This is a game about Iteration.
If you like attempting a process/workflow, seeing the results and then trying to do it again but better than this game is for you.
I say this because I work for a tech company, love my job, and see a mirror of what I do at work in this game - only it's much more fun!  This is a developer's game.
This game has many layers - you will not understand everything.  The idea is actually that you don't.  The devs want you to react to what happens from an emotional standpoint and the game will respond in a way that actually makes sense.
Want to be an awesome Barbarrian King and conquer the world?  Go ahead!  Oh, you died and now are playing as your spoiled son?  Will the bloodthirsty, barbarian generals your father put in power respect and obey you?  I highly doubt it.  Maybe next time you'll arrange for one of those generals to be your heir insted.
After nearly 1400 hours logged into this game I can say it is the best gaming investment I've ever made.  Their are hundreds of starting locations and each one has different nuances that you will only learn through trial and error until you get to whatever you consider perfection.  Even when you achieve what you consider perfection you will look back at that playthrough and realize countless mistakes you could fix the next time around.
My adivce on playing this game is to start with the western religions, then india, then the middle east, and finailly the tribal religions.  This will progress your learning of the game in a stable way and also present ever increasing challenges.

[Introduction]
Cowboy's Adventure is a memento of the well established Western Deathrun genre.
It offers three levels of diffculty the Player can choose from
and it sets out to achieve what many of its modern predecessors fail to accomplish
[Story]
You play as the Ghost of a Cowboy Adventurer which finds himself trapped in the Underworld.
The Player isnt given any Information about the previous life of the mighty Adventurer and left to guess
wheter the Protagonist has fallen in a Western duell and finds himself in the Afterlife or if a Dark Spell has been laid upon him. After you find yourself stranded in a Strange world with a deep-blue Ocean and a castle with seemingly no way to escape you feel the pull towards a portal. You manage to overcome the traps and hurdles thrown at you, and clear the first portal. You find yourself in another world and ask yourself if this is just the beginning or already the end. There is nothing else to do for you other than continue, there is nothing else in the world anymore and you find the thrill, pain and challenge of the portals more satisfying than waiting for the never coming end.
[Controls]
I really admire the choice of the Developer to keep the Controls simple, you may Jump Spring and choose the direction in which to move. Simple. Perfect.
[Visuals]
Unfortunatly i have to say that there is room for improvement for the visuals.
I do understand in the business there are hard time-limits and the stress can be overbearing.
BUT i completly support the decision to invest the End-stage Development Time into the Gameplay so you can release a game that the players enjoy PLAYING and not LOOKING at.
[Music]
Generally, im happy with the decisions made, implementing the Music into the gameplay of the game.
Instead of using single songs the Developers decided to Use one Soundfile that gets Looped over and over again.
The Soundfile is 30 Minutes and 28 seconds long and gives the player enough repetition to feel as uncomfortable as a Cowboy trapped in the Underworld.
All in all the perfect Music to underline the general concept of the game.
You can find the Music in your Steam library under Music>Album>Music.
[Level Designs]
There are 14 Game Worlds which range from castles flooded with rapid currents, heated lava levels inside a volcano to throat tightening stuctures that suck the air out of your lungs.
I found the Difficulty levels adequat altough i found the hard levels to be too easy relative to the easy levels.
[Summary]
I would give this game a 7/10.
I appreciate the games existance and hope it helps the Western Deathrun Genre to turn into the right direction.

Mind you this is easy mode.
The loading screen honestly looks like something just added in a few minutes before release, it is just the same font as the logo thrown onto what I think is a fire background video.
Then we have the music, and that in and of itself is worth not getting this game. You would think that, being the deathrun game this claims to be, there would be adventure music, maybe cinimatic music, but no, the music in this game can best be described as slow horror music.
There is also no animation or transition when you fail/die, you just restart the level.
This game is trying to be a temple run game where you can go at your own pace, and I did really want to enjoy it, the problem is it is broken in its current state, and I could even forgive that IF it was labeled as early access, but it was not, this is the finished product.
This game was an adventure, but an adventure I regret.

This is the first time I've felt compelled to review a game, which hopefully indicates the strength of my conviction. If I  sound harsh, I'm sorry.  I just want to be honest.
In the current form of this game, as of 2:49 AM on April 9th, 2015 I can't recommend it for purchase.
Let me start out by saying something very positive- this game has great potential.
And I do like the graphics, for the most part, and I've had no major issues with the A.I. on both sides...
Okay,
Now my biggest complaint is that the game is simply not finished.  I thought and believed I was purchasing a product ready for use but that is not the case. For instance, playing through the campaign I found numerous placeholders where names of characters should have been marked. I know that might be insignificant in the whole scheme of the game but details matter and this game is just not there where a product should be when brought to the marketplace.  It is not polished, it is not complete, and it is not worth a purchase at this current time.
The campaign felt untested, like I’m a paying beta player and they still expect feedback on the balance of gameplay.  But I’m not a paying beta tester, I’m a disappointed consumer who feels bamboozled.
The game is buggy as all get out (and I've heard they have been working on the situation...and I can forgive a few bugs...but not when the games crashes or freezes over and over.) I must applauded how quick the developers have responded with patches.  This act has given me hope.
The loading screen, which takes forever, reminds me of games dating back to the earlier 2000’s, and not in a good way. Actually, this game feels like an early 2000 release but it isn’t…which makes me sad…because at least then I could have given it a pass for being out dated.  But, that is not the case.
I have read this game is trying to emulate Dungeon Keeper 1 & 2, a game I have not played, so I can’t speak from that point of view. However, as a newcomer to this genre I have felt the uneasy tension that this game doesn’t have a personality of its own. It feels bland, a dime store novel filled with stock everything.  I have not had one single WOW moment during gameplay that inspires me to continue playing or advocating my friends to purchase this game.  It just feels generic.  I loved the idea presented in this game but the execution is lacking.
A few functions of the game I found odd, wait, no, I actually found missing, are common place in many other strategy games I’ve played.  For instance, I have yet to find any indication of a pause button, a min/max speed button, or a restart option on the menu.  Frankly, a restart option would be fantastic because of how many times I’ve had a campaign with unclear directions and a steady stream of escalating forces pushing down on me from the start, killing me off quickly and forcing me through the torturous load screen once more because apparently I’m a glutton for punishment.  Ugh, it’s just bonkers to me that these three options are not presented in the structure of the game.  I digress, for maybe I’m a foolish gamer who has become spoiled on what I thought were considered common place functions built into modern games.
Something must be said about the lost art of creating your dungeon, alas, maybe I assumed too much about the game actually allowing you to create a dungeon to fit your deepest and darkest desires.  More often than not, it comes down to pure function overriding any hope of creating  something to satisfy that hunger of building a dungeon worth calling a dungeon.  I feel the fast, pushy pace of the game doesn’t help, but again, there is no pause button to allow you to form a creation you can be proud of to counter the speed at which the game opperates.
I am also amazed at how fast you can bring down walls.  The sensation of seeing the walls crumble in mere seconds pulls me straight out of the game because I don’t experience the satisfaction of ripping the earth out bit by bit in my endeavor to create something worthy of occupying the space.  To be clear, I’m not saying it should take an hour per wall, but I do feel that the balance is not correct when it comes to the speed of clearing a cavern for your lair and monsters.  I don’t feel like I’m accomplishing anything due to the speed at which this process occurs, especially when I wish to make hallways to connect my rooms and an enemy can come through and burrow through said wall with remarkable ease and speed. I think the economy of the overall game structure doesn’t feel balanced to how I hoped or expected it would be. Did the developers plan on games/matches to occur and finish under ten minutes? If so, then I have chosen poorly with my purchase.
And last, but not least, the mini-map. Really, it feels like it was created in Microsoft paint? It's dreadfully painful to use and basically takes up space in it's current form. Again, if this was a game made in 2001 than I wouldn't be as upset to the design of the mini-map, but it's 2015.
I've read this a small develpement team funded by kick starter and that's all awesome, truly,  however, I don't think that should excuse them from releasing a game in this current form. I get giving them slack where you might not with a larger studio, but at some point that slack runs out and they run the risk of accidently hanging themself...and letting the game die...and I hope that doesn't happen.
Let me end by saying something positive- this game has great potential and I hope that somehow it becomes nurtured and turns into what it could be, a great, fun, challenging game…but until it happens, stay away.

I'm a long time player of Dungeon Kepper 1 & 2...and am old enough to remember the thrill of loading these games for the first time.
Although I've been a supporter of this project since they first started, well before when they had a different team and a different goal, the amount of progress these absolutely hardcore lovers of DK have made is quite astonishing.  This game is stonking amazing...it literally is the third coming of Dungeon Keeper.
I've been a backer, but I honestly only played occasionally, feeling that it would be best to play when the game was pretty much feature complete and also since I don't have much time to bugtest it made the best sense for me.  I am absolutely THRILLED at what they've done here...what they have managed to accomplish.
I have played up until the 5th mission in campaign as well as some putzing around in the other modes for several hours (30+), and I can truly say that this has been the time of my life.  The heart and soul of DK is there.  Yes, sure, there's a few bugs and glitches, but this is a massive undertaking that they've done here and the end result is quite simply astonishing.  It looks brilliant, and the humor is there.
I experienced zero crashes and very few bugs on my playthrough today.  I played about 4 hours straight and had an absolute blast.
I've enjoyed checking out every room and looking at the tiniest details in each of their design.  Posession is quite fun and reveals the amount of work put into each of the models and objects.  It's exquisite.
I have absolutely no doubt that given a month or so, a ton of the early bugs will be squashed. This developer team is hardcore committed to making this project a success and you can see it everywhere.
If you're a fan of the original DK, or are looking for a game where it's good to be bad, please check this out.  It is quite simply a load of fun with an immense level of detail that puts other games to shame.  This is truly an incredible job they've done and they deserve a swift pat on the back for what they've accomplished.
Buy it!

Pfffff okay, here goes.
I played Dungeon Keeper 2 almost non-stop for an inconceivable amount of time. After which, I wondered if they were going to make a Dungeon Keeper 3. I was elated to hear that the answer was "yes and no". There would be a Dungeon Keeper 3, but it wouldn't be *called* Dungeon Keeper 3.
This game lives up to and surpasses my wildest expectations. It's fun, comical, challenging, and intense. This studio did an absolutely incredible job on this game, and I highly recommend it.
That being said, you should be prepared for a few bugs and glitches, at least at the time of this review. I am quite certain that they will get everything resolved at some point, but at the moment I've had to handle a few hair-pull worthy issues.
At one point, when hitting the ESC key to save my game, the game froze and eventually crashed on me. In another instance, two of my minions appeared to be stuck in a lake. They were wandering around in circles incessantly, clearly befuddled by why their master had abandoned them. Not to worry, though. A quick spanking or three sent them back on their merry way.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. I paid 36$ for the Underlord Edition and do not regret my purchase in the least, despite a few hiccups that are presently in the game.

Maybe the game will be finished and fixed through patches.  It looks like it has great potential when finished.  But it is still in beta stage, and releasing it like that is awful.  Don't buy this product.

Hard reset is a morbid and gritty first person shooter set in a decrepit world that seems to have been taken over by soldiers made from a fusion of man and metal. The story is so incredibly vague and Hard Reset gives you so little to go on that the whole way it feels like you're being teased with what could have been an amazing story of a dangerous trek through a volatile and almost dystopian city. Instead you're left wondering about the context of some of the character exchanges and even in some cases, who these characters are. Seeing as there's no introduction to most of these characters you don't know whats going on half the time and the other half you're still trying to understand the last cutscene. A very important aspect of Hard Reset is that the developers took a very heavy inspiration from old style FPS games such as Shadow Warior, DOOM, and Duke Nukem and it really shows all throughout.
As I mentioned before the story is pretty sparse and when you end up being given story segments they're pretty lackluster and hard to understand. This means that Hard Reset essentially has little to no story or character development throughout the whole game. In this case however, I personally would say that Hard Reset is better with no story since that isn't what the game is focused on. Instead, since Hard Reset is essentially an old-school shooter from the 90's, the games main focus is on gameplay and mechanics rather than story and character development. Speaking of game mechanics, Hard Reset really feels like a classic FPS that's taken that genre and fine tuned it with modern game mechanics that are implemented in such a way that they subtly enhance gameplay without driving away the classic feeling. A huge downside to the game is that the level design is absolutely horrendous for a classic FPS since every level is incredibly linear with only a handful of side areas to explore and most of those aren't even side areas but instead are secret rooms with loot in them. This was incredibly disappointing since the environments the game lets you explore are absolutely gorgeous and would have been absolutlely stunning to explore. All the levels feel like you're window shopping at your favorite store; you see all the cool stuff but you have to just stay outside and look.
A critical mechanic in old-school shooters is gunplay and that's something that Hard Reset has absolutely nailed. You're only weapons are a futuristic plasma rifle and a run of the mill machine gun but both of the guns can change into one of many different forms. The plasma rifle can change into a rail gun or can let you see through walls and the machine gun can change into a shotgun or a rocket launcher. This unique take on gun mechanics makes Hard Reset very memorable and since you have to unlock every different firing mode, each one feels like an achievement to unlock and a powerhouse to use. The enemies you fight, as I mentioned earlier, are these macabre robot-human fusion monstrosities that range from being normal foot soldiers all the way to being giant mechs that are ten stories tall. Each different enemy type has different weaknesses to various different guns and you have to find those weaknesses and really push them to your advantage if you want to survive the later levels. My main problem with the enemies of Hard Reset is that there's only three or four different types of them and they start to get repetitive very quickly. Hard Reset could have been so much better if they just would have had a few more enemy types and made the game much less linear.
Hard Reset creates an immersive world dominated by abominations of flesh and machine and throws you into it with nothing but guns and an attitude.

Beware hyperbole.  "Best game ever" this is not.
Story is pretty interesting, and the first act of the game is fun.
The combat overall is pretty poorly balanced.  The armor mechanic, while seeming interesting at first, really hurts the balance later in the game.  Crowd control is basically neutralized, as you can't apply any status effect while a character's armor is still up.  There are certain battles which require you to protect certain NPCs under a time limit.  The enemy will all tunnel vision on the one NPC you're supposed to protect, in some cases this is 6+ enemy combatants.  You can't possibly outdamage that many enemies so normally your strategy would be to use crowd control to delay them until the time limit is up.  However, due to the armor system, this requires you to essentially outdamage 6+ enemies AND apply crowd control to them BEFORE they can kill your VIP.  This is simply impossible, especially with a 2-man Lone Wolf group.  The issue here seems to be a lack of playtesting all the various options that are available to the player.  Many power combinations are too powerful and others are not competitive.  Look no further than the infinite damage loop bug that the developers almost kept in the game because it was "creative".  The higher difficulties just exacerbate these issues even more.
The combat overall just lacks nuance, it doesn't feel tactical, mainly due to a lack of defensive options i.e. ways to negate or deter enemy actions.  This is putting aside all the combat bugs which are incredibly frustrating, such as Attacks of Opportunity not triggering and your character's turn being skipped for no reason.  This is all very sad after hearing laughable claims like "More strategic than XCOM."
I've put about 40 hours (half of that being pre-release) in the game on the higher difficulties before I couldn't stand the poor combat any longer.  I may start over on explorer simply to experience the story, which was quite good in my playtime.  I will give big kudos to the developer for adding full voice-overs, as it enhances the immersion and engagement of the story ten-fold.
Maybe I've gotten my money's worth already, but I am overall feeling disappointed, and I expected a lot more.  Wait for the inevitable Enhanced Edition I guess?
P.S.  For goodness sake, make your story achievements hidden.

You may be thinking to yourself: "Is this game as simple and bare as it looks on the screenshots?" It's a not a bad question. At first glance, Recettear looks like a rather dated game centered around the niche topic of running an item shop in medieval-style world. Characters are 2-D sprites in a 3-D game world that would look at home on a PS1, and dungeon crawling is a simple hack-and-slash with different unlockable adventurers bringing a different class and playstyle to the table. While the game is hardly complicated or difficult, it is definitely charming and captivating. However, it is so much more than that, and the game really impressed me with it's hidden depths.
To shorten things a bit, the core game and plot is about Recette, a little girl whose missing father has a large unpaid loan about to default. In order to not lose her home, Recette, with the help a 'loan-shark' fairy named Tear, open an item store and begin trading in order to make enough money to make the weekly loan repayment. As you might expect, as the weeks pass, the amount required to pay grows exponentially until you either fail or manage to make the final payment. The main plot spans about 5 ingame weeks, and should you fail to make a payment, you start a new 'loop' from Day 2 with every item you owned as well as whatever cash you had left - this greatly helps remove the frustration of having to start all over from scratch.
So you might think that this is an easy game to beat. Well, yes, but the real meat and potatoes comes from post-game content. Beating the main game unlocks Endless mode, where you simply continue running the item shop with no more loans to pay back; New Game+, which starts a new loop with money and items carried over; and Survival mode, which has never ending weekly loan payments that grow until they overwhelm you.
Is there a point in continuing your save free from debt? Hell yes there is. You see, the core game with its dungeon feature only barely scratch the surface of the content and characters the game has to offer. Within the first in game month, you are highly unlikely to meet even half of the available adventurers you can hire, unlock all dungeons, or even make a dent in the item encyclopaedia. In fact, there is essentially a post-game questline to still follow through to the end!
Considering that I expected the game to be focused on that one lone month of paying bills, I was impressed with how polished the gameplay mechanics are, and pleasantly surprised by the amount of content this game has that adds to replayability. For how the game looks to the average person viewing the store page, this game is diamond in the rough, and I wholly recommend it if you want a light-hearted game to drop hours into

I don't know if this is a new concept but I have seen some games with a similar idea, its a card game at heart with real battles playing out when you encounter a monster card or when you reach the end of a card set. (you battle a boss at the end) Certain cards will have you playing for tokens which if won will unlock more cards for you to build your deck at the end of the match.
Various times you will find gold, food and you will have the chance to upgrade your max health or refill it. The gold can net you some interesting items, armour and/or weapons, you can also buy food so you can continue your journey. Various pathways can be taken on later decks which will lead you to other battles or extra loot and/or tokens.
Overall the game plays well with a batman battle system and a nice card game thrown on top which gives you an incentive to play on to unlock more bosses and more cards for better loot and/or scenarios.

This is essentially Game Of Thrones: the game.
In my first game, I played as an Irish ruler, and got him married to an English lady to cement an alliance, allowing me to begin a conquest of Ireland. My wife proceeded to bear me daughter after daughter, which due to the country's male inheritance laws left my vassals unhappy.
Then, her father dies and she is left as his heir - she returns to her home county in England. Whilst there she bears two more daughters (seven in total now!), which seemed a bit off with me as how can she have my children when in another country?
It emerges that she was sleeping with a local Bishop. I realise I need a new wife if I'm to ever have a male heir, yet I can't divorce her or I'll end up making enemies of the English. So, I start a plot to assassinate her.
The very first person who offers their help with killing her? The bishop she was sleeping with! And he'll be most valuable, having lots of "access" to her! My plot is in motion!
And then, said Bishop gets royally drunk and blabs about the entire thing to everyone, my wife is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everyone thinks I'm scum, and I have a troop of daughters at my ankles.
Damn fun game, the emergent gameplay is outstanding.

I tend not to like games that stay in early access for 2 years as this one did then gets released unfinished. It defeats the point of early access in my book.
It is now July 2015, 4 months after War for the Overworld was released and it finally has enough Skirmish maps to make it worth playing in single player. An update to Unity 5 seems to have improved performance too.
It has enough units, powers and spells to keep most dungeon keeper fans happy, and it brings enough of its own tricks to the table so it cannot be accused of being a straight forward clone of the old classic.
If it has any problem it is that it has too many rooms and monsters for most maps, you will find your self without the room to the build them all. So your going to have to choose what you want and what you do not want.
Previously I recommended this game but only just, stating a lack of maps and other unfinished features meant you would be left waiting to play it because it was not finished.
Also, previously, I said 7 out of 10 on metacritics user score was about right, it is now at 7.3 and rising on metacritics because the game is finally playable. In it is current state it is worth about an 8.
Though the campaign pretty much sucks with its timers and shows a distinct lack of imagination, mind you so do the new maps.
What is it with devs these days and their symetrical maps ?

I would recommend this game, it might be a bit hard to get into first, but after a little while you quickly get the hang of it, but it will still kick your♥♥♥♥♥at points. I went into this game with no expectations whatsoever, the only thing i really knew is that it was a twin stick shooter and had a cyberpunk setting. Thankfully it proved a very enjoyable experience even if it falls a bit short some places.
The cyberpunk setting is oozing out of every crack and it is wonderful, it captures that feel like very few other games do, the atmosphere is thick and the soundtrack is incredibly enjoyable. It nails it down incredibly well aesthetically, like I said, it oozes cyberpunk. Each level has its own theme and style to it and getting back to Rengkok South always feels nice.
Gameplay wise it can be a bit cluncky. At times it feels like hits dont register or that you lose health for no reason because the depth can be a little confusing at times and hitting enemies three to four times can be a bit strange at first, especially if you come right from Hotline Miami. Guns dont have a super impactful feel, unless you have something that has incindiary shots, generally it's best to go melee, guns are your back up.
Bosses all have their unique flavour and fit the area they're placed in, most often its a healthy mix between ranged and melee bosses each with their own weakness, some more obvious than others. The first boss you meet for example can easily be defeated if you go up close with melee, the second boss is easier if you go ranged. Not all bosses feel good to fight though, some can be quite annoying or just boring to fight in length because of the extended health bar.
Sadly the Hubworld Rengkok South and its characters are also underused. The games hubworld shines and is very intriguing on the surface, but when you delve down into it you discover that there is not a lot too it, the characters that inhabit this place could be used more and have some more interactions. It's especially sad since you only really visit this area twice, it would seem that the developers planned to have more stuff thrown in here, but maybe had to cut it due to time constraints. Rengkok South could atleast have been used better.
overall it could need some polish here and there, but it's a good game and can scratch your cyberpunk itch. Although do not go in expecting a Hotline Miami clone even though it takes inspiration from it.

RUINER captivates you with it's cyberpunk aesthetics from the get-go, while also mesmerising you with it's amazing soundtrack. All important mechanics are presented in the very first level: high stakes, high reflex combat, shoot to kill, dodge to survive. You're also introduced to this world's story, a rather forgetable story, but that's not what everybody's interested in such a game anyway.
is a great take on the Hotline Miami formula. However, enemies don't outright die in 1 hit, and neither do you (under certain circumstances anyway). There's no shortage of fights, each level presents you with rooms that dish out all sorts of enemies your way (ala 2016 DOOM) that drop weapons and karma, the game's XP system.
Karma allows you to level up, unlocking new skills or skill upgrades. You can switch skill points on the fly, be it before or during an encounter, at no cost whatsoever, allowing you to approach each encounter in a unique way if you want.
are unique, each with a different set of skills, each can be (and should be) approached in different ways.
is smooth and responsive, hitting an enemy with a melee weapon feels satisfying and looks gruesome.
require some getting used to, especially on M+KB; going "UP" on your keyboard is more "UP-RIGHT" in-game, quick-dodging is directional (if you're going "LEFT" then you quick-dodge "LEFT"). Not a big deal, you should get the hang of it post-tutorial.
Overall, game gets a solid
, it's got everything you need for a
afternoon, while also offering replayability to those that wish to S+ each level.

Based on Indonesian mythology, DreadOut joins the ranks of atmospheric horror games with some glaring gameplay flaws. It's obvious the developers put their heart and soul into this charming title and it definitely shows. However, a bunch of issues, mostly regarding the controls, make this title only worthwhile for fans of the genre.
The premise is simple: Five students and a teacher on a school trip come across an abandoned and, of course, haunted village and decide to investigate. With the help of a smartphone and later SLR camera Linda, the silent protagonist, is able to see and combat different kinds of ghosts. Designed after Indonesian folklore and shortly explained in notebook entries, the variety of spirits shown is refreshing and frankly insightful. Just as the character design, the environment is pleasantly authentic and believable. DreadOut is thankfully above any superfluous westernisation.
Regarding its flaws, DreadOut unfortunately contains passages that are either just a little bit odd or straight up enraging. It's rather dated graphics are forgiveable, as are a few weird animations and minor bugs, but the controls in boss fights made me throw my hardware across the room. Ab ovo, Linda's movement is sluggish. Her run speed resembles a slow and careful jog and her stamina that of a feverish person. So far so good, slow protagonists in horror games are the norm and often enough contribute to the apprehension and suspense especially in boss fights. Usually the player needs to run away to gain some room, turn and quickly whip out the camera to attack. Easy, if only all the following issues wouldn't occur: The arenas are barely big enough, there's only a small annulus of allowed distance to trigger the camera glitch and successfully attack an enemy and of course the enemy is faster than Linda. Throw in some input lag on camera use and the experience is ruined. Dili ana!
Nevertheless, when these two or three passages have passed, DreadOut is fully enjoyable and incorporates many ideas that shake up the gameplay until the very end. The Indonesian music and synchronisation give the game an appealing touch and show how thoughtful the developers have woven their origin into the project. Some scenes are more strangely confusing than mysterious, but that's Asian horror for ya.
All things considered, DreadOut is satisfying to beat. I like it, despite its flaws, but I
be biased towards my Southeast Asian kin.

If you liked Total Annihilation, you will like this one. It's more or less the same game, but it has 3 factions which are actually different from each other. The campaign spans 6 missions per faction on ever expanding battlefields. This makes the missions fluid and you have to adapt to new situations on the fly.
Apart from that it's still "build mass extractors and energy generators to supply your constant building of army units". Yes, this game is not about micro, but macro management. Your units don't cost "money" per se, but each building and each unit cost a certain amount of resources/second. If you're spending more than you're generating production slows down considerably. Different builder units and production facilities also have different outputs. To build an army quickly you will need to use builders to speed up production. It's a big old turtle and siege game. Whether you use artillery supported by main battle tanks, anti aircraft units and mobile shield batteries or different navy ships or a combination of bombers with fighter escorts and perhaps some gunship strafing runs, it all comes down to who can cripple the enemies economy better. Since there are no finite resources a skirmish can practically go on forever and end in a stalemate.
Luckily there are also super units and long range nuclear and artillery gun emplacements to potentially kill the enemy. After all, all it takes to win is to kill the enemy commander, which can happen almost instantaneously in the late game. That's also why rushing in this game isn't very effective. The command unit will take care of most Tier 1 units pretty quickly, unless you have a ♥♥♥♥ton of them.
To be honest, unit control could be a bit more precise. Often your units will simply clump up and die one after another. It's a big grind fest. Especially naval and air units are problematic. Air units told to resupply will often just circle the resupply pads for ages, despite being "done". Naval units need too much space where none is available, so in a group of 10 ships it often happened that only 1 moved to the destination... Also unit information when selecting an actual unit and not just with mouseover would have been cool. All in all it's a neat little macro strategy fest though with clear rock, paper, scissors gameplay: Break base with artillery, protect artillery with tanks, protect all of them with anti air and add some shielding into the mix. Done.

The initial storyline is engaging.  You are a member of what seems to be a security team for some large coorporation dispatched to a planet by the boss himself.  Upon arriving you are shot down (technically forced to use the escape pod) by the company's arch rival.  Your comrads are dead and you must find a way to send a distress signal and get off the planet.  As you investigate deeper into the planet you discover that there is more at stake than losing a dig site to your rival company.
The gameplay is fun and the controls are good.  The game itself is reminiscent of a watered down version of metroid where you have essentially an open world to explore and advancing is controlled by what powerups you have so far.  That said, there aren't that many powerups total and the enemy diversity is minimal.  There isn't anything which I would call a boss fight.
I've seen that some complain about no map and no music.  I admit, music would've been nice but its absence does provide a certain tension that is condusive to the games atmosphere.  Having no map makes me think of those old games of yore (NES that is) where one had to draw one's own maps and keep track of where you were going.  From that perspective, I like the no map option.  It is a different kind of game design that stems from giving players value in a game by making it more difficult.
So finally, would I recommend this game?  Well, the story builds and I was very excited to see how they would end it but ufortunately the ending was, in my opinion, the equivalent of a book ending with suicide.  It is like the authors couldn't write their way out and so went with a very unsatisfying solution.  Maybe I just didn't get their point but sadly, it was enough to make me feel as though my time spent playing was in vain.

Thought I'd write a quick review since I just played through this this weekend and it has shown up in another bundle.  I want to like Inescapable more than I do.  I followed it for a while during development because I like the retro graphics and "metroidvania" always gets my attention.  But this is not a metroidvania.  It's a rather linear experience of fetching a relic, back-tracking, and opening the corresponding door.  Lather, rinse, repeat.  Oh, and that back-tracking?  That's about 75% of the game.  Not exploring and the sense of progression you get with a true "metroidvania", but endless back-tracking.  And there is no map, and most of the backgrounds are just palette swaps.  So you will get lost.  A lot.
Also, no music.  Which I didn't mind because the ambient sounds helped set the mood.  No story either.  There is some vague, generic sci-fi stuff going on.  But it is never explained.  And then the game just ends.  Seriously, the least-climactic, most unexpected ending I've ever experienced.
That being said, there is still something about this game that I like.  I won't recommend it at $5, but since you can get it in a bundle like I did, it's worth a shot.  It won't take more than 2 hours of your time.

First of all, this game does still have some bugs.  If buggy games bother you a lot, maybe give it another few weeks.  The devs are working hard, and they're making a ton of progress, but they're not quite there yet.
That said, this game is to Dungeon Keeper 2 what DK2 was to DK1.  If you feel (as I do) that DK2 was a drastic improvement over DK1, you're in for a hell of a ride with this game.
So many improvements to what, at it's core, is the same system.  Take traps/doors, for example.  In DK1, they would build whatever they wanted, then you could place it.  Kind-of annoying, since they would produce all the low-level stuff first, so if you wanted, say, a Steel Door, you'd have to wait.  Then, in DK2, you could place a door/trap, then they would get to work on it.  Definitely an improvement, since it didn't waste resources, but if you didn't currently have a place that you knew you wanted a door/trap, your workshop workers would just be slacking off.  In WFTO, they finally solved it.  Workshop workers build generic parts.  When you place doors/trap blueprints, your imps bring those parts to where they need to be, and after enough parts are brought, the door/trap exists.  It doesn't waste anything, and it's perfect.
Everything in the game is like that.  They took a look at the systems in the DK games and said, "How can we make this better?"  They've done a remarkable job.  Researching rooms/spells is done through a sort of "skill tree" so you can spend your research points as you wish.  You can fill back in places you don't want dug out; one of my pet peeves with my DK dungeons is when they could be ruined by intruders, and now you can fix what they did.  There are all sorts of entirely new systems, like alchemy, constructs, and rituals, each of which have a different purpose and interesting uses.
All that, and I'd already be willing to pay more than the $30 MSRP.  But you know what else they decided to do?  Write a plot.  DK1 basically had none.  DK2 had a bit of one, but it was always, "Do the thing, this guy's trying to stop you from doing the thing.. yay, you did the thing!"  In this game, I'm only halfway through the campaign, and I'm already wondering what's going on and questioning the motives of certain characters.  Did you ever expect a DK-style game to have you questioning a character's motives?  I sure didn't!  It's a blast.
So yes, I'd recommend this game, even in its very-recently-launched state.  Like I said, if bugs bother you a lot, give it a bit more time, but if you're willing to forgive a bit (and if you played DK2, you should be; that game was never 100% stable) then you should just pick it up now.

Put it this way, I've played plenty of games where you can beat your enemies into submission, but never one where you can shag their sisters afterwards. Politics, Intrigue, War, Diplomacy, everything. This game has it all. No tactics to speak of but that only adds to the depth in its own way. On a different game you might say, "hmm, his army is twice the size of mine, but hey, I can probably beat him, I'm a good general'. On this game, you are more likely to think, 'If I go up against him I'm going to get my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me on a plate. I'd better stay on his good side until I'm strong enough.' This is a great strength of the game, and you have to set long term aims and goals if you want to win. For example, at the start of my most successful game, which was as Duke Ethelred of Wessex on the Old Gods campaign, I ruled a small Duchy in the South of England, with a massive Norse army making its way south to burn and kill everything. Through a hefty bit of luck involving several strategic alliances, I was able to secure control of England. By putting a woman on the throne of West Francia, who my heir then married, I was able to begin a process of conquering all of France. When the crusading era arrived, holy wars brought me muslim spain and the Holy Land. In 1140, The House of Wessex now rules as Emperors of Britannia, the masters of Western Europe and the Levant. It won't be enormous military might alone that brings you success, you need to utilise every ounce of political acumen you posses, taking advantage of every opportunity that comes your way, praying that you don't make the wrong choice. "My Lord, the Duke of so-and-so is rallying your vassals against you". "Oh I'll be fine, I've never been more popular." Next thing you know, ten thousand men are kicking down your door. In my view, the perfect strategy game.

-Dig out a dungeon and stock rooms to attract creatures and then attack the enemy
-Torture Chamber is fully operational
-Devs are patching bugs and paying attention to player requests
Cons (at the time of this review):
-Some features are not available yet (sandbox mode & multiplayer)
-Creature path finding can be somewhat haphazard
-Rooms and creatures do not have enough detail about what they do (still calls things "prop x")
-Possession can be difficult to control and once in possession mode no clear explanation about the controls
-Memory Leak? Game tends to slow down a lot over the course of playing and occasionally crashes (devs stated they are looking into solving this problem)
War for the Overworld is a refreshing change in the standard RTS genre given that you build a dungeon and attack the "good guys". As many know, WftO is the spiritual successor to Dungeon Keepers 1 and 2. This is the game I have been looking for since finishing DK 1&2 in 2000 (15 years!). I am sincerely happy that EA has allowed Subteranean Games to create this clear clone of the Dungeon Keeper franchise.
Do not get me wrong, War for the Overworld is not just a facelift for Dungeon Keeper 2. It does have it's own story if you are a plot addict like me. However, the look and gameplay feels just like DK2 on the surface, but is a bit buggy with path finding which I expect will get ironed out. If you have been looking for another Dungeon Keeper look no further and pick this game up since it is what we wished that "Dungeons" was or "Overlord 1&2" were. It is certainly worth the $30 USD (half of what EA would charge if they made it, and it would not be as good) even though it does have some flaws as detailed above. I expect that these flaws will be polished away with a bit of time since these devs are extremely devoted to supporting their product and are enthusiasts themselves for the Dungeon Keeper series.
Buyer with a low-end system beware (i.e. less than 8 GB RAM and less than a Quad Core processor running at 2.0 GHz) as this game is somewhat CPU and definitely memory intensive which manifests itself particularly during battles. I know this because I recently had to upgrade my system to run smoothly (I was capped at 3.25GB RAM and it bottlenecked my Quad Core AMD Phenom II @3.2GHz processor). If your system does not meet the minimum requirements, either upgrade or expect slow downs, stability issues, crashing, and even unplayability during gameplay, and don't downvote simply because your PC cannot handle it (I see this too often).
All these things being said, I cannot recommend this game enough. WftO is exactly as advertised with regard to being the spiritual successor to DK 1&2. I played this game when it was in early access and enjoyed it then and now even more. This is the only game that I have ever been happy with after purchasing in early access, and I have purchased a fair few.

Yeah, not bad overall. The gunplay was satisfying, the weapon upgrades were a lot of fun to use, the enemies were fairly varied and the final area was really well done and enjoyable. They didn't reinvent the wheel but the game is fun to play for the most part and it's not too long either which to me is a plus, a lot of games these days tend to overstay their welcome. I also enjoyed their comic book style cut-scenes.
Hard Reset does have some major flaws though, the first is the voice acting and dialog, it's best described as cringe-worthy and amateur, there was only one major character that wasn't laughable, and sadly it wasn't the main one. I can't tell you just how bad it was, you need to experience it for yourselves. Another big problem was a surprising one, performance, I couldn't maintain 60fps on any visual preset, drops into the 40s were common on the major boss battles and even some smaller events, I can only imagine how poorly this ran on 2012 hardware. The final complaint was the constant micro-freezing whenever the game autosaved which was often enough to annoy me. So there you have it, Hard Reset is an OK shooter that does have some fun moments but suffers with performance issues and comically bad voice work, for 99p I'd say it's well worth a shot if you're bored and have run out of better games to play.

This game is pretty bad and has alot of flaws that make it very frustrating to play. RNG being the main factor in the outcome of most attacks makes no sense in a tactical game. Setting up a great strategy just for your character to miss a point blank shot makes this game bad. The game does not take things like distance into consideration when attacking and leads to many failures, especially where snipers and lancers are concerened.
The characters are very cliche but are done very well. However where the game gives you many options to add to your squad I find I use the same ones over and over due to them having better traits. The game does a bad job on pacing also. Where you can get new types of weapons they are often terrible in terms of range and accuracy causing the bad RNG to pop up more often. This can be offset by buying upgrades for these weapons but the upgrades are not available until towards the end of the game. As of this review I have been through 8 chapters and still no upgrades for weapons that I have taken off of enemies leaving my only option the starting weapons.
Balance is very poor also with scouts being your best unit in almost all battles and lancers being some of the worst, only really good for taking out tanks and getting the very rare lucky shot. The game also gives you access to skirmishes which are good and allow the player to repeat past battles but they also give the player access to special class only skirmishes which are outright impossible in the beginning.
All in all it is a shame as this game has all the bearings of a classic but the devs took it into a lazy direction. If the devs put a little more time into the game and did not rely on RNG so much then this would have been a must have. Do not buy it unless it is on sale and your thing is trial and error gameplay rather than tactical planning.

Do you enjoy slot machines? Do you enjoy games of chance? Do you enjoy games that you have very little control over the outcome?
Then we've got the game for you. Desktop Dungeons. 95% luck-based gameplay! It's a hoot. Everything is determined by random number generation. The map layout and enemy / item placement factors heavily on whether a dungeon is beatable or not. You can carefully work your way through a dungeon for 30 minutes, just to realize at the end that you don't have enough health and there is no way to recover the health you need to win. This happens most of the time.
So if you enjoy gambling and dislike strategy having any influence on whether you win or not, this is the game for you!

While ostensibly a roguelike RPG, each dungeon is basically one or two levels, so it's ideal for short gaming sessions. The main thing that makes this one interesting is that combat is basically deterministic; you can predict the outcome of each fight pretty accurately, you don't have to worry about getting screwed by the RNG at a critical point.
The thing is, this may not sound like a big difference, but  it completely changes the flavor of the game. Instead of an RPG, it ends up being more of a puzzle game, where the objective is to figure out how to maximize XP gained and minimize the waste of health and mana, by deciding where  to go and what to fight next. Adds a sort of minesweeper aspect to the roguelike gameplay.

This will be a fairly detailed review--the gist of it is that this is an extremely well polished game whose core mechanics--which is managing your item shop--are splendidly executed and introduced to the player smoothly, but this is all rounded out by the charming and endearing--optional--story, as you meet and interact with the townsfolk around the area. The characters are likeable and you learn more about them as you take more time out of the day to explore the city. It's almost like Final Fantasy 6 in the second half of the game.
All I can say is--this game is amazing. Honestly--the best way I can describe this game is a item shop tycoon/dungeon crawler/visual novel, all jumbled into one game. And yes, I said visual novel, which I will get into later.
So the primary premise of this game is that you run an item shop on a day to day basis, kind of like a Diner Dash-esque sort of game. From start to finish, the primary goal of the game is to make enough money to pay off your debt in weekly installments. That might seem boring, but in actuality the plethora of options that are given to you at every given moment make the game so much more than an item shop tycoon game, and it makes for such a fun and unique experience.
Regarding the item shop tycoon aspect of the game--it is spectacularly done. There is just so much that goes into managing your shop, that it just feels fresh while you progress through the game. What do you decide to put in front of your window, which will affect what kind and how many customers will come in? Should you decide to invest in expanding your shop? Should you buy vending machines for your shop, which allow for increased and automated sales at the expense of customer interaction?
But I think the absolute best thing they did with this game is the PROGRESSION that you learn all these things. Sooner or later, as you start to buy and sell more things, and decide what to do with your shop, you start to distinguish between the different kinds of customers that want to buy things. There is simply a consistent pattern--this kind of customer just won't pay that much for an item (and you will learn to hate those customers), and maybe this other kind of customer has a bit of coin left in their pocket, so you can maybe offer him a higher price. It's all very subtle and unstated, but learned by the player as you sell more items. It's honestly magical.
And what will be your main strategy to earn your keep? Should you go buy from the market and take advantage of item booms and lows? Or go dungeoneering into the depths to procure items and sell for 100% profit? Should you choose to go dungeoneering, you will learn that it's a very difficult balancing act of opportunity cost. Should I keep this item, or toss it to pick up this one? Should I use this healing item, or risk killing mobs to wait until I level up, which will heal me fully? Should I progress through the dungeon to use the day more efficiently, or not take the risk and use the checkpoint to go back home?
The day is divided into four slices. For each slice, you can choose to open your shop, go to the market, explore the city, or go dungeoneering, all consuming a certain number of slices. However, should you choose to go to the market, exploring the city will not take up any additional time. It's an ingenious way to make the player able to enjoy the story-side of the game. When you explore the city, you will interact with the townsfolk, which will bring up a short scene with your characters and their friends. As you take the time to explore the city more and more, you realize that each character has a backstory to them, and they develop more and more. It's one of the things I enjoyed most about this game.
The only gripe that I may have about this game is that the dungeoneering is actually very difficult. The controls are tight and fair, but some of the bosses spike in difficulty and you may easily die if you are not prepared for them. Dying in a dungeon renders your day obsolete, and all the time and effort you put in getting up to that point.

I met the Devs at GamesCom 2014. Around noon on Friday they sat me down in front of a PC and had me try the game - apparently I did well (I looked at the goblin before attacking it and noticed it had first strike). After a merry but short romp through the introduction dungeon, which ended with a green blob of slime eating my poor adventurer, I went on to explore the rest of the Indie Megabooth. Friday night though, before I went to sleep, I knew there was a bit of unfinished business: I bought the game, and not just because the developers are great guys (but that too).
The game delivers what it promisses: bite sized adventures you can play during a break. The other day I had 15 minutes to spare: 10 of those were used by a berserker clearing a swamp of monsters.
It may look like a simple game, but it has a suprising amound of depth, with many abilities, items and other things that lead to multiple ways to tackle dungeons and may have you adapting your strategy based on what you encounter.
And there is a lot to encounter. Just when you think you have seen all the races, seen all the classes, you find one more. Then you check the journal and see just how much you haven't seen yet (I found it more fun not to check how much I am missing so as not to spoil the pleasure of finding something new).
But how do you play? Simple: you select a dungeon to explore and write an adventuring permit. The permit is the "character creation" process of that dungeon. For example it could say: To [dungeon name], For Generic Adventuring, Race: Human, Class: Warrior, Equipment: starting adventurer's kit. Then you would play the dungeon with a simple lvl 1 human warrior.
As the game progresses you unlock more races, classes and can provide better starting equipment and other bonuses, making each run unique.
So what are you waiting for? Your kingdom needs you! Oh, you need a permit? To: Unnamed Desktop Dungeon Kingdom, For: Kingdom Administration, Race: Human, Class: Gamer. There you go, your permit to play the game.
And yes, the alpha version is available for free to try out :)

So with almost 30 hours in i think i got enough to say a thing or two about the game:
Good things:
1: Amazing intro to the game which makes you get a little understanding of what is going on around you, compared to where some games just push you out into a world where you got no clue wtf is going on.
2: Once you are in the game and start playing you spawn outside the map in the desert. Not far off, but just enough for you to breathe.
This is really nice as i wouldn't feel like i have controll over my surroundings if i got placed in the middle of the jungle.
You start off nice and slow with a little bit of basic things laying around.
3: The farming and building game!;
In some games where farming is a huge role to get somewhere, you will often find yourself spending many hours in the start just to be able to build a little house. And litterly for the rest of the server session...
Were in Conan starting off with gathering resources is quite simple. Getting maybe a 4x4 house will take at most 15-20 min, and with this as a start you are off to something good!
4: Exploring time!
Once you have settled down somewhere you can go begin the exploration of the world of Conan.
Conan has ALOT to offer when it comes to exploring:
-Different types of monsters all around the world!
-Different types of NPC'S all around the world!
-Different types of animals all around the world!
-Many different caves around!
-Dangerouse areas with even more powerfull creatures!!! And this is in the undead City! (Or whatever you wanna call it)
-A god damn beautifull world in general <3
5: The leveling system!
The leveling system is both interesting and really well done!
Figuring out what to unlock, and what skills to improve is all up to you as you gotta figure out how you want to play the game. And if you are scrolling down through items you can unlock and find an interesting one, you can get info about lvl requirement and what other things you have to unlock before this one will be avalible just by klicking on it.
Also if you wonder what different skills does before you upgrade any, you can hold your mouse over the text of the skill and it will tell you what advantages it gives.
For the first 35-40 lvls you need to spend your points (for unlocking) wisely as you will have limited points to spend!
Same for skills but spending some points on the ''wrong'' place there wont be as crucial as a wrong unlock.
In the beginning i would reccomend you to increase you stamina pool and how much weight you can carry as farming and running is the most common thing to do for starters.
Also if you are playing with a friend try to avoid unlocking the same things ;)
6: Solo/duo mode!
This mode is amazing. You can think about other survival games and how often do you see a solo mode? I would say very very rarely... BUT! In conan you can run solo!!! *Woooh*
''But mr unicorn. Wont it take away the fun of having other players around you? And the pvp and all that?''
No.. Not really. On one side yes, but on the other side no. I will tell you more about the no side on a bit further down.
Yes side is that some npc camps, places to farm and so on is hard to get through alone, and having someone with you would always be nice. You can do so in duo mode with friends, but online there will always be people around.
But more about why it is amazing. In solo mode you are the admin yourself. You decide how fast things are gonna go. Everything you now do and want to do, you do in your own speed.
Maybe you are one of those who is waiting a little before you buy the game, and once you do you kinda wanna learn the basics before jumping into the populated world. Solo mode let's you do that. It lets you learn, descover and understand how the world of conan works, and this is why i love it <3
You can even reset points as admin. On online servers if you screw up, you screw up. But on solo mode you can fail as many times as you want and it wont matter cause you will always have the oppertunity to redo something.
-Bad things about this game :(
( I really don't know which order im gonna do these in so they will be a bit mixed! )
1: Crashes, lag, stutter, server issues and so on...
The optimization in this game is awefull... aswell as the servers are the most laggy ones out of any games out there...
Yes i know it is a pre-release and it came out a bit over a week ago, but seriously... online servers are a pain inn the♥♥♥♥♥♥to play on. They bring more pain than joy...
I'm running this game on this system: I7 6700k (4,7 ghz), gtx 1080, 16gb 3600mhz ram, 200gb ssd and a 1tb hdd.
I cranked the game to max setting plus 6x msa, and well the visual is amazing, but in so many scenarios the fps drops to below 30 and makes the game less enjoable. I tried to turn off msa and it helped out making the game smoother when it ran above 60 fps, but stil got the same frame drops and stutters as before.
I have even been in the situation where conan used 13gb of my ram!!! It nearly crashed my system cause of the ram usage... Also. If you have an higly overclocked gpu you should probably crank that down a little as this game wouldnt run when mine was oc just a little...
If you know pc specs and see that this system have trouble running this game you know the optimization is not at it's best.
2: Online gameplay:
There are positive things about playing online like meeting new ppl, pve together, epic pvp battles as so on. But these things are also what makes this game bad to play online.
As the game is insanely laggy pvp-ing is really hard as you just teleport back and fourth while slashing your sword into the air. In the beginning you could destroy someones base with your bare hands... They fixed that, but alot of the raiding problems are still there. Let's say you have started fresh on a server and the first day you made it to lvl 15. You go offline. And boom you are raided... ''But i put a door on and sealed off the roof and everything... how did this happen?''.
Well. Once you get iron pickaxe and hatchet you can breake into basic doors just in a few hits... Raiding is so easy that new players will go to sleep knowing that all the stuff they worked forr is now gone... In early lvls it's so hard to defend what you have managed to get. It's more or less impossible to defend your poor home.
And may i ask how in hell is this even close to fun?
It isn't. And most groups/clans you will find around on servers will do whater they can to screw you over and make sure you wont have an enjoyable time playing.
This is one of the main reasons i stay away from online servers...
Oh btw. PVE servers which are ment to be ''friendy'' servers... you can stil raid people and steal stuff. So it's litterly the same as pvp just that now you can't defend your base at all.
3: Communicating online. You got global chat, nearby chat and voice chat. Everything works...aaaand then they don't. Typing chat might just randomly dissapear and you can now not communicate with the world <3
Voice chat is on and off. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. And sometimes you just hear stutters.
Also there is a voice range indicator which will tell you how far away someone is from you while talking ingame. This thing might also get stuck to the left of your screen and never leave. So for the rest of your gaming session or untill you restart the game you will have this text saying ''Unicorn: 46m''.
4: You remember the yes and no side to the question ''But mr unicorn. Wont it take away the fun of having other players around you? And the pvp and all that?''
Well. I told you i would say more about the no side, but by now i think you know why it wont ruin anything. It will honestly make it more fun...
Do i recommend it? Yes. It's not that expensive and gives you so much back. The map is bigger than you think and there is always things to do :)
But solo/duo mode is the way to go untill the online things are getting better!!!

Changing to maximum armour, you ambush them with a well placed grenade and then finish them off. But now the Koreans have heard the noise and seen you, and are closing in to flank you. Best PC Metroidvania You Didn’t Play of 2013? Must've been no other metroidvanias that year. It's pretty but the actual gameplay, the stuff that matters when making a game, is crap. The game is short and empty. You backtrack through huge cave areas picking up items to open doors and 'upgrades' to let you explore more huge caves all while fighting the same three enemies and their recolours over and over.
Seriously, you got walking thing that has stronger forms that can shoot, flying torso ghost thing that takes one hit and it's stronger form that takes two, and evil soldier with a gun.
The bosses, if you can call them that, are a bigger red version of the walking thing and at the very end you fight a soldier with a gun that fires a three way shot.
You get three weapons. Grenades which are limited, there's maybe fifteen in the whole game. A pistol with infinite ammo. Another pistol that fire a three way shot but costs energy.
As for the upgrades? Let's see if I remember them all, no longer take fall damage, ability to read the ancient tablets, double jump, breathe underwater longer, breathe underwater even longer than that. Yeah, real fun stuff there.
As for plot, the game just throws info at you that means nothing as there is no context. You go to this mine where there are these guys from some other group that aren't supposed to be there and there is a name drop about Templeman, whoever that is. You find they dug up some ancient temple and this other group is trying to awaken something. Along the way you find tablets that ramble about ancient magicks and technology and sealing this thing the soldiers are trying to awaken.
Who were these ancient people, are the enemies related to them? If not where did these monsters even come from?  Who are the soldiers that are trying to awaken this thing and why are they doing so? Who is Templeman? Who are you? All I know is that you walk around picking up keys shooting things that get in your way.
The ending is what was really a kick in the teeth. You kill slightly different soldier, which I thought was the first real boss not the last unique enemy in the game, and take an amulet and another orb to open some tomb thing. The tomb is of course back at the other end of the game's areas so you can backtrack more. You get sealed inside, the end. You get a view of the planet and a quote about how heroism isn't glamorous and no one is entertained by it.
Now I admit, I like the
of the ending, but not the execution. I would enjoy it if something had happened actually happened or was explained. All the amulets and stuff are sealed in the room with me, does that mean I stopped them? Did I save the galaxy by sacrificing myself? Did I fail to stop them and humanity gets destroyed? I don't know, the game told me nothing.

Part of me wishes this was longer;  but it really is just the perfect length for what it is.  I really like this buy for five dollars.
If you hear the "Metroidvania" tag and expect something along the lines of Super Metroid, Fusion, or such, you may be disappointed - the MV genre is the closest easy genre to throw at it, but this is something a little different.  It's less like a modern era Metroidvania throwback, and more like a Metroidvania era Amiga throwback.
Compared to what one expects from an indie MV style game, it's simpler in many ways, but with a little more push on narrative.  I'd really like to see what the fellow making this can do with a few more resources.
It's stripped-down approach, while it may just be an artifact of the single-dev approach, is quite suiting to the game.  It comes across as slightly haunting, really.  It's like a really good indie record from the 80's - rather than being hindered by it's limitations, it has embraced them into part of the aesthetic, and made something better for it.  I think trying to make a game with the same sort of emotional resonance that is attempted in modern titles, within the confines of a vintage-styled 2D game, and to succeed on the level this game has is quite the accomplishment.
From a gameplay aspect, while I often like something in this genre with a more open and less linear map (Aquaria was one of my favorites in this regard) given the size of this game, and the slow speed of movement, I appreciated the "looping" nature of many of the paths you take - while it does create a slightly more linear experience, it removes a lot of the "grind" of making your way across repeated terrain.  Teleporters and shortcuts and other work-arounds wouldn't have worked as well with the feel of this game, really, and allowing the character to move through the environment faster would have ruined the feel and mood of the game.
Really, there's been an incredible balancing act in a lot of aspects of this game.   Every decision in it's creation seems to be quite deliberate.
Honestly, I have a hard time not recommending this to anyone - the dollar and time cost are low enough to not feel like a waste even if you don't like it, and it's an intriguing game.  It doesn't quite hit every note it reaches for, but if you like 2D styled games, and games driven slightly more by story than action (without being action free) this is a good try.

I can recommend playing Inescapable, so long you understand several very important things about this title. First, despite the visual similarities, know that this is
Super Metroid. A comparable situation would be like saying a triple decker sandwich is proportional to a single slice of lukewarm bologna. Second, this game is very short, and I would suggest not even playing unless you have ample time to finish it in a single go, because, third, there is no map (or hidden collectibles). Even though the game’s world is relatively small, I imagine most will simply give up upon booting back up and realizing that they can't recall where they'd been. And that would be a shame, because once you get past the fact that the supposed similarities to Metroid don't really exist past the visuals, you will still find a competent and mysterious adventure that ends long before it has the chance to overstay its welcome.
To better explain what this game is, lets again bring up the beloved Super Metroid. Now, remove the myriad of hidden hallways, collectibles and bosses, remove the enemy variety and all music, remove all but a few non-linear pathways, and cut the world into, oh… 1/5th the size, if even that. Now, you might have an idea of what to expect upon starting Inescapable, an
take on the metroidvania style.
As bad as the all of the above may sound, know that I enjoyed my time with Inescapable, as brief as the 2 hour journey was. The game is
“indie”, with only a handful (read: 3) of enemy types, lack of weapon variety beyond a pistol and variant thereof, and whose combat consists solely of ducking below enemy bullets. Worse yet, there are doors that can only be opened upon finding the proper jewel or thingamajig that fits a slot, and so backtracking becomes an integral part of the experience. You may understand now why completing this title in a single sitting becomes paramount, as “misplacing” that blasted door was will undoubtedly infuriate, and the likelihood of such an error may lessen if you’ve yet to pause your journey and allow forgetfulness to set in.
What story exists is told through snippets of dialogue found through interacting with computers, murals, plaques and the like, but it’s typical sci-fi nonsense of “ancient alien power” and man’s greed. What gets me most, in regards to the story and this title’s aforementioned
quality, is that this story doesn’t end, or rather, there is no ending. In typical indie nonsense fashion, the game ends with a “deep” quote and a
screen. The story sees no resolution, and the player receives no reward for their work.
So why, then, the thumbs up? Simply, the journey was enjoyable, and the lack of resolution to the meager story did not diminish that feeling. The world that you explore, as lacking as it may be, and the adventure it brings ends before it becomes stale. Lack of a proper conclusion in favor of a silly quote screen notwithstanding, I enjoyed this short title for what it was. And if you can forgive the lack of a proper finish (and that it sure as hell isn't Super Metroid), as I did, you will likely look fondly on your time with Inescapable.

A feat that is.. hard to pull off for games that devs try to stay ontop of performance, exploit as well as "balance" wise.. some may know which games i refer to.

This game is an absolute BLAST to play in co-op with a group of friends, as well as Guild runs if you are lucky enough to call a Guild your home here. there is more to do every time a major update comes out, which i have seen about every month or two within this past year and it doesnt look to be slowing down, i actualy have ALOT of new gameplay features and mission types to try now since the game has updated so many times since i last played it.
That being said, this game can feel rather lonely or at least, more tedious and plogging when playing alone, or at least that is how i feel.. being OCD and trying to "do everything and find everything" in a level if i can before leaving (something which sometimes gets on the nerves of friends or fellow public players who wish to rush to the end)
So this may not apply to everyone. And yes this game is indeed a slow grind.. for everything.. meant to be in order to stretch out progression in the game, in this case NOT to make microtransactions speed it up.. as it only does so the building process or trading for parts and blueprints.. and yes it takes a long time to max level gear in order to mod it the way you want, as well as rank up to gain access to building and using other gear..
That being said.. don't expect to try everything within a year, but DO be ready to TRY EVERYTHING. the game doesnt realy let one feel comfortable with a certian loadout for too long, enchoraging one to experiment with new gear as they manage to obtain and build it and get comfortable with other gear in order to level up and RANK up. so if you want to rank up and try new things, you have to try everything you can first to reach it, forcing teh player to be a Jack-of-all-trades as it were, but still let you master what you feel comfortable with.. even if you have to "master" the weapon in-game to rank up. with the amount of gear as well as expanding missions and gear, you will always have something to do or a goal to reach ingame for yourself, even if you may have to grind for up to a year or more to reach said goal, which is indimidating but that is life right?
AGAIN that being said, you will likely get hooked to this game, especialy with friends or an active guild and to reach said goal you will need to devote alot of time as i said already.. so you may end up becoming addicted easily and spending large parts of your free time binge playing this game. nothing wrong with that unless you are usualy very busy with a tight schedual. the other cons i can think of arent to do with the game itself, after all the movement and combat system, while it has a slight learning curve becomes rather intuitive once you learn which button combos do what and you will find yourself gleefuly sprinting and jumping about the level feeling like a true space ninja!
Oh right.. well con wise i can think of is the time it may take to install or update which depends on internet connection speed and bandwidth.. same goes for connecting to games online too though, and be wary that because of frequent content updates that this game will take a good chunk of your HDD/SDD but it certianly feels worth the investment in hardware resources if you do enjoy the game.
TL;DR: This game is a rollar coaster experience that will always leave you with a goal to accomplish and friendly players to team up with. It's a blast with friends if you all can find the time and you will likely be hooked and play for hours a day!
ALSO this is TRUE Free To Play! you need not invest a cent into the game in order to play or progress.. and the actual microtransactions for "Platinum" are only needed for cosmetics, some starter weapons if one chooses to, as well as spending on "halving" gear construction time.. oh and for trading for items and parts ingame unless you have similar items to trade with anyway.

The game is very forgetful and seems something of an unfinished game that could have been great if more effort was put into it. The download size is 2.5MB, so very small even among today's lightest indie games. I don't recommend buying the game at full price but it you get it as part of a bundle or as a gift then at the very least it's a decent way to waste some time.
Longer, more detailed review below:
You start out with nothing and gain weapons and upgrades. Gun, upgraded spread shot gun, and grenade... very simple.
The enemies are blan "alien" creatures that come in two types with about two or three variations on them. One type is like a zombie that shuffles around slowly on loop and only attacks with projectiles when facing you. The second is sort of a ghost of a half corpse and persues you with flight. They both do little damage and are nothing more than an annoyance. You do find actual human enemies towards the end but they're so few apart and are only really just another upgrade of the first alien type only they shoot and walk faster.
You progress through the game by using items/keys you collect to open doors that lead to more areas. The collecting is so horribly repetitive it gave me a headache just doing the same thing over and over again. Obtaining an item/key is usually just killing an enemy and it popping out of them or just finding it on the ground at the end of an area. There seemed to a sort of attempt at puzzles in various parts of your quest for these items but they just consist of making your way to a switch, lighting fires, or using a water filled pot to set on a floor switch. All of it very unimpressive.
As you play the game you'll come across what seem to be small parts of an actual story forming. It's not that interesting and horribly written, giving the player no real reason actually pay attention and read any of it. There was a sort of "build up" to the story as you progressed through the game and made me think I was in for a boss fight of some sort...
The game abruptly ends when you get to a sarcophagus to insert the last item you found. (a stone circle) I'd of thought this would trigger the final battle that I was hoping for while playing through this but NO, NO NO NO, your character just says he'd rest there and the game pops up an image of the planet in space with some saying in front of it. The saying being a BS message about "your heroic adventures as kid mean nothing" or something along those lines.
Meh.
