Divinity Original Sin 2 is one of those rare games that comes along very rarely these days. In a market full of AAA cash grabs full of DLCs and microtransactions, DOS2 delivers more content then games at a higher cost point. But its not just about the quantity of content, its also about quality, and quality DOS2 has.
From the ridiculous amount of builds you can do on characters, to the addicting looting and item sets, DOS2 has me hooked. I find it fun to the point of I'm losing entire nights replaying the same beginning part over and over and still finding new ways to do things. There is so many ways to complete quests, that the replay value is astounding.
Also, the combat, while not changed too much from DOS, is just as creative as ever. Every fight players are outmatched and have to utilize creative elements of the map/abilities to come out on top.
I'm only on Act 2, so maybe this will change, but as of right now, its the best RPG I've played since Witcher 3 and highly recommend it to any fan of RPGs or Baldur's Gate style games (a more casual/modernized version of BG, granted).

This was one cool game in my book. Made by the devs of Painkiller, Bulletstorm and Shadow Warrior.
It's an old school type of FPS - think of Serious Sam, but in a Cyberpunk future.
The story is presented between levels, simplisticly drawn and in a comicbook style. The story lacks... but this is a "Robot masacre simulator", so the story is there just to have something to follow and move forward.
Now the great part of this game are the graphics. They nailed all design elements:
* a world taken from DeusEx combined with Terminator future
* also the DLC has a more junkyard vibe... think of the "Enslaved: Journey to the west" game
* lots of details in all elements, from world design to enemies
* great weapons
The sound effects are also great, the music is there and is not bad, but the voice acting lacks... luckly there is not much of it. Gameplay ways... had lots of fun. These are the things I want to point out:
*the weapons are originaly implemented, but not perfectly
*enemies are really cool and engaging, but only 3 types with 3 variations on each
*bosses are lots of fun, but again, too few
*linear levels, but the secrets are a cool addition, giving you a reason to explore
*environment traps are amazing and one of the most fun part of the game
* ~8-10 hours of gameplay for the main game+DLC
The DLC has a few more enemies, new setting and is equaly as fun as the main campain - worth it!
The Redux version brings 1 more enemy type (zombie like), 1 more weapon (sword) and a dash move, this along the improved graphics, performance and more balance to the game - if you own the original, I would say that this is not worth it, unless you want to support the devs or have extra cash at hand.
PS. Also made a YouTube vid with My Thoughts on it

This "format" is primarily changed through physics, as the golfing balls in this game are prepared to go to mars and back just to get into that damned hole. I think a way to counter this issue is allowing the community to have a map maker with a workshop for other users to browse, play and edit other users levels.

This is quite possibly one of my favorite puzzle games of all time.
At first it seems rather simple - your goal is to take a level one character and find a way to kill the level 10 boss at the end of the map.  The challenge comes in how you do it - the amount of XP and healing items are limited, so every step counts.
As you progress through the quests, (which are nothing more than fixed starting criteria) you'll unlock new items, characters, classes, and gods to help (or hurt) your progress through each map.
If you're looking for a well-paced evolving challenge, I highly recommend this game.

It's not a terrible game, but certainly has "doujin" taste to it, despite it's look and presentation.
This game is a mixture of dungeoun crawler and monopoly sim together. Is this fun? It sure is.
As the game was released (the first copy, not steam release) you do have to accept the fact that this game is aged. The graphic is near PS1, or early PS2 titles. Music is nice and cheerful. Story is charming, despite its actual story isn't. I think the character is helping out a lot. Recette, the protagonist, needs to pay her runnaway-father's debt of his house, otherwise she will be homeless.
The sim itself is well made- you have certain amount of time in each day (works like turn basis) and you have few options to get yourself a money; buy/sell from other store, hire a client for dungeon crawling, or open your shop. Your merchant level increase by selling item in FAIR prices, and as it goes higher, you can sell things differently- such as custom order, or purchase vending machine, etc. Each customer will have different preference. So, you likely don't sell long sword to a little girl well, she would likely want to get food or books. Time also affect what kind of customer you'll bring in.
The dungeoun crawling is very straight forward, but the dungeon is randomly generated. You can use an item you find in dungeon, or save it to sell them later.
Unfortunately, the game has 1 massive issue for me- the sheer difficulty. Almost to the point of unnecessary. Each week you have a set of debt that you need to pay back. The debpt increases by each week, however, it increases in such a rapid pace- first week is 10,000 second week is 30,000... so on. This is caused by the fact that you only have 5 weeks to finish the payment. In order to finish game fast, you have to have pure luck, as the entire game is randomly generated. The random event occurs from 2nd week (such as gold booming or bad reputation towards all of sword) and I truly mean randomly generated- even if you save/load, you will get random event. The meeting with important character (playable) is also randomly generated. All of the treasures in dungeon is randomly generated.
To cover this issue, the Recettear allows you to carryout your items once you hit "game over". Your money will reset to 1000 while all of your items remains the same.
I understand that forcing you to cycle the game was their only plan to make this game feel less short then already is. THe problem? Well, once you got gameover, you will be sent back to day2. You can repeat this over and over until you beat the game. It gets repetitive, I also felt less encouraged to go back to day 2 from day 30.
This game is impressive "doujin" game, as this entire project was done by single person. Still, $20 price tag can seriously compete with other titles.
The game itself is good, however, it may not fit for everyone. It's worth giving a try.
If I had to give a score it would be 6.5/10.
Another nice note: this game is old enough to play with my crappy 8inch tablet. Nice.

This is a surprisingly fun and addictive game.  It short it is a procedurally generated micro solo dungeon crawl.   It has basic rpg theme elements of classes and races which set your base skills and character progression.  Add in a layer of equipment and inject a play strategy based upon one's deity of choice and you have a pretty large degree of freedom and replayability.  While the layout and enemy composition change between runs of a given dungeon there are consistent parts.
1. a set number of mobs of each level up to 10
2. a set # of glyphs (spells)
3. a set # of skill ups
4. a set # of shops
5. Undiscovered tiles which restore health and mana when explored
6. A set # of potions
Like some gameshows you can retire from the dungeon at any time and keep your winnings thus far.   Which is helpful when it is impossible to defeat the dungon boss and just need to amass gold to improve your town.  A run becomes an optimization problem, in which the player needs to maximize each step and attack to best utilize the resources at their disposal.
This game scratches the itch of a turn-based roguelike rpg that can be played in 10 minute chunks.

Owlboy was 10 years in the making and when you see the amazing artwork, the great animations and its carefully crafted characters you can see why. I respect the work that was put into it. But I just can't understand how the gameplay ended up such a mess.
The game starts out great. Lots of character driven moments and interesting locations promise a terrific experience. But later parts of the game are not that great anymore. The "dungeons" overstay their welcome and become tedious quickly and the level design is full of flaws.
This game frustrated me so much. When you get hit you fly away so far, lose your only means of defense and have such a small invincibility timer that I found myself in stunlocks more often than not. Bosses are huge bullet sponges, sometimes you don't even know if you are dealing damage or not. Often a boss room is just a small room where you get attacked by waves of enemies.
There is a huge difference between challenging difficulty and frustrating difficulty and this game provides the latter. The difficulty lies in your characters limited moveset, the weird controls and the frustrating control loss after getting hit. I never felt fully in control over my character and regaining that limited control after being hit is a huge struggle. Pair that with levels where you can't even see the obstacles, lava that kills you instantly when you touch it and lots and lots of backtracking if you want to get the collectibles.
I wanted to like this game so much but the gameplay dragged the whole thing down with its frustrating combat system and dragged out level design. The artwork, the music and the characters are amazing and there is so much potential. Currently I felt miserable while playing, never feeling fully in control of my character, fighting through rooms with hordes of enemies just to get a glance at what this game could have been. More than just a pretty game you want to like because the developers put 10 years into it.

So far I'm on my second set of matches, having won one of the artefacts (marks of your progress which increase both your abilities and the challenges you face), and I am -very- intrigued to play and learn more.
By far its greatest strength is the dealer opposing you across the table; both sinister and likeable, with a great line in sardonic humour and musings on the nature of games, alternately chiding and encouraging, mocking and praising, the player. On the surface, it is a neat little game. It reminds me a lot of a sega master system title Zillion in that it really isn't a metroidvania as advertised. You just have to get through each screen and a branching path either results in a key or a door.
In terms of presentation, the animation isn't great but the controls are ok, the graphics are fine and it is "just" interesting enough to draw you in. There is some story here, but it is mostly told through snippets of text that appear at the top of the screen. I feel you would really need to be in the right "mood" to appreciate them. I probably wasn't so I found it really hard to care. Still, at least there is an attempt at a narrative here (not so much an attempt at an ending).
On the negative side, I think it can be compared to something like Cave Story+ in style. But where cave story shows you all the "cool" scenes, inescapable tends to skip them. For example the game starts and you are told there is 2 minutes until everybody dies on the spaceship. Then the game cuts to you leaving your escape pod on another planet.
Going through those two minutes to escape, even as a tutorial area is the type of added detail that is missing at the moment. It doesn't ruin the game, far from it, but it could just do with things like that to elevate the game further.
These initial impressions of an underwhelming experience carry through to the later stages. It was ultimately fine, but nothing much happened and the game only really made you back track more towards the end, with no real changes or challenge to keep it interesting. The areas you go through (some several times) are large, but mostly empty and any combat resolves down to a careful strategy of simply ducking all the bullets.
Even the upgrades are rather unexciting. They seem to centre on letting you last longer underwater. This sounds fine and "metroid-esque" but you still need to tackle these sections in a linear order and they are just long empty sections where you can only move slowly. As such, you never feel like you are getting powerful and strangely can still drown by the end of the game (it just takes ages).
All up, it only lasts an hour and I kind of enjoyed it well enough, but I don't think it is worth buying at this stage. Hopefully the developers take this solid base and really make something exciting next time around.

If you're looking for a metroidvania, stop, close the page, and don't look back. If you're looking for a good game, rinse and repeat. If you're looking for tedious garbage that lasts 2 hours then you've found the right place. Inescapable's page asks the questions of "Unravel the mystery uncovered by a remote interplanetary mining operation. What did they find? What threat does it pose? And ultimately, what does it truly mean to be a hero?" None of those questions are answered.
You "explore" this planet in what is pretty much a straight path majority of the game. Other times it will acknowledge you picked up an item and ask you to return to another previous location 10 minutes away because it happens to open a door that lets you pick up another item. You'll also occasionally complete braindead puzzles that required you pressing a switch and then continuing on your way. The creator seems to have played a Metroid or Castlevania sometime in his life and decided to make a game about it without realizing what makes those games any good.
In those games you usually picked up upgrades that had a meaningful impact on your movement or how you dealt with enemies. In this game you acquire 12 total grenades off random bodies throughout the game and a spreadshot gun that depletes your suits energy/health every time it's fired. Besides that you'll be running around with an average gun majority of the time shooting the same enemies for 2 hours. There is 3 different enemy types. There is a regular mutant, a flying mutant, and about 3 enemy soldiers you fight in the game. Take that regular mutant and change it's size and color palette and that's 95% of the enemies you will be killing in this game.
Now another one of the things that makes Metroid and Castlevania good is they include a map and each area is very distinct so you always have a feeling of knowing where you are. There is about 5 or less different tilesets in the game. Majority of them are present in the screenshots provided on the page. There's rocks, lab looking stuff, temple stuff, metal stuff, and I can't honestly think of any more. Majority of it is just different colored rocks. I think it's an accomplishment that a single guy made this, but I can't believe no one told him to maybe make the game fun or interesting.
The only thing that could be construed as interesting in the whole 2 hours would be the broken up narrative that you get from reading tablets throughout the game. It's to be believed that this planet you crashed on was being dug up and researched by some group of people we don't care about. We're to believe they found an old ancient civilization that had a secret thing no one has ever discovered. This secret thing had a lot of power and was cool or something so people wanted it. I might be wrong in my synopsis, but it's not like it really matters when at the very end you don't even get an ending. It mocks you instead. You put the final item in an old tomb, the game cuts to black, and then shows a shot of planet you're on. You are then presented with a completed unrelated quote from an author named David Foster Wallace. The quote tells you how your childish entertainment was just that. It was childish entertainment. It was theatre, smoke, and mirrors. It was all meant to excite and gratify an audience. In reality though, there is no audience. There's no one to clap for actual heroism.
The ending is a slap on the face to anyone who might of bought this. If I were to take a guess, the creator might of enjoyed the authors books and this quote. He also might of just needed a quote that talked about how entertainment is meaningless that could also be construed as why do you need an ending. I imagine the guy working on this didn't know where he was going with the story while writing the three pages or less of text in the game. He then realized at the last moment he needed an ending to his 2 hour affair. He then couldn't think of one that left the audience reasonably satisfied and maybe one that also left them a few questions so they could possibly theorize what was going on. Instead of thinking of an ending like that, he decided to just go with a quote. Again, a quote that basically said that you completed the game and because of that, you don't deserve any praise and contentment you might of gotten from a real ending.
I hope the guy who created this takes his skills and applies himself to another endeavor, but actually gets feedback throughout his process to realize what makes games good and fun. I hope the creator can learn how to make a video game engaging and enjoyable. Maybe then he could go on to make something that actually is like a Metroid or Castlevania. Still,  looking at this overall, I'm left with disappointment. It had the possibility of being a tightly packed metroidvania that lasted a few hours, but instead we got a straight path through the same rocky areas and fighting the same enemies for 2 hours. The only thing I think I enjoyed about the game might of been the art and animation on main character, but that is not enough for me to care about this game.
Ultimately, it's just a bad indie game that could of been much better if the creator put more time into it and actually had feedback on what makes video games fun.
Also, a side note. Most of the reviews in the description of the game are either badly written, misleading, or links to a random person on tumblr who doesn't know what he's talking about.

Inescapable is a metroidvania-style game reminiscent of the early 2D games of that type.
In terms of game mechanics it also resembles the older games -- tight long jumps that require jumping only once the character's feet are 90% off the platform, simple crouching and knockback on getting hit. By today's standards it is pretty bare-bones. Even the upgrades typical of metroidvanias are rather lackluster: shock absorbers to remove fall damage, handgun, energy shield, double jump. There's also grenades and an improved gun but there's hardly any need to use them more than once. Combat is a non-factor and once past the fall-damage part there is almost no danger of dying.
Presentation-wise Inescapable looks like an early snes-era 2D platformer and lacks any music other than a few ambient sounds. Sound effects are basic as well so really most of the game is spent in silence. Dialogue is scarce to say the least and mostly takes the form of the ship's AI providing basic narration and translations of alien script.
Yes, it seems like there isn't much to the game at all. Still, it is a short metroid-flavoured adventure that'll help fans of these games pass an hour or two of time.

WftO is the first game in one and a half decades to get the Dungeon Sim right. It's tonnes of fun, and brings a great mix of old features from the old classics, improvements to the formula and new ideas.
I've followed this game since I backed it on Kickstarter in 2012, and honestly, I'm impressed by what's been achieved, and proud to have been a part of it.
[Update]
WftO was a bit of a car crash at launch. No denying it. However, unlike some indie let downs, Brightrock have worked hard, forging thorugh the early negative feedback until they had a real gem. WftO is now (and, in fairness, has been for some time) a game to recommend vehemently. A true spiritual descendant of the Dungeon Keeper series, WftO exceeds DK in so, so many ways.
The Heart of Gold expansion pack in particular is wonderful: the missions are all about building a base, rectifying my only remaining critism of the base game (I play a dungeon management game to build my dungeon, and didn't enjoy the campaign levels in the base game that either did away with that or placed a timer on it). I've not enjoyed playing a game this much for ages and am looking forward to expansion #2 immensely!

Inescapable is not quite what it's been billed to be by many reviewers. As a gigantic fan of Super Metroid, the cavernous screenshots practically had me salivating, but the Metroid influence is only part of the story, here, with considerable influence coming from early DOS and Amiga platformers. Another World would be a good talking point, although the visuals are less stylized. Whether you grew up with games on those platforms or, like me, you were raised mostly on consoles, you have to appreciate the dedication and authenticity at work here. The pixelart is excellent making great use of the limited color palette. The game lacks music, but it lends a harshness to the proceedings with nothing to accompany the player except the ambience of gunshots.
What's more, though, is that the game plays well. Some have complained about the lack of a map here, but perhaps that just shows that people have become too dependent on them. The world is well designed, small but quite labyrinthine. Despite that, the gameplay itself is rather straightforward with the focus on finding a series of keys and powerups that enable the player to progress through the game. It's nothing that we've not seen before, but it hits all the right notes, getting a nice balance between obscure and obvious by usually showing you where to use keys before acquiring them. As usual with open-world adventures, the amount of backtracking may bother some, but over the course of the game, you do find a few shortcuts. The game also adds a few twists that are less common such as severe limitations on drops early in the game and a health bar that doubles as ammo for a special weapon, though admittedly the action rarely gets heated enough to necessitate the risk.
All of this makes for a decent game, but it's the storytelling that makes it stand out. Many will find the obfuscated approach to revealing the plot frustrating as there is very little traditional exposition, but I appreciated the subtle way that the details are graually revealed. There's an elegaic quality rarely seen in the loud and fast world of video games. The ending, in particular, has clearly rubbed some people the wrong way, and it can't be called anything but an anticlimax, denying its audience of any reward, but by way of a quote from David Foster Wallace, the game makes some interesting metacommentary on the hero worship we often see in games and other media and how it disconnects from the reality of courageous people.
Undoubtedly, Inescapable is designed for a very specific audience, and while it's well made, it does have problems, particularly  in its challenge or lack thereof. While the level design is good, there is very little variety in enemy types and there are far too few puzzles. It lacks the polish that we might expect from a Metroid or Castlevania. This game is unlikely to be seen as a classic, but developer Mangetic Realms shows a lot of potential here, and the conclusion while unexpected is gutsy and smart. Although the game left me wanting more, it's a testament to the craft here that I would have been willing to keep playing.

Quick Summary: A first person shooter with a variety of weapons, no reloading, and swarms of bullet resistant enemies. The bad guys all have enough life that you need to focus your fire to bring down even the little dudes, but they usually come in packs so survival is all about crowd control. The game was developed by the same people who made the Shadow Warrior remake, so if you enjoyed that game, you should like Hard Reset.
You play Fletcher, a kind of cyborg cop on the streets of Bezoar city, investigating a breach in the city walls that allowed killer robots to enter and run amok killing civilians. As you progress, you’ll find that the robots had help from the inside, but the reasons are convoluted and I don’t fully understand after playing through the game twice. Suffice to say that there are bad guys everywhere, and not all of them are robots. Most of the “story” elements are told between missions in hand drawn art, kind of like a motion comic rather than rendered cut scenes. This is at odds with the game’s modern graphics, but you’re probably not playing a game like this for the story.
In terms of gameplay, Hard Reset is probably closer to Serious Sam or Quake than other modern shooters like Call of Duty. You have numbered health and a regenerating shield, but you’ve got to keep moving and pick up health packs to survive. There’s no cover system to protect you, so if you stay in one place you’ll get squashed, especially since a lot of the things you might think to hide behind can be destroyed by charging enemies.  I mentioned earlier that your opponents have just enough life to be a threat, and they usually come in small groups that will keep you walking backwards as you try to spray them with your guns, but one thing that makes your life easier is the massive amount of destructible environment objects. By this I mean explosive barrels, exploding cars, and a whole lot of items that spray electricity when shot. There’s a steam achievement for destroying environmental items, so I was able to count about 2500 destroyed items in one playthrough (and I wasn’t even really trying).
Technically, the game has only 2 guns: the CLN firearm (ballistic gun) and the NRG gun (lasers). As you move through the levels you find nano, which will be the “money” of the game. Nano can be spent at upgrade stations to buy attachments for your guns, turning them into different weapons. For example the CLN gun has shotgun, grenade, RPG, and mine attachments, as well as upgrades for each attachment (like a passive upgrade to make the shotgun fire faster). There isn’t enough nano in the game to buy all the upgrades but you’ll probably not be using all the guns anyway and you’ll have enough for the good stuff (grenade, RPG, and railgun, smartgun).  Damage per second is incredibly important in this game, second only to crowd control. Note that since there are only 2 guns, there are also only 2 ammo types (CLN and NRG). This means your RPG, Rifle, grenade, etc. all use the same ammo, just different amounts per shot.
Pros:
+Very nice graphics with explosions, lasers, and robo parts being blown all over the place. Bear in mind that the collectibles (nano, health, and ammo) can also be blown around by your guns so be careful not to shoot them too far away. A few of the hidden nano packs can only be reached by knocking them around with explosives.
+The game is hard, but reasonable (once you unlock quick save with the console). Note that the game has a set of about 25 steam achievements, repeated for each difficulty level. For example an achievement for killing 10 enemies in 10 seconds, with different tiers for easy, normal, hard, and insane difficulty. If you’re like me and only play normal mode you’ll only have about half the achievements by beating the game. I was able to beat hard mode with some effort, which I normally don’t even attempt on most games. Insane difficulty just eats your ammo though, with the enemies laughing at your bullets while they stomp on you.
+Free DLC included: Exile, which is a series of missions almost as long as the main game. The DLC takes you out of Bezoar city into the ruined post-apocalyptic world, though most of the enemies are the same and there aren’t any new weapons. A few new bosses and mini-bosses show up though.
Cons:
-Below average story, which I mentioned earlier. It’s mostly old school run and shoot.
Overall Hard Reset is a fun game that will take about 9 hours to complete. You can’t just run through it because unlike many other modern shooters, you need to watch your health bar (non-regenerating) and even small packs of enemies can overwhelm you if you’re caught on more than one side. A redux version of the game is available on steam for a steep discount if you own the original. Supposedly it has better graphics and some new weapons.

It was very interesting to come to this game AFTER "Shadow Warrior." Flying Wild Hog are seriously the kings of building nifty-looking environments, as well as giving strong nods to classic PC game mechanics. You can also see their lineage of "lock you in an arena and spawn enemies" tricks, but what's rather strange is that they did it MORE blatantly in "Shadow Warrior" than in "Reset."
"Hard Reset" has its interesting moments, especially with it feeling like a playable homage to "Blade Runner," but it only has a few tricks to pull. The enemies are actually interesting to fight (which is an excellent bit of craft), but you'll encounter lots of copies of every baddie. In that way, the experience can get quite "samey" after about the halfway mark. Plus, there are only so many corridors and corridor-esque situations that can be strung together before the magic starts to wear thin.
The upgrade system is decent, but the overwrought interface sometimes gets in its own way. (It looks really cool, though.) The weapon balance is sensible, if seemingly a bit tilted towards the CLN weapon. The "physical ammo" gun feels like it hits much harder than the NRG weapon. A rocket launcher with laser guidance will really clean up the battlefield in a hurry, and the plain-vanilla assault rifle is actually very accurate for a rapid-fire weapon. Even with that sensation of CLN favoritism, the NRG weapon can become almost a touch ridiculous. Yes, it feels generally underpowered and slow, with a parallel tendency to run you dry of ammo at a critical juncture, but the sticky EMPs are very useful...and just wait until you get homing projectiles that you can fire through level geometry!
This original iteration of the title has no manual save, so there are times when the checkpoint spacing can be inconvenient at times. Even so, the devs were nice enough to hand out a pretty decent number of checkpoints overall, and those checkpoints do tend to occur in helpful spots. The only real complaint here is that, come on, quicksave is pretty much a basic feature anymore.
The story elements are something of a rougher ride, because of how "lurching" they are. Tantalizing pieces of world-bulding are dangled in front of you, but then very little actually gets done with them. I felt like a real opportunity was missed there, especially since it wouldn't have taken much more to tighten up the narrative side of the presentation.
"Hard Reset" is a good, shortish diversion of a shooter. It's not a jaw-dropper, but it does a decent job without overstaying its welcome. I hope Flying Wild Hog keeps honing their craft, because they've come out of the gate doing quite well.

This game has a little bit of everything: management, tycoon, random loot, crafting, and even RPG. I do mean "a little", too. The biggest regret of Recettear is that it doesn't achieve greatness in any individual category, but it's a great combination of genres. All the different things you can do keep you from getting bored at any one task, and each benefits the other. When you go adventuring, you earn goods to sell and ingredients to craft with. When you craft an item, you can sell it to your fighters for better stats. You get the idea.
I got about 50 hours worth of play out of my first go-through (though to be fair I had it running in the background for some off that), and I may play it once or twice again before retiring it for good. Definitely worth the price on sale, and maybe even at full price.
It would be great to see a sequal, or even the concept adapted by another company!

I wanted to like this game. Everything I saw for it made it look like a cyberpunk Hotline Miami. As it turns out, it's just a twin-stick style corridor runner. You run through samey environments and fight the same bosses over and over again.
Pros
- I think the atmosphere and style of the game are great. I thought the world was interesting and I kept wanting to know more about all the different groups and the city.
- The combat looks smooth and the game has great visuals.
Cons
- The game lacks variety in its environments for how long it is. For the first hour or so, you go around different types of areas and fight different kinds of enemies. After that, you end up in the same metal platform littered with gore and bodies, with sparks flying everywhere. They throw you a red fog every once in a while, but it's all the same.
- You fight the same bosses over and over, and they even make a "clever" joke about fighting an enemy again. In that same fight, you fight the enemy for 3 phases, where nothing changes and you just beat on him some more.
- The game feels inconsistent.
- The different gun types are cool, but guns and most of the skills feel weak compared to just using melee attacks on everything.
- The story is weak, and pulls the "your princess is in another castle" trick to drag the game out even longer.
I really wanted to like this game, but I can't even recommend anyone buy it at full price. Maybe pick it up for $10, but I just didn't have fun after a while.
TL;DR - Stylish game, meh everything else

I played and really enjoyed the "coffee break"-length first freeware version of Desktop Dungeons, and was looking forward to see what the full, fleshed out version was going to look like.  The core mechanics are still there - strategic turn-based dungeon crawling that plays out like a puzzle you're trying to solve, maximizing the efficiency of every attack, every move - along with a beatuiful music and graphics upgrade, heaps more of the dry, witty humour, more classes and races, and bit of a story arc/narrative progression through the missions instead of randomly generated encounters. (although it's got those too)
It also feels like the difficulty was amped up a bit more, it seems a lot harder to get up to Level 10, so the game isn't as "casual" as the freeware version. DreadOut is a fun, albeit mediocre videogame developed by an Indonesian company. The game uses similar mechanics to those of Fatal Frame, a game released exclusively on console more than a decade ago.
+++ great concept: the game is played from a third-person perspective, but changing to first-person view is a must with our smartphone and digital camera if we want to hurt / eliminate the enemies that are all ghosts and possessed beings
+++ an interesting story: our characters (students probably on a schooltrip) find themselves in an abandoned town out of a sudden and they start to investigate (and soon nightfall arrives and spectres appear)
+++ appropriate longevity: this seems to be a typical indie game, yet, its 6-hour long story offers a good length; extra walkthroughs can be done for missed-out 'cheevos
--- ugly graphics: Unity or not, the game was released in 2014. Some of the textures look pretty ugly, while the monsters and related effects are quite decent.
--- story not finished: I know there is an expansion or some sort of sequel, still, the story ends with a cliffhanger which bothered me as not much was explained as to what was happening. We find some articles here and there that barely shed light on the story of this abandoned settlement
--- extremely tedious, irritating boss battles: there are some sequences that are extremely annoying. For instance, at one point we have to run from a possessed being who occasionally jumps at us lowering our life in the process. We have to restart a couple of times to know where to go, however, even when we know our destination we know we're going to be captured a few times. Not many hints are provided as to how to eliminate the bosses and even when we know it the process is very tiresome
DreadOut is a good game for those loving the horror genre. It has some mistakes here and there that for me can only mean it was left unfinished. There are some annoying sequences that almost made me stop playing - parts that were challenging not because of the real difficulty but because of the awful control mechanics. In case some of these were revamped in the sequel then I'll gladly complete that one.

Saw trailers for it. The setting and tone of the game drew me in from right off the bat. While I loved playing it, I noticed some typos in dialogue and some minor graphical glitches, though nothing that severely detrimented my gameplay experience. A note: dying in this game is pretty much expected. You will die and, and it will probably happen often. The game minimizes any need for "backtracking" when this occurs, and you start at the beginning of the fight where you died. I'm far from the most patient person, but the fact that I managed to get through this game without rage-quitting says a lot about the care in its design, in my opinion.
+Challenging and rewarding gameplay.
+Amazing soundtrack. Mostly.
+Very fun art style.
+An immersive and interesting world. I was thirsty for all the info on Rengkok City as I could get.
+Incredible atmosphere. A real love letter to the Cyberpunk genre.
+Very reasonably priced at 20$. If you love immersion and want to wring every bit of enjoyment out of the game, a full playthrough can take up to 9 hours if you don't replay sections.
+Runs extremely well on my mid-low end 6 year old desktop, with no frame drops or visual stuttering (mileage may vary).
+When you get used to the game, you'll feel really badass.
~Mindscrewy Gainax-style ending (though this is arguably fitting given the genre).
~I feel like the setting and gameplay have a lot more potential than this game seems to have time/budget to explore.
~Replay value is centered on achievements and personal enjoyment of the gameplay - there seem to be no real major mechanics designed to encourage repeat playthroughs.
~Will be supported later with (presumably) paid DLC.
-Unintuitive default control scheme on M+KB. This is the main source of difficulty early on, which is unfortunate. A few hours of practice will get you into it... if you're not left-handed.
-Building on the above: there are no keybinding/button-mapping options (Devs have said this is coming soon, for what it's worth).
-Limited gameplay tweaks (It'd be nice if you could disable the slow-motion effect on kills. I don't mind it, but others do.)
-Mediocre weapon balance. Winning strategies, generally speaking, are melee-focused in my experience (with very few exceptions).
-Occasionally repetitive tunes.
-Short. If you speed through the game you could beat it in only a few hours, especially true on easy mode.
All and all, I believe Ruiner marvelously achieves its goals of being a fun-to-play cyberpunk action game. It's very reasonably priced and Reikon (the devs) have said they intend to support this game with patches and DLC in the future. Ultimately, Ruiner is a neat game with a tricky learning curve and a lot of love poured into it.

I went into this game after seeing a few clips of gameplay from PAX thinking that the combat would be similar to that of Hotline (one shoting enemies, peaking corners to avoid getting one shot yourself).
RUINER almost takes that one shot route if you play on
, enemies will do a good chunk of damage and you will need to use your abilities to chip them down with swings of your pipe or gun shots from distance.
With the mention of abilities I currently use a few, not the full skill set even though I have abilities bound to each of the keys. RUINER gives you the option to customize your playstyle, personally I took the tank or I know I'm going to get hurt in each stage I need more health/healing abilities. You could change this type of style to a high damage dealing, quick, mind controlling bad boy, but that's just not my style.
You can always change your abilities if you want to by using the ability wheel (mid-combat even).
Gameplay is just as fast as Hotline, you'll be dashing around blowing up dumb nerds with shotguns point blank. Stunning multiple enemies, then calculating a multi-dash slicing through for some sweet combo-murders.
Soundtrack is great, playing into the second area I can hear similarities to the Hotline soundtracks. Is the soundtrack better than Hotline? I don't think so. If you're bummed out just pop in the Hotline soundtrack, lower in-game music volume to 0% and carry on killing.
I think there is a quick learning curve to this game, the tutorial will not get you ready for the gameplay ahead. And that's fine no one wants to get bogged down with a long tutorial. I began the game on HARD and debated a few times changing the difficulty, during the boss battles. Stuck it out and learned that you're meant to
, without doing so you'll soak up shots from goobers with shotguns around the corner.
As you progress your enemies get stronger/more dangerous with more abilities they will seem more similar to you and more difficult to kill. However you will also get stronger as time goes on with you skill set.
I'm interested to see where this game ends.
If you're on the fence I won't push you over, if you're looking for something similar to Hotline I'm drop kicking you to this side.

I play ETS2 to relax, and i have sunken more than 150 hours into that game and still am coming back to it. ATS is practically the same game with new trucks and scenery.
If you played ETS2 you know exactly what to expect. It‘s literally the same, even the menu is the same. But i don‘t consider that a negative thing, though some things could‘ve been improved.
After the ETS2 graphics upgrade the game looks gorgeous. ATS is no different, it looks great. Developers put a lot more work into scenery and cities. The American environments never gets old and is always nice to look at and the cities feels alive and real.
The game core didn‘t change. You must drive from pont A to point B and deliver various goods. There are only three trucks in game so far, but it‘s enough for the start, and they‘re badass American trucks! There‘s only two states for now – Nevada and California, you will drive through them in no time, but it feels developers have put more work into them than ETS2 Europe map. Scandinavia DLC looks much better than default EU map, and ATS looks even better than Scandinavia. So i‘d rather have less but quality content than more but shallow and bland.
The game is only 20€ on steam, so you kinda get what you pay for. The more content will be added through DLC and this is one of those rare games when i wait for DLC because i know these developers will not disappoint, they want to make the game better and are always looking for ways to improve their games.
After ATS was released the steam workshop was added to both games. People were asking for it for years and finally these amazing developers done it. Thank you. Now applying mods is as simple as clcking the mouse button.
What i think should be improved is physics and force feedback. The physics feels too arcadey, i know developers are doing their best, but for a new game they could‘ve improved physics. Also Force feedback could use some improvements. But overall driving feel is good.
Graphics are nice and all, but not having anti-aliasing in this day seems a bit stupid huh? I know maybe it‘s because engine limitations or something, but it‘s really not my problem, AA is a must! Other than that performance is inconsistent. I'd say the game runs worse than ETS2, but it also looks more detailed.
There‘s nothing more to say, if you liked ETS2 you‘ll like this one. Just start the engine, open a beer and drive trough beautiful American scenery.

Owlboy is a platforming game based on flight. I went into this game for the most part completely blind, apart from the beginning bits shown off in one of Jim Sterling's Jimpressions videos in august of last year. He said he had been following and waiting for the game since 2008. He was the reason I had interest in this game, and the little bit of knowledge of this game's existence. It had been on my wishlist for almost a year and during this summer sale I did get the game and within the 15, amost 16 hours I have currently put into this game, I pushed through the story. And that was an experience I will remember for quite some time.
A bit off for my standards but, definitely something I could look past once I got used to the controls. w is to jump and press twice to fly, then the controls are fairly easy to get behind. A and D to go left and right, w is up and s is down. A lot of the controls pop up in some areas, especially in the beginning during the tutorial. Some boss battles are pretty difficult, others not so much. The puzzles aren't terrible, just require good timing in some cases, though some others can be a pain. The platforming isn't bad at all, actually quite simple during most parts of the game. It's only in portions where you cannot fly that it gets a bit more difficult.
The story section here is going to be short and sweet to avoid spoiling anything. During the course of the story you play as a young owl named Otus, someone who in the beginning can't do anything right, but later goes on to be one of the heroes in this story as he goes on this great adventure when a terrible threat endangers the world he lives in.
The novelties... Collectible coins the player looks around for to obtain trinkets as a reward for searching for them. The soundtrack is incredible. There is a minigame, which was addicting. There's a global leaderboard if you're one of those people out there who enjoys that type of thing. I spent quite a while in that area myself. The level design isn't terrible, actually quite fun in some areas where in others much is to be desired. And of course, who can forget about the stunning pixel art graphics in this game.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys platforming games and games with great stories. D-pad Studio has earned their place in my list of favorite game studios for this gem of a game.

I'd say this is definitely the best Crysis game, as usual the modern shooter trends like iron sight aiming, regenerating health and limited weapon capacity (thanks a ♥♥♥♥ing bunch Halo) prevent this game from being anything better than above average, but it still finds ways to get around these issues, with varying levels of success. You can equip laser pointers on all of your weapons which allows for much more accurate hip firing, and entering speed mode (one of the game's features allows you to augment one of your abilities at any time) gives you faster strafing, but your aim waivers a fair bit when you move and it can be pretty difficult to see the pointer against the sun's lens flare. The closest it gets to countering the regenerating health bit is giving you the option of a regenerating shield as well, and represents these as a standard percentage bar, which only serves to make it very difficult to determine when you're low on health. And while you CAN only carry two individual submachine guns/assault rifles/shotguns/sniper rifles, the smaller submachine guns (which can be dual wielded) and explosive weapons like rocket launchers still carry their own slot (and can be laser guided for hitting flying vehicles) and you can put a scope and silencer on of your weapons and put it into semi-automatic mode. This is also the only game in the series that has both a melee weapon slot AND a melee button, embodying the PC attitude of giving players options. The gameplay centres around giving you large open areas in which to do your objectives, providing you with many different options for success. This is the direction all linear games should be leaning towards, even if they aren't as open as this game. It looks stunning in both its setting and its graphics. Unfortunately, the whole story is told through these hilariously godawful CG cutscenes. You have to watch these though, I'm not even sure if Crytek intended for them to be this comedic. But still, this is definitely a must-play for PC users, and if you only intend to play one Crysis game (even though you should play them all), this should be it.

Detailed Review now.
Ok first off i were sceptical, as its a card game and they mostly rely on luck with a random die but this game flips that die the finger and lets the skill of the player in combat encounters, so difficulty really is about players skill although i dont want it to be said that if you are bad at the combat you will get destroyed as that is not the case. There is multiple different things you can do to in order to make the game easier, there is a option in the in-game wildcard menu to give the player more in-game items and better ones at the start for those whom do find it abit difficult and that is a nice move, havent used it so cant go into specific but thats what its description is so i like it. The game has simple but enjoyable mechanics which i will run through. Note all different things or mechanics will be described.
Movement: In-game movement has 2 stages, card movement and combat movement.
Card movement is the player moving around on the cards, you move 1 card at a time and for each move you consume 1 point of food and regenerate health if you have lost some but if you dont have any food you will starve and loose health instead. All cards are flipped upside down on the movement board so you never know what you will encounter or what you might see in the current stage.
Combat movement is the movement is when in combat (no♥♥♥♥♥♥ during that phase you will be given a your gear and dropped into a combat arena, how it selects the arenas i dont know although it feels random on occations it also doesnt some other time. Depending on your gear your speed in combat will also be effected, for example heavy armor will protect alot but slow you down quite alot aswell, there is speed changing magical items in-game aswell. Myself have had for example some tiara or crown of some kind which locks the players speed to maximum in-game. Once you finish a game and defeated the boss in it then your gear is reset when you enter the next game and pursue a different boss. Nice they made it so as to keep it challenging.
Card deck: When you are about to embark on a adventure and enter the card movement phase during that you get the option to customize your item deck which consists of what type of treasures you can find and also what type of encounters you can meet on your journey. The encounters deck involves people and general creatures or events you meet on your adventure, some might be bad and some good while others are a quest line you can do and complete during your adventures. Notice the s, many encounter quests and missions take place over multiple adventures and wont be completed during a single run but during the course of multiple. An example is in the games featured screenshot, the one with the text - The Hall of the Goblin King, that encounter for example is a quest line that does just so happen to take place over multiple runs.
Food and Gold:
Gold like equipment is reset after each completed run of the game, gold is used during some encounters where you may give it freely, some might try rob you or spent when encountering a shop. In-game shops have different items depending on what type. There is for example a magical shop which sells magical items and blessings (passive effect) that cost alot of gold mostly but are also very powerful and useful, all shops however sell food that you can buy if you are low or if you have alot of gear or junk items then you can also sell it to them to get gold.
Food is amongst the most important thing in the game i'd say, while good gear helps with getting away with less wounds and bruises or just save you from death. Food can be both a great thing or horrible thing, depending on your current food supply. For each card move you consume 1 point of food, so you need to be careful with it. At the sametime if you are low on food then it can be terrible, as if you reach 0 then for each card movement you will loose health with the amount of health lost i belive is depending on your current max health which can increase or decrease during the adventure.
In summary before i end this i will say that this an amazing change of games and one that stands out alot more than most modern games, i would say it belongs in the nice pairing with new and innovative games like papers please and deserves to be noticed, its a shame it is sort of in the dark like many as it really should be in the spotlight. With just 3 hours i understand i might grow some issues with it but currently i have none and so far i love it.

Eventually you do pick up a few more weapons and powers, but what's the point when 99% of the game is wandering around empty terrain, occasionally shooting a bunch of identical monsters in the face and ducking to avoid their bullets?

I'm a big fan of Shadow Warrior 2013 and could feel a lot of the same in Hard Reset but ultimately I think Flying Wild Hog missed the mark here.
The old school shooter vibe they were going for was fine and dandy but they really dropped the ball with the movement. It just wasn't fluid enough movement for the style of game. You feel bogged down in what is otherwise an endless assault of great action and eye-candy. And things were rather flat. Jumping was clunky and thus underutilized in general. You remained on one plane despite some vertical level designs. And jumping was never involved in battles, just strafe til things are dead. Then your character just feels half a step too slow for a game where you need to constantly be moving. By the halfway point the movement was begging me to call it quits but I ultimately stuck it out thanks to some highlights like the boss battles.
There's a lot of other bad aspects though. All of them I would've forgiven if the movement had been smoother! But instead, they stick out. Like how much of bullet sponges the enemies really are. it isn't a valid complaint on it's own because, well, they're suppose to be! But when it feels like you're strafing through mud it gets tiresome. Another annoyance was the slight bit of RNG "dodge" or "miss" involved on top of them being those bullet sponges. Enemies had dodge animation that would only show half the time you missed an on target shot... The other half of the "dodges"? Well... I'm left guessing, but I will; I think the animations just don't kick in. And this leaves your shots literally going through the enemies with no effect. It was quite odd and visually off putting. Again though, something I would overlook if I had smoother control of my movement and things were just faster overall.
Regular enemies just come in waves and you strafe and shoot hoping you can absorb more shots than they can. Weapons didn't need to be elaborate or varied and they aren't. Plenty of secret areas to be found during downtime. Extremely sparsely sprinkled platforming jumps that are just out of place. All sectioned off by absolutely awesome boss battles. And all packaged in underrated good looks, honestly don't get the need for the Redux as far as the visuals go. But supposedly there's a little more to it than window dressing. But I do believe I will be passing on Redux nonetheless. I had hints of fun and appreciate Flying Wild Hog's approach, but was one of those games that becomes a chore to finish rather than a thrill. And really really odd abrupt ending by the way. I mean I felt it coming but just weird.

It's quite similar to FTL - at the highest level the game is a series of text-base random encounters, some of which initiate a combat mode. Combat itself is a third-person brawler, simiar to the batman series. The unique hook of this game is the deck of cards, which you can build to influence the sort of encounters you'll find in the game. That bit works farily well.
What really brings this game down are the noninteractive animations that are sprinkled everywhere. I was planning to stream the game for a bit to try it out, but ended up playing for 6 hours. Here's what you'll expect.
The main focus of the game is to run a store to pay off a debt. Every week, you have to meet a payment and each time you pay, the next payment increases. If you fail it's game over, but not really. If you fail to pay your game timer is reset, you lose all your money and start from day 1, but you keep the items, store progress and character progress meaning the next attempt is easier. It does however count as a second run so you won't have a "perfect" save file if you lose at all.
To help run your shop, you hire people to run dungeons for you. You explore at least 5 floors of a dungeon, 4 large areas then a boss. During these dungeons, you find items to sell in your shop but your inventory is limited, so you have to pick amd choose what you want to bring with you. The combat during these sections is simple, but engaging. Think of classic Zelda as a reference. You have a basic attack and later you learn a few skills. You will find yourself dying quite quickly if you just run around spamming the attack button, especially on bosses.
Aside from the shop managment and dungeon crawling, anothre thing I adore about this game is the dialogue. The interactions between the different characters is well written, funny and sometimes pretty random. There are even small bonus dialogue events if you take the time to head into certain areas of town when you have the chance.
Overall, a fun, cute, engaging game that offers alittle of everything from different genres. If you are skeptical about if you would like the game, wait for a sale like I did. You won't be disapointed

I went into this game after seeing a few clips of gameplay from PAX thinking that the combat would be similar to that of Hotline (one shoting enemies, peaking corners to avoid getting one shot yourself).
RUINER almost takes that one shot route if you play on
, enemies will do a good chunk of damage and you will need to use your abilities to chip them down with swings of your pipe or gun shots from distance.
With the mention of abilities I currently use a few, not the full skill set even though I have abilities bound to each of the keys. RUINER gives you the option to customize your playstyle, personally I took the tank or I know I'm going to get hurt in each stage I need more health/healing abilities. You could change this type of style to a high damage dealing, quick, mind controlling bad boy, but that's just not my style.
You can always change your abilities if you want to by using the ability wheel (mid-combat even).
Gameplay is just as fast as Hotline, you'll be dashing around blowing up dumb nerds with shotguns point blank. Stunning multiple enemies, then calculating a multi-dash slicing through for some sweet combo-murders.
Soundtrack is great, playing into the second area I can hear similarities to the Hotline soundtracks. Is the soundtrack better than Hotline? I don't think so. If you're bummed out just pop in the Hotline soundtrack, lower in-game music volume to 0% and carry on killing.
I think there is a quick learning curve to this game, the tutorial will not get you ready for the gameplay ahead. And that's fine no one wants to get bogged down with a long tutorial. I began the game on HARD and debated a few times changing the difficulty, during the boss battles. Stuck it out and learned that you're meant to
, without doing so you'll soak up shots from goobers with shotguns around the corner.
As you progress your enemies get stronger/more dangerous with more abilities they will seem more similar to you and more difficult to kill. However you will also get stronger as time goes on with you skill set.
I'm interested to see where this game ends.
If you're on the fence I won't push you over, if you're looking for something similar to Hotline I'm drop kicking you to this side.

Recettear is a very cute game about a girl and a fairy running a shady item shop with the aim of
working earnestly to make a living. There are two modes of gameplay: running the store and stock procurement. Running the store involves a lot of haggling and knowing
the market prices. Stock procurement involves paying hard-working
adventurers to accompany you into dungeon where they would risk their lives to kill monsters while you go around collecting their hard-earned loot, which you can then sell at unfair prices.
Seriously though, I love everything about this game. Running the store has been a fun, relaxing experience while the dungeon exploration provides a very exciting, interactive combat system that makes your grinding very bearable. Coupled with a lot of cool character interactions, cute and catchy musics and a lot of end-game exploration/content, the game really offers a lot of
replayability.
Overall, a very realistic item shop simulator. 10/10 capitalism, ho!

Terrible game. If the N64 graphics, horrible voice acting and broken controls don't put you off, the awful combat and idiotic level design will.
This is a game where an enemy can lock you in a corner and keep knocking you down until you die, and if you happen to quit from the respawn screen you will be stuck with an autosave in that situation, forcing you to start the game over from scratch.
Add to it blurry graphics that would have been panned in 1998, "Michigan: Report from Hell"-level of cringy voice acting, invulnerable enemies that chase you around and can only be killed if and when the game decides so, broken controls with glitchy mouselook and poor controller support, along with horrible level design where it is never clear or intuitive what to do next, and you have an abysmal package.
The horror atmosphere is effective and I would love to cut some slack to the first effort by a studio from Indonesia, but this is beyond unplayable and cannot be recommended to anyone, not even the Fatal Frame fans this is made for.

I play ETS2 to relax, and i have sunken more than 150 hours into that game and still am coming back to it. ATS is practically the same game with new trucks and scenery.
If you played ETS2 you know exactly what to expect. It‘s literally the same, even the menu is the same. But i don‘t consider that a negative thing, though some things could‘ve been improved.
After the ETS2 graphics upgrade the game looks gorgeous. ATS is no different, it looks great. Developers put a lot more work into scenery and cities. The American environments never gets old and is always nice to look at and the cities feels alive and real.
The game core didn‘t change. You must drive from pont A to point B and deliver various goods. There are only three trucks in game so far, but it‘s enough for the start, and they‘re badass American trucks! There‘s only two states for now – Nevada and California, you will drive through them in no time, but it feels developers have put more work into them than ETS2 Europe map. Scandinavia DLC looks much better than default EU map, and ATS looks even better than Scandinavia. So i‘d rather have less but quality content than more but shallow and bland.
The game is only 20€ on steam, so you kinda get what you pay for. The more content will be added through DLC and this is one of those rare games when i wait for DLC because i know these developers will not disappoint, they want to make the game better and are always looking for ways to improve their games.
After ATS was released the steam workshop was added to both games. People were asking for it for years and finally these amazing developers done it. Thank you. Now applying mods is as simple as clcking the mouse button.
What i think should be improved is physics and force feedback. The physics feels too arcadey, i know developers are doing their best, but for a new game they could‘ve improved physics. Also Force feedback could use some improvements. But overall driving feel is good.
Graphics are nice and all, but not having anti-aliasing in this day seems a bit stupid huh? I know maybe it‘s because engine limitations or something, but it‘s really not my problem, AA is a must! Other than that performance is inconsistent. I'd say the game runs worse than ETS2, but it also looks more detailed.
There‘s nothing more to say, if you liked ETS2 you‘ll like this one. Just start the engine, open a beer and drive trough beautiful American scenery.

This review covers Supreme Commander and Supreme Commander Forged Alliance. Get both!
One of the greatest RTS games of all time.
If you like commanding hundreds of sea, air, and land units please read on.
Don't let the low hours on Steam trick you. Eight of my friends and I bought this game on CD years ago. We would reoutinely play 6 to 8 co-op or multiplayer (free for all) games on LAN before the Internet speeds really got fast. I've got at least 1000 hours in this game with all the weekend LAN parties hosted at a bachelor pad.
This game ruined my RTS experience by introducing or near perfecting some techniques.
1. Virtually unlimited queueing of orders (patrol, move, etcetera). I've never hit a limit. I would reckon that I have had at least 100 orders queued without any issue to tens of different unit groups.
2. Large scale battles. Each side can have hundreds of units (we've had 8 sides in one large battle).
3. Mouse zoom in/out. I can't explain in words the many ways this feature is plain useful and should be the standard in RTS games. You can zoom into a low level (one unit) and out to see the entire map and units are then represented as particular icons (easily identifiable). You can issue any command or select any unit from low to high level zooms. It's plain awesome.
4. True faction faction and unit differences. Big difference between tier 1, 2, 3, and experiental units.
5. Interesting upgrade paths for commander with multiple paths (Builder, fighter, stealth, etc).
6. Short cut keys to do same thing as mouse.
7. Four factions that look, feel, and really behave different.
8. True land, sea (above and below), and air units.
9. Transports (air or sea) with fantastic transport queueing/ferry options.
10. Graphics look great, even for an old game.
11. Replayability (different campaigns as different factions, co-op, multiplayer, maps)
12. Experimental units.
13. Game balance. Almost every unit has a counterpart. Want to nuke people? Want to build anti-nuke system?
14. Automation of engineers (patrol duty) to clear battle fields of wrecked metal or terrain.
15. Massive selection of buildings and units
16...I'm sure I'm leaving stuff out.

I have two personal stories with Crysis 1 and Crysis Warhead. First one is not really a story. It's more just a fact that Crysis 1 with Warhead was my first PC DVD retail copies ever. I was buying PlayStation 2 games before, but for PC they were first. I got them in supermarket and not in gameshop, during late 2008 with currency that doesn't exist no more (Slovak Crown) and during times when inflation basically didn't exist over here in my country, where only games and movies had prices of the Western World. To give you comparision, so you can imagine that - range of game prices used to be from 300SK as cheapest to 1999SK new ones. For 300SK you could easily have full varied food for weeks, even for a month.
Second one is kinda rare. I saw Crysis 1 in 2007 on maximum settings running smoothly and looking stunning. It was not on any convention or expo, it wasn't in any gaming club. It was just next house to the right from ours. My schoolmate knew the guy that lived there, and he just told us that his older brother wants my schoolmate to go visit him (well, I was lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ so I went with him also, uninvited, and before I saw that tropical island on the max settings I ate all of their fries with ketchup :D) And then I saw it.
Well, enough of childhood sentiment, let's get straight into the Warhead. Released year later after first Crysis,
In terms of graphics, game runs smoother, so I believe optimalization was done a little bit better. I had problems with the sound to be honest, cracked speakers, sound cut off, but when I used headphones, sound was working correctly, so it was error on my part.
While Crysis 1 will last you above 8 hours, also it depends on how you play it, and if you enjoy it, if you using slow approach, it can go up to 10 hours or so, with Warhead you will be done within 5/6 hours. I have feeling that some parts even outside caves might feel like a corridor, but almost every is just up on your approach. Also, infiltrating last airfield was super easy, and you could easily reach the container in stealth without notice. Yes, on hardest diff.

Brilliant game, best described as a mix of dungeon crawling and puzzling.
Its basically about "solving" small dungeons, not bigger than screen size, by succesfully optimzing the game mechanics (rules, spells, character abilities, environment). And as simple as that sounds: dont plan every of your moves carefully, and you will fail. Be prepared for a tough mental challenge if you choose to play this game, in which the depth has no limits...
Concerning the graphics, dont let you fool by its simpleness- there is an AMAZING amount of content behind it: a lenghty campaign, random generated dungeons, optional puzzles, tutorials, achievements, (upgradeable) buildings, unlocks (races, classes), quests...
I played for 30 hours now, am still discovering new ways to optimize my play, and still have tons of stuff to do!
On the negative side, the game suffers from a lack of final polish (refinemen and comfort):
Some descriptions and tooltips are lacking, few are even wrong, which leads to several bad experiences and losses, until you have learned the game properly. Be prepared to play all tutorials and use the Wiki in order to really understand this game.
Additionaly, the balance is lacking, and thats the only
bad thing i could say about this game. Some monsters and gods are (in relation) stronger than others, and since dungeons are randomly generated, frustration is a part of this game.
It goes as far, that some challenges and dungeons are not always beatable, as a certain constellation is necessary to succeed, and thats the point where it hurts.
In the end, some will love this game, while others will hate it.
Patient people with a preference for mentally demanding, turn based games will find hundreds of hours of enjoyment in this game, while the casual and/or action gamer might get frustrated by the learning curve, the slow pace and/or the randomness.
For me, this was one of the

I am someone who loves the more challenging and strategic games out there such as FTL and the Banner Saga. Even though Desktop Dungeons are both these things, I am going to tell you why you should not purchase this game (even at sale). Desktop Dungeons is a game that exhibits a little of roguelike quality into a strategy game that is mainly about killing the boss for each "dungeon." You start off with availability to one class and one race and slowly progess by upgrading your town to obtain more classes/races/items/bonuses/etc.. The progression in Desktop Dungeons is fine. The game never forces you to use the same class or race at any prolonged period of time. Because of this, the game is entertaing for a couple of hours as you discover all the ways to utilize your classes/races abilities to give you the best shot at defeating the boss at the end. However, for me, the fun stopped pretty quickly after you unlock the grunt of the different loadouts you can have when entering a dungeon. The reason why it stopped being fun was because in order to beat the level you have to use the bonuses that each race/class has effectively. Thus, when you use a class/race you never deviate from the approach that gives that class/race its edge. Therefore, after you unlock the basic classes, it feels as though there not much deviance from the game to keep the dungeon runs refreshing.
The Last couple of hours I played consisted of me logging on to play a dungeon run or two, and then logging off because I felt bored. Since I have stopped playing this game though, I did not experience what the rest of the game had to offer. It is possible that the runs got more interesting, but to me it was not worth the time to go through it, or the money i spent to buy it (while it was on sale).
Before I end this review, I do want to share some positive aspects of the game because there were good implements of the game that kept me interested for awhile.
-Game has a sense of humor and keeps the game in a light mood even though it is difficult.
-There are puzzles in the game which put you in a situation in which there is one method that will make you successful.
-If you want to be tested to the limits, these are great
-The game explains everything very well and there was nothing that terribly confused me when playing
-Game does take good planning to be successful. You cannot simply just click everything to death.
Overall I would have to give the game a 6.5/10.
I encourage you to look at the other reviews for there are things that I left out about the game. Also, make sure to watch the video on the store page, for that is what the general gameplay of the game looks like. Lastly, just make an informed decision before you hastily bought it like I had.

For this review, I will also be reviewing Crysis 1.
Nothing makes you feel old like realizing this game is 10 years old. It still holds up as well in terms of gameplay and graphics. I loved the level of customization the player has in terms of mission accomplishment and fighting the enemy with a stardard assortment of weapons. Planning and executing a plan felt rewarding if it payed off, like sneaking into a military base without a single enemy noticing, or going prone in a rice-field to ambush an enemy platoon.
The few issues I had with it were its' physics. Overall they were good but sometimes my character would die instantly just by touching a crate very slightly or even throwing an object, which can be very iritating. The vehicle combat is clunky, and often I find myself more interested in blowing up vehicles than driving them. The enemy A.I is smart for the most part, but often I will see them pushing themselves against a wall like Kim-Jun Ill ordered them into time-out.
Warhead itself is a good stand-alone expansion, being able to play as the great British Psycho we all know and love from the series. The level designs were done well and some of the vehicle combat was improved. Though it may be great campaign, don't expect much in terms of a couple new weapons and vehicles.
Overall, the graphics hold up even after 10 years, and the camplay is just as good as I remember it.
I give Crysis 1 a 9/10, and Crysis Warhead a 8.5/10
