This game absolutely BLEEDS atmosphere. It is a fantastic contribution to the cyberpunk genre, which I think it's plain to see, is seeing a resurgence. It's also pretty obvious how much inspiration it took from anime of the 80s, like Akira. Well, Akira, Ghost In The Shell, Alien, etc..All of it coming together to form a very beautiful baby, indeed. The kind of baby where you genuinely go "Aww, look at that" without thinking "I mean..It's a baby. They all look the same." Now, I suppose you're wondering to yourself "Hey, this is like a cyberpunk Hotline Miami". Stop right there. Just stop. Gaming journalism CONSISTENTLY writes articles saying "CHECK OUT THIS INCREDIBLE DARK SOULS-TYPE GAME", or "This game has rogue-like elements like FTL". And it's ridiculous.
Ruiner is..As best as I can describe, a twin shooter that is very difficult, and incredibly fast paced. I've honestly haven't experienced such fast paced gameplay since I played Doom. It also has the elements of your typical "bullet-hell" game, but it gives you a plethora of tools at your disposal like dashing, deflecting bullets, super-charged melee strikes, etc to make sure you're not riddled with bullets every three seconds..As well as many fun weapons like a giant flamethrower or freeze cannon. The soundtrack is amazing and it wants to pull you into this beautiful and bleak world where your brain is taken on a joyride, like a character in Ghost In The Shell. My favorite part, however, are the visuals..The style..The grime. The neon. The game does atmosphere well.
My only gripe, which hasn't prevented me from enjoying Ruiner, is that the weapons don't have much "oomph" to them..Which is a shame, considering the weapon variety. I haven't finished it yet, because I chose the hard difficulty, but some people report finishing it in 10 hours? That's kind of a bummer. Only because I do not want to stop living in this world. I really hope Reikon Games adds different modes or expansions.

Owlboy gave me an emotional ride I won't soon forget.
From Otus' first struggles until the very end, I felt for the characters on a deep level, and I cherished every tear I shed watching them fight on. This game just wouldn't stop growing on me, and I think I feel a bout of fanart coming on!
I'll admit, the controls took some getting used to. It's not really a criticism though; I get a little tired of the same control scheme every time. I've played a lot of platformers, and they're one of my favorite kinds of games, but sometimes I need something fresh, and this game gave me a few challenges I wasn't expecting!
Reading through some of the other comments, maybe I need to admit that Owlboy is not a perfect game, if there ever even was one. But, I don't think it needs to be to get my stamp of approval. I don't believe this game was meant to be a fine-tuned action platformer with super-tight controls and speed-running potential. Maybe I can't say for sure what this game was 'meant to be,' but if I could make a recommendation? Put on something comfy, silence or ignore some of your social media for an hour or so (please try to ignore your Steam friends blowing up your chat with cries of "HOOT," yes, I know it's hard), and take your time with Owlboy. Break it up into a few sessions of play and follow the story, smell the roses, bump into the occasional secret room and look for hidden dialog scenes between the characters.
And as for the pricetag? It's shameful that games keep having their prices dragged down just because another game may have sold for cheaper. Taking it easy on your wallet is good, but don't forget to support people who pour their energy into making beautiful things. I'd gladly pay $25 for this game, but if you catch it on sale, then treat yourself to a fun, easy-going platformer that won't fail to make you smile.

Are people so wowed by pixel art that, even in a world where Ori and the Blind Forest exists, this game receives such praise? I could barely stand to play this game for an hour. I think I never understood what people meant when they said "the controls are clunky" because I had never played a game with bad controls until Owlboy. In Ori, the mere act of jumping around is delightful. And Ori's levels are designed so that basic navigation is satisfying, not trivial (and certainly not frustrating). If attempting to perform mundane actions in a game routinely makes you go "that's not what I wanted my character to do!", you're playing a poorly made game.
And the game starts off with almost no direction. Nothing makes me go -_- like a game that begins with "explore your surroundings". Why did the designers think I'd want to awkwardly flop about and interact with their dull NPCs before I knew anything about the world or my place in it? A good story-driven game takes care to firmly place you in its world before assuming you'll want to explore. Even the most open-ended games know to start off with a heavy dose of linearity to hook players before letting them roam free. It takes a real amateur to spend 10 years on impressive-for-20-years-ago art while ignoring every other aspect of their game.

Now, before I get into my review of this game, let me give you a bit of advice. Play Mass Effect 1 first. You'll thank me later on in this review.
Here we go into the neat-y (yes, neat-y) gritty that is Mass Effect 2.
The game is by far my favorite of the Shepard Trilogy a.k.a. Mass Effect 1,2 and 3.
The story is by far the best, most fleshed out of the 3 games but that isn't to say the 1st and 3rd have terrible storylines.
This one was much more in-depth especially if you're like me and can spend hours reading through the data you find in your Codex and Journal.
I had more connection with the characters in this game than I did in Mass Effect 1, mainly due to the Loyalty Quests that you can do to unlock each character's "Special Abilities". The choices you make in this game have a slightly higher impact in Mass Effect 3 than the 1st had on the 2nd but don't worry. Replayability is great in this game, making it much more immersive than the 1st.

I could go on but I rather you didn't TL;DR this. :P
On to the gritty portion. Each choice you had in this game was pretty straining on me, not knowing how the outcome would affect the storyline, especially nearing the end of the main storyline. Why am I placing this on the gritty part? Because of what happened in my game. I kid you not, I nearly threw my laptop across the room near the end, thankfully I was able to restrain myself.
Some of the voice acting was a little subpar but only because I have a higher standard for games with full voice acting.
Other than that, the voice acting is phenomenal.
Sometimes the game made you feel "rushed" to complete certain missions, which I found out after, doesn't really have much of an impact on the story itself.
Overall, this is an excellent game that's worth putting a fair few hours of your life into, most particularly if you like fleshed out storyline.
Highly Recommend playing.

Here is where the game failed.

is mediocre. It is cliche, there is no depth to it. It just felt bland. The characters, while charming, have no backstory.

of the game is really annoying, too. Sometimes, a new mechanic is added, and it feels interesting. But then they drag the same thing for way too long, until it becomes *really* irritating. Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of the best RPG experiences I’ve ever had, but it has a few imperfections that could lessen the experience for others.
Having played and greatly enjoyed the first game, this sequel takes most of the ideas and dials them up to 11, which is exactly what I want out of an RPG experience.
The amount of choice involved in most scenarios is astonishing, I feel like there are at least three ways to finish the majority of quests with many of the possibilities depending on your character, finding secrets or just getting a crazy idea in your head that you want to try.
I’d go as far to say that Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the closest I’ve ever come to a D&D tabletop experience in a video game (excluding Tabletop Simulator).
If you’ve played a top-down RPG before most of the concepts will feel familiar. You create your character, recruit a party (or not if you are hardcore like that) and explore the world presented to you.
Most locations, or indeed virtually every corner of the various world areas have something interesting to do or uncover. There is so much to do and see in fact that it would be difficult, if not impossible to see it all on the first playthrough. Some of this is due to certain choices and experiences being locked to specific character races or abilities. An undead, elven thief will have a very different experience than a human mage because they will both be able to find secrets, get to areas or interact with the world in ways the other could not.
Personally I love this part of the game, it feels like something you could have a blast talking with others about at the water cooler at work, with each person having something completely different to tell. The drawback is that for players that don’t have time for more than one playthrough, some of the content will never be seen by them. This is a problem that many developers face when making branching stories, but I’m happy Larian decided to go balls deep with it.
The combat in Divinity: Original Sin 2 is something I’m torn about. On the one hand it has just as many possibilities as the quests in how you complete encounters. You can fight most enemies straight up, or find alternative, cheesy tactics to take them out such as teleporting them off ledges, setting everything (literally everything) on fire or simply charming them to become non-hostile while you beat them to a pulp.
The issue I have with the combat comes down to A.I behaviour and I believe this is due to the amount of options I just mentioned. Often times there is so much going on during a fight and so many abilities active that it seems to throw the A.I through a loop and sometimes makes them act wonky. During some fights a boss character would use a very powerful ability to wipe out the entire party in a couple turns, upon reloading they would sometimes forget about that power completely which makes the combat feel like luck of the draw.
This can be very frustrating and I believe it is the reason behind many of the complaints about difficulty. Unpredictable difficulty spikes are much more infuriating than a set difficulty level.
It’s a bit of a double edged sword in that the amount of choice for your party is great and lets you be overpowered from the get-go, but this can also work in the favour of the enemies.
There are glitches and bugs present in the game. Things like items becoming invisible, characters doing wonky poses and other minor visual irks will happen in a game of this size. There have also been reports of major, game-breaking bugs including memory leaks after the first portion of the game. I have not personally experienced these but it does seem slightly widespread.
The campaign mode includes a built in four player co-op mode for those that can get a party together. You can do any amount of players up to a full party of four and it supports drop-in co-op, so you can keep playing even if your friends are all working that night or whatever the case may be. This works very well and is a better experience as a whole when there are others to share moments with. It also makes managing the loot system easier as you will only be micro-managing one or two characters instead of a full party.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 also includes a full set of modding and construction tools for people to make their own worlds, stories and quests. There have already been some released on the Steam Workshop and it seems like upcoming user content is going to be of very high quality.
The other mode built into the game is the Game Master mode, which is oriented at D&D groups. The Game Master of the group can set up some basic story slides and locations on a map, then load into these locations and place NPCs, items, environmental effects and more on the fly while the group plays. It’s a neat idea for role-playing groups but I would like to see it expanded upon further. The GM is supposed to voice all the characters it seems, but it would be nice to be able to add dialogue options and other things to some of the NPCs in this mode.
Overall, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a wonderful experience for those that enjoy choice and role-playing. It immerses you in the world and makes it feel like an open ended sandbox while still offering solid story. Some may become frustrated with the combat as the A.I has a lot to deal with, but the majority of the game works fantastic.

Hand of Fate is a relaxing little game, which deserves to be recommended.
Firstly, what is Hand of Fate? The game is somewhat unorthodox, as it is a mixture of genre. It's a "marriage" of a card game, a dungeon crawler and an rpg. HoF is mostly a card game, where you create and use your own deck of cards. It's also a dungeon game, the style of "dungeon master". You play with the dealer, who reveals the environment before you. A map constitutes of cards and when you move onto the next card you reveal it and face the adventure or the event described on that card. When you face combat, a separate level design opens up, where you move your character freely and fight mobs. The combat system is extremely simple, which is not necessarily a bad thing.
What's absolutely fantastic about HoF is the atmosphere created. It's magestic, mysterious, with dim light and a shady dealer commenting on your actions. The game certainly has the wow factor, especially when you first launch it. In a sense, it's eye-candy. The voice acting of the dealer is very well made. The buttons and graphics are excellent, the art on the cards really impressive. The dealer's pot is awesome and that sound when he reaches for the token and closes the pot, the token then hovers in the air avaiting for you to take possession of it. Attention to details is commendable.
The game system is very very well balanced. It really is. It's simply, but well thought out. As you make choices, it's all about risk and return. It's simple, it's fun, it's relaxing.
On the downside, when you play HoF for some time you realize it is shallow. I hate to say it. You play matches with the dealer and unlock new cards. Then you need to use the cards in practice to learn them. You need to progress in that manner, unlock better equipment to deal with stronger bosses. Et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Purely repetitive. There is, sadly, nothing more than that in this game.
That doesn't change the general recommendation for this game. It's good, it's definiately worth getting and I believe you are guaranteed to enjoy it.
I've read that HoF2 is under development. Definialy a good decision. The game has a lot of potential. Let's just hope that they will bring more depth to the game.

TL;DR - There is absolutely nothing bad I can say about this game. It's a bit slow, but it fits the game. There's a lot of reading, but it fits the game - it's a "choose your own adventure" type game. It's amazing. Strongly, very strongly recommended.
Positives:
1. Atmosphere. It's really well made. It's consistent with it's themes and atmosphere, the ambient noises, dark visuals, hand drawn beautiful cards, etc etc.
2. Presentation. Amazing. The way your avatar appears on the battlefield from a card, the way each item appears from the cards... The way randomness is made - you pick a card from a shuffled deck. Great ideas, and implemented very well...
3. Variety. This game is a huge mix of CCG, RPG, Dungeon Crawler, Action Adventure, Exploration, etc etc etc... There is so much to do, there are so many different things to do, and all that is hidden so well in the cards and general gameplay mechanics...
4. Visuals. Yeah, it's not as great visually as Crysis or Witcher 3 or whatever. Still, the visual art style is fitting, consistent and overall really great looking, and that's the most important for visuals - to look good.
5. Gameplay. That is kinda covered in the variety point, but again, you are playing a choose your own Dungeon Crawling adventure CCG with RPG elements, customizable equipment and fighting style, as well as doing quest chains, mini quest chains, beating guys up, well, everything.
6. The Dealer. Oh, the dealer... I will leave it at that. The dealer.

Used to love this game, but it seems that every update brings us farther and farther away from that game that used to be fun. Used to feel fast paced and frenetic, now it just feels really slow. I mean really, really slow. In the effort of making the blocking system easier, they seem to have significantly slowed the characters' attacks and movements. This ends up meaning that two players fighting face to face will pretty much never kill one another, and it falls down to another player to attack from the side or behind. Contrast this to Mount and Blade, where the fighting is actually faster paced, and much more satisfying with a challenging and rewarding directional blocking system.
They also fixed the old system where the player had to aim directly at the target to hit them, instead having weapons damage in wide arcs. This would be fine by itself, but the addition of the ability to hurt and kill allies mean that you are far more likely to kill a friendly than an enemy. On the plus side, the community seems to have given up on getting angry at a player for teamkilling, since this is almost entirely unavoidable.
Finally, and this is a bit nitpicky, but the game is poorly optimized, especially for all the more graphical fidelity it offers. I've got a 4 GB video card, and it hovers around 60 fps (no V-sync). All in all, I'd have recommended this game in a heartbeat 2 years ago, but today I have to say: Don't buy it.

Questionable level design and awkward shooting. Shadow Warrior remake (by the same studio) is essentially the same game but polished. Consider that game instead; this one I cannot recommend.
NOTE: I always play games on the hardest available difficulty level.
PROS:
-Cool voice acting
NEUTRALS:
-The "all in one" weapon is functionally the same as multiple weapons that simply share ammo.
-There are 2 weapon types (ammo and energy) which each have 5 subtypes to them. Unfortunately, the 5 subtypes are literally identical between the two weapons....major missed opportunity and lazy design.
CONS:
-Some enemies simply stand there trading damage with you regardless of what weapon you hit them with or where you shoot them. This becomes especially problematic in areas against several waves of enemies as you may end up in a situation where you simply don't have enough health to kill the next wave of enemies no matter how you play it.

Is it polished? No. Does play well? Not really. Does all of the challenge come from the darkness being so obnoxiously in-your-face that you're not quite sure where you are? Kinda.
Would I still recommend DreadOut? Yeah alright. Sure.
This is a PS2 game in spirit, that would've been lost to time before the magical garbage world of now. A bargain bin pickup that you spend an evening with and decide that, while it's not perfect by any stretch, it's somewhat enjoyable and does some interesting stuff, then you see a couple years later and think "Hey, it's that game" with a half-cocked smile.
This is that, and there's no bargain bin bigger than Steam.
It's hard to make a case for recommending DreadOut because there's really not much that it does well. The enemies are varied, unique in design and patterns, and tend to show up once. The first "act" has some nice level intricacy, the second has a bag of interesting moments. When the music decides to play, it's nice too, from the folk music to the contemporary rock.
If that sounds weak, yeah. Most of the good aspects are those second-half interesting moments and first-half moments of "oh this is very close to being good."
Unlike most games that have the habit of opening up as you come to grips with the mechanics, DreadOut starts off with some explorative elements and then immediately clams up, withdrawing into a shell of scripted sequences. The two "Acts" are night and day, the shift in development couldn't be more blaring if it tried.
A weird situation. I want to say that the game is more fun in the open section out of principle, but there's half a dozen encounters and the rest is just wandering around completely pitch-black areas. But yeah, the darkness. It hurts to look at. I can count two situations where it's used well, and the rest of the time it's just pain.
Pitch-black and wide open with a sight distance of "no" or pitch-black, enclosed and wholly repetitive. Pick your poison.
Lamp or two wouldn't have hurt. I know dark is usually viewed as scary, but none of those old games were ever really that dark. Some were grey. At the very least your torch actually worked. Wasn't just a suggestion of a torch that lit up nearby walls while you otherwise ran blind.
Most of the interesting moments are in the scripted second half, even with the scripted sections themselves are just weird and not that fun. That sentence itself should tell you how weird this situation is.
So to fight all the spooky ghosts, you've got the fairly mediocre mechanics of weaponized selfies and running away.
You look through your camera, point and click and hope that you've got the whole hitbox in your line-of-sight. It's not exactly precise, and the hardest enemy in the game is the one with the dumb hole in its back that refuses to register. It's hard because patience. The rest of the time, simply just putting away the camera and going for an emergency jog solves your problems.
Movement is weird. Your default walking speed is more of an upright crawl, so don't put away the jogging shoes. You will run into stuff, but health regen has your back. There's no health pickups. No real ammo types either. There's some collectable stuff, but after the first half they pretty much stop with that.
I'm just confused as to what DreadOut wants to be. If it wanted to be an oldschool Fatal Frame/Resident Evil clone, why does it just stop? Why do all the NPCs just disappear in the first half and are promptly reintroduced and killed in the second? If it wanted to be some litany of weird moments and inventiveness,  why even bother with the lame scripted corridor inbetween sections? Why not marry the two ends and become a great game?
DreadOut is a meandering, confused and somewhat irritable game, just like a player wandering that first school area. And that's the weird situation.
The final product is... alright. And thus goes the most lukewarm recommendation I've ever put to paper. It doesn't so much leap the minimum bar as it does get a running start, break out into a confused dementia tapdance and then stumble over it.
Are you interested in a game that's janky, somewhat interesting and has some surface oldschool appeal? Then this is here for you. It doesn't push either the oldschool intricate half or potentially insane half nearly enough, but there's an attempt made in both and that's enough to stick out.

This is a weird one. On one hand, it has all the bad practices of social/mobile games. Food mechanic that forces you to wait every couple of battles to refill (or, of course, pay money), unlimited 100% pay to win characters, et cetera. On the other hand, it's very well done. There are tons of varying monsters, the fights are somewhat strategic and the entire monster leveling and evolving thing is well thought out. The game isn't too harsh on free players either, the food refills at bearable speed (most encounters cost 20 food, you refill 1 food per 2 minutes) and can be taken back by various means (random food drops, random food refilling item drops, completing a level without losing any character for the first time gives you 10 food back) and gems, which are the premium currency, can be earned somewhat easily, allowing a free player to use nearly every 'premium' aspect of the game, albeit rarely.
Do I recommend playing this game? Depends, if you like Pokemon-like collecting everything and training monsters and don't mind playing casually only a bit at a time, you'll probably like it.
But do I recommend supporting this game? No. If the food mechanic was taken out and the game revised without all the microtransactions, I would pay for it handsomely, because it's rather fun and interesting. But as it is it really needs to die a horrible death.

This game does well as a grand strategy game and dynasty simulator. It’s all about elevating your dynasty to high prestige and power through conquests, devious schemes and morally questionable management of heirs.
It’s not a mindless conquest game where you constantly invade whatever is nearby. Except for the pagans, they get to do that. More than half of your time is spent maintaining a stable rule over your land and vassals. The rest of your time is plotting up ways to invade and acquire more lands. This is because to invade other provinces would require Casus Belli. CBs are reasons that allow one to go to war with another ruler. Fortunately, there are many ways to acquire said CBs. Claims for lands can be inherited through betrothals and marriages under pretence of an alliance and then pushing those claims against them two generations later. Being a different religion from them is reason enough to go to war too but risky as that gives the others the same reason to attack you.
Maintaining stable rule is another kind of challenge the player has to constantly face. Rulers must maintain a favourable reputation to his vassals and manage their vassals so they won’t grow too powerful. Or else, the vassals will revolt and put someone else on your throne. A sinning arbitrary ruler can rouse a lot of rebellions if not careful. Sometimes, there are some things that you just can’t prevent and your ruler becomes an old mentally-challenged possessed homosexual lunatic. Just the flavourful element of fun in CKII that you have to deal with.
Heirs must also be carefully chosen and groomed to ensure the transition to the throne on your death goes smoothly. Or else, the vassals will revolt and put someone else on your throne. So there’s nothing wrong marrying your sister/aunt/mother/daughter to ensure your heir inherits good traits that would make them popular to your vassals. Of course, there’s the occasional premature death, you end up as a child ruler, the vassals are revolting because they don’t see you as a mature adult fit to rule them and your personal spymaster is plotting to assassinate you. But that’s just one of the many obstacles you have to face in CKII. Hopefully, the previous guy saved up enough money for you to inherit and hire mercenaries to aid your army in fighting off the rebels.
There's actually no true endgoals to win the game. You play until 1453 AD and what you do with your time until then is up to you and whatever self-imposed challenges you’ve made. Be the king of England and wish to unite Scotland and Ireland into the Britannia empire and then storm France through Normandy? Go for it. A traitorous count in the Byzantine empire with a desire to overthrow your emperor so that your dynasty may rule it instead? Nothing’s stopping you. Be a possessed lunatic, convert to heresy or a foreign faith and spread said faith through Europe by force? Very hard but possible.
The base game only lets you play as a Christian European ruler but that’s enough for a sufficient crusader king experience. Many playstyles and start locations are available to the player, even more with the DLCs, giving it solid replayability value.

Now, before I get into my review of this game, let me give you a bit of advice. Play Mass Effect 1 first. You'll thank me later on in this review.
Here we go into the neat-y (yes, neat-y) gritty that is Mass Effect 2.
The game is by far my favorite of the Shepard Trilogy a.k.a. Mass Effect 1,2 and 3.
The story is by far the best, most fleshed out of the 3 games but that isn't to say the 1st and 3rd have terrible storylines.
This one was much more in-depth especially if you're like me and can spend hours reading through the data you find in your Codex and Journal.
I had more connection with the characters in this game than I did in Mass Effect 1, mainly due to the Loyalty Quests that you can do to unlock each character's "Special Abilities". The choices you make in this game have a slightly higher impact in Mass Effect 3 than the 1st had on the 2nd but don't worry. Replayability is great in this game, making it much more immersive than the 1st.

I could go on but I rather you didn't TL;DR this. :P
On to the gritty portion. Each choice you had in this game was pretty straining on me, not knowing how the outcome would affect the storyline, especially nearing the end of the main storyline. Why am I placing this on the gritty part? Because of what happened in my game. I kid you not, I nearly threw my laptop across the room near the end, thankfully I was able to restrain myself.
Some of the voice acting was a little subpar but only because I have a higher standard for games with full voice acting.
Other than that, the voice acting is phenomenal.
Sometimes the game made you feel "rushed" to complete certain missions, which I found out after, doesn't really have much of an impact on the story itself.
Overall, this is an excellent game that's worth putting a fair few hours of your life into, most particularly if you like fleshed out storyline.
Highly Recommend playing.

TL;DR - There is absolutely nothing bad I can say about this game. It's a bit slow, but it fits the game. There's a lot of reading, but it fits the game - it's a "choose your own adventure" type game. It's amazing. Strongly, very strongly recommended.
Positives:
1. Atmosphere. It's really well made. It's consistent with it's themes and atmosphere, the ambient noises, dark visuals, hand drawn beautiful cards, etc etc.
2. Presentation. Amazing. The way your avatar appears on the battlefield from a card, the way each item appears from the cards... The way randomness is made - you pick a card from a shuffled deck. Great ideas, and implemented very well...
3. Variety. This game is a huge mix of CCG, RPG, Dungeon Crawler, Action Adventure, Exploration, etc etc etc... There is so much to do, there are so many different things to do, and all that is hidden so well in the cards and general gameplay mechanics...
4. Visuals. Yeah, it's not as great visually as Crysis or Witcher 3 or whatever. Still, the visual art style is fitting, consistent and overall really great looking, and that's the most important for visuals - to look good.
5. Gameplay. That is kinda covered in the variety point, but again, you are playing a choose your own Dungeon Crawling adventure CCG with RPG elements, customizable equipment and fighting style, as well as doing quest chains, mini quest chains, beating guys up, well, everything.
6. The Dealer. Oh, the dealer... I will leave it at that. The dealer.
???
1. The game is a bit slow, but it have a lot of reading. So it's understandable. I don't consider it a negative, but some people may dislike the slow progression speed. Some rounds can go WAY over an hour if you read every encounter..
2. There is a lot of reading. A LOT of reading. The writing is good, which helps, but still, there is a lot of text, that needs to be crunched. After a few rounds some basic cards will start repeating themselves, so repetition may become an issue. I still don't consider that a negative, but some people may not enjoy the literature aspects as much as me.

Owlboy is a touching story about overcoming disability.
It's also an amazing game. Zelda-style exploration and puzzling is combined with a touching (albeit cliche) story and beautiful pixel art to create a stunning experience that is well worth the price.
The gameplay itself is a unique system for a platformer; your only ability is flying, picking things up, and spinning into stuff.  To make up for this, you have the ability to call upon your friends to help you with their own abilities that are used both for combat and for solving puzzles. This mechanic also ties wonderfully into the narrative arc and themes of the game, and really increases your attachment to these characters.
Outside of the critical path, there are many secrets and collectibles to be found, yielding the player cute cosmetic items, touching story moments, and useful upgrades.
The game's sotry is well paced and engaging.  The game takes the "silent protagonist" trope and ties it into the narrative, helping create one of many personal conflicts that make this game's story so emotionally charged.
If you love story-driven platformer/puzzle games, I'd highly recommend you give this game a chance.

The art was beyond beautiful (I can't stress this enough), but I play games for the gameplay first and foremost, which was disappointingly average.  It was a relatively simple stick shooter with very simple puzzle elements thrown in sporadically.  I also found the story to be rather predictable and boring (Yes, I did find the secret area's with more exposition, but the exposition offered could be inferrred easily from the core story, so they really didn't add anything).  One major problem I had with the story was the fact that the story would have played out the exact same way if the protagonist, Otus, had been absent.  In my opinion, any story where the protagonist's actions have absolutely no effect on the overall story needs to seriously consider making a different character the protagonist (or make the protagonist an observer or scholar, not someone trying to change things).  I know I'm coming across extremely negatively on here, but I did have an enjoyable time with my first 3-4 hours of the game.  The next 4-5 were a bit of a repetitve slog, but I wanted to see what all the hype surrounding the story was about (as mentioned earlier, I was disappointed, but the gameplay was decent enough that I don't feel like it was a waste of time) The hour+ spent on that stupid cannon mini game was straight up awful, and it did feel like a massive waste of my life (Cannon's only necessary for 100%, so don't worry too much about it if you're not a completionist).  I would recommend it if it ever goes on sale for ~$8 or cheaper, just don't expect the game of the year like everyone is making it out to be.

This is a story about outcasts, people who fail and the losers. How many games, movies or IPs say such a thing but quickly you find out it isn't true.
Owlboy is different.
A touching story with humor and deeper themes (not existential angst but mature and thoughtful themes). The writing is entertaining and the characters share a motiff that I'm sure the vast majority of us can relate to (at least during certain parts of our lives).
The gameplay is fluid and offers variety depending upon the companion character you use. The main character can fly, roll and spin and mixed with the abilities added by 1 of the 3 companions you can not only fight in different ways but also solve puzzles.
In fact the game has action and platforming, in a sense, but also puzzle heavy. These puzzles aren't very difficult but works well with the games mechanics.
Bosses follow a a forumla we are familiar with where they have patterns and to reduce it to the bottom, bosses are essentially puzzles that hurt you.
The animation is simply put, really ♥♥♥♥in great. The subtlest of emotions or actions prompted more than one "ah how cute..." moments.
It doesn't reinvent the wheel but what it does is solid. The game doesn't over stay its welcome either clocking in anywhere from 7-10 hours depending upon how fast you go and if you plan on unlocking the achievements. Give or take some time depending upon player skill.
I don't want to spoil much. The story is thoughtful with a strong message at the end which is geat but honestly...the story shines on the characters. Look at the characters and you undestand the theme of people who are different. They might be losers, or shunned because they fail. This is a game that reminds us failure isn't the end.
Failure doesn't define you. I could explain for 100 pages what I mean and what I believe this game tells us, but I don't have the space nor do you have the time. That said, I bring it up just so people open up their mind to see this kind of theme so we can ponder and dwell about ourselves (i.e. Socrates the unexamined life is not worth living).
In short, I give the game a huge thumbs up but I do recommend snagging it on sale. Why?  Because I mostly recommend picking up every game on sale.

The game is hard, but fair. Any time you die, you'll realise your mistake or you'll wish you were a little luckier in finding the monsters you needed. Many of the puzzles will have you banging your head off the wall as you ponder just going online for the answers, but the game can be beaten normally.

Supreme Commander
I have to say that Supreme Commander is a very fun RTS game, which is probably the first one to ever have a unit cap of more than 200, heck, it goes up to a 1,000!
In Supreme Commander, your a commander of robotic armies of mass destruction, trying to conquer the galaxy for ultimate supremacy.
In campaign, 3 factions fight for ultimate supremacy for the galaxy, like I just said. The war has gone on for I believe over 1,000 years, making the World Wars look like small skirmishes.
Supreme Commander has a wide variety of units, and is more complicated than its sequal, Supreme Commander 2.
Although the down part is that the matches can be SUPER HUGE and possibly super long, and with the addition of possibly 200-1000 units for each player, the game can get Pretty Sl-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-ow-w-w-w...
Despite that, the game is great and fun.
Do I recommend this game?
1. If you are going to get this game alone, I recommend getting it on-sale. It's usually 80% off. (3 bucks)
2. If you get the game AND the expansion, go for it. But I also recommend getting on-sale. It's usually 5 bucks for both.
3. If you get the expansion, Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND, let me repeat...
HIGHLY HIGHLY HIGHLY RECOMMEND getting Forged Alliance Forever (FAF).
*NOTE: FAF is not compatible with the vanilla game, Supreme Commander, only Forged Alliance*
FAF is a community made for Forged Alliance so you can play matches with others online.
TL;DR I recommend this game if your an RTS fan, but get it on-sale, it's more worth it.
But I HIGHLY Recommend you get this and the expansion for the story mode and get FAF for multiplayer.

I didn't understand why there were only two weapons, nor why there was a separate command to select each. I didn't understand why i was moving from area to area, killing hordes of robots and i didn't understand why i was so bad at it...
For the next few months, Hard Reset sat in my games list, with just 1 achievement, mocking me.
Recently, I’ve been aiming for perfect games (a 100% achievement score), trying to increase my average completion rate. So with only one achievement, the time came back around to re-install Hard Reset, and try to bump my rating back up.
After it was re-installed, i had the option to continue my last save, so i clicked the resume button, and in i went. Still on the first level, i continued my desperate struggle against the machines, and again, trying to make sense of the area to area robot horde killing gameplay.
This is probably the point that changed the game for me. My next challenge was to fight one of the bigger robots (the kind that charges at you), and i hadn’t realised that i was being awarded points for destroying the enemies, as well as collecting the orange pickups. “A new upgrade is available” flashed on the screen, and having already seen an upgrade terminal, i quickly found the next one. I took a grenade launcher on the CLG Firearm.
Now i had an incentive to carry on. To become more powerful, i would have to continue, and the achievements had already started popping up in the corner. Then, i think i started to like Hard Reset, i was looking forward to getting past the next section, getting my next upgrade, and finding all of those delicious secrets.
Currently, i’m playing it through on hard mode, which involves many re-tries. Every section is a case of trial and error. You go in, get horded, die, then retry, positioning yourself in a better place, to get past the first spawn. The second and third hordes of the area, will no doubt kill you again and again. Forcing you to retry, each time, remembering where the enemies come from, and to be ready, bottlenecking them with the scenery, and using the environment to your advantage.
Hard Reset would probably describe itself as an environmental shooter, as half of the scenery is either explosive, or has electronics wired so badly that a light kick would force it to short out and electrocute everything in a 2 metre radius.
So, my advice would be, to sit it out, play the first level to the end, try not to give up immediately. I understand now, why there are only two weapons, and generally how the game is compiled together giving the player individual challenges, and i understand why i struggled at first.
The only thing i don’t understand now, is why i like this game so much.

If you've played Total Annihilation, you'll know the basics of how this game works already. And yet, this spiritual successor improves upon its unique RTS formula in almost every way possible. The price was worth it just for the single player campaigns, and I haven't even touched multiplayer yet.
There's a simple hierarchy of 4 tiers and gives you so many options in combat. Unlimited resources (in a manner of speaking) lets you do more than other RTS games would. Even though Starcraft 1 and 2 are my favourite RTS games ever, this game is very refreshing in comparison with the freedom you have. You can turtle effectively with an impenetrable base and use long range nuclear missiles or artillery battery to destroy your opponent. You can send a swarm of 200 gunships to take them out. Or use an army of Tier 3 siege bots and AA bots. And you can use aircraft, land units and naval units. Then there's the unique, experimental units which take a lot of effort to build but are very fun to watch wrecking things. And let's not forget the ability to zoom out or in to almost any degree you feel like.
The main campaigns are good and fun, even though the pacing could be a little better. I'd like to use the tier 3 siege bots, battleships and gunships a bit earlier. And you don't get to use the experimental units until halfway through the last mission- which is a little disappointing.
There are only a few things I would say are bad about the game. Compared to Starcraft, it feels a lot slower. You need air transport to get your engineers anywhere other than your main base in an acceptable time fashion. Queing orders when selecting multiple units sometimes results in them repeating builds that have already been done, wasting precious time. The campaign also has an annoying unit limit that applies to buildings as well, and there's no quick way to delete units if need be. A simple "delete" command would have been nice. Commanding armies has advanced controls but the units themselves still bump into each other and not attack as a clumped group (like Starcraft 2 handles very well). Projectiles operate in an immersive way, with bullets or missiles homing or not depending on the unit, but some units are nearly impossible to kill efficiently without transporting engineers and building defenses (tier 3 air superiority, ugh).
The graphics are very impressive considering how old the game is, and I still like zooming in to inspect all the high tech lights and power networks I construct.

Let me start off saying RUINER is not a type of game I would normally play. Twin stick shooters generally are really simple and not often too fast. Ruiner decides to throw away both of those normal twin stick gameplay styles, and creates a very fast game with lots of abilities to vary up combat.
RUINER is also made to be pretty challenging, and so far it has been. Starting out, you will most likely die a bunch until you get used to the controls/handling and flow of combat. Which speaking of, the flow of the game is generally go through a really pretty/atmospheric area and then into a combat arena, and this repeats through most of the game. Although, it did suprise me to see a hub level within the game as well as simple dialogue within it. Even with that, the level design still seems a bit lazy, and could have been fleshes out a bit more into something along the lines of exploring multiple different paths to get the means with which to open another path or area.
But besides the super satisfying combat, it also has both a phenominal atmosphere and soundtrack, some of the best I have seen in a game in a while. The dialogue itself is generally a mix of hit or miss lines (and a decent, but heavy accented voice line occasionally), which is the only really glaring issue I have seen so far. But all of the character designs are great, with the main character being one of my all time favorites nearly instantly. The helmet light images shown and silent body language he conveys during dialogue are great, and really make him pull off the silent badass character stereotype well.
Overall, I would say it is definitely worth the full price if you are willing to overlook the eh dialogue and somewhat lazy level design for a game with astoundingly fun and fast paced twitchy combat drenched in atmosphere.

Bought this on a whim, looked okay, and a friend had it, so I'z like.. why not.
Had read a bunch of comments about it being an Ark Clone, which sorta had me worried.
(Heads up, I've only done Single Player so far, waiting on Multiplayer till they fix more bugs)
Started it up, began to make my character. The moment I had completed my character creation, I knew this was nothing like Ark, It was much better.
In Ark, there is no back story, there is no reason to why you're there, and there are dinosaurs (I really don't give two poops about Dinosaurs...)
In Conan Exiles, there is a slight back story, there is more story which is laid out on notes that you pick up while exploring, and on top of all this, the premise is great, and leaves a bunch of room for your own imagination to fill the blanks, so that you can add your own taste to why you are doing what you are doing.
So far, I'm loving it, and with all the planned features, especially the city building, it cud be my fav game of 2017. If they nail the NPC life-ness in cities right, this game will be among the Top 5 Games of 2017 easily. If they screw up city building, then this game will barely make it to the Top 20 because it will leave it looking like just another Survival Builder game... (The city building portion is what I believe will make this game shine brighter then any other survival game)
Some may not think swapping out Dinosaurs for Mythological Gods and Sand; is enough to make a difference.. But I will tell ya, they are either massive dino fans, or don't like survival building games. The Mythological God aspect set in the Conan universe feels to be a perfect setting for this type of game. They are also squashing bugs up, left, and center, already been 2-3 patch releases this week.
So, if you like Survival/Crafting games, get this.
If you liked Ark, but didn't care much for Dinosaurs, or got bored after you tamed all the dinos, then get this.
If you like city builders (from and first or third person viewpoint), and mythological gods, then get this.
Edit: Also if you liked the Black and White games, then you will likely love this game.

RUINER is a little bit on the short side. I've never played a game like it and I can say I enjoyed it quite a bit. Just wish it was a little bit longer. For the price though it's worth it.
The game has some flaws. Other than the main storyline there's not much else to do. It would have been nice to have a few extra modes to kill some enemies or maybe some interesting side quests given there's a hub in the game.
The characters in the hub do give you some extra tasks to accomplish but it doesn't really move the game forward much and the game doesn't really make it clear how to go back and get some of those tasks done, or why you would want to. Most of them you accomplish in the main story anyway so it seems a little pointless. Maybe the developers ran out of time while fleshing out the hub.
Storywise, once you've finished the game there really is no reason to go back and play RUINER again, unless maybe there's a different ending that I didn't get.
The enemies are for the most part similar to each other. One of the bosses is recycled three or four times. Even though every enemy in the game gets its own introduction, they vary very little in actual gameplay mechanics. The game can be very tough but once you get a certain moveset it's easy to figure out how to cheese the game. The harder difficulty modes are definitely tougher but I didn't find them more fun, just more frustrating.
I think the developers should have foregone with the difficulty notches and instead make the first playthrough at a tough difficulty (normal) and then added a new game plus with a very tough difficulty (hard) and completely have gotten rid of easy. I think this would have not only stretched out the longetivity of the game but also provided players with a little bit more reason to go back and explore the game.
I would say the game is highly style over substance. The presentation is flawless but the game itself is lacking a bit. That being said it was a hell of a lot of fun and I enjoyed my time playing it.

I've now joined a guild (MIB, based on another steam reviewer's suggestion) and one member has taught me a lot about the game.
It's not pay to win but a premium subscription makes the game more fun (eg automatically reloads your guns, you can auto-collect loot at the end of a solo mission, 50% bonus to xp and rewards). I bought a premium sub because I see real potential in this game and so I want to support the developers.
I can see why some see it as a grind. But I'm a casual player and I'm more interested in the long term, and so I'm in no rush to level. However, this almost put me off the game when I first started, until I did the coop missions.
My main suggestion to the developers is to have a separate English server. It's frustrating when you can't understand half the players you meet!
Edit: You can now respec your attributes and skills for free until you're level 10, which is really useful.

This game is gorgeous, with unparalleled pixel art and incredible music. It's also pretty enjoyable, and I liked playing it, even if I knitpick it a lot below.
This game is very expensive for what it offers. The story is fairly short, and not in a "Leaves you wanting more kind of way", and evolves in a fairly rushed manner. You go from enemies to friends with various persons very quicky, in a way which feels pretty rushed.
For a platforming and 2D fighting game, the actual fighting mechanics are pretty bad. The main mechanic involves picking up your friends and wielding their abilities as your own. There are two problems here - the picking up mechanic, and the abilities themselves.
On the mechanic: Getting hit by enemies causes you to fly backwards, playing an animation of you falling and standing up and requiring you to go and collect your friend from wherever they fell or teleport them back into your hands, which can only be done while flying. This is very annoying, and in some boss fights can lock you into a loop of getting knocked down and not being able to fight back.
On the abilities: There are too few. You have a basic Mega Man style pea shooter, a heavy shotgun and another similar pea shooter ability which comes with kind of spiderman-style web slinging which would be more impressive if you couldn't also fly. The most fun one in combat is the shotgun, however it reloads far too slowly to feel like a viable option most of the time in combat. They also have an annoying habit of taking them away from you periodically for story reasons, which means that you don't have access to all your abilities at once until the game is closing up.
The game has a flying minigame which is just awful. It is heavily memorization dependant, and I don't believe it is possible to complete at the pace it goes without trial and error deaths at nearly every new section. It also has some weird difficulty spikes - two bosses in the lava area in particular are way harder than every other boss in the game.
The game also feels fairly uninspired in terms of area design. Cave, temple, jungle, underground lava place, icy place - it feels like a little more inspiration could have been taken. Owlboy himself is also fairly underdeveloped - he has friends, he goes places, he gets scared, he feels bummed out when he lets people down, but ultimately for the central character in a game with as much narrative as this game has. It's odd that I really have no idea why he's doing the things he's doing beyond, in a videogame sense, those things being the next thing to do.
I had a nice time playing through this beautiful game, but I didn't have much of a desire to dip back in and finish things off when I completed it. For a game that took so long to make, it's a shame that the final experience ultimately had so little sticking power.

From the moment I started playing Owlboy, it was very clear that more effort was put into Owlboy than anything I've ever made. I kinda just assumed that the game was a big hit that I just now found.

Owlboy is a coming of age story about Otus. He’s an Owl, he’s a boy, and he’s also a mute. Unlike most silent protagonists, Otus has many insecurities due to this. Just like all the NPC’s that populate the world, Otus is a true believable character.

The world matches these characters. It is well developed and a mystery of it’s own. There are tiny details everywhere, and I never thought it was boring to backtrack through. The pixel art is some of the best I’ve ever seen. I was genuinely wowed when the game booted up. Videos and screenshots don't do this game justice. Videos also don't do the soundtrack justice. They got an orchestra to perform it for ♥♥♥♥s sake.

Thematically, this game actually reminded me of Dark Souls. Both games present the world as a cold and unforgiving place, but also a beautiful one. It will knock you over and kick you while you're down. The best way to tackle it is with the help of friends and positivity.

The one place where Owlboy falls short is the gameplay. Its mediocre, at best. There were times where I couldn't bring myself to play the game for a day or two. Those moments were when the story took the game inside, where there are many stealth bits and puzzles. There was one puzzle that I had to watch a walkthrough to solve because I couldn't find the door. (It was in a low light area, and I walked past it at least 10 times.) But I feel that at least half of my problems with the gameplay are personal. I’m kinda just burnt out on video games in general, you know?

Overall, Owlboy is an amazing adventure. It deserves a lot of praise for it’s tone, artwork, soundtrack, and characters. I would highly recommend Owlboy if you enjoy story driven games where gameplay takes the backseat.

It's pretty.  It tries to do something interesting with the weapon system.  That's about all the good I can say about it.
The game mistakes "challenge" for "swarming you with several hundred tiny enemies".  Imagine HALO if The Archive had been the only part in the game.  Every single area area has tiny holes that are very obviously meant for the two tiny enemy types (walking tiny screwdriver, walking tiny chainsaw).  Attempts to create tension by having something run by just out of sight fall flat on its face and just make you groan, "goddammit not this♥♥♥♥♥♥again."  Literally every room has this happen.
The offering of choice in weapon upgrades is purely illusory; if you don't take the specific upgrade paths intended by the designers, you are hilariously incapable of dealing with anything.  -EVERYTHING- is a bullet sponge.  There is very little variety in either location or enemies, and any rare moment of uniqueness is immediately spoiled by yet another uninspired slog through a sea of tiny screwdrivers and micro-chainsaws.  Many of the enemies are supposedly maintenence/industrial robots gone haywire, but the designs for the most part make no sense for their setting.  What in the world are all these bipedal chainsaws supposed to be used for?!
Speaking of things with no use, apparently everything in the future explodes in horriffically dangerous ways with the slightest provocation.  Not only that, you are expected to make use of all these wacky exploding background bits despite initially working for the city.
The game tries desperately to invoke the difficulty of "old school" shooters almost as a badge of honor.  It fails miserably.  I can, to this day, pick up and play Doom 1 & 2 and other old shooters that Hard Reset claims to strive to be.  I really tried to give this game a chance, but it just falls flat.

Since my previous review got minused a lot, I think people didn't understand my point, as I put it in two lines. Ok, here we go, a full review.
Crysis Warhead and Crysis Wars are two separate games in one pack. While Crysis Wars focuses on 64 players high-speed mayhem, Warhead appears to be a spin-off from original Crysis game. A very sloppy spin-off. From narration, ridiculously long and boring cutscenes, to obviously badly designed parts of maps, this... game feels not like a game, but a desperate urge to squeeze a tiny bit more money from bright and proud name of Crysis Franchise, sold by EA and made by some group of part-time students instead of the team behind original Crysis. Action and combat is still the same, same AI, same enemies, same decorations placed in different order. Oh, hey, look, you can shoot akimbo smgs. Great, another useless feature on fourth, max difficulty. But the plot? Narration? Cut-scenes? I wish there weren't any, instead of that boredom.
On the other hand, Crysis Wars is an update to original multiplayer mode. It's fun, vast and deep experience, that can wipe Battlefield's♥♥♥♥♥with Maximum Power. The Wars half of that pack was the sole reason I purchased this pack. And you know what? ♥♥♥♥ Gamespy, ♥♥♥♥ EA, they discontinued so many games, that I don't want to ever buy anything from them. So here we are. We have halfassed mod, that cannot compare to original in its wildest dream, and butchered multiplayer game, which does not work out of the box, and needs community patch to run on community servers. On top of that, game does not run well on modern PCs, because for some reason steam does not download x64 binnaries, you need to google them. Is that worth any money? No. Do I recommend to purchase this pack here on steam? No. Do I recommend purchasing anything that has EA on it? You've guessed it.

Ok After 65+ hrs time to review.
I nearly didn't try this game, mainly cause of the massive amount
of neg comments about P2W and overall "fairness".I am thankful at these times i make
my own choices and not follow the "trendy" crowd looking for games to play on "easy".
Firstly, This game is NOT pay to win. There are NO weapons, armour or items in the
game to buy that you cannot get by grinding or crafting. so lets stop "crying" about P2W.
Pay to progress is more like it, I see nothing wrong with this as dev's have the right to get
paid for there efforts.... Right.
The basic concepts, (as i see them)
Firstly, i see this as a game of "sheep and wolves", You can be a sheep or a wolf, your choice.
This game is basically a "sandbox" style of game, meaning you have a lot of choices as to
what you do with your character and how you play the game.
1: The Sheep. You can "farm" resorces from monsters and refine them. you can "mine" resorces
from bots in mines and refine them. You can take these resorces back to "factorys and make nearly
anything you can buy at the shop. You can then set up as a trader and either provide vital resorces
for your clan or just be a merchant.
2:The wolf. Basically you hunt, you hunt sheep of course if they are stupid enough to wander out of
the Safe zones. Better yet you get to hunt outher wolves.
3: the hero. Tool up and become a "gladiator", fight in the arena for exp and rewards.
You may choose one of these styles of play or try to be a little of each, It is YOUR choice.
That is the cool thing about this game.
I would suggest this game is sutable for players who like an EXTREME challange to there gameplay,
Certainly not for the fainhearted, if you never max out the hardness on your games this might not
be the game for you.
Personally i think it is an exellent game that rewards thought and planning and REALLY punishes
stupidity and "rushing.
[EDIT:]
Now after over 200 hrs and nearly level 10 of 21, I can update my review.
This game is still NOT pay to win. I got where i did through normal gameplay.
I am pleased to find this game has incredable depth both in skills training and
crafting. the Gfx are nice, down to the empy brass ejected visibly into the minig
cart next to me filling it up...
After the 1.7.1.0 Patch last night, you can now travel fairly safely between the 2
main settlements. Looting in [yellow] squares has also been halved meaning they
can only nick half your stash. All this from dev's that apparently don't care about
the players concerns. Not the picture i see. You can feel the presence of the dev's
evrywhere in the game. They appear to be very active and from what i've seen in my
paltry 200hrs care a great deal about the english speaking players game experience.
Then there are the clans. As a new player you will not encounter ANY higher level
players for a long time unless you do something really stupid. There are warnings about
this built into the game so.... Some of the clans Drip menace while some, most noteably
MIB clan are very friendly and extremely helpful regading advice. These guys are solid
and you can trust them as a new player. Whilst im still a bit of a sheep, I have BIG nasty
upgraded teeth and a kevlar fleece. I will get the "wolf's clothing" one day.
My personal decision to buy a bit of gold at this stage is not because i can't win....
I just REALLY want that wolfsuit.... I do hope you find this review helpful i will update
again if needed.

Owlboy is a 2D platform-adventure game.
+ Excelent animations
+ Excelent soundtrack
+ Interesting story
+ Right amount of collectibles
+ Never gets boring
You control the owl Otus. He is a young mute owl that is learning how to perform tasks in the small village. You start your game by perfoming simple tasks but as the story goes along something unexpected occurs and that's were your adventure begins.
Otus can fly, spin and carry objects that can be thrown. However Otus cannot kill most enemies by itself. As the story you will find friends with special abilities. Otus can grab his friends to make use of their special abilities which you will have to use to continue your adventure.
Gameplay wise it is a metroid-vania style game. There are many puzzles and things to find out. Nothing too hard but neither too easy. The boss battles are entertaining as well. Some bosses have an interesting design while others not so much. The level design is mostly linear, so it is an easy to game follow. You will probably never get stuck. It's not an hard game but it still manages to be very entertaining.
Owlboy has a good mix or charming but also dark story. The flow of the story is well designed, keeping you interesting through out the entire game. There are even hidden story pieces that you can find. I have personally found everything there is to find but your milleage may vary.
The game has an excelent classical style soundtrack. Each soundtrack reflects your current location and mood. The soundtrack contributes a lot to the atmosphere of the game. The graphics seem to be hand drawn and have excelent animations. Just like with the soundtrack every map is carefully detailed and colored to reflect the current mood. It feels like a NeoGeo game but even better.
So does the game deserve the very positive reception? In my opinion yes it does. It is an excelent game recommended to anyone who likes simple metroid-vania games.

is novel in concept, if only slightly poorly executed. Just off kilter enough to make it not super enjoyable for repeated attempts. Given the nature of it being a rogue like that probably isn't the best direction to go in.
Now, it's only sort of a rogue like; it isn't really a rogue lite either.
It behaves much more like something in between. There are campaigns to go on but these essentially equate to choosing an enemy or final boss at the beginning of a dungeon and trying to get there afterward by pulling encounter cards
“
” in this regard. Albeit, with much less engineering.
You build each deck that you enter the dungeon with; the gamemaker lets call him, has his own deck and cards are drawn from each to create the dungeon itself and also provide all other aspects therein. For example: Equipment, Blessings and Curses, and Encounters among other things.
It's sort of contrived in that there is a definite progression in each dungeon regardless of the deck. One odd thing however is when building your deck you have the option to manipulate equipment cards AND encounter cards. It sort of feels like you have your hands in both pots. Due to the nature of knowing the encounter cards intimately you can use them to manipulate what the gamemaker throws at you giving you an advantage.  He even comments about this as you play occasionally.
The main problem is, the game can feel TOO formulaic. Dungeons become repetitive almost immediately as new encounter cards are earned only through earning the token attached to the encounter card by successfully completing the event of previous encounter cards. This is where the real rogue-esk feeling comes from. Not the separate campaigns. Once the token is earned it breaks open in a very slow and dopamine filled reveal animation. The cards are set up in very Mercenaries 1 sort of way wherein the suits and numbers that correlate to types of enemies and higher up more specific enemies.
On top of all that there is the real time combat-- or, as I like to think, the Card Game is the main draw and the fighting is the
injection to set it apart. Problem is, its extremely clunky. It's the Batman/Shadow of Mordor combat that depressingly has become a standard. It is functional at its very best and can feel even more cumbersome depending on what equipment/blessing/curse cards you may or may not have. Hit detection is weird, movement speed is weird, though this is highly variable due to the cards, animation is clunky and unsatisfying BUT, as I said-- the card game is the main draw. I often avoided fighting if given the option or decided to fight to make should the odds not be in my favor as it really isn't that challenging without a ton of variables stacked against you.

This game is a lot of fun, but I can only recommend with caution as it has some extremely frustrating issues.
The devs did an excellent job blending a deck-building game with Batman/Arkham style combat sequences. As you progress through the game with the starting deck, you get to unlock more cards that build up equipment, gold, stats, blessings (buffs and other bonuses), curses (debuffs and other penalites), and different story-driven encounters. This helps as you grow more powerful through the game as you play randomly generated matches from your deck (with cards added by the Dealer) and each culminating in a mini-boss fight.
A mini-boss is a stronger version of an ordinary mob with a unique and deadly uninterruptible attack that will be spammed with gusto. If you see them preparing to launch one, your only defense is to get away.
During a match you will have any number of encounters that throw you into a succeed/fail situation, a choice-making situation, a pit stop to buy/sell stuff, or a combat situation. Combat has all the basic Arkham moves: Strike, Counter, Stun, and Dodge. There's also a combo meter that improves your damage if you can keep chaining hits. If you've equipped a weapon that has a magical power it will have unlimited uses + cooldown. You can also have an artifact equipped with limited uses + cooldown (artifact vanishes after last charge is spent).
if you run out of health for any reason (damage from combat, starvation or a failure on a random event) you have to start the entire match over again, but any new unlocked cards are always added to your permanent deck. A match contains 3-5 levels made up of 6-12 randomly drawn encounter cards per level. The random layout of the cards at any level determine if you have to proceed through all of them or get to pick your path while searching for the exit to the next level. Also, you start every match with basic equipment. You
get your upgraded equipment via card draw awards or having enough money to buy an item from a shop. This means it's entirely possible to reach the end of a match and face off against the mini-boss with only starting armor/shield/weapon. There are no guarantees. You can even lose your starting items along the way from failed encounters and be forced to use light armour, a rusty axe, and/or no shield.
Despite the set-up sounding a bit tilted against you, it actually tends to balance out pretty well.
Well, most of the time. Then you get into the clunky stuff:
Unlike the Batman games, you have no camera control. Therefore in a 3D space certain maps will have blocked lines of sight due to poor camera placement -- either you won't be able to see enemies or you won't be able to see your own character. While most combat scenarios don't suffer too much from this, it can cause serious health loss when fighting large numbers, especially if a mini-boss is thrown into the mix. Imagine playing an Arkham game where a building suddenly blocks your view of the combat and only resolves if you blindly roll some direction until the camera clears the building. The same thing can happen with a ton of mobs in the foreground, so being near the back of the map is almost never a good idea. Healing in combat is tied to a handful of items and even then it's all passive (except for one weapon's magic ability) and almost never enough to make a difference. So there is no failsafe against taking hits due to camera issues -- the only rule of combat is "don't get hit".
This alone wouldn't cause me to dislike the game. In fact I was having a blast despite this. Until the final match...
Normal difficulty was already plenty challenging, but the final match of story mode where you face off against the Dealer is close to impossible without extremely good luck. (I don't even want to think about the odds at hard difficulty.)
Your only true advantages in the Dealer match are:
The disadvantages are:
The entire match leads up to the final combat against the Dealer. But you don't fight him. Instead he summons four waves of enemies each containing
mini-bosses you fought before and sometimes a few adds. You'll have at least 5 curses unless you spent money to remove some, no blessings, most likely a 10-25% health penalty, very possibly not at full health when combat starts, no healing, mostly the starting armor/shield/weapon, and possibly a useful magic weapon or artifact. And that's assuming you actually make it to the fight. If you die at any point, you have to replay the entire match.
So while normal story mode keeps raising the challenge gradually from match-to-match, in the last one the difficulty spikes drastically. The imbalance has caused the average player to either give up or spend more time on the last match than the rest of the game combined to beat it. This is the most commented topic on the game's discussion boards.
And yet, would draw cards again in Endless Mode. And looking forward to ...

I was skeptical but bought it anyway as I'm having to spend a lot of time off my feet at the moment, damn am I happy I went with it though!
In short, for the Too Long Didn't Read, it's purely a strategy game and not for the faint hearted. For those who like a brainy challenge however this game is a must, it combines many elements of strategy with a tidy interface and no dithering about. It allows and even encourages you to plan far in advance and won't interfere with these plans - as a result however when it gets hard it really doesn't mess about.
It takes a few games to get your head around it but it's very simple to pick up. The outcome of every move is predicted and even an entire fight is easy to plan beforehand with little indicators showing how many attacks it will take with the selected move to take down your opponent and how many he will need to take down you. In this way you can easily see for example that you each need three attacks so if you attack twice and then use a GETINDERE glyph to ensure your attack lands first you will win the encounter.
It has found an interesting balance for exploring a dungeon. On one hand you want to find new glyphs and stat boosts but health and mana is regained by exploring so ideally you need to utilise that first, but otherwise it is not punished.
Monsters only ever retaliate so braving the unknown is at practically zero risk. Just as long as you set right click to attack to avoid inadvertently killing yourself against a higher level monster.
If I were to have any gripes it's the lack of direction the game gives you. Not so much the Minecraft sense in "here's a world go amuse yourself" but more in that it gives you TOO much to do. I currently have about 15 quests, several requiring multiple dungeon runs to complete. Completing one will often generate two more. But monetary rewards are good incentive to upgrade your kingdom to provide more options for starting a dungeon.
Overall it's a beautiful game, a true challenge but not in the "haha I instakilled you now do the last half hour again" way. More like an elaborate chess game with increasingly complex challenges.
It's what you want Destiny to be with even more content and free to play.

So I've got over ten hours in the game now, and feel like I've got a solid idea of what Funcom is offering. Is the game buggy? Oh yes. Has it broken the game for me? Only on a couple of servers I tried out. I finally found a server that worked well for me, and I've had minimal lag and rubberbanding issues, no worse than a lot of games that have been available for much longer. The game is early access, and with that designation, particularly in the first week, comes the expectations that there will be issues. Case in point, the phantom spawing issues for crafing materials. But the devs have so far been wonderful in fast and frequent updates towards bugs and seem determined to release an optomized game.
The second reason I'll reccomend this game is that the devs seem to have a clear vision of where the game is headed. The closest game to this one I've played is ark, but they shrouded a lot of their end game goals, particularly in the beginning in mystery, and never have seemed to have a clear direction beyond adding more dinos. Now, I'll be the first to say I love ark, but I appreciate the effort that conan has already put into fleshing out the world from the start. There are ruins to explore, notes to find, different races with seperate lore, entire cities, dungeons, etc. It feels more cohesive, and it's a wonderful launching point, and I'm excited to see what they add to this.
Finally, there entry level building system is a lot better than equivalent games. It has a similiar placement mechanic as Ark, but already has rugs, tables, braziers, trophies, chairs, banners, etc, that help me immerse myself in the game and really make my base feel special to me. I'me still waiting on a dying system and maybe a paint system for walls, but I really appreciate that the game is already open to rp-ing builders.

Divinity Original Sin 2 is one of those rare games that comes along very rarely these days. In a market full of AAA cash grabs full of DLCs and microtransactions, DOS2 delivers more content then games at a higher cost point. But its not just about the quantity of content, its also about quality, and quality DOS2 has.
From the ridiculous amount of builds you can do on characters, to the addicting looting and item sets, DOS2 has me hooked. I find it fun to the point of I'm losing entire nights replaying the same beginning part over and over and still finding new ways to do things. There is so many ways to complete quests, that the replay value is astounding.
Also, the combat, while not changed too much from DOS, is just as creative as ever. Every fight players are outmatched and have to utilize creative elements of the map/abilities to come out on top.
I'm only on Act 2, so maybe this will change, but as of right now, its the best RPG I've played since Witcher 3 and highly recommend it to any fan of RPGs or Baldur's Gate style games (a more casual/modernized version of BG, granted).

A First-Person Shooter taking place in a dystopian 24th century setting where machines have taken over much of the planet and only a few scattered, human cities remain. WASD controls with mouse targeting.
There are two weapon types: a physical-based weapon for bullets, grenades and an RPG, and an energy-based weapon for plasma, electricity and laser railgun. Various alternate-weapon modes for scopes, stun and seeking rockets. Left-mouse for firing; right-mouse for alternate mode. You can also target objects in the environment to create explosions or electricity discharges that will destroy the enemies for you, but if you're too close, you'll take damage as well.
Ammo is plentiful as are healing power-ups, and the machines drop them as well. Lastly, there is a 'nano' resource that you need in order to unlock and upgrade weapons, and you can improve health, shield and recovery rates as well.
The enemies, of course, are the machines. They range from small anti-personnel devices with blades, saws and explosives, through human-sized robots using energy-blasts, rockets or brute-force ramming, up to huge, towering bosses with multiple, active weak-spots that need to be destroyed in order to take the thing down.
The saving is automatic at checkpoints and the zones between those checkpoints are pretty small, so reloading after defeat may cost you maybe five minutes of gameplay.
The graphics are good with decent explosions, discharges and flying pieces but not top-notch and no particle effects. Maxed-out, everything runs smoothly on Windows 7 with 16GB, a 990X CPU and SLI-coupled Nvidia 970's. There were no glitches, crashes, lock-ups or slow-downs.
The story that underlies the game is only partially present and things go on that don't make a lot of sense, nor does the ending resolve anything presented throughout the game, but it's enough of a shell to make the activities coherent and move the game forward.
It is a solid FPS, and mostly you'll be mowing waves of enemies down. You have to keep moving and using the environment for protection or you can easily be overwhelmed. Overall, it takes maybe 10 hours to complete a run-though, so it's a distraction for a single day, and there is some replayability though different weapon choices, as well as improving performance and finding all the scattered nano and secret areas. Nothing beyond nano is found in the secret areas, though.
Recommended.
