I really wanted to like this game.
The setting is cool, the visuals are neat, the soundtrack is solid...
But mechanically this game is a few mistakes away from being a total trash fire.
Probably my biggest gripe is that the gameplay in the trailers makes the game seem like Hotline Miami, in which you're dropped into a level & are free to dispose of enemies as you see fit when you come across them. In actuality, it's quite the other way around- you walk down some form of linear corridor before reaching a slightly more open area that you will inevitably be walled into while enemies spawn in around you & you're forced to survive them in small waves, like some kind of half-arsed top-down Killing Floor.
Past that, certain key mappings are very awkward, & they are all seemingly hard-coded so you cannot remap them to be more convenient.
Many "cover" objects/obstacles in maps are flat-out broken, allowing you/your enemies to press up to them & become completely damage-proof from one side, yet still shoot at enemies in any direction without being impeded whatsoever. I could forgive it if we were talking about thin barricades & walls, but most of the objects I'm referring to are more along the lines of solid rectangular shipping containers.
Guns are underpowered while a charged melee attack has nearly as much range, far greater & more accurate spread, & doesn't break or run out of ammo while being a one-hit-kill for most enemies; saving you from having to expose yourself long enough to put multiple shots into a gun-wielding enemy & effectively making a majority of guns useless. While I'm sure there are plenty more options that open up to the player the further they progress & upgrade their abilities, for the first few levels that's the single most effective strategy & it makes the gameplay go stale almost instantly.
In all, it could be a lot worse for the price tag, but the issues I've listed just flat-out make the game frustrating & boring to play. I can't recommend it in good conscience.

To begin with, a quick note on what Conan Exiles is. This is not a full game, but an Early access project that you sign up to test.
A test in Early Access meens that you sign up to TEST. A few of the main goals of an Early Access test is to
1: Find and report bugs, glitches, exploits etc.
2: Stresstest servers for the developers.
3: Provide constructive critisizm in regards to game content.
4: Provide feedback on how to best progress and develop further until launch etc and so on.
It is NOT about being "first" or to get an advantage over your buddies, because yes...what you test now will NOT be brought over to release day, so NO..you cannot stockpile stuff now and keep it.
Review.
My experience from day one in it´s early hours has been possitive mostly. There are indeed issues connected to a Beta test project, but it´s far better than both expected or claimed by many.
You play as an Exile. You are banished to die on a cross in the Desert with your crimes pinned to your chest. Conan emerges and cut´s you down, and from there on..you are on your own.
The features that are mostly working right now is
* Basebuilding
This is a Fallout 4 " snap and attach " build system that works very very well. You can lower and raise, tilt and angle every item you place, so you can build pretty much to your hearts content. Materials for the building proccess is spawned in as enviroment all around you in forms of trees, rocks, grass etc...and the re-spawn ratio of it is high enough so you don´t empty an area too fast and have to wait for it to come back.
* Fighting
You cannot escape it, but i´d avoid it. AI is very dodgy and overpowered from time to time. Stuns on you stacks with multiple hits, hitboxes not working properly, but in it´s foundation..it´s sort of working. It´s bringing you food as well when killing animals, or body parts if you want to go that way.
* Survival management
You need food, water and shelter. Eating and drinking etc is set by the admins in the admin tools. Consider talking to your players / Admin if you feel the settings are off and tweak it.
You will die..a lot, so don´t go full Conan mode the first you do but slow and steady and preferably in teams.
Cons of the present state.
* AI not fully working and having far too high output damage all the time + aggro range is set at max for everything.
* Crafting material amounts are as way off as i have ever seen in any game. 50 rocks and 30 sticks to make a small campfire is one example.
* Rubberbanding and floating movement here and there.
* No VOIP so far ( Or chatbubbles for that matter )
* Server browsing is a bit dodgy ( Recommend Steam server browsing instead )
All and all, i reccomend this project for testing and even in it´s present state, it´s a lot of fun and will only get better.

Be advised, this isn't a full review (mostly just me ranting about bugs and poor gameplay choices) so take this into perspective along with someone else's review.
I want to love this game. I want to embrace it's uniqueness and charm, but the details turned it sour. The game has bugs. Alot of them since it was ported to PC. Tanks get caught on parts of the environment which causes them to move slowly and can't turn unless you completely stop the tank, but by then you already used a quarter of your movement and can't  execute your plan. Soldiers shoot walls that are a foot left from where they're aiming and waste your entire action. Soldiers get more accurate when they can see an enemy and from your third person perspective, you can see a dude only slightly that your character can easily shoot from theirs, yet the targeter is finicky and even if their bullets can hit the dude, if you don't see the whole guy, they are essentially blind firing.
Things like that caused me to get easily frustrated and made me reload time after time, but there's more. The game doesn't give you many specifics and displays some strange choices. Like how you don't know the radius of mortars or grenades and that you character can only throw grenades one meter. Shraight shot explosives like their infantry anti-tank lancers and AP tank rounds have an obnoxiously large circle for their spread. The game uses two reticules for spread on a shot: one which shows the maximum spread of that weapon and a smaller one which shows whether or not you can see a target/within your maximum range. For some reason the smaller is the one that gets smaller when you can see a target and your accuracy increases. This leads to a confusing predicament of trial and error on how much more accurate your shots can be and on one shot weapons, this can be killer. The overhead map that they show you also isn't very detailed at all and you can't see if the enemy is behind a sest high wall or waist high sand bags and also whether or not that enemy is crouching or stnding (which is a big deal in this game). The list goes on: Your units can't crouch behind anything that isn't sand bags, trying to position a unit to be slightly covered by wall but still be able to shoot an enemy is a nightmare, etc, etc.
Look, the game has a great storyline and it's combination of RTS and Turn-based strategy is really cool. You will reload so that no main character gets knocked out ever, because you care that much. In case you haven't noticed, I've only played like 6 hours on this. While I can't tell you about the endgame, I can say that I already consider my buy worth it, even with all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. But I cannot in good judgement recommend this game without a lengthy warning exactly like this.

Medicore combat used pretty much for making the rest of the game feel better. It's essentially a CYOA with roguelike elements to it that expand the game more  the long you play, for the most part. Unfortunately, bad luck in this case can elongate how long it takes to even look at certain types of cards, which means if you really want to look at all the cards, you'll probably just have to grind easier difficulties to anywhere any time soon.
While the CYOA part is fun, eventually it unfortunately tends to be more boring than fun as you see the same dialogue for the same choices over and over and over, and the same dialogue over and over and over and over, and it begins to feel less like an exploration than just choosing which buffs you'd like to get and hopefully getting good rolls. If the rolling was more fun or more interesting, it would be great. If the choices felt actually varied, that would be great. If the combat and items supported the rest of the game better, that'd be great.
Unfortunately, none of that is true, and it becomes a mediocre roguelike where the main selling point is the uniqueness. Being able to influence your dungeon is kind of fun, but not nearly as much as it sounds unfortunately. Certain items are worthless or absolutely BoS, so instead of having a variety you usually just end up picking up stuff to make things better.
All in all it was a fun experience in some part, and an absolute drudge when combat took precedence over the rest of the game. Combat's only benefit is the item choices you get to make, which means bad items make the combat absolutely boring, even when difficult. Really only recommended if you like CYOA, really.

Owlboy is a beautiful game with a good soundtrack. But mechanically, it's so terrible that the rest of the experience is ruined. There are a multitude of one-hit KO areas and other areas that chain damage until you die. The game's language in conveying mechanics to the player is bad. And all of the bosses have inconsistent hitboxes relative to the owlboy.
Furthermore, the story is bland and predictable. Owlboy the character is one-dimensional, all he does is either make a happy face or sad face. Other NPCs not part of your party pretend to have personality by having a few lines of conversation. But they have nothing to do all day but mope about the main plot. They have no lives of their own, and they offer no knowledge about in-game history.
Overall, the frustration caused by the game and the bland story is not worth the graphics and music.

Great setting, cool combat, etc....love the destructible environment....but fails on so many basic design levels its disgusting.
I don't understand how these people managed to make shadow warrior a decent game because it sure doesn't show for this game.
1. God awful maneuvering, you can't quick jump/dash away from a charging enemy.  All you have is a sprint, so if you want to strafe quickly you need to turn and sprint to the left or right.
2. The scenarios are generally garbage....There are tons of explosives everywhere you'd think at some point they would say "Hey, maybe we should give our player some room to move around?",  Nope...you are always finding yourself in crowded environments full of boxes, crates, pipes, indestructible fences, etc.
I got to one boss fight so far....was the most cringeworthy thing I've seen. At no point in time do you EVER have never ending enemies spawning in an FPS.  Thats absolutely lazy design.
3. Every battle scenario is accompanied by cutting off your escape route....no running back, pacing yourself, etc.
4. At no point in the time does the game teach you what or how the guns are used. I still don't understand and I'm just guessing that you work off their armor with one gun, then plasma blast them...but consistency isn't easy to find.
5. No crouch....seriously....they added jumping but no crouch.
6. Invisible walls everywhere to the point where the enviroment is very misleading and causes you to waste tons of time trying to jump around on things.
7. Minor complaint, but the story is awkward.  You are not properly introduced to anyone or anything, its like literally jumping into the middle of a book.
8. Terrible hit and collision detection.  Those gorrilabot things will still hit you with their charge despite them never physcially colliding with you.
I'll commend them on the cutscenes, the compromise on a regenerating shield instead of health, decent voice acting, graphics, and destructible environment, and even cool combat when the game isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on you...but the general battle scenarios suck.
It gets very tiresome constantly being stuck in a crowded environment, with enemies swarming you because they seemingly pop out of nowhere.  If you are going to buy it, make sure you get it on sale.

First, let me say before hand that this is a really great game.
The Narratives and Strategy are simply superb.

However, it has several design flaws and bugs that really bugged me and ruined my experiences.
I'm going to give this a negative review until some of them get solved.
- It's too hard to keep track of ongoing Quests.
During exploration, I would encountered some Quest specific Events, without knowing that I did.
Leading me to do things that I should not have done, result in the quest became close and unsolvable.
Displaying a warning beforehand could really help.
I know that it's Player driven narrative, but I prefer to have my quests solved.
- Shovel in Fort Joy.
Even if there was a hint, I couldn't find it.
And I didn't want to bring the Dragons along just to dig things.
- Trial & Errors Dialog result
There was really little hints in the dialog that could show how the result will end up,
making me do Save&Load again&again just so that I can clear those quests.
In this kind of game, the results can be swayed by the traits of your characters.
Thus, how the Players develop their characters became a fun part of it.
But in this game, additional choices from traits do not guaranteed benefits.
As such, I do not feel that traits are fun to play with.
Please reference Shadow Run on this.
- Map & Key Object Display
It took me too much time just to clear Fort Joy,
with more than half the time spending on finding that exact thing to do in order to progress.
I went pass both the drawbridge lever and the fort tunnel, because I didn't realize they are there.
And then end up slaughtered the entire Fort before I could progress on.
- Bug - Not everyone in the party Entered Combat
If a Party Member entered combat or flee, please teleport everyone in,
instead of having to make me select and manually move them one by one.
- Bug - Party Members don't follow Player
This occurred sometimes. Party Members will just stand still and didn't follow.
Coupled with the above bug really ruined it.

90% of people complaining about the gameplay seem to lack the attention span to just sit down and learn the proper movement, shield and blinking (three things which you'll be doing the most in this) during the tutorial, which takes a whole of five minutes to grasp and a further ten to start really getting good at. There's no clunkiness, no forced mouse acceleration, or anything unreasonable or uncomfortable to get used to.
The game absolutely has issues, but they aren't major, and they certainly have nothing to do with how the character controls, you're given tools to very easily achieve that visceral combat edge where you just act without thinking and clear entire rooms of enemies. That part of it alone is extremely enjoyable, and that's of course disregarding the stunning audio-visual presentation.
If I had to point out any cons after five hours on hard with this (so, roughly, half of the game) I could only say that the inclusion of the hub area that you go back to after each mission, while packed with NPCs and some small pathways that change over the course of the game, leaves you wanting for a bit more. But that's a minor thing which I'd say borders on being a nitpick. Additionally, there's the lack of the option to rebind keys which kills some of the appeal for those who like to try out different control schemes.
Also, for those who're wondering about the length of the game, RUINER judges you after every encounter and level (ala the Shadow Warrior reboot or something like DMC/Bayonetta) and gives you an appropriate rank and a picture of the reaction of your female, hacker partner. The better the rank, the better the reaction. It's not spelled out for you, but it's obvious that the game has been designed from the ground up with the idea of constantly improving your rank and trying to ace all of the levels, which means that you'll probably be playing this for way longer than just the ten hours that the main story wraps up in.
Decide for yourself if that's worth the equivalent of 19,99 euros.

There are all the small bugs you would expect from an early access title, like being able to glitch jump over walls, mobs teleporting around randomly in online play where they run normally when playing locally, and the duping exploit they fixed in a patch recently. But when servers randomly start crashing on reboots or updates, or even when players do specific things, and when buildings randomly disappear with some regularity, IMHO the game is not stable enough to recommend it yet.
The crashing and database corruption issues were so widespread that a majority of official servers fell victim to it before they eventually shut all of them down. And being Funcom, they're not telling us what's going on with them either other than "soon" (for the last week). If you were hoping to play this on an official server, I can't recommend a purchase right now because of how they handled this situation and would suggest to give it a few months at least.

Owlboy is a charming, but not perfect game.

Visually, Owlboy is superb. That being said, I’m a sucker for for retro art styles. Characters have vibrant designs and great animation that brings them to life. Backgrounds are well constructed and are something I wish I had payed more attention to. Levels have layers upon layers of sprites that use parallax scrolling to show depth. The few moments where things slow down, letting you to take in your surroundings are serene and much appreciated.

Music fits moments well and works well with environments, creating memorable themes for memorable areas. A few pieces are genuinely stunning the first time you hear them. The sound design of sound effects for every action and enemy are unique and pairs nicely with Owlboy’s unique visuals adding to the game’s signature feel.

Owlboy’s story started out a little weak but after the game ended I found myself wanting to wikipedia lore and see if there was any planned sequel or prequel. Without giving much away, Owlboy’s setting has a lot of potential and every character is memorable and great to be around. There are plenty of serious moments and moments of levity and comedy to balance things out making this game stand out in my mind as a happy memory that seemed to go by all to fast.


While playing I got weird flashbacks to Super Mario RPG, likely due to that game also having a very signature sound, appearance, story and characters that might seem comparable to experience I had with Owlboy.
I dunno, just some strange side thoughts.


Despite the overall very positive experience I had with Owlboy, there were plenty of moments that took me out of the experience. A few general bugs here and there are all right but I did have a rather frustrating experience with a boss who freezed while on the way to their second phase forcing me to restart from the last checkpoint. Cutscenes tend to have awkward transitions with characters teleporting in and out before dialogue starts. While twiddling the thumbs sticks during cutscenes the reticle also shows up briefly, surprising me if I had been doing it unconsciously. There were also about three instances where I attempted, over and over, to do a puzzle a frustratingly unintuitive way, but that, more likely than not, was just me being a fool. In the moment, however, it did feel like I was being swindled a bit.


My one other gripe with Owlboy is that it could’ve done a lot more. I know it’s just an indie game and a game doesn’t have to be long to be good or worth your time/money, but what little there was of upgrades, allies, environments etc. had me full of ideas and wanting more to sink my teeth into.

With combat, encounters don’t change much from start to finish, even with new allies. Weapon upgrades are minimal and owlboy stays the same, besides health increases, throughout the game. Upgrades are collected through finding rings which usually appear very linearly through each area and it didn’t feel worth it to spend time going back to find secret ones just for a few small embellishments. The metroidvania-fan side of me wanted to see this idea expand but sadly it was only lightly touched on. It feels like the only thing that shows Otus’s improvement over the game is story. Not a bad idea by any means but one that could’ve been further encouraged gameplay-wise with a few upgrades to physically get the player to feel like they had gone from zero to hero.

With story, every character and new area seemed to flash by so fast that the more world shattering moments didn’t touch me as deeply as they could’ve. I felt ready to get really into the world Owlboy had put together for me. I genuinely thought the real ending of the game was gonna be, like, end of act 1 just cause I had some many little theories about where the plot could go. That sounds like a critique but I guess it just means I was enjoying the game.


Owlboy is was a blast and there is plenty more I could say about it.

As for purchasing it, I’m someone with no constant source of income, so a $25 price seems a bit steep, especially if you strictly compare how fast the time flies by. Regardless of if you have the money, add this game to your wishlist. I think if you’re at all interested, you will eventually want to play this game.

I have played this game nearly 1,000 hours on record with steam, and another few hundred of hours outside of it. I started by buying the $150 "Trailblazer" to make it into the Alpha.
When I first encountered the game it was like nothing I had ever seen before. The community was small and active enough that you really got to know who is who on the server. Guilds were much closer knit than any game I've played previously, and it really felt like you were a part of the community.
Beyond this, the game itself was beautiful. The landscapes were amazing, the world was fairly big, and there was so much to do that I almost never got bored. It was a brand new experience that shocked me at first.
As time went on the magic faded a bit, I began to rally up with fellow players complaining about 'Pay2Win' (P2W) aspects constantly being added to the game. I complained about normalizing of mounts. I complained about the ridiculously RNG gated end game. I complained about  a whole like of things. I spent more time sitting around complaining than actually playing the game. It burned me out, I psychologically convinced myself the game was not worth playing. If I honestly looked at my actions I'd realize I wasn't even trying to experience the game anymore. I was too focused on complaining.
So I quit. Then I returned, then I quit, then I returned, then I quit. I went through the same cycle over and over again. Starting again, returning to a state of bliss when playing the game, slowly becoming more and more cynical again until I quit.
Until I finally realized it was myself that was ruining the experience more than the P2W aspects I would always groan about. I disregarded the fun experiences I had while playing and only remembered the times where I was sat around doing nothing, because I had convinced myself there was nothing worth doing in a game where I would always be behind players who P2W. I realized that I did have insane amounts of fun in this game, and all it took was to play it my way, ignoring the fact I would always be behind P2W players.
If there is one thing you will need to understand in order to play this game, it is the fact that you cannot be more geared or more wealthy than the players willing to pull out their wallets 24/7. But what you can do is get a much better experience than they can. We crave rewards for our hard work, and when we work towards a goal like slowly gearing up a character, we feel a sense of accomplishment that the P2W players never will. Their enjoyment of the game is much more hollow then ours will ever be. We can train our PvP skills, increase our wealth, improve our gear, and be genuinely proud of the progress we've made all on our own.
In the end the biggest thing stopping you from enjoying this game, if you really do truly enjoy the gameplay, is yourself. You can't let others overshadow your accomplishments or happiness when playing this game, you have to really play for yourself.

I love Dungeon Keeper Gold and was excited for the release, but sadly I was rather disappointed. The game if far too buggy to recommand quite yet, and personally I preferred the style of DK1 over DK2, which obviously seems to have been the main source of inspiration.
Nevertheless, here's a list of noteworthy bugs, issues etc. I encountered while playing the campaign:
- Options. No settings for controls, especially mouse. Also the graphics options are slightly limited.
- Cursor. Its size and the animations, often make it difficult to click precisely. It's also a bit laggy at times.
- UserInterface. Most tooltips contain a lot of unformatted placeholder data. Some of the buttons etc. are a bit too bulky (Add UI scaling option?). Sometimes clicking the buttons won't register, or they're otherwise a bit unresponsive.
- Performance. Frequent lag spikes after a while, and in the bigger levels the game begins to slow down quite notably.
- AI. The minions act just plain stupid at times. Ignoring enemies right in front of them, fleeing while having plenty of health, stuck somehow unwilling to attack while in combat, imps selecting task far away when there's stuff to do right next to them, and the list going on.
- Voiceover. The periodic taunts get annoying really fast. Having a very limited number of variations and starts repeating pretty quickly.
- Pace. For whatever reason, the game seems a bit sluggish.
- Map. There is no fullscreen map and the minimap isn't really informative enough.
- Crashes. Some stability issues. Nothing recurring or gamebreaking yet.
- Glitches. Some of the 3d models get stuck on the user interface. Such as while holding a minion, dragging the cursor over the minimap.
I'll check back later and edit this review to reflect on the game's state at the time.
Next I'd like to do a little comparison for those that might deem it helpful. As said before, WftO is far closer to DK2 than DK1, what's the difference. Well I certainly can't break it all down here, but here's some things from the top of my head.
- Mana. DK Gold used gold for everything.
- Imps. In DK Gold they were unlimited, limited only by their increasing price.
- Graphical tone. DK Gold was darker, grittier and in general more sinister.
- Overall feel. With verything combined, the music, the visuals, the narration, the jokes and the gameplay, in my opinion DK Gold had far superior athmosphere.
- Language. Apart from the occasional taunt and the narrator, there was no real language. Now, for example the cultists speak and in plain english.
- Voiceover. It's great to hear a familiar voice, but it just seems too cheerful and cheesy.
- Upkeep. In DK Gold imps and traps require no upkeep.
- Statistic. Such as the mood and task of minions, was clearly modelled after DK2 rather than DK Gold. Especially the combat log in DK Gold was invaluable in making sense of the chaos. No such feature here.
- Walls. In DK Gold, fortified wall were indestructible, except by a special spell, making quick land grabbing and fortifying of key locations, an important part of the strategy. Also walls could not be recovered once dug out, forcing you to really pick and choose.
- Handling of minions. DK1 didn't add any penalty to manually moving minions around, nor was there a limit to where you can pick them up from as long as were alive and not in the enemy's custody.
These may seem like minor details, but put together they drastically affect the gameplay and the overall feel. I'm making this point, just in case you were expecting more DK1-like feel rather than the DK2 that this game currently has.
TL;DR
Do you prefer?
- DK2: Wait for patches, and buy the game.
- DK1: Wait for patches, consider carefully.

I don't recommend this game unless you really enjoy turtling.  It has good ideas, but they are poorly implemented.  Painfully slow build times on units and structures, mass fabricators destroying any need to control the map and the resources scattered across it, and incredibly powerful defenses turn this into a painful slog.  The ability to control and upgrade the commander who represents you in the game is neat at first, but they quickly become the big can which sits in the middle of its defense riddled, mass fabricator clogged base and never leaves.  Because if the commander does leave, it runs a good chance of dying and losing the match.
You play as a commander aligned with one of three factions which can build basic structures.  The factories let you get fabricators which build even better structures.  Upgrade the factories to get better fabricators for better structures and units.  You also need to balance production with your resource income, so make sure you're building mass pumps, power generators, and mass fabricators to meet your base's growing needs.
When it comes to crushing the opposition, you are given many options, and your three starting ones are land units, naval units, and air units.  At higher fabricator tiers, you can get long range artillery, stealth, experimental units, and strategic missle launchers (nukes).  Of course, all of this can be countered easily at lower cost by defenses.  In order to defeat an enemy, you need to either catch their commander while it's exposed or have an overwhelming advantage to push through their defenses.
Mass pumps provide the most mass at the lowest energy cost, but they can only be built atop mass deposits scattered across the map.  Ideally, the game would become a battle to control and defend mass pumps for a production edge over the opponent.  Sadly, mass fabricators destroy this by allowing a player to acquire all of the mass they will ever need from the comfort and safety of their own base, often at a faster pace and at less expense.
The factions are almost entirely aesthetics, with their only major differences being what experimental units they can build.  They all have the same unit classes and structures which do the same jobs.  There are small bits of fluff like "Aeon bomber does damage over (a very short) time, cybran bomber does slightly less damage over a slightly larger area, and UEF is a typical bomber with a large explosion and good damage."  But ultimately the differences are minimal.
The story is decent in each of the three races' campaigns, but the basics makes them a slow mess.  Even the first map in the campaign takes at least forty minutes to finish simply because of how long it takes to build everything and amass enough firepower to win.  And it only goes down hill from there.  Expect one to two hours for each campaign map.
These often take just as long as the campaign maps, although tech rushing (spending all of your resources on obtaining max tech units and structures as quickly as possible) can end an AI opponent quickly.  It is impossible to beat the AI at spamming mass fabricators, so be prepared for a long slog if the battle isn't ended quickly.  The AI skirmishes also seem to be buggy and occasionally crash to desktop for me, so beware.
As other reviews have stated, look at Forged Alliances if you want an active online community.  I haven't tried it, but from what I have read online, expect cheese.
This game may be worth buying on sale.  If you're really liking some of these ideas, I'd recommend Planetary Annihilation when it is on sale instead if you don't mind its lack of a story filled campaign.  It uses a large number of the same ideas in Supreme Commander, but is a better tuned experience overall.

An interesting mix of a shopkeeping simulation in a fantasy world with the added feature of being able to hire adventurers to go down into dungeons and restock your shop with newer and better items instead of buying them.
Essentially you have three parts of the game - in your shop you can move items around, or swap them with your inventory to ensure your best and most profitable items are on the shelves (you generally can't sell items not on display so choose carefully), and then wait to see who comes in the shop and see if they want anything you have on offer. If they do you will get to haggle with them to try and eek out that extra profit if you think you can, conversely they will try and haggle down the price.
In town you can meet all sorts of people - other merchants you can buy items from (haggling again, but in the opposite direction), the guild where you can craft items or also buy more stock, or the tavern and elsewhere where you can meet adventurers sometimes.
Finally there is the action RPG dungeon crawler where you can persuade adventurers you have met to risk their lives getting you more stock for your shop, this is probably the weakest part of the game as the controls aren't great, the monster variation is quite small, although there are a few reasonably well done boss fights to open up new dungeons.
Overall a great game and well worth playing, just don't expect too much from the dungeon crawling side of things, that is more of a chore than anything else. The story is fun and endearing, and it is interesting to be on the other side of things in an RPG for once.

While not a fan of space themed settings, the game is surprisingly good gameplay wise. It has an addictive gameplay with its mission based focused It is pretty linear though with the assignments being minor side tasks, scouting anomalies for some extra loot, and the rest being compromised of crew recruitment or story missions. The actual story mission is really short with 75% of it being to recruit allies to help in the fight. It would have been nice to see a lot more on the aliens and less focus on what felt like side tasks.
It could be more difficult but the play style is tactical oriented by hiding behind stuff and getting into shootouts, so there aren't many options to make it more difficult. Some of the weapons seem rather pointless with the most effective being a mix of assault rifle, sniper rifle, and heavy for the large enemies. Which allies are used doesn't feel like it mattered much, so pick some favorites. They tend to die easily by running into open areas, although you can command them to sit somewhere (though they don't seem to respond to commands always).
A large amount of time can be saved by not depleting the resources on each planet and just scout for anomalies. The million stockpiled up served no purpose. You only need maybe 500K or less. This planet scanning was the only bad part of the game and knowing this would have been great.
Personal experience score: 9/10
Story: 9/10 - Cool enough for a shooter taking place in space. A typical save the galaxy from aliens scenario
Sound: 10/10 - Sounds good, pretty much a new track for each mission
Graphics: 7.5/10 - Pretty good considering the release date. Could use more detail
Controls: 8/10 - Fine overall, but the camera turn speed even at max is far slower than other games. Would require a separate mouse sensitivity adjustment
Game Length: 9/10 - Around 40 hours with doing everything within the game

I've been following Ruiner for awhile now.  The mix between Hotline Miami and Ghost in the Shell/Akira really stuck out to me as being something unique, especially with the more refined looking gameplay mechanics.
I can safely say that the time I spent waiting for this game and the money I spent on this game was well worth it.  More than well worth it.  If you have a somewhat sick Cyberpunk fetish like me, ♥♥♥♥ing buy this you nerd.
Controls are a little odd, but combat ends up being very satisfying.  I'm playing on the hardest difficulty and it's great.  Dying is just part of the game and (like Hotline Miami) once you accept that you'll start to improve.  Each death is kind of a learning experience.  Instead of getting buttblasted, think back on what you did wrong and try again.  The powers the game gives you are pretty fun and can change combat a decent amount.  Weapons feel good, both melee and ranged.
I'm probably going to edit this review later on.  I usually don't put reviews only 2 hours in, but ♥♥♥♥ me if I don't love this game already.  I only expect to love it even more going on.
EDIT: Finished the game and my opinion definitely did not change.  This game is art.
Combat becomes even more fun as you go on with many different playstyles opening up.  I chose a slow-mo melee-centered build that let me precisely land hits with my sword and deal massive damage at the cost of huge amounts of energy.  Energy that I of course could gain back by shooting people.  It was super fun.  Bosses are still just okay design wise later on, but I feel that the versatility of the skill tree and combat makes them fun even if the design isn't perfect.
Music remains fantastic throughout the entire game with each piece that plays fitting each area perfectly and providing additional atmosphere to a game that's already DRENCHED in atmosphere with the spot-on lighting and art.
Story was good cyberpunk fun.  Had enough of the cheese, violence, and edge necessary to create a perfect Japanese-Cyberpunk feel.  Ends on a tiny cliffhanger though and I hope the story will be continued with either additional DLC or a sequel (sequel ♥♥♥♥ing please).  Characters were fun too with my personal favorite being the "Her" your hacker friend.  She's super cute and her dialogue is pretty great sometimes.
Overall this game is a very solid 9/10.  Easily my Game of the Year and I think this game offers a fun time for any Cyberpunk fan.

Where to start with this incredible game.
For starters I guess I should say I wasn’t really expecting much from this game, or any other game for that matter, in the current state of affairs that the industry is in it’s a tad bit difficult to get excited for anything, but that’s just me.
For the first 30 minutes or so, I was frankly disappointed nonetheless, and that was simply because the game spends 30 to 40 minutes explaining you how a lot of it works.
In reality it’s fairly simple until you began combining a lot of your abilities, getting into the flow of the combat, and finally being able to get into the “rhythm” of the game, once you push through that first barrier of sloppiness, and tediousness the game opens up both figuratively, as well as literally, there’s a hub area in the game in which you’re literally in only two times during the campaign, in it you can find a grand cast of particular, and very strange characters that go into toe with the whole dystopian insanity of the universe of the game, reminds me of those good ol’Ranxerox comics from back in the late 70’s, the whole idea it’s that the future has somehow been overrun by A.I. and now, “it”, simply is part of people’s life’s, throw a bit of violence, modern cultural references into the mix, and generally a massive amount of inspiration from Hotline Miami.
And you pretty much have Ruiner.
The inspiration from Hotline Miami can be seen not only in the isometric point of view that follows the character around, or in the fact that the character’s design it’s similar to the one from Hotline Miami’s main protagonist, Jacket.
The narrative it’s also similar, with the main character being driven on one side for a personal motive in a thorough, and brutal search for a lost family member, while at the same time searching for “Boss” a character which it’s controlling the main protagonist through the entire game through a “hack” implanted in his brain.
The true brilliance from the game, for me, comes directly from the incredibly well design, and “fast-paced” gameplay mechanics, and systems that the game allows the “user” to play with.
Everything in combat flows incredibly well, it’s not at all like Hotline Miami, in which every hit it’s a life, or death decision, instead the game focuses in delivering a similar style of feel to the one of say… Something like the newest DOOM.
You constantly find yourself getting weapons, that no matter how many upgrades you set to increase de ammo capacity, or duration/resistance of both guns, as well as melee weapons, you’ll keep trading for new ones, simply because each and every single weapon in the game feels amazing, and while not every single one of them is particularly effective in all cases, fundamentally, the vast majority of them, to not say, all of them, feel great.
There are traditional ones like the ones you’ve come to expect, shotguns, machineguns, pistols, but then out of nowhere the game starts getting progressively, and gradually, more and more bizarre with the type of weapons that you obtain, after a while you’ll get a shotgun that can ricochet bullets of walls, only to then have them explode when touching an enemy, in other cases you’ll find yourself using a “ray” gun that shoots out a “laser beam” that turns your enemies into skeletons, then you can find stuff like katana’s that freeze your enemies or simply allow you to turn them into amorphic pieces of meat, and blood.
It’s amazing, and each time you get into a firefight everything turns into a quick, and exhilarating match.
After a while you’ll get karma which serves as your experience, level up enough times with it and you’ll find yourself getting karma points as well as abilities that you can then unlock and use to improve both core “powers” as well as add other types of “specialties” to your character.
Some are as simple as delivering a crate that contains a powerful weapon, while others can regenerate health in exchange for energy, the “currency” that the game uses to measure, and limit, your power consumption.
Some other abilities however simply are always activated, I believe this are the one’s that are referred to as “passive abilities” in rogue like games, or games in general.
Abilities such as general upgrades to your health, and energy capacity, or alternatively to your ability to dodge, one of the game’s “main” mechanic’s is the ability to dodge through enemy attacks while at the same time reducing the damage that you take while receiving damage in the middle of a dodge.
This serves an almost “tele transportation” of some kind that allows you to travel from one place to the next in the blink of an eye.
Soon after upgrading this ability, I found myself not only dodging in fights, but even while just traversing the map.
It’s pretty satisfying.
Probably the problems that I have with the game land in the game’s misused potential in actually using the hub world, and the universe of the game, for something a bit more promising, I’m pleased with what we got, but I just wish in a way the game would have had a bit more content for me to “sink my teeth in” I just left Ruiner with a bit of a necessity for more, you can replay the levels with all the abilities that you’ve previously unlocked, but so far it doesn’t seem as if you can get more.
Something that also kills some aspects of the game for me.
Having to use a trainer to unlock every ability for my second playthrough just to experiment, and feel what it’s like to have everything unlocked and be a “power machine” right from the start, just doesn’t sit right to me.
Thank god that in pc you can do stuff like that, but I really would’ve wished for a new game plus mode, I’m sick an tired of seeing so many games that put such an incredible degree of emphasis in it’s upgrades, and powers, and skills, only to then lock you out of all of them after playing the game for the first time.
Besides that, Ruiner it’s an incredible game, in regards to the difficulty which I personally don’t like to address that much in any of my reviews/critiques, mainly because it’s a bit of a delicate subject (just like many in this industry) but the game wasn’t hard at all.
I finished the game in 4 hours but I played the game on easy (I play all my games that way, go ahead, Judge me!) and I really enjoyed it, you can change the difficulty at any time as well, so if you’re feeling up to some more challenge you can “bump” up that all the way to the hardest level of difficulty, and vice-versa.
Overall, I’m really satisfied with my purchase and I’m planning to simply play the game once again with everything unlocked, just to see what else you can do with such a “smooth” gameplay style.

Valkyria Chronicles is truly a one-of-a-kind game, bringing a gorgeous graphical style, fun gameplay and a heart-wrenching story, and although it suffers from a few issues, still shines as one of the best games I have yet to play.
The story itself is cleverly written, and throughout the game's roughly 60-hour campaign, will make you laugh, cry and cheer in victory as you conquer another level. The voice acting, although sounding slightly weak in English, does not dampen the enjoyment at all. Gameplay is solid, smooth and addicting, being a mixture of a third-person shooter and a tactical RPG, however the controls can sometimes lead to awkward maneuvering and the enemy AI can occasionally be silly. The grameplay stays fresh throughout the entire game and doesn't become stale or repetitive, thanks to the large variety of weapon upgrades and customization, and the ability to change your squad roster, letting you create and devise your own strategies without becoming overwhelmingly difficult.
I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys strategic rpg's, and I also feel that the gameplay is exciting and immersive enough to be great fun for everyone.

I won't be recommending this game. The reason is that WASD doesn't move you around relative to YOUR perspective but rather to the environments. Imagine the upper edge of your screen is north. Holding down W would make your character move north-east.
This might not sound so bad but from my experience, it really is. It's not easy to get used to and having weird, wonky controls in a game with hard and punishing gameplay is a bad mix.
Combine that with how the isometric perspective makes it difficult to land shots, when using ranged weapons that aren't shotguns, and you'll end up fighting the controls more than the enemies, as a few other reviewers have already pointed out.
If you want an example of how to do it right, take a look at the Hotline Miami games, which RUINER seems to be often compared to.
The HM games have a top-down perspective where holding W will take you north, just like you would expect.
Reliably hitting enemies with ranged weapons that aren't shotguns is also not a problem, since the top-down perspective eliminates any ambiguity as to wether your bullets are going to hit the target or travel juuuust behind their back, leaving them unharmed.
In the end it's up to you to judge wether you believe the controls won't really be a problem for you or if thats a deal breaker or wether a guy with less than 2 hours of play time can accurately judge a games controls.
I just know that personally, if the controls were different, maybe if the gameplay had a bit more variety, i would definitely want to play more, because this game is incredibly stylish, has a great atmosphere, great characters (from the few i saw) and has a nice cyberpunk feel to it.

This is my first review on a game and I must say the game is special enough to make a lazy person like myself to write a review. Okay, here are some pros and cons I picked up while playing this.
Pros:
+ Unique characters, all your squad members have different stats, likings and potentials so choose carefully when deploying them on battlefields
+ There are 5 classes of foot soldiers with different roles and you are free to deploy all the people of one same class or one of each to a battle.
+ Gameplay is unique, a combination between Third person shooting and Turn-based (where you use command points to decide which characters to act, then after spending the CP you control that character in the 3rd person)
+ Can issue orders using CP during battles to create even more strategies
+ Various battlefield types/maps
+ Can upgrade units and weapons between battles, it also is carried on to the DLC.
+ Suitable for different gamestyles (sneaky or full-on massacre) as well as gamers (A-rank goers or casual time-killing)
+ Can save at anytime between the Command Points
+ AI is decent enough though not persistent SOMETIMES, e.g: anti-tank units know to run behind your tank to destroy it quickly but I have seen scouts charge directly towards shocktroopers.
+ Gamepads work perfectly, I tried it with my joystick and Xbox Controller.
+ DLCs included! YAY, less money spent but more content!
Cons:
-  The dodging mechanics and the random factors (for triggering potentials or missing a target when shooting) can be frustrating at time, especially when you go for A-rank
-  No Auto-save means if you forgot to save and screw up, then well, err, rage quit?
-  There are some good moments in the story but overall it has many plot holes (typical for anime type of story)
-  Some class is more OP than the others, e.g: scouts with defensive boost & Demolition boost can clean up officers + heavy tanks in like 1 turn.
-  Units can only hide behind sandbags to get less damge, so yeah, no full/half covers like in Xcom or Company of Heroes (but they are made up with the orders or the dodging mechnics, which make your units 90% bullet proof!)
-  No tutorials, so you better learn quick in the first few easy missions or be prepared to get rekt later.
Overall, this game is worth buying if you don't mind the plot holes, anime-ish art style (though imo it's pretty) as it offers hours of unique gameplay as well as satisfying feelings, either when you see your snipers head-shot the enemy or get a surprise A-rank.

I really, really, really wanted to give this game a thumbs up. It takes inspiration from lots of horror games (especially Fatal Frame) and has a good many easter eggs to series like Silent Hill and Resident Evil in it but I just can't bring myself to recommend it. The best part of playing a game is that a game can take you out of reality for a time. This game makes you very, very aware that you are playing a game approximately every two minutes. There's some nice scares occasionally and some decent atmosphere here but bugs, glitches, and just plain bad storytelling/writing break the immersion constantly.
***SPOILERS OF A SORT LIE AHEAD***
A classmate friend turns into a sort of "zombie-like" creature at one point and then something happens to him. But the game gave us absolutely no reason to care about this person at all so you feel nothing when it happens. If they had set up the game differently, you may have grown to care or become personally invested in the story but the story that is here is bare-bones at best and gives us no reason to want to save anyone.
Your soul motivation is to get the heck out of this place and away from these ghosts that are running around everywhere.
Cheap deaths abound! This is my main gripe with the game actually. There were many, many, many times when I'd have the camera out, take the picture completely on queue and then get hit anyway and the monster takes no damage whatsoever. There were at least five different fights that resulted in cheap deaths, after which, you have to walk down this extremely long corridor to get back to playing the game which completely broke all immersion for me. Many times after having just booted the game up, then dying inexplicably again, the death screen would tell me I'd been playing too long and to take a break. I don't need the game telling me to take a break after five minutes of play time. It's like the developers don't even want you to keep playing the game at all. Deaths are fine when you learn from them and adapt as a player. There was no learning here. There was nothing I had done wrong or could have done better. The games mechanics just really are not sharp at all.
The AI is terrible and the camera glitches through walls and turns the game into first person sometimes for just a few seconds. I'm fairly certain that almost all of the framerate drops I experienced (which were considerable) were because of the camera glitching through the environment. One of the enemies in the dining hall, I never even saw. I'm still not even sure how I beat it because I never once saw it. I just randomly flashed the camera until it was over.
Are there some good things about Dreadout? Absolutely. There were several scares that caught me completely off guard and one time I jumped about two feet in the air. These moments were not nearly as often as I'd hoped and for the most part, this game was a buggy mess. It oozes atmosphere and then ruins it almost immediately.
I don't write reviews often and I'm fairly certain this is my first negative review but I just can't give a pass to this game. I love games like this, I want there to be more of them - I just wish this particular game was as good as it should have been. There is a lot here to get excited about but unfortunately, it mostly just disappoints. Perhaps the DLC is better. I'm wary of buying it at this point though. I believe another year of development would have done this title a great service as it could have been great.

10/10 - Pixelart platforming perfection.
I will probably be playing through the game a second time for these four reasons:
1. The art is incredible, absolutely fantastic, and I wish more time was spent in each of the areas as it was obvious that the team has spent an enormous amount of effort in making every new area look as good as possible (excellent and memorable aesthetics for each area, a huge number of unique assets for the areas, and loads of detail in many scenes).
2. The soundtrack is great, far better than I would have expected in a $25 game.
3. The story is very well done, although I do feel like I need to qualify this point a little. The actual events which take place in the game, including the character development and plot twists, are perfectly executed, and there are some real emotional moments in there. The backstory for the world is fairly straightforward, but the big revelation is told in a confusing manner and only really reveals half the story (the rest is hidden behind a postgame sidequest).
4. The characters! I know I basically covered this in point 3, but they definitely deserve their own point as well. These characters felt real, with real problems and motivations, and they (for 99% of the time) stayed true to themselves and didn't feel like they were acting some way just to advance the plot. I love that they don't each have convoluted backstories which take ages to tell; they just are who they are and everything you need to know about them is told through the dialogue of the game itself, with a couple of nice but small character focused scenes.
Things I was not a huge fan of:
- No map. The game works fine in the main story without one as it is super well designed in terms of directing you to the next location, the problem lies in returning to old areas (if you missed something) in which case you will struggle a fair amount, I never needed a detailed map, but a basic one would have been nice, or even if there were more signposts and they were actually useful.
- The gunner selection buttons/wheel. It just never got to the point of being intuitive, choosing the right gunner at the right moment was sometimes a struggle.
- The pitch dark sections. Definitely could have cut out a few of these sections.
- The game ended but I want to stay in this world with these characters for much longer. It's just such a fantastic game, I would be hyped to play a prequel or sequel but from what I've heard about the team and their long development cycle, it doesn't seem likely.

What can I say?  I love Total Annihilation, Planetary Annihilation is an abomination, and I wanted a TA-like RTS.
is how you do it, a gem by Gas Powered Games and THQ (now replaced with Nordic, who moved the game to Steamworks servers).  It's got a great artstyle, three exceptional campaigns with intriguing and well-executed stories, and a small but dedicated and polite online community.
There's literally nothing I can say against this game.  Total Annihilation, Age of Empires II, and Red Alert II remain my all-time favorite RTS games, but this game has completely replaced TA on that list.  It crushed my nostalgic love for the game with full 3D visuals and fantastic gameplay, an accomplishment that should never be overlooked.
Whereas most RTS's fall apart in the singleplayer department, this game's campaigns stand the test of time with quality writing and great missions.  While some lack proper multiplayer-ing, this game's netcode gets the job done well, now under the eternal watch of Gaben and the Steamworks serverlist
in the clouds.  It's also very compatible with modern hardware and runs well on a variety of systems.  There's plenty of lasting value with three campaigns and factions who all play differently from each other and an active multiplayer scene.
I seriously can't recommend this game enough, it's one of the best RTS's I've ever had the pleasure of trying.  Ever.  Simply put, you need to buy this and Forged Alliances as soon as you can.  You're doing a disservice to yourself by not giving it a chance.

If you like DK1 and 2, you should definitely give this a go. It sticks extremely close to the formula.
Pros:
* Feels like other DK's
* Similar DK humour (Lol'd at Chunders)
* Overall just really good!
Cons:
* Subtitle text is too small and is pure white meaning it's hard to read on bright backgrounds
* All of the buildings have the word 'Prop' in them. e.g. Instead of 'Barracks' it's called 'Prop Barracks'...not sure why.
* When you look at buildings/creatures and what they're doing it's not very specific whereas in DK2 it was very specific about what was going on so you could micromanage very well.
EDIT: I've been playing it for a bit longer since my initial review.
The game is too buggy. Here are a list I've encountered so far (The good aspects of the game still stand, but it's also buggy).
- Frequently getting 'Insufficient mana' when trying to cast a spell even if my mana is full.
- Imps ignore the boundaries set by the flag to stop them possessing land
- I played a skirmish game and nothing happened. No units came at all.
- Several graphical glitches
- The sidebar buttons are wayyy too small to hit with a cursor. The whole UI is a bit finnicky, I'm not sure if it's just too small?
- Placeholder variables in the actual game content. This is unacceptable. Things like 'Identified : False' and 'Team:null' are very lazy placeholders which they need to remove asap. I also encountered one where a beast was going for food and it's status was something along the lines of 'Going to HUNGER_VAR at slaughterpen'...not cool.
- When you possess a creature, the movement feels janky and jerky.
I think more than anything, they need to seriously review their code. By the sounds of it, they're rushing it and introducing more bugs.
Still, If you like DK (not donkey kong) and don't mind a few annoyances, I'd recommend it.

Valkyria Chronicles is truly a one-of-a-kind game, bringing a gorgeous graphical style, fun gameplay and a heart-wrenching story, and although it suffers from a few issues, still shines as one of the best games I have yet to play.
The story itself is cleverly written, and throughout the game's roughly 60-hour campaign, will make you laugh, cry and cheer in victory as you conquer another level. The voice acting, although sounding slightly weak in English, does not dampen the enjoyment at all. Gameplay is solid, smooth and addicting, being a mixture of a third-person shooter and a tactical RPG, however the controls can sometimes lead to awkward maneuvering and the enemy AI can occasionally be silly. The grameplay stays fresh throughout the entire game and doesn't become stale or repetitive, thanks to the large variety of weapon upgrades and customization, and the ability to change your squad roster, letting you create and devise your own strategies without becoming overwhelmingly difficult.
I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys strategic rpg's, and I also feel that the gameplay is exciting and immersive enough to be great fun for everyone.

This is my first review on a game and I must say the game is special enough to make a lazy person like myself to write a review. Okay, here are some pros and cons I picked up while playing this.
Pros:
+ Unique characters, all your squad members have different stats, likings and potentials so choose carefully when deploying them on battlefields
+ There are 5 classes of foot soldiers with different roles and you are free to deploy all the people of one same class or one of each to a battle.
+ Gameplay is unique, a combination between Third person shooting and Turn-based (where you use command points to decide which characters to act, then after spending the CP you control that character in the 3rd person)
+ Can issue orders using CP during battles to create even more strategies
+ Various battlefield types/maps
+ Can upgrade units and weapons between battles, it also is carried on to the DLC.
+ Suitable for different gamestyles (sneaky or full-on massacre) as well as gamers (A-rank goers or casual time-killing)
+ Can save at anytime between the Command Points
+ AI is decent enough though not persistent SOMETIMES, e.g: anti-tank units know to run behind your tank to destroy it quickly but I have seen scouts charge directly towards shocktroopers.
+ Gamepads work perfectly, I tried it with my joystick and Xbox Controller.
+ DLCs included! YAY, less money spent but more content!
Cons:
-  The dodging mechanics and the random factors (for triggering potentials or missing a target when shooting) can be frustrating at time, especially when you go for A-rank
-  No Auto-save means if you forgot to save and screw up, then well, err, rage quit?
-  There are some good moments in the story but overall it has many plot holes (typical for anime type of story)
-  Some class is more OP than the others, e.g: scouts with defensive boost & Demolition boost can clean up officers + heavy tanks in like 1 turn.
-  Units can only hide behind sandbags to get less damge, so yeah, no full/half covers like in Xcom or Company of Heroes (but they are made up with the orders or the dodging mechnics, which make your units 90% bullet proof!)
-  No tutorials, so you better learn quick in the first few easy missions or be prepared to get rekt later.
Overall, this game is worth buying if you don't mind the plot holes, anime-ish art style (though imo it's pretty) as it offers hours of unique gameplay as well as satisfying feelings, either when you see your snipers head-shot the enemy or get a surprise A-rank.

I have a few grudges with Valkyria Chronicles however. First off: The presentation is really weak. And by that I don't mean the graphics, I mean the way your missions are presented. That just feels tedious. I like the characters, but I want to play a game. For example: Once you get to the army academy you are told to explore the academy, and from now on you can go to the armory, R&D etc. But why do I have to do that via menu? Why can't I really explore the academy by walking through it?
Also, going into this with Fire Emblem in mind I was hoping that I would bond with all of my characters. I don't, because while they do have unique names, looks and properties, they don't really have a personality and you just recruit them via menu. You learn nothing about them.
Now I listed a lot of negative things, but I really do enjoy this game. If you like FFT and Fire Emblem and you want a game with a different type of world, this is for you. It is just not perfect.

It's usually a great sign when a game has gotten me engaged for this many hours and this game is really no exception, the story welp it's supposed to make a direct reference to World War II but with magical elements and typical RPG tropes. Dive into the role of commander Welkin Gunther and Squad 7 while you fight to stop the ambitions of an evil empire.
The presentation of it is just absolutely gorgeous and clever with it taking the format of a compiled book going about the legendary exploits of Squad number 7 and  their day by day lives, you get to see every moment of joy, sadness, agony, every argument and even get a glimpse on the bad guys lives too, the game focuses a lot on certain characters but they are usually well written and are generally likeable, seriously it manages to convey that feeling of urgency to keep everyone alive that Fire Emblem was usually well known for but in its own way(more on that in the next few lines).
Gameplay wise this is a strategy game, however rather than just moving all  your units and go combat happy you get a limited amount of movements per turn, meaning you gotta select a few units and think carefully about your moves, unlike Fire Emblem there's no perma death unless one of your troops gets shot down and then an enemy comes around to finish them off. Also depending on how well you do on missions you can collect better rewards, which in turn help better train your troops, upgrade their weapons and other stuff. There are a few classes, each with their own sets of advantages and disadvantages that you really have to get the grasp on quickly in order to succeed, but the game for the most part is lenient... EMPHASIS on "For The Most Part" cus if you're unprepared then prepare to get your nuts(or ovaries) squeezed till you beg for mercy, also most maps are well thought out but of course a few times I felt it went nuts and suddendly just decided to ramp up the difficulty out of nowhere, I'm looking at you ♥♥♥♥ing huge tank mission.
All in all if you ask me wether you should buy this game then my answer is ♥♥♥♥ YES, I personally give it an 8.5/10

Bite Size Review - Mass Effect 2
The Good:
+Good Characters
+Graphics Look Great
+Optimization (Runs really well on my PC)
+Fast Loading Times
+Lots of Quests
+Story was Good
+Good pace to the game
The Bad:
-Simplified RPG Elements compared to First Game
-Mini Games for Hacking or Unlocking things gets old fast (why not just have it be a skill?)
-Resource gathering in required to get upgrades, and is also a boring and very tedious minigame
-No Mako (Don't get me wrong, the mako wasn't great, but in this game it's all chest high walls all the time now)
-Ammo is limited (in the first game, there was a lore reason why you had unlimited ammo for your laser guns, now you run out pretty easily and have to switch)
-Less skills for everyone to experiment with
-Nerfed Biotics (so unless the enemy is down to their health you can't pick up people anymore, which makes it kind of useless)
-Removed loot from the game, now all upgrades are found in parts of the levels in the game just lying in containers
The Verdict:
It took awhile but I finally beat this game. I enjoyed it for the most part, and it did correct a lot of things that I did not like about Mass Effect 1. Crysis is the original game.
Crysis Warhead is this game.
Crysis Wars is defunct multiplayer.
Crysis 2 is the proper sequel but plays very differently than the above.
Crysis 3 (and 4) are on "Origin" not Steam.
Background:
See my earlier review for Crysis the original.  This time you play as Psycho during the sections spent apart from Nomad (the player) in the original game.  This game looks the same but runs smoother on modern cards (GTX 970) and all but the hardest difficulty now use auto ammo pickup which is so much better.  Vehicles start in third person.  The UI isn't really improved from the first, though it tries.  There are definitely more weapons to play with but it doesn't change much.  This game is very clearly the polished version of Crysis original.  Way more fairly long cut scenes.
Gameplay:
Another first person shooter in a mostly open world.  This one is more linear but has less sections that you get stuck working through and hate.
You start off with all suit powers (hold middle click and drag in a direction):
- default is armor which includes faster health regen
- then cloak is overpowered (drains power as you move and drops if you attack) yet fails at melee range.
- strength makes you jump higher and absorb more falling damage
- speed makes you run faster, really fast for a short time
Good to know:
Fairly unforgiving again (seriously consider playing on easy and you will still die a bunch).
Falling damage can kill (use strength to minimize).
You can breath underwater.
There's also a separate night vision that drains a separate power meter.
Armored vehicles require explosives to destroy.
You can only carry a few kinds of weapons at a time, but can swap on the fly and recall a previous weapon's ammo pool (which is the only reason to swap late game).
Health is regenerative but the meter is on screen.  No achievements or collectibles, just secondary objectives with no impact aside from providing another ammo cache.  Relatively short compared to today's titles (7-10 hours).
Verdict:
Worth $5.  You could skip the original to play this one in a pinch, but it explains a lot more of the story (maybe watch YouTube videos of the original).  But play 1 first if you're planning to.  Read my review of 2 before you buy it, it's a very different game.

This game is a Strong standalone expansion to the original Crysis game which was released on September 2008. Warhead follows a plot that happens during the original story of the first game and explains lots of things from the first game! You follow a Tough as Nails englishman Nicknamed "Pyscho" and he has a very interesting story to tell, although a short one!
Warhead features a  clearly optimized version of the Cry Engine 2, with 720p graphics (good for the time.) with lots of settings to choose from. Lots of Mods are also avaliable for people who want current graphics and extra options. (Shooting chickens instead of bullets, infinite energy and custom enemy skins are my favourites.)
Determined players will have arange of options with graphics and tweaks if they look hard enough. But the games look itself should be enough for the average player. It is something that it prides itself on, although it is less desirable nowadays.
The Idea for the story is very well done! The Fact that is isnt a prequel nor sequel really shows the sophistication in the story. It happens exactly on the side of the main plot. Which is rare to see nowadays! It basically deepens the overall story that you play through.
The Length is obviousy going to be shorter. But at 3-4 hours, it isnt what players really deserved here. No matter how deep the plot might be, the raw length has to be at least 6-10 hours. Although since this tells a side story, it can be let off.
In terms of new addition to gameplay from the first game, not much has really changed. Although there is a new weapon which is amazing (Dual SMG's). Overall Combat and Gunplay hasnt changed, this is mainly because it was released very close after crysis 1 so the devs didnt feel like they needed to add anything. Also since it happens at the same time, itd have to make sense on that scale.
Thats enoguh Briefing, heres the Pros and Cons:
+ Better optimized to run with more Builds/systems than Crysis 1 since it is newer
+ Beautiful graphics and scenery, much like the first game which provided a Lush wide area for most of the game.
+ Good choice of main character with a mysterious past and a great personality. Tough Guy persona, with some english stereotypes and friendly rivalry with his squad mates.
+ Large Levels with some side objectives at times. (Go to x to extract intel is a common one.)
+ Intense firefights and action packed gameplay often possible with multiple approaches (eg: Stealth and Action), much like the far cry series!
+ Nice straight forward story that features Crucial aspects of the Lingshen Island Incident.
The Ending is great as well! It basically ties the two games together like a neat knot at the end.
+Stealth and All guns blazing approaches add some Replayability, especially in the harder difficulties.
+The Vehicles included (Same as the first game) make travering the map much faster! You wont want to rely on your suit for travel, unfortuntely.
+Explosions and other visual effects are very well done (Always reminds me of Far cry).. Basically all PC's can run this game now, and thats awesome! The only things that stop people from getting it are the price and a basic interest in FPS games.
+Once again, the pacing is reminiscent of an Action Movies such a Rambo and even some general parts from Independance day!
Thats a really dumbed down verison of the summary. If you even remotely liked any of that. Please Get this!
+Did i mention shooting
- As it is a standalone game that has to live in the first games shadow, it is going to be very short (3-5 hours max played at the highest difficulty=Delta) Although length of playthrough will obviously depend on the players approach (Completionist, speedrunner, Stealth-focused, etc.)
- Unimpressive voice acting from some of the cast, some scenes could have had a stronger impact if the voice acting was more convincing!
- Most levels have a much smaller map-area than Crysis 1, i guess size does matter..
- Not much long term replayability since it is very linear and theres no unlockables or a big reward for finishing it either.

Overall I really enoyed this game, but i had to pay attention to cutscenes or i would miss lots of important info! Flashbacks were a great addition as well, but having a Main Boss to pursue throughout the game was definetely my favourite Section. If you liked the first game and want to continue the ride, Definetely get this! However if you like the information that i provided about it and want to understand the whole story, start from the beginning. I makes a big difference. I played the original alpha freeware version of DD years and years ago, and I loved it. The strategy and careful planning, combined with many choices in which the player must weigh opportunity costs, appealed to me as someone who enjoys both puzzle games and roguelikes. This market version, however, is a bit disappointing.
Almost immediately I noticed that the quick and seamless gameplay of the original has been replaced with lots of flashy graphics and animations, most of which are far too long and prevent input until they have finished playing. While these animations are relatively short, the slowness becomes noticeable the longer you play. Those little microseconds add up. Yes, this is a turn-based game in which you cafrefully think through your decisions, but let's be honest-- the first 2/3 of every session is pretty much blasting through the weak monsters or exploring in hopes of finding the right item with the RNG. The real magic of the original was in the last 1/3, when things start to get tense and you really have to plan ahead. So it's frustrating when this version forces you to slow down at the part that deserves to be sped through.  These slow animations carry over to the menus as well, and it's  exacerbated by the dull, mediocre banter which tries too hard to be funny, and which takes forever to skip.
And of course, there are tutorial levels you can't skip. Really? Really?? This is 2014 and you are still making unskippable tutorial levels?
Perhaps the newest feature of this version is the introduction of the gold-to-buy-buildings (which then unlock new heroes or give small upgrades) system. There was absolutely zero reason to add this, because they do the exact same thing as simply completing the challenges in the original alpha. At least in the alpha, you didn't have to click through twelve haphazardly scattered menus-- once you beat the dungeon, the next level or hero was unlocked automatically. Seriously, why even add this?
The artwork is polished, but the style is just ugly. There is really nothing redeeming about it. While the alpha had simple, easily distinguishable 16-bit pixel graphics, this version tries way too hard to be detailed. It's like staring into those gross Ren & Stimpy  or Spongebob Squarepants closeups for hours on end! No one wants to do that. The music is also unmemorable-- it sounds like generic stock medieval fantasy music, versus the ominous, synthy fanfare of the original; it says a lot when a 5 second introductory song is more appealing than an entire soundtrack.
Lastly, I want to talk about how QCF Design has trolled other indie developers. Back when DD was still in development, League of Epic Heroes, a game by a single dev on iOS, got a cease and desist and was threatened with a lawsuit for "copying" the gameplay concept. At the time, LoEH was actually superior to both the DD alpha and the beta. The main developer of DD complained about intellectual property, but honestly, who hasn't copied game concepts before? Every action RPG since Diablo has been a rip-off of it, but we understand that they are still original in their own right. League of Epic Heroes had a unique inventory system, original graphics and assets, and only borrowed the gameplay of DD. The developer said it was unfair that someone else was releasing a Desktop Dungeons-like game on iOS before he could, but that's what you get for taking four years to finish something! Now there is still no iOS port of DD, and of course, there are two Android games which are like DD but very conspicuously, they have not been removed-- sounds to me like the dev just wanted to cut out the competition.
So: A release that is actually worse than the original, and an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ developer who can't handle market competition. If you want a fun, puzzle dungeon crawler, save yourself the money and go get the original freeware version of this instead.
