This review may contain spoilers.
DreadOut is a game developed by Digital Happines that immerses the player in a dark, nightmarish, foreign town riddled with utterly terrifying paranormal entities. You play as Linda, a high-school girl with a keen insight for the supernatural. Equipped only with her cellphone, you must navigate through an abandoned school, a ghost town and a haunted mansion in search of your friends and an escape from this nightmare that started off as a cultural school road trip.The puzzle-solving aspects of the game are also solved by using your camera to find hidden objects through intricate perspectives and weird angles.  What I also enjoyed about this game is its unique lore. You must use your smartphone to see, capture and kill the enemies of this town that are based on pagan Indonesian folklore -- a definite ode to the classic Fatal Frame series.
The inclusion of Indonesian horror lore as the main scare factor of DreadOut serves as an effective strategy to instill a deep feeling of being a stranger in a foreign country. The player will notice common tropes of the horror genre, but thanks to a highly stylistic Indonesian influence in the game it becomes new and interesting. The Indonesian folklore doesn’t stop at just the text – the soundtrack of DreadOut riddle with jarring, startling and disorienting tracks that truly create a terrifying atmosphere and intimidate the player. This game excels in world building by creating an ominous and hypnotizing sound design that crawls under your skin and has you at the edge of your seat. It manages to do so by combining flute-type instruments such as
, a 12-string guitar known as the
and wooden percussion instruments such as the
.
The plot is impressive considering its length. As Linda you piece together the reason you are in hell by collecting posters, journal entries, and odd tokens that reveal some bits of information behind the town’s troubled past. Moreover,  there are moments in the game where you interact with friends who have been possessed. The game occasionally asks the player to make a choice through dialogue.The cinematic style of these episodes also heightens the whole experience. Character building is aplenty, albeit in a decidely primal and evil manner. You get to see characters that were introduced at the beginning as the stereotypical high-school bunch turn their bodies into abnormal contraptions or pursue you in demonic rage. All in all, DreadOut is a worthy entry into a promising franchise that manages to stand tall on its own merits while still paying homage to classics of the genre like Fatal Frame and Silent Hill.

Hand of Fate has some interesting ideas going for it and I’m excited for the sequel, but after playing and finishing the first entry in the series, I’d feel more comfortable with saying that waiting for the second game would the better move. This game has some rough edges around it that make me extremely cautious when recommending it.
The combat for this game is a painfully average Batman clone with not much to distinguish itself from similar games. The animations, the muffled enemy sounds, the uninspired graphics, and the somewhat simple gameplay that doesn’t change much make me loathe the combat sections whenever they come up. The light ragdolling is a little bit of fun and some of the more advanced weapons can at least make the screen light up with weapon abilities, but overall, combat is not the real draw of the game despite there being so much of it.
Now if we’re talking about drawing cards, that’s a different matter entirely. I enjoyed the Dealer’s voice acting and sound quality which is important since he’s the only character that talks. He also makes some smart remarks every now and then depending on which cards are being played for a second time. The artwork for the all the cards also stood out and looked great. The table itself also has some little touches here and there. It’s kind of strange that this part of the game looks so much better than the combat areas you’re thrown into when those encounters come up.
Navigating the game board is just a matter of selecting a card that has yet to be turned over. What makes you decide on which card to reveal next depends on the situation you’re in and the conditions of the current run. There are a dozen bosses that each have their own negative special effects that are generally tied to their theme. Sometimes it’s gold loss or maybe everyone moves faster and deals more damage. You have to keep track of health, gold and food (0 food means health damage per turn) when making your way through the unturned cards. Occasionally, you just have to take an early exit if backtracking to reveal the other cards could mean a cost of 7 food. The worst thing about navigation is hitting the same merchant card multiple times and having to select “Pass it by.” after continuing past the initial screen. It’s a bit of an annoying time waster.
Every card, except shops and bosses, presents a situation that you can resolve through making choices. There’s usually a correct and obvious answer that’ll reap the most benefits, but many of them will have RNG dictate your success or failure. The RNG presents four cards that will have a combination of Huge Success, Success, Failure, and Huge Failure. Sometimes, if you’re watching carefully, you can spot where the card you want is going. Other times, it’s really up to chance and you just have to hope that the Dealer is merciful.
Defeating any of the 12 bosses and successfully handling the various situations that certain cards throw at you reward you with even more and higher quality cards. You can gain cards that let you complete the next step in a quest, new events, start different combat encounters, better reward cards (gold and food), and different pieces of equipment to wear. By the end of the game, you’re not going to be wearing standard gear anymore since you’ll have cards that help you easily gain powerful equipment fairly early in a run.
Finally, one other negative aspect of the game was the final battle which turned out to be a somewhat long and very boring boss rush in a boss run with very difficult conditions. There are blessings and curses in the game, but for this final run, imagine being unable to gain additional blessings and only able to gain curses on each new floor. It’s not an impossible feat, but sometimes the combination of curses can become extremely frustrating. For example, all my food converted into gold and I ate five gold per move. After going down to a new floor, I gained another curse that made me lose gold depending on my remaining health. Yuck. I was disappointed with how the final fight turned out and hoped for more in a game that provided a mostly positive experience for me.
Hand of Fate’s card gameplay and narration are the only parts I truly like. It’s a somewhat rough experience and the RNG aspect can sometimes be harsh towards the end. There is an Apprentice difficulty if you need a helping hand, but I think that you’d honestly be just fine with skipping this title completely and waiting for HoF2. It might be a better realized experience that’s building upon the first’s foundation which is what any good sequel should do.

I'm always a fan of small groups of people coming together to make a memorable game. And Owlboy is certainly memorable, a little messy at times, but memorable.
For the first two or three hours, Owlboy is pretty straightforward. You play as Otus, a mute boy chosen by the great leaders of the world The Owls to take up the mantle and be the local village's future protector and overseer. He isn't very good at this however and his teacher's strict teaching style only stresses him into some self-esteem issues. Then the game begins and everything goes steadily from bad to worse as no matter what you do, you screw up. You do your best, but you still screw up. But you know there's a direction to it, that eventually everyone's going to see that you're not a screw up. You're going to show those other Owls that you're great. Then the second half of the game happens, the developers pick you up and put you somewhere else. It still fits the story, but suddenly the characters largely vanish and instead you're sticking with the few in your main party. Owlboy is very focused in what it wants to do and gives various characters just enough time to be memorable but not enough to feel very important. They feel truly alive and full of personality, so I wish I could do more with them or see them more. In this I feel like Owlboy was made up of two halves, both sides equally amazing, but the middle part doesn't completely fit together with both ends. Almost like something is missing. But Owlboy had a long development cycle and I feel like at some point the developers came to the realization that things just have to go forward.
As I said, however, Owlboy is structured well, many plot threads are tied up nicely while others are left as vague yet defined enough that you can draw your own conclusions. The plot can be rather predictable at times (*cough*theentirefinaldungeon*coughcough*) but there's more to find out if you explore around the world. Really Owlboy does a great job when you can explore and find little subtle things, typically in how Otus reacts to things. Like he knows something, but can only really say it through his emotions rather than speech. These points aren't often, but are enough to feel substancial at least.
Owlboy also has a pretty great amount of game to it too. Most of the game you'll be switching between two characters, one with a fast shooting weak weapon and another with a slower recharging strong short range weapon. This allows for great fluid combat - firing off the strong shot and then poking at other foes with the rapid fire between recharges - along with various puzzles that are challenging enough on their own without being "too much". Owlboy's difficulty spikes in the middle and falls off soon after sadly. Still, it's a memorable enough game that offers freedom yet remains rather linear in its execution.
So yeah, all and all Owlboy is a solid title. It's very pretty and poetic at the right times, but still feels flimsy in places. Character is its strongest asset, and yet it doesn't really capitalize fully upon it. If anything I feel like it just makes up for the game's shortcomings. Not enough for me to give it anything more that a solid recommendation, which is still a good thing all things considered.

Hand of Fate is an innovative roguelike RPG card game with heavy top down slasher gameplay. You play a game of chance and adventure against the Master in a similar fashion to Dungeons & Dragons with hands on combat.
Hand of Fate is visually beautiful. There are a plethora of maps, equipment, enemies, and, of course, the cards. The small maps are all unique and different from the last and are very nice to look at. Whether you're in a forest or arena, the backgrounds are all detailed and very well done. Every card in the game as it's own card art as well as it's in game model. The animations are done quite nicely and the Master's animations are top notch.
Hand of Fate is both luck-based as well as skill-based. Luck is a big portion of the game as it is in Dungeons & Dragons. Whether you succeed or fail an event boils down to whether you pull a successful card or a failure which can have positive outcomes or disastrous complications. Before every "campaign", you can choose the deck; what equipment cards there are, randomised events, and enemies that all have set required amounts to keep the game both challenging and interesting.
After every campaign you complete, you are rewarded with new cards, events, and bosses. Every campaign can completely change the next, for better or for worse. Completing a campaign isn't completely rainbows and sunshine. Everytime you beat the Master, he bites back; with increased difficulty in monsters, and bosses. The amount of replay value in Hand of Fate is astonishing. There is never a dull moment. The first campaign can very well be your last because of how your deck varies with the increasing amount of cards added to the pool.
The music in Hand of Fate as well as the voice acting are amazingly well done. The voice actor for the Master is both mysterious and beckoning. To whoever did the voice acting; well done to you, good sir. The Master narrates the story that unfolds before your eyes with lulling words that pull you in the more you play. He taunts you but also supports you. Is he a villain, anti-villain, or a silent hero?
The music is also very well done. The genre in music varies but keeps you on your feet with adventurous music pushing you forward toward the final boss and the sweet rewards that await you. As I previously mentioned, the music varies through the levels and campaigns and never bores you with endless looping tracks. The atmosphere the music creates is like no other and can help create impact with the narration of the Master.
The story for Hand of Fate is rich and interesting. Every campaign has a different story that seemingly interconnect. Every boss has a different backstory that the Master pulls you into. Some bosses have stories that make you pitiful for the hardships they went through, while other backstories make you want to drive a stake through the heart of the scoundrel. The Master is simply that. A master. He crafted all the stories, cards, equipement, and events himself. He is the storywriter of the whole game and everything that happens is from his creation. Hand of Fate is a game about a game that the Master has invited you into.
I don't have much to complain about Hand of Fate, but if I were to complain about any one thing, it would have to be the controls. The combat is fluent only after you really get a hang of the controls. The first few hostile encounters I engaged in had me beaten and battered as I tried to figure out how to really dodge and roll around the enemies before they attacked. Combat against ranged enemies is also a little bit awkward but once you get used to the contant running and rolling, you'll be good to go.
Hand of Fate is one of my favourite games so far. It's fun, and that's what I look for in a game. It drew me in from in the first 20 minutes and just like that; I'm hooked. I want to defeat the Master and come out on top of his elaborate story. I believe that everyone should try out Hand of Fate, even for a couple minutes.

I got this with the Humble Freedom Bundle. I started off really enjoying this game, and was digging the deck building aspect, with the combat system as a nice bonus. However, the longer the game went on the less I was enjoying it. I played the King of Skulls level, 75% of the way through the game, about a dozen times before I just gave up in frustration.
The roguelike elements of the game are just not balanced correctly for the difficulty and RNG, and I found myself trapped in a loop where I needed to draw better weapon & equipment cards to be able to reliably beat the random combat encounters, but instead drawing encounters that would either inevitably kill me or were designed in such a way (hello White Minotaur, you miserably stupid pile of dung) that getting through them was a total slog.
In particular, I had multiple encounters where I drew two bosses from earlier levels, which with the starting gear were basically unkillable when paired with a dozen mooks. The ranged attacks in particular start to happen so often that you can't block or counter all attacks, ensuring you will (eventually) take so much damage the level becomes unbeatable.
When coupled with the fact that the game insists on showing you every card flipping animation, store loading animation and level setup animation, I just couldn't take it anymore.
Also, the RNG is just a royal, unfun pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Theoretically you can follow the cards when there is a single shuffle, but on multiple shuffles it just isn't possible (regardless of what smart alecks on the Interwebs claim) and it would be kinder to just tell me if I pass a 25% chance instead of forcing the player to pointlessly scroll across cards, pretending that it matters.
So while there are some really interesting ideas in Hand of Fate and it starts promising, and the voice acting and art remain fantastic throughout, it ultimately is a very poor set of cards the game deals you.

Conan Exiles
Early Access
Funcom
Funcom
Open World Role Playing Game
31st of January, 2017
Singleplayer & Multiplayer
I’m sure that most gamers, comic book readers or film enthusiasts have heard of Conan the Barbarian, at some point in their lifetime. It’s the inconic definition of a savage warrior in an equally savage world, in which physical strength is crucial to your survival. Utopic Social Darwinism or not, the genre has had its fair share of popularity in the pulp fiction of the ‘30s and mid ‘40s. Arnold Schwarzenegger’s unintentionally hilarious performance while starring in the two (now cult classics) Conan movies from the 1980s, most certainly revived interest in everyone’s favorite barbarian. Conan Exiles has quite a legacy to uphold and for the most part, it manages to convey the savagery of the fictional lands inhabited by Death at every corner. Developer Funcom has had extensive experience with adventure games in the past and MMOs in more recent times. So no rookie dev looking for a quick cash grab while making empty promises. *cough* Hello Games? *cough*
I found the game’s initial difficulty scale quite refreshingly in tone to the source material’s themes. As an Exile in a strange and deadly world, you don’t need someone holding your hands and you have to make do with what you find for yourself and craft, eat, find shelter and ultimately survive or die trying. I would still have implemented a barebones tutorial of sorts if nothing more. Anything is better than having to quit the game and head to its Community Hub on Steam while hoping that the Guides already published there might shed some light on the game’s aim and fairly complex crafting mechanics. For a novice player in survival games (multiplayer-centric as well) the start of Conan Exiles must be confusing to say the least. The title could have only benefited from a proper introduction, instead of just cutting you loose at the outskirts between a desert and an oasis.
Even if it’s barely explained, I can’t deny the appeal of this game and its encouragement in regards to freedom of choice. A few lore bits are scattered around but other than that, you can head in any direction of the sizeable map you wish without much interference from the wildlife, if you keep your wits about you. It is true that strength is a paramount trait for a barbarian, but I strongly recommend you invest you initial points in Vitality and Survival. Yes, Conan Exiles features an RPG character progression system that provides both skill and attribute points as you level-up. Speaking of that, you seem to increase your level outside of combat too, simply by gathering resources, materials and then using them to craft tools, weapons or even structures. If you do wish to be constantly on the move and travel across the map, that is by itself a feat worthy of any warrior.
Provided you find a peaceful spot on the map where something or someone isn’t trying to eat you, you can settle down at least for a bit, while putting your architectural proclivities to the test. My advice in this regard would be an initially small sandstone hovel, built on one of the several islands near the starting position of your journey into exile. Why build in a relatively secluded place? Simply because the odds of critters or hostile natives spawning near your place of rest, are minimal. Beware of getting too close to crocodiles before you’re able to craft some proper armour and weaponry. Also, treat most NPCs with caution since I’ve only met a handful that don’t attack you on sight. Most creatures found while you’re still low-level, will happily ignore your presence if you maintain a safe distance.
It would be a blatant understatement for me to accuse Conan Exiles of lacking in activities. Everywhere you look there's stuff to gather and things to kill. Timber to chop, stone to mine, plants to harvest, wildlife to hunt, buildings to erect and natives to defend against. Even PvP combat, should you be inclined towards a truly competent form of opposition. I just wish the game will provide a backbone to all of this. A storyline worthy of Conan’s fantasy setting and something to certainly set it apart from ARK: Survival Evolved and Rust. All three titles seem to remain close to Early Access status though, at least for the foreseeable future. And yes, you don’t have firearms in Conan Exiles. THAT would have severely been out of place. Dev team promises the implementation of sorcery though, so you won’t be left wanting for very long. Afterall, slashing, bashing and shooting arrows gets boring eventually.
The gameplay is diversified enough, as are the enemies and resource distribution. What about game modes? You’ll be satisfied to hear of both the “relaxed” character of singleplayer (as much as hosting your own server and the haste with which you learn to survive, can provide) and the fiercely combative nature of multiplayer servers where you can guess how well you can mingle with the other players. Never played DayZ for a considerable amount of time, but I still recall the fact that monsters weren’t the true threat to your survival. Other human players were. So the multiplayer experience has always been met with mixed feelings by myself but that should certainly not deter you from joining someone else’s server instead of creating your own. There are sufficient options to be taken into account upon creating your own “playground”. Slides with modifiers for anything from experience gain and down to food spoilage rate.
Graphics are beautiful, courtesy of the Unreal Engine 4. Does that beauty also allow for a smooth experience? I’d say that’s still debatable for now. I never expected to run the game maxed out on 4K resolution and stable 60 frames per second. But even 2K res was met with stability issues as I had frame rate drops seemingly random and definitely annoying. On an overclocked GTX 1070, might I add. I was simply flabbergasted when the “mighty” GeForce Experience software, suggested that I play the game at 4K and medium details as OPTIMAL settings. Are you for real, Nvidia?
Religion and urban centres are subjects both the game and myself have yet to scratch far from the surface but I am convinced of Conan Exiles huge potential, as long as the developer keeps receiving support from gamers and buyers of his project. Slightly ironic since I think the game is a bit on the overpriced side but at the same time I am fully aware that without future customers, the outcome for Conan Exiles shall be quite typical. Funcom, please provide your new project with Trading Cards and as many Achievements as you can. Gamers have come to rightfully expect that, from a title of excellent production value. Steam’s a metaphoric graveyard for some developers’ dreams and you can find so many de facto abandoned Early Access games, that they’re beyond count. Don’t allow the one promising game featuring iconic barbarians go silently into the night. A warrior’s end is faced standing with sword-in-hand!
+ Beautiful graphics and sounds.
+ Large map with lots of potential.
+ Complex crafting (still work in progress).
+ Terrain and foe diversity.
- No tutorial and so far only feeble attempts at a storyline.
- Slightly overpriced since it’s still an Early Access.
- Inexplicable frame rate drops.
- No Steam Trading Cards nor Achievements.

Now, lemme point out that I do understand that this game is in Early Access. (at the time of this review)
I actually really enjoy this game's concept. And it pulls it off nicely. The game basically has you "race" against 1-3 other opponents in a stage that loops endlessly. The objective is to leave your opponents in the dust and leave them off the screen. Think of it like Smash Bros. You leave the screen and you're eliminated. The game even includes a little "Test Your Luck" sort of game mode where you can get random effects on a spinning wheel. These effects include running faster, flipping the stage in a mirror mode, and having rockets rain down from the sky and knocking everyone off course. This is a great feature and adds a lot of replay value to the game, so it doesn't remain the same every time. The game's a lot of fun and during the Free Weekend, I found myself coming back to it every few hours just to play a few rounds. It's a small game that you can pick up and play whenever. I can totally see myself picking this game up after the Free Weekend to keep...
... And then I tried playing online...
... The game's online is pure
, which is a bummer because the game is a lot of fun with others. You'll fall through the floor out of nowhere, your powerups won't work half the time and just zip through the enemy due to lag and the race will start and immediately kill you off without any reason. There's no dedicated servers, it's just random matchmaking. And nobody plays this game online, nobody with 0 XP at least, because "Ranked Match" gives you either nobody or the same people over and over again. I haven't finished a single match due to the constant lag, glitches and crashing. You CAN set the search range between Country, Continent, and Worldwide. Setting it to country would probably help with the lag and glitches, right? Nope. I couldn't find anyone in my country, and when I found ONE lobby in the continent, the game crashed.
And that's another thing. The game crashes. A LOT. It'll crash in the menu, it'll crash while loading the character select, it'll crash mid-game and it'll sometimes crash you use the Web Browser in the Steam Overlay. And before you attack me because I'm on a laptop, it's the game that crashes and not my PC. The game runs just fine, there's no frame drop and the game doesn't slowdown at all in-game. And then out of nowhere; Poof! I'm at the desktop with a pop up saying the game couldn't handle a certain operation in the programming. It's unstable.
Another feature is a Level Editor, which isn't as easy as it sounds. I literally cannot find the item pickups for the life of me, and if you place an item down that you don't want, it'll be a ♥♥♥♥♥ to delete as the item seems to go away every time you hover over it. I'm assuming this is so you can place other objects around it without clicking on the item instead.
The game has a "Level Up" system. You play the game normally, and you get "XP" for the bonuses you achieve, and the rounds you win. There are unlocks inbetween levels, but these unlocks... are just weird. I can't undo everything and see it again for myself but I swear you unlock things that are already selectable from the start of the game. Salem, an anthromorphic black cat in a witch outfit, was available at the beginning of the game but halfway through playing the game notifies me that "she's been unlocked". All of the "Test Your Luck" effects were also "Locked", despite always being there. I'm not sure if I'm just going insane but this needs a serious fix.
The only fun I've had with this game is offline, with bots and friends in local multiplayer. Online is garbage and the Level Editor is frusturatingly complex. The "Tips" for the level editor doesn't help either, it just tells you the controls. I'm hoping by the time this game is complete that there are some normal servers up, instead of this random matchmaking crap. And for $10? You could probably get another multiplayer game that's more stable for $10. Until the game buffs out it's scratches, get it on sale. Right now, the only fun you'll have is by yourself or with a friend. I'm still recommending the game though because online multiplayer isn't everything in a game. I still have a ton of fun with bots and friends offline and I'm sure you will too. But you should probably get this on sale while it's Early Access.

If you're looking for an enjoyable, relaxing, immersive platformer that requires precision and has a thumping soundtrack and clean, simple, "Japanese" esque graphics look no further. The animations of the main character (mostly the run animation) is a bit goofy looking but also fits the overall game created. The presentation of the game itself is pretty solid, however, with cool introductory bits for each level. Checkpoints are scattered throughout the level, but are sparse enough to balance both a challenge and avoid frustration from having to redo too lengthy of a section should you fall off. Numerous abilities beyond "just jumping" ie divebombing onto certain platforms to trigger other effects, as well as a midair kick to activate platforms round the game out from being too simplistic. Add to all of this the occassional "boss fight" and the game is an all-around pretty solid package.
If you see the aesthetics and gameplay and think you might be interested, it plays better than it looks, and offers a unique experience.

This game actually isn't that different than a typical RPG. You go in to a dungeon, kill things, take their stuff and sell it back in town. Except it's adventurers you hire that do the killing, and instead of selling the stuff to a shop, you're the shop keeper. What drives you forward isn't a quest to save the world, but the need to pay off the massive debts inherited from your father. Otherwise you'll end up kicked out of your home and end up living in a cardboard box.

I feel it was worth the couple hours of my time it took to complete. It was quite amusing, and the ending was... Interesting. If you are looking for a small game to pass the time that makes you feel properly rewarded, it's worth a play through. My only frustration was that, when you get to a certain point, a guide might be nessisary because it's somewhat specific about its requirements. Even so, I felt most of the game was pretty well-made in that I could intuit what I needed to do next, and the dialog was entertaining.
Just don't expect too much from a free, two hour game, and it may surprise you. Overall, a fun experience. Those who are in a bad mood, who don't like dialog-based games, or who are easily frustrated may not enjoy it though.

This is my first sandbox survival & building multiplayer game. I got hooked on it very hard. The main strengths of this game are its fantasy setting, relatively great graphics style, but most of all: absolute overall savagery in terms of everything that can and will kill you.
You have to learn how to deal with spiders and other enemies. You have to learn how to build bases in a PvP server. Every mistake is punished brutally, but somehow you always come back even more motivated to beat the odds, and that's what this game is about.
I love the fantasy and the mystery that surrounds it. There are plenty of different levels of challenging PvE stuff to do out there and obviously the best stuff is to be found at the most brutal places.
In its current stage, the game does suffer from desynchronisation between your client and the server, often causing moments where you have no idea where the enemies are really at and that kills you too often. That's the main weakness.
But overall a superb adventure. It has my recommendation.

One of the best examples of FPS action games out there. Only downside is a flat ending. Great difficulty, nice score system, nice story, I can make some critical judgments aside - but honestly - if you enjoy games like COD or Bioshock - this one is very playable and enjoyable. The weapon system is interesting. Two weapons, four fire mode functions and each of those functions have an auxilory function. All of the weapon modes add to gameplay and that's a big deal. When you unlock new functions and what function are choices you make along the way - which change the gameplay.
You are also to 'play into the enviroment' by damaging objects for destruction bonus points and AOE damage on enemy swarms. It's worth at least $15 to someone who can appreciate nuanced FPS action. If you play games from start to finish - that in itself is decent in this title. Scenes move forward, the action makes sense. I recommend playing on an advanced difficulty - but whatever floats your boat.

78.8 hours within a week. I'm a Day 2 Player.
180 hours now over the month and due to constant updates and improvements, I feel now is the time to change my review.
As this is still in Early Access my recommendation for this game will be temporary, but I'm sure I won't have many reasons to change that.
Conan Exiles is an online Survival game set in the Conan the Barbarian world, where players create characters exiled to die in this new and extremely hostile land. I mean seriously, the animals and monsters have insane aggro range.
I started playing on Day 2 of the games release and it started amazingly. The game worked great, apart from a few bugs involving Thralls, Strength, and the occassional Desync. For an EA game it worked amazingly, and we were always excited for the next update. Early patches caused more problems than solutions and it wasn't until about two weeks later that the patches actaully fixed server issues and exploiting. The Devs definitely listen to their customers, however as this game is still Early Access there will always be issues found while playing. So far, I have found no game breaking problems yet.
The game can be played solo but is not recommended. For most of my server gameplays I was solo. It's only recently I joined an active clan and with that I have made more progress than ever.
When starting an Online game, you are given the option of joninig PVP, PVP Blitz, or PVE. PVP Blitz is a competitive PVP server with players fighting for power over each other. The strongest players are named the Champion or whatever after 30 days have passed, in which the server wipes the map for a fresh start.
PVP and PVE to an extent allow for more types of servers to play. From standard PVP to Relaxed(for like minded players who want to kill each other and be civil), and even Role Playing where you play your character and station. It's a nice change from trying to find friendly and dedicated servers and helps to spread all the players to their prefered play style.
The character creation is limited to a few changes, and a nice and random change is Breast and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sliders. It makes me feel weird whenever I see naked people walking around and their balls are just bouncing so much. Balls should not bounce so much! It's not as wide of a creation as Ark, but it offers more than most EA survival games normally do. Such as Genders(Looking at you H1Z1 and Culling).
The In Game Spawn when starting a game immediately sets you up with one of two or three spawn locations leading into the map with access to a waterskin and some Lore. Seriously listen to the Lore, the voice acting is so good.
The area leading to the game world has access to water and very weak enemies, but it's futher on where things get rough, assuming you can get over the severe lag and crashes.
There are two big attractions that makes the game special and that Ark players may enjoy. Thralls and Avatars.
In Ark, I remember the enjoyment of being able to Tame a new Dinosaur and place a Saddle on it to ride around on. In Exiles, you're able to capture and break Slaves and turn them into Thralls, who can take up jobs at your crafting benches, like a Tannery or a Blacksmith, and others can be placed on guard such as Archers and Fighters. There are different Thrall classes and each Tribe excel in different classes. The most common Tribe to find are the Dafari, a cannibal tribe who utilize bone weaponry. Their specialist who spawn most of all are Tanners and Blacksmiths.  They cover most of the South, East, and center of the game World. In my game, I managed to capture up to 40 Thralls, mostly Dafari, and set them up all over my Castle, making my little Kingdom that much more lively. Their Temple also happens to spawn one of the strongest weapons in the game. Don't let its name fool you, because it does double the damage of Iron weapons.
Then there are Avatars. To players who chose a religion to follow with a God that desires worship, they have a chance to summon their God, an Avatar, into the World to wreck havoc for a limited time. These colossal monsters are virtually invulnerable but can be slowed down. It's a lot of fun to find a town or village and just destroy it entirely in a single swoop. Much like the Dragon or Mega-Ape of Ark, these god bosses make the end game feeling that much more rewarding.
At this stage, the game is functional, the devs are highly supportive of the customers and the player community is large and active. Servers have mostly kind admin, but you will find the few servers that have abusive admin. Simply avoid those and find another server. Don't worry about losing stats upon dying as the stats are saved, so you can train your character up, die, come back and kick butt later.
I very much recommend this game.

Warhead was the successor of Crysis in 2008; a stand-alone expansion pack that was specifically released for PCs and, interestingly, did not require the original Crysis game to run. I remember this being praised for its better optimisation while the game at the same time had the exact same requirements as its predecessor. Also it looks better, there's not much difference, though, as it uses the same environments / assets as the original Crysis game.
The story is a tad bit unusual here - instead of this being a continuation to Crysis it actually takes place at the same time. However, the game puts us in the shoes of Psycho instead of Nomad. We pick up the story just after the two buddies get separated - with Psycho alone there's more focus on fighting the Korean military (initially, that is) as the emphasis is on retrieving / destroying the nuclear warhead they have in their possession (hence the title). I liked the in-game cutscenes they made for the game and the fact that we have a Korean colonel as the game's antagonist.
The campaign is, being part of an expansion pack, shorter than that of Crysis but is a BLAST! I found it more action-packed and interesting (even though we know there are aliens rampant on the island which is not a surprise anymore). Since multiplayer services no longer exist (see the disclaimer re GameSpy on the store page) there's no point in elaborating on that one.
Perhaps there's a solution for that, but this would definitely be something unofficial. Thus, at this point, this game is only worth purchasing for its short but satisfying campaign content. If discounted, it may just be a decent purchase and then you can make up your mind whether or not you want to see what Crytek achieved with Crysis 2.

Pretty solid game. There were a lot of complaints about its length, but if you play through the base game and the DLC, you're in for probably 10 or more hours of shooting good times.
The weapons are interesting and the difficulty is high enough that I found I needed to use the crowd control mechanics extensively in order to get by.
I played the game on Hard, which is the default setting I use when playing shooters, and this one was by far the hardest one I've played in recent memory. There was one boss fight in the original chapters I died 49 times on!
One cool thing about the level design is that there are a lot of secrets tucked away in the levels which is something a lot of corridor shooters have lost over the years since the Doom II days. Some of the secrets are pretty easy to find, but some required really studying the options available in the room to figure out how to get to them.
I highly recommend advancing to the Rail Gun or the RPG as fast as possible (accomplish this by checking the pre-reqs on it and focusing on them as high priority upgrades). The rest of the weapons do not do enough damage to really chip through the harder enemies fast enough. Again, this was on Hard. Maybe Normal is a cakewalk, I dunno.
Overall, good game, probably didn't get the acknowledgement it deserved.
One final note - the story is nigh incomprehensible, the VO often cringeworthy, the cutscenes okay, but the Cyberpunk setting is cool and you don't need to understand the story to enjoy blowing up endless waves of robots with a creatively versatile arsenal.

On paper, it sounded like an incredible idea; reviving the spirit of Fatal Frame, and shifting the focus on Indonesian folklore. There's something beautiful about the legends and myths coming from Southeast Asia, and being able to experience that would have been a refreshing change of pace from the saturated crowd of J-Horror.
Unfortunately, on paper is all it ever delivers.
The game is largely unfinished, unpolished, and a mish-mash of different ideas that come together in a ferocious mess. There are moments of brilliance, but too few and far between. There's hardly any character development, there is hardly enough time to get to know these characters, and there is hardly enough sense put into the game to understand what the hell is going on. All of this culminates into a climax that's actually good, but feels hollow - it's like we skipped a few cutscenes and levels in-between and went straight for the final boss.
The team is understandably small, but they've bitten off more than they can chew. There's signs of troubled development and broken promises. The game had potential and should have been longer. Splitting into 2 parts meant the game had been rushed.
It's more of a proof of concept rather than a real game.
The Demo for the game is actually better than the full game. Even the prologue sequence, which is supposedly identical to the Demo, is a step down, perhaps due to the new engine.
It's a shame, really. I was one of the people who looked forward to the full release, and was ultimately let down, twice.

This title is pretty much European Truck Simulator in a different area. Some of the glitches and jewels are present in both. However, there are some glaring exclusions in ATS that shouldn't have made it to release. One of the most annoying are the stop signals on interstate highways. These do not exist in America except in very rare instances, and stop signs at T-corners that should have signals. Some if these intersections are nearly impossible to get through due to the amount of traffic.  Another annoyance is the lack of beacons. There are required for oversized loads. These are available in ETS2  and should be included in ATS also. Perhaps SCS will add them at some point.
The geography is very compacted also resulting in fairly quick trips. But,  I'm sure some feel this justified due to the size of the American west. Whether this is valid or not will become more evident when new DLC is added.
Even with it pimples and the number of shortcomings at release, if you need a break from Europe and want to drive in pretty much a desert environment, then by all means purchase it. My hope is that with more DLC the game will only get better as it matures.

Review for Owlboy
I finished the main story with a playtime of 12 hours, did not do any collectibles.
+++Excellent, stunning pixel art graphics and animation that exemplifies the pinnacle of what the art style can achieve in modern gaming
++Amazing soundtrack that sets the mood and is just as crucial to the Owlboy experience as the pixel art.
+Well written, mature yet lovable characters that compliment the gameplay well
+Good, simple controls that handle well.
+A wide variety of fun encounters and boss battles that can be very challenging
~Story that you play through during the game is pretty good, and hints at a potentially very interesting lore, but unfortunately the game fails to elaborate on the game's universe and setting. Some lore books/collectibles would have been much appreciated. That said, I enjoyed the experience nevertheless.
~Many side characters were poorly done and had zero character development or explanation as to their role or prior relationship to protagonist. They exist just because. It's a shame as the pixel art for these characters are really good.
-Story's ending was disappointing in my opinion and an unfitting conclusion to what I otherwise deem a remarkable experience. I was left with a lot of questions and the game did not provide any answers even after the credits roll. The narrative (and lore) has room for improvement.
Summary score: 8/10. A remarkable experience that is tarnished by nitpicks that prevent it from being a perfect game. Still, could be considered in the future as an indie classic and a must-try.

Attention! If you are searching for a new experience in an MMO RPG that isn't just PvE or PvP, ArcheAge offers many other options toward seeking those thrilling and dangerous adventures!..
It's a pretty fun and easy going game when compared to a lot of other MMO RPGs. The UI and game mechanics are very familiar to others of the same genre. Here is an opinionated list on the fun and positive connotations to the game as well as the flaws to the game. Hope this gives a little insight on the game for the viewer. I did not include everything about the game, just generalizations and minor suggestions.

UI- As previosuly mentioned, the user interface of the game is very similar to others of its genre making it a little easier to grasp and understand.
Settings- ArcheAge can be a very beautiful game when its qualities are cranked up. As contrast, it can be just as optimizable for people with lower performance computers. The small issues with putting the graphical settings on low for those people, they will unfortunately have to deal with a slower rendering rate, making the world very dark or models not properly loaded.
Gameplay- As it is an MMO, the story is a bit stale and somewhat predictable, not to mention that the race that you choose to play, decides which side you are on in terms of the story. Thankfully, specializations that can be made to your character to offer more in compensation. Instead of picking from a small pool of classes, there is a multiclassing system, adding a huge dynamic for your character as they are leveling.
Professions- Like great MMO RPGs, there are always ways to make gold. ArcheAge has a variety professions that you may take up and specialize in as you are playing the game. For example, Fishing, creating trade packs and commuting large distances to turn them into a trader, or just the basics like smithing or farming. The one major flaw to ArcheAge that limits your ability in the game when it comes to these leisures is a Labor system. As you are playing the game, every 5 minutes in real time, you acquire 5 labor that accumulate to a total of 2,000 if you are a free to play person. When you log out of the game, you do not gain any labor from being offline, thus, crippling some enjoyment of the game as the labor costs become higher for certain things as you level up. The only way to have an advantage or be able to gain more labor while being offline, is by paying for a subscription to be what is called a Patron. In my personal opnion, while being a patron has many more benefits than just increased labor cap and collection, I would not suggest investing any real money in the game, unless, of course, you are enjoying the game so much so, that you would like to show your support, and get some benefits in-game.

I got this as part of a Humble Bundle and knew nothing about it before trying.
I'm a huge fan of tabletop board gaming, so I was interested when it was described as a deck-builder mixed with an action combat game. The concept is really neat, but the game ultimately falls flat, in my opinion.
As you'll read in other reviews, the game does have solid voice acting and graphics. I agree with those assessments, but that's about as far as I can go with the positive aspects.
My biggest concern with this game is that the card gameplay is extremely shallow and random with very few interesting decisions; it's full of illusion-of-choice where the game shuffles 4 cards and you pick one -- the act of picking a single card from a shuffled pile is NOT the same as making a decision. The game ultimately feels like a fancy skin over a bunch of die rolls and linear movement. After 5 minutes of playing the game, it becomes apparent that this is the core gameplay loop.
The pacing of the card gameplay is sluggish, with animations being just a tad too slow. And with so many of these animations being the same and/or with nearly inconsequential effects, it quickly feels repetetive and grindy. Couple this with the lack of decision making, and the game begins to feel like a chore.
The game uses a tarot style graphic design on the cards, only showing a card name in addition to the art. The issue with that is that there are at least dozens (hundreds?) of unique cards that each do different things, and they these effects are not immediately apparent. So when you complete a mission and win a booster pack, it totally takes the excitement out of the reveal because you have no idea what you just opened. This may seem like a small detail, but it sucks out SO MUCH of the immersion and underlying story. When you have a wall of completed missions with no descriptions, the experience feels hollow.
The combat is very similar to Batman. I didn't know this before playing, and if I did, I probably would have avoided the game based purely on personal preference (I didn't care for the Batman combat system). This game really tried to capture the same feel, but is again ultimately quite sluggish in its execution. As well, this combat system feels at odds with the balance of the card system. With so many opportunities to block and counter and dodge, what even is the difference between a +25 ATK weapon vs +27 ATK weapon? Part of the excitement and strategy/tactics of a more traditional card game is working out lines of play that let you edge out small victories with just enough damage in different situations. The action combat in this game blurs this aspect of gameplay to the point where it begins to feel arbitrary and lacking a cohesive design.
In conclusion, even if the gameplay itself was more compelling, the user experience (card descriptions, pacing, etc) really made a mediocre/boring game into a frustrating one. I definitely do not recommend buying this at full price, and would only recommend getting it on sale if you enjoyed the combat in Batman and are intrigued by the concept of a mixed card game/action game. DO NOT buy this if you want deep card game experiences because you will be disappointed.

This game is very innovative and beautiful and I like it. You can clearly see the effort made in this game, which is substansial with as small team as this game had. It apparently took nine years to develop, and I would say that it is time well spent.
This is the second game in a row that I review that seems to have taken influence from the art of Roger Dean in it's visual scenery with the floating islands. Which is great.
Gameplaywise I found it very interesting, as you are able to fly during most of the game which is understandably quite rare for a platformer. It still proved itself to be quite challenging at times, but not too much so for my tastes. I'm not very talented in platformers, so I understand if some other person thought it was too easy.
There were some confusing times during the game where it wasn't all that clear where I was supposed to go, but it was still quite manageable. Some sort of maps could have been helpful, as this was, in a sense, an open world game.
The music fits very well with the overall mood. It has high quality and with an actual orchestra instead of computer generated music that is quite regular in this kind of pixelated games.
I don't agree with some of the reviewers on that the game was badly explained. There were numerous references done during the game on what the story was about, and there were no illogical quirks that would have ruined it overall. I was very happy with the ending, which seems to be surprisingly hard to accomplish in games. It made some kind of closure with some things left very open, but in a good way.
It's hard for me to tell whether the pricepoint is correct or not, as I think that any game over 15€ is too damn high and I buy all of my games during sales. I bought this from humble bundle, so it was only 12€ with many other games to come with it and I'm very happy with the purchase.

I reviewed this game in May of 2017, and loved it then. In July, I played through Team Cherry's "Hollow Knight" My twin brother eventually convinced my to replay Owlboy, as I had Started comparing the two games. This was one of my biggest mistakes, no doubt.
Owlboy cannot be compared to Hollow Knight just because they are both Indie Games.  While Team Cherry made a remarkable Metroidvania game, D-Pad Studio chose instead to make something unlike any other game i've played. Owlboy doesn't fit into one genre, which the best part of the game. At first, you see a large world to explore and learn about. This is the only major thing that stays constant. After the start, the gameplay goes from adventure to adventure shooter, to stealth, to puzzle, back to stealth and puzzle, and then to a runner for all of 20 seconds. Thats only in the first 2-3 hours. Before you know it, you are being chased by gnats and then riding a snake out of a continent Dr. Strange Love style. There is no knowing what to expect at any given time, and this always leaves the player hungry for more.
Unfortunately, after the main 11 hour entree (8 if you know what to expect), there is very little dessert. After the main story, all that is left is too gather all of the Buccanary coins, (which is not the most fun) get higher scores on the Boguin cannon, and find and place the 3 owl tokens. While Indie games can't be expected to provide as much content as AAA games, this is pitiful. A game that is 10-11 hours long the first time around only gets extended by an extra 1-2 hours. The reward for the 3 tokens is great, but the same cant be said for all the Buccanary coins. The game can be a bit loquacious at times, but the dialogue is never too long.
The immediate appetizers of gorgeous visuals and an unforgettable OST help the case of Owlboy tremendously. It just becomes so much harder to stay away from a game when its so goddamn gorgeous.
All things considered, Owlboy is worth the price and the almost decade of development. While the adventure isn't exactly a long one, its filled with content all the way to pour line. Unfortunately its not overflowing with it, as their is not much to be outside of the main story. A story of Friendship, Acceptance, and Adversity await you. If you have $25 to spare and you like having fun, there is nothing to stop you from having a good time.
TLDR- The gameplay is fun because it switches up a bunch, visuals and audio are fantastic, except there is very little to do outside of the main story. Very fun, would highly recommend to lovers of Indie games.

Warning: Long personal opinion review ahead.
TL:DR version: As someone who was introduced to PC gaming through Dungeon Keeper 1. I love it, It's great for those nostalgic for the classic "Dungeon Keeper" gameplay and a fair introduction to those new to the Dungeon Management RTS genre. Only negative i have is in the games on/off freezing times when alot is happening at once such as a large scale combat.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
For those of you who were very upset over EA games mobile abomination and black mark against a beloved PC cult classic "Dungeon Keeper", War of the Overworld is in my regards a true to form successor that delivered what it's Kickstarter set out to do 2 years ago.
Players who have played or are still playing Dungeon Keeper 1/2 you will find that this game will make you feel right at home as nothing has really changed in terms of theme and gameplay with the only a few small exceptions in regards to the naming of creatures and rooms.
At this time I have only played the campaign and sandbox mode so I do not know what the online multiplayer or skirmish modes are like. But as far as the campaign goes it is a trip through nostalgia lane. As you play through the campaign you find that not only do you play the standard "Build, Manage, Defend" gamestyle Dungeon keeper made famous.  You also have to play different play styles in order to accomplish your mission goals or to respond to the mission's situation, This can provide you with a very refreshing or frustrating challenge depending on how view it. To me the very icing on this cake is that your in-game mentor "The Overlord" is voiced by Dungeon Keeper's very own Richard Ridings who delivers the same grand performance he made in Dungeon Keeper while also providing the games comic releif in the lines he delivers during gameplay.
Sandbox mode is essentially DK's "My Pet Dungeon" where you are given all and unlimited resources to allow you to build your very own perfect dungeon with out any worry of being invaded or having to accomplish some mission. I think it's a bit dull but it's something to do in your downtime all and all.
Now while I have praised the game alot so far and I still recommend it to those interested, There is one negative I have in that the game will slow down to a stand still if there is alot going on at once, This happened to me multiple times on one mission in the campaign where there are 3 different teams all with large sized armies. There was so much going on it would freeze the game up for a minute or 2 and my PC has been setup to run most of the latest games on high graphics, So far the game has not crashed but I do recommend saving your progress every now and then.
A classic to the genre.  A must have for Total Annihilation fans looking for more nostalgia.
Incredibly intricate, vastly rewarding.

78.8 hours within a week. I'm a Day 2 Player.
180 hours now over the month and due to constant updates and improvements, I feel now is the time to change my review.
As this is still in Early Access my recommendation for this game will be temporary, but I'm sure I won't have many reasons to change that.
Conan Exiles is an online Survival game set in the Conan the Barbarian world, where players create characters exiled to die in this new and extremely hostile land. I mean seriously, the animals and monsters have insane aggro range.
I started playing on Day 2 of the games release and it started amazingly. The game worked great, apart from a few bugs involving Thralls, Strength, and the occassional Desync. For an EA game it worked amazingly, and we were always excited for the next update. Early patches caused more problems than solutions and it wasn't until about two weeks later that the patches actaully fixed server issues and exploiting. The Devs definitely listen to their customers, however as this game is still Early Access there will always be issues found while playing. So far, I have found no game breaking problems yet.
The game can be played solo but is not recommended. For most of my server gameplays I was solo. It's only recently I joined an active clan and with that I have made more progress than ever.
When starting an Online game, you are given the option of joninig PVP, PVP Blitz, or PVE. PVP Blitz is a competitive PVP server with players fighting for power over each other. The strongest players are named the Champion or whatever after 30 days have passed, in which the server wipes the map for a fresh start.
PVP and PVE to an extent allow for more types of servers to play. From standard PVP to Relaxed(for like minded players who want to kill each other and be civil), and even Role Playing where you play your character and station. It's a nice change from trying to find friendly and dedicated servers and helps to spread all the players to their prefered play style.
The character creation is limited to a few changes, and a nice and random change is Breast and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sliders. It makes me feel weird whenever I see naked people walking around and their balls are just bouncing so much. Balls should not bounce so much! It's not as wide of a creation as Ark, but it offers more than most EA survival games normally do. Such as Genders(Looking at you H1Z1 and Culling).
The In Game Spawn when starting a game immediately sets you up with one of two or three spawn locations leading into the map with access to a waterskin and some Lore. Seriously listen to the Lore, the voice acting is so good.
The area leading to the game world has access to water and very weak enemies, but it's futher on where things get rough, assuming you can get over the severe lag and crashes.
There are two big attractions that makes the game special and that Ark players may enjoy. Thralls and Avatars.
In Ark, I remember the enjoyment of being able to Tame a new Dinosaur and place a Saddle on it to ride around on. In Exiles, you're able to capture and break Slaves and turn them into Thralls, who can take up jobs at your crafting benches, like a Tannery or a Blacksmith, and others can be placed on guard such as Archers and Fighters. There are different Thrall classes and each Tribe excel in different classes. The most common Tribe to find are the Dafari, a cannibal tribe who utilize bone weaponry. Their specialist who spawn most of all are Tanners and Blacksmiths.  They cover most of the South, East, and center of the game World. In my game, I managed to capture up to 40 Thralls, mostly Dafari, and set them up all over my Castle, making my little Kingdom that much more lively. Their Temple also happens to spawn one of the strongest weapons in the game. Don't let its name fool you, because it does double the damage of Iron weapons.
Then there are Avatars. To players who chose a religion to follow with a God that desires worship, they have a chance to summon their God, an Avatar, into the World to wreck havoc for a limited time. These colossal monsters are virtually invulnerable but can be slowed down. It's a lot of fun to find a town or village and just destroy it entirely in a single swoop. Much like the Dragon or Mega-Ape of Ark, these god bosses make the end game feeling that much more rewarding.
At this stage, the game is functional, the devs are highly supportive of the customers and the player community is large and active. Servers have mostly kind admin, but you will find the few servers that have abusive admin. Simply avoid those and find another server. Don't worry about losing stats upon dying as the stats are saved, so you can train your character up, die, come back and kick butt later.
I very much recommend this game.

Never written a review before. Felt compelled to add my meager compliments to the authors. Holy cow... this is like mellow mediatation. After a couple hours in a FPS or RTS, or straining my brain cells to the max in a 4x monster map with hundreds of items to track this is relaxing and elegant. The backstory is very clever and engaging, and the artwork sucks you in. Its like an interactive alternative history daydream. Being a 19 Delta or 11 Bravo in anime land is fun. I love the old school SKS style Gallia-1 rifle, and the Finnish/Baltic WW2 references. Do NOT expect this to be fast-paced, complex or difficult, or big on replay value. Its not meant to be. I could teach an 8 year old to play well; that being said, I enjoyed teaching my kids to play Risk and other simple games and got my booty kicked. I find Valkyria a pleasant break from the heavy hitter games, or a good way to wind down after a tough day. Milk, cocoa, cookies before bed along with an hour of Valkyria is good medicine. Let me say, from the first few minutes of this game to the first few hours, I HATED this game. The only thing that eventually saved it for me was that I liked the story that much, but I had to force myself to play it to get that far.
For every bit of progress they made in this game over ME1, they messed something else up just as bad. Just some examples off the top of my head:
+melee is now it's own button! no more doing weak melees with a shotgun because you got too close.
+you can now sprint out of combat, though it's much slower and still as mostly useless as it used to be.
-you now have to hit a button to get into cover, rather than doing it automatically
-that button you have to press is a context sensitive button used to: use everything, sprint, get into cover, and jump over cover. These actions will interfere with each other and get you killed, enjoy that. There was no reason for this on the PC.
+no more tedious inventory management!
-actually no more inventory management of any kind. You can swap weapon loadouts, however the stats are obscured so you'll have to use the wiki if you're trying to min max, and then new weapons are few and far between so you'll rarely touch it. Your armor is something you select at the beginning of the game, and there's literally no reason to ever touch it again because you never get anything new to choose from. No customization of weapons or armor of any kind. Weapon mods are in fact abilites now.
+much shorter ability cooldowns
-much fewer abilities per person
-global cooldown meaning there's little reason to use anything but your strongest skill
-Weapons. What were they thinking?
-Got rid of the heat mechanic in favor of reloading and ammo drops. Maybe this sits well with some people, but to me that heat and accuracy management mechanic was what made the combat of ME1 so fun.
-Cannot bind weapons to quick slots. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I cannot stress enough how much this♥♥♥♥♥♥in my salad. I played a soldier in ME1 and I would quickly swap weapons on the fly using quickslots as the situation demanded it. In this game, I just used the sniper for everything. Not because I wanted to, but because it was less painful than stopping every few seconds in combat to pause the game, mouse though a tedious menu, and then wait for the weapon switch animation to finish.
-Hide for 5 seconds to regenerate all life and shields. NO. STOP IT.
+Remember that kind of annoying ring puzzle that was on everything in ME1? that's gone.
-Now you have these two bypass and hacking puzzles that are on everything and are a hundred times more trivial and tedious
+No more mako bouncy house planet exploring for meaningless minerals and crap.
+They replaced it with a hovercraft sort of deal for the few missions that have planet exploration in the dlc, and it's way better. Way to go. good job.
-Now you have this planet scanning game to get minerals, and it's not optional because you actually need the minerals to get upgrades instead of just a meaningless collection quest. And boy is it tedious.
I'm sure I could sit here and think of more but you get the picture.
At the end of the game, while I hated pretty much everything they did to change this from ME1 to another boring modern shooter, it didn't ruin the game. I still recommend it, but it wasn't better than ME1.

It is an understatement to say that Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy is not a good game. The Mystery of the Mummy (MotM) is not a good game in the way that Dungeons and Dragons 2000 is not a good movie, which is to say, it manages to get absolutely everything wrong in a way that I felt compelled to see. Yet, MotM is far less enjoyable than a cringy bad movie, because unlike a film where the observer has the power to sit back and watch an entertaining trainwreck, in videogames, one is forced to experience for themselves the clunky mechanics and glitchy systems almost to the point of madness.
The Story: Sherlock Holmes, independent of Watson who is on vacation with his wife, is asked by his cousin, Lady Elizabeth Montcalfe (almost cousin by almost marriage, I believe) to investigate the mysterious circumstances behind the suicide of her father, Lord Montcalfe. The entire game takes place over a single evening inside the Montcalfe Manor, where Sherlock apparently unravels the mystery through a series of deductive hunches never completely explained to the player. The solution to the mystery is nonsensical and strange. It makes some sense if you reach, but not enough to be satisfying. I tried to type it and its dangling plot threads out and my review got cut off for length, that's how bad it was. Not only that but I have to mention that Sherlock sits his cast down and explains the answer to his mystery inside a mansion that is actively on fire in several places while he does so, try as I might I just can't ignore that fact.
The Graphics: Terrible. 2/10. This game was made in 2002, so there is legitimately no excuse for how bad the graphics in this game are. Some great stuff came out in and around 2002, this game wasn't among that stuff. Seriously it looks like it belongs somewhere in the very early 90s.
Progression: Extremely linear. In most cases you are required to solve one puzzle before moving onto the next, meaning there's little to no freedom of location within levels and you'll only have a few rooms of wiggle space at a time at most. This annoys me. I would much rather be able to stew on a puzzle for a while and go see about something else in a different location until it clicks, but no dice here. There are also no NPCs to question or anything like that, the only speaking NPC outside of a cutscene is in Level 5, and he says a series of preprogrammed nonhelpful phrases.
The Puzzles: Not Good. I don't know how to objectively rate them in numbers honestly. There are a few different kind of puzzles, none of which make much sense. Early on, it's a lot of pixel hunting. Actually it never stops being pixel hunting, but the pixels you hunt in Level 1 are a lot more obscure compared to later game in Levels 4 or 5. Sometimes there is no indication of what you need to pick up, you just have to scan your mouse across a large expanse of screen until the little hand changes to indicate something important is there. This happens say, in the wine cellar, where you can and must pick up specific wines which all look exactly alike, so good luck cursor hunting. When it's not pixel hunting its either arbitrary object placement which is mostly a guessing game (The last puzzle is basically the creation of a Rube Goldberg machine, when MOVING THE OBJECT SHERLOCK WAS TRYING TO DISABLE WOULD HAVE WORKED JUST AS WELL) or it's interacting with a clunky puzzle interface over a timed set. There are two slider puzzles, those are timed. There's a thing where you literally have to click and drag letters with no basis for elimination, only a series of obtuse hints you need to open a submenu to reach, and that's mega timed. There's a really annoying nonogram (japanese origin numbers game where you fill in a grid to create a picture) and that one is timed, and also changes solutions with every new game. I only got through it because a year ago I had a nonogram obsession, yay me. So the puzzles are really bad in just about every way. I play Nancy Drew religiously, I've beaten Myst, and Riven, I know a good puzzle when I see one d*mn it.
Additional Stuff: The voice acting is really bad too, and Sherlock's is the worst of the bunch. He's constantly making inane observations that are either incredibly obvious or legitimately impossible to deduce on logical reasoning, so he's the game's walking talking "look player this is what's happening and I can say it because I am very smart and can deduce things better than you can huehuehuehue" machine.
The game is buggy as hell. On windows 10, I experienced the following problems. First, on trying to play the game wouldn't load. It would crash or not respond immediately, right on launch. There's a quick fix for this already on the forums, but as the forums are down as of me writing this review, I'll leave it to you to google at a time when they are up and working once more. Second, sometimes in the cutscene transitions the game will just stop working altogether. Save before the Level ends (save frequently anyway this game is a minefield of timed puzzles and crashes), watch the cutscene once if you wish, then reload the game and hit 'esc' right as the cutscene begins to not deal with this crash.
I'm going to admit that I used a guide on this entire game, I did. I wanted to get through it, review it, and play other Sherlock Holmes games. I was also amused by the spectacle of a really bad game and got to laugh as I played. I recommend a guide, the game is bash your head against a wall stupid without one. There are some youtube walkthroughs and one on gamefaqs, but I used Witchen's walkthrough on Gameboomers, which comes collect with some explanation and great commentary, so I highly recommend it. Once again, a google should suffice.
So would I recommend this game? Not really. If you have to play things in sequence like I do, then yes. If you want to see how bad it really is, then yes. Otherwise steer clear, even if its free, if you aren't a consumer of terrible media for fun like I am, you won't have a good time. If you're looking for a good mystery game for your child, this one does show a character get shot (non graphically, this game couldn't do something graphically if it wanted to) on screen, and it makes no sense. Invest in a good Nancy Drew or get a Sherlock Holmes farther down the dev line than this one.

The few times I do them, I usually go into windowed mode to leave it on auto-move while watching a show, occasionally tabbing back in to turn the vehicle.
Being in a large guild can lead to many fun experiences, which include raids, pvp, etc.
A majority of the costumes are well made and become the "most wanted" for that period of time until a new costume is released.
Unfortunately, another aspect of this game is the Pay to Win system.
While this will turn many players off, hear me out.
The Pay to Win system helps Free to Play players get their subscription paid.
The P2W players supply an item called APEX, which when used, gives 2000 credits.
Credits can be used to purchase items from the Cash Shop, which include costumes, consumables, and basic luxury items, one of which happens to be a summonable mailbox.
Credits can also be used to pay for the subscription. This allows F2P players access to all the perks that subscribed players have, without the need to actually pay $15 a month for a subscription.
And in a way, the P2W system is better described as: "Pay for a chance to win".
Most gear that need to be upgraded are subject to RNG.
High grade gear is very expensive and it is incredibly rare to see anyone with top tier equipment.
Each upgrade has 5 different outcomes: Success, Great Success, Fail, Great Fail, and Destruction.
Destruction is the most painful outcome to receive. The equipment you attempted to upgrade disappears from your inventory permanently, which prevents players from truly paying to win.
I personally have sustained a year of subscription off of this system and enjoy my time playing this game.
