I'm going to start off by saying that Hand of Fate is one of the most original and entertaining games I've played in a long time. My friend got it for me for Christmas, and I can definitely say it was an excellent gift (even if it took me a while to get around to playing it). It's well worth the $20 it costs; if you find it on sale, even more so. That being said, there is a very, very big issue I had with it.
If I had to rate HoF based on everything except the final boss fight, I'd easily give it a solid 4/5. It does rely quite heavily on luck, which can be frustrating at times, which is the only thing preventing it from being 5/5. However, if I were to rate the entire game as a whole, the final boss sadly drops it down to 3/5.
Yes, it's that big of a sore spot for me. The first time I reached the final boss (not an easy feat, I should add, given the high degree of luck involved in dungeon and loot generation in the game), I was in very good shape, and cleared the first part of the fight without much difficulty.
Then, out of nowhere, there was a cinematic Quicktime Event. A QTE that, if failed, causes instant death. Now, I'm not a fan of QTEs in general, but this one was particularly egregious because prior to the final boss, there is not a single QTE in the entire game. The player has absolutely no reason to expect one. Not only that, since the game revolves around enemies that correspond to various suits of cards, when a giant Q popped up on my screen at the start of the event, I thought it meant the boss was summoning a Queen enemy. A moment later, however, SPACE popped up, and I realized it was a QTE, but by then it was too late. Instant death. And in Hand of Fate, death means having to start the entire randomly generated dungeon over again from the beginning, losing all your collected gear and gold, and getting reverted back to starting equipment.
Quite frankly, it was a dirty move on the part of the developers. It's the gameplay equivalent of a jumpscare; the fight would have been legitimately fun and challenging without the QTE, but they decided to randomly give the player a chance to die instantly, regardless of their gear or combat skill. Not only that, it actively punishes the player for not spoiling the final boss fight for themselves; reading online guides or FAQs beforehand would have given me advance warning, so I would have known to be ready for the Quicktime Event, but since I wanted to get through the game on my own, I was sucker punched.
Regardless, I would still recommend the game, but I will definitely not be picking up the sequel until I have determined that it is free of 'press X to not die' moments.

There are a few things needing to be discussed when it comes to ArcheAge.
1. P2W
2. Community
3. Content
4. Quality
5. Other stuff
To start out we have to adress the P2W argument everyone likes. hear me out; its not P2W. Archeage is Free to play till about lv 30, then you just about need a monthly sub to get stuff done. This is understandable seeing how the servers must cost a lot. YES you can but stuff with cash, but nothing i have seen in my 1500 hours of play time in the ingame market houe would give you such an advantage over others that it is P2W. Now it is true that you can buy APEX and sell it for ingame gold, however to put this into proportion, if i was to spend $500 USD i would still not be able to get the best gear. If you Grind with the monthly sub (seeing how grinding is a part of ALL MMOs) you could have the best gear in the game (wit hfair RNG luck) in under 6 months.
compared to other games to where it may not even be possible to get the best gear in a mortal life. Also know that you do not need top gear to do PVP. most players do not have amazing gear, and i have been killed by people with worse gear then me. its about skill.
On the topic of PVP it brings one to ask about the community. It may change from one server to another, but at least on Aranzeb, the community is pretty nice. there may not be 50k players, but there is no shortage when it comes to raids or events. And those are often. lots of content, player wars, etc. Like with every game there are a few Cancerous tumors that play Archeage. Ignore them or block them.
On the Topic of content there is a lot to cover. This game has a pretty damn big map, 2 factions, 4 races (6 soon, and an even bigger map) so there is lots to explore. Not to mention the ocean. From sunken ships, to islands, and all 3 major land masses. There are events constantly. every other hour there is a raid for both Nuia (west faction) and Haranya (east faction) that 50 people can do, or more if another raid starts. There are huge battles where it is PVE, or some that are PVP. and there is alot to choose from for PVP. your class is based off 3 skillsets that you can mix and match from out of a list of about 15. Lots of options, and pretty good for all types of damage. Magic effects look pretty good, and the cast times are fair in preportion to damage. Lots of combos for people that like pvp. Crafting is another thing where they did not skip on content. There are your basic skills like Mining, Farming, Smelting, Armor and wepons crafting, and it goes of longer then i cae to mention. there are even skills just for fun. Artistry for example: It has no other purpose other then for enjoyment. you can craft songs and copy the code from online databands of codes. so basicly you can be playing just about any song you want while your raid charges to battle. Its the small stuff that matters. Lots of Easter Eggs, hidden quests and areas. Overall great content. And its gonna get even better: in December when 3.0 comes out there will be give aways of items, 2 new races, new zones on all 3 major land masses, and all new events and bosses. Dungeons are fun and level balanced.
As far as quality goes, This game has some fair graphics even on low, and if you have even a basic internet connection then you are fine. I live in the middle of nowhere and get 2Mb download, and have only slight lag. That is not half bad considering i cant play any other online games where I live. Dosen't crash often. The graphisc on med look great, and on highest settings.... I'll just say Amazing and let you be the judge.
The other stuff is the fact that the game is slightly dead. This is because this game used to be ♥♥♥♥ to be honest. and the ratings have never recoverd. They fixed most everything, and now only annoying thing is Labor system. You need labor to do most things. All Vocational Activities from making music, armor, wepons, mining, farming, etc... This is the reason you need the monthly sub. you get 5 labor points every 10 mn of play time and that dosent go far. so you can be afk labor farming 24/7 or pay $15 and have 5k labor pool. With Patron (monthly sub) you get 10 labor points every 5 min online. This is my one Anger wit hthe game, but it is still fun. Id rather have a pay to play game that makes everyone even then a true P2W where someone can drop $100 and become unkillable. That wont even get you boots in ArcheAge. Just grind a bit and you will be fine.
I understand That this game is not for everyone, but if you take the time to read this and have not tried it before, ask yourself this. Do you like games that have : Crafting? Exploration? Grinding? PVP? PVE? Naval Combat and Sailing? Good Music and Graphics? Open World? if you like these things then try it out. If you are one of the people who clicked dislike on it ask yourself this : Was it worth the $0 you spent? Thats right, its free. If you spent $ trying to be P2W and it dident work then try to play ligit someday lol. Its a good game, and give it a try.

I really really like this game. Nice storyline, nice visuals, nice classic Jump&Run(Fly) Elements, surprising bosses, overall nice level design (with some flaws here and there). So this is definetly a recommendation...
BUT all the aforementioned pros turn in to cons here and there.
First of all the controls: During most parts of the game this is not a problem but I just spent one hour managing a simple jump&run part. The game uses the same button for jumping (pressing the button longer makes you jump farther) and when you are in the air and press the button a second time you start to fly. My high and mighty Steam-Controller has some trouble differentiating pressing long and pressing two times which just a few minutes ago made me toss the controller across the room...
The there's the classif jump&run bosses. Some are beaten very very easily if you try the right way to fight them directly (of of there are several ways to beat them). Some of them hit away at you without leaving you much of a chance to react. Other bosses kill you a dozen times before you figure out in what pattern they hit and what you have to do to beat them but afterwards they are very wasy to kill if you get the pattern right.
Level design can be quite repetitive in some levels (and sometimes you have to search for the right way to go for some time) but the style changes often enough. The diversified level designs affects the style of gameplay in some levels which is quite refreshing.
So this is a recommendation if you get a chance to buy this game in a sale but with some grains of salt...

First off, great work Stubterranean games! I've been a backer of this project from its inception, and other than the occasional 5 minute bout every six months to get a feel for how things were coming along I've all but avoided every piece of news about the game in the hopes that I wouldn't spoil myself for release.
I'm a long time fan of the Dungeon Keeper series and fondly remember as a 10 year old sinking entire school holidays into figuring out how to deal with digging into clusters of level 10 Samurais. Dungeon Keeper has and always will have a place on my hard drive alongside many of the Bullfrog classics, back when Peter Molyneux could keep up with his big ideas. How the mighty have fallen! Anyway my review ;
It's no secret that this game is a spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper, and while I want to keep in mind that it is it's own beast and I shouldn't directly compare for the sake of biasing myself, inevitably, and inescapably, this is something that will be part of this review. Thankfully whether that's right or wrong, WftO in my opinion has nailed the atmosphere extremely well. The background hum of dank dungeon corridors and the deep, thumping beat of your dungeon heart, alongside your insidious sounding, witty assistant has thrown me back to my schooldays.
Dungeon design itself I have mixed feelings about. There doesn't seem to be as much of an incentive to place down traps or dig your dungeon out in areas to encompass rooms and a necessity to mine out entire areas to make use of the tiles you get is apparant.
I feel like the actual map sizes don't compliment the number of rooms given particularly well, even if the rooms themselves are well thought out in terms of theme and function. Something as simple as converting particular rooms and their functions into room addons may be able to accomodate this where it makes sense - The Sanctuary's functions placed in the centre of a library with an expensive altar for example, or unlocking an arena pen to attract your Beast Master which you could then place on the grounds of an expansive and somewhat barren Beast Lair to fill it out.
I would assume at least for the campaign, fiddling with map sizes would require a horrendous amount of work, so combining rooms with a usefulness that seems somewhat saturated would possibly be a good direction. Some rooms feel a little empty and as a whole the sheer number of room types doesn't translate well to the room you tend to have on each map.
The maps themselves from a campaign standpoint are well thought out, the variation of mission types is welcome and I'm glad as it brings a particular flavour to each map which allows you to apply your creativity in different ways. Dungeon planning was always a big part of Dungeon Keeper and I feel like the variation offered in each map is similar enough to give you that "lets get to work, I got this" feel, without making everything too samey and keeping you on your toes somewhat.
My biggest gripe is creatures and battle. I have found myself a few times leaving rally flags sitting up against an enemy keeper after all but wiping each other out, resulting in a 30 minute long battle that pumps every level 1 spawn on either side into one place until something ever so slightly tips the balance. It doesn't feel decisive enough to be satisfying, as does the level increases for each minion. Level 5 and 6 creatures feel somewhat irrelevent, especially when you consistently go up against them in the campaign with swathes of level 1s, and having a level 10 creature doesn't have that feeling of acomplishment that DK had.
There is a feeling of overwhelming higher level units which again is not a good thing - I just feel like something is missing when it comes to how satisfying this is. I feel like more emphasis should be placed on the power of each level and battles should feel a little more decisive, in return I'd welcome a higher difficulty although I understand if some people would be put off by this.
Another couple pointers is the minimap. More clarity would be helpful, as would a little more intuitiveness in regards to what's going on where. And the hand! The actual reference point is lost on the hand and I really feel this needs redesigned to better handle some of the UI. The rally flags on the left for example require pinpoint precision to the point where the concentration to do so successfully is immersion breaking, and I regularly find myself missing torture racks when I try to drop heroes, even when it feels otherwise.
Bugs I don't particularly want to go into - Every time I check my downloads on Steam there's another massive patch and I'm quite happy to hold off negativity regarding this (which other than a restart of a map due to a broken ritual doesn't bother me. If you're playing this kind of game specifically to win the map you're on then I suggest you sit back, relax and enjoy letting your creativity run wild instead!), but it's nice to see so much work getting put into addressing issues that other players may have a harder time dealing with.
All in all, WftO is a great spiritual successor to DK, most definitely one of the best, you can see from the outset that the team really understands the intricacies and have most definitely made it their own while paying homage. I love to see what happens next and all in all I'm very satisfied with backing Subterranean.
Whether you're an old player or new to the whole concept, I suggest you take a look, regardless of whether it's for nostalgia or just for a new experience. I hold DK in a VERY high regard and consider Bullfrog part of a golden age which wasn't swamped by corporate fatcats, and true creativity was something to be welcomed and encouraged. I'm very happy to see a dev team capture the essence of this in a way that really pays homage to the concept as a whole. A modern DK has been a long time coming and I'm glad to say it's almost there. Just a little more work Subterranean, a touch more clarity and you got this.
Keep up the good work, you won over a venerable Keeper!

A nice blend of card strategising, and Batman-isque combat to keep you at the edge of your seat. Just as you're getting settled down strategising cards and managing your resources, you have adrenaline-fueled encounters to ensure you never lose your interest.
I never fancied card games, I always like a good ol' FPS. But with this game, I kept telling myself "one more stage and I will stop" and lo and and behold, I look at the clock and it's already 2am.
The dealer is both witty and engaging and relevant to your gameplay. His commentary adds spice and keeps the game from getting stale. Although the voicelines were sometimes repeated, it is still amusing to hear him commentate. There were numerous times where I just went "you little♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; as the dealer destroys me with a witty one-liner.
"Chance" events are exactly that, with 4 cards spawning for you to choose ranging from "Huge Success" to "Huge Failure"... except you realise it's not complete chance. You can increase your "chances" significantly if you have a sharp eye on the "Success" card when it gets shuffled to see where it goes. This is the mechanic I love especially, because it introduces a skill based mechanic within a chance mechanic.
And then comes the encounters, which I thought were highly engaging. On the first few stages, these encounters were simply boring. And then as I played, and encounter chained into another encounter, I grew more and more hooked. "I must finish ALL the encounters for "The White Council", I mutter, as I add every single chaining encounter to my deck.
Overall, this game has been extremely enjoyable, which surprises me considering I do not have any love for card games. Will be on the lookout for the second installment for sure!

- Do you like torturing your enemies to recruit them into your own ranks and send them fighting their own brethren?
- Do you think it's appropriate to slap your minions around your dungeon to speed up their work?
- Do you think that itsy bitsy micro piglets are the right way to stop underworld hunger?
- Do you characterize with some kind of higher being, e.g. a god? Loving, caring, just in a twisted kind of way?
The developers are a quite small team but have delivered a high quality game, even though it is still a bit rough about the edges a few days after the release i'm sure these things will get patched up quickly.
The price may look hefty at first but is ultimately rightful, as the game offers tons of quality content and delivers it in a fun way, especially if you dig the dungeon keeper "it is good to be bad" humour. However, you may want to wait until the price drops and more content is delivered / patched.

I have a certain bias when it comes to cyberpunk things like this, Blade Runner, Akira and Deus Ex are some of my favourite things ever created and RUINER is probably going to be up there. I don't want to say too much but the gameplay is excellent forcing you into crushing difficulty but giving you tools to push forward and when you do its incredibly satisfying. It is also drowning in style, the first time I walked into the hub area and heard Island Door by Susumu Hirasawa softly playing amongst the chatter and ambience of this dirty futuristic city, chills ran all over me. Yes its bad that you can't rebind your keys but the controls really do feel solid on keyboard and mouse (cant speak for controller), that really is the only criticism I can find thusfar the brutally difficult, fast paced, cyberpunky top down action game that is RUINER. I'd reccomend it to anyone who is up for an insanely stylish challenge.

Stunning pixel art dragged down by atrocious pacing. The story is barebones and rushed, resulting in a 6 hour long game with dungeons that still manage to overstay their welcome and turn into a slog. Boss fights are tedious and are far too often waves of increasing number of enemies until the boss just shrugs and walks off. The others you will know how to fight if you've played any video game in your life before, through the amount of damage those sponges take will still make you question whether you're on the right track anyway. All of this isn't helped by Otus' propensity to fly all across the room, splat on the wall and slide down when hit, which was funny the first time but gets old long before you get your first visit to stunlock valley.
Death is without consequence considering the game auto saves every 3 seconds, so the game compensates by having said tedious boss fights and enemies placed maliciously just out of sight but in your direct path so they can jump you like highway robbers, down to literally appearing out of thin air or out of the wall to whack you over the head. The final dungeon completely switches gameplay on you and spikes into being unforgiving when the rest of the game before was arguably too easy.
And if you're tired of that old trope where the villain is always a step ahead and arrives at the MacGuffin before you, even if it's entirely impossible, be ready to fall asleep at this game because that's what the entirety of the fairly predictable plot boils down to.

This game is flawed as hell but damn if I didn't have fun with it. It's a platformer with an emphasis on speed running and mild puzzle solving where you play as a girl trying to escape a virtual world called the Nexus. You can double jump, air dash, and ground pound. You can also bounce of the heads of enemies or kick them around with an air kick. You also have an emergency jump that's on a timer that allows you to jump really high every 30 seconds. You basically just race to the finish while doing all these things in order to progress.
The big flaw of the game is that sometimes the controls just feel like they don't respond. You go to bounce of the head of an enemy that is your ticket to the next platform and then suddenly you fall past it to your death. This maybe happened 1 in every 30ish enemies but it was really annoying. However, I feel as though the developer may have understood this was an issue which is why I believe the emergency jump was put in. It saves you from mistakes and keeps you going when you should have failed. The only other real issue was the final level's "boss." The boss uses different attacks at different stages but sometimes you advance into the next stage when an attack from the last stage is happening. It results in a mechanic that was easy to avoid in the last stage killing you in the next since it is not really fair for that stage.
This all seems bad but the game does so many things right. Movement is fluid and the music is amazing. The graphics are not great but there are still a few moments that look really good. I would recommend it on a sale since the game is short but for 5 dollars I would say it's worth it.

While truly there are lots of things to enjoy about CK2, and everyone finds his own most favourite part in this game, I personally find the stories it creates the most exciting part about it. For example, this story happened just yesterday.
One day my character was chilling in a carriage in his old family lands in Hungary when suddenly he was ambushed and taken prisoner by some weirdo in Brittany. The freak tortured my character with rats. What is worse, I had no money to buy my way out of the prison. At the same time, my lovely new wife became pregnant, and, for obvious reasons, this could not be my character's child. After the first daughter came the second and only then my unwitty spymaster uncovered that the weird guy and my unfaithful wife had an affair! Sadly, due to my liege's incompetency in managing the realm, my lands were constantly pillaged by vicious pagan tribes, leaving me with almost no income. Moreover, the regent that was installed to rule in my character's place was a nice and a charitable guy. He shared all of my petty income with the starving and underprivileged. He did not like my character either and never agreed to anything I have asked him to do.
My poor character ended up in a dark and cold oubliette after his friend tried to rescue him and failed. He soon passed away, betrayed by everyone. He only needed 20 more gold coins to buy his way out...
Soon after the news reached Hungary, king's brother was selected as the new king. Being an envious, lustful and ambitious fellow, he always found his brother's wife to be prettier and more attractive than his own. He immediately divorced and married the unfaithful widow. A few months later, the new king decided to relieve his stress by embarking on a carriage trip to his old family's lands, when suddenly they were stopped on a road by a group of french-speaking hoodlums...

The Dungeon Keeper feel is certainly there, but since buying the game as it was released I've run into a LOT of bugs. Does this ruin gameplay? No, but it does get annoying up to the point that I had to quit and go do something else. I do really like playing as long as the game works, so I'll list a couple of pro's and con's.
Con's (or bug report, rather):
-Loading saved games sometimes messes up the level you're loading, making minions and creatures just stand about, unresponsive to commands. Also the fog of war is sometimes reset, so anything you may have explored before will be covered up again.
-Tooltips that pop up when you hold your mouse over creatures or items still show the programming code instead of an anctual tool tip. Really? In a released game?
-Creatures sometimes get 'lost' inside a wall and can't be interacted with anymore. It also happens that they just get stuck in some trance and just stand in one spot for the duration of the level.
-Bugged dungeon state reports. For instance the food shortage message keeps repeating even though you have plenty of food available.
-The Desecration level. A dungeon building game and then they put in this level where you don't build a dungeon, but rather go Warcraft III and walk around with a selection of creatures and have to make sure they don't die. It's not a difficult level, just annoying.
Pro's (or the game as it is when the bugs don't strike):
+As I've said, the Dungeon Keeper feel is certainly there. Love the gloomy interiors and the demonic voice that accompanies you as you slap minions and such.
+Interesting spells/traps/etc. I also like the mechanic of researching those things in your library before being able to access them. The potions option is also a great new addition.
+Humor. Random messages of random sillyness going on in your dungeon.
+Potential. If the dev's buckle down and get this game steampressed (and *cough* the multiplayer option working *cough*) I'm sure it's going to be great fun to play.
So overall, I would recommend this game, but advise to maybe wait a while longer for all the bugs to be worked out. Because even though it's been released, it's far from finished.

I'll get this out of the way : This is very much an EARLY ACCESS GAME. What does that mean? This is the START of something-  and it's the start of something amazing.
My experience in multiplayer hasn't been the best, but that's simply because of lag / desync issues. That more than anything is my big unhappy point: I love playing survival multiplayer, so it's a little frustrating when I die to a monster that's only just aggroed and, to my vision, is still ten yards away. :(
HOWEVER!
☼The game stays very true to the feel of the Conan universe, and has amazing starting blocks for really fleshing it out.
☼Seems to play just fine for me, with graphics at a perfect ground of 'gritty' and 'fantastic'; jiggle physics could use a bit of tweaking, but it's not too unrealistic!
☼Customization is amazing, for an EA survival game
☼Basebuilding is a delicious mix of ARK's recipe learning and FO4's NPC staffing, Conan style: beat some hyborian exile into submission and enslave them!
☼Interesting 'corruption' mechanic
☼Summon your gods! Become the avatar of Yog! Destroy entire civilizations!! BLOOD FOR THE BLOOD G-
☼Mining. Mining is so oddly satisfying. The rocks crack where you strike, and crumble. It's hard to explain, but it's just SATISFYING. Try it.
All in all the game has GREAT building blocks to leap off from. With a bit of multiplayer optimization I'd have no gripes! As  it's an early access game, there isn't an infinate amount of things to do- aside from level level grind mats build build - but that's the core of any survival game, isn't it!
The survival mechanics work just fine, though I'd like to see a little more variation : sandstorms are wonderful, but I'd like to see a few more things? Maybe heatstroke during the day and hypothermia at night? The day is bright and great, HOWEVER nighttime results in some interesting reflection mechanics... and it gets VERY DARK. Not a complaint, just a comment!
Overall, 7.5/10 ! Definately something to keep an eye on if you're not willing to dive in so fast and enjoy the experience of watching it grow~

Link: The Unleashed Nexus is a fast-paced action puzzle platformer made by Reminisce. You start off as an anime girl who seems trapped in some sort of void or chamber filled with ethereal beings which you can pass through. Afterwards, you jump into the actual puzzle platformer aspect of the game. There’s a very helpful tutorial that teaches you the basics of dashing, moving, flying, etc that should appeal to newcomers to this genre and game overall. Soon after the tutorial is finished, you get placed into the game where you have the freedom to dash, fly and move around the area to reach the goal piece which is a glowing statue of sorts that you have to hit in order to proceed to the next room or level. I’m going to list some pro’s and con’s this game has to offer and finish off my final thoughts on this game.
+Intuitive Gameplay let’s you make your own choices and act accordingly
+Japanese and English layout and subtitles
+Challenging to the point where I got stuck on room 2
+Fast Paced
+60 FPS
+High resolution settings
+No cutscenes or dialogue saves the developers a lot of money
+Full Controller Support (I personally use the Xbox One Controller)
+Only $10
-Single Player makes it so there’s no interactivity with other players (not even leaderboards)
-Little sense of direction
-Decent Graphics (if you’re looking for Unreal Engine graphics, look elsewhere, they’re decent enough)
-Very few graphic settings. (Only “resolution”)
-Not an original concept (lot’s of other devs have made games like this; i.e Cloudbuilt)
-Hit detection for certain models slightly buggy
-ONLY Japanese and English layout and subtitles
-Puzzle layout’s feel familiar (copypasta)
-No cutscenes or dialogue makes the gameplay slightly stale
Honestly, this game is pretty decent for this dev studio’s first indie release and for being only $10. If you don’t mind the slightly repetitive levels, little sense of direction, no cutscenes or dialogue, the game offers a cool experience if you’re looking for something you can play for a little bit at a time and if you’re a fan of the genre, you should get it.
By the way, you can also find this review on my review site

You have one goal in RUINER: Kill the Boss.
RUINER is set in a wonderfully realized cyberpunk world where you play as the nameless, faceless protagonist hell bent on revenge. From the very beginning, the game presents one of the most aesthetically pleasing and cohesive games I’ve played in a long time. The graphics are fantastic and the world has such a thick atmosphere that it’s clear to see that it’s been lovingly crafted.
As for the gameplay, well it’s nothing short of phenomenal. The isometric, twin-sticks shooting feels great and when combined with the dashing and powers available yields fast and brutal combat that flows and feels great. Dashing around the arena, throwing up a shield barrier and switching to a supply drop (from which you can choose any gun that you have already picked up) feels super snappy and intuitive. Visceral is term in the gaming sphere that is often overused but I think it is quite apt in regards to RUINER as the brutality of the game is extremely satisfying. Melee weapons have a heft to them that you don’t usually see in an isometric game.
The game boasts a killer soundtrack that pulses along with the ultraviolence unfolding on screen. In this regard, it reminded me a lot of Hotline Miami. It’s a perfect marriage of gameplay audio working together to create an exceedingly memorable experience.
I’m going to keep this review short because frankly, RUINER is a must-play game. Along with What Remains of Edith Finch, it’s my favorite indie game of the year as well as one of my favorites overall. There’s so much to like here and pretty much everything that the game sets out to do, it knocks it out of the park. It’s an easy recommendation even at full price and one of the best games of the year.

Normally i don't bother writing reviews, but for this game, I'll make an exception. Valkyria Chronicles is an amazing game in which you will love the characters, story, original gameplay and visuals. It is probably one of the best games I've played in the last year, and I've played a ton this year. The best way to describe this game is: a great anime with gameplay mixed in. Even if you aren't into anime itself, but are just looking for a game with a good story, Valkyria Chronicles got you covered. The game is presented to you in a book with different chapters, each chapter has a number of episodes which can contain: gameplay, cutscenes or dialogue scenes. Visually, Valkyria Chronicles is also very appealing. The game looks like an anime, but with a sort of painted vibe to it.
Valkyria Chronicles' story isn't always about the pure fighting in a war, but really gives you a look at the lives of those soldiers fighting the war. Because of this, you really start to care for the characters, and might cry when one of them dies in battle (because the game has a permadeath system, but I'm not sure if this also applies to the main characters). But the main characters aren't the only ones you will get to know, because every unit you can use in the game has it's own backstory (although not as extensive as the MC's). During the game, there will be moments where you go through all kinds of emotions, from laughing to even crying.
The gameplay in itself is pretty solid and an entirely new take on the turn-based strategy. Each turn, you have a number of Command Points (CP). These CP determine the amount of moves you can make, so you can move the same unit more then once. Using a birds-eye view, you determine which unit you're going to move and to where. Once you pick a unit, the game changes to a third-person perspective, and you can move the unit like in third-person games for as long as you have action points (AP). Once per move, the unit can also take an action.
I would love to see this kind of gameplay again, the only throwback is that the screen in which you choose which unit you want to move doesn't always have a clear image of the environment (especially in the beginning). This resulted in me sometimes picking a unit, thinking i could move somewhere, only to realise that there's a steep hill in the way.

Desktop Dungeons is a rogue-like miniature RPG unlike anything else that could fit that description.  The game advertises that it operates primarily in 10-15 minute instances, which is appropriate, but not necessarily accurate, as the serious player will quickly discover that you will be well rewarded in later levels by careful consideration and chess-like strategizing.  The aim in each dungeon instance is to clear out the dungeon boss by leveling up, acquiring items, and making use of every possible resource at your disposal (including the unexplored areas of the dungeon: every new tile revealed restores health and mana) - which is deceptively easy in earlier stages, but will prove frustratingly difficult in later levels.  Think of it as much as a strategy/puzzle game as an RPG - and an excellent, if unorthodox, example of all these genres.  If you're on the fence try the alpha - available free at the developer's website - for a taste of what the game offers: the full release is both more accessible at first and more difficult at last, while providing more control over your circumstances at every step of the way.  Whether you are a casual gamer looking for a new fix, a hardcore gamer seeking new challenges of your wit and will, or simply a conoisseur of the quirky - I cannot recommend this game enough.

If you want to play just one mass effect game, this is the game to play.  No doubt about it, storyline, animation, detail, combat, music and sound, and overall game structure make this probably the most impressive game in the series.  You don't have the growing pains of the first game, you don't have the linear feeling and (well known) terrible ending of the first game.  It's not using generic situations to pull at your heart strings to make its point.  It is really the most well crafted game in the series.
The world of Mass Effect is incredibly well detailed.  A glance at the in-game codex (the major subjects being fully voice narrated) shows that they spent quite a lot of time fleshing out the universe and even the physics of how things work.  This borders on 'Hard Science Fiction' level descriptions of how everything works, and not just your average star-trek style technobabble.
The main characters, and even quite a few side characters and even some very peripheral characters, all have a story and a personality.  There aren't many games out there that make you really feel that a character who is otherwise completely alien can have their heart warmed or frozen by what is happening around them.
The graphics, considering the INSANELY LOW REQUIREMENTS this game runs very well under, are simply stunning, even in 2016 it is still one of the best looking games out there.  Sure, there's some low-res textures here and there, but they nailed it where it counts in a highly narrative game: Facial structure, animation, and texturing.  For a game that came out when the 8800GTS was around, and for a game that will basically run on anything, it's amazing what they managed to do.
That being said, sometimes the level designs do feel somewhat simplified (which makes sense), and the collision and physics model is incredibly simplified.  This sometimes leads to some VERY interesting bugs, and while this would be a pain on the console versions, quicksave and quickload on the PC makes it a mere hicup in an otherwise great game (especially considering that it loads very quickly on modern hardware).  The combat is very simple compared to what we've seen in more modern games as well, as this was technically an early title in the PS3/XB360 era.
Overall, though, this is a game that any science fiction lover absolutely needs to play through and experience.  It has become a sort of standard since its inception for games of this variety and shows that bioware was, at this time, the upper echelon of adventure games.

First off, I would like to give Crysis Warhead a neutral rating.
The game is good for many reasons which other reviewers already discussed and I agree.
There is graphical fidelity, exploration of the gameworld (though I did not bother with it) and mostly satisfying combat.
Unfortunately when facing many enemies and the bullets started flying my rig would not keep up the performance to show fluid combat in those high ("enthusiastic") graphics. This may be due to my hardware but other more knowledgeable reviewers find the engine lacking.
The island, i.e. the outside levels, is not overwhelmingly pretty which makes the beach huts somewhat comical. In contrast I really liked and enjoyed the inside levels. They were less forgettable and I were misssing those in the original Crysis, although Crysis had "The Core".
After I passed this initial boredom of the tropical trip I started getting annoyed by the badly directed cut-scenes. Those were too long and really slowed the experience of the "story". I wouldn't blame anyone for not understanding the "story" if they had not played the original.
In terms of presentation I felt like Crysis Warhead tried and someone had some nice ideas but those were not thought through and the execution was severly ragged.
As an example I once expected one certain pilot to die and see Psycho (protagonist) experience some emotional turmoil. But instead another nameless pilot (/soldier) died and Psycho copes with this heavy loss by drowning some unknown, unlucky, wounded enemy. Which I came to realize later.. disappointing me subsequently again.
If Crysis Warhead were an expansion or DLC of the original Crysis (which it is in a way) I would have given it a positive rating but since it is considered a standalone I see it falling just below the threshold to recommend you playing it.
I would recommend buying Crysis Warhead on sale if you liked the original. Anyone else might save their time.

What is DreadOut?
DreadOut is a horror game that is heavily influnced by Fatal Frame, or else Project Zero. Instead of an old camera however you are equipped with a modern smartphone, the Irisphone. Your enemies are ghosts that are based on Indonesian mythology.
Now then, let's talk about the story. You play as Linda, a high schooler that returns from a trip with her fellow school friends and teacher. You arrive at a broken bridge and while you try to think what you are going to do next, a troublemaker finds a way through the bushes and towards the village where the broken bridge leads to. Soon the whole group follows suit and you arrive at a school. You found nothing and no one along your way. The moment you enter the school, all hell breaks loose. Linda is seperated from her friends and now has to grit her teeth and get on with it in order to find her friends and escape from this place.
The story is nothing too fancy, is actually kinda vague all the way, but it's a standard one and doesn't go to the exremes in experimenting new ideas. However, the Indonesian mythology of ghosts, their origins and story as well as the visual perception of the ghosts are spot on!
The soundtrack of the game is also kinda vague, nothing too memorable, but the ambient sounds of your footsteps, the voices of the ghosts and so on add to the overall atmosphere of the game which is absolutely fantastic; you feel the immersion of the game, something very rare in horror games nowadays. Jumpscares are nice, but actually feeling dread, THAT is what horror fans such as myself are looking for! The voice acting is average at best unfortunately, something that destroyed the already bad character cast.
The characters of the game are not memorable at all. The only one that they did absolute justice upon is Linda, the protagonist. Through her voiceless acting, her demeanor, her composure, her unwavering willpower, you come to see Linda in a new light, someone that you actively want to protect.
The graphics are old and the game does indeed show that. They are not ugly per se, but they are indeed outdated, something that lowers the atmosphere score in my opinion. However, there are some details out there that are very nice when you spot them.
The game revolves a lot around the camera, as most if not all of its puzzles are solved through it. Sometimes the controls are clunky but once you get used to them you shouldn't have too many issues! If however you are using a controller for Steam, ensure the button configuration doesn't change, especially if you switch from Big Mode and so forth.
DreadOut is a game I personally loved and enjoyed till the end. There are some fun achievements as well, for those who actively seek them out like I do. It's not a groundbreaking experience by all means, but DreadOut taught me a couple of things. One, that you don't need a game to be overly complicated, it can be enjoyable if what you present you really worked on. And two, this kind of gameplay is not dead yet!
A game for horror fans, a niche even in that and a game that anyone can play, even if they are squirmish!

The game feels like it has a lot of potential, but it's just too damn awkward to play, which is a real shame.
- Clumsy menu navigation with a gamepad, with a menu to re-do your key bindings that seemingly does not work to re-bind controller keys.
- Confusing button layout on the controller: press (not hold) RT to bring up cellphone? Hold LB to run? It's not terribly complicated but you will fumble with it for a while. You actually seem unable to even go into first-person mode with a controller, which is one of the ways you find weakspots on enemies.
- Inability to adjust the camera sensitivity with a controller. You can again do this for a mouse, but not a controller, and the default sensitivity on the controller is way beyond what any Fatal Frame-esque horror game should be at. The combination of this, plus the completely free over-the-shoulder camera makes this game downright nauseating to play on tight quarters. Attempting to adjust the camera in these scenarios leads to it swinging around, gliding against walls and just generally being a pain to manage.
- Item scavenging is just plain bad. When you character can "sense" something, a blue aura will enshroud the corners of your screen. However, this works for points of interest *and* items at the same time, so when it starts shining, you don't know if you should be pointing your camera at an object or if you're meant to be looking around for an item. This is exacerbated by the fact that the aura seems to be triggered on a 360-degree sphere around the character, ignoring walls and anything in-between, so if you're on the second floor of a building and the aura triggers, you don't know if the item is in your floor on a different room, the next floor or the previous floor.
- Lack of a map. I don't know if I didn't just advance enough through the game to get this, but I looked around for a while and could not find a map of the school. Once I came across a couple of locked doors and had to start backtracking through that relatively big enviroment, I had enough.
- Kind of an ugly game texture-wise. This is just nitpicking, but there's a very big contrast on the texture quality of objects in the game. Some walls can have a respectable UV mapping while others look like the texture is blown out of proportion.
It's a fascinating window into another country's culture, but aggravating to control.

If you're looking for a card game / dungeon crawler / Batman simulator, this is the game for you, but you'll probably get bored before the end of the story mode.
It does a lot of different things, and most of them work really well. The art is great, the dialogue is well written, well performed, and well programmed (even by AAA standards), and it's just a really sexy premise. However, a lot of the elements clash against each other, rather than gelling together. For example, the Dealer is a fine character, but his dialogue distracts you from reading all the text (PRO TIP: you can skip all the text boxes and not miss anything). The tone of the dialogue is awesomely dark, which makes some of the goofy card text feel inappropriate. The card illustrations feel realistically medieval, and so it's really jarring when the combat looks like superheroes smacking each other in the middle of a laser light show, and the player is represented by a comedic murderhobo with a silly beard.
The first big problem is the combat system. It's exactly the same as the Batman: Arkham games, except much MUCH slower, more forgiving, and less exciting. The camera is useless, the hitboxes are vague, the animation and voice acting is terrible, and the rhythm just feels wrong. It simultaneously feels insultingly easy, and unfairly hard. If you're familiar with the Batman games, this game will just be really frustrating.
The second big problem is that the game feels really slow and sluggish. Every single thing takes a few seconds more than it should, and it really adds up to a big frustration. In FTL, when you get to a store, you click the "store" button and it instantly pops up. In this game, you need to wait for a loading screen to load a completely pointless 3D environment. When you make a decision with a random outcome, it shows this long unskippable animation of cards shuffling. And don't even get me started on how slow the combat is--it's like the battles are taking place underwater! And in case it's not slow enough already, it goes to slow motion whenever you do a special attack. That made sense in Arkham Asylum, because it's a very cinematic game about a badass superhero, but it just doesn't work in a gritty roguelike. (And in Batman, it doesn't slow down EVERY TIME, and you can push a button to cancel the slowmo.) I really wish I could set the entire game to 200% speed.
Ultimately, despite all the time you spend on exploring the board and managing your resources, the game just boils down to one combat encounter after another. All the methodical slowness on the game board feels like pointless delays. And since the combat isn't fun enough, it just gets boring after a while. To me, a good roguelike (like FTL) is one you can play over and over again. This game, I'm pretty much done with it before finishing the story campaign. So while there's a lot of good stuff in this game, and I had fun during the short time I spent with it, I have to give it a thumbs down.
(The "hours played" on my account is not accurate; I accidentally left the game open in the background one day.)

In the initial stages of Early Access for Conan Exiles, this game is just more of the same in its genre. It hardly adds anything new, nor does what it have retain much depth. While the developers are vocal and mean well, they have a lot more to do to set this game apart from others. So no, I don't recommend this.
More details below...
The combat system desperately needs improvement, as all you do is swing a sword and clumsily roll around to little effect. Higher tier weapons are weaker than lower tier, and there is little distinction between the weapons when learning a recipe, so you don't find out any of its stats until you actually craft it. Because of the way the level up system is generically constructed, you sacrifice being able to make a lot of other things just to see what weapons are better. Bows are all but useless, they hardly fire from far.
That just leads into the RPG system being lackluster. Since there's no point in using Bows, the archery stats such as accuracy have no utility. Stats only have one basic function for each one, and appear to have little effect on combat and the player so far. And what there is, doesn't explain itself well to the player.
Mobs aggro in a radius, and so there's no hope in sneaking past them. The landscape, while beautiful, is mostly the same. What survival aspects there are mostly just revolves around players killing each other, or just the player dying in the clunky combat. Not really surviving the elements, nor food and water. The rate in which your character consumes those resources is so slow that you end up throwing out stacks and stacks of meat because you simply have no use for them past a certain point. You can easily wander across the desert and forget the need for water.
It just seems like right now, this game doesn't have enough that gives it its own personality, and doesn't provide enough challenge and engagement to the player. I'm hopeful this may change over time. Unfortunately, Early Access games tend to stay just that, and don't dramatically change over the course of this development.

Normally i don't bother writing reviews, but for this game, I'll make an exception. Valkyria Chronicles is an amazing game in which you will love the characters, story, original gameplay and visuals. It is probably one of the best games I've played in the last year, and I've played a ton this year. The best way to describe this game is: a great anime with gameplay mixed in. Even if you aren't into anime itself, but are just looking for a game with a good story, Valkyria Chronicles got you covered. The game is presented to you in a book with different chapters, each chapter has a number of episodes which can contain: gameplay, cutscenes or dialogue scenes. Visually, Valkyria Chronicles is also very appealing. The game looks like an anime, but with a sort of painted vibe to it.
Valkyria Chronicles' story isn't always about the pure fighting in a war, but really gives you a look at the lives of those soldiers fighting the war. Because of this, you really start to care for the characters, and might cry when one of them dies in battle (because the game has a permadeath system, but I'm not sure if this also applies to the main characters). But the main characters aren't the only ones you will get to know, because every unit you can use in the game has it's own backstory (although not as extensive as the MC's). During the game, there will be moments where you go through all kinds of emotions, from laughing to even crying.
The gameplay in itself is pretty solid and an entirely new take on the turn-based strategy. Each turn, you have a number of Command Points (CP). These CP determine the amount of moves you can make, so you can move the same unit more then once. Using a birds-eye view, you determine which unit you're going to move and to where. Once you pick a unit, the game changes to a third-person perspective, and you can move the unit like in third-person games for as long as you have action points (AP). Once per move, the unit can also take an action.
I would love to see this kind of gameplay again, the only throwback is that the screen in which you choose which unit you want to move doesn't always have a clear image of the environment (especially in the beginning). This resulted in me sometimes picking a unit, thinking i could move somewhere, only to realise that there's a steep hill in the way.

"Hard Reset" is hard, really hard. I don't like the so called "retro" or "old school" shooters, which this game seems to pay homage to. Despite it all, I somehow loved "Hard Reset".
You're Major Fletcher, a human badass with bionics who fights all kinds of robots who want to take over the world. You've got only two weapon types - one that fires hard ammo, another with energy charges. Each of the two weapon-types can morph into different weapons. For example, the hard ammo type can become a rifle, a shotgun, a grenade launcher, an RPG, and a mine launcher. Each weapon-mode can further be enhanced to feature alternate fire modes. In short, there's actually a lot of weapons to choose from, and to survive you'll have to switch between them a lot.
The enemies are BRUTAL. Even the weakest ones can kill you with little to no effort if you're not careful. The enemies come in mini waves, and each wave is very much lethal. You can get blasted to pieces in a second, if you don't dodge, run, and shoot appropriate targets with appropriate arms. There's an amount of strategy involved here, too, although the game does at rare times feel cheap due to the sheer amount of enemies it throws at you. The few boss fights are pretty damn impressive, too. "Hard Reset" will challenge you a lot; it took me 17 hours to beat it on my first run ever (on Hard), because I died a whole lot. Yet I never truly felt like quitting, because the game always made it obvious WHY you died and WHY it was entirely your fault: you backed yourself into a corner, you ignored the little enemies, you chose your weapons poorly... every time I died, it just motivated me to try once again and turn those damn machines into scrap.
The game also seems to be nicely optimized, since it ran at 55+ FPS with medium-high settings on my rather weak HP laptop.
Criticism goes towards kinda samey level design, and the "Secret Area" mechanic, which often felt more like an in-game glitch. One example is walking on very tiny ledges - otherwise it's not possible, but on a specific level suddenly you CAN walk those ledges, but only on this exactly pre-defined spot in the level because a secret is hidden at the end of it. That kind of thing.
But overall, "Hard Reset" turned out to be a hidden gem, and a true surprise. So yeah, recommended!

Even though I gave this game a thumbs up in my original review, now that I've played Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, I realize that there is absolutely no reason to play Supreme Commander 1.  Forged Alliance is better in every respect and it's a stand-alone expansion, so just play that.
-----ORIGINAL REVIEW-----------------------------------------------------------------------
I would recommend playing Supreme Commander - at the end of the day it's a really fun game, and it has its incredible moments.  However, this game did not live up to its legendary reputation for me.  Granted, I don't like playing RTS multiplayer because I don't find it fun spending hours optimizing every mouse click, so this is based on my experience with singleplayer.
This game puzzles me because some aspects are mind-blowingly cool, and others are absolutely moronic.  Examples of the mind-blowingly cool stuff:
- Battleships that grow legs and walk on land AKA the most radical amphibian assaults you can imagine.
- Giant artillery guns that can fire on enemy bases continents away.
- An incredibly deep economy based on "Mass" which is used to produce things, and "Energy" which is consumed while you produce things.
- Experimental units AKA GIANT LASER SPIDER ROBOTS WTF!!!
- Tactical nuclear missle launches.
...and the list goes on.  But then you get to the moronic crap:
- Units and Buildings share a unit limit - if you build too many units, you can't build anymore buildings.
- Tutorial is basically "Welcome to the tutorial!  Here is a button that opens the in-game 20-page manual.  Thanks for playing the tutorial!"
- Units have no sense of self-preservation and make no attempts to escape enemy fire - if a unit cannot fire back at the attacking enemy, it will just sit there like an idiot and let itself die.
- No unit formations (that's kind of basic for an RTS).
and also (and this is absolutely infurianting), all your land units act like distracted people at a stoplight.  When you give them a move order, the ones at the front will
, then start moving, and the remaining units will not move until the ones in front of them have moved.  Imagine giving a square formation of tanks an order to move into an enemy base - that nice tight formation will spread itself out into vulnerable line, and instead of a wall of firepower overwhelming the enemy, your tanks will end up entering the enemy base one at a time politely letting the enemy defenses individually pick them off.
This is unacceptable.  I don't know if it's intentional, or if there's some way to prevent this I don't know about - but in a game that's all about large scale conflict, it's unacceptable to give a large group of units a move order and end up with some of them still at your base waiting for their turn to move while the front of the column is already at the enemy base getting killed because they have no back up.
But like I said, at the end of the day, it was fun to play and the cool moments this game provides are worth it.  I just don't think this is the RTS masterpiece that everyone claims it is.

Hard Reset Exteneded Edition (otherwise known as the finished product) is a sci-fi first-person shooter developed by Flying Wild Hog; a team consisting of a few members who worked on Painkiller. This was their first published title and you can tell that some aspects of the game were experimental or not fleshed out as well as it could be.
: The primary focus of the game is its gunplay. The game revolves around a kinetic weapon and a energy weapon with each having five separate forms and each form having an alternate fire function. The kinetic weapon functions as a rifle, a shotgun, a grenade launcher, a rocket launcher, and a proximity mine deployer. The energy weapon functions as a rapid-fire pulse rifle, a close-range lightning arc, an EMP grenade launcher, a sniper rifle, and a homing weapon. The weapon models look great, but it can get confusing in-game knowing which weapon is in what mode which can lead to some unwanted splash damage. Enemy variety is sub-par up until the later levels, where it upgrades to servicable. Another problem is that the enemy models, all of them robots, don't stand out against the environment often enough. The health system involves a non-regenerating health bar which can be replenished with medkits (some enemies can drop small medkits upon their defeat) and a shield system that regenerates when you're not under fire. The game also boasts a light RPG element where you spend currency to upgrade your armaments as well as your combat suit. There are also environmental hazards littered throughout the levels which you can employ to take out enemies. The few bosses in the game are a delightful distraction from the masses of robots you destroy as you progress through the stages. On a sidenote, the in-game interface is cleverly done since everything in the game is mouse-driven. Overall, the gameplay can keep you engaged through completion.
The story is easily the weakest part of the game, with voice actors phoning it in and the plot convulutes itself to a lackluster ending. The level design is cyberpunkish buildings through two-thirds of the game until it changes it up with a more varied environment at the final third. However, the design is also very linear with "secrets" that can be found by turning the other corner before going down the beaten path. Technically, the game runs smoothly with a benchmark inside the extras menu of the game.
I would recommend picking this one up if you want a shooter that doesn't adhere to the modern military standard. Before getting into  this game, you need to understand a few basic points:
1. This isn't a AAA game.
2. This is a "linear" game, and no, it isn't a downside, neither a flaw in design, it's what it was intended to be and what its target wanted.
3. No, you don't have -fake- "choices" to make or "waifus" to fulfill your needs of self-worth, it is an "old school" shooter with a half-decent story (with really bad dialog and voice acting) and it is heavily focused on gameplay and FUN.
When you play it on the hardest difficulty setting, it is actually HARD and sometimes it can feel unfair, you will get stuck at some parts and feel it is impossible, The game is broken! But when you beat those parts it is very rewarding and you realize that you just had to get out of your comfort zone ( your gameplay style and strategy). The reason I used  quote marks on the "old school" term, it is because this game is old school, but in a 2k FPS style. You aren't a minion jumping around in a big level as you do on Quake and Doom, your mobility is mostly horizontal and although you can jump over some stuff in the map, your mobility is not close to the one you had in 90's FPS tittles, but like Doom 3 instead.
The game has a "currency" called N.A.N.O. which helps you to get upgrades and some packs if such currency can be hidden in a variety of places, many of them are hidden  in the fashion some games hide their "collectibles" behind walls you have to destroy, others are just behind a box or a corner and they are very easy to miss of you don't explore a bit (but just a little bit).
Although you "technically" use the same two guns through the entire game, the guns change their form with a very nice animation each time you change to another weapon. There are good, feel nice, and aside from the basics, one of them uses energy and the other is a more "classical" projectile based weapon, they have many variances and again: they feel really well to use.
Lenght-wise, well, this game isn't an RPG, but after the complaints about its duration when the first edition was released, the game got this free expansion (Extended Edition) that added around 3h reaching  solid 6-7 hours,
The game is very replayable and it has some "arcade" characteristics/features:
Replayability of each level
Survival mode
Final screendisplaying completion time, percentage of available nano collected, secrets found (X/Y), etc.
Interesting bosses.
About the graphics: as you can see by the screenshots, it's very well done and rounded, artists really focused on making the metal look "real" and although ultra-realistic graphics isn't the main focus it  features very good good visuals.
Flaws?
Yes, it isn't a "perfect" game, although I struggle trying to not find this flaws on almost every TPS/FPS out there:

Crysis Warhead - When the expansion pack is way cooler than the original game.
Game runs on the same engine as original Crysis, so again you have great visuals, huge draw distances and so on, but Crytek Budapest did some improvements as well, like better optimization and so this title isn’t as resources heavy as the original game, but don’t get me wrong, you still need at least a good mid-range rig to run it on ultra settings. Developers also did improve the texture quality and lightning effects.
However game still runs like nightmare on 64-bit systems, and that's a shame, so you’ll have constant crashes, random FPS drops and so on.
You now play as Sergeant Michael "Psycho" Sykes, who were your teammate in original game, but unlike Nomad from Crysis, Psycho is voiced and has some character to him, maybe his lines and behavior is a cliche, but still I had a great fun filling his shoes. Psycho story-line is a parallel of Nomads from the original game, and he goes on to hunt North-Korean officer Lee, who's in charge of evacuating a mystical container which might have a nuclear warhead in it.
Gameplay is pretty much the same what you expect from Crysis, however, game escalates pretty quickly, you  acquire most powerful weapons early in the game and combining it with Nano-suit's abilities you feel like unstoppable Juggernaut of death, and to be honest, that's just so much fun to play. Maybe if the game was bit longer it would outstay it’s welcome, but for campaign that is about 8 hours long, it was perfect. Standalone expansion also introduces some new weapons like dual wielding fully automatic pistols and granade launcher, new vehicles as well as some new enemy types.
In the end, I really enjoyed Crysis Warhead, it’s a definite improvement in every way, but the technical problems and Crytech’s attitude to fix them for new’er systems just pisses me of. Again minus technical side, the game would be 9.0, but for current state – it’s 7.0 maximum.

My favourite game series of all time. God knows how many times i've played through all 3 games.
Great stories, great characters, great set pieces and great gameplay too.
Everyone has already praised its story and presentation so i'll just talk about the main shooting gameplay. I find it addicting and indepth. I can't think of another game like it. Closest would be binary domain or the division. Its essentially a 3rd person shooter with a skillbar akin to mmorpgs. The shooting feels tight though the mouse sensitivity controls could improve(the 3rd game is better in that regard). In addition to great shooting, there is strategy involved in a battle with the skilled management and execution of your skills (including your team member's). For example, some abilities are more effective against shields or some skills against shields and even different enemy types are more susceptible to certain ammo buffs or weapon types (assault rifles, snipers, smg's, heavy pistols and heavy weapons). You could also combo certain abilities with another to create a devestating biotic explosion.(Priming with Reave then detonating them with a Heavy Warp)
It may sound overwhelming but this game has a kind of Dragon Age -esque pause system. You can press Shift and slowly manage your team members and abilities tactically. Once you get used to it, I suggest hot-keying everything and playing the game in real time. Its more thrilling and fun. Especially on the harder diffculties. You feel like a complete badass.
Plus, having a bunch of different classes to choose from encourages mutliple playthroughs with vastly different playstyles. (my favourite being the vangaurd/shotgun combo class)
I also suggest playing the game on Veteran so you'll be making use of the abilities and strategies involved in properly managing your team member's positions. It might get frustrating at first but it makes the game itself deeper and fulfilling. Adding that deep gameplay to its already almost perfect story and presentation, you get a masterpiece of a game experience.
(though my current pet peeves is with its awkward and dated looking animations during the gameplay cutscenes but this is me noticing them after many many playthroughs)
p.s. Liara is best girl, don't cheat on her in this game. (Shadow Broker DLC is a must)

Crysis Warhead represents the apex of the Crytek sandbox FPS genre. This is the one and only time the formula's been applied flawlessly. Far Cry 1 brims with promise but is plagued with staggeringly unfair AI and bad checkpointing that can make the game sometimes unfun. Crysis 1 starts off incredible but devolves into linear COD-esque nonsense two-thirds of the way through. After Warhead, Crysis got consolized and turned into a generic linear shooter, and Far Cry got open-worldized and turned into a generic Ubigame.
But, for the brief duration of Crysis Warhead's 7-hour running time, the style is done perfectly. It's linear, of course, in the sense that you need to go from point A to point B, but there are innumerable paths to take and a variety of available playstyles. Want to stealth through most of the game? No problem! Want to kill everybody? No problem! There is a slightly more linear train level, but you can just jump off the train and sneak through the woods if you want (in fact, on the highest difficulty, you have to - staying on top of the train means insta-death).
The story is inconsequential and won't make sense if you haven't played Crysis 1, and the game's still a system melter just like the original, but neither of those things diminish how much fun it is to play around in these environments. Thankfully, this game has quick save, so you can play around to your heart's content and try different things without worrying.
Definitely worth the $20 asking price.

This is easily the most polished game I've played since Witcher 3. The small bugs have been demolished patch after patch with incredible speed. There remain only a couple potential problems and one warning for potential players.
First, combat can get drastically easier in the later acts of the story if the player is competent and meticulous. Second, load screens can be awful in party play, even if everyone has a solid state drive. Last, a warning. Co-op can be frustrating and requires patience.
That being said, Divinity Original Sin 2 is an immersive RPG. Quests are challenging and rewarding. The crafting and spell systems are inspired and expansive. Character customization is impactful and engaging. (Take the Pet Pal talent.) The world is simultaneously whimsical and dark throughout yet somehow manages to be thematically consistent.
Divinity Original Sins 2 is a gem of the fantasy RPG genre. Larian studios should be proud.

This game has many flaws:
- the graphics are PS2 era quality,
- the gameplay mechanics are painfully simple and lack any kind of depth,
- the story is told in such a way so that people have to puzzle it together and interpret it, but it pretty much fails, since not enough story is presented, and what IS presented, is a mess,
- Act 0 and Act 1 play like old school survival horror games but Act 2 is full of scripted (obviously experimental) sequences,
- the voice acting is poor,
- some of the achievements are broken...
And despite all of this, it is still better than 95% of the indie horror garbage on Steam. While it is not particularly scary, it does create tension (which is very rare in horror games these days), it has bucketloads of atmosphere, and some of the ghosts and sequences are really well done. Overall, I hope the developer gets more funding and gains more experience, since there is a LOT of untapped potential here.
<edit>
Forgot to mention. The gameplay is heavily inspired by Fatal Frame / Project Zero series of games (taking photos of ghosts), however DreadOut  tries not to blindly mimic it. Unlike FF, DO has something I call "monster ghosts" as in ghosts not of people, but monsters, paranormal beings. Additionally, the story is nothing like FF. It is safe to say that DreadOut's developers managed to create their own identity unlike some well received indie horror games *cough* Lone Survivor *cough*.
</edit>

Supreme Commander is one of the granddaddy Real Time Strategy games from the era of Starcraft 1 and the Command & Conquer games. Like its predecessor Total Annihilation, Supreme Commander is all about huge battlefields and hordes of units running around. No need to worry about building pylons or supply depots to increase your build limit, just mass produce your favorite units from your half dozen factories and overrun your enemies.
According to the game’s opening cinematic, the Earth Empire spread out over the galaxy and eventually fractured into 3 factions. The UEF is the “old guard” faction that is probably closest to modern day United States. The Cybran Nation / Symbionts were born from a fusion of human brains with computers to create enhanced artificial intelligence. And the final faction Aeon Illuminate is kind of an enlightened (or cultish) group who follow an alien religion called The Way (even though the aliens themselves were wiped out long ago). Each faction has their own single player campaign to conquer the galaxy, and even though they cross over each other, they have mutually exclusive endings like Command & Conquer. They don’t all form a single story, like Starcraft.

At first glance, Supreme Commander seems to be built around the ACU (Armored Command Unit) which is a giant human shaped robot that strides across the battlefield blasting enemies and building structures. In reality though, the ACU is more like a mobile command center. Other than being a really tough builder unit, the ACU doesn’t have too much going for it. It can’t build the more advanced structures and it’s not such a great fighter. However, if you lose the ACU, you lose the game. If you’ve played the Command & Conquer games, you should be pretty comfortable starting up with Supreme Commander. For one thing, fixed defensive buildings (turrets) are extremely hard to kill, so turtling in is a really effective tactic in the single player campaign.
If you’re used to playing real time strategy games, Supreme Commander’s build system may seem counter-intuitive. You don’t need to have the money up front to buy units or buildings since everything is paid for “over time.” As soon as you start building something, the mass supply (your money) starts being drained a certain amount per second. If you run out of mass, the build pauses, but since your mass is also gained over time (not in little clusters like Starcraft), the actual effect is that your build just gets slowed down (as soon as your mass goes up +1, it gets drained for the building). This means you can start building your entire base at the start of every level, but you should probably let some of the buildings finish first, like power plants and mass extractors (money makers). It sounds weird when I try to explain it, but it makes sense when you play.
Probably the biggest difference between Supreme Commander and a lot of other real time strategy games though, is the size of the level maps. The maps are so large that you need to use your mouse scroll wheel to constantly zoom in and out at different locations to see what’s going on. There’s no mini-map in the corner of your screen. The “tech levels” for Supreme Commander are also unlike many other real time strategy games. Your engineer (builder unit) can only build structures up to its current level, and the engineer cannot be upgraded. For example, a level 1 engineer can only build level 1 buildings. If you want to build level 3 buildings, you need to build a level 3 engineer. Every production building also upgrades tech levels independently. So if you have 2 land factories and one of them is level 2, only that factory can create level 2 buildings until you upgrade the second land factory. Honestly it seems like a waste of time to me, especially if you like to build large numbers of factories at once to really pump out the units.
Pros:
+Huge maps with room for massive battles between armies of units. The Air, Land, and Sea are your battlefield, and along with the expansive area, there’s a huge variety of units to choose from. There is a unit cap, but it doesn’t seem to be explicitly stated anywhere. If you just set all your factories to autobuild units, you’ll reach the cap eventually.
+Artillery! Long range bombardment is probably my favorite weapon in real time strategy games. You can have mobile missile launchers and even fixed artillery launcher buildings pounding your enemies. There are also strategic missile launchers (nukes) but the enemy can build strategic missile defense structures that automatically counter your nukes, so I don’t really see the point.
+The game is quite long, so if you are enjoying yourself, you can kill over 30 hours just playing through the 3 single player campaigns. There only seem to be 6 levels each, but they’re not straightforward “kill everything” missions. They usually expand the map several times each level (complete an objective, boom the map doubles in size and you’re now surrounded). Fortunately, Supreme Commander has a “speed up time” option that increases the rate the game plays. You can play at up to 10x normal speed, but you should really only do this if you’re waiting for your buildings/units to finish construction.
Cons:
-The game can be hard to get used to, especially the formations of troops when you have a large army. The naval units especially take multiple commands to get them to form up how you want them. The game’s tutorial is not in an obvious place in the main menu. It really should have been either part of the “campaign menu” or right above “campaign” at the start. Instead, it’s kind of in the middle of options.
-Since you’re constantly zoomed out on the battlefield to get an overview of the map, you really don’t get to see much in the way of graphics. You mostly just see dots firing more dots at enemy dots. Granted, the game is pretty old so you shouldn’t be expecting top notch graphics as the main draw.
Overall, the game is fun for people who enjoy real time strategy games. There are no steam achievements, so if you just want to see the story you can set the game to easy and slog your way through. Yes, even on easy mode it will take quite a while to beat the game because of just how massive the levels are. Remember to build up your base defenses, and the computer will crack its head open on your turrets.
