25% chance to just game over on an ironman style game. Game over, and very very angry.
Let me explain.
This is a game where many of your decisions are opaque; you have to make so many choices without full information, and without an idea what might go wrong. This is generally a bad design decision, but in Hand of Fate it is a feature. Early on there are simple challenges with simple outcomes. You keep encountering the same things, and discover through trial and error which things are worth attempting, avoiding.
The game screws with you a bit. The same card can have different outcomes that are not visible. When you're out of food, there seems to be a bias for gaining food from encounters, even ones you would not expect it from. There are variations of the same encounters too, which keeps the game fresh. These are excellent designs, though not perfect. I've had at least one run where I found 0 food. Which is annoying, but it's a proceedural game. It's bound to happen from time to time.
Settling encounters is done three ways: Decisions, chance and combat
Combat, which is often difficult depending on circumstance, but largely skill based (though having the right equipment and blessings will make you into an unstoppable monster). It's possible to win almost every fight regardless of what you are fighting, and your circumstances.
Decisions, as I have mentioned are largely opaque, until you have encountered a card many times, and seen all the outcomes.
And chance is settled by four cards, which are shown to begin with, then shuffled a number of times depending on the difficulty of the check. A 1 shuffle is really slow, and you can follow the cards with your eyes easily, so can more easily pick the success or failures. A 6 shuffle is so fast you are basically choosing at random.
BUT, the great success/success/fail/great failure is again opaque. Sometimes less successful checks bring greater boons.
And this brings me to where the system starts to have trouble: Sometimes to progress stories you must fail. Narratively, these make sense, but it takes away your agency. You are already making blind decisions. But now you're expected to go for a failure, when the rest of the game has trained you to avoid it?
Finally, the situation I found myself in. Play this game of chance with some devils (the fourth in the chain, I believe, and might be the first time I encountered this particular one). Yes/No. Hrm. These guys have cursed me in the past for failing. I can deal with more curses, if it comes to that. See the range of cards. Keep an eye on the great success... shuffleshuffleshuffleshuffleshuffleshuffle. Oh well. Ok. Hm. Pick. Total failure "At least you got an achievement, (12 fails/total fails in a single session)". Great, probably going to get two more curses... Auto dead. Game over.
So:
Opaque choice.
One random, skill-free check.
Automatic game-over despite all other conditions.
Automatic loss, on an effective total random 25% chance.
OK. That just happened. Can I play a game, that through no fault of the player, you can simply lose?
I could just avoid that card... but I also know that other cards have several variations. This same run I lost 150 gold and an artifact to a card that I thought only had beneficial effects. So yeah. Instant death can be in other places too. It could be on every card, hidden behind a check I have so far never failed before, or a variation I haven't faced.
My trust is broken. I cannot play this game anymore.

While I've my fair share of criticisms of the series as a whole and both the 1st and 3rd entries, I count Mass Effect 2 among the best games I've ever played and believe it not hindered at all by the imperfections of its predecessor nor its sequel.
Oh hey, I'm going to spoil some stuff by the way so careful reading. You've been warned.
It is, with some caveats, a masterpiece in writing, cinematic presentation, character design, middle-entries-in-trilogies, world-building and tight, focused gameplay.
For the most part, it's also pretty and varied in its art style and variety of environments, the only rough bits to look at are the splotchy textures on a few things that look like they're from ME1.
The soundtrack is incredible and memorable, and I count it as being among the best game soundtracks. Perfectly matches mood and builds suspense.
Fair to note at the outset I've got 130 hours logged on this copy and an additional 130 on another copy, so a little over 250 total.
Shooting and cover are responsive and enjoyable. While ME2 lacks the cover-rolling and melee maneuvers of ME3, I'd argue that the health systems, enemy types and level designs make for much better shooting and gameplay in the 2nd title than the 3rd.
ME3 segments enemy health into blocks or chunks, ME2 displays it all as one bar continually draining, the same applying for your health and shields. Very clear how much progress you're making towards killing a target.
More importantly though, most of ME2's engagements can be handled with methodical patience and careful use of cover and squadmates -- it makes even the hardest difficulty a joy to play on all but some of the collector missions.
ME3, on the other hand, is filled with missions involving reaper-type enemies that run at you and force you out of cover and involves more luck than it does method or thought. It was only after running through ME3 a couple times I realized just how well-designed ME2's experience is.
You'll get more frustration-inducing kind of difficulty out of ME3's experience than you will the kind of careful, well-designed and enjoyable difficulty you'll get out of ME2.
Of course, one can also look backwards and respond to the opposite complaint about this game's sheer divorce from ME1's RPG mechanics. If you want to argue ME2 has departed from ME1, you'll hear no argument from me.
Given what an awkward, bumbly experience ME1 was though, I don't think it hurts ME2 at all being a responsive, well-designed third-person shooter with RPG elements. I'd rather it was that than ME1 -- a third-person shooter that isn't sure if it wants to be a shooter or an RPG and just ends up doing the shooting, cover and RPG elements wrong.
(Hey, I can see those fanboy tears welling up in your eyes! Before you start writing some inane comment telling me just how wrong I am, I recommended ME1 too.)
I mentioned caveats, let's cover those. For those who did the majority of the side quests in the first game, you know that Cerberus is an evil human-supremacist group willing to do horrible things to achieve their ends.
In a fantastic writing twist, that same group decides to recover Shepard's body after he dies and reconstruct him, bring him back to life, make him into an effective tool both for humanity's interests but also their organization's.
In a not so fantastic writing twist, Shepard seems pretty chill about this. The player is given some opportunity early on to object but for the most part Shepard seems pretty okay with cooperating.
Given Shepard's history with and knowledge of the group coupled with his loyalty to the Alliance and affinity for not being a terrorist, you might think Shepard might look for more ways out or the game might present the player with such an option. At a minimum, it seems strange that we are basically funnelled into this path with little recourse in an RPG.
There are compelling reasons why Shepard might cooperate. They might feel, rightly, that they owe a debt to them for resurrecting him and they might also be tempted by that shiny new Normandy and the support of former allies Cerberus recruits. They also might agree, as the Illusive Man argues, that Cerberus is the only organization that recognizes the reaper threat at the moment, and will help him/her investigate and stop them.
That's all fine and dandy, but the player is mostly left to decide whether they accept these reasons in their head, There's not a lot in conversation and dialogue involving Shepard that makes it clear Shepard understands or accepts any of the implicit or explicit reasons for accepting their present situation.
However, that all being said, ultimately the choice the writers made to take the narrative in this direction pays off. We're presented with a complacent and careless galactic government that won't acknowledge countless colonies dropping off the map.
Cerberus recognizes it though, and has given you the resources and people to investigate. They suspect it's the 'Collectors'. A mysterous race that most have never seen that dwells beyond the equally mysterious Omega 4 relay. Of course, no one has ever returned after going through this particular relay.
Once this is all confirmed, the game sets you into a broader framework of building a team, one that is in it to go through the relay and stop the Collectors.
The team you build must be perfect, include the best, most committed and skilled operators the galaxy has to offer.
The Council has pretty much disavowed you at this point, and, even if you're nice to them, don't really want to see you poking your nose where it doesn't belong in Council space.
All of this sets things up perfectly for the game's setting: an adventure through the dark, criminal underworld of the galaxy. It gives the writers opportunity to flesh out new characters, species and places. Stark tonal shift from the first game. It gives them, basically, an opportunity to hugely expand the depth and breadth of Mass Effect's world. And this they definitely do.
Missions span hubs like Omega, Illium and the Citadel to war-torn Tuchanka to mercenary-infested Korlus to distant, hazardous Haestrom. Many more. You're introduced to a lot of corruption and dirty, self-interested politics and characters. Mercenary groups. Extortion. Racism. Murder. Not that you participate in these things, but you see them happening.
This dirtier, darker galaxy immerses the player quite well and really sucks you into the subplots of the places and people it affects. You'll care about the people and places of this world.
Many more varied places and situations to discuss, not enough space here to write about them.
In the context of these dark, horrible places, you're introduced to characters new and old and even the old ones are given new stories, as time has passed since you last saw them. You see characters evolve, change attitude and outlook. Great writing.
Past the old characters, the new ones are compelling and interesting. Everyone loves Mordin. Okay, not Jacob. He sucks.
Each potential team member is given their own mission with a completely unique level design, objectives and context surrounding their recruitment. Missions are varied and replayable.
The team that you build though, after all this world-building and character development has occurred over the better part of the game, is meant to undertake a suicide mission in going through the relay.
To say BioWare excellently builds up to this climax wouldn't do it justice. Your choices and the amount of time and effort you invest into the team you build play a decisive role in the outcome of the mission and you get a strong sense about how everything has built up to this point.
There are few moments in gaming that I can think of that compare to ME2's suicide mission.
There's so much more to say about this game and how amazing it is, but Steam recommendations have character limits.

This is an excellent puzzle game.  It's really a puzzle game more than it is anything else.   I'm going to recommend this game with on big caveat attached.  With all its frills, and new graphics, this version isn't all that much better than the FREE version currently available online.
Actually the free version is much more pure and streamlined version of this game.  The original is even better in some ways.  All of the extra stuff in the steam version of this are mostly just bloat.  All the "outside the dungeon" town building interface is really poor compared to the version slick a brilliant puzzle game that you are trying to access from the town.  Also it takes quite a while to unlock everything.  I have nearly 30 hours clocked and still have not unlocked all 9 basic classes.  Having to run 2-6 dungeons just to get the 2000 gold for an unlock seems grindy and is something the original free version lacks.
So what is improved over the free version?  The graphics are greatly enhanced.  The Deity system is better handled although they are a bit too powerful in the sense that using the deities is often key to conquering higher end maps.   The biggest upgrade is the amount of new diversity added to the maps.  There are just more scenarios and variations applied in each new challenge.  If you enjoyed the original desktop dungeons, this one takes what was there and adds to variety 100 fold.  With puzzles, challenges, interesting bosses, 2ndary rooms, and much more.
So yeah its good stuff, but I feel it's a little odd that some of the simple purity of the original gets a bit bogged down in some unnecessary bloat in its steam version.  And they should patch in reduced town upgrade prices.

My wife and I love couch coop games.  We're always on the hunt for new coop experiences to enjoy together and often times that means purchasing two copies of a game just to find out that after 4 hours in, it's just not quite what we were hoping for.  And while our itch is especially difficult to scratch, this game has finally done it.
This review is going to focus entirely on the coop experience.  I have about 35 hours logged now and while probably half of that is single player, the coop is what I feel sets this game apart.  If you're not interested in coop or multiplayer in general then this game could still be perfect for you, but this review might not be.
My wife and I continually came across Divinity: Original Sin over the last few years when searching for coop games but never wanted to bite the bullet and try it for one reason or another.  But when the sequel released I decided that it was time to give Divinity a chance.
First loading up the game my wife and I were overwhelmingly excited about how diverse and open the multiplayer system seemed to be.  While it'd be nice to load in characters from a list in your profile into any game, we still appreciate that you can not only play local coop/splitscreen but can mix and match up to 4 players with a combination of online and local play. And fully functional controller support (while a bit of a different experience compared to keyboard and mouse) means that our Steam Link just got another title that we can load up while lounging on the couch.
And for the cherry on top, Nvidia's Experience application means that we can share the game with friends and family who haven't discovered this gem yet for free over the web with a split screen connection.  No downloads required for them.  All they need is a basic computer with Google Chrome and a game controller and we can invite 2 more friends to our party to explore this beautifully crafted world.
Let's talk about gameplay though.  As Dungeon and Dragon veterans, we were astonished at how well Divinity captures the magic and freedom of that experience.  While you can't do ANYTHING you want, the limits of what you can do are seemingly endless in comparison with other games in the genre.  Even the WoTC licensed D&D games don't pull this kind of immersion off as well as Divinity does.
Within the first five minutes my wife was pickpocketing story NPC's and provoking combat in situations where no other game would ever allow it.  Not only were we able to provoke combat but when succeeding in killing these NPC's the game just continued on like it was totally normal and expected.  This is such a liberating feeling, knowing that if your character feels the need to murder someone for any particular reason, you're fully able to do so with just and immersive consequences, such as jail time or otherwise. And while we've seen this type of system in RPG's before, we haven't seen it much in such a deep story-based coop experience. And definitely not to this extent.
Let's talk standard RPG mechanics and how they're affected by coop play.  Going into Divinity we expected to run into roadblock after roadblock where one of us was stuck waiting for a conversation or twiddling our thumbs while someone micromanaged their inventory and gear slots. But wow.  Were we ever surprised when the game automatically shifted to splitscreen and gave the second player an unintrustive option to listen in on a conversation or to go on about their business.  What a breath of fresh air in this stuffy genre of late.  It was so nice carrying on two conversations at once, even if the voice acting took a slight hit by being cut off to start the next player's voice clip.  While this could get confusing, we quickly adjusted and still very much appreciated the developer's generosity to let us play the way we wanted to play.
Now we haven't got through even the first chapter yet, so we don't know exactly how much freedom you have in a split party, but from what I could tell, each player could go their separate ways entirely with little repercussion.  Of course, this isn't recommended in a coop game, and why would you want to in the first place?  But by separating at times with a plan of attack you can head into combat from different angles, or completely leave one player out of combat to be doing something else entirely. The freedom here to work as a team with your friends is just astounding.
But the best part of coop might be the freedom to work AGAINST your friends. At any time you can pickpocket your allies, give them stolen goods to have them arrested, teleport them out of (or into) a prison cell, poison them anonymously or even attack them when they're least expecting it.  This makes drunken game nights better than ever in my opinion.  With no rules your party could be a well oiled machine or a ticking time bomb waiting to kill each other at the next opportune moment.
And if all of this wasn't enough I haven't even touched the endless possiblities of GM mode where you can create your own stories and adventures for a party of 4 to embark on while you run the show much like a dungeon master would in D&D.  This is evidence of Larian Studios appreciating their audience and respecting the genre by going above and beyond. This feature could have been a standalone game by itself, but now it's a way to keep this game alive for years and years to come.  Endless content in a game with endless possibilities.  Needless to say, I'm smitten.
TL;DR
In essence, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the cream of the crop when it comes to multiplayer RPG's.  The freedom to do your own thing as one part of your party is just simply breathtaking and the attention to detail in this game wraps it all up nice into a perfect 4 player package that's just begging you to dive in.
I fully and highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a primo coop or D&D experience. The price tag is a laugh for what this game offers. Do not be deterred, it's worth every penny.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is what every D&D player always wished video games were like.

The combat mechanics are promising. But it just feels broken because the direction of the gameplay is shoddy. You'll spend 90% of your time bracing for an epic 1v1 battle and staring down your opponent, looking for that that one really awesome kill, only to suddenly die when someone cuts you down from behind and your character is too damn slow to back into a defensible position before you're completely ripped apart. Even when you're the guy ruining someone's day like this- it isn't really fun because you have to constantly worry about whether or not your team mate has their♥♥♥♥♥♥together enough to not accidentally kill you in the process.
Usually, one really good player carries the game. So I guess it's fun for the one guy who plays nothing but this game and learns the many ways that you can cheese players who are still trying to make it over the learning curve. You'll look at this game and think wow, this game has a good concept. But that's where it stops- the concept. The idea of this game sounds like tons of fun, especially when you consider the level of chaos that team damage and relatively small maps in which you're usually completely exposed on all sides because of the amount of open space there is everywhere.
It all sounds like fun, but in practice is just leads to a mess of people cutting each other down from behind and double or tripple teaming. You never get that 1v1 battle the game makes you want so desperately. The objectives feel meaningless, and few maps control traffic enough to create combat encounters that come down to anything other than sheer numbers or how you position yourself before you engage your opponent.
I have high hopes for this dev team because of the concept they've managed to deliver as effectively in terms of production value as they have. It's not the development that needs work- mostly design. A combat rebalance and map overhaul would do a lot for this game. So I can't recommend you pay $25 for this. It's just not fun.

Run the item shop, swindle old men out of their money, and send adventurers to their death for your profit!
Buy low, sell high! Get the money! Be the little girl!
Pay off your deadbeat dad's debt?
This is Recettear! You play as the adorable Recette Lemongrass, a little girl who is saddled with her missing father's debt. With the cooperation of the fairy named Tear, you run an item shop, buying low and selling high. Customers have differing personality types, some are willing to pay a lot more, while some will pay very little over base price. There are also times where a certain item will see a sudden, temporary hike in value, which is great if you already have that item, but you will also pay more for it if you don't have any to sell.
But that's only half of the game. The other half is a dungeon-crawler, where you take control of the adventurers that Recette can "sponsor." They get to make a name for themselves, and you get to keep the loot. This is where the big money is, as you can often find very valuable items in dungeons, and not having to pay for them greatly improves your profit margins.
You also have to effectively manage your time. You have to make payments on your debt every week, and running your store, buying from wholesalers, visiting dungeons, etc. all chew through your time slots in short order. You'll have to get a feel for what times are best to do certain things. You really need to rotate your saves in this game to avoid getting stuck in an unwinnable state. Keep at least one save at the beginning of the week, so that you will always be able to go back far enough to fix your mistakes.
Good game, great timesink, definitely buy it if you catch it on sale.

Stable. Haven't seen a single bug or glitch.
The world map immerses me. It looks good.
Cons:
Repeatative and Grindy. Biggest issue is skill learning which is need to use better gear and advance in the story.
Lots of waiting as a gameplay mechanic (healing = wait, moving a square on map = wait).
Same free noob gear, same mobs (dogs) for hours. Game feels unrewarding to play... and repeatative.
Stupid AI, which means there's really no need for tactical choices. Stats on gear > tactics.
Graphics outside the world map aren't inspiring. No character customization
Gear breaks quick. Extreme prices to repair so you will have to get new stuff all the time.

Honestly, I'm not very satisfied with this game. I'm about four missions in, and it is essentially the same game Dungeon Keeper was with a graphical overhaul. Feels almost like it's running the exact same engine with higher resolution textures.
It's been about 18 years since Dungeon Keeper came out, but War for the Overworld plays essentially the same as it's predecessor. Games have changed and improved quite a bit in that time, but WFTO is stuck in the past.
The Good:
Same quirky atmosphere you likely enjoyed with Dungeon Keeper.
Simple, casual gameplay. Nice voice acting. A pleasant way to spend a few hours.
The Bad:
AI is generally clunky and bad on both sides. Your minions are not very bright, but neither is the enemy.
Many maps are so full of caverns and holes that you can't really design a dungeon the way you want it to look. The map forces your hand in most cases. Combat is a complete mobfest, and usually involves dropping everthing and the kitchen sink onto your enemies heads, spamming heals and shooting some lightening. There is no strategy required.
The Verdict:

Summary (TL;DR):
+ True to the original Dungeon Keeper recipe
+ Fantastic graphics, sound and animations
+ Additional mechanics are fun, but feel natural to the genre
+ Challenging and rewarding gameplay
+ Return of an old familiar friend (the mentor from DK)
+ Frequent updates from an invested developer
- Minions lack style and personality
- Minor bugs, however, not game-breaking
I was a huge fan and hold many fond memories of the original Bullfrog Dungeon Keeper games, so seeing a "spiritual successor" to them made me raise an eyebrow. As many may already know, a handful of developers have tried to recreate the magic that Bullfrog crammed into the DK franchise.. they all failed miserably. However, these guys, swearing fealty to the original successful formula had a crack at making a worthy successor, and by god, they made it better.
What they have created is a maleficent and joyous game which remains true to the style of the DK franchise, however, with the addition of a couple of other game mechanics and room types. What is surprising in this case is how natural the game mechanics fit, the developers have clearly given a lot of thought into exactly how these extra mechanics can fit without disrupting the experience or alienating old players of the DK franchise. As a result, the additions make it stand out on its own as its own game and not some mere clone of DK2.
The game itself is beautiful to look at and smooth to play, hearing the return of the old DK mentor was a nostalgic and welcomed addition. However, if I was to be picky, I would criticise that some of the minions just do not have the charm, style, nor variation that the DK franchise had. Additionally, the minion character models seem to be of a lower quality than the rest of the game, whether this was done for optimisation, I'm not sure, but I did hope for better.
Many others have reviewed that the game has many bugs, I would partly concur with this. While the game does have a few bugs, I found that none were game-stopping bugs, just very minor niggles such as menu responsiveness. I take my hats off to the developers who have seemed to be updating the build like crazy trying to iron out some of the issues (we've had 2 patches in 24 hours of official launch at the time of writing).
Would I recommend? Yes, definitely. If you are a seasoned DK player eager to find a game that fills that evil chasm in your heart, or a casual player looking for a fun yet challenging strategy game, I would wholeheartedly recommend this War for the Overworld.

Alright, first attempt at a nice
Art: 10/10, no question asked. One of the best looking games I've ever played unless you're not into 16bit art.
World: I honestly wish the world was a little bigger and that I can travel more freely but it's not a big deal, especially without a map. Not having a map is a good move as it helps building that feeling of exploration. Worldbuilding is absolutely amazing, they managed to flesh out a full world and make it feel real in my 7.6 hours of playing the game. Still, it remains that we only got to visit two cities in this wide world that was created.
Music: Fits very well with the game, boss music is pretty goddamn lit.
Story: A few unresolved plot points and kinda abrupt conflict near the end, but it's still very good. I was quite surprised a few times (in a good way) at the plot twists in the story. It brings a lot of things and is much darker than you would expect from a game like Owlboy, and I think it succeeded in that regards.
Character: The characters are well crafted, and the protagonist is super likable. There's not much in terms of character development, luckily the cast is fun and enjoyable right off that bat so that is not as necessary. Still, I don't really understand Otus' mentor and why he did what he did.
Design: The level designs are various and creative, showing off multiples type of environment (all pretty as hell). A lot of people say the game was pretty easy, to me the latter boss fights really picked it up and unless you're quick with your reflexes and familiar with the controls, it's going to be pretty hard. Final boss fight were easier than previous ones in my opinion, so that's kind of disappointing even though it was probably the coolest.

I fail to see the actual game in this game. It is far too simplistic to be called a video game. Unless of course the target audience is somwhere between ages 4-8. It could be described better as "an addictive task" perhaps.
You basically make your way through side scrolling maps with an  army of creatures and collect more creatures, gold, and one-use buff items. There isn't really any combat or control for the player to engage in, Things just attack what's next to them for x damage vs y defense and hp. All you do as a player is hit the big green go button over and over. Once in awhile if you are feeling especially tactical, you might move one of your creatures up or down a grid space to go around a wall or to line up with a particularly threatening enemy approaching on your next click of the green button.
As you collect creatures, you "evolve" them, which caters to some kind of psychological yearning people have for pokemon "collect them all" addiction. Collect and evolve creatures over and over, building a bigger and better army. That's the entire basis of the game.
You just keep running maps until you progress your creatures, over and over. You don't play against anyone or anything. You just run maps.  If you get bored with running maps, you spend money to get gems, in order to buy more creatures, then you are powerful enough to run more maps. Keep clicking that green button.
The game claims that you do PvP fights, but all it really does is take a snapshot of people's armies and then you run a map with that snapshot facing against you, while you click the green button. No human is actually playing against you, and if they were all they can do is click thier green button, and perhaps move a guy in front to the back, or a guy from the top to the bottom. A tactical challange it is not.
I don't understand how anyone finds that to be a satisfying experience. There is no challenge. There is no game.
It is strangely addictive to collect creatures and watch your army get more powerful, but I remind myself that the progression is meaningless, because there really isn't any challenge to be overcome. It's just a matter of time or cash to get to the next map, not skill or thought.
Speaking of money. This game is not unlike the other games of its generation in that, it wants your facebook friends, it prompts and pestures you to invite freinds and hit social media. It begs you to spend money to accelerate progression and offers to give you creatures for your cash that are insanely more powerful then what you get in the game for free. I'd call it pay to win, but there really isn't anything or anyone to "win" against.
The worst attrocity is that, even if you do like the game, the game itself is designed to stop you from playing for more than an hour or so at a time, per day. They put a system where every map takes an amount of food and that food regenerates very slowly over time. If you don't have enough food, you can't run the map and have to eithe spend cash to buy more or log out and wait. Essentially, you'll be running 3 maps or so, do a little "PvP", upgrade a unit or two and log out for the day. I don't know many people that install a game and then hope they can't play it. If I am off from work and want to play 4 hours in the evening, I shouldn't be forced to log out and wait for 2 of them. It's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and annoying system. I suspose that if they didn't have it, everyone would just run through thier content so quickly that they wouldn't have time or need to make microtransactions.
This ironcally, makes the entire strategy for beating the game - not to play! Do not advance, do not get ranks, keep running the lower level maps as much as you can possibly bare, getting crreatures to fuse and evolve until the next map is easy as pie. The only way you can do that, is by logging out so that the timers reset for chances to get elites, and the food replenishes for you to run.
It's the same in PvP. The best way to win is not to play. Log out, run lower level maps. Consider that the game rewards you for getting a PvP streak as long as possible. So get 3 wins or 6 wins, and then log out, run lower level maps as much as you can bare for 1 exp a run, such that you dont gain rank, and then PvP again with you more powerful fused and evolved army.
Tha's all that's to it. Log out until food replenishes and all timers reset, then go in and slowly progress by running lower level maps.

This game is absolutely charming, is very well made and innovative and an absolute pleasure to play.
The gameplay is really unique, since everything you do, from your health, to your food, to your inventory, to the adventures you have to complete, is represented by cards. You "craft" the encouters for your adventure by building your own deck, but you absolutely don't have to like card games to enjoy this one. This gives the game a really distinct look and charm, while also being a system to add replayability and a choose-your-own-adventure vibe.
When you enter the combat, the whole game transform into an action RPG, with WASD + mouse controls to move and attack monsters. The equipment you have found during your journey in the card game will transform into real weapons and armors. The combat encounters lasts for a mere 1-2 minutes on average (excluding boss encounters). I have to say that this part of the game seems a bit out of place, the main fault being the spamminess of the attacks, which don't look like they carry lots of weight. It is not my favourite part of the game at all, but it can be enjoyable nonetheless.
The encounters are really varied, some are luck-based, some may require combat, some advance the story a little. There are really lots of them, from the simplest dialogue-based ones, to events having multiple possible outcomes. Most encounters form an arc, spanning multiple encounters and playthroughs to reach the end of the narrative. Some events, if kept in the deck, can become a bit stale and repetitive, of course, since the outcome of an event is scripted (at most depending by 1 or more luck/skill based card draws, or a combat encounter), but they can be swapped out for other cards to keep the game fresh and enjoyable.
The DLC Wildcards, which I got for free during a promotion, adds even more events, on average more complex than the base game ones.  It also adds talents to the player, which change a bit the way of playing. You have to choose one talent before starting your next adventure, with can increase/decrease the combat proficiency, the speed of cards in the card draw minigame, the health and damage of the monsters etc. I find that the DLC increases exponentionally the replayability of the game. The only thing I didn't like of DLC (up until now, at least) was the Goblin Hall event series, which have the player try to reach the end of a little maze filled with traps: since the game was not made for a platformer, avoiding traps and obstacles is way more cumbersome than needed, making that section a little frustrating. Except for this, I recommend getting the DLC for this game, for the replayability and variations it adds.
Huge props for the card dealer, which makes the game really interesting and fascinating.
Overall I find this to be a really great gem of a game, I absolutely recommend this to everyone.

Firstly, I need to enter in my overall bias for the game. It's Australian made, therefore it's freaking awesome!
That aside the game delivers a turned based competent along with a live-action platform environment. I'm going to describe both for you.
The turned based competent is a card delivery system where prior to going on your adventure you can select your deck of cards for scenario's and then select your deck of cards for equipment (ranging from weapons, sheilds, armour, rings and spells). The higher you rank in your adventuring quest the more cards you can have in your deck.
You start your adventure on a 'dungeon crawl' in a turned based environment where food and gold is your life essence to get to the end game/boss. On each move a random card is flipped to tell you a tale or a random scenario that you will need to select your course of action. The course of action may having you flipping on a x4 success or failure card. Failure could result in lost health or food/gold. Getting to traders and selling some of your gear helps you move on.
A scenario based could result in an encounter - which then brings you to the live-action platform part of the game, you have your warrior in a rear facing fight controlled by mouse and keyboard (gamepad optional). The card flip will result in the amount of monsters you are engaging and the tier level of monsters. Your fight then has you fighting trying to keep your hit sequence as high as you can to score crits, so it can bea a fast flowing combat.
Overall this is a great go to game when you have 15 minutes or 2 hours to spare gaming. End of game will score you 'chips' which give you more cards to play with.
There are modes you can play in for difficulty and an endless mode to see how far you can really go too, which is highly enjoyable or at times distarous based on your choices.
A great game for the avid casual gamer market.
Oh and the dealer has pure sex for a voice :)

Hand of Fate is... a strategic action brawler game? I'm not quite sure how to categorize Hand of Fate, other than the words "pure genious".
Picture this: you are a traveller seeking what destiny awaits you. A mysterious fortune teller deals cards face down as if they were the lay of the land, and you move your token across them. Upon contact, the card is lifted and revealed: you have an encounter. You do not necessarily have to fight to resolve most of them, nor should you shy away from combat, nor should you attempt to engage in combat. Each and every choice has potential outcomes and you are encouraged to experiment them all.
Of course, you might consider the above description of the gameplay a little vague. Simply put, gameplay revolves around four phases.
1) The choice of which adjacent card to move onto, searching for the exit or the boss encounter.
2) The event is revealed, which in turn requires that you make choices on your actions and/or throws you into combat.
3) The event is resolved, or you died, or something good or bad happened. Either way, consequences.
4) You appreciate or despise what happened and move on to the next event as you continue your quest, or start anew if you got killed.
The reason this game is so good isn't the simplistic combat when you do fight, nor is it entirely the great amounts of rich descriptions of the events you encounter (although that really helps). It is the dealer's words, commenting on what appears before you, your choices, his scorn when you take his pieces or his joy in seeing you suffer for what torments you. The dealer is an entire third of your enjoyment in this game, and it doesn't disappoint.
Frankly, this is the game that I return to play sessions of between 10 minutes to about an hour every now and then. It is wonderful, even when you have seen practically all the possible encounters over and over again. But don't let my words deceive you: you will start the game with few things unlocked. You must complete the dealer's challenges, and with them you are rewarded cards to add to his deck. From better equipment to harder monsters, crossing through new and mysterious encounters as the game naturally progresses to a harsher state with more variability.
You will rage. You will laugh. You will listen to a story in which you are the protagonist and the story-teller is your opponent. And you will love the Hand of Fate.
Buy it, definitely. Maybe with a discount, but it's really a good game. As of the time of writing, there's also something else you should consider:
If you like the Hand of Fate, or if the Hand of Fate 2 is as good or better than the first, buy them both!

Confess my Love is a cute little RPGMaker game with very basic elements, short and bittersweet.
The main character is a nice guy that keeps being rejected by his love interest. Each new playthrough offers different stuff to examine or items to collect, although those are very limited in scope and number, and new dialogue options are unlocked. The game works on two levels: Time and Conditions. There is a clock that will count up to 5 minutes, during that timespan, you can confess your love and collect \ use items, combining their usage with the passing of time.
Admittedly, of the 20 endings presented by the game, the first 15 are entirely based on your patience (they all require you to do something at a certain time) while the remaining 5 are based on luck (a certain condition has a 1\3 chance to be met) so chances are you will have to repeat the process at least a couple times. All in all, the flow of the game is quick enough to keep you busy but I would have personally preferred a quicker clock - not a real-time one - maybe 30 seconds equals 1 minute in game would have been better. Regardless, that's a minor complaint, the story is already short as it is.
As a simple story, once you start figuring things out a little, you immediately know where it's headed, but in this case it's not a disappointment. It's competently done, tells what has to tell, and fades away like a fleeting memory from another life.

Hard Reset is a slick, unforgiving FPS that feels ripped from the genre's roots. Were it not for the updated graphics and more responsive controls, you'd swear this direct was kin to Wolfenstein, Doom, and Quake. Coat it in a lusciously dystopian cyberpunk coat of paint and you've got me by the sensitive bits; just be aware that Hard Reset is liable to kick you in those bits just as readily.
Pulling no punches, Hard Reset puts you in the shoes of Fletcher, hands you a strange energy weapon full of upgrade potential, and then starts lobbing wave after wave of robotic foes at you with little time to breathe in between. Action becomes stick-and-move most of the time as you work your way around each level, avoiding fire more than taking cover from it and taking as much advantage as you can of the environment. That environmental element was probably my favorite aspect of the game, as traditional exploding barrels are joined by things such as electrical boxes that can short out your opponents, and just natural-feeling static elements like barriers and columns that can, to some degree, help control enemy direction and flow.
Unless you've been maintaining your twitch reflexes since FPS' toddler days or you're gifted with ungodly reaction time, Hard Reset is likely to kick you around quite a bit at first. Stick with it, though, and explore your upgrade options for your weapon. Once you've gotten the feel for the game's flow and found a setup that suits your needs, things start thrumming like, well, machinery.
I'm very impressed with this game. It's got a surprising amount of strategy in the combinations and timing of the simple mechanics. Thumbs Up!

A tip: if you want to try this game out, there is no on-Steam demo, but a good way to get a feel for how it plays is to mess with the ancient alpha build, still on the company's website.
That said - this is a quick yet strategic take on the roguelike concept. The world only moves when you a) take an attack (ie, cast  a spell or hit someone, maybe use an item to do so) or b) explore uncharted tiles. But barring specific enemies, you're the only one who ever moves. Meanwhile, your stats and the enemy's stats are visible at all times, including a convenient little tooltip that will tell you what effects come of performing X on Y target (up to and including "DEATH" - do not do anything that will result in this!).
The game, as a result, comes from mixing risk and reward: do you try and take out a higher-level enemy to start for the bonus XP? Do you spend more time exploring the map (which will potentially raise stats, but also deny you HP/MP regeneration later) to find a weaker first target? Maybe there's a potion a few tiles away, or a handy spell glyph to use? Everything becomes second-nature over time and soon you're playing each race/class (there are plenty of combinations - races give specific bonuses, classes a set of three skills/boons) like... well, not a pro, this game gets hard as heck. But a veteran. A war-torn, blood-stained veteran with plenty of your own corpses in your wake.
I absolutely recommend it, but you should really try that alpha if you haven't to get a gist of how this works. It's not your standard take on the genre at ALL. (The new edition includes plenty of new tricks and a continued kingdom to develop via your conquests, though, so don't assume it's worth sticking with the freebie.)

This little thing has been sucking up a wholly inordinate amount of my time lately.  It is on its face a little rpg lite type game, where you maneuver a little adventurer around a series of procedurally generated maps looking for loot and baddies to win to level up to face the boss.
That on its own would be cool and fun and a little enjoyable time waster, but there is a second 'meta' level of developing your town between quests to gain access to better starting goodies, more classes, races, etc.
Even then, I would have been happy to play on its own, but theres something more devious and hooking (for the right kind of personality) than either of those first two aspects.  When it comes right down to it, the game is quite simply far too hard to enjoyably play on just its face value.
The tutorials begin to show you the true way, which is that really every map is not so much a dungeon to adventure in, as a very cunning and difficult puzzle in the shape of a dungeon.
There is absolutely a 'right' way to pass through each little dungeon that maximizes your xp, items, and chances to victory, and it is almost never the straight forwards way of just running around and clicking enemies as you come by them.
You want to slow down, pace yourself, calculate each new move, each new click to maximize the value that you can extract from each scenario.  Sure you can fight a bunch of random level 2 or 3 enemies, when you are level 4, and you will win each fight easily.  However if you alter the pacing, and fight one of those level 3 enemies when you are level 2 instead (and have the right mix of skills/stats/items to win) you'll get a serious XP boost for defeating it.  Multiply that out by the 20 or 30 enemies on a map and you can be a whole level or two higher when fighting the final enemy.
Each class and race has some little unique twist which lets you change the rules around and re-optimize your approach, and you can mix and match some of the random dungeon attributes (as you level your town up) to maximize your chances with the mix you choose for each map.
TLDR?  This game is far deeper than it appears, its much more tactical/strategic than it is a cute little rpg, and the difficulty level absolutely demands you play to the higher level if you want to get through all the various scenarios of the later game dungeons.

Its a real shame that this game isn't more well known, it's a fantastic game. For a Japanese Indie game made in 2007 that hasn't seen any sort of franchise continuation or update aside from the 2010 english port it still holds up. It's worth every cent and if you catch it when it's on sale for 5$ there's absolutely no reason on earth that you shouldn't buy it.
Game Mechanics you can look forward to:
- Simulated real world economy: There's a famine? Time to sell high, sorry folks. War in the north? Boy have I got the weapon stock for you.♥♥♥♥♥♥everything made of metal has gone down in price, allright when I said weapons earlier I meant wooden staves/bows and gloves, back you savages.
-Dynamic customer interaction: Customers can place orders to pick up items, randomly ask if you have items even if they aren't on display, influence what type of customers come into your store with decore and choosing what window items you display
- Bartering: This is a game about buying and selling, and one of the best things about this game is the bargainning you do with each customer  that comes in. Try and charge to much/too little and eventually they'll get fed up and leave, but are they bluffing? See how low you can buy what they're selling and how high you can charge.
-Dungeoneering: As you progress through the game you will meet various adventurers who you can eventually choose to take with you into dungeons once you've earned it. While in the dungeon you play as the adventurer and each one has unique special abilities and regular combat abilities.
-Acquiring Stock: Don't feel like going through dungeons? Go to the market place and stock up on whatever you want to sell you coud play the whole game without setting foot in a dungeon if you want. And you know that Dynamic economy I mentioned earlier? Those events also apply there so buy low so you can sell high later. Alright so you want to dungeon? Grab the most valuable loot and gather crafting ingredients so you can craft the highest value items
-Elaborate, tiered crafting system (Maybe somethings will be highly profitable to craft and sell maybe some won't you'll have to find out)
-Charming Character cast: Throughout the game there will be oppurtunities to take a break from the life of a shop keep and interact with the guild adventurers and townsfolk. Sometimes people will even come into your shop specifically for dialogue events.
Non game mechanic Things you can look forward to:
- Trying to sell 500 dollar alcohol magazines (with tasting samples) to kids
- Having an old man come into your store and sell you a highly expensive vase for cheap, and then coming back the next hour and buying it for 3x the price he sold it to you.
- Throwing your hands in the air and ask "WHY DO YOU EVEN NEED THIS!?" when an old man comes in with a request for 5 pieces of heavy plate armour
-Ripping off kids and having kids try to rip you off.
- Having a fairy loan shark who's not all bad but still going to take your house unless you make your payements since your dumb dad went on an adventure and left his 12 year  daughter with a massive debt.
Seriously, this is my top game to buy as a random gift for friends because chances are they've never heard of it before. 10/10 you'll get your money's worth

This game is fantastic. I haven't played an RPG that has had me this involved in strategizing the fights before they even start in so long. This was the fight I had last night that made me know I was playing something special.
I barricaded myself in the room on top of the keep with dressing room walls, chairs, and chests. The NPC's came after me chasing my rogue who I had used to pull them. She ran back into the room where we were barricaded, and I had my undead warrior use telekinesis to move the stuff into place before they got up there. They consisted of 2 ranged 2 melee and a dog. The dog couldn't climb the ladder to get up there, and the other 4 chased. When they got up there, they started hammering away at my barricade. I used my teleport gloves to port the ranged guys in one at a time, and massacre them with my whole party, (wayfinder, inquisitor, summoner, rogue). By the time I had ported both the ranged in and killed them, the melee had made in through. I used my wayfinder to shoot a poison arrow at my undead inquistor (basically a deathknight) who is healed by poison. I then summoned a bunch of poison totems/poison incarnate. My inquisitor was nearly invicible at this point. I teleported one of the melee enemys in while the other took care of the last barricade I had made. At this point they were screwed.
After that, all I had to do was take my party down the ladder and massacre that poor little dog. RIP doggy. I could go on and on about different fights and things that I've had to figure out ways I would have never thought of to win, but this was my favorite fight so far.
TL;DR, This game has some of the most engaging and interesting combat I've ever seen in an RPG. If you know what you are doing, and can figure out how to use the terrain to your advatage, you can win fights that seem impossible. I love it. The game does not hold your hand, and that's what makes it amazing. The freedom you have to figure out how you are going to take care of every single situation you get yourself in, and never knowing what's around the next corner, or who is actually an enemy or friend is amazing. I love this game. Worth the money I spend already, and I'm still on the first island. Must buy game if you love tough RPG's with combat like The Old Republic or Final Fantasy Tactics but with more strategy thrown in, mixed with tough story driven choices.

Like many early 3D games, the game is pretty much unplayable in 2015 without lots of patience and tolerance. Basically, the player clicks around with the mouse to interact with the 3D environment, to turn around, to move. There's no free movement. The greatest challenge of the greatest detective ever is apparently to figure out what the low-resolution graphics are supposed to represent: what of the stuff is actually clickable and what is just some obscure mess. This difference can be found out by panning the mouse on top of everything and seeing if the pointer changes. Its not even clear where you can click to move, without doing this panning. The inventory handling is also terribly clumsy. If this wasn't all, on my Windows 7 the game reliably crashes on each alt-tab.
The mystery of the mummy might have been a nice game to play in its time, but because of its technical problems its no use to go to the actual content, and I wouldn't recommend it for the modern age.

So, you're looking for an RTS to play, and this one has popped up in the list.
You've played a fair few RTS games, and certainly most of the mainstream ones.
This one claims to be different, better give it a look.
Now, there are reviews that have gone into far more detail than I'm going to offer you, but what I will say is very important.
There are a few games where economies are progressive for units - that is, the resources you have amassed drain away as the unit builds.
Now, you'd think this method would be used more wouldn't you? Well, it's hard to balance properly - you've got 3 unit factories building units, and then you run out, so all of them stall, wasting more time than if you had built one at a time right.
What Supreme Commander does is sort out those balance issues, and expand on the progressive economy aspect.
Units, buildings, upgrades, super weapon use... all of these things are linked into the economy almost 100%, with time being the only real drain on that percentage (super weapons take a proportionate amount of time to build etc).
Building thirty different buildings including factories, defences and superweapons as well as running 12 different factories and existing artillery/superweapons and out of resources?
Simple! Pause production on a few of the factories and some of the superweapons production.
Not enough? Stop the artillery from firing, maybe even turn off some shield generators or resource converters.
Sounds simple, but it's on such a large scale that it feels like running a proper future war economy.
Now, maybe you've decided that you REALLY need to get some of those buildings built. Ok then, convert dead units into resources. Not enough? Convert functional units into resources, or maybe one of the buildings you don't really need?
Haven't got the time to convert things into resources? Ok then, build your buildings over the destroyed remains of the same kind, that'll cut the time and resource cost by up to half!
Or hell, you could go full city planning mode and arrange your resource-consuming buildings next to your resource-producing buildings.
Why do that? "Does the electricity not have to go as far, so therefore it's more efficient?" you might smirk and say, but yes actually.
Building like this puts in place what are basically powerlines between the buildings. This synergistic effect is incredibly noticeable almost immediately - a building produces 20 of a resource, or produces 20 of a resource and reduces the cost of the same in another building by 1%, and you can fit 20 along the sides of the building?
This actually adds another element of risk though, big resource producers take a lot of synergised buildings with them, and those that survive take pretty hefty damage, which is what you'd expect - energy substation just got blown up, it's going to take some appliances down with it.
And on top of all of the above, on top of all the super weapons you'd expect in an RTS, there is the commander unit.
A core engineer unit isn't anything new to RTS games, but have the same potential for hilarity.
Ever rushed an enemy with SCVs in StarCraft just to mess with their heads?
What about rushing them with a veritable super weapon that unleashes a thermonuclear explosion when it dies?
Not even Michael Baysplosion could hope to top that.

If you were a fan of the classic robot armada strategy Total Annihilation you will be right at home with Supreme Commander.
With land, Air and Sea battles, constant attacks, limited resources and vast battle grounds there is plenty of warfare to be had. At times the pace feels slow, particularly when setting up your initial base on a large map, however, when you find yourself being hammered by endless hordes of your opponents forces, almost in a panic trying to grind out a force good enough to repel the attacks, all the while desperately defending your resource production line, you will at times miss the slower pace of the base building phase.
The story is somewhat shallow and is really just a hook to guide you from world to world, ultimately leading to that all important end-game battle, but you didn’t come here for the story, did you?
Multiplayer is the most fun aspect of this game. It is even more enjoyable when you play locally and can hear your opponent scream and curse you when you expertly execute a fast air attack, taking out metal production and temporary shutting down his unit production. The matches can be long arduous events and occasionally the victor might be determined by someone giving in, rather than a skilful victory, but still there is much fun to be had, just choose the map according to the intended game time.
With all that said Supreme commander is a lot of fun and well worth your invested time and energy.

This game already has great reviews so I will just add my short two cents.
Pros:
- Very fun gameplay - Even an extremely casual game like this can have tense moments when you are 2 strokes from beating your friend who's right behind you.
- Mechanics - The gameplay mechanics are above decent. Not perfect, but great. I can judge my direction and power pretty easily, and have an idea of what I am doing.
- Freeform Camera - Pressing "C" in game will let you fly around in "noclip" mode, so you can view the courses. This needs to be made more clear from the get go, it took me several games to figure this out, and until then, I was shooting blind hoping for some kind of miraculous Hole-in-One.
- Random multiplayer server support, you don't HAVE to play with...your friends...
Cons:
- Early Access Game, so there are some bugs. A hole (I don't recall which number) in the Candyland map allows you to fall off the course behind the hole, and if you roll back underneath the map, you can hole your ball underneath it, due to the detection trigger the map uses. It was very annoying that one of our friends tried to tell us it was a fair shot when clearly it was a glitch.
- While teeing off is simple and you can jump right into it, some other commands and ideas are not so easy. It was very hard to learn what to do on some maps (candyland specifically, the water slide hole with the 3 ramps) without direction or previous experience with the game. Another problem as mentioned above was no inclination to use the "C" button to fly around and see the course you're on before teeing off.
Overall, great casual game. If you're looking for a cheap time killer, Golf With Your Friends is a good boredum killer and has replay value.

I used to play Total Annihilation back when a Pentium 2 was a fast, unaffordable machine. Despite claims to the contrary, SupCom is a 100% remake of TA. Really - it is the same game. No innovation whatsoever, unless you count the pointless super-zoom-out as innovative. The game is about extreme amounts of tiny units clashing on huge battlefields, as it always has been. But I find it rather surprising how badly this is done here. With so many units doing different jobs, it is completely impossible to micromanage all of them in a meaningful way. And yet, that is what the game expects you to do. No AI scripts you can employ (Warlords Battlecry and Dark Reign had those more than 15 years ago), no platoons or even the most basic combat formations (like Earth 2150 had back in the 90s). Without any kind of aid, managing your army is a tedious chore. Once you get into actual battle, it is an exercise in frustration. I fail to understand how seasoned developers could ♥♥♥♥ up so badly. But they did, and this game sucks.

A Must-Play Game
+Beautiful art
+Some of the best game music I've heard
+Compelling storytelling
+Enjoyable gameplay
Storytelling
The delivery of the story is very by-the-books for film and novel narratives, but it's very well executed, always leaving the player waiting for more, and, despite being typical for film and novels, it's rarely used in games making Owlboy an all the more refreshing take on narratives in games.  All of the characters have a lot of personality, aided by top-of-the-line character design and animation and a masterfully detailed text-based dialogue delivery system that really gets across cadence and tone in a way that few games of its kind have done before.
Gameplay
While the rest of the aspects of the game shout "game of the year", the gameplay is where this game isn't phenomenal, just good.  It's enjoyable and never gets boring, putting it well beyond most games of its kind, but never really wowed me in the way the other aspects of the game did.

A spiritual successor to the Dungeon Keeper series, War for the Overworld is everything you could have wanted and more! It does not try and reinvent the wheel, but instead keeps things as similar to the original as possible while adding some of their own (and community’s) great ideas. The initial release had several bugs - some major, many minor - but the team is currently hot fixing like crazy and improving the game immensely every day.
Some people have complained about the state of the game upon release, and although their opinions are not without merit, it should be said that the team that brought you this game is a collection of DK fans. A team who loved the series and wanted to bring the franchise back to life and have worked tireless to do just that. They do not have some large studio behind them – just us, the community. And I actually see that as a good thing, lest we get a horrid game like the Dungeon Keeper mobile game that EA released!
If you were a fan of DK then this game will satiate that burning desire to imprison heros before you torture them to death, slay princes and their kin, mine gold to stuff your coffers, and recruit evil creatures to your dungeon all in an effort to rule the Overworld!

Stupendously fun game that is essentially a modern day Minesweeper infused with the most potent distillation of role playing mechanics!  You play the wise administrator to a budding town that is pestered by the hardships that accompany being located in the very center of a dense labyrinth of dungeons.  You must hire dungeon-invading heroes of unrestricted race/class combination, outfit them as you can afford and send them into harms way in service of the kingdom!
Your first order of administrative business is recruiting a weakling, level one hero, because all of the powerful heroes retire immediately as just reward for surviving a dungeon.  This requires making decisions on which buildings to initially construct with your limited resources.  Your choices determine what race/class combinations you can choose to send into the nearby dungeons, and with what items or services you can furnish them.  Assuming your coffers can afford such bonuses.  Each building you construct provides its own set of bonuses and a unique item selection that can be upgraded.
Actual dungeon gameplay consists of moving your chosen hero around a tile-based grid which is covered in the fog of war.  Under each square of fog exists either a monster (level 1-10), an item (or a place to purchase one), an altar dedicated to a specific god, a stat boost, some treasure, or a staircase to a sub-dungeon.  Sub-dungeons offer mini challenges with their own rewards, boost/items enhance your hero's stats or give them new abilities, gods alter your playstyle by forbidding certain actions while rewarding others, and monsters are what you will be primarily hunting for.
Apart from scenarios and puzzles, your objective will always be to kill the boss monster, who is always level 10.  In order to slay such a beast you need to equip yourself, and gain levels by finding and eliminating all of the other monsters in the dungeon.  However, they fight back!  Monsters will NEVER initiate attack with you, but they will retaliate when you strike.  After each fight you will need to recoup by exploring the fog of war.  Each square revealed from the fog will replenish your health/mana, but also the health of any unpoisoned enemies.  Once the fog is gone, though, your only means of healing for additional fights are potions or appealing to your chosen god.  Fail to take out the boss before you've expended all of your available resources and you have to retire in shame, with the entire venture possibly a net loss after the cost of preparations.
Both the meta-game of kingdom administration, and the individual dungeon dives are very enjoyable.  Spending your limited gold feels critically strategic and there are many possible strategies given the available combinations of race/class/equipment/deity which lead to some very satisfying combos.  Every dungeon is a challenge, and by the end of 10-20 minutes you may actually feel kind of attached to your valiant hero that you will never see again.
My only real complaint with the game is that the puzzles are too difficult.  I played about eight of them and each one had a VERY specific solution that had to be performed EXACTLY with no substantial deviations in a chain that can be up to fifty actions in length!  One mistake at any point in that chain and you need to start over.  Some people may enjoy the mental gymnastics necessary to plot out every possible way your hero can move across the board, finding at which points to use which abilities/itemsY and finding the sole solution from a myriad of possibilities - but I didn't.  Thankfully, the puzzles are optional and if you skip them the only thing you'll miss out on is a relatively small sum of gold and some items you could just as easily unlock from doing any of the quests.  Had the game penalized me for not playing the puzzles it would have been a dealbreaker, but mercifully this is not the case.
Far more enjoyable than the puzzles are the scenarios in which you play a themed, semi-random dungeon that has an objective that may be something other than killing a boss.  Some of these scenarios feature unique classes specifically for the story, and can be humorous if you read the notes, signs and story.
Also, the game uses a cloud sync independent of Steam which allows you to log into an account from any platform (including web) and continue playing!  Overall I'm very impressed with this game and would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys casual role playing condensed into 20 minute play sessions, fans of Minesweeper or strategy, or anyone who enjoys mind-numbingly difficult puzzles!

I only got round to playing Crysis in 2015, although I've been meaning to for years! I have now also played warhead, the followup which takes you through the same timeframe but on the other end of the island, playing as Psycho instead of Nomad. The game is identical in most ways to the previous one, so I'm copy-pasting much of what I wrote about that here.
From what I'd seen prior to playing Crysis, I was under the impression that you'd play a kind of semi-indestructable super soldier in this game, dashing and jumping around at high speed and slicing through dozens of enemy soldiers with ease, but really it plays more like you're just a fairly standard FPS soldier dude with a few perks. I found myself not bothering with things like the stealth and speed mode very often as they both drain your energy incredibly quickly. On hard difficulty, a few well-placed enemy bullets can still take you down if you're not careful so you don't really feel invulnerable.
The gameplay is fairly standard FPS fare, akin to Call Of Duty or whatever, with open-ish world elements but lots of set pieces. The game world never feels as open as, say, the Far Cry series and you are pretty much railroaded into tackling things in order, though how you approach each set piece is up to you and you do feel that you can take a variety of approaches to solve the obstacles you encounter.
The graphics have really stood the test of time, It didn't feel particularly dated.
The Crysis campaign only took me 10 hours to play through and I didn't exactly rush through it. Warhead was even shorter, at a shade over 6 hours! The storyline is very standard and unengaging, following a rather cliched 'US saves the world from alien invasion that is unwittingly aided by the nasty Asians' formula that's all too familiar by now. In this iteration, you play as stereotypical Brit hardman with a heart of gold Psycho, who constantly has to remind the racially stereotypical Korean baddies that he's a Brit, not a Yankee. Warhead's plot and ending were even weaker than the first game, sadly.
Overall, I'd say that if you've never played Crysis before, play that first. If you enjoy playing that game, this is just more of exactly the same! Pick them both up when on sale with a heavy discount and you can't go wrong, really.

It is the first in the Adventures of Sherlock Holmes series of adventure games developed by Frogwares and Viva Media. Other than the frequent game crashes, if you like puzzle games this is an ok game.

Like other reviewers, this game is a hard recommendation.  Made originally in 2002, The Mystery of the Mummey certainly shows its age.  As a note, the screenshots on Steam show interaction with people, but those shots come from in-game cutscenes.  The control of the game is similar to Myst/Riven, a first person view where your movement is cell based rather than fluid control over your character using directional keys.  The game is essentially a hidden object game which is perfectly fine, but the problem is that because the game is so old, the resolution of the game does not keep up with the times and objects become even harder to find on higher resolution monitors.  Additionally, the game is available in only full screen mode (unless you use DxWnd) so imagine trying to hunt for objects on a wide screen monitor while the game is originally designed for 4:3 ratio and at a lower resolution.  Everything becomes stretched out and pixelated.  These two issued combine makes this hidden object game less pleasant to play.
I actually enjoyed a bit of the game but only because I used an online guide every now and then.  The story is mostly told through the pieces of notes found in the levels and cutscenes, and while not very intriguing it kept me interested enough to listen to Holmes thoughts and keep playing.  Puzzles can be very hard due to lack of feedback from the character (and due to the low resolution of the game).  For example, sometimes keys are used to open locks but other times a knife or hairpin can be used instead.  Sherlock Holmes only mentions that its locked, and because it's a hidden object game, it's likely that instead of trying different objects on the lock, backtracking for a missing key will be the first thought instead.  There's not many soundtracks in the game, about one per level, but they were nice to listen to, and while the game is low resolution the environmental design was pretty cool.
The last problem is that the game crashes.  I'm able to alt-tab the game with no problem, but whenever the level ends on a cutscene and begins loading the next level, the game crashes.  The only solution I found was to skip the cutscene by rapidly pressing the esc key once it starts, so be sure to look at a guide every now and then to know to save before the level ends.
All in all, it's a hard to recommend this game.  I gave up on the last level due to one puzzle (combined with all of the previous issues mentioned).  It was simply too much.  I can only recommend this to those who are hard core adventurers, but otherwise if you got this game in the Sherlock Holmes Bundle, play a bit and watch the rest of the game online once you get your share of enjoyment and frustration.  If this game was remastered to a much higher resolution, I might give it a shot again.

Great way to deal with resources (one of the most tedious aspects of all strategy games), makes you focus on the real thing: STRATEGY. The unit/building limit is another way to stay focused on what's important and not. In addition to the variety and levels of units and structures, the game builds up and evolves very naturally, make you switch between tactics as you get new units, tech levels or scenario modifiers.
The story flows in parallel for each faction, this means that the first faction you play will give you insight of the perspective of the scenario, making the next faction you play a little more predictible (as you now know where the enemy is, and from where it will come). Not a bad thing (if you like to take advantage of this) nor a good thing (if you wanted a linear story, one episode after the other).
In a nutshell: you must think out of the box, it's a new and better kind of strategy!

You will never get enough to do anything unless you are a premium member.  Just to open loot bags that nine times out of ten, have nothing but a few coins, you spend 20 minutes worth of your labor points.  When you are out grinding for quests, you can collect hundreds of bags that will never be able to be opened if you ever want to attempt to craft anything.

If I come into a large amount of free cash flow, I will definitely pay for a premium membership and grind on.

It's been a long time since a game made me feel so "at home." Not just immersed, but genuinely embracing the game world and enjoying just being in it. The art and music contribute largely to this feeling, but also the very charming characters and refreshingly original setting. I don't play metroidvanias often, but this one hit all the right buttons for me with its oldschool-like level design including several new and unique mechanics to spice up gameplay, its manageable difficulty curve with challenging bosses that require practice but never outright overpower you if you adapt to their patterns, and a satisfying share of optional hidden rooms and collectibles.
A few parts of Owlboy annoyed me, but the high praise is certainly justified in my opinion. Perhaps a bit short for its current price, but I beat it in 11 hours without going for achievements and collectibles and can see myself playing it again at some point just for the good vibes. I would have loved to spend more time with those characters and get to know them better in a longer game, but maybe we can get something like a sequel someday.

I jumped on this bandwagon about two years ago. I was excited about what they were doing and hoped beyond hope for a game that truly was more Dungeon Keeper. I participated in their discussions and made suggestions. I watched their videos and read their reports. I was all about this game... For about 6 months.
In the following months, I became very bored with this game, I admit. I actually felt that things were rolling out too slowly and was concerned that I had bought in to yet another "early access" game that would actually be "forever alpha access" instead. About a year ago I uninstalled the game and moved on, chalking this up to another learning experience.
Yesterday, I noticed it's full release. I have no idea why I went to their page and ultimately installed the game to try playing it again (I really had given up on it) but I guess I was bored enough? I braced myself for disappointment.
I think that having so many other early access disappointments really made me far too over-harsh on this group and what they were doing. I was giggling in the first mission and I was hooked in the second. This game is exactly what they said it would be. It's DK without major publisher taint all over it. It's DK's successor.
Is it perfect? Nope. No game can be. Is it broken? Nope. Everything is playable and fun. Is there a learning curve? Yep. But if you played DK, you have completed the basic tutorial. Are there bugs? Yes. And the team is already all up in that.
I don't approve of people giving this game poor reviews due to the multiplayer not being in full function (at time of writing) or because their system can't handle it (I have a decent system at best and have had very little lag when my dungeon was huge) because that's not what these reviews should be about in my mind. DK was mostly single player, and the single player game is awesome.
My only real complaint (and it is easy to remedy) is the voice acting for minions can be a little repetitive.
Having seen where they started and looking at where they're finishing, this game did not fail at it's task. If you miss your DK and the other dungeon manager games have fallen flat, then this is what you've been waiting for. You won't be disappointed.
