Yesterday i played around 7h and I like the game so far.
A few parts in this game feel a bit like eve online.
You have to do something to collect your xp to get a skill leveln. You learn the skills like in eve, you buy them, inject them (will train the first skill level if a point is available). If you want a weapon you have to Train the novice skill (5 is max). With lvl 4 in that skill you can use at least the first sniper, MG etc. Better weapons will also Need then their subskills. Like for the m16, you Need like 4-5 in the weapon skill and also the assault rifle skill. Like if you Need in eve eg. for the assault frig, the frig skill and then the subskill (assault frig). There are some skills that boosts different stats and so on too.
Crafting is also bit eve like, because all the items can be crafted and sold by Players. You also might find rare blueprints.
You reprocess ressources in the laboratory and craft items in the factory via a blueprint.
As a old eve Player i like those mechanics a lot.
Beside that, its possible to craft weapons also in higher Qualities.
There are a lot of different weapons and armor ingame, that also can be modded.
Also there are different Kind of ammunitions, like em bullets against robots, poision bullets and so on.
I like the evil games where you may loose all your Equipment on death (full loot System). Games where you dont rly risk something getting bored very fast for me. In this game u dont loose you Equipment on death, but at least the stuff you collected while you were outside and what you didnt stored meanwhile. That risky enough for me and makes the game exciting for me. I was a few times too greedy and had to pay for it.
You can also Play with a friend and do pve and pvp. Quest battles dont work in a gang, but it still may help to travel to the Mission spot in a Group, because you will have to fight stuff on the way to there and back for sure.
A friend can also a great help when you mine. Theres a Titan armor that let you carry a lot of ores, but with low defense. In case you wear such a armor it may be wise to bring a friend with better armor that will fight in the front, while you mainly shoot from the back and collect the stuff.
As far as I know you can also conquer strongholds or something like that.

Owlboy is a visually beatiful game that falls short in just about every other category.
Gameplay:
- Level designs: Certain level designs just didn't strike me as fun, in particular the jungle where you spend most of it flying around in the dark. Another example was the short area with gnomes where flying will cause you to be swarmed with enemies. In theory something where you can only jump is fine (the end of the game does it decently), but flying is on the same key as jumping so you can accidentally screw yourself pretty easily.
- Fighting enemies just didn't feel satisfying to me.
- Since you already start out the game able to fly, there is much less of discovering and using cool new moves as the game progresses.
Value: This game is not very long, doesn't have good replayability, but comes with a $25 price tag. Fortunately I waited to get it through a humble bundle and didn't pay the full price. I don't think the amount of content justifies the price tag.
Audio: The music is generally very good, but various areas would just not have any music playing. In other places, the music would be way too short for the amount of time you have to spend in an area and loop multiple times.
Plot/Concistency: Don't expect anything special here - very cliche/predictable story. Also random inconcistencies "the air is too thin to fly up here", but then you can fly anyways with no explanation.
Achievements: This is a less important point, I'm sure plenty of people don't care about achievements at all. However, in a game with so few achievements, I think it's ridiculous that ~4 of them require you to do the same thing, namely collect all of the coins. There are two achievements for collecting trinkets, but both require you to collect all of them, and to do so you need all of the coins (which, again, there are two achievements for) .

Decently fun, though the devs state in the official forum rules that they'll ban people that disagree with them, which raises a lot of red flags for the future of the game and the community. Cautious recommend for now.

Hard Reset is a FPS creation in the style of the old school shooter.
The game offers an interesting take on guns, and while not perfect, they do a lot to mixup the play-styles throughout the 8 hours on offer here (including dlc). The process of unlocking upgrades leaves you with something new and interesting to try until the very end. The proximity grenades that you can detonate whenever you want with the second mouse button was a personal favorite. Flinging a proximity mine over a group of enemies then detonating it just as it sailed above their heads (sending them flying in all directions) never got old.
On the negative side the levels are quite linear. Throughout the game you find yourself either in a narrow corridor, a wide corridor, or a big box with scattered obstacles. The environments look nice, but I feel like a big opportunity was lost by keeping it so linear. It's pretty evident what gun works best where, so a lot of the time you feel quite railroaded in tactics.
That said the enemies have been well designed with the linear levels in mind and certainly keep you on your toes without ever feeling unfair. They do tend to the "charging straight at you" variety, which again, reduces your tactics quite a bit. To somewhat make up for that there's a great deal of destructible objects in the environment which can hinder your enemies in different ways.
The game prides itself on its 'old-school' style. But though the weapons feel right the player control doesn't. Compared to the classics the movement speed is slow, and jumping feels like you're wearing lead boots. Oh and I found too may places which the player should be able to reach via jumping but are blocked by invisible walls.
And the less said about the plot the better.
So If you're in the mood for a short, fun & mindless shooter and this is on sale, sure, give it a whirl. Otherwise I can't recommend Hard Reset. It's simply to limited.

This game took every issue I had about the original Crysis, and improved upon them to the fullest extent possible. The result is a game that stands on its own as "better than the original". The characters (now you play as "Psycho", Nomad's former SAS teammate) are now vastly improved, with the game exploring the depths of Raptor Team's  former history. Whereas I did not find General Kyong to be a wholly believable character, I found the ruthless Colonel Lee to be a far more engaging (not to mention competent) villain- it's a pity one could not fight him at the end, like the General in Crysis. So yes, the characters are better. The storyline is slimmed down, which in my mind provided greater coherence throughout the game. Essentially, the player pursues Colonel Lee, who is in possession of some valuable alien technology, all over the island. The missions are now highly varied, from standoffs with hordes of aliens in the frozen mountains to a vehicular frag-fest atop a moving train. The missions absolutely kick♥♥♥♥♥ The weapons have now been substantially modified, with tons of new ones being added in. I absolutely enjoyed the new turrets, the 20mm definitely being the superior one. The Gauss rifle is slightly weaker in this game, which was a little disappointing, but the Sniper Rifle is as accurate and deadly as in the last game. The Hurricane minigun is as good for throwing up a wall of lead as in the previous installation. The last thing I want to point out (aside from briefly mentioning the awesome soundtrack that accompanied this game) is the massive changes to vehicles. The APC has its moments, but without a doubt the best have to be the BMP-esque tank with the 30-or so-mm autocannon, and the AA installation, with its' guided missles and awe-inspiring flak cannons. I missed the vehicular combat in Crysis, and felt that that was an avenue which the developers could expand upon. Here, they have done so. Nothing is quite as thrilling as manning the AA battery and shooting down alien after alien during the final swarm (I have a thing for AA vehicles, as seen by my admiration for the Shilka in Arma: Cold War Assault).
This game DESERVES a 10/10, but JUST because it is not Arma: Cold War Assault or Stalker: Shadow of Chernobyl, I have to take off a small point. It's a clerical issue- anyone who reads this review will know what the real score is!

I rate the game Crysis: Warhead 4/5. Good.
This game is better than the original crysis in every respect except it seems to have no idea how to tell a coherent story. Indeed, if I had not played the original game first I would not have any clear idea as to what is going on in this game and as a result it is very necessary to play the original to understand what this game's plot is about. But....the graphics are better, the game runs better, there are even fewer bugs and the same great enemy AI has been retained.
Like its predecessor, this game encourages you to "think outside of the box" and come up with more innovative solutions to tactical situations than some other games would have you do...but also like its predecessor if you think too far out of the box or get too innovative you can fully expect the game to come up with some crazy, contrived way of instantly killing you. Good example: I decided to bypass a large battle area and outflank all the opponents in an entire battlefield by swimming underwater. A giant shark came by and instantly killed my character, despite the fact that he's wearing a power armor that can deflect .50 caliber bullets with relative ease. Oh well.
But despite its intrinsic and inescapably linear design, this game is still a lot of fun to play. It's loud, action packed and full of between level cutscenes that somehow bridge the gap (or straddle the fence between irritating and campy. This game also gets an honorable mention from me also because it has one of the best train battles (where you jump from one railroad car to another wild-west style) that I have ever seen (the very best was still in Soldier of Fortune however). The music was better in this iteration of crysis also but still not spectacular enough to warrant getting a soundtrack for it. This is a game that was fun enough that I'd consider playing it through on an even higher difficulty sometime or other...if there wasn't such a huge selection of other games out there vying for my attention. In short, this game has all the strengths of the original (except anything approaching a coherent story) and none of the weaknesses. Be warned though, it is unfortunately rather short. Intense but short.

Crysis Warhead is a first person shooter, and is a standalone expansion top the original Crysis game. This was released in September 2008.
Warhead follows a side plot to the original story of "Psycho", an ally of the original protagonist, Nomad. You are thrown into challenges on the other side of the island at the same time as the original story.  One change with the gameplay that Warhead brings, is the chance to customize your weapons, allowing you to put silencers, different sights on, and other additions such as flashlights. All of the weaponry which was in the first game is still present here, with the addition of a few new guns such as dual wielding SMGs which are absolutely bad♥♥♥♥♥  We see the return of the super human style nanosuit too.
Warhead features a optimized version of the Cry Engine 2, but it still lacks 1080P resolutions which is a real shame. The game still looks really nice and blows alot of recently released titles out of the water graphically, even though it is almost eight years old now. The graphics menu has interesting options available, you are basically having to pick the style of gamer you are; you get pigeon holed into categories such as "gamer" or "enthusiast" for example - to me this really doesn't look good. I should be able to pick the graphics options with their regular choices, and not some predefined garbage categories which we see here.  The lack of high resolutions slightly lets the game down. There is a hot-fix you can do by changing .ini file settings, but this also messes with frame rates, and lord knows what else.
The story is a complete stand alone to the original game, you can play this game first and still be none the wiser that their is a prequel to it. I really like the idea that all of this story is going on at the same time as the original though, it makes the plot seem even deeper than before.
Warhead has some well recorded voice acting, all be it a very generic English accent on the main character, but all of the other dialogue and sound effects are all very good.
This game has various difficulties, much like the original. Playing on Delta mode, which is the hardest, will certainly give you a well worthy challenge if you are an experienced Crysis/FPS player, stick to the lower difficulties if you just want to see the story as enemies and gameplay takes a significant drop in difficulty.
Warhead, much like Crysis 1, could sometimes be considered as an open world game. The levels which you are playing in, are absolutely huge. There are so many different methods of reaching the same location, that you can play this game exactly how you want it. I personally opted to try a more stealthy approach, and normally games don't really cater for different methods like that, but I was still able to experience everything the same. There are tons of little nuggets of extra story to find throughout each level too, from computers to checkout, to radio broadcasts of propaganda. Plenty of stuff to keep you looking in every building you come across.
A full playthrough of Crysis Warhead will take you just about five hours; depending on how you play. My first run through was a regular all gungho all guns blazing playthrough, which took me just about four hours to complete. My second run, which was my stealthy approach, took me quite a bit longer. Normally I don't get as much enjoyment out of my second run through a game, but I was able to get the same, and if not more enjoyment out of a second playthrough, I was able to see a different side to the game which I didn't see before in the regular playthrough, and the higher difficulties add a little bit more replay ability too.
As well as the aforementioned resolution issues I had. I did notice a little bit of screen tearing on the cut scenes. Turning on v-sync tanks the frame rate to sub 30, which is unacceptable. nVidia users can enable v-sync in their control panel but you will still get a bit of tearing sadly. I guess that's what you get from older direct 9 version of games when you are running more recent operating systems/direct x versions.
Crysis Warhead definitely stands the test of time when it comes to gameplay and story; it's hard to believe that this game is almost eight years old now. You wouldn't think so with the quality of the gameplay on show. It is a welcome addition to the Crysis franchise and one that should almost certainly be played by fans of the series, and just FPS fans in general.  For the low price of £7,99, you will be getting a significant length story mode, with plenty of replay ability with a very fleshed out story line to boot.

Among the worst adventure games I've ever played.  Everything it is possible to do wrong is done here.  I'm glad though that I got all the Sherlock Holmes games together in a pack because they get much better.  And if I had just bought this one alone, I surely would have avoided the rest.

(I played on Explorer mode, so bear this in mind)
The World:
There are four areas in the world that you explore through, essentially four chapters of the story. However once you progress through one area, you will never be able to go back to the previous. The notion of NPC vendors is also somewhat odd; few actually have anything specific to what their appearance would suggest; a fish market vendor may just as well have some expensive armor, weapons, and magic components. Items also scale with your level, so no matter where you go, everyone's stock has amazingly upgraded to suit you. This is a quality of life issue so I'm not too annoyed with it, but sometimes I really just wanted a specific thing and couldn't find anyone who sold it. In the final act, I needed to acquire a specific skillbook in
Shouldn't be a problem to find this skillbook? Nope, no where to be found! Not even a magic shop that I could find, just general vendors!
Story:
The story was engaging, and overall well constructed. I played as Fane, and the story was very interesting up until the end. The ending specifically felt very abrupt and rushed. During the final moments,
as I struck the final lethal blow the game instantly began cutscene/conversation mode, and basically asked me
So what happened to
So all in all the story was very interesting and kept me eager and excited to see what was next, but the ending was a letdown. I wanted a proper epilogue to see what happened to everyone, but this game seems to end on a cliffhanger of sorts with everyone just saying "wow that was fun, wonder what comes next!".

There's not much else to say about this, really. The game is dull and features way too many "This door is locked" or "I need something to open this" lines. I'm a big fan of Doyle's Holmes, and that Holmes would, quite likely, just have bypassed those locks in some ingenious way - not just looked around for a bit and hope to stumble upon the key.

After playing all of the Sherlock games from 'The Silver Earring' onwards, I wanted to go back right to the beginning and play them all through chronologically before the new one due out this year. I'm giving this one the thumbs down as much as I want it to be a thumbs up because of so many speed humps that actually interrupt the flow of the game. Probably the first thing to mention is the continuous crashing, particularly at the end of cut scenes and chapter ends. MAKE SURE YOU SAVE OFTEN. I cannot reiterate that point enough. Much frustration comes after completing a devilish puzzle to have the game crash and redo it ALL over again. However, these crashes can be overcome with the good ole ESC key, for the most part.
The second most disappointing element is the visuals in relation to the difficulty of the game. I appreciate the age of a game and God knows how many adventure games I have played over the years but to find a hairpin, for example, on a floor that frankly is blurry and the object resembles a smudge is poor form. Being penalised via having to consult a walkthrough so often for locating objects is not on. On the plus side the story is engaging enough to make you restart again and again and finish it but it feels a chore to 'get through'. The voice acting/recording is atrocious (knowing in the future this becomes its' main selling point) and the dialogue itself is poorly written. After almost no interaction with characters the game finishes with a huge cutscene that wraps it all up with way too much assumption and frankly insults the gamer who has been there all the way by solving the whole thing and saying goodnight with silent credits. Fans of the games NEED to play this one to experience the whole saga but this one cannot have it's age to blame because in its era there were many other adventure games that got this formula right with less frustration. Anyways, onto the next game :)

Ever since the first demo was released about 3 years ago from now I planned to ignore DreadOut completely. I was never a huge fan of Fatal Frame, but always had respect for that series trying to keep some of it's identity and some of the core of the classic survival horror concepts, instead of devolving into a simplistic jumpscare fest. Which DreadOut is. I suspected it after the demo. And now, after deciding to give it a try (I mean, they supported the game for so long and even made a standalone expansion, there HAS to be something?), I can say that with certainty.
DreadOut, from the very beginning, until *almost* very end is the same kind of game most horror themed products on Unity engine, ever since SCP and Slender games got popular, is - a linear jumpscare fest of BOO in your face moments with loud screaming. It has the most basic of mechanics, quite clumsily taken from Fatal Frame, sometimes has "puzzles" and sometimes even has an item you need to take. So exciting! But most of the time it's very guided experience that holds exactly on one thing - on trying to be spoopy, because freaky ghost, baby. But butsin doesn't make you feel good here. Because it's barely a mechanic, unlike the complex system in Fatal Frame. It's here just to give an illusion of another mechanical layer and make sure you have first person view with limited visibility to do jump scares more effectively.
The only good things the game has are, amazingly, in the very very end - there's one actually pretty interesting in concept (but boring in reality) boss fight, another good in concept, but more frustrating than hard boss fight and actually good with visuals and some concepts final boss fight, which is, however, terrible mechanically. It actually feels as if the developers finally realised how games could be made right as they were finishing it. Shame they didn't scrap the entire game and make a new one, though.
Is DreadOut worth it? Well, if you're playing horror themed games just for spoops and video/streaming scarecam silliness, you will be able to get some enjoyment out of this. If you want anything more than have jumpscares at different intervals... Hell, if you want the game to perform and not glitch, you better look elseware. It's not like there's a shortage of horror themed games on PC lately.

Let me start this review saying that I am very strong fan of horror games, like Silent Hill, Clock Tower and Fatal Frame.
Dreadout is a short, but entertaining game, worth the price tag. Admittedly the duget for the models and textures are a bit lacking comparing it to recent horror games, but it is still quite the decent effort. Dreadout plays like your stereotypical horror movie, with a group of students and a teacher arriving to a ghost town. You take control of Linda, one of the students, and the only means for survival are her physical condition and a camera to fend of the ghosts, much like in the Fatal Drame series.
If there are some complains about this game is the camera during 3rd person, which is kind of unstable in small places and corners, being a bit jerky, which leads to disorientation. Another issue is death, which after being defeated you are thrown into Limbo, in which as punishment you have to walk some distance in order to try again (the distance is diminished if you collect certain items). However, you are placed exactly at the location of your death, meaning that if you were completely surrounded by enemies, you will be stuck there being killed over and over and will have no option but to start anew. Lack of knowledge of indonesian mythology and folklore may affect, but I would use it as an opportunity to learn about other cultures.
All in all it is quite the entertaining game, worth a shot in one of those cold, dark nights.

The aesthetic is great, but the game feels poorly designed and the story lacked depth and closure. It's a wonderful game to look at, but not much else, in my opinion.
The game's mechanics and level design felt unintuitive and in need of improvement, especially later on. Movement isn't very tight for some of the more precise bosses, and later platforming and stealth sections felt more like guesswork. Seriously, though? A boss that can throw you into insta-death lava pits? A completely dark section with spikes, enemies, and practically no light to go by? Insta-death stealth sections? Precision platforming with loose gliding instead of flight?
The pacing was also a problem - bosses and levels alike felt almost random in placement and difficulty. One boss halfway into the game felt more like Silver Surfer NES, while the final boss I was able to finish on my second try. I also counted several times in play where I would move to another screen thinking "please don't be another boss...".
The story in particular left the most to be desired - like the rest of the game, it felt like elements were cobbled together from a much larger and deeper story, with just enough plot holes to leave half of it up to speculation, which is maddening. And - minor spoiler alert - the game ends on the worst cop-out ending I've seen in a long time.
There's still glitches several months after release - most notably collision. I was pushed out of the map several times during play, which explains the "load from earlier checkpoint" button they inexplicably included...
To put it simply, I don't recommend it, but I would recommend a sequel if the devs learn from some of the shortcomings of this title. It just feels like D-Pad's 9 years of development on the title were spent solely on the visual quality of the game, instead of the gameplay, and while I appreciate the wonderful aesthetic and still respect the game somewhat based off of that alone, it's just not worth picking up because of the frustrating gameplay and poorly executed story.

After 255 hrs of playing, I think I can write a review for this game.
Let's start off with the negative aspects:
The worst part about CK2 is that there is absolutely no challenge. Not to say, the game is easy as it can be. I always started with a county as crappy as possible in the hope of a real challenge but it never took me long (never more than 50 years I think) to become emperor of a great realm, either by killing & marrying (HRE / Byzantine) or by founding the British Empire by conquest. This limits the fun with the game for me, because once emperor, there is nothing left to achieve really, you can basically just conquer province after province. The only thing that slows you down at this point is that you have to wait until the next claim was fabricated somewhere. Never really managed to play longer than 150 or 200 years before I lost interest due to being bored.
The main issue about the game being much too easy is the broken marriage & inheritance system. Most of the time you will easily find a heir of a duchy or even a kingdom somewhere in the world whose heir is perfectly willing to marry your daughter matrilineary. Then just kill the current title holder and your son inlaw (which isn't difficult at all) and voila, you got a new realm. If you don't happen to find a direct heir who is willing to marry your daughter, just take his brother instead and then kill the heir. Tata, you matrilinearily married daughter will now produce the sons of the new heir.
The second reason which makes the game too easy is the very dumb AI, and I hate to say this because I'm a fan of Paradox and they are usually known for having great and challenging AI in their grand strategy games. In CK2 at least, if you manage to lose any war, you really suck. It is so easy to practically ally up every empire even as a small count, so you dont even have to fight your wars on your own. Byzantine will happily ship 20k troops to britannia to conquer that welsh scum next to you - just lean back and wait. And your opponent only rarely ever thinks about sieging your county. If against all odds he really raises troops and sends them to your place, just raise some 50 men from a liege and let them run all over the map. The opponent's 10k troops will chase those 50 peeps until his whole realm is crushed by your byzantine friends...
The reason why I still gave the game a thumbs up? It's a damn unique game concept, based on the medieval feudal system which keeps me locked up and makes me start a new game again every now and then. Forming a dynasty, managing your vassals, getting the right guardians for your promising kindsmen to build a decent heir for the next generation - it's really addictive. So sad, that the AI doesn't care about any of this either, and so you will see a lot of very crappy rulers in the realms bordering you.
Summary:
+ Very unique game idea
+ Addictive dynasty management
+ Great replay value
- Lousy AI
- Unrealistic and too easy marriage / inheritance system
- No long term motivation
5/10

Owlboy is a charming little platformer, with the type of story and aesthetics that you can only expect to get out of a small dedicated indie team; it's basically the platforming version of Stardew Valley. Perhaps not quite as indie as that, looks like the Dev team behind Owlboy has 5 folk instead of one, but still, you get the idea.
The action is polished; sufficiently complex to avoid becoming boring, while at the same time not being overtly complicated. The addition of flight to a platformer game might come across as a bit of a strange choice, but it works quite well for this game.
Art direction and soundtrack meld together quite well, and fit the story in an excellent fashion.
I wouldn't play it if you're expecting some sort of hardcore challenge. It's not a difficult game by any stretch of the imagination, nor is it all that long. The boss fights are varied and interesting, but for the most part easily doable with just a few tries each.
I didn't engage in the "hunting out every coin" challenges; I just played the game through to the end, following the main story line. Took about 10 - 12 hours I believe (a significant portion of my registered playtime was the game on pause).
The achievements should be mentioned; there's no "gimmies" here. Every single one of them actually requires you to go out of your way, or at least do something that you have an option of not doing while still contining the story line. I only ended up getting one of the achievements, and that one could have easily been missed.
I'd say that the main downside would be the overall lack in replayability, or at least, I personally don't think I'll be replaying it, I'm sure some folks might wish to. Then again, I think that's a factor that is pretty much common to almost all platformers.
All in all, I'm pleased enough with what I got for the price I paid (currently $13 as the sole game in the top tier of Humble Indie Bundle 18). I think this is a game where people's impressions will be met; if it looks like the type of game that they usually enjoy, then they probably will; if it looks like a type of game that they wouldn't be interested in, then they'd probably be right there too. Would I pay full price, however? Yeah, probably not.

There's a lot to learn to the game, which is why progression being slow isn't too big of an issue.  Lot of inventory management, but the gameplay itself when it gets down to the combat is smooth and comprehensive.

While I haven't participated in it yet, there seems to be some form of PvP system where you can enter someone else's PvE battle and ♥♥♥♥ them up. Though I could be wrong, and it might be PvP only. I honestly can't tell, I only know that you can jump into random's games and help them, but there is also an option to PvP however I've always been told I can't do that(Because of some mechanic that probably involves clans??) Update: So PvP works weird. There are safe areas, which are towns and buildings that you can't be attacked at perior. Then there are "Secure" areas where you can be attacked by creatures but not players. Then there are "wastelands" which are unsecure areas and you can be attacked by players in those tiles. There are also PvP arena matches in the main starting city, but those usually have level requirements to enter so that is mostly end-game stuff. As for that one guy complaining about not being able to level up your stats: He's an impatient♥♥♥♥♥♥who didn't wait long enough.  You buy skills from the market, or get them from quests, and use those to level up your stats directly. If he had paid attention to the tutorial he would know this.
As well, at level 4-5 when you get your weapons skill up to level 4, you go into an arena and get to try out classes from the looks of it. Seems to be Machine gunner, sniper, and tank class. Very well designed. Frustrating at points, but nevertheless an enjoyable romp.
A quick overview:
Gameplay: Classic metroidvania, with a twist - you can fly from the beginning. This almost completely removes jumping puzzles, which I for one was glad to see. Still, all the staples of the genre are there - collectables, false walls, secret areas, and steady progression through progressively harder areas connected to a central hub. Combat, especitally with bosses, strikes a balance between high difficulty and low consequence for failure. You will lose often, but the game's autosave rarely sets you too far back. This makes the game challenging but removes the impulse to rage-quit.
Story: Again, remeniscent of classic games, though with more in common with a zelda title or an older Final Fantasy. Bad guys threaten your home, magic mcguffins from an ancient civilization, making friends with former enemies, etc. etc. However, thrown into the mix are many moments with real emotional weight, often backed up by game design. For example, your character starts walking slow when visiting the graveyard. Little details like this help drive home a dramatic atmosphere, and cement the game's themes of the need to combat loneliness and fear, making an otherwise generic story strike several authentic chords.
Art: Beautiful. Good music, good sprite art, good backgrounds, good animation, good everything. Smooth, well polished, and well presented.
No bugs, glitches, or other problems so far as I've encountered. 10 solid hours of old-school sidescroller exploration gameplay. Enjoyable, resonant, and with several design choices that I hope other developers are looking at. Much can be learned from this game's successes.

This game commits just about every sin in the point-and-click genre:
- pixel hunting (the environments are incredibly grainy / blurred, and on multiple occasions, you are expected to pick out sand and hair pins from what you see)
- a poor interface (items taken out of the inventory have to be put back before a new one can be chosen, and the inventory icon is at the edge of the screen, which means you often spin around when trying to access it)
- meh voice work (Holmes sounds like a weird British Inspector Gadget, Elizabeth is dozey, and Watson sounds so bad that I thought he was Lestrade at first)
- timed, esoteric puzzles (a tile puzzle that requires you to inexplicably make Holmes' profile, and the fact that inventory items have to be combined in a certain order)
- a half-baked plot (the start of the game mentions a made-up cousin, and Lord Montcalfe (or Metcalf) who was found burned to death, yet Holmes is called in to investigate the Lord's disappearance).
On the plus side, the first time you hear the music, it sounds alright, and some of Holmes' actions are actually given animated cutscenes.
Even Hound of the Baskervilles is better than this, and that's saying something.

Confess my love is a little free title I have wanted to try for a while now actually - And it fitted perfectly, now that I have been behind.
The game is about - confessing your love - to the girl you like in class. You decide how/when you are gonna do it, if you're gonna do it at all.
The game "resets" after every time you either leave class, hesitate, confessing your love or waiting for your love to leave - Every decision give you a different ending, and some endings are opening up for more choices.
It's a quite interesting game, and a neat little concept of a story. Rather sad too.
It gets pretty frustrating quick, but when you finally find out what you are missing it give a rewarding feeling of "some kind of progress".
I like this simple way of telling a story, and I can easily over-analyse it. Haha.
If you just want a short little 'story', you should try it.It's a cheap (... free is pretty cheap, right? ;)) way to try something different.
The idea of the game is better than the game IMO tho.

You will not be prepared for the beauty, horror, sadness and fantasy of this little gem when it hits you. But that's the most genius thing about it: it's an unassuming little title with more to offer than it seems.
Going into this game, it seemed to me like it was just going to be a cute and simple little game. After all, it was free, the graphics were simple, and the game itself seemed simple: an RNG/time-reliant love confession simulator that takes place all in one room, and with only three characters.
But all of that simplicity is its beauty: this game builds upon its various, sometimes arduous-to-get, endings, and its ultimate ending can only make sense in a simple, low-populated environment such as this game's setting.
Work for all those endings. Use a walkthrough for the later ones if you need it, because the true ending of this game is incredibly worth it. It puts all of your rejections into perspective, and explains the point of all this heartbreak and why it keeps happening.
This is the most amazing game I have ever played for free, and I recommend it to all.

Yeah, it's tough to review games like this one. Frogwares' first, the game with which they started their succesful SH series, so of some minor "historical" value for the genre - and yet a letdown in most ways... Released in 2002, this game looks dated even for that year. Looking around might be smooth, but moving is clunky, and sometimes an exercise in pixel hunting, which is hardly a recommendation... Inventory management is annoying and slow, and (unless I'm mistaken) no usage of keyboard doesn't help.
The setting is, yeah, SH meets Egypt (with a bunch of other clichéd influences & touches), quite uninspired, as is, more or less, the story (Doyle was likely turning in his grave because  of this one), along with voice acting, which goes from "so bad it's good" to "meh"... Sherlock himself, apart from being a Frankenstein of Sherlock clichés has "accent issues", failing to convince or interest. Music? I was just playing Transport Tycoon Deluxe before this, and the quality is eerily similar at some points... I honestly didn't expect almost midi level music in a commercial (if budget) 2002 game.
So, OK, there are all too often great adventure games hidden behind an unimpressive technical side. Is it here too? No. The puzzles are (so far, I only got to the beginning of the 4th chapter) as uninspiring as they can be. Generic slider puzzles? Check. The "5l and 3l buckets & you need 4l" puzzle? Check... Illogical / obscure solutions? Check. Poor & simple puzzles have likely been obscured by, in some cases, a complete lack of hints on what you're supposed to achieve, some backtracking, and extreme pixelhunting in a 360 environment, requiring from you, sometimes, to go from place to place and pass your cursor everywhere in hope it changes. And timed puzzles... They are a personal peeve of mine, but they're quite badly and annoyingly exectuted. Like someone figured it was damn too easy on its own, wasn't capable of creating interesting puzzles and just made it harder by making it more annoying.
Basically, it's a dated, generic, dull first person adventure game. It's amazing how much Frogwares have grown and improved since then... but this one you should avoid unless you're a completist & hardcore Sherlock Holmes fan.

It is hard to put this game into words that describe it well. It is in some way a deck building / card game, but all fights are conducted as hack&slay 3rd person fights where the moves are a bit similar to the batman games (evade, counter, attack, some special skills). So what happens in a standard round of Hand of Fate?
1. I select a story / main quest to play
2. I select a preset deck and review it to exchange cards
3. Play (the following steps a & b repeat multiple times):
3.a. Move your character across a map made of cards which are revealed upon reaching them. These may then trigger sidequests, encounters, shops, traps etc. They come along with stories where you can often choose how to react to an encounter, which gives you different results.
3.b. In case you engage in a fight, you go into the battle mode. This is classic hack and slay action with block, dodge, attack.
4. You complete the round by beating the final boss (or dying). During 3. you have completed many events that gave you tokens. These unlock future side quests, weapons or other cards to be used in future rounds. So once done, go back to step 2, to make use of your sweet loot!
I really enjoy RPGs, good progression systems, deckbuilding and a fresh gamestyle. In my opinion, Hand of Fate combines these mechanisms into an oh so refreshing and satisfying experience that anyone with similar preferences should not miss!

Alright, here we go.
If you've played the original Bullfrog Dungeon Keeper and/or Dungeon Keeper 2, then let me just say, this is it, this is what we've been waiting for (and if you haven't played them then skip to the later part of the review). WFTO *IS* truely, more than anything else has ever been, the spiritual successor to the Dungeon Keeper franchise. Its made by DK fans, for DK fans. Don't hesitate (well maybe, see my next point first), just buy the game and play it.
Now, before I continue, I must concede that yes, there have been a number of major bugs since release. HOWEVER, the game is most certainly release ready, enjoyable and playable. Many of these bugs have been related to the campaign, cutscenes etc, however the majority of these have already been fixed. The development team are fully committed and have been doing a great job. There will always be bugs on release, especially for a small indie team like this, you cant get around that. Even major publishers often have bugs on release, sometimes massive ones, and they have millions to spend. If you've played the game for two hours, encountered one bug, and called it a bad, incomplete game, you really don't deserve to be writing a review. In a few hours you've played 2, 3 levels? Get some perspective. Almost all of the bugs people have talked about in the negative reviews were fixed within 24 hours of release.
So look within yourself, and if you're the kind of person who is extremely nitpicky about their games, and can't handle a few little bugs or a couple of placeholder texts, then fine, just wait a month, they'll be gone. For me, that's certainly not worth giving a bad review over. As someone who has been waiting for this game for almost 5 years, I'm completely satisified with it.
Now, for people who haven't played the original Dungeon Keeper games, then you've never played anything like this. Really. The DK games, and now WFTO, are a genre in themselves, once which hasn't truely been seen for 14 years since DK2. Its a mash up of the RTS and God Game genres, with elements of RPG thrown in. Its like mixing a classic RTS like Age of Empires or Warcraft, with something like Sim City or Sim Theme Park, and then throwing in rudimentary elements of an RPG.
So it's Sim Age of Diablo, you ask? That's hard to imagine, what do you actually do?
Well, you start by building a dungeon, you mine out caverns and hallways around your dungeon core. Then you fill them with different rooms, attract hordes of monsters, minions and beasts into your employment, make them train and work, construct traps and defences, explore and expand your territory throughout the map and ultimately use your army of creatures to destroy the enemy, be it the forces of good, or a rival Underlords dungeon.  There's far more to it than that, but you'll have to play it to see.
10/10, fully recommend.

This feels like it could become something great.
I'm completely sick of Early Access games so I'm keeping a healthy dose of skepticism nearby however FunCom is making this, an actual MMO studio with a reputation to worry about. The fact that they are responsible for Age of Conan hopefully kicks up the chance that this'll become something great with all of the source material and assets to draw/steal from. You can already see the lengths to which they're going to make the player characters extremely well implemented. The character models and animations are already outstanding and feel great.
That being said, the AI sucks, the combat sucks, the spawning right in your face sucks, your body vanishing sucks, and a whole host of things suck... but it's early access... so whatever.   I hope they can come up with an interesting approach to melee combat like they did with Age of Conan...
I have high hopes for it and have to give it a thumbs up for now.
EDIT AFTER EXTENDED PLAY:
The whole experience feels very much like playing a MUD if you're old enough to remember those.  The fun is in the interactions between players and that means PVP, treachery, alliances, villains, and the occasional acts of kindness or mercy.  Withought a somewhat balanced mix of dedicated "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s" and "nice guys" the whole thing falls apart and becomes stale.
That being said, you may have to switch servers several times to build up relationships with players and acquire confidence in server rules and administrative consistency.  It's up to the admins to provide the landscape for a thriving ecosystem to evolve.
Don't expect to build bases without drawing interest from raiders. If it's got a door, there's treasure behind it.
Do not, under any circumstances, try playing on an Official server unless you really know what you're getting into and have a clan of likeminded people who enjoy that degree of challenge.  Make sure at least 1/4th of your clan are vampires that do not require sleep.
Do not expect worlds to persist for longer than 6-8 weeks.  Get used to the concept of starting over with a strategy to cement your clans place in the fresh world.
If you don't want to PVP or can't find a way to navigate the above, avoid the game.

HARD RESET sets out to provide old-school run and gun fun, and it succeeds admirably. The combat is frenetic (and tough at times) with waves of enemies being punctuated by simple puzzles and a light story line. The graphics are good for an indie game and the environments are impressive and immersive (it’s clearly influenced by Blade Runner, and that’s no bad thing). Physics play an important role: there are plenty of explosive and electrifying objects in the environments to help with the frenzied firefights. The enemies are well-designed and quirky (some even have propellers on their heads) and, although there aren’t that many classes, their attack methods develop as the game progresses to keep things mixed up. Although you only get two weapons both can be upgraded to add lots of additional fire modes (I liked this aspect -- some games have too many weapons). I really enjoyed this game despite the fact that I normally prefer a more nuanced shooter. It’s fast, furious, and a whole lot of fun. 4/5

You can only play it at fullscreen (in which everything is pixelated and hard to look at - and I only have a 13'' screen, which is considerably small), you can't alt+tab away from the game unless you're in for restarting it (you can't even access the Steam layer) and it happens a lot that the game crashes at cutscenes (that stuff you spent the last hour working on? Lost!).
If that is not enough to harden your way through, items are very very well hidden, which is not a bad point per se, but I found they were just overly hidden for it to be fun. I don't know whether this was made on purpose (since Sherlock's primary skill is observing it makes sense to make it hard to "see" useful stuff) or not.
Also, the puzzles are really difficult (difficult enough they're no longer fun) and most of the time will require you take paper and pen (since you can't alt+tab out of the game) and spend some long time on them, which could be fun if you like it (like I do), but, in this case, it just isn't.
Yes, the story is fine, the way you can get letters (backstory) is well thought of, moving through rooms/levels is a very good mechanic, but the bad points weight, by far, much more than the good points.
So, unless you enjoy very difficult and time-consuming games, don't spend your money on this.
If you get this in a SH bundle and need to check it out just because you're a fan, don't be afraid to have a walkthrough ready on your phone!

I have been playing Chiv on and off from free weekends since the game came out in 2012. I've owned the game for about a year now after picking it up from a sale when it was like $2 so I've gotten the chance to play with essentially every combination of class, weapon, and map. When the game first came out it was a ton of fun; easy to play, but hard to master.
Unfortunately, the game play has devolved from having correctly time strikes into people cranking their sensitivity all the way up, spamming a combo button and throwing their mouse around while jumping and crouching. This wouldn't be a huge if Torn Banner Studios wasn't a smaller developer. The animations are not very well done which makes the cheesy way people play almost impossible to fight against as a player will attack behind themselves while their character, and more importantly, weapon face an entirely different direction. Most of the time when someone complains about it in-game they complain of lag, but it isn't. It's poor animations being exploited by an exploited combat system.
Additionally, when I first started playing the game the weapon stats listed in-game actually meant something and now those little bar graphs seem to be meaningless. Do you like playing first-person precision fighting games where every enemy no matter what weapon they're using or you're using (regardless of whether you block, parry, or stun-block them with a kick) can attack you faster? Then this game is for you! Seriously though, it seems like the only way to kill anyone is the gang up on them which is another thing I see people griping on in reviews. Plus, it is super apparent the maps were not fully tested as just about every piece of collideable environment will get your player character trapped and killed because the skeletal mesh can't walk over a pebble on the ground.
All in all the game is still really fun, it looks cool, and it's one of the few good options in an under saturated market. All this being said, you should definitely not pay for full price and the DLC is ludicrous. However, it is definitely worth a dollar or two during big steam sales.

I put in a lot of time with the original PS3 release and thought enough of the game to add it to my library and work my way through it again on Steam.
The art direction is top notch, and the cel shaded look will help to ensure that the visuals stand the test of time.  The soundtrack is solid, while the effects are nice and satisfying.  The story is very straightforward but remains engaging due to an interesting cast of characters.
With all that said, the gameplay is the real standout here.  A glorious hybrid of strategy and real time elements makes this game truly unique and engaging.  The top down map view lets you plot your next move and observe friendly and enemy positions, assuming you currently have eyes on them.  Spending CP during you turn will then allow you to either issue orders or jump into the shoes of one of your units on the battlefield.  Once you're directly in control of a soldier or vehicle, you'll be free to move about the field and fire - or be fired upon - in third-person mode until you've exhausted the unit's AP and/or manually end the turn.  The whole thing works beautifully and really opens the door for a wide variety of attack strategies depending on map layout and squad composition.  Sprinkle in some nice leveling and crafting mechanics, and you've got one heck of an SRPG.

I really enjoy the mechanics of this game. Reading your opponent and surprising him with a kick or fake attack is awesome. The combat system has some variaty, for example the three different attack types and the option to manipulate the moment of impact with your body turning. It is all about knowing the range of your attack as well as its speed compared to your opponent's.
Enviroments are various and the objective maps feel like epic battles.
The only Problem is the lag srewing you over while playing online. As said before reading your opponent is key. When lag comes into play you are suddenly surprised by a superfast heavy attack or a crazy long leap which is quite frustrating. I had this issue often already with a ping of only 25.
Some other things I did not enjoy are that objective descriptions a sometimes not clear and that the distances between spawn and current objective location can be quite long and it is often not clear which way gets you there quick and which is a complete dead end, resulting in lone attackers running into a bored horde of defenders.
Concerning the importance of your awareness of nearby enemys as you cannot take many hits the FOV option is very limited because of the fisheye effect being very noticeable. This may screw over your understanding of your reach which as said is very important.
Non the less I recommend this game if you enjoy the theme and the brutality. Keep in mind the price tag as the animation quality is not the best and that the game seems to be quite demanding concerning resources.

Finally, the main missions are all about recruting and training your team, upgrading to be ready for the final mission. This is not a bad thing on itself, the interactions are great and let you know your main crew completely, but there is so little variation in the way is developed that it feels repetitive. Do a mission to recruit a team member, after recruiting do another to make it loyal, use resourses to do an upgrade to the ship from an idea that the new recruit has. Rinse and repeat until you got everything to go to the final mission.
Now the positive aspects on the game are the interactions with the characters, the dialog is what keeps this game going and surprisingly so, the actions you took previously really make themselves noticed, there is a lot of continuity, if you saved a minor character in the previous game, you will know about them, find them for a small mission, receive a letter from them, it makes you really care about your choices and make them carefully.
The game motivates you to complete the upgrades and the loyalty missions, hinting you that should you be lazy and be unprepared, your team and you will face a grim end in the final mission. So this gives you a push to explore for extra missions, complete all main quests before the final act, and it also motivates you to read the codex and know more about the universe and the relations between all the races.
Also, though I complain that the action gameplay is too similar to other titles, it does not mean it's boring. There is great action and gunfights in the game, I just wished they sticked to a more polished version of the previous gameplay instead of trying to use the same style and feel other popular games of the time had.
In the end is a very recommended game, if not as satisfying as the first game, because the story is great, the graphics are great, but most importantly, because the characters are great. And because Tali is still best waifu.

After 255 hrs of playing, I think I can write a review for this game.
Let's start off with the negative aspects:
The worst part about CK2 is that there is absolutely no challenge. Not to say, the game is easy as it can be. I always started with a county as crappy as possible in the hope of a real challenge but it never took me long (never more than 50 years I think) to become emperor of a great realm, either by killing & marrying (HRE / Byzantine) or by founding the British Empire by conquest. This limits the fun with the game for me, because once emperor, there is nothing left to achieve really, you can basically just conquer province after province. The only thing that slows you down at this point is that you have to wait until the next claim was fabricated somewhere. Never really managed to play longer than 150 or 200 years before I lost interest due to being bored.
The main issue about the game being much too easy is the broken marriage & inheritance system. Most of the time you will easily find a heir of a duchy or even a kingdom somewhere in the world whose heir is perfectly willing to marry your daughter matrilineary. Then just kill the current title holder and your son inlaw (which isn't difficult at all) and voila, you got a new realm. If you don't happen to find a direct heir who is willing to marry your daughter, just take his brother instead and then kill the heir. Tata, you matrilinearily married daughter will now produce the sons of the new heir.
The second reason which makes the game too easy is the very dumb AI, and I hate to say this because I'm a fan of Paradox and they are usually known for having great and challenging AI in their grand strategy games. In CK2 at least, if you manage to lose any war, you really suck. It is so easy to practically ally up every empire even as a small count, so you dont even have to fight your wars on your own. Byzantine will happily ship 20k troops to britannia to conquer that welsh scum next to you - just lean back and wait. And your opponent only rarely ever thinks about sieging your county. If against all odds he really raises troops and sends them to your place, just raise some 50 men from a liege and let them run all over the map. The opponent's 10k troops will chase those 50 peeps until his whole realm is crushed by your byzantine friends...
The reason why I still gave the game a thumbs up? It's a damn unique game concept, based on the medieval feudal system which keeps me locked up and makes me start a new game again every now and then. Forming a dynasty, managing your vassals, getting the right guardians for your promising kindsmen to build a decent heir for the next generation - it's really addictive. So sad, that the AI doesn't care about any of this either, and so you will see a lot of very crappy rulers in the realms bordering you.
Summary:
+ Very unique game idea
+ Addictive dynasty management
+ Great replay value
- Lousy AI
- Unrealistic and too easy marriage / inheritance system
- No long term motivation
5/10

I think the most important point of this review is that this game is very much the typical affair you would find on facebook like farmville or any facebook game nearly. What I mean by this is how the game is structured with a stamina system, level of progression, and many other similarties. If this is not your cup of tea then I would walk away. Reviewing I am basing my evaluation that it is free. It does carry it's fair share of cons but for me the pros outweigh them. For the cons I think the largest hindrance is the stamina system. For any level you play it requires food and once you have depeleted your set amount of food you have to wait for it to regenerate. I think this would not be a problem if it was not for the fact that the levels require large amount of food and you will often find yourself replaying levels in attempt to get more ideal elite creatures for evolving. If the cost of food to play levels were reduced then the game would be much more enjoyable. As of now you will find yourself with a short game session and waiting for the energy to renew. I wanted to play a shooter again, it had been a while. And here came Hard Reset on a sale, looking like a shooter with cool weapons, retro-gameplay and fancy graphics in a dark megacity setting. Sounded like something I would enjoy.
I completed the game on Hard and when this game says Hard, it means HARD. I rarely finished a level with under 2-5 deaths, some arenas cost me close to 10 deaths, because I either didn't choose the right weapon upgrades and consequently struggled, or I simply got overwhelmed by a surprise wave of enemies.
Hard Reset is pretty simple in terms of game mechanics, the gameplay could be summarized like this:
Enter arena. Run around in circles, relentlessly firing, dodging and switching between your poorly performing weapons, while trying to run from hordes of almost endlessly spawning mobs until you run out of ammo and powerups. Die. Try again. Finally beat arena. Proceed through corridor. Get ambushed. Enter next arena. Repeat.
Occasionally you have to press buttons to proceed, that's really all there is to it.
I'm usually the type for deep and rich gameplay, thinking up clever solutions, progressing tactically. I like games that make you think. This game is nothing like that and I'm aware this sounds like a full-fledged rant so far, BUT: what it does, it does well. The mechanics in place are well balanced, sprinting, jumping, shooting, environment damage, powerup placement and strength, enemy strength vs. weapon damage. It all was balanced with the grand scheme of gameplay in mind.
Some arenas feel a bit overdone, the developers just love to throw in waves and waves of mobs, probably to extend the playtime a little more. However, once you learn what enemy types to expect in which quantities and where the powerups are, things get more manageable. And still, each mob does crazy damage, there is little room for mistakes. Mobs also have tons of health and the big boys take quite a bit ammo to take down. Smaller enemies come in larger quantities regularly and still each have quite a bit of health, so you're often better off using the big calibers with AoE for small enemies as well. Enemies mostly feel like bullet sponges - and that's okay to make the game work as it is designed, given the design of arenas and the circumstances of powerups etc. The problem is that the game just doesn't give you the feeling of real weapon impact which is a big factor of fun in most shooters. Not so much here.
What's fun on the other hand is the management of space to run, retreating into the right corners, using the right weapons, dodging in the right moments, leaving powerups on the ground until you actually need them, it's all enough to consider to keep the game interesting.
Boss battles are well done as a combination of getting swarmed by waves of distractive mobs and having to hit special zones on the boss's body that need to be destroyed to take the boss down.
I like the AI in this game because mobs seem to cooperate to take you down. Mobs often run around you through adjacent corridors in order to attack you from all sides. Other than that, the AI is reasonably predictable once you've observed each mob's behaviour.
The level design overall is pretty linear and one-dimensional. Visually most of the game takes place in a dark Blade Runner'esque megacity, most of which is beautifully built. Unfortunately it gets repetitive after a while and leaves you longing for a change. It's not until the Exile DLC expansion that the overall setting changes to a brighter scrapyard wasteland, which to me was a welcome change at that point.
Many level elements return quite often, like forklifts blocking paths, while lifting the fork allows you to progess, or optionally powering up or down button panels to open doors. A little more variety wouldn't have hurt here.
Quite often you'd bump into invisible walls blocking progress or keeping you from jumping over obstacles. This can be quite tedious when there's only one supposed way to get to a secret, but there's no way to tell where there's a hole in the invisible wall.
So how does that add up? Let's take a look at the pros and cons:
*Pros*
+ Graphics are really good, performance is sublime for the visual quality
+ Sound is amazing
+ Good soundtrack (with a few exceptions)
+ Immersive dark and gritty atmosphere
+ Fast-paced non-stop action, bug- and glitch-free
+ Smooth user interface
+ Motivating upgrade system (at least until midgame, in endgame all the necessary weapons and defensive stats are maxed out and there's no more need to upgrade)
+ Interesting and tough boss battles, really gets you on your toes
+ Good AI - enemy groups split up and try to attack from all sides, even sometimes taking the longer path around an obstacles to sneak at you from behind
*Cons*
- Often repetitive and easily predictable level design
- Few enemy types
- Weak weapons (or too tanky enemies)
- Often unnecessarily prolonged battles - too many waves of mobs
- Some weapons are useless - I almost exclusively used the RPG, Mortar and Railgun and did just fine. Assault Rifle and Plasma Rifle never got used anymore when other weapons were unlocked
- Weapon switch times. This game requires frequent weapon switches and there are a few occasions where you just don't have the time to switch weapons. So if you're not prepared, you getting swarmed and you die.
- Less than stellar German translation and synchronization
- Some annoying songs in the soundtrack
- Invisible walls, often annoying placement of N.A.N.O. (currency) requiring you to make fiddly jumps. I sometimes couldn't be bothered.
So, do I recommend this game? Overall, yes! Buy it if you don't mind the simplistic gameplay and if you have a high-ish frustration tolerance. Do not buy it if you don't like arena battles and the circumstance of being constantly ambushed, surrounded and swarmed.
Overall rating: 79/100

Graphics: Mystery of the Mummy uses a Myst-like 3D-ego-perspective with pre-determined points-of-view. It does look worse than the ten years older Myst, though. Washed-out brown and grey tones are dominant, in later levels smoke, which is basically illustrated by a transparent grey layer above everything else, makes this even worse. To be fair, Myst had static frames while Mummy allows the player to look around with the mouse freely in its 'frames'. The possibility to look around freely is implemented badly, though, seriously hampering gameplay.
Gameplay: Surprisingly for a Sherlock Holmes game there are only very few logic based puzzles. It has ome stereotypical adventure puzzles: f.ex. the old 'get a key from the other side of the door with a pointy item and a pice of paper' trick makes a return and it has the infamous sliding puzzle (twice!).
Unfortunately most of the puzzles consist solely of finding and combining the correct items. The free camera together with the washed out graphics make those puzzles utterly frustrating. Making places in the gameworld that Sherlock can interact with more apparent would have helped making this game a lot more enjoyable. Instead you are supposed to find things like a tiny hairpin (seriously, it was only barely visible after I *knew* where it is) in a room with lots of broken stuff and junk in it, without even knowing what exactly you are looking for to begin with.
Having a time limit in one of the levels doesn't really help either.
Some of the few better and more complex puzzles which usually open a new frame to solve them, suffer from the somewhat arbitrary way of ending them: Some end automatically as soon as the right solution has been achieved, in others nothing is happening after getting the solution until the puzzle frame is exited. This results in situations where little oversights in a overall good but very tedious puzzles leads to the player exiting a puzzle, thinking it's solved, only to be forced redoing it from the beginning.

I want to like it.  I really do.  And for a student project, it is excellent.  The team should be proud of their work.
TL;DR: only focuses on addition skills, a bit boring for an adult, not entirely polished
The good:
-It's great practice for addition.
-The difficulty scales with spell power or quest.
-There's plenty of rewards to keep someone playing.
-It's linear, so it's difficult to get lost for too long.
The bad:
- It is painfully obvious that English is not the native language of the developers.  "In" and "on" were misused a couple of times.  In/on/at can be tricky for ESL'ers (some languages combine these words).  This is a relatively easy, though tedious, fix.  I doubt it would hurt the developing language skills of children, but it may be a bit confusing.
- I'm forced to play a male character.  I could input my name, but not choose my gender.  This may have been something that was planned but never implemented.  It may have been too much work to include.
The ugly:
-I don't expect it to get as much play time as other games.  The linear story line doesn't seem to branch, so it would be the same story every single time.  I don't think choices really matter much.
-I find it boring.  Neat, but boring.  I'm not sure I'd be really engaged in the game if a child was playing it nearby.
If I get the opportunity I'll try to a kid to play with me.  That way I could get more accurate feedback -- it *was* designed for kids afterall.  But as it is, I wouldn't recommend it to parents for kids.

It is an awesome, awesome game in its own right, but as a part of a trilogy, it is the ‘dark’, characters front and center, middle chapter of a sprawling space opera, à la “Empire Strikes Back”. BioWare took all that was great of the first Mass Effect, trimmed the fat, and made the game just that much better. ME2 has the most interesting crew out of all three Mass Effect’s, from good ol’ Garrus (now a vigilante which makes him even better) to Mordin, the very model of a Salarian scientist (who has studied species turian, asari, and batarian). What fits in-between are a master thief, a grizzled war vet, a tank bred Krogan, a crazy tattooed psychic lady, and many more. Colorful people, I must say. The story (sans the ending), is a great one, so far away from the ‘normal’ story of ME1. In ME1 you were a Spectre, the cop of the galaxy, giving you access where ever and whatever. In ME2, the only thing you have is your gun, sweet honeyed words, and a couple of good friends. Even though the game came out ~4 years ago, I still implore any one new to try to keep themselves as pure of spoilers as possible, and to experience the story on their own. Just as a final word, the combat of the game is very much the same as it was in ME1 (cover based 3rd-person shooting, with the ability to control squad mates abilities), just with the introduction of ammunition. It has just been sharpened in all regards. Just go out and buy it! Though, if you are one that wants all three in the trilogy in one place (with easy access to DLC, sort of), just use Origin. Not at all a bad service. This game truly is 'Mom's Spaghetti'

After playing this game for about 10 hours, I feel I can write a faily solid review in relativity to the state the game is now in under release.
This game is a surprisingly amazing throwback and spiritual successor to Bullfrog's series Dungeon keeper. The gameplay is a breath of fresh air in an industry over saturated with Indie Devs creating stale replications of more popular games.
This game features dungeon building (which is amazingly satisfying), RTS elements. And economic balancing. Kind of a Towns/RTS if you will. The game features 4 modes, Campaign. Survival, Skirmish, and sandbox. (Multiplayer skirmish)
Campain acts as a story setting and tutorial for the game's research system, building and running your dungeon effectively. With brilliantly evil voice acting, fun and exciting missions that challenge your abilities as an Underlord. Campaign will keep you busy for hours and help you refine your skills as an underlord.
Skirmish is unfinished but the basic format for a skirmish game is 2 or more Underlords facing off in an attempt to destroy eachother's dungeon core (Larger player games are being worked on) This game gives you a fully unlocked Veins of evil tree to research the rooms nessesary to defeat the opposing player.
Survival is very much what is says on the box, and like skirmish, is still relatively under construction. Survival places you in a premade dungeon and gives you 3 lanes to defend where opposing heroes will try and breach your dungeon's defences and destroy your core. Sounds simple right? Its hard. Really hard. Good luck.
And sandbox, a dungeon building wonderland, where the game gives you the freedom to construct a dungeon of ludicrous size, and this mode, as free as it is, will only last you a certain amount of time, as the lack of enemy contact makes it feel.. empty at best after all of your rooms have been made.
At the time of review I can give this game my approval and definetly recommend this to any person who is a fan or the original Dungeon keeper series. And anyone who is a fan of RTS and "Towns" Style games. But do not be afraid to try if you normally stray away from these styles of games! This game has somthing for everyone, and deserves as many sales as possible.
However, this game is still for the most part, an unfinished release and I have to deduct points for that. But the negatives far outweigh the positives in my eyes, and everyone should keep this game in mind, even if you don't plan on buying immediately post lauch. Please keep this in mind.
Credit is given where credit is due as Subterranean games breaths fresh life into a industry that is lacking new ideas recently (At least in my opinion) This game is a work of art and deserves your money.
I rate this game a solid 6/10 in its current state. I'm sure the score will rise to a 7/10 or a 8/10 in coming patches.
I have had tremendous fun so far with this game, and cannot wait for more content to arrive as Subterranean games have promised in free updates post launch. If you are looking for a solid throwback to Dungeon Keeper, and a great new IP to keep you busy for hours. War for the Overworld Certainly deserves to be a game in your library.

Fantastic game, sadly, it's F2P of the worst kind, the one that forces you to buy something to get the full experience.
First off, let's just adress the thing that ruins the game: The labour system.
The Labour system they've got going in Archeage works like this: You regenerate 5 Labour points every 5 minutes to a maximum of 3000 as long as you're online, these points are used to do ANYTHING except for combat, most of the quests, traveling and buying stuff from stores. Examples of it's uses is: opening loot bags that drops after killing an enemy, mining, crafting, chopping wood, etc.
You can boost this buy paying for 1 to 12 months of "patron" which makes the regeneration of labour points as well as the maximum labour points one can have double (for the duration of the Patron) It also makes you regenerate Labour points while offline.
At first, it doesn't seem so bad. But as soon as you get to higher level areas you'll notice that it becomes a big problem if you lack Labour. Crafting consumes waaaay too many points and the loot bags steadily increase the ammount of labour points you need to open them. It just doesn't make it fun.
Other than this, bots instantly claiming land is also a big problem, which makes building a house impossible.
More games should take after Warframe's way of making a F2P game. Wait times are acceptable if they're done in that way. I had a ton of fun with this game, but overlooking flaws in games just because they were enjoyable is something I won't do. The game's bad due to greed and unless this is fixed, I can't say I'll see myself coming back anytime soon.

Hand of Fate is a fun little indie game which at a 6$ purchase price(steam winter sale) makes an easy recommendation if you like dungeon crawlers or card games. It offers a fairly unique premise with excellent visual presentation as well as the excellently voiced narrator, your opponent.
With a sequel well on the way already, i view this game as the first step in a new series of games which will get bigger and better from here on out. With this viewpoint in mind here are a list of things i find holding back the game that i hope are addressed in the sequel.
1.Combat becomes monotonous. Enemeies have far too much hitpoints, sponging up attacks, and the game penalizes you for attempting to finish off knocked down opponents. It becomes worse as new bosses are unlocked and start appearing randomly in old encounters. The bosses are very tanky and will appear as often as weak enemies.
2.Deck building is of little importance. The most important part is unlocking extra fortune cards(gold, food, equipment drops) but there is no choice involved;these cards simply stack up. The most powerful gear is a no brainer to toss into your deck with no downsides.
3.Beating bosses gives no repeat reward. You may as well forfeit at the end of a dungeon and save yourself the grind of repeatedly killing a boss. It would be nice to be able to earn one-use extra fortune cards that could be deployed in endless, for example.
4.Dungeons lack thematic impact. You are in a cave dungeon, yet got spotted by a giant eagle. There is no terrain graphics for deserts and forests.
5.Dungeons are small and straightforward. The later dungeons are slightly less so but are never complex.
6.Beating the game is anti-climatic. There is virtually no acknowledgement that you have done so, no new abilities or cards for doing so. This is where you would expect a New Game+ to come into play.
7.The final boss is very poorly designed. Its filled with quick time events and spams waves of previously beaten bosses with no way to earn health or save your progress in between. You will have to replay the final dungeon many times in order to begin this encounter with epic-tier equipment to stand any chance.

This is a very strange and interesting rogue-lite.
You play a game of cards, where each card represents an encounter. There are many different encounters, some beneficial, some perilous. Many, you can solve in both a positive or negative way. Depending on the outcome, you may get "tokens", which are simillar to booster packs. They each contain one or more cards you can eventually add to your deck in order to make it richer in encounters or equipments or whatever it is you fancy.
The catch is, though, that in order for you to claim your rewards, you need to finish the entire run. If you manage to do so, all the tokens you've collected are yours, and you are free to move onto the next, more difficult and varied adventure.
The game is not purely played through the cards. Whenever there's combat, you have to play it out manually, and these can get pretty intense. The gameplay is extremely simple, though: just mash buttons and time your attacks according to the in-game prompts. If you've played the Batman: Arkham games, you know the drill. This is similar, but far less fancy in its acrobatics and overall animations. It gets dull rapidly. Yet, each combat doesn't last more than a minute or 2, depending on the difficulty, so it's not that taxating.
The game has a Story and an Endless mode, besides different difficulty levels. As it is with most rogue-lites, this is a very replayable game, and also kind of unique in both its presentation and its development. In some way, it's more text driven than most rougue-lites, which demands a more active imagination with the encounters, but in a good way.
I'd say if you're interested or like rogue-lites, check this one out. Is cheap and very good for its price.
