I believe I'm about halfway through, though I haven't touched the endless mode. Nonetheless, I think I can say this game is pretty cool. Unique concept with a polished execution. Combat is simple, but its difficulty ramps up quite quickly, especially on hard mode. Sometimes it feels like bad luck really screws you, but almost always skill and good decision making can make up for some bad rolls (and in fact, I think maybe you can even watch the cards as they shuffle to increase your chance of choosing the right one, but I'm not sure if it's just completely random anyway). The "Loot" is pretty satisfying, though so far it doesn't seem to dramatically change your playstyle (like, you can't play ranged characters or a mage or anything, just basically a melee character possibly with 1 or 2 ranged attacks.)
I will say the overall writing and setting, while solid, is kind of generic darkish fantasy. There are various story arcs that play out through extended encounters which are entertaining, but don't expect anything profoundly creative. I also find various parts of the game kind of slow, like entering into shops, and when the dealer deals the initial cards and you have to watch him for like 15 seconds. It's not a big deal, but it's one of those little things that takes away from the game.
It's the kind of game that would be fun to imagine with 10x the budget, while still maintaining the core gameplay and feel, only hiring some better writers and adding a few more mechanics, various secrets, more of a character creation, and just fleshing it out more. Perhaps Hand of Fate 2 will end up being like that.

Hard Reset is developed by Flying Wild Hog, the people behind Shadow Warrior and its upcoming sequel. Hard Reset was developed before Shadow Warrior and you can tell that the company did not have as much of a bigger budget as Shadow Warrior did
The story basically follows a dystopian world where robots have taken over by a sophisticated A.I., you play a major known as Fletcher, throughout the story you have to try and find out the reasons why the robots have turned against the humans and stop those who are responsible. The story is very cliche and does follow what many other sci-fi films back in the day managed to achieve
The environments are absolutely stunning, and the lighting effects in particular really make the enviornments come alive. The explosions also play a big role in Hard Reset and really make the game more explosive in its action, however, even though I have a PC that can run it on ultra settings, I did suffer with some minor frame rate drops when there was a lot of action going about. Now, I don't know what the developers where trying to go through the environments, but the game really reminded me of Blade Runner, a sci-fi thriller classic. The high rise buildings, the flying cars and that Chinese/Japanese (sorry can't tell the difference) adevertising on large blimps, I think the developers where heavily inspired by Blade Runner when they were designing Hard Reset
Talking about game performance, this game does suffer with poor game performance. Sometimes the game freezes monetarily even in heavy combat areas, this may be due to the high amounts of enemies and explosive effects taking place
The A.I., the game's difficulty changes drastically, especially in the last bit of the main story and then the rest of the DLC story, I first played on Normal difficulty and it was so annoying that I died so many times that I had to lower it to the Easy difficulty which lowered the amount of times I died and these robots sure do have precision aim shooting, because in Hard Reset they have precision aim shooting!
The music and sound effects were okay but what really made me happy was that whilst playing, it did remind me of Blade Runner quite a lot!
Like previously said, you will die, a lot, thankfully there is a fair checkpoint system in the game. The voice acting was bad and I mean really bad. You can tell that in Shadow Warrior they had a bigger budget because at least in that game the voice acting was good, in Hard Reset, they were really bad. The only good performance I would say was from the professor, nobody else
The gunplay is okay, nothing special though. I think the game was also heavily inspired by old shooters like DOOM, as it does try to bring in that same formula to Hard Reset
Lastly, what really made me not want to continue playing was the re-use of the enemies. I don't know how many times I saw the same enemies over and over again every single time through my whole playthrough. It really made me not want to continue playing... Plus, what is up with the endings!? The main story's ending is really bad and ends on a huge cliffhanger leaving you helpless as to what has just happened and what will happen, thankfully Flying Wild Hog made an extended edition which includes the Exile DLC for free which continues the main game. But even that ending, it has that ending of, "Oh, don't worry, everything will be explained in due time", and just ends like that...
I had fun playing Hard Reset, even though it did have its fair share of problems here and there, but on the whole, it was a really good action game. I wouldn't recommend Hard Reset for its full asking price as I feel it does not satisfy me to pay full price, but if it is in a sale, price drop, etc... I would definitely recommend you buying it, if you love sci-fi or Blade Runner or both like me

A strong contender for the retro-style pixel art video game scene. Visually it looks amazing, from the the amazing detail in the level design to the subtle emotions portayed on the sprites themselves. This unfortunately is the games strongest aspect. The music which accompanies climactic moments is strong yet often brief, and exploration is lonesome with the music cometimes seeming as if its altogether not there.
In regards to exploration, that is another strong weakness for a game with a metroidvania-styled map layout. Shortcuts that bring you from area to area are few and far between and the inconsistent size of screen transitions can make it difficult to fully grasp your general location. That and there is no map feature to aid you in the 100% collection benefits the game teases.
As for mechanics, the game itself feels strong, being more of a side-scrolling shoot-em-up as opposed to a platformer with its two-man system: Owlboy for movement and a secondary companion on attack. Sadly, while it does make you get creative with the unique combat features of each companion, it only does so for a brief moment, never really taking it a step further especially with the sparse boss fights throughout the game. There are also a few seqeuences, namely the stealth ones that feel out of place with the design philosophy of the rest of the game and severely hinder the enjoyment of the game.
Overall however the experience was a positive one and I recommend this game on a sale.
Also I would suggest a keyboard and mouse, controllers had issues with responsiveness and forced a double-tap when fatal (Such as hitting jump thrice which cancels flight mode).

The Good, The Bad and The...possibly awesome?
I'll try to keep this short.
Good:
- Crafting System
- Looks beautiful
- Well optimized for a new Early Access release. Running all Maxed out @1440p on a GTX 980 at 45-65FPS.
- Hidden secrets and lore around the map
- The universe of Conan has a lot to bring to the table, and it stays pretty true to it.
- Potential (There are so many things coming that are gonna be awesome.. The Purge, Sorcery/Necromancy using Corruption, new biomes making the map larger and larger by each one.. and much more)
The Bad:
- Official servers have had some lag and big rubberbanding issues. Funcom has decided to move all official servers to a new provider. Hopefully that fixes a lot of it.
- Some bugs involving crafted items going missing, Thralls dissapearing etc. on server restart.
- VoIP issues. Atm not the easiest to RP using ingame VoIP. Sometimes it works, sometimes it works halfway, sometimes not at all until you restart your client.
- Needs a little balancing on XP gains, so that you don't have to grind one certain type of mob to level quickly.
- Durability on shields needs to be buffed big time. Breaks too easily.
With all this said, i am a fan of Survival sandbox games, and so i love this game. It's my new favorite (Used to be ARK).
Even with the issues, i see soo much potential, and the game has given me close to 40hours of fun so far, and i'm not even close to having seen everything or done everything.
IMO well worth the money so far. And knowing a little of what they mentioned is to come, just gets me more exited to play even more.
I have to give credit to Funcom for delivering patch upon patch, and being active both on Discussion and Twitter. This is important for Early Access games. If they can keep this going, this game will go far.
TL;DR
Great game that will get even better with the roadmap of stuff coming.
Well worth the money if you like Survival sandbox games.
Be aware of lag and rubberbanding though if you play on Official servers at the time of writing they are

I rate the game Hard Reset (extended edition which includes the Exile DLC) 4/5. Good but not great.
This highly linear first person perspective action game has truly fantastic and highly detailed graphics (heavily inspired by the movie Blade Runner) but ultimately has far more style than substance...but what wonderful style!
+Fantastic graphics!
+Extremely fast paced, streamlined and highly optimized gameplay
+Extremely efficient use of existing computer hardware to produce fantastic, fast moving graphics.
+A great use of multiweapons (rare to see done well in any game). Multiweapons are single weapons which act, though the use of different modes, like multiple weapons thus making it seem more plausible (barely) that you should be able to carry around 12 different weapon systems.
+Cool cyberpunk style throughout.
+Great, fairly tight controls.
+Cut scenes have a nifty anime/sketch work style going on.
+Game objectives are almost always clear despite the fact that the plot (and the reason to complete the objectives) isn't often clear at all.
+Good sound effects.
+Graphics and lighting effects are so nifty that it may be worth it to play it through a second time just to see them all over again. Quite a special effects extravaganza.
+Often challenging but rarely frustrating with a generally great automatic save system.
-Extremely linear game with one ending
-The single ending which this game has leaves you hanging and feels abrupt
-Fairly short game (but it does have some replayability as you may want to play again on a higher difficulty level and get all the weapon and other upgrades (which the game is to short to allow you to do on a single play through).
-The enemies don't have great variety
-Bare bones plot
-Unintentionally funny and bad dialogue sequences which often fail to significantly develop this game's general lack of specific plot.
-Occasionally confusing plot elements which aren't important anyhow which may nonetheless leave you wondering 'okay...why exactly am I doing this? What is my plan here?' etc.
-Unbelievably crappy music throughout. It's hard to believe how craptacular the music in this game is.

Another part of original story of Crysis 1 following sgt.Sykes (aka Psycho) who goes to the isle steal alien artifact which Koreans possess.
Classic and good 'old' FPS with good story and atmosphere.
Beautiful semi-opened levels acting as large sandboxes where solution of level goal is only on you - scout area carefuly, observe guards/enemies, look for possibilities to i.e. draw attention on one side of map while you sneak through it on other side etc., or go rogue in Rambo style (but you maybe will die a lot then ;)).
Not bad AI, definitely one of smarter, they can hear you very well and they can see you even if you are cloaked if they come too close (they see 'something', not exactly you, but they will go investigate etc.).
Badass super hi-tech nano-suit with four modes:
- cloak - sneak through almost anywhere unseen
- power - jump higher, deliver super strong punches with your hands or throw grenades/stuff/enemies over larger distance, lower recoil, even with large guns like mounted 20mm cannons etc.
- speed - no explanation needed :)
- armor - withstand much more damage to your suit like from enemy bullets or simply drop down from large heights
Every ability can be very useful, use is only on you how do you combine them during gameplay.
Beside cloaking there is possibility to hide behind stuff and even in bushes uncloaked.
Pros:
- nice story about saving humanity from alien race's raid
- smart AI
- even with linear story game gives you feel of open world due its large and open levels/maps
- amazing graphics (with some lighting and HD textures mods even better)
- bugless (i didn't encounter any bug)
Cons:
- game needs a lot of tweaking (not in menu but in config files itself) to deliver reasonable framerate even on nowaday's beast rigs, but funny fact is you can tune it to actually look much more better and yet increasing your framerate ;)
- gameplay do not differ much from original Crysis 1, this is more like an DLC which is expanding orignal story
Conclusion
Overall very good game (yet typical scenario 'go save our world'). I had wait some years to play it in desired quality, but waiting was worthy :). If you like sci-fi and stealth possibilities with sandbox play i'd definitely reccomend it to you. Anyway Warhead involves much more aliens and less humans than Crysis 1 - i am fine with it, but someone could find it boring as he likes 'pre-sci-fi' part of orignal Crysis 1.

You start out selling a single bread only to expand and broaden your stock, take advantage of price drops and increases and items trending amongst certain townsfolk. You can decorate the shop which will infuence type of customers coming into the shop, and set up auto sellers for items you don't particularly want to haggle on.

Playtime: I played through the whole game 2.5 times on PS3. Will eventually get around to play it on PC, too-
Know that kind of games that innovate genres by creating interesting new gameplay concepts, instead of re-iterating stale franchises?
Valkyria Chronicles is one of those. It combines squad-management(with limited upgrade-possibilities and character-specific boons and drawbacks), a turn-based battle-concept(where you get a limited amount of activations per turn, but CAN spend multiple activations on the same unit(which gets less movement with each activatio)) and semi-real-time during those activations(best watch a video on this, it would take take too long to explain in a way that could not be misunderstood).
The plot and characters are good, if somewhat over-the-top, but if you played any japanese games in the past 20 years, you'll know what to expect.
The art style is as unique as the gameplay, very fitting, and I definitely wish more games would use it. Sound is good if not outstanding.
Most importantly, the settings(urban, grassland, desert, woods...) and mission objectives(interception, defense, reach point, destroy specific enemy, capture base, eliminate all enemies...) are varied and interesting. There are a few slight balance-issues(Scout OP), but on the whole, it's awesome, and not easy getting the best ranks.
(Unless, of course, you play on NG+, which is a thing).
TL,DR: I found this game and concept so awesome that despite already having played it several times on another system, I got it on Steam in the hopes of eventually getting the sequels released on steam as well.(even if the second part for PSP was inferior). It's a fresh new concept with unique gameplay, and the positive aspects vastly more dominant than a few small drawbacks.

The only problem is that due to it being a small indie game, it's pretty short, and sometimes their ideas don't quite live up to their execution (like a large mansion area where almost all of the doors are just scenery), and sometimes the player camera can be a bit buggy, particularly with getting your phone's light to shine in the right direction sometimes in the school area. Just like Crysis.. i wish there was a vote inbetween thumbs up and down. This is another "meh" title.
I had high hopes for Warhead. Crysis leaves you on a MASSIVE cliffhanger and I figured this game would go back and you would continue on. In Crysis the characters "Nomad" and "Prophet" go into the alien sphere for what seems like an epic battle. That game ends abruptly right there and leaves you hanging.
Warhead instead of doing what it was supposed to do, just puts you in the shoes of a completely different soldier "Psycho" who you see for a short while at the start of Crysis. Worst still, it takes place along side Crysis on a seperate part of the island. Its not a prequel or a sequel. That's pretty annoying. The only justice in this title is that at least is wraps up Psycho's story somewhat.. problem is the ending of Crysis happens after the ending of Warhead, so even though Warhead wraps up, it can't close off the open story created by Crysis.
Seriously, this is another example of a tech demo and not a full game. Worse still, Crysis at least showed off some amazing design and some really interesting visuals... even if there was no gameplay present during those moments. Warhead on the otherhand just recycles literally all of it's visual content from Crysis and doesn't add anything to the experience. Psycho's storyline is uninteresting. You spend the whole game trying to capture a "thing" in a box. Once you get it the game doesn't have the good grace of even telling you what it is... however by the time I was done I was so burned out on the experience I didn't care. I didn't expect the game to answer the questions it poses so I wasn't dissapointed this go around. I was expecting mediocrity and I got it.
By why still a thumbs up? True I want to give this a nuetral rating, but it is still fun in it's own right. It barely leans towards a thumbs up, even less so than Crysis did and I was feeling conflicted by that one. I'm 7 years late to this party, but at least writing out this review feels cathartic.
Unless you have a good amount of money to blow, your level of enjoyment wont be too high.

I tried this game because I am looking for some games to play with my little cousin who needs help with maths. It doesn't really cut it.
Good:
Cute/pretty as far as RPG maker games go.
Ability to sprint which is always nice.
A lot of drills and problems and varying difficulties for kids learning arithmetic.
Cute simple story with a simple path to follow.
FREE - and good length of gameplay for a free game, I spent a bit over an hour playing it through.
Bad:
Very unforgiving. The questions from the villagers only give you one try and even though you can take all the time you need the longer problems, which are more difficult, disappear once you get to the second screen so you have to rely on memory for what the problem is. The combat problems are timed and then disappear but are easier. You are not given the answer if you get it wrong.
If you forget to lift the sprint key when you talk to someone it works like the enter or space key and causes you to do whatever action or miss part of the conversation.
The combat system isn't intuitive. You have to hit enter before you can put in your answer. The easy difficulty has a tutorial that explains this but the normal and difficut difficulties don't. Even so, it's not a very good set up and the problems having a short timer and disappearing when you go to answer aren't good for kids with dyscaluclia or dyslexia, which my cousin has. Those tend to be common problems for kids who need help with maths.
The menu is awful. I don't know much else to say there. It's just... weird? And even in the tutorial I didn't see anyone tell me how to access it (by hitting 0). I fell upon it by accident, which I'm glad I did because it's also the back button. It's only called "the pause menu".
It was boring. I received quite a few of the same problems. The problems had all the same setup; either ? + ? or "I had __ amount and then got __ amount. How much do I have total?" There were a couple word problems with three numbers you had to sum. (It's ONLY addition. But thats in the game description so it's expected but a bit odd to not have any other arithmetic)
Quite a bit of memory testing without reminders which isn't all that great. It seems a bit more heavy on memory than maths. The one mistake I made was from a more complex word problem that I couldn't re-read the problem and forgot the figures I had to add.
The English was pretty bad. Some things had really bad grammar or didn't make much sense. Usually I don't care as long as I know what it meant but I don't know how good that would be for a kid still learning English grammar. There were also some words that were really beyond the level of the target age group.
"Side quests" are actually required to advance. That's a bit weird.
Overall, its like a good start to a game but I wouldn't really recommend it to older players because of the simplicity and tediousness unless you want to practice some addition for some simple brain exercises. For my little cousin I can just see her getting frustrated at how unforgiving the word problems are and the combat set up.

'Dungeon Keeper'. Yeah. You can't escape the fact that this is the game that you buy if you wanted a Dungeon Keeper 3 (or a decent DK2).  You will typically start the game looking for a creature portal, building rooms for sleeping, eating and training, and finding the starting gold vain. Nothing new there.
But this game stands strong in it's own right. Obviously, it just isn't quite DK. Hating it for this seems to be a hobby for many fans. But the game deserves to be treated as though it stands on it's own: and it certainly can. If DK had never existed, this game would be hailed as an innovative marvel. Instead, it is simply a fun, workable game using the same formula.
An early example of a nice little innovation is the Tavern building: Minions will pay some of their wages back to you for cooked food and beer, but you need to keep it stocked, giving an interesting strategic choice. Things such as this give the game a feeling of depth without making it micro-manage hell.
The game is worth the money. You will have fun playing a dungeon-building strategy game. It is not DK. Get over it.

This game is everything I wanted and more. It's brilliantly made and has a very fun and easy to enjoy battle system. I first saw this video in a paid promotion and I was pre-emptively gagging, expecting some cash grab. I watched on and what I saw looked amazing. It's a game of chance, requires some strategic thinking and is loads of fun. Sometimes you feel awesome and super lucky, while other times you just feel wrecked, but usually you can play well enough to mitigate the bad outcomes. I wholeheartedly recommend this if you've ever enjoyed a roguelike game before, or a card game. It's the best of both, with tons of progression.
Pros: Good lore, fun gameplay, interesting character designs, interesting encounters, a surpising amount of progression and a ton of depth. Lots of replayability, extremely addicting. Once you begin collecting tokens, you just can't stop.
Cons: There's barely any music, but what little there is, it's pretty good. There is a lot of luck elements, but it's a card game all about fate and chance, so this is barely even a drawback. Also, this game is extremely addictive. Hard not to play over and over and say to yourself "Alright, last game- Ah crap it's 3 am? Whatever, just one more."
Would buy again, especially while it's on sale. DEFINITELY get this if you're considering it, you won't regret it one bit! (Unless you hate getting unlucky, then maybe. But pro tip, you can track cards with your eyes so it's never that luck based!)

This a beautiful game that simply isn't for me. From the time I put in, it appears to be a decent Metroidvania platformer--if you can still consider a game a platformer when you can fly from the get-go.
I have a few minor quibbles about the art, but they're very minor, and one is related to consolitis. I don't know what resolution the game was made in, but it apparently only supports one resolution. Fortunately, it has a full-screen option.
What turned me off to the game was the opening cut-scene. After the opening sequence, I simply didn't want to be Otus Owlboy the Helpful Hero. I wanted to beat the crap out of my mentor and burn the village to the ground. But neither of those goals were options, and I found it to be a major buzzkill. While it is common for games to dictate what your goals are, this game made that weakness more keen to me because the storyline left me not only completely unmotivated to perform those goals, but highly motivated to shirk those duties.
I couldn't get past actively not wanting to do what the storyline demanded I do. But someone who is motivated by abuse and humiliation, someone who sees such things as a challenge to prove themselves rather than a reason to flip the bird and move on, will no doubt find a lovely game here.
I'm not that person.
Edit: I'm not against a story where the protagonist begins as a pariah. But if you're going to have your protagonist be a pariah, it only works well if there's some sort of redemption arc. I obviously don't know how the story goes beyond the opening, but the opening wasn't a setup for that. That setup involves either a history of malevolence and a period of soul searching, or some sort of traumatic event resulting from a mistake--either a crime of passion, or just a bad choice with terrible consequences. Being a disabled orphan taken in by an arrogant jerk and treated like crap by the village doesn't qualify as something someone needs to atone for.
A pariah beginning can also work if there's a vengeance arc against the community, but I saw no indication that was forthcoming, and while those can work, usually they just end up turds like Postal or Hatred.
Owlboy gets two enthusiastic birds from me--but kudos to the art and programming team. From what I saw, they did excellent work, and I hope to see more from this studio, and more high resolution side-scrolling sprite based platformers.

This game in my opinion is a rethinking of an "old school" shooter similar to Serious Sam or especially Painkiller.  If you like either of those games at all, you can stop reading now and just buy and play Hard Reset especially given the price.
Many of the game play elements, points accumulation and level crafting are very similar to those of Pain Killer.  But Hard Reset has a Cyberpunk/AI based theme and evokes the sensibilities of Blade Runner including Industrial/Urban rainy scenes in low light though it is has many scenes that are very bright.  It actually has some truly beautiful though Industrially themed scenes.
It has many secret areas and collectable items.  The character movement is fairly traditional though is not too stictly scripted -- you can fall to your death in many areas.   There is some tricky jumping and climbing involved to access the secret areas (some are as difficult as those in Pain Killer).  There is a weapons/armor crafting system that allows one to buy upgrades for weaponry that suites your style (the shotgun is authoritative, I like it).
While it is not an open world, and has no optional quests, the level design is very complex and involves significant maze running.  You  won't likely be bored by traversing similarly designed levels -- the scenes are all quite different.    The visual quatlity is very good and the game performance is remarkably good and has no real bugs or jarring graphical artifacts.  The AI's are very good and at higher levels will brutalize you.  But this is well suited to an aggressive style of guns-blazing play style that starts in the first 30 seconds of play.  It's a shooter :)
The game is very replayable which I think makes up for it's main problem -- it is a bit short and difficult (think of it as a Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥short story).  So you might want to try it first on a difficulty level that is a notch down from your typical settings.  You can replay the game at higher level using the weaponry you acquired on a lower level.

The best thing I can say is this: in my first play through, I was sorry that the game came to end.

Originally I had written some sarcastic words about how the game was cool (haha he's so funny) and I have come to regret this. Here's why...
There's no doubt that if this is your first time to the CE store page than the first thing you noticed was the mixed reviews. Now reaching above the 40 hour mark, I have not just grown to like Conan Exiles. I have grown to love it. In a world where the witch hunt continues for “money hungry devs” its not a bad thing that players are so cautious with how their hard earned money is spent in the industry, but perhaps we are all a bit too lenient with who we throw these words at. After spending more and more time with CE I fall deeper and deeper into pondering just why the game is receiving so much negativity. And thus I do my best to take part in the effort to shine some light on this growing little title that has big potential.
Let's tackle the EA thing shall we? I have purchased a lot of EA titles. Some helped me to realize the magical possibilities of the concept. Some are an ever looming regret. Now there are generally two sides of people in this story and though each side insists the other is wrong, the truth lies somewhere in the middle.  Bugs should be acceptable in early access material. Place holder content should be acceptable in early access material. Lack of content – to an extent – should be acceptable in early access material. This is the whole idea of Early Access. Games are not magically awesome one day. It takes hard work, dedication and time. But its also important to understand that the devs are not invulnerable just because they put the EA sticker on their game. Bad choices are bad choices, regardless of the state of the game and to some extent we consumers are the investors here.
So where does that leave CE? CE had a bit of a rough start. Server issues ran rampant and some pretty serious bugs were discovered. If left unattended I would not be so lenient, but due to Funcoms diligence and perseverance I am only left with admiration. As a community we need to start supporting devs like these, if not with our money than with our words. There are so many devs out there that do not have the motivation or possibly the skills to right what they have wronged. Funcom has been more active with their game development than I have ever seen personally in an EA title. The news log should speak for itself. This game is updated on average about twice a day. I've seen more than the average two before and so far have yet to see them take a day off. Why are we not applauding this?
Nearly every major issue has already been squashed and they are working hard to rectify some others. Though CE is in EA this game feels far more complete than any other EA title I have played at this stage. The devs need to continue their ambitious approach and maintain this work ethic. If things continue in this direction, mark my words, Conan Exiles will be a major force in the survival genre.
Currently i'm running a GTX 1080, i7-4790, and 16 gigs of ram. Performance has never been an issue for me though it could vary for AMD owners as I have not tested this myself. To be fair I have only played CE in single player and on privately owned servers, so I will be unable to verify performance when it comes to official servers.
Conan Exiles is stunningly beautiful on Ultra Settings. It is definitely the best looking title in this genre. Everything from your surroundings to character models, to the water and the way your clothes sways in the wind is painstakingly detailed. Some of the games animations are a bit on the rough side, but I would imagine these will get cleaned up over time. If ultra smooth animations is a must for you, you might want to hold off on picking this up.
Mechanically CE feels very streamlined compared to similar titles. Funcom have seemed to put a great detail in fixing small issues i've encountered elsewhere like being unable to stack foundations (why is this even a thing?) and simply telling you what side of a wall you are placing is faced. Little details like this really enhance the experience and gives me a lot of hope concerning the dev teams attention to detail and efficiency. Though most of the core aspects of the game look promising and provide a great base to build off of, CE is moderately lacking in fluff. Unfortunately I'm talking about the good kind of fluff. Recipes are not as plentiful as they should be, the level cap feels a bit on the low side and there needs to be at least twice as much in the crafting material department. Again it's important to note that this game is very early in development and these type of things generally get placed in a bit later in the games life. With how proactive the devs have been, there is no doubt in my mind that this stuff will be implemented asap.
Combat is pretty par for the course but is delivered in more manageable doses then we are used to seeing in the genre. This balance makes exploring very enjoyable as the game stays engaging but rarely gets overwhelming. I found the games block mechanics help to keep combat interesting and dynamic. Trying to time blocks with oncoming arrows and still managing to get swings in can be very satisfying.
Though Conan has a gorgeous world map it does leave a little to be desired. It's not quite as large as one might expect. Though I have not gotten bored of the map yet, I can see how its smaller size might factor into premature boredom. Thankfully the devs are working on new and interesting biomes that will be added supposedly within the year.
Conclusion:
Conan Exiles is one of the most promising EA titles I have seen and as long the devs keep up their hard work there is no doubt in mind it will succeed monumentally. That being said, the game still suffers due to its early stage of development, lacking in map size and some content. Though CE feels much more polished than most EA games on release, if you get bored of a title very easily you might want to hold off until more content has been added.

Miniature golf on Steam, what’s not to like?
Pros:
+ Unique courses and game modes that separates this game from other golf games.
+ Connecting with friends and players online is fairly easy and there has been little to no connection issues playing with friends from all over the country.
Cons:
- The learning curve is very steep. Of the six courses available (at the time), only one was suitable for beginner/intermediate players. With the other five ranging from challenging to frustratingly hard. And a handful of the holes in the courses will rely on precise geometry and “parkour-like” trick shots to make it to the goal as opposed to playing like a real miniature golf hole. I’m not asking for them to make the game easier, but I am asking for them to offer a more wider range of difficulty among the courses. Have a handful of relatively simple and easy courses as well as “medium” or moderately challenging courses to accompany the more difficult ones.
Overall: A decent game for what it is now, still an early-access game in development but it looks like they have some good ideas for future updates. If you have friends who would enjoy playing this with you, I recommend you and them buying this game.

Playtime: I played through the whole game 2.5 times on PS3. Will eventually get around to play it on PC, too-
Know that kind of games that innovate genres by creating interesting new gameplay concepts, instead of re-iterating stale franchises?
Valkyria Chronicles is one of those. It combines squad-management(with limited upgrade-possibilities and character-specific boons and drawbacks), a turn-based battle-concept(where you get a limited amount of activations per turn, but CAN spend multiple activations on the same unit(which gets less movement with each activatio)) and semi-real-time during those activations(best watch a video on this, it would take take too long to explain in a way that could not be misunderstood).
The plot and characters are good, if somewhat over-the-top, but if you played any japanese games in the past 20 years, you'll know what to expect.
The art style is as unique as the gameplay, very fitting, and I definitely wish more games would use it. Sound is good if not outstanding.
Most importantly, the settings(urban, grassland, desert, woods...) and mission objectives(interception, defense, reach point, destroy specific enemy, capture base, eliminate all enemies...) are varied and interesting. There are a few slight balance-issues(Scout OP), but on the whole, it's awesome, and not easy getting the best ranks.
(Unless, of course, you play on NG+, which is a thing).
TL,DR: I found this game and concept so awesome that despite already having played it several times on another system, I got it on Steam in the hopes of eventually getting the sequels released on steam as well.(even if the second part for PSP was inferior). It's a fresh new concept with unique gameplay, and the positive aspects vastly more dominant than a few small drawbacks.
Thumb up, no doubt.

Hard reset is a game that tries very hard to be like the old school shooters like Serious Sam, Pain killer, Duke and Shadow Warrior, unfortunately it falls very flat.

I bought this game as soon as I found out about it last week, and the moment I got it, I have been blown away.  I like the graphics a lot, and it acts like a turn based strategy, but in a good way.  I never played the first one, and I don't feel like I am missing out that much.
The class system is very simplistic.  You pick a preset and an origin.
The origin can be a premade character with its unique story or you can play your own character, which is great if you are wanting to play an undead Lizard or a male elf.  How people react to you really does change based on your origin, which is great for those of us who loved games like Skyrim but felt like our race didn't matter to the story or plot of an otherwise lore rich game.
Your preset is basically your class.  You have a ton to pick from, each with the weapon styles they are meant to use.  But just because the preset has two or one school of magic doesn't mean you are stuck with those for your main character.  You are capable of mixing and matching as you see fit.  You can pick a conjurer for example, and instead of just one school of magic and "leadership", you can dump leadership and pick up a school of magic you might feel is helpful.

Crytek creates another epic continuation onto the Crysis series. Crysis Warhead offers an alternative story from the eyes of Physco another one of the nano-tech marines.
On the same island as the original Crysis Warhead starts the story with Sergeant Sykes, Physco, who is on a vital mission to capture Korean cargo. It is up to you and your friend O’neil to push through the forces of North Korea and aliens alike to complete your objective.
The campaign consists of approximately seven missions, which vary in length. The campaign lasts anywhere from around four to seven hours depending on your play method. The initial missions are before are against human AI, but as you progress the enemy shift begins to occur as you start fighting less humans and engaging more aliens. The enemies, weapons, and abilities are the same as the original meaning this expansion only adds new missions and story. Regardless the campaign is well planned and the levels keep you wanting for me. They offer  dynamic play-styles that allow you to choose your completion style.
As in the original the gameplay varies based on your difficulty. I played Delta and noticed most of the game was more about utilizing my cloak ability and catching enemies by surprise. The enemies will fire in the same place if you cloak and run, but if you hide for a few seconds they tend to forget you even existed and continue on with their business. Realistically this game is pretty fun and the combat can be dynamic – if you’re looking for run and gun you’d probably want to play on an easy difficulty. On the other hand if you’re more into sneak and strike then I’d recommend going for a harder difficulty. The abilities are fun, but you’ll notice you tend to use some over others. I rarely found myself using speed or super-strength, but instead almost exclusively cloak and shields (which auto selects when cloak deactivates).
All and all Cyrsis Warhead is a great addition to the series and even if you didn’t play the first Crysis I would recommend giving it a go. It doesn’t really ruin any elements from the original if you play them backwards, but adds more depth to your Physco who in the first game seemed rather annoying. The campaign offers great complexity and amazing new environments. The graphics are of par to the original, annoyingly not 1080p, but still it looks good enough that you couldn’t tell anyway. I’d definitely recommend this game for someone who loves FPS games.

Crysis Warhead is something of a mixed bag for me. I played it almost immediately after Crysis, and all sorts of strangeness abounds. For example, I played Crysis on maximum settings and didn't notice anything (aside from the occasional frame rate drop in larger levels) that would impact gameplay from a tech side of the house.
But Warhead? I had to turn everything down. I wanted that 60 fps sweet spot... but it wasn't happening without minimum settings. I didn't play it on minimum, I compromised for about 40 fps, so I could actually see things like grass (which is necessary for my play style, as I like to be the Predator and kill from stealth). I'm curious as to why this stripped down expansion was literally more taxing on my system than the 2013 Tomb Raider (also played on max - but without the PhysX hair).
It may be the combination of age, poor optimization, and video drivers (which age has a pretty big factor on whether or not your drivers will play nice with the game) that prevented me from getting the sort of performance I was getting with the original game (plus, the original game underwent a series of performance patches after it was released).
The gameplay is essentially unchanged, which is good if you like it (I do). All the old weapons are present, though they did add a couple of new ones. However... again, the overpowered alien enemies rear their ugly heads (as expected) and the game becomes less fun as a result. You basically have to carry the gauss rifle at that point forward, and cloaking is a waste of time from there on in. Worse, like before, as soon as the aliens arrive, you're given linear paths and objectives (though Warhead is in general, more linear than the original).
Story wise, I like Warhead better, mostly because you play as Psycho and get some great character development out of the experience. From the first game, the only thing I knew about him was that he was British and slightly sarcastic. And that his callsign probably meant he was a daredevil or just deranged. Psycho is much more interesting than Nomad, and actively defies orders at certain points for fairly justified reasons.
I actively despised the Korean general who is the antagonist of Warhead, and hated it whenever he got the upper hand on Psycho, but the ending was made all the sweeter for it.
On the whole, I recommend Warhead for fans of the first game, with the caveat that it has the same issues of said first game, as well as a few new ones. It's also short, about half the play time of the original Crysis (which I think is fine - it doesn't overstay its welcome).

In many ways this is a game with great potential. I only got 2 days ago, and after playing for a bit I figured out that ok, it's an early access game and there's a lot of work ahead. It's a fun little game, but by no means a full fledged game ready for release. As many people mentioned it borrows heavily from DK, and anyone who has played it back in the old days will feel at home. The UI is in many ways exactly the same, and it has a few cool new features like alchemy or tech tree. But as I said it's still an underdeveloped beta game. There are major bugs in the campaign, in-game textures are very poor, skirmish offers only 3 maps (all for 2 players only), battle animations are wonky and/or look like temporary placeholders, with a 5x5 study you plow through the entire tech tree in 4-5 minutes tops... Don't get me wrong, THIS WILL BE A GOOD GAME. In a few months. Todays release is a mistake, and if you're considering buying the game hoping for regular gameplay, keep in mind that as of today, you're still signing up for beta testing. Buy a copy of DK2 somewhere and fiddle with it for a month or two, then come back. Maybe it will be a full game then.
EDIT
After this game had a chance to grow up and mature I feel it now deserves the recommendation. As for people who downvoted this review, I am sorry your feelings were hurt. I still firmly stand by every word. The game release was so rushed there were still placeholder names on some units.

At times the game feels slow and I often found it annoying on large maps, that half of the time my creatures were angry simply because they had to traverse massive distances. The prospect of a new Dungeon Keeper made me back this with little hesitation back in 2012 when the Kickstarter ran. Videos from the beta I watched about a year ago gave me some trepidation, but I had hope that it would turn out alright given that there was still more time to improve it. Now that time is up and version 1.0 is out - and I'm
to see what the project has come to: This is a woefully unfinished game, not at all ready to be released! It's not just about lack of polish: Animations are jerky and rough or simply missing (slap a piglet and it simply disappears), creatures in combat move around chaotically making it hard to know what's going on, glaring bugs are aplenty -
bugs - some game modes are unfinished, the minimap is nigh useless and on top of that the game is poorly optimized. I've never seen such an incomplete game pushed to release and can only surmise that it has to be desperation move by the developers.
I suspect this project has been seriously mismanaged and poorly planned out from an early stage. There are many additions beyond the mechanics of the original games and many good ideas among those. The textures are pretty nice and it has the same narrator voice as the originals. How then are basic features like a proper minimap not in place? Why does the core gameplay feels so erractic and why is the relevant feedback on what's going on in the dungeon so sparse? After all this development time? Poorly balanced fluff features? And from the steam achievement you can see that the campaign only has 13 missions (compare that to the 20 of DK1)
I must conclude that the developers didn't have the experience, skills and resources to make the game we all wanted and thus failed to deliver.
"Game will be patched." "More content to be added." "It has potential." Yadada-ya! - These are the funeral hymns
usually receive.
this game will be completed at some point in the future. I wouldn't get my hopes up though, and based on the development speed up to this point it definitely won't be soon. Don't buy this game before you hear convincing reports that it actually has been completed!
Instead, get the originals from GoG if you're craving for a dungeon sim.

In all seriousness, this game looks pretty at first. It's got the most massive sandbox world i've seen yet in a game, the gliders are fun as all hell, the battle system's not too bad either, and raising your mounts and pets is pretty fun.
Unfortunately after you've done those three things, this game gets old, old, OLD really fast. The storyline drags on and on without much payoff even after a "Boss", you can hardly do ANYTHING without either grinding for hours upon hours upon hours or PAYING for it, and even gliding over the land gets boring when you realize that down on the ground there's practically nothing going on. The only areas with activity are the main cities and towns where you pick up sidequest after sidequest after sidequest, with the hope of getting the main storyline someday again getting further each time you complete ONE.
And the PAYWALLS. Everything you've heard about them from other reviewers are true. If you don't have a deep enough wallet or a big enough credit card most things in the game are just blocked from you, leaving you wanting more and never able to get it. And the worst part is, even if you pay for it or grind enough in-game currency or points or medals to get it, it's not even yours to keep. It's got a 30-day time limit, forcing you to stay behind to "enjoy" it before it's gone. Because it's not even a "Play for 30 days worth of time" timer, it's 30 days from the time you GET it.
Take a break and come back? Forget it. You'll be so lost and confused as to what you were doing that trying to pick it up again will leave you battered and bruised from the enemies you forgot how to fight, if you don't just stare at the screen in blank confusion as a multitude of colored arrows reaching up to 8 or 10 point you haphazardly in every direction on the map.
It LOOKS pretty, it plays almost pretty, but in the end it's not all that worth it.

Here comes an unpopular opinion that will sure make people scoff and turn away from this review but... I don't think Last Light is as good as 2033. 2033 was flawed but still gave an engaging and atmospheric experience where everyone's actions, however cruel and disgusting, were at least understandable in a world that has gone to complete hell. Last Light gave me a sour taste in my mouth with some of the plot decisions and some of the villians were almost equivalent to a cheesy Call of Duty villan. With that however, the game is still good and has some stuff that it did better than 2033.
PROS:
-Stunning visuals, nuclear war has never been so beautiful and saddening at the same time
-Voice acting is still good
-Atmosphere is at the peak with Last Light, dark and dreary with a few hallucinations and you have a game that's equivalent to survival horror
-Sound design is still amazing
-Level design is a step up from 2033
CONS:
-The story, some may like it, but I felt it was a major step down from 2033. There are some interesting moments, but a lot of them aren't engaging and just seem pointless. Villains are the equivalent to Call of Duty and they weren't at the least intimidating.
-Performance can be average to unplayable, even above recommended specs, I got frequent crashes and frame rate drops
-The moral points are confusing and are odd to calculate. Every chance I got I did every kind action that was given to me but still I got the bad ending
-The strip club scene, seems so out of place and it just takes away from the immersion. Feels like a cheap way to get some cleavage.
-Little weapon variety and most are not even effective at all.
-The final level is the most frustating level in the game. Starts off amazing and then goes to order you to do things where you have no idea how to do them.
To conclude, Metro Last Light is still an engaging experince, however it has way more flaws than 2033 and it feels like a small step down. On the upside, Metro Exodus looks amazing, so hopefully it will be a major step up from this. I still reccommend you get the game for the atmosphere and visuals, but don't expect a story of the year.
Verdict: 7/10

First of all it's a mobile port on PC, everyone wants those. It's also a very poor mobile port, first couple of battles go smoothly, then you notice slight decrease of fps with every consecutive level played, after 10+ levels the game becomes nearly unplayable, for a game where all you do most of the time is clicking on one button, yeah. To be fair only a portion of players have this issue, not an excuse to have the issue live for at least 3 months.
Secondly it's a "pay to win" type of game, starts off pretty fast and fun while you learn those 1.5 mechanics that this game consists of, then comes some challenge when you need to think strategically, even though the strategy is a bit too strong of a word, still kinda fun. Then the difficulty ramps up into the sky, you learn that those simple mechanics have a ton of handicaps and you also need to use them properly to not to hit a brick wall somewhere further into the game. Absolutely everything is handicapped but has some sort of workarounds with gems, you can receive some gems via the game, like 1 here, 5 there once in a while but you need hundreds of them to have noticeable progress or you will end up wasting days and days and days for the same results. Yes, you can buy gems for real money.
Game playtime is very limited by a "meat" mechanic. You need a certain amount of meat to enter a level, meat regenerates in time or with level up (or by buying it for gems of course) and couple of other small sources which leads to a very unsatisfying experience when you play not when you want to play the game, but when the game lets you play it.

Absolutely stunning graphics combined with a moving soundtrack, incredible level design and responsive, flexible, and feature-rich gameplay. Each aspect on its own wouldn't hold up on its own, but together, every moment of gameplay was a delight. If you're only playing for the story, I'd wait for a sale - you could easily clear the entire game in about 7-8 hours - but if you're an actual gamer who likes poking around in the games you play, the full price is well worth it. There are SO many secrets. So much collection. The game is short, but LUDICROUSLY dense.
If you've heard people complain about it, it's usually due to a conflict of play styles. The shadow section is totally easy...if you're already constantly testing the environment and making safety precautions. The final level is Nintendo Hard, but not particularly frustrating...unless you were coasting through the game by depending on the mechanic it takes away, leaving you helplessly learning how to play from the ground up. When you play Owlboy, you should be playing with the understanding of how dense it really is, and the more superficial you are, the harder it's going ot be on you. Each map trains you to be at least passable at the next map. Nothing comes out of left field. It will make you suffer if you're trying to shotgun the whole thing.
The game also teaches by showing, instead of telling. Beyond the ridiculously brief story-driven 'press this button to do this thing' control setup tutorial at the start, the game just teaches you by putting you in a simple, controlled environment, lets you figure out how things work, and then sends you on your way. It makes you feel like you're the one making all the achievements, you're the one triumphing over the game, and it makes the whole experience fun.
The plot is...well, the narrative is the closest you can get to literal perfection in a video game, told in a way only a video game could communicate, and all the characters are interesting, memorable, and compelling. In terms of an actual story... If you like simple stories enhanced by gameplay with a clearly defined objective that delivers on its themes, it's a damn good plot, very servicable, makes everything feel worth it. If you're in it for the worldbuilding, you're constantly blueballed, being blocked from enjoying the setting at every turn, most egregiously by presenting the most fascinating, compelling, and fresh take on the Ancient Civilization trope and then just going ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ and zeroing in on the themes and characters with an agonizingly deliberate motion.
Hey, I say to the game, no, go back, you were telling me something.
I was only telling you that so the ending has clear narrative stakes, the game explains patiently.
Yeah, I say, yeah but also it was real cool, keep going?
No, says the game. You know what's going on. We've got a story to finish.
Good plot, though. Really top notch stuff.
The game has a a handful of actual design flaws too - some bosses and sections are a slog, and the all Lava Snake-related stages are just the game screaming 'THIS IS WHAT BAD GAME DESIGN LOOKS LIKE, AND YOU HAVE TO SUFFER THROUGH IT IF YOU WANT MORE CONTENT', but overall, this is a fantastic product, and I can't recommend it enough.

Have you ever experienced a cheap gunfight in a game? Well, just imagine that stretched out to an entire game and you have a pretty clear image of what Hard Reset is.
You fight your way through waves of enemies from point a to point b, and occasionally push a button or two. Now, this formula is fine, as long as the shooting is solid. However, in Hard Reset the shooting is far from solid. The combat in this game is dull, irritating, cheap and unenjoyable. There are a few levels of♥♥♥♥♥♥i have to get through to properly describe just how broken the combat of the game is, and that is what this review is gonna focus on, the combat.
1: WEAPONS
There are two weapons in the game, one standard bullet and expolsive rifle and one energy rifle. The twist with that though is that these two weapons can become five different weapons each, wich is a cool concept. The problem with this is that there is barely a difference between the different firing modes, especially with the energy rifle. Expect to accidentally blow yourself up, alot. All and all they feel alright to use, nothing special though.
2: ENEMIES
Now this is where the♥♥♥♥♥♥truly starts to thicken. The enemies and the placement of those enemies is so cheap that you'll want to throw your keyboard out the window. Almost all enemies are extremely damaging, and can take you down in a few seconds. Now combine this with tight arenas, constant flanking without any warning, fast and unpredictable movement, slow player movement and you are set up to have a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ time.
There are a few different enemy types that you'll encounter on your "journey", and they all share the same tributes. They are all annoying as sh*t to fight, they dont feel fair, the designs are repetetive and uninspired, the color pallets are bland and boring and you'll have more fun smashing your face with a hammer while masturbating with sandpaper. You have a generic fast little bloke with two legs and some sort of melee weapon, a generic ranged humanoid robot, flying turrets and, you guessed it, a generic ♥♥♥♥ing large robot that runs at you. Those are 90% of the enemies you'll face. Im only going to go in depth about one though, the common large ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
So, you'll face some big robots that just run at you like a ♥♥♥♥ing bull, and there is nothing wrong with those types of enemies. Serious sam had those enemies, and they were great fun to fight! You could dodge them pretty easily if you knew where they were coming from, and it was the player's fault if they died. In Hard Reset, you have barely enough space to dodge these guys! The arenas are filled with tonnes of dead ends wich the robots can easily trap you in. And if you even manage to dodge them, you'll still magically take damage as the w*nker passes you (poor hitboxes). And as an added slap to the face, there are probably billions of little small, fast sh*theads waiting behind you, because some fuc*ing sadistic developer REALLY enjoyed placing enemies in the most annoying, autistic locations. WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ HAPPENED HERE? DID ANYONE ACTUALLY PLAYTEST THESE AREAS?  The combat is just a ♥♥♥♥ing chore, and I really had to force myself to complete this game.
3: LEVEL DESIGN
Your level design should compliment your gameplay, wich in Hard Reset it does not. Levels are usually semi large areas with a bunch of clutter and dead ends purely to annoy the player. It's also repetetive as balls, you just shoot some guys, push a button, shoot some more guys repeat. Basically, it ♥♥♥♥in' sucks.
Other notes:
-The optimization is absolute sh*t
-The comicbooks are poorly made, downright laughable at times
-The story is a joke, it tries to tell this serious story about ai and robots, but just falls flat on it's face. It makes litterally no sense and you'll find yourself skipping all the cutscenes before long
-Really short, however, I consider that kind of a good thing considering the quality of the game
-Poor english localization, typos and strange pronounciations are common
-The visual effects are everywhere, don't look good and make it hard to see
Conclusion: Don't buy it. Flying wild hog improved significantly with their second game, "Shadow Warrior", and is a much better game. 4/10

A while ago I played a lot of the earlier, lighter, version of Desktop Dungeons, and had a lot of fun doing so, but even playing that didn't prepare me for the fantastic game that DD has become with hard work and polish.
Its essentially a rogue-like puzzler, with an overworld progression that doesn't get reset when you die, but you do have to replay the dungeon you were in when you succumbed to evil.
Pace is very good, the game makes sure that you don't end up in an unwinnable situation unless you really, really try hard, and if you do, there's plenty of sidequest you can fall back on, and improve your town and unlock new items, races and classes to improve your chances.
Theres even hand-crafted puzzles, that beside being fun and really challenging, teaches you advanced tricks and tips, which you can then use on your next quest into the dungeons around your settlement.
Classes and races are varied and play very differently, and the quests are different enough that there aren't just one uber combination thats going to win every dungeon for you.
Dungeon runs take somewhere around 15-20 minutes, some faster, some slower, but the game can be played at exactly the pace you like.
Highly recommended!

I am overhauling my review since beating the game.
First - this is a JRPG with a unique combat sytem. In many ways the combat system makes the game and ButterChain has done a great job on the pacing. Its loads of fun, well worth the price, and extremely engaging.
Gameplay - Gameplay consist of story, followed travelling across overhead map (more on that in a sec), followed by a boss fight and then more story (with story potentially pushed in at any point in a stage).
Overhead map - Each stage consist of overhead map with various routes (all leading left). Each of these routes has various sprites distributed on it. These can signify battles, money, items, traps, etc. The arrows along the bottom of the screen choose your route. Along with the arrows are various other effects that are only good when used in battle such as special attacks and health recovery. This is interesting as it introduces an element of resource management into each stage. As you use an arrow or item the remaining tiles will slide to the right and a new tile will show up at the end of the line. Some of the arrows allow you to go more than one direction and you get to choose which one.  If you choose an item that is not an arrow it sends you in a random direction. Once you reach the far left hand of the stage you have a boss fight.
Combat - the arena is broken up into three different areas. You are controlling three characters (fighter, general, magician) that share a health bar. So its all or nothing for everybody. The enemies will attack by moving from left to right towards you. The fighter is the one you will controll the most and who is in the main portion of the arena. You attack by click into empty space in the arena and your fighter will do a dash attack to the place that you clicked. The fighters attack power will go down over time but can be recovered by standing still (but this opens her up to attack), The General controlls a line of troops that are protecting your magician. They do this by firing projectile weapons and bouncing the enemy back, The magician fires projectiles across the screen with more damage being done the closer the enemy gets. Additionally attacks can be pulled off by using any of the arrows or items on the row at bottom of the screen. Those arrows now literally fire lasers across the screen. The main attack area is split into three lanes, so if the enemies are up top it helps to send a laser down the top lane and so on. Its always awesome to have a laser that fires down all three lanes at once. This is where the resource management comes into the game by controlling the row of tiles on the bottom of the screen - because you need a balance of health by holding on to hearts, choices of where to move on the map by holding onto arrows, and choices of attack by holding onto anything else. One strategy I would often use is barrelling through as many of my attacks as possible in an attempt to load up on hearts right before the boss battles. The combat continues to grow and evolve througout the game - I could cover it detail but it would only detract from the experience. Needless to say there is a rudimentary elemental system to the attacks but it soon becomes easy enough to switch that up to suit the needs of the indvidual stage. ButterChain did a great job of introducing new gameplay elements/mechanics all the way up to the end. This really helps keep the player engaged and stops the game from becoming what might otherwise become a tiresome experience.

Overall I say Overwhelmingly positive for my review. Supposedly all created by one guy... maybe 2? Maybe a girl, not a guy? I don't know. Props either way - beautiful, engaging, JRPG with a unique battle system.

Real Review
I really loved the game overall, it's extremely easy to run and I doubt you'll find a computer that can't run this. I felt like the music was pretty good, it wasn't amazing or bad but it was plenty memorable. I haven't exactly finished the storyline, but it it's straightforward and good. The characters are well made and well rounded, I actually like every single character, who have their quirky traits and converstaions with Recette. Battle-wise, all of them are well made and are very well rounded when they gain all of their skills, making each person have a different style associated with them. (Movement, range, damage, attack speed, abilities all vary) The gameplay is pretty standard, it doesn't change that much because there aren't that many varied enemies, but bosses are unique and sometimes frustratingly hard (which is good). The amount of ingredients and items that you can make is extensive and really, I mean REALLY hard to complete, there are some items that you need to find in rare drops or take rare drops and make it into an even rarer item. The shop managing aspect is the most relaxing part of the game, you buy and sell items to people, building friendships with them. There is some thinking required at first, but you can automatically do it after a while, Market changes in items that reduce or increase the value of certain items keeps the process fun, creating chances for high profit margins of 250% a lot of the time. So much of this game is really fun, though, I recommend they put in more enemies and expand it a little, but, hey what can you do? It's a really fun game m8, I r8 8/8.

Impressions & Score:
Story: 9.5 out of 10
This is an expansion for Crysis, not a new game and is intended to tell the story of Psycho,  one of your teammates in Crysis I. During the story in Crysis I, Psycho get separated from Nomad, in order to fulfill another important mission. This new story is quite good and it's connected to the story in Crysis I, which is awesome. Even though it doesn't provide too much info about aliens and characters, I liked the way it was linked to the main story, so this is why I gave a better score.
Graphics: 10 out of 10
The graphics are almost the same as for Crysis I but with some improvements in details in almost everything. This is quite a good thing, I didn't quite noticed at first, but after checking some videos on youtube, the differences are pretty big. If I could have given a better score, I would, this expansion is improved on almost every aspect.
Gameplay: 9.5 out of 10
First of all, I like to mention that this game is a bit harder than Crysis I, but this isn't because of AI improvement, but mostly because of more difficult enemies throught the game. While in the first Crysis, you fought KPA soldiers over 50 % of the game (which were quite weak even on Delta difficulty), in this DLC you'll only fight KPA soldiers during the first 10 % of the game. Instead of KPA soldiers, in Crysis Warhead you'll fight a lot of KPA Special Ops (which are bassically nano suit soldiers just like yourself), which are pretty damn good. The producers also included some alien packs that are immune to damage until you destroy the one that generates their shield. All this makes the game a bit more challenging than the first Crysis, which is a good improvement from my point of view. They also added new vehicules and new weapons like grenade launcher, new pistols, new grenades, all this further improves the overall gameplay. Great job !
Audio: 10 out of 10
The audio is similar to the previous Crysis, so that means is excellent. Didn't noticed any differences here.
AI Behavior: 9.5 out of 10
The AI is better, because you don't have to fight too many KPA soldiers, instead you have to fight a lot of aliens, KPA Special Ops and some bosses. The KPA Special Ops are quite good because they use nano grenades to deactivate your suit before moving to attack, the aliens instead, have the same behavior like in Crysis I, so for more details see that review.
Multiplayer: not tested
As with Crysis I, I couldn't test the multiplayer since the servers were deactivated. There are some instructions on the internet on how you can play multiplayer, but I didn't bother to try.
Overall: 9.7 out 10
A lot of improvements done in this expansion compared to the previous Crysis, that makes this game even better. On top of all this, Crysis Warhead is a stand alone game and doesn't require the original Crysis to be played, but in my opionion is very recommended that you play the first Crysis before checking Crysis Warhead, so that you may have a better understanding of what is happening during the storyline. 100 % recommend, a true clasic masterpiece to the fps genre.

It's a good time for maths: games about them keep appearing on Steam. After
and
(links lead to my reviews), here's Mathoria: It All Adds Up, developed by a student team, with a teacher as supervisor, who happened to be also a little publisher in Philippines.
Mathoria: It Alls Adds Up is telling the story of a young teen, happening to be The Chosen One, whose mom is abducted by goons. It's up to him to save her, by visiting the island, by defeating obstacles and by helping others. His skills maths will be useful, especially his addition knowledge.
The game is simple: you lead a character thanks to the arrows or ZQSD/WASD (forget the mouse), you speak to other persones who will ask you to answer a problem, like "My brother ate 20 apples yesterday, I ate 35 today, how many apples in total have we eaten?". The answer field consists in 4 cases for each number (the first one is for the thousand, the second one for the hundred, the third for the dizain, the last one for an unity - for the answer of the problem above, it should look like 0055).
You have also some fights to handle: you have the choice between a simple attack (with adapted calculs, generally, the easiest you can find during a battle) and powers (with calculs that are more complicated to answer like 465+354). The equation is shown on your screen, you have a timer (ranging from 5 seconds to 30 depending of the difficulty). Hit "Enter" so that the answer field is appearing, write the answer and hit "Enter" again. If your answer is right, the damage will be inflicted to your enemy, if it's not, it's you that will loose health.
Like in a RPG, you can use potions to double the damage, speed up the process of using again your powers or heal yourself. However, it's not the only items in the game: you can also put a set of clothes that can improve or decrease your HP or your damage. It means that you have to be careful for answers as a set can inflict 60 damages but leave you with 10 HP only. A single wrong answer and you're dead - though in the game, dying isn't accepted: goons are putting themselves on the side when defeated, much still alive.
You have three difficulties: I've played the Easy one, as I didn't want to be confronted to harder calculs, even if in the end, I was because of the powers.
There are several problems that can be improved if there is any sequel.
For me, the most important is probably the one that will never be taken in account: the game is in English, which means that any non-English speaker kid can't answer the problems unless an adult can translate. However, as the game is only about addition, you know that you need to add this number to this other one. But still, for sequels, if there is a mix of calculs with substraction or multiplication or division, there will be a problem.
The second one is related to the fact that I've explained the controls above: you don't have really any tutorial in real time: you have to read what is explained (again in English), if you don't miss the characters that will tell it (for the fight, it's included naturally, not for the problems). You're speaking to kids, it's way more useful to show them in real time than rely on the fact that they've understood the mechanics just like that.
The third problem is that it's short. In more or less 1h30, I was already at the end. Not that I don't complain, because for kids, it's not too short. However, it would have been much better to have a little more of exploring. However, given the end, it seems clear that the idea of a sequel was in their heads and that substraction could be the next focus.
The fourth problem is the difficulty: an easy difficulty for me means calculs like 1+9, 10+10 but not 345+114. For any young kid that can't handle these, they can't use the powers and are just stuck to use simple attacks, which means that some of the enemies will take long to defeat. The developers should revise the difficulty at least to stick more to it.
I don't mind the fact that the game was made with RPG Maker - a blog post explains the beginning of the conception where Unity wasn't easy to handle for Mathoria. But it's not a bad move as the game can still attract children.
Mathoria isn't as bad as the reviews seemed to say. Many of the players missed the full point of the game, which is drilling in mental calcul and only saw the fact that they didn't get a RPG. Anyway, while Mathoria isn't perhaps the best educationnal game out there, it's still a nice try. It's free, so, your wallet will not be hurt by this one. It's worth a try.

I wanted to be freaked out a little (as I sometimes get the urge for a good horror game) so I played Dreadout... Instead, I uninstalled after 1.5 hours.
Besides the graphical stuttering, pop-in, and wonky controls, in one and a half hours of gameplay I experienced:
1) An "intro level" with zero story elements to segue into the actual game, nor any reason for the actual intro level.
2) A ghost of an insect to kill as your first enemy. A ghost of a slightly oversized bee.
Allow us to take a moment to fathom the strageness of this... Moment over? Okay...
3) A little girl (the same age of the girl you control) creepily runs around an cries and runs some more. Great, so more stereotypical "creepy little girl to scare you" trope.
4) Insert random abuse of the number 666 because every culture in the world knows thats a bad number. And its badness is second only to its overuse in videogames to try to scare the player.
5) "Creepy little girl" turns into evil pregnant ghost girl to fight.
I sense a another plot point coming soon... I didn't play enough to see this plot point develop, but my spidy sense is tingling here.
6a) Okay, so, "Creepy little girl" and "pregnant ghost girl" combine for their super-trope-abusing attack! ... Moving on.
7) Aaaand now I'm dead. No seriously, dead. I have to walk a bit on a bright white path to get alive again. Aparently this is a thing. I know this because the menu has a "how to play" section artfully depicting the main character walking to become alive again...
7a) This "how to play" section shows a lack of conveyance in the game design. Something that game designers should learn. You want to see conveyanvce in action, the intro stage of Megaman X teaches you every thing you need to know without a menu screen and panels of text.
7b) Walking in a horror game is wonderful when done right. It can work wonders for building tension when done correctly. But snotty and repulsive and downright aggravating when done wrong. This game does walking wrong, time and time again.
8) And now I'm alive again and... The trope centeral station train has left the track... It was all a dream maybe... or maybe it was just a random level to get players in the mood of a scaaaary game. I rolled my eyes so hard, I think I tore my corneas.
9) Aaaaand now were exploring an abandoned town. Why? Because we're kids on a highschool trip aparently. And because our chaperone is a complete moron who doesn't deserve the minimum wage she's getting paid.
10) And now I realize I'm a silent protagonist who doesn't talk when her best friend is talking to her. But she breathes. I know she breathes because the run speed (which is only slightly faster than my walk speed) causes her to respirate loudly into whatever mic she's wearing.
11) Also, here's that walking complaint again. I walked through that darn abandoned town for like 10 minutes. No development. Just badly rendered ghost town straight out of the stock assets of a bad indy game. Shame.
11b) Again, if the developer tries to create tension by making me control the main character through a stupid environment for ten minutes with no development... then they really need to revist some classic scary movies. Just to get an idea of how horror works, how terror works and the difference between the two. Failbot.
12) Aaaaand now it's nightime and I'm hanging with my best friend on a bench outside an abandoned school while my other classmates have checked out the environs... Being a silent protagonist, I can only imagine how riveting that conversation must have been.
12a) Someone's lost in the school, aaaaand now I'm facing a giant boar with a human face who's only damaged by me taking pictures of it with my camera...
I'm done.
I'm just done.
Uninstalled.
I'm going back to knitting. At least it's more engaging than this game.
