A Game I Will Not Soon Forget
So much positive to write about this game. At the very least I would describe it as ominous. One part, however, gave me cold feet, and not in the sense of being so frightened I didn’t want to continue, but because a certain “boss” cheated and made the game frustrating. I was inclined to hit the uninstall command.
Every time I see a pair of scissors from this time forward I’ll feel nauseous. The only way I finally figured out how to defeat the cheating AI was to use the key that was the back-step key, and twirl the mouse so that I was using that key to run forwards, instead of backwards. The AI got so confused I was finally, quite easily, able to defeat the scissor wielding cross-dresser. In spite of this, the game is one I will not soon forget. It took me just over 12 hours to complete, which I am beginning to believe is just about the perfect length for a game.
A school building being a big part of the game you eventually enter requires a cognizant approach in adventuring as it is full of spirited rooms joined by dusty halls that you’ll have to comb through in order to pick up necessary items; a process I thoroughly enjoyed. After all, it is a school, so just as one would expect the rooms and hallways to be similar, they are. Yet the classrooms and hallways are only similar in their shape and dissimilar in stains and dirt, the placement of desks, chairs, and items students have long left behind, teaching tools, etc.. Again, just as it should be. Afterwards you'll play in different "spiritual" locales; a garden, dirt pathways, a small village, a mansion; but will eventually wind up back in the school.
DreadOut is filled with atmosphere, thus wandering and coming across ghosts makes every step threatening. There is always a sense of dread and danger. The Indonesian team of Digital Happiness have created an amazing, bone-chilling survival horror.

Red barrels - the videogame.
Eh... I picked it up for 2 euros, so I can recommend it at the pricetag, but honestly, compared to Shadow Warrior (2013) this game is not very good for the most part.
Especially if you get the wrong upgrades. Some weapons are useless even after you get the upgrades (looking at you, assault rifle). It wasn't until I painfully played through half the game when I realized, that the way to go here is to permastun enemies. Get all the CC upgrades, use RPG and railgun for dealing big damage, shotgun for wave clearing.
There's not a lot of enemy variety either. You got the little annoying ones, you've got the big charging ones, the rocket spammers and the scarabs. They do have a varied look based on how much armor they are packing, but at the end of the day they have the same abilities with a different paintjob.
The enemies are bullet sponges as well. UNLESS, you use the red barrels to kill them. The game puts a lot of emphasis on that, rather than the gunplay, which is a shame. 1-2 red barrels can kill the bigges enemies, but if you try to do the same with your guns, it will take a long while. There are plenty of red barrels in the first few chapters, but later they get more scarce and therefore the fights are needlessly prolonged, because you are waiting for the day the spongy enemies will finally die.
I also noticed a lot of inconsistency in this game. Sometimes the little sawblade enemies deal only like 20 damage, sometimes up to 80. I have no idea wtf going on whatsoever. Is it because of my shield? But even if my shield are full, I still lose HP when I'm hit. Is it proportional? Is the damage only halved? Are shields only protecting from ranged attacks? I have no idea what's going on.
This game does one thing pretty damn well though, and that's the boss fights. The boss fights with Atlas and the Overseer from the Exile DLC are particularly well done. I really liked how I had to get the Overseer to suck in the barrels. That was a bit creative and unusual. Really good boss fight, that one. The parts of the game between the boss fights are really not enjoyable though.
In conclusion you can very much tell that this is the studios 1st game. It was an experiment. I'd say play Shadow Warrior instead, if you haven't played already. That's a much much more polished version of all the ideas this game experimented with and therefore a thoroughly enjoyable game. Get this game only at a huge discount and only if you are very bored.

So this is more of a first impression kind of thing I will update this as I play more of the game.
So at first I had trouble getting into the game, it seems as though it doesn't like amd cards.  So what you have to do is go into the AMD Catlyst Control Center and alter the AA to use the applications settings.
So with that out of the way,  what I have played so far is very, VERY reminiscent of Painkller, The music, The graphics, it almost seems as though some of the people from the Painkiller team have worked on this project.  It is awesome just the fact that they managed to capture the atmosphere and feeling of Painkiller (just with a Sci-fi setting.) is awesome to me (I am a huge Painkiller fan.)
The game looks sharp, the graphics are just really well done, like I had said earlier very reminiscent of Painkiller (more specifically Hell and Damnation.)
The weapons in this game are interesting you have two weapon types N.R.G. and CLN.  The N.R.G. weapons are energy weapons (shocking I know.)  However instead of picking up entirely different weapons you get currency to upgrade the weapon you have (HOLD ON IT GETS COOLER.)  Each of these upgrades makes the weapon take on a different roll (The assault rifle turns into a shotgun and other weapons.)  It is very interesting, however the weapon that you buy shares the ammo for the other weapons (at least from what I have seen so far.)  I can't wait to see what this game has in store for me, I am already in love with it.

The guns are still awesome I just unlocked a Alternate fire mode for my shotgun, once again very reminiscent of Painkiller,  it fires flak that paralyzes enemies very similar to the shotugun of Painkiller in which the alternate fire mode frezzes enemies. This game is fantastic. I haven't played an RPG that has had me this involved in strategizing the fights before they even start in so long. This was the fight I had last night that made me know I was playing something special.
I barricaded myself in the room on top of the keep with dressing room walls, chairs, and chests. The NPC's came after me chasing my rogue who I had used to pull them. She ran back into the room where we were barricaded, and I had my undead warrior use telekinesis to move the stuff into place before they got up there. They consisted of 2 ranged 2 melee and a dog. The dog couldn't climb the ladder to get up there, and the other 4 chased. When they got up there, they started hammering away at my barricade. I used my teleport gloves to port the ranged guys in one at a time, and massacre them with my whole party, (wayfinder, inquisitor, summoner, rogue). By the time I had ported both the ranged in and killed them, the melee had made in through. I used my wayfinder to shoot a poison arrow at my undead inquistor (basically a deathknight) who is healed by poison. I then summoned a bunch of poison totems/poison incarnate. My inquisitor was nearly invicible at this point. I teleported one of the melee enemys in while the other took care of the last barricade I had made. At this point they were screwed.
After that, all I had to do was take my party down the ladder and massacre that poor little dog. RIP doggy. I could go on and on about different fights and things that I've had to figure out ways I would have never thought of to win, but this was my favorite fight so far.
TL;DR, This game has some of the most engaging and interesting combat I've ever seen in an RPG. If you know what you are doing, and can figure out how to use the terrain to your advatage, you can win fights that seem impossible. I love it. The game does not hold your hand, and that's what makes it amazing. The freedom you have to figure out how you are going to take care of every single situation you get yourself in, and never knowing what's around the next corner, or who is actually an enemy or friend is amazing. I love this game. Worth the money I spend already, and I'm still on the first island. Must buy game if you love tough RPG's with combat like The Old Republic or Final Fantasy Tactics but with more strategy thrown in, mixed with tough story driven choices.

A heads-up; this is my first (seriously) written review. Feel free to criticize and give tips on how to improve my writing.
Owlboy is an indie platformer developed by D-Pad Studio. It has been in development since 2007 and was relesed November 2016.
The plot of Owlboy is set in the land of the sky and the islands of the world below has been separated by a catastrophic event. You play as Otus, an owl-human hybrid race called Owls. The game has a unique mechanic in the fact that Otus cannot really defeat any enemies, just stun them. Luckily, you get the help of your best friend Geddy, whom you'll be able to carry around and shoot enemies with his gun. Your duty as an owl is to guard your village from Pirates whom have recently united under a ferocious leader named Molstrom.
Let's start by pointing out the obvious; the game is bloody gorgeous. The pixel-art for this game looks amazing and it is, in my opinion, one of the prettiest looking games I've ever seen. The world of Owlboy is extraordinarily pretty and the attention to detail is amazing. The characters all have their unique design which, in turn, makes all of them very memorable. The game's writing is also something you have to thank for that however, since all the characters have their own unique written personality. The people you meet all feel like genuine and real people.
The soundtrack is great. It's not perfect, it's a rare thing that games pull that off, but the people behind the orchestral tracks of Owlboy has done a great job on tracks that are supposed to be more happy and adventurous, my favorite being the Tropos Day music. Unfortunately I can't really mention any boss themes that I found memoreable, but on an overall scale, I'd say that it's one of the best I've heard in recent years.
The gameplay is simple. You fly, walk, shoot, jump, roll. Basic stuff. You have to fight your way through many bosses and puzzle your way through ancient dungeons. If I have to criticize something, it's the fact that a lot of the puzzles are too easy. The fact that you can fly makes a lot of the platforming almost non-existant. However, the boss fights are interesting, they are fast-paced and they are exciting. The pacing during fights can be a bit off sometimes, as there are bosses with attacks that are way too fast for a first-timer. Bosses should start easy, then scale up in difficulty, but Owlboy unfortunately often throws too much at the start of the fight and then doesn't up the difficulty enough to make the fight truly feel like a threat.
Enemy variety gets a bit stale, but seeing how the game focuses around puzzles and platforming, it's not much of an issue.
The story of Owlboy is simple. As I've mentioned above, the characters you meet during your journey really is what makes this game interesting. However, if you come to this game and expect a story as deep and touching as Undertale, you're wrong. The story works well, it has its plottwists and touching moments, but unfortunately it feels rushed. The pacing feels off sometimes and there are moments where you're supposed to get deep emotions, but because the pacing is too fast, you don't get enough time to attach to things. There are of course moments where you do genuinly feel sad or touched, but not as often as the game would like you to.

Speaking as a person who cannot buy everything I want, 22.99€ is quite a price for an 6 hour game. After beating the game, I don't really have any feelings of wanting to go back to collect every item or coins either. The Bougin challenge is not fun either.
It seems like I've been bashing the game more than I have been praising it, but I am really fond of this game. It's not going to be the next big hit like some might've expected, but it is an extremely polished game with some of the best visuals and characters that has come out over the recent years. The music is good, the visuals are fantastic and the characters are memoreable. I do highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of platformers or just wants to have a good time, cause you'll certainly find it in this game. The 9 years of development time has certainly paid off in this happy and touching story about one little Owl.

I'll play Devil's Advocate since it seems like only one other reviewer actually bothered to play this game all the way through.
Mathoria: It All Adds Up is a RPG-Maker game inspired by Pokemon with a combat system where the player must answer simple math questions in order to defeat opponents/obtain items.
The math aspect isn't particularly interesting (though it probably helps that my mental math skills are terrible), but anyone who rates this game negatively on the basis of 'it's teaching me math and too simple for me' likely isn't the intended demographic. This game is for parents who want to spend time together while teaching their kids. In that respect, this game does well. After playing through it, I'd say that if I had a kid I probably would do just that.
That being said, a few aspects of it didn't quite feel right for a children's game. The plot was much too deep for a children's story, especially the ending. Not only this, but I feel like a child 10 or under would have trouble with some of the words in the game as well (such as Vegabond). The story didn't even need to be as intricate as it was - most children beneath the age of 10 are usually willing to forego most plots in exchange for gameplay, so having a compelling story isn't too big a requirement.
There were also a few moments, such as someone saying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off', that didn't sit well with me for a children's game. The rest of the game is good, innocent fun and there were actually a few sections I found myself genuinely enjoying, such as the minotaur puzzles and some of the villager interactions.
The controls are definitely clunky to begin with but you get used to them in time. As another reviewer mentioned, having to press Enter to enable the answer prompt and removing the question from the screen, as well as having a timer on the question itself (which the game claims makes you answer when it runs out, but in reality fails you if you don't), feels like a bad design choice. Especially when learning math on an easy difficulty, timing the player feels too difficult and forcing them to remember the question can easily be too complicated.
The game also focuses solely on addition and not any of the other modifiers like subtraction, division or multiplication, even on higher difficulties. I suppose it makes sense for younger children, but adding this as higher-level option would extend your demographic in a fitting enough way.
The delay between the answer box popping up and when you can type feels too short as well, causing me to mistype whenever I typed too fast, but somehow I don't see that being a problem for children who may type more slowly.
An options screen would be nice, however I find I didn't have much of a problem playing at a fixed resolution, and something tells me a child wouldn't mind it all that much either and possibly wouldn't even notice.
Visually the game uses a lot of RPG maker assets, which is fine since I feel like most children won't mind much unless they've played an RPG Maker game before. What looked like custom assets, however, stuck out like a sore thumb, such as a certain type of house and the ship at the end. Music felt very RPG maker-y and I hardly noticed it (which is a good thing) except for the credits/title music that felt far too hard rock.
As a game designer myself, here's my two cents: Dumb it down more. Even if you're targeting it towards parents and children, parents won't mind playing a more child-like game if their child is playing it with them. Your Pokemon references were enough to appeal to the older side of me, but most kids would be left behind by much of the game's design. This applies to controls as well - I know kids aren't stupid when it comes to controls, but an unintuitive interface could interfere with a child's enjoyment who might get bored easier than an adult. It's doubly bad if gamers are complaining about it!
All that being said, this is a student project targeted to children, so coming out of it those are my only notes. I got much more into it than I expected to, it just needs some tweaking to actually feel like a final product. At this stage I'd liken it to a prototype - one that's just about solid enough to play with a child.

This game is a RPG math game for children. It's like Pokemon, but to fight and win you have to solve the (very simple) equations. Unfortunately the game wouldn't recognize my keyboard inputs like my name, so I became known as:    . It also made it impossible for me to win any fights ever, because I couldn't enter the answers to equations which is the way you win fights. So basically that was game over for me... So I can't really comment on the story.
The difficulty of the game is basically in the equations, and for the three difficulty modes it's something like this: Easy: 3+0. Normal: 3 +10. Hard 18 + 15.
This difficulty level makes the target audience quite narrow. There is a lot of english text to browse through, so it essentially rules out english speaking kids below 7½/8 years of age because they would simply not be able to read through all the text essential to understand and play the game. The equations themselves however are so easy that 'easy' difficulty can be quite easily be solved by kids 5-6 years of age; medium is about 6/7-8 years, and hard 7/8-9 years. So basically the target group is between 7½ to 9 years, add to that kids above 9 years with special math difficulties, or kids aged 7½ year and down with super english reading skills.
For these reasons alone I find it hard to recommend the game. Perhaps if the story is interesting, but unfortunately because the inputs bugged out I will never know.

I recommend this game if you're into games like Fatal Frame, which is exactly what this game is like, only with mythological creatures and spirits of Malaysia and Indonesia. I really enjoyed this game, despite some of the slow paced events and a few glitches here and there.
What I liked about the game are the enemy concepts, and how creepy everything is. It's always interesting to see mythology from different countries, and how things can change when the camera's armed. I also really liked on the strategy inputs on how to defeat and see specific enemies. Pretty interesting idea(s).
Now, I have read quite a bit of negative reviews on here, and what boggles me is the whole thing about "graphics". Games shouldn't be just about graphics, they're called 'video games' for a reason, not an animation or simulator. In my opinion, I find the graphics to be fantastic for an indie game. Believe me, I've seen indie games out there with way~ worse graphics than this. I would compare these graphics to be equivalent to an HD remake of a PS2 game on the PS3 and Xbox360. Of course, I'm not just talking about the graphics, I enjoyed the game itself through my own experience.
What I didn't like about this game were how at times the cutscenes would drag on to the point where it confuses you on if you're able to control Linda again, or not.
I also encountered a few glitches. One had to do with the camera mechanics, another had to do with lag, and the last had to do with disappearing walls at one point.
For the camera mechanics, I would be clicking the button on taking it out and putting it away. At times, she wouldn't. And I wouldn't even click anything and she would put the camera away after taking it out.
For lagging, it would lag whenever a lot of action occurred and when I ascend staircases, or turn a corner of a hallway. Even when I would have the camera out and there's a lot of action occurring, I would move slightly over to where the enemy is and Linda would be aiming either all the way behind, on the ground, or up in outer space.
And for disappearing walls, it happened when I was in the Grand Hall. I just finished with the mirror puzzle and as I exited, the walls disappeared, confusing me on where I am. After making a full circle of the upper level, the walls reappeared.
The other negative thing I should point out is the voice acting. It does need work.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

I've been a fan of Bullfrog's Dungeon Keeper games since the first one was released in 1997, and so, when I heard that a spiritual successor called War for the Overworld was in the works, my interest was piqued to say the least.  I followed the development of WftO during the past year or so, and when I saw its release date finally come around, I excitedly offered up my $26.99. After all, the hundreds of reviews for the game in early access were "very positive."  How could that many people be wrong?  Right?
I've never been impressed with the concept of "early access" games.  If I wanted to pay for the privilege of using broken, buggy, unfinished software, I could just install and boot up Windows.  This is why I wait for official releases before I start playing any game.  I don't need the added frustration and tedium that early access games bring to my PC, so I respectfully abstain. Or at least that's what I thought before I bought War for the Overworld.
When I first launched it, the game told me that it was version 1.0, the official release build, but damned if I can tell from how it plays.  And this game isn't easy to play, by the way.  As soon as I got to the third mission, the game's video began to freeze for what had to be ten to twenty seconds at a time - an unplayable mess. From what I read now, I'm not alone in this.  The mini map is completely useless, looking like some pixelated mess dredged up from two decades ago.  When I first saw it, I had the idea that this must be what people who read tea leaves see in the bottom of their cup.  One would have to be some kind of mystical seer to divine any useful information from it.
I'm tempted to go on, but it's all been said in other reviews.  You should read some of them.  I should have waited to read some of those reviews BEFORE I made my purchase, not AFTER.  I've got only myself to blame for wasting my money.  Please don't waste yours on this unfinished game.  Don't stand for "release now, patch later (if you're lucky)" business practices.  Vote with your wallet, and maybe game developers will start to realize that they're not doing themselves any favors by pasting a v1.0 on an obviously unfinished product.

I have always loved and enjoyed playing real-time strategy games, and Supreme Commander satisfied my hunger pretty well.
If you like real-time strategy, alien/futuristic themes, and challenging gameplay, you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very good, with nice special effects for the different weapons and units. There are 3 factions, each with a fairly large pool of different units to choose from (land, air, and water). The music and sound is decent.
The controls are typical of an RTS-game - lots of hotkeying and keystrokes if you are familiar with this type of gameplay. The learning curve is moderate to challenging - especially if you are unfamiliar with the RTS genre. The tutorials are very helpful and recommended if you want to get a quick grasp of the game. There are a number of difficulty settings when playing agains the AI (I always start of with a skirmish against the AI whenever I first try a new RTS).
There are two types of resources, energy and mass, and managing/balancing your upkeep of both is critical to being successful in this game. You can actually hit a standstill if you try to build/produce too many things at once and run out of resources. I still have not been able to find a way to cancel/delete buildings in progress, however, you are able to pass construction to free up resources.
The feedback in the game is very good - health bars over each unit, a +/- number indicating how much of either resource you are gaining/losing per second (you can switch this with an efficiency %). There are tabs for each research level when you are trying to build structures or train units. There isn't much detail on each unit type (I am used to seeing things like attack damage, defense, etc). From what I've seen, you are only provided with the unit/building health, type (ex: attack submarine, spy plane), and amount of time to train/build.
The story is pretty interesting, there is a nice cutscene in the beginning of the game that paints the setting for you.
You have a commander unit who can attack, build, and reclaim resources. This unit must survive, and you lose if he is defeated. To give a quick boost to resources, you can use your commander (or any engineer/construction units) to reclaim/absorb materials from things like buildings, forests, and destroyed structures/units. The commander unit can also upgrade his components (chest piece, left/right arm piece, back). For example, you can either give the commander a resource boosting arm (for when you use him to relaim material) or a weapons boost on his left arm (you can remove pieces if you wish; upgrading your commander is very expensive and usually done later in the game).
Gameplay is similar to many RTS-games I've played like Red Alert and Tiberian Sun series - there is a faction with cloaked units (radar sensor building to counter). A lot of the battles are decided by rock-paper-scissors mechanics (bombers to destroy buildings and/or slow-moving artillery, fighters to destroy bombers, anti-air to destroy both, tanks to destroy gun emplacements, etc). I do like the versatility of your commander - you can upgrade him to be more of a combat specialist or a building expert.
Overall, I think you should give this game a try if you are interested in the theme or RTS-genre in general, however, the sequel is out, and for a cheaper price too. That being said, I would still give this game a playthrough - especially if you are an RTS-buff/junkie.

I'm not going to lie: DreadOut has quite a few rough spots. Graphics are a little plasticky and rendering is a little weird and doll-like. Controls can be a bit of a pain, as mouselook tends to be oversensitive. Loading a save game sometimes causes the game to get stuck, forcing you to start again. The camera mechanics are implemented with a couple of issues, the biggest being that it takes at least 3 seconds of aiming before you can fire.
However, don't let that detract you from playing, either. DreadOut is a fine homage to the Fatal Frame series. The atmosphere is genuinely frightening, the monsters freakish and terrifying, the music and sounds perfectly moody and foreboding, and the slight kitschy feeling of Southeast Asian horror movies washes over everything and brings out the folklore of Indonesia like no one else can. I would recommend it, but wait for a sale.

My First Steam Review:
First things to point out: Don't let my Time on this game fool you I am very much knowledgeable on this game
-Back Story:
So I was recommended this game by a friend on Xbox Live, he more like nagged the hell out of me to get it. Even though this game disapeared off the shelves before I could snag it on Console, and since I prefer RTS on PC (Obvious reasons). For years he would Nag and I would always say: "I still can't find this game in stores, nor on the Xbox Live Marketplace" and then I found it on Steam. All I have to say is this is a beast of a game and is definitely worth every penny you pay for it, and if you don't like the Classic RTS then you can get the Second one which favors rushing tactics were this game makes that difficult or if not completely impossible.
-Debate:
Now I am aware of the HUGE debate on which is better the first or second, let me just settle that here: The First game(s) are more for RTS with emphsis on the S (Strategy). The second one is more for the newer people to RTS it is less complex and is much more fast paced. You can say this is better in which you are right as a RTS but for people who want to start or try a RTS the second one if for you.
-!WARNING!-
My friends used to play this game ALL DAY LONG and I wondered why and I found out it was a huge time consumer. If you buy this and play it expect to spend atleast 30+ minutes in a game, as I am writing this review I was up till 4 AM Playing the second I think campaign level it lasted 4 hours legit. However those four hours were the most intense four hours I've ever had in a game.
-Gamemodes:
If you are anything like me, you won't buy a single RTS unless it has a Skirmish mode or some sort of Scenario mode were you fight AI as this mode is were this game shines
- Skirmish - 1-8 Players/AI 1,000 Unit Cap for all on massive maps as one of the three factions and is highly customizeable
- Campaign - Restricted version of Skirmish where you only get certain units (I'll go in depth later) with objectives thrown in from time to time and smaller unit cap
- Multiplayer - Same as Skirmish but with Players/AI (Haven't touched multiplayer yet)
- Sandbox - It allows you to test out units as you want to test them for all factions all at once
-Graphics:
(N/A) Lol, really? You shouldn't really care about this since it is a RTS game but graphically it looks like a HD RTS, it doesn't look dated at all to me and it can be set to look equivalent to the sequel. Some of the models however look really ridiculous in my opinion compared to the newer looks in the second.
-Sound:
(10/10) Excellent sound track it fits so perfectly and it changes depending on your Status, the sounds of units are typical of RTS with some older RTS annoyances absent.
-Gameplay:
(9/10) In comparison to both the first and second they play identically, other then progression were this game utilizes the Tech system while the Second utilizes the Research system. The amount of units you deal with is truely massive and it is kind of required to use atleast 100 units to do most of the campaign missions. This game is brutal to strategies as you have to execute them perfectly in order to achieve victory and that is due to the double edged sword that is how forgiving this game is. You can easily fix a mistake in this game but it will make the game last longer and the AI aswell as other players benefit from this. However when you play this game they make it feel underwhelming dealing with the mass (Pun intended) of units you deal with, which is actually very beneficial. The big issue this game suffers is the polished Strategic view in the second game and requires more micromanagement then the second, but the AI for this are not stupid and won't blindly follow orders like they do on the second.
You win by Killing the Enemies ACU (Armed Command Unit) who then explodes into the most rewarding nuclear fireworks show ever nothing is more satisfying then this and even the campaign does a slow mo Zoomed in view during this. However most of the game units feel more like cannon fodder in comparison to the second where all units can be made effective via researching. Building and researching is a slow process it litterally tells you how long it takes to research something or build something and they usually range in the 3 minute section (You can speed this up with engineers).
-AI:
(7/10) The AI are no push overs, and WILL AND DEFINITELY WILL ADAPT TO YOUR STRATEGY and counter it (This is why games take so long). They will rebuild, make defenses and play EXACTLY like a player would difficulty does nothing but give them abilities to cheat. Teammate AI however is a Joke and they will almost never assisst you and will always try to expand even into your Territories regardless of your needs and take what they want.
Now the Unit AI is a big problem in this game even more so then the second one: Units can be stuck in the most stupid situations and they usually cannot be recovered or they will not follow your orders at all.
-Balance:
(9/10) In terms of Balance all factions are literally EQUAL and no faction is better then the other unlike the second were they favored certain playstyles (However those Aeon Morter anti unit cannons kill wayyyyy too quickly in my opinion). Until you get to the endgame (Experimentals).
Strategies are equally difficult including Rushing.
-Economy:
Resources are infinite but runs on a resources system absent in most newer RTS's, in which economy management has to be done such as: Shutting down factories, Supply and Demand, and Constant expense of resource. If you play smart you will never run into this problem unless you need to do a 180 on your strategy.
-Strategy:
This is were the first shines in its many ways to win:
- Cold War -
- Weapons Race -
- Nuclear War -
- Ground war -
- Turtling -
- Rushing -
- Sabotage -
- Economy Crashing - Unique to the first game
- Assassination -
Just a few different ways/strategies that can happen in game
-Tutorial:
(9/10) The tutorial is pretty good at covering everything, but doesn't teach you anything, and I did NOT notice any learning curve that people been complaining about.
-TL:DR-
(10/10) If you played RTS games that are old, you'll like this game (Your anti-virus won't however). If you are new, you should still give it a try it is not as difficult as people say it is or try the Second then return here young one. Even if you aren't interested in this game it is definitely a must own for any Hardcore RTS player like myself.
- Troubleshooting -
Oh you are reading through the reviews and you cannot get the game to run? Well I had a few issues and I will clear up a few here.
- Compatability: This game is Compatable with Windows 8.1 unlike what most people say, however it isn't with anti-virus software.
- Trojan Virus: This game is Not a virus despite your dumb as hell Anti-Virus program would like to say, and your anti-virus will cause it to bug out and crash and corrupt its files
^ How to fix ^
1.) Go to your anti-virus software's Fire Wall settings;
2.) Go to Allowed/Ignored/Whitelist
3.) Click add
4.) Click browse or find the program listed then click allowed
You'll find it in C:\ProgramFiles(86)\Steam\SteamApps\Common\SupremeCommander\Bin it will be the Supreme Commander.Exe make sure you also add the other executables in the bin too as I found that makes it not happen a lot less
Pro Tips:
-Never Launch this game at start up as your Anti virus may freak out as it is still "Waking up" and will cause it to delete the executeable
- Executed Executable: Missing your Executable? Heres how to get it back
1.) Go to Library on Steam
2.) Click the Game go to options on it until the options submenu opens
3.) Now find the option that says Verify Cache and run it
4.) Wait about 10-30 minutes for it to fix deleted files
*5.) Re-add Supreme Commander.exe to your whitelist on anti-virus software

I have heard of this game since years ago, and eith the praises it got recently, I have decided to give it a try. And it is amazing. At first glance it might not seem great, but it had a great core gameplay that makes you play and not realize that it has been two hours. The action is simply that smooth and slick. Melee is simply satisfying, the shooting is good (helped by the unique and different weapons handling differently giving a great amount of variety to the game), the customization is deep, and that mobility is simply amazing - you really do do feel like a space ninja in this game.
The waiting might be frustrating for some, but they managed to pace things so well that with each sessions, no matter how short, felt like you've accomplished something. It helps that the rewards are amazing - a bunch of very cool and unique weapons and character classes that are fun to use. Just don't get fixated on one thing too much and just try as many things as you can.
The implementation of Microtransactions in this game is very good - I didn't feel like anything was kept away from me and you can earn everything for free; but if you want to progress quickly or get the cosmetics quickly then you can buy the premium currency when you got a 50-75% discount from the daily login bonuses. A very generous discount, especially when you can definitely play the game without paying with barely any major hassle.
It is also very well optimized - bugs in the new Plains of Eidolon aside - as I can run it with my weak laptop and even at lower settings it still looks very good. There are some bugs here and there, but rarely anything severe and the developers listens to community feedback and communicates constantly with the fans via many different channels (most notably a weekly stream). They're not perfect - there are some things that they still fail in addressing - but they are miles better than most other developers/publishers, I'd say better than CD Projekt even, which is a very high bar. The community themselves are great and full of helpful people with very little elitism and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ry you'd have expected from most online communities, making playing and talking about the game simply a joy to do.
This is the game that Star Wars: Battlefront II and Destiny 2 could have been.  It has been a long, long journey, and it seems that it hasn't always been smooth. But it is a rare game where they continue to polish what they have until it shines and stood tall amongst the crowd. It is a game that is worth your time and, dare I say, worth your money. Play it. Give it a go. Even if it's not your cup of tea, I would say it is worth a try as I'd thought the same at first - and now it is my fallback game when I don't feel like playing anything else.
9/10 - Need polish but I have faith in the developers so I don't hesitate giving such a high score (for me).

Hard Reset is no more or less than the quintessential old school shooter. It lacks any real form of cover, leaning, and most shockingly crouch, and the maps are incredibly linear. There's no notion of stealth or sniping or any serious problem solving. It's a very spam-y game. You just take on waves of enemies as they come. There are different sorts of enemies, but it doesn't matter much in terms of just sinking enough ammo into them until they die.
Enemies drop four kinds of drops: health (green), rifle ammo (red), plasma gun ammo (blue), and nano (orange). You also have a shield but it regenerates automatically. You collect enough nano and you earn an upgrade. Both of your weapons as well as your general gear upgrade the same way. Everything has 5 modes (the last two of which get unlocked later) and each mode has 2 additional upgrades beyond the first for a total of 15 upgrades for each weapon and your gear. For weapons this tends to mean a primary attack, and secondary function or attack, and a passive bonus in each of the 5 modes. Each weapon uses the same ammunition for each attack and each mode, albeit at different rates.
Your environment is pretty dangerous, there are high explosives all over the place as well as electrified items which, when damaged, shock everything within range for a period of time before exploding. Additional from time to time you encounter random flame-throwers in the walls. You can take down entire waves of enemies with just the explosive and electric death traps lying around.
That's basically it. That's the entire game (as far as I've played it anyway).
On the down-side, the gun play isn't all that imaginative and you don't always have time to swap to all your cool new upgrades in the heat of battle. This combined with the high linearity, wave format of enemy encounters, terrible terrible voice acting and story (not that it has any real impact on the game), and the fact that, despite what the pictures look like above, the artistic style really isn't all that nice, makes me sort of sigh and dream of what this game could have been.
IMHO, what this game could have been is Shadow Warrior (Redux), which I believe was a perfect and shining example of what happens when you put modern game technology and philosophy into an old school shooter. In a sense, Hard Reset is like a poor man's Shadow Warrior. Definitely not worth the same amount of money (I just picked up Hard Reset for like 2.50 USD, sooo not complaining). On the upside though, if you do like your old school shooters, this is a good game. It does what it sets out to do. It's fun, it's destructive, it's fast paced (during combat sequences), and you can just go insane. Ammo conservation hasn't been a problem yet (normal difficulty). Over all, I haven't found the game to be really difficult at all, which is not to say that I haven't died yet. Bottom line is, I'm enjoying it, I'd recommend it, and though I haven't played it enough to comment on the complaints about its short length, I'd say even at full cost (15 USD) I think it's fair.
TL;DR : Solid game, proper old school shooter experience, no major faults besides♥♥♥♥♥♥story and acting, but nothing mind blowing either. I'd recommend it to friends.

Valkyria Chronicles is a game that I didn't expect to like at first. I was worried it was going to be too silly, that it was going to be over-the-top. It had been a while since I had really enjoyed a Japanese RPG style game as much as I had done in the late 90s. But this one surprised me.
First, I'll mention some of the negatives. There's this one character who always has one eye closed and it really bugs me. There is a supporting character that is a small pig with wings. There's some fan service bits. It's occasionally very difficult. It's unplayable and ridiculously cheesy with the English voice acting (in my estimation).
There are many positives. I like any game that enables me to form a team of distinct people from a large number of options (in this sense, it scratched my Genso Suikoden itch). It means that, while there are some characters that aren't to my tastes, unless they are part of the main cast, I don't need to suffer them. The characters I put in my team become heroes in my own mind, as I recall times in which they've saved me from almost certainly having to start a level from the beginning again. There is an extensive cast of female characters, with a diverse range of personalities and appearances. It's also worth mentioning that there are quite a few LGBT characters in the game, but they aren't particularly well represented in some cases. The game does have an anime style, but it's very subdued--everything from the colour palatte to the behaviour of the characters is mostly just a bit less in your face than what I've come to expect from modern anime things. The combat system is fairly intuitive and it can be very satisfying when you've developed a strategy for defeating a level with little to no casualties. The psuedo-European setting is a pull for anyone with an interest in historical things. All the details about guns and tanks will no doubt be of interest to people with certain inclinations. The story isn't amazing, but it's simple, and it's effective (and sometimes affecting). It touches on some delicate issues such as racism and slavery, and isn't too tacky about it. Soundtrack is also very nice.
I was so involved in this game for a few months, I went to a themed cafe when the remaster came out on PS4 and there are really chunky art books to buy that flesh out the story, characters and development process. It was a good time. If you enjoy the characters in this game, many of them also make appearances in the sequels on the PSP, and are set to be featured in DLC for the recently announced VC4--so it's worth getting invested in!

Valkyria Chronicles is one of a kind. This has two sides: the good, and the not so good. The good thing is, you're going to enjoy playing it. A lot. The not so good: you won't find another game like this once you've played the heck out of it.
Valkyria Chronicles will keep its appeal for years to come. The reason is some outstanding design choices. By placing the action in a fictional, I World War-alike game, situations and characters ooze proximity and realism while not offering any surface for attacking the game's historical accuracy; the technology will never feel outdated; the comic-style art never goes out of fashion; and the technology chosen to blow life into that art is perfectly capable of moving everything in your screen smoothly enough.
The story and characters are also likeable, and the gameplay itself has set a standard for games like the latest UFO: Enemy Unkown iterations: a mixture of turn based strategy game and first person shooter that works like a charm (I was skeptical at first).
All in all, VC is a timeless classic. You owe it to yourself to try this game.

A decent, challenging cyberpunk FPS. Hard Reset is a great looker, boasting both an amazing artstyle and great graphical fidelity. Nothing bad can also be said about the technical aspect either, since gunplay is solid and the weapon animations smooth. The soundtrack is okay and fits the game, albeit is nothing to write home about.
That being said, Hard Reset suffers from repetitiveness, especially in the later stages. Fighting bullet sponge enemies in similar, dark rooms can be fun for only so long. The game follows the Serious Sam formula of locking you in an arena with hordes of enemies, and that inevitably gets boring during long sessions. The game shines when you treat as a time killer you boot up every once and again, not when you marathon it from start to finish.
It should also be noted that Hard Reset gets really difficult at times. It is a challenging FPS for the veterans of the genre, not a game for newcomers.
While Hard Reset might not be worth the full price of 13,99€, don't hesitate to grab it when it's on at least -50% sale. It has flaws, but it's certainly not a bad game.

This is another case where I wish there was a "neutral" option when reviewing a game. On the plus side, Owlboy is a beautiful game. Otus controls well,  picking up new allies whilst playing through the game was motivating, and altogether the game was a relatively enjoyable experience. I understand the development that this game went through, and I think that it makes this game all-the-more inspirational.
Despite all of this I couldn't bring myself to recommend this to everyone, so therefore I cannot leave a thumbs-up. Don't get me wrong, the game is a relatively good platformer. It looks good, it plays good, and the fact that it was created at all is incredible.
There are a few small nitpicks here and there. Thanks to the art style some of the jumps can be frustrating, and Otus' rolls never quite seem to make it. I don't care about these things, however. Again, the game controls amazingly well anyway, and any small frustrations caused by them only last a minute or two.
My reasoning is that the game is incredibly unfulfilling to the moderate gamer. Casual gamers will have a blast reading through the story and enjoying taking the game one step at a time. Hardcore gamers might get bored, but Owlboy clearly has some potential for them a long as they are patient.
This game is incredibly unfulfilling, even tedious to the middle-of-the-road gamers. This is not because the game is bad, but because it is both a puzzle-action platformer AND a collect-a-thon.
The smallest issue I had with the game came in the form of the monsters. Any monster not part of a puzzle was practically worthless. This is fine by itself: add some filler monsters to add some life between getting from point A to point B, but then the collect-a-thon bit comes in.
While playing the game players will find coins littered around everywhere. Reaching certain coin milestones will grant rewards, although they are entirely unnecessary to beating the game. Still, getting gun upgrades and the such is usually worth it, and coins tend to be everywhere. The is a finite number of them, however, and this is where things took a dive.
For as quick paced as the game can become during key moments Otus is SLOW when trying to move around the gargantuan overworld. If you want to find EVERYTHING the game has to offer get ready to triple your playtime. If you expected to play through the game casually and then collect everything you must first figure out how to turn your brain off.
Because you WILL spend hours just circling around the same dungeon over and over again to find the last 10 coins you need.
And then you will spend 5 minutes to get back to the next dungeon.
And then you will spend another hour or so going through that one.
I don't think that this sort of thing is bad by itself. Collect-a-thons are usually tedious anyway, so that's all fine. In the end, I collected all three owl thingies and put them in their corresponding pillar thingy. This is when I started questioning my decision to do so.
Many similar games that require you to re-explore dungeons give you something as a reward. An alternate ending, perhaps. Maybe it'll grant you some special power, or maybe it'll be the final nail-in-the-coffin to figuring out the story.
I got nothing. Just a few holograms that gave me some information I already knew. I felt like I might have missed something, perhaps I needed to go through the end of the game cutscene for my reward. Still, nothing. There isn't anything else to find. No alternate endings, no bonus cutscenes, just the credits and back to the title screen.
I didn't even bother getting all of the regular coins. You can see the reward before you nab them all anyway: just a spiffy looking cloak, probably some funny dialogue along with it. I wasn't going to try watching and re-watching a youtube walkthrough a million times to find out.
In the end, playing through the game itself wasn't so bad. It slowed down painfully at times, but it was okay nonetheless. The pixel art is great, and if you just collect the extras that you come across you probably will enjoy yourself.
If I could go back in time, this is the information that I would have told myself. I've spent hours of extra gametime flying back-and-forth in the world to no avail. But my biggest complaint is that there was no real reward for doing so, at least not any award that was worth the extra hours gone to waste. If you wish to buy the game: play through, enjoy yourself, and if there is anything that would be tedious to do, don't do it.

Just kidding, I loved this game. If you played the first Mass Effect, expect more of the similar styled gameplay. For the most part, not much has changed in Mass Effect 2, but there are a few changes that alter how the game is played. One of the most obvious changes is that you now use ammo instead of an overheating system. Honestly, this wasn't too different, but there are instances where it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥having to run outside of cover to look for ammo. Aside from that, the sidequests are much more interesting and they're managed in a way that you actually want to get this done. Rather than having to have these sidequests on your mind, the galaxy map simply shows you what system corresponds with your currently available sidequests. This added a few hours of gameplay to my playthrough and I greatly enjoyed that. Despite that, at one point you simply want to get through the main mission to progress through the story line.
The loyalty system with your team is another good feature of this sequel. Not only does it fill out your team members past, it also rewards your completion of them with alternative costumes and power ups, a positive.
A few things I disliked about the implemented changes.
1: The levelling up system feels almost worthless. Besides levelling up specific abilities, you can almost go through the entire game without upgrading your abilities and you'll still do well. The implementation of a research console is what mainly contributes to you doing well in this game. Rather than searching for weapons like in Mass Effect 1, most of the upgrades are done through a research console on the Normandy. Instead of looking out for new weapons on various planets, it's the research upgrades that you need to look out for.
2: The final boss battle is a bit lackluster. Maybe it would've been harder at a higher difficulty level, but some fire fights were more of a ♥♥♥♥♥ than this final boss. I'm not saying that the boss needs to be near impossible to beat, but it should require a higher level of difficulty than what other enemies throughout the game offer.
For the most part, those are my immediate thoughts in regards to this game. Needless to say, this game has increased my love for the Mass Effect franchise and I look forward to playing Mass Effect 3 and eventually waiting for the arrival of Mass Effect 4. I give this game a 4/5 and I definitely recommend this game.

Back when i got this game in a box from target, it introduced me to the gnere of RTS. With its big battles and complex strategy, i thought of this game as the standard of all RTS games. After trying other RTS games like Command and conquor and Empire Earth, i realised how exceptionaly amazing this game really is.
Supreme Commander lets you make and take control of your own army while trying to destroy someone elses like all RTSs. But while most RTSs let you control a few units to make armies, this game lets you use hundreds of them, giving rise to situatons of "how do i defend agaisnt their 500 bombers while not losing my factories?" or "Wheres the best place to attack with my 700 gunships and what to do with these nukes?" and minutes later "HOW DID THAT NOT WORK?" (NOTE: do not try to use nukes in combination with gunships, gunships are not nuke-proof)
The game has a resource system based on 2 resources that are required for everything. Every little bot you build for your armies of mass destruction will cost mass and energy to build, bot of which are easy to obtain and require little maintenance to keep up with your production unless your opponet destroys them. The game also has 4 tiers of units from the basic light tanks of tier 1 to the experimental lazer eyed and nozed colossal sized bots of tier 4 ( also called the experimental tier)
I thought the game was better from the box than from steam as some of the units are borrowed from Forged Alliance here. (Forged Alliance is better than the original Supreme Commander and totaly worth the 5 extra dollers in the gold edition) Not that the units are bad, but the gameplay changes when one faction has suicidal bombers. The game also tends to crash a bit when you get 8000 unit battles going but i dont know any computers that can handle that many units and their animated shells and rounds too.
If your getting this game for the campaign, just a warning, the plot isnt the best ive seen and the AI is a bit annoying reminding you to complete your objectives every few minutes. However, any game that lets you carpet nuke an uninhabited part of Hawaii is worth the annoying AI. (no offence Hawaii but the only missions on Earth featured part of Hawaii)

Speedrunners is one of those rare games where four people can sit (without splitscreen) on a single machine and just play for hours. It comes to us from developer Double Dutch games, who have released nothing else on Steam as of this interview.
Falling into a catagory of "racing platformer", Speedrunners tasks you and three others (local or online ranked/unranked multiplayer) with racing through intricately designed arenas while dodging rockets, blocks, grappling hooks, lazers, and drills all thrown by your competitors. Grab items of your own, and use them against your rivals to quickly gain the lead, but if you fall out of view of the camera, you're knocked out of the round.
When the first player is knocked out, the screen begins to shrink rapidly (the "camera" 'zooming in'), shortening the "kill zone", and raising the stakes. This keeps the game extremely fast paced, and I and my friends have found ourselves playfully yelling at the screen in frustration.
Price is a little steep, but replayability is very high. In game unlockable content (including characters and skins) but you are not encouraged or asked to purchase any dlc content in order to unlock out-of-game characters. Excellent for fans of Mario Kart, Smash Brothers, and racing games respectively.

DreadOut is one of the best new original horror games to come out in some time. In a genre over saturated with shovelware, this game is truly a diamond in the rough. Not to say this game isn't a little rough around the edges itself at times. Heavily inspired by the horror genre juggernaut 'Fatal Frame', DreadOut hits its marks, but misses a few as well. The game features a 3rd person over the shoulder camera angle, that I love, but I still would have liked an option for 1st person. In terms of voice acting, it leaves a lot to be desired, but works well enough. The main character "Linda" is a silent protagonist, which is a HUGE disappointment and a little awkward when it comes to cutscenes. The sound and music are good; except for a couple scenes missing score where there should have been something there. In terms of story it's very thin and could have been slightly better explained as well. it's also a VERY short game (about 4 hours).
I want to point out that I actually like and enjoy DreadOut very much, but want to give constructive criticism. Although it has its problems, It's a great game that I definitely recommend to anyone who likes/loves the horror genre. The horror genre needs more good games. This is one of them. In what negatives it has, theres so many more positives to be found.

Dreadout is an Indonesian indie horror game, which focuses on Linda Melinda. Trapped in an abandoned town, and armed with her trusty Irisphone, she whips it out to exorcise ghosts with her trusty camera on her smartphone. If that sounds similar, it's because it's quite similar to the Fatal Frame series.
Linda will encounter many types of ghosts, some visible normally, some only visible by the camera, and some only visible by the camera by certain means. To exorcise them, she needs to take a picture of them in the camera. Some ghosts can simply be exorcised by taking a picture of them normally, while some can only be done so by taking a picture of their weak points. Once exorcised, their entry will enter Linda's book of ghostbusting, in terms of their relative origins. And as the background of the game implies, most of the ghosts are based on Indonesian horror folklores.
You can swap between third person or first person view. First person view is obviously for camera snapping, while third person is mainly used to navigate Linda across the town, or to reposition her effectively, as in first person view your movement is slower than usual. Ghosts will attack you physically and magically, and when she dies, she will enter a limbo realm, which she is allowed to return to the realm of the living.
As there are very few games that are similar to the Fatal Frame series on PC, I must say, this game is pretty unique. Also, unlike many games, the hints in this game is extremely vague. If you are playing it for the first time or so, you may be clueless as to what to do next, since it doesn't tell you what to do completely. It's pretty interesting, yet frustrating at the same time. Also sometimes the ghosts actually gets bugged out, where even though they should be dead, yet they aren't. This will occur if you do something which is not exactly as the game dictate, for example, using the SLR camera instead of the Irisphone for a certain event. It's avoidable, but if you are playing it on your first playthrough, then it may happen.
This game actually have quite a lot of jumpscares. It's shocking for the first few times, but when the ghost attack is so, it gets pretty annoying. I don't want to get screamed right in my monitor repeatedly. Also, as I mentioned earlier about the limbo realm, you can't actually die. She will never move on, but continue to return to the land of the living. The biggest issue about this game is that, it's short. On your first playthrough, it will take much longer, since you will be cautious of the environment and also get stuck due to the lack of hints. However, once you know how it goes, you can finish it really fast, within 2 hours or less. Even in one playthrough, you can get many achievements in one go, which is something achievement hunters will actually like.
Overall, I say it's a decent indie horror game. There are not many horror games which uses a camera to exorcise ghost on the PC, so it's pretty unique. Horror fans will love this game. However, it's kinda short and jumpscares tend to get really annoying over time. I would suggest to get it during a sales though. Also get the Keepers of the Dark standalone DLC. It will explain the story a bit more better as the plot of that game occurs somewhere within this game storyline, though don't play it first, as you will really be clueless on what to do.

Fantastic deep and complex strategy game, it will have you cackling with evil glee when you pull off an assassination attempt on your idiot son, in order to get him out of the line of succession so your smart son can be your heir. It will have you jumping up and down with joy when you finally manage to knock up your gluttonous, maimed wife with a son so that scheming vassal of yours won't take over when you die (at least not immeadiately). It will have you wailing in agony when those pesky vassals rebel right at the tipping point of your war to take the English crown, forcing you to beg the incestuous midget King of England for white peace. You will curse and throw things at your screen when your ambitious wife succeeds in her plot to saw through the railings of your balcony, causing you to fall to your death (I knew I should have never acknowledged that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ son I had with my lustful hedonistic courtier). Most of all, it will have you engrossed with the unfolding story of your dynasty.
Be warned though, this game has a fairly steep learning curve. For me, at least, the tutorial wasn't nearly enough. I grasped the basics only after watching a lengthy Let's Play/Video Guide on Youtube, that could be just because I'm slow on the uptake so your results may vary. I'm still learning new things every time I play, as I'm still fairly new to the game so don't expect to master this game quickly. Another possible negative is the amount of DLC (it could also be considered a positive), some may say that the DLC should be free updates to the game. I'm not sure where I stand on the issue when it comes to this game but I will say that the DLC goes on sale quite often, and because the game is so incredibly good it really doesn't bother me that much. These guys aren't releasing a new Crusader Kings game every year, so they continue to build on this game to give us new avenues and situations to explore. Whether or not it should be free isn't for me to decide, it's just something to consider when you buy the game.
Bottom line: If you want to become immersed in a deep and complex strategy game that really makes you feel as if you're a ruler in the middle-ages, this is the game for you. It's amazing. Just be prepared for the learning curve and for spending a little more on the DLC if you decide it's worth it.

I bought this game in 2013 apparently and since the have not played it while patiently waiting for the developers to finish it.
While they did add a lot of rooms, spells, traps, sounds and a voiceover since then... it still feels unpolished.
Personally i've got several issues that persisted through every version of the game:
1) Cursor is hard to use. Yes, you are reading it right - the cursor. They made it look like a finger from an original game, unfortunately as far as using it in the game it somehow became harder, probably due to increased resolution. Clicking on stuff is mostly "hit and miss" situation since the active part of the cursor is just the fingertip. Combine that with the fact that you have to click directly on the stuff, like treasure chests and tiny imps - you've got yourself an annoying issue.
2) Tooltips. Many reviewers already mentioned that they do not make any sense whatsoever and its true - instead of clear information about rooms its just some strings with numbers and abbreviations.
3) UI. There is no way to soften the blow - its horrible in every possible way. The buttons are too small. The cursor is too big and hard to use (read 1). The minimap (again, made to resemble an original DK minimap) is completely useless and would've been appropriate in the year 95 - Microsoft paint blocks instead of actual rooms and enemies just won't cut in 2015.
4) I've expected that with time and better optimization the game would demand less PC resources but unfortunately the opposite has happened. So just a heads up - you really DO need 6-8gb and more, as well as good CPU.
Unfortunately the game has not met my expectations yet (in the basic controls department at least) and i've waited quite a bit already. I might change my mind later on, if the developer updates the UI though.

How to make a random cash-grab game with mindless mechanics and lowest cost: this game is the result.
You step a party through a predefined area by pressing space for each stept, and nothing else ever. If any enemy is adjacent, the party will automatically attack, you may however choose one target that should be attacked first. But in the end it doesn't really matter anyways. So basically you slam space till some game window tells you that you earned stuff. You can get the creatures you fight (by chance) and random loot that boosts your party. Creatures can be used to evolve them into stronger versions (kind of like a levelup+), or can be "eaten" to grant free XP.
The game starts easy, but already after a few levels, enemies sometimes just one-shot party members. And the only way to get through those levels is to use boost items. Some of them you get for free, the rest need to be payed with ingame cash-shop items. And just so you use a lot of them, the game doesn't even ask you if you actually want to use cash to activate the boost. One miss-click and 9 gems are gone. One boss that just cuts everyone's HP in half per turn, and all your cash is gone.
Thanks to the very primitive gameplay this game gets boring rather fast. All levels are the same, enemy abilities rarely matter, evolutions and new creatures are plain random, if you even manage to understand how it is done at all. Maybe it gets more tactical on the higher levels, but then you better already emptied your wallet into the cash-shop, or you have to endure a mindless grind of pure random luck.
The translations show the effort that was put into this game, namely none. I started with German, but everything was so wrong, even Google translate could have done better. English language is ok-ish, but the game only lets you enter the options menu after you played through the tutorial. Till then you have to read things like "This egg artifact must get. Beware!"
Unless you are a big fan of mindless money-grabber flash-games, stay away from this game. It is a pure waste of time.

By the time you get anywhere meaningful (say, the point where your gear is good enough to even roughly equalize your playing chances when fighting higher-geared players) you'll have spent either hundreds (if you've paid a bit) or thousands upon thousands of hours. Unless, of course, you buy cash-store items for an exorbitant total price and sell them to buy said gear, then level accordingly.
Sure, you COULD spend a bunch of money to accelerate your gear acqusition to "only" a few hundred accumulated hours (most likely among multiple people) for competitive gear. You also COULD spend many more thousand hours as a free player trying to get even anywhere near that, smart play or otherwise.
Alternatively, you COULD take your money, time, and give it to a game that isn't going to tell you
whether or not you *might* find it fun that many hours down the line. Regardless of whether or not you play smart, so many other games would reward you more for your effort that if I had to make a list, ArcheAge would be a tiny and, deservingly, an obscure part of that review.
Believe it or not, I have actually seen someone defend this game by saying that you can't judge the game until you've spent "at least 1000 hours" on it. For those of us who might, gee, know it's possible to know if a game is enjoyable (judge-able) or not in a few hours without a thousand hours of grinding, it is not a valid choice.
In my few hundred off-Steam hours, I've been a bit on both sides of the aisle. I am happy to say that I didn't spend a lot of money on this (even if I was still a paying customer) game and also managed to get Patron mode by simply using free labor -- but most of the reward in that was just another tier to grind, assuming the game didn't decide to randomly scrap your item and make you restart the building process.
Saying "Sandbox experience" is cool and all until you realize it's all just a numbers game, both in terms of player counts and in terms of how much money and time they've spent. For those of you who want to gape at technical marvels, go ahead and spend your money. For those of us who think that the sandbox experience is icing on the cake, it will not matter when the cake (actual practical value to your usual players in terms of combat equalization and labor usage) is made of glorified mud.
I will happily change my view if this game somehow does a 180, but that would require a total redesign of labour and gear, which is far, far more than I expect this game to ever accomplish. Until then, I'd say steer clear and find a game that will give YOU more for your time, effort and money.

I've been playing AA outside of Steam for almost 2yrs now.  Well over 1500+ hours and still going strong.
This game, despite its flaws, and it has a few, is still a truly amazing game.  The sheer depth of it boggles the mind.  Even after almost 2yrs of playing, I still learn something new almost daily.
From the number of classes to the ways to play the game (farmer, pvper, pvper, AH player, etc), ArcheAge offers a little bit of something for almost everybody.  There are days when I'm a pure potato just planting and growing stuff.  Other days, I get bloodlust and goto pvp/pve events.  Being a sandbox, we have those choices.  You can play the way you want.
What really stands out are the faction/guild alliances and how they play out during in-game events.  We have Easterners who regularly visit our CR/GR events which turn into a PVP scrum.  Imagine trying to kill a boss while reds are picking off your teammates from the rear.  Or going to Abyssal to see one faction working with pirates so now you have to fight twice as many people!  PVP in Diamond Shores or conflict zones can go from a 5 man fight to a full raid in minutes.
The landscape in AA is some of the most beautiful I've seen in over 20yrs of gaming.  My first time roaming through Windscour, for example, just took my breath away.  The mountains, those funny looking trees, the elephants, the lions...  Villenelle is straight out of a Japanese town and looks so breathtaking that I moved there.  Hasla has a very Korean feel to it.  Lots of mountains, tight paths, and, of course, Veroe.  Karkasse looks like...well...the worst place in the history of video games.
Music is another win for Archeage.  Who hasn't heard that, I dont know how to describe it, the "Hasla Tune?"  I could literally sit in Hasla and listen to that tune for hours.  The music in Austera is something straight out of a middle-eastern city.
Sea Combat in Archeage is where things get truly crazy.  We have a large pirate faction on our server and they make sea travel dangerous.  They hit hard and will gank you for looking at them funny.  Still, the game wouldn't be the same without pirates and Growlgate island.  When we do Abyssal and Lusca, the s hip-to-ship combat is both intense and deadly.  I once had an enemy ship launch itself in the air and land on mine!  Gold Traders on Freedich are regularly camped which makes sneaking packs into Freed a risky but exciting deal.
Crafting in Archage is so deep, you could write a book about it.  There are actually people who specialize in crafting just a few of the hundreds, perhaps thousands of things that can be made.  The folio, the crafting database, is just packed with info.  Not a day goes by where I'm not discovering some new item to make.
Finally, there is always some kind of faction / nation / server drama involved in Archeage.  Whether people are complaining about green pirates, packs being stolen, or just complaining to complain, it is there.  If you enjoy hijinx and comedy, you shouldn't miss it.  Just bring a thick skin because chat can be a bit...well...toxic.
This game has brought me so much pleasure I feel I should be paying more for it.
In fairness, the game does have some flaws.  Some of them are serious.  Yet, overall, the game is just a blast to play.  I highly, highly recommend it.  I'm on Kraken server so if anyone needs help getting started or has questions email me.  My email is in my profile.
