"Normally, with puzzle games, if it seems too hard then you're generally just doing it wrong. With Desktop Dungeons, it's just too hard." — Kakie, Corsual Live Viewer
I have a confession to make. I'm not proud of it, but I haven't finished Desktop Dungeons. I strive to complete all of the games I review prior to writing, but in this case the cross was too great to bear.
My failure came not through lack of trying — I tried for many, many hours — but from an overwhelming level of difficulty. Not the bad kind of difficulty, where cheap opponents consistently barrage you until you die hurling an overpriced controller against the nearest wall, but the good kind of difficulty, that will see you thinking — really thinking — about every move you make, every time you make it, lest your adventure come to a inconveniently early end.
Fortunately, I appreciate a challenge. Hell, I crave it. But in the end, it turned out that there was more to accomplish, collect and unlock in this roguelike dungeon crawler than I could ever hope to discover in just 2 weeks, and so, I began my review in advance.
WITHOUT FURTHER ADO...
I first saw Desktop Dungeons while watching MANvsGAME; Danny Baranowsky and Grant Kirkhope, who composed the soundtrack, were there alongside one of the core developers, Danny Day.
They discussed many of the basic game concepts; the randomly generated dungeons and roguelike nature, spell-casting warriors, the coming mobile release, the difference between a harpsichord and clavinet and the origins of Granny Kirkanowsky.
Listening in, amidst the constant laughter, I quickly learned that DD has something of a cult following that grew around an alpha build released to the public years back and available free today, which led to it winning the IGF Award Winning for Game Design. Immediately, I downloaded it to take a look.
IN THE BEGINNING
The alpha turned out to be a crude version of the one MAN was playing. It looked very different — the hand-drawn art wasn't present, instead offering a more traditional pixel art style, and the entire progression mechanic was missing, so choosing a dungeon was as simple as selecting a race, class and difficulty.
Though I was watching MAN play a clearly superior version, I still felt entirely engaged playing the alpha due to the 'roguelike' nature of the gameplay. Every dungeon was different, and though my imminent demise was almost always a single click away, the ability to head straight back in, new knowledge in hand, to a completely new dungeon, maintained my interest throughout the entire night.
That's when I made my purchase, gained access to the browser-operated (sans-soundtrack) beta and began to compare.
NEW IS ALWAYS BETTER
After a brief serving of story and a short tutorial explaining the basics I was directed to my very own kingdom, a world map of sorts, comprised mostly of open space and human inhabited houses. After completing a dungeon, more buildings appeared.  An elven habitat, a mage tower, a church...
I quickly realised that the original 'choose race, choose class, choose difficulty' menu featured in the alpha had been replaced here with progressive RPG elements via the kingdom, including a huge host of quests, and that unlike the alpha, races and classes here required an unlock before they could be used.
The game continued forward, revealing multiple new features. Gold could be collected from dungeons and kept afterward, and then used to purchase preparation items that could be used in future dungeon attempts, or saved to unlock new buildings in the kingdom.
Eventually, I was introduced to the tavern, which served as a hub allowing access to multiple dungeon types. It was here that the largest difference between the alpha and beta made their appearance — there's more than one dungeon type in the full version. A lot more.
DON'T♥♥♥♥♥♥OFF THE DEITIES
That's when things started getting tough, and it was at about that time that the full Steam release arrived, this one complete with Granny K's masterpiece soundtrack.
I was happy to learn that the progress I'd made in the beta was saved, and too, that even though I could now play the full release on Steam, I could continue to do so from my browser if I chose. Everything is saved online, so portable gaming is a legitimate option. A good thing, too, as Desktop Dungeons lends itself perfectly to quick gaming when you've only got 10 minutes to spare. Come on mobile version...
Where was I... oh, right. It's hard. Even the normal dungeons are hard. And the hard dungeons are a lot f@&ing harder. God only knows if there are even harder dungeons around the bend, but if there are, you'll likely need God's help to complete them. Well, at least one of the Gods, anyway.
Yes, yes... I know. Terrible segway, yada-yada. Gods are the key to victory in many of the dungeons, yet they're also a leading cause of death. The decision to adopt a deity is usually a hard one — on the one hand, they offer amazing buffs and bonuses that are generally the key to victory, on the other, they'll restrict you in various ways, punishing you severely for whatever they deem misconduct — though mastering their ways is essential.
THIS IS THE GAME THAT NEV-ER ENDS
That's where the other 'game mode' really helps: Puzzles. After unlocking the Explorer's Guild building in your kingdom you'll have access to a series of puzzles - dungeons that aren't generated randomly, but instead, have a single specific solution that you must discover in order to succeed.
They double as great ways to learn more information about the various items, weapons, spells, deities and conversion materials on offer, and though not everyone will need them, they're highly advised if you're having difficulty completing certain quests or dungeons.
And that's everything I know. Almost. I know that of the nine classes I've unlocked there are another nine to go. I know that of the four races I've unlocked there are another... actually I don't know how many more there are. One, at least. I found him once — a Halfling trapped in a dungeon within a dungeon who nicked my last potion— but failed and haven't seen him since. That's a lot of the fun in Desktop Dungeons; every dungeon is different, and you never know what you're going to get. If you like The Binding of Isaac, or Spelunky, or more appropriately, Rogue Legacy, which offers a similar style of 'progressive roguelike' gameplay, then there's a great chance you'll love Desktop Dungeons, too. It's as hard as the others — perhaps even harder in its own way — but if you're not one to shy from a challenge then there's a lot to enjoy.

So I didn't want to write a review for Owlboy until I finished it. Because this game does have a story to tell and I wanted my review to make use of that. After 10 hours of gameplay, I have done so! But I'm not a 100%er so there's probably a good amount that I've missed.

The gameplay. This is what mattered. And after playing it, I can say it was like if you took the flying mechanics of Kirby, mixed that with the level design of a metroidvanie type title and you'd have Owlboy. But there is more to it than that. The ally system is the unique thing that stands out for Owlboy. Otus, the protagonist can pick up his allies and switch between them at will to use their different abilities.
The abilities are used for combat and puzzle solving in a delightful way. I loved it.
The story has a great twist. And it has a relationship arc between the protagonist and his mentor that really struck a note with me.
I highly recommend it. It's landed among some of my favorite games of all time.

I felt like there was so much wasted potential here. I played ME1 and had a blast with my Shep despite the fact that the game was really showing its age in terms of graphics and whatnot. The gameplay however was still solid and the plot was epic. When I finished I had an immense satisfaction with a story well-told and the decisions I had made to get there.
And then I played
.
The graphics -- much better. Changes to the gameplay -- if anything they smoothed out the clunky stuff from ME1. The story -- well... ME1 was epic in scope. 80% of ME2 was about how you acquire each team member while navigating your mission accomplishments under the eye of your shady new employer. Meh.
And let's be clear, you don't need each one of those team members. They only serve as a pool of people to assign different roles to in the final ME2 fight, which is capped by a ridiculous and laughter-inspiring final boss.
And the whole death/resurection thing at the very beginning? Probably the most contrived way to hit the reset button on the character for the sole reason of returning him to level 1. Seriously. Destroy his ship, kill him off, bring him back, put him on a more-or-less identical ship owned by bad guy, staff it with the same crew. (I guess the Alliance couldn't find them decent reassignments?) Isn't that awesome!?! (Some restrictions apply. Memories do not include any previous skill training. See resurrection offer for details.)
Overall though the game isn't THAT bad, just a bit of a slog. I probably spent the standard amount of time on the game as any other player. But it spread out over many months because bite-sized two-part missions (acquire team member/do optional loyalty mission) doesn't lend itself to "I gotta see what happens next!"

I guess I was expecting more RPG and less Strategy because this game seemed to me to be too difficult to be fun.
It starts out easy, you have to clear single-screen 'dungeons' that are tough but defeatable.  By the time I had finished the tutorials (and even some of those I had to cheat and look for solutions on youtube) that was the end of any successful dungeon clearing that I was able to do.
Game in a nutshell is: The playfield is dark except where your character begins.  You always begin at level 1 but can choose your race/class and optionally pay some ingame gold for starting equipment (example: a shield that reduces all damage by 2).  You are placed on the screen and have to move around uncovering the darkened squares and ultimately defeat the level 10 boss of the dungeon.   Sounds fun right?
The only way to heal yourself and your mana (used for skills found as you explore the dungeon) are potions or uncovering darkened dungeon squares.  Both are in limited supply.
The 'casual' rating of this game is true in the time required to play sense, but if you don't exploit every single weakness of every enemy, and if you don't kill higher level enemies for the bonus exp (which is harder than it sounds, again, very limited healing) you have no chance of killing the level 10 boss monster.
Because every move counted so much, and because ultimately it takes a lot of moves to clear a dungeon, I found myself getting frustrated at how incapable I found myself of clearing a dungeon.  I'd get to level 8 or 9 and simply not be able to kill enough enemies at that point without dying, to get to level 10 or have enough of a stockpile of potions for the final boss of each dungeon.
So, instead of surely dying to the higher level boss, I would exit the dungeon, able to keep whatever gold I found in there and selling off the potions for 50-60 gold, take away 10-15 it costs for the items you bring with you.  At that point I was looking at minimum 500 gold upgrades to unlock anything more fun about the game, and I decided to uninstall and give up on the game because there was no other difficulty setting.
If that kinda game sounds fun more power to you but I was looking for a much more casual game, as in not an intense experience.  I wanted to shut my brain off for a bit but this took all of my concentration and was, for me, not a fun game to play in hindsight.

With gorgeous sprites, engaging music, and colorful, creative enemies and environments, Owlboy is a captivating experience soured only by a handful of control quirks; it explores platforming design space that most platformers avoid entirely with the usage of flight as the main form of travel, and challenges you to think on your feet at several intervals.
The story itself isn't of extraordinary depth, but is fitting for the world the game takes place in. The characters are relatable enough, and are a nice bit of seasoning to the taste of exploration and adventure; the gameplay is reason enough to feel compelled forward, so a story that won't have you falling asleep is just sugar on top.
All things considered, I could list a few nitpicks, but I highly recommend trying this game, ESPECIALLY if you are lucky enough to grab it on sale. Easily worth the $25 I spent in terms of entertainment value.

Owlboy is the worst kind of bad game- a game I had high hopes for; a game which had so much potential that it shines through even the crud that is its final form.
Let's go back a step though- what does Owlboy do right? From the very first trailer I and almost everyone else who saw it was enchanted by the visuals, art style, and music. That part still holds. Retro art is ironically old now, but it's done well here unlike in some indie games, and the music is strong enough that I bought a few tracks from the OST on the composer's website. The thing is, Owlboy never really goes beyond that.
The Combat is incredibly barebones. Owlboy lifts up to 3 partners, which basically means 3 different guns you can freely switch between unless the partner is missing for story reasons. These get 1 minor upgrade each over the course of the game, and are otherwise unchanged. Enemy selection is very limited, with 1-2 types in each area. Thankfully, the boss fights at the end of each area are a bit imaginative and mix things up, but that's just not enough variety and challenge. You do not gain any extra movement abilities or powers beyond the guns (which unlock slowly over the course of the story).
Let's talk about the Rings. I hope I wasn't the only one getting serious Superman 64 vibes from that part of the trailer. Owlboy can fly around opening chests to get coins, or fly through rings to get coins. This isn't currency, though. Think of them more like Feathers in Assassin's Creed. They're collectibles and they unlock things in a "shop". The quotation marks are because you can't choose what to unlock, they simply unlock automatically at certain coin thresholds, in a linear order. These are mostly cosmetic changes for Owlboy (content padding) with the 3 minor upgrades for your weapons mixed in. The whole thing reeks of unfinished features and playtime padding, which is kind of sad for a game that took 10 years to develop, regardless of the dev team size.
The worst part of the game is the Level Design. The devs simply went full retro with these. Owlboy levels rival the worst of nonsensical NES level designs with nonsensical layouts that aren't very interesting to play through. I cannot describe the disappointment I felt when I entered the second major dungeon area- apparently a bunch of samey looking steel girder grafted to literal clouds, which formed a maze on the way to a major bad guy airship. The idea that some reviewers have described Owlboy as a Metroivania is a joke. There's no exploration here; routes are 90% linear and the only thing that can be missed are small hidden alcoves with extra chests and floating rings.
In summary, just stay away. Watch the trailer again to experience a quick sense of wonder, without having it spoiled by actually playing the game.

I bought this game because I was attracted to the interesting gameplay screenshots (and the anime-esque graphics), and I must say, I am so glad I bought it. The difficulty of the game ranges from I'm-gonna-walk-through-the-crossfire-of-dozens-of-enemy-soldiers easy to full-hp-to-dead-while-transitioning-to-aim-mode hard.
(winning in less turns means a better rank, A is the highest)
Yes, you will get less EXP and DCT (money) for a lower rank, but that's what skirmish missions are for.
Once you beat the game, then you can go for perfect runs. Personally, I never had a problem with the wide range in difficulty (there exists a balancing mod though). The only real gameplay problem I had was the tank controls.

On the technical side, the game does not frame skip. So if your computer can't keep up with the FPS setting in the configuration, then the game will slow down in order to render each and every frame. For example, if settings are at 30 FPS and your computer can only do 15 FPS, the game will run half as fast (but sounds will continue at the full speed). This allowed me to play this on my crappy laptop without worrying about dying because I couldn't see the enemy in time. I find this as more of a blessing rather than a curse.
I fell in love with Valkyria Chronicles, and even shed man-tears at one point.
Additionally, if you loved the game, go watch the anime for it. It is definitely a ride of emotions, and stays mostly similar plot-wise to the original game, as well as elaborating on each of the pasts of the major characters. If you haven't played the game yet, though, I personally recommend at least beating the game before watching the anime.

Crysis: Warhead was released in 2008 and serves as the stand-alone expansion to the 2007 hit game Crysis. (Famous for being one of the most technologically advanced video game in terms of graphical and visual fidelity back in 2007, but at the same time, infamous for making most, if not all, gaming PCs at that time obsolete.)
The player takes the role of former British SAS Sergeant Michael "Psycho" Sykes. He currently serves as a member of Raptor Team (a Spec Ops unit equipped with Nano Suits) who were sent to Lingshan Islands to investigate the presence of North Korean forces. The story takes place after Raptor Team is split up and Psycho is sent on a one-man mission to sabotage various North Korean targets and to capture and recover a mysterious container that the North Koreans are very eager to get their hands on. Discover a new side of the island and join in Psycho's action packed adventure that made some players during the first game wonder what he was doing while Nomad was waging a war as one-man army.
+ Better optimized to run with more systems than Crysis 1

+ Large pseudo-open world map but...(see CON #3)

+ Chicken bullet secret DRM

- Full price tag does not justify the short campaign. (May be the multiplayer holds it up but then again, I don't play multiplayer)

GOOD EXPANSION but I can only RECOMMEND this game if it's bought while on SALE or with the Maximum Edition (Crysis 1 and Warhead) or Crysis Collection (Crysis 1, Warhead and Crysis 2).

DreadOut is a PC clone of the Fatal Frame series spiced up with an Indonesian background. Playing as the schoolgirl Linda, you have to fend off various ghosts by photographing them with your camera while also solving various riddles.
The game certainly has many flaws - it is not very long (I'd estimate a playtime of 6-10 hours), the graphics are mediocre at best, and the game's difficulty can vary wildly; doubly so as you are sometimes required to do things that seemingly defy all reason (such as not attacking a certain ghosts in a certain moment).
Nonetheless, DreadOut is quite capable of scaring the living daylight out of you. The unfamiliar bestiary of Indonesian ghosts alone is unsettling enough, but the camera mechanic takes the cake - for the better part of the game, you will be moving forward at a snail's pace with your cellphone cam at the ready, expecting ghosts to pop up from every corner. This is only made worse by the well-done lighting and sound design - unless the light of your cellphone or camera is up, you're practically blind, and the constant noise in the background doesn't do much to alleviate your paranoia. DreadOut may be one of these games that only are scary on the first walkthrough because you don't know where the fiends are waiting to ambush you, but let none say that they didn't get the ambush part right.

TL;DR: If you are looking for a standard energy driven collection / battle game on the computer, this is an excellent choice!
FULL REVIEW:
At a glance it is your standard micro-transaction driven collection and battle game. There are countless similar titles available in the Google Play and Apple app stores. That may seem like a reason to look elsewhere, but that would be acting too hasty. Just because it has a lot of common features doesn't mean it's bad!
Micro-transactions:
YES, THIS GAME IS FREE TO PLAY.
Through regular play you earn both "gems" (purchasable currency) and "gold" (earned currency). Gold is used to level up units. Gems are used to buy items / save time.
Energy:
You have a set amount of energy for questing and attacking. This resets to full when you level up, and refills on a timer. Its a good thing there is energy, otherwise I would never stop playing. (highly addictive)
Controls:
Everything is either click or drag. Unfortunately the in game help references touch commands.
Collecting:
You can spend in game currency to buy eggs to hatch. Each egg has a random unit with rarity based on the type of egg you opened. You also can capture units while you quest. You can only hold so many monsters before they start to run away. Fortunately you can use gem to buy more space, sell monsters, or grind them into XP as part of crafting. I would like to have more space, but I have enough that I don't feel hindered by it.
Crafting:
The crafting system is a little buggy with respect to clicking. This is likely a side effect of porting from a touch app. You need to "fuse" monsters to max level and then "evolve" pairs of them. Sometimes these evolutions generally completely new monsters.
Questing:
You have more control over your questing than many other games. You have a 5x3 grid of boxes to place your units which impacts who they can attack. They advance one column at a time so you can adjust your strategy and targets each click of the “go” button. Alternatively you can simply fast forward.
There are multiple types of quests you can do.
Story Quests (which are available in multiple difficulties)  advance the plot and can give healthy doses of XP.
Daily Quests which can be used for farming specific things like gold or evolution components. These daily quests do NOT give XP.
Guild Quests (raids). These help your guild as a whole earn prizes.
Leveling:
Each player gains experience as they play allowing them to level up. Each level grants a bonus ranging from increasing your squad size, to unlocking game features, to expanding your friends list, increasing your energy max, etc. One of the features you unlock is your castle. Your castle can be further leveled to make items work better, earn gold and resources, or achieve other bonuses. Each of your individual creatures level up as well, gaining a stat bonus.
Missions:
Every day you get missions you can complete for items / XP / etc. These bonuses are helpful, and there are enough of them you are unlikely to run out unless you spend money (in which case you really don't need their bonuses as much).
PVP Battles:
This is basically the same as questing, except you are fighting a squad created by another person. Depending on how many wins you achieve, you get rewards and harder opponents.
There are three types of PVP fights:
PVP Tab where you actively battle players for gold. You have a choice of 3 opponents.
Ambushes which randomly happen when you start a quest. You have a choice of 3 opponents.
Guild ranking where you fight for your guild’s rank. You can choose any undefeated member of the enemy guild.
Guilds:
The benefits of guilds are already discussed under Quests and PVP!
Summary:
I know this was fairly scattered but I hope it helps. It may seem like a standard micro-transaction collection game, but it does an excellent (and addictive) job of it. Give it a try, you literally have nothing to lose!

War for the Overworld: The Kickstarter that succeeded
This is a short honest review that addresses the good and the bad about this game in its current state. I waited until official release to play, so I have no beta-bias or bonding with the developers.
THE GOOD:
-The game feels and plays like Dungeon Keeper, for real.
Let's be honest, no game has come close to the DK experience in over 15 years... until now.
-The game truly feels like DK3, and not just DK-2015.
Not only are all the core elements of the DK experience in place, but new concepts have been added (contructs, sins, and the tavern for example).
-The visuals are nice, the music is great, and the voice acting is amazing.
Remember the primary voice actor in the DK games? Well, they found and hired that same guy to play his role again.
-The developers have announced that new content is under way, both in the form of paid and free additions.
The fact that two patches have been rolled out within 24 hours of the game's launch tells me that the developers both care about the game and are in dire need of some sleep.
THE BAD:
-The game needs polish in certain areas, especially in regard to the first person "possession" mode.

Despite having finally been released from early access after nearly two years, it’s hard to see where all the “early access” quality assurance efforts have gone. The game remains a buggy and poorly paced mess.
As far as I can tell the game is about strip mining your dungeon, as there is little obvious incentive to construct corridors, rooms and doors. Wall demolition is practically instantaneous, so there is no time cost to be saved. Strip mining also seems necessary to improve pathing (nothing to get stuck behind). In contrast to demolishing walls, however, trap setting is painfully slow, despite having numerous foundries, so there’s no encouragement to spend any time thinking about subtle traps and dungeon layout. Furthermore, each door and trap appears to have a maintenance cost that reduces your overall available mana pool, so there's a perverse disincentive to building any dungeon structures at all.
I’ve yet to crack mission four due to either game breaking bugs or poor pacing. My first game was abandoned because, despite having taken 90% of the map, my flow of minions completely evaporated and I was left watching the one or two I did have lasered by the AI. My second attempt at the mission lagged out, with around one screen refresh every 20 seconds or so – a problem in other maps, although one the game had previously recovered from after a minute or two.
Game boot and load times might easily be the longest of any of the 1300+ games I currently own. It’s a trivial point, but given the elongated load times I spend a lot of time looking at the loading screen, emphasising how bland and amateurish the loading screen looks.
The giant evil hand pointer is vastly too large, and it’s consequently difficult to target precisely, not least because you’re hovering above an isometric 3D plane and it’s often not clear whether you should be clicking on the base of the 3D terrain block or the top of it (which might instead result in selecting the adjacent block instead).
Pathfinding is poor, and minions repeatedly get “lost”, often stuck behind single objects completely out in the open. For example, I had to rescue a mob of about 8 units bouncing off a spawner, despite there being two clear paths on either side. Units often run out of food or don’t get paid, presumably because they can’t route to food or cash, despite half my dungeon being micropig spawners, taverns and treasure.
The minimap is largely worthless, with no clear signaling about where an attack might be coming from, and little attempt to distinguish rooms, enemies, minions, etc.
Ultimately, the game seems primarily a fairly traditional, uninspired RTS; spam barracks (monster spawners or whatever) and rush enemy - he or she who builds the most barracks (or barrack-like spawners) fastest wins. You are basically forced to have all your units running around in one mass mob due to the single rally flag, so any kind of subtle tactics are out.
There may be a good game under the surface here, but after five hours of perseverance I have yet to see it.
edit: I have now flirted with skirmish mode because I desperately want to give this game a chance, and I can see that there's a little bit of complexity here be unlocked, at least as far as research paths. The campaign is the tutorial however, and as the campaign is borked I'm finding skirmish mode to be a little too overhelming to take on for what looks like a fair bit of trial and error to get anything out of. And to be honest, without a campaign to get me hooked, sandbox mode was always going to be a bit too open-ended for my short attention span.

I tried to like this game.  I really did.  I booted this game up on three seperate occasions in an attempt to get through it, but why bother if it's not fun?  The whole ordeal was a slog through slow paced shooting sections.  There is obviously an attention to to detail here, but the core elements of the game are just fundamentally broken.  The story is delivered through minimal character voice overs during gameplay and short comic strip-like segments between loading screens.  The voice is acting is...decent, and the comic style of the cutscenes is interesting.  But beyond an interesting comic style and a neo-future cyberpunk setting, this game falls flat.
There is an attempt at interest, but the cyberpunk setting is washed out by a spew of browns and grays in a variety of dark and blue-tinted areas.  The setting never really feels different between two locations: street level and underground.  The enemies are all bulletsponges and their design are both from an aesthetic standpoint, and a gameplay standpoint, uninspired.  Every enemy is a one trick pony, repeatedly attempting to kill with it's one attack mechanism.  For most enemies, you simply dodge while holding down the trigger until either they blow up, or you run out of ammo.  The topic of dodging leads me to my next point that the level design is awful.  I would expect this kind of design from a student project, not a full release game.  The areas are excessively linear with obvious tells for every single ambush of enemy robots.  Environmental hazards play a large role in the combat, but everything is incredibly played out.  If there is going to be a wave of enemies to ambush you, there will also be a series of explosive barrels or electrical spouting conduits to fry them up.  Most enemy encounters are simply there to pad the experience.  Many times enemies seemed to just appear in an area because the game said so.  Most combat was either myself against a large charging enemy in an open area, or myself against many small enemies in a closed area.  When you are required to dodge many small enemies in a closed off corridor like area with minimal movement, it's not fun, it's not a challenge, it's frustrating.  In one instance, an ambush blew through a wall, but upon inspection of their entrance point, it was a closed concrete block in a hole.
You only get two weapons in the game.  Each one has it's own twist, and the weapon variety is accomplished through allowing upgrades for each of these two weapons.  Through the usage of upgrades, your bullet based weapon and your plasma based weapon can each turn into 4 other weapons, totalling 10 different guns.  However, these guns feels the same.  None of your attacks seem to have presence.  Accuracy is abyssmal, and when combined with the fact that all enemies have massive amounts of health (or you simply don't deal any damage) any combat interacting is simply tedious.
The movement is a joke too.  For a game that so heavily relies on dodging telegraphed enemy attacks, movement is stagnant and stale feeling.  Your characters jaunts around at a slightly sluggish speed.  You have the ability to sprint - if I could even call it that - but it really just makes your character move slightly faster for only a few seconds and makes your screen and HUD shake a lot.  The jump is floaty, as if your character lacks weight, and you also can't jump while sprinting.  There was a speed puzzle where a lift needed to be activated by a button across the room.  You then had to run down a staircase and across the room before it went back up.  With the sluggish controls, it was tedious and took multiple attempts before realizing that to get there faster, I should not sprint, so that I could jump into the lift as it was going up.
There are definitely some cool concepts here.  Floating UIs for upgrade panels and actual interaction screens for devices in the game are interesting and function very well.  The visuals themselves are very good.  Everything is for the most part impressively rendered and the visual effects are nice to look at.  But the art style, the sluggish controls, unvaried weapons, and completely uninteresting and uninspired combat really sink this game.  I tried to like it, but I can't and shouldn't have to force myself to clear a game out of my backlog.

I remember playing and enjoying the earlier version of this game while at work a couple of years ago (2011), and  it's nice to see that the paid version has built out the features nicely without losing sight of the original design. Don't be fooled by the cutesy artwork either - under the brightly colored hood lies an engine made of pure unadulterated mathematics. Do you fight the stronger enemy while you are lower level, earning extra xp you may need later? Or would that fight require you to eat into your valuable potion supply? The answer is right in front of your eyes, 95% of the time, it's up to you to figure out the optimal path if you can. Or, have a calculator handy.
I'm not joking about the math either. This game is like a combination of Soduko, Minesweeper and the popular roguelike Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (I mean this in the best possible way). That's isn't to say that the rpg theme is painted on. On the contrary there is a satisfying asymettry to both the challenges you face in terms of levels and bosses, and also to the way the various classes and loadouts need to be deployed in order to surmount those challenges. The number of abilities and potential interactions, combined with a high degree of randomization, means that things stay interesting and fresh.
Expect a game to last anywhere from 5 or 10 minutes from the early levels/challenges and upwards to an hour when attempting to successfully navigate some of the later dungeons, where a single miscalculation or wrong move can snatch sudden defeat from the jaws of victory. Murdered: Soul Suspect is a game developed by Airtight Games and published by Square Enix
You play Ronana, a street thug turned detective who gets brutally murdered and enters the spirit realm as a ghost, he finds out that his soul can not move on until he resolves whatever is holding him back. SHORT VERSION: Do you like highly-difficult thought-based games? If so, get this game.
LONG VERSION: Despite the developer's claim that "reviewers have trouble with genres", the core genre is simple: At heart, Desktop Dungeons is a strategy game. Success requires careful management of limitted resources. There are plenty of RPG elements in the game, but RPGs are typically centered more on their story, which, lets face it, isn't exactly this game's strong point.
Each dungeon has a simple goal: Defeat the boss(es). This is, of course, easier said than done.
As mentioned, fulfilling that goal will require very careful management of your resources. Obvious resources are health and mana, but there's also item slots (you can only carry so much stuff), blankspace (exploring unexplored parts of the dungeon regenerates health and mana, but re-exploring already explored parts does not), conversion points (turn items into something else), levels and experience (levelling up fully restores health and mana, which is highly abusable), gold (for buying stuff!), and piety (too complex to explain here). In addition, your class (as well as many other factors) helps define just how efficiently you can use these resources. For example, wizards use less mana for the same bang, monks regen double health from blankspace, and fighters gain experience much faster. Mastery of the game will come from a thorough knowledge of its mechanics, intelligent use of resources, and at times, a bit of luck.
It's worth mentioning that this game is HARD. The learning curve is very steep. While you are guided through the basics via tutorial, the rest of the mechanics will need to be figured out on your own. Do not expect to win every time. (However, also notably, this difficulty rarely stems from randomness issues; a highly skilled player should lose in only the worst random situations)
This game is also humorous. In fact, it's rarely NOT humorous.

Gameplay- SUPREME COMMANDER is an amazing game which startles with its ease of execution of global conflict and easy to get into user interface while still offering a challenging thought provoking ai to go up against. At first i thought i was going to end up with a very chugging along slow grand scale war situation like the old gargantuan wargame from the early 1990s UMS (UNIVERSAL MILITARY SIMULATOR). Instead i found something that played with the massive variety of units of TOTAL ANNIHILATION and depth of such old time classics like BATTLE ISLE and THE PERFECT GENERAL done in real time with stunning movie like battle visuals. It was a eerie scary sight to see a huge enemy frigate when destroyed actually roll over on its side and sink like something out of a old time war reel. Plenty of time will be spent on building bases and units but you are free to acttack or do recon missions etc at any time. Building bases is alot of fun with plenty of upgrades which one has to invest heavy resources of mass and or energy to make possible.
Graphics- Very immersive with plenty of visual detail when it comes to things like air units going into and dive and crashing with 3d depth not to mention the consequences as the explosion from the crash can damage any nearby structures and or units. Everything is done in layers of depth and mass so all that wreckage on the field will actually get in your way the cool thing is you can get it out of your way by salvaging as resources or in the case of one of your own buildings being wrecked you can rebuild the same building over the wrecked one taking half the time it normally would to build it. There are plenty of video popups of the other commanders friendly and enemy reminding you your not alone on the battlefield and you have objectives to complete. The enemy on the other hand is sending plenty of threats and taunts your way which enrich the war mood of battles.
Sound- Excellent use of sfx making everything seem like you on another world in some futuristic time with sci-fi weapons designed to deliever devastation to your enemies and your own units if your too close when they explode in a raging fire storm of nuclear death.
Sum Total- A must buy sci-fi wargame which really delievers. If you have not played it yet now is the time with the beefy computer systems of today and the past year that can easily handle its beefy overhead.
Thank you Chris Taylor and company for the fantastic satisfying work :D

Crysis Warhead's level design is noticeably different than that of Crysis 1. It still has both open and tight levels (which are alternated between for better pacing), but they are presented differently this time around. The open levels don't quite offer the same freedom of approach and alternate routes as the first game, presenting instead a wide but more straightforward route to your objective. The tighter sections are much better designed and are pretty fun to fight in. Warhead is also more action-oriented, often rushing you into a battle rather than letting you approach a potential encounter from a distance. Fortunately, the game still offers plenty of freedom and options for the player to handle confrontations. Improvements over the first game include the alien enemies, boss battles and vehicle controls. Overall, a short but highly enjoyable campaign.

Despite having finally been released from early access after nearly two years, it’s hard to see where all the “early access” quality assurance efforts have gone. The game remains a buggy and poorly paced mess.
As far as I can tell the game is about strip mining your dungeon, as there is little obvious incentive to construct corridors, rooms and doors. Wall demolition is practically instantaneous, so there is no time cost to be saved. Strip mining also seems necessary to improve pathing (nothing to get stuck behind). In contrast to demolishing walls, however, trap setting is painfully slow, despite having numerous foundries, so there’s no encouragement to spend any time thinking about subtle traps and dungeon layout. Furthermore, each door and trap appears to have a maintenance cost that reduces your overall available mana pool, so there's a perverse disincentive to building any dungeon structures at all.
I’ve yet to crack mission four due to either game breaking bugs or poor pacing. My first game was abandoned because, despite having taken 90% of the map, my flow of minions completely evaporated and I was left watching the one or two I did have lasered by the AI. My second attempt at the mission lagged out, with around one screen refresh every 20 seconds or so – a problem in other maps, although one the game had previously recovered from after a minute or two.
Game boot and load times might easily be the longest of any of the 1300+ games I currently own. It’s a trivial point, but given the elongated load times I spend a lot of time looking at the loading screen, emphasising how bland and amateurish the loading screen looks.
The giant evil hand pointer is vastly too large, and it’s consequently difficult to target precisely, not least because you’re hovering above an isometric 3D plane and it’s often not clear whether you should be clicking on the base of the 3D terrain block or the top of it (which might instead result in selecting the adjacent block instead).
Pathfinding is poor, and minions repeatedly get “lost”, often stuck behind single objects completely out in the open. For example, I had to rescue a mob of about 8 units bouncing off a spawner, despite there being two clear paths on either side. Units often run out of food or don’t get paid, presumably because they can’t route to food or cash, despite half my dungeon being micropig spawners, taverns and treasure.
The minimap is largely worthless, with no clear signaling about where an attack might be coming from, and little attempt to distinguish rooms, enemies, minions, etc.
Ultimately, the game seems primarily a fairly traditional, uninspired RTS; spam barracks (monster spawners or whatever) and rush enemy - he or she who builds the most barracks (or barrack-like spawners) fastest wins. You are basically forced to have all your units running around in one mass mob due to the single rally flag, so any kind of subtle tactics are out.
There may be a good game under the surface here, but after five hours of perseverance I have yet to see it.
edit: I have now flirted with skirmish mode because I desperately want to give this game a chance, and I can see that there's a little bit of complexity here be unlocked, at least as far as research paths. The campaign is the tutorial however, and as the campaign is borked I'm finding skirmish mode to be a little too overhelming to take on for what looks like a fair bit of trial and error to get anything out of. And to be honest, without a campaign to get me hooked, sandbox mode was always going to be a bit too open-ended for my short attention span.

DreadOut is an indonesian horror game and features alot of indonesian mythology/horror lore when it comes to the enemies and their backgrounds.
However, this game from a critical standpoint is not on par with current games. Not even with the Fatal Frame Series (which somewhat inspired this game).
The graphics are very outdated for a game which wasn't released too long ago.
The sound design is very outdated aswell, but still at least features some interesting sounds. Especially some monsters got some really FAK'D up sounds they make.
The gameplay is probably what I hated the most. Not because it is similar to the Fatal Frame series (which I actually REALLY love) but because it is waaay to slow compared to the size of the game world.
The beginning is the worst, because you literally have to jog in snail-speed for HOURS.
The puzzles however are really not good at all.
They make 0 sense, there are no god damn hints on what you have to do, and they are pretty random, even for a horror game. I really didn't like the puzzles in this game at ALL!
5/10 as a horror game. It may feature an interesting lore, but compared to other horror games, especially horror games which got released in the same year as DreadOut, it just isn't on PAR at all.
6/10 as a game in general. The idea is good, and some of the games features work nicely. Still there are alot of things I didn't like, as mentioned above. I still can recommend this game however, because unless it's underneath 5 points, it's worth to give it a try and see for yourself if you like it or not. It is indeed special, and some may like it, while others like me won't like it too much.

A game that I assure you will surpass your expectations and take you on a wild ride of emotions. Including frustration at times. I downloaded this as a means of passing half an hour before bed. I ended up playing the game non stop for 4 hours and refused to leave my chair until I 100% it.
Gameplay:
The gameplay knows what it is, simplistic, and works well within those confineds. Giving you challenges to work against that, like the gameplay mechanics, are simple, yet offer enough of a challenge to warrant multiple retries without rage mode getting to hard to destroy your keyboard. But, I could certainly see someone getting a little too agro. So if you know you're easily wound up you might wanna take a lot of breaks playing this game.
Music:
There aren't a lot of sound tracks or SFX in the game but the ones that are there are decent enough to not drive one insane. However, they're nothing to write home about.
Art:
The pixel art itself is astonishing but the character sprites when entering more, VN style, conversation (which is every conversation) is also lack lustier. Lack lustier but not so awful you can't stand to look at it.
Story:
Without spoiling the story isn't anything super original but it's execution is what makes it. It feels like there is no story to speak of at first. But, stick with it.
Overall. This game is a great way to spend (not waste) around 2 hours (if you're good) or 4 hours (if you're me level bad). I really enjoyed my time with this game and if you're a weeb of culture you will too (you don't have to be a weeb to play this game, it's by no means a weeb game). It reminds me of Corpse Party in many ways. Try to go into this game blind. You'll thank yourself for it.

SHORT VERSION: Do you like highly-difficult thought-based games? If so, get this game.
LONG VERSION: Despite the developer's claim that "reviewers have trouble with genres", the core genre is simple: At heart, Desktop Dungeons is a strategy game. Success requires careful management of limitted resources. There are plenty of RPG elements in the game, but RPGs are typically centered more on their story, which, lets face it, isn't exactly this game's strong point.
Each dungeon has a simple goal: Defeat the boss(es). This is, of course, easier said than done.
As mentioned, fulfilling that goal will require very careful management of your resources. Obvious resources are health and mana, but there's also item slots (you can only carry so much stuff), blankspace (exploring unexplored parts of the dungeon regenerates health and mana, but re-exploring already explored parts does not), conversion points (turn items into something else), levels and experience (levelling up fully restores health and mana, which is highly abusable), gold (for buying stuff!), and piety (too complex to explain here). In addition, your class (as well as many other factors) helps define just how efficiently you can use these resources. For example, wizards use less mana for the same bang, monks regen double health from blankspace, and fighters gain experience much faster. Mastery of the game will come from a thorough knowledge of its mechanics, intelligent use of resources, and at times, a bit of luck.
It's worth mentioning that this game is HARD. The learning curve is very steep. While you are guided through the basics via tutorial, the rest of the mechanics will need to be figured out on your own. Do not expect to win every time. (However, also notably, this difficulty rarely stems from randomness issues; a highly skilled player should lose in only the worst random situations)
This game is also humorous. In fact, it's rarely NOT humorous.
A great game to get if you like playing with friends and family, and a addicting game!

TL;DR: plays a bit like an interactive movie at times, but has enough involvement to keep you invested. Good graphics overall and interesting mechanics. A main character you can get behind, though a rather annoying sidekick, and a story with just enough twists and turns to keep you hooked. It's a bit too short to justify its full $30 price, so definitely wait for it to go on sale. It probably won't appeal to players who dislike slower paced, exploratory mystery-solving games. Overall, I guess I would give it 6.5/10.
Now for the full review. At first I found this game to be phenomenal, one of the most intriguing and fun games I've ever played, and that's something I don't by any means say lightly. The mechanics of being able to walk through (most) walls and objects, read peoples' minds, and poltergeist electrical items in order to get the attention of the living were well-executed and quite entertaining. It was so cool having to find ways to use my powers to influence the environment and people around me. I especially loved communicating with other ghosts and using my detective skills and ghostly abilities to help them resolve their problems and shift off to the next plane of existence.
If only the game had stayed as open-ended.
Yeahhh, unfortunately after you get out of the apartment building, which is essentially the first level, the world slowly begins to "shrink" from there on out, giving much less room to explore and eventually no ghosts to interact with outside of a few lines of dialogue, and towards the end there isn't even that! It's especially frustrating when the game puts you in a new environment where there should be plenty of interesting fellow ghosts to interact with and mini-mysteries to solve, yet somehow there aren't. (For example, you go through both a cemetery AND an insane asylum, two extremely underused environments in videogaming as a whole, and there's virtually nothing to do in either outside of tasks pertaining to the main storyline. It would have been amazing to visit with a small community of ghosts or solve a dead asylum patient's troubles, but we get none of that. You can't even talk to ghosts you see in the asylum. Wasted opportunities, guys!) It's as if the developers became progressively lazier as work went on.
Another complaint that I have is that you get a companion about halfway through the game. I have to be honest: I found her to be annoying and unlikable, and in the end I was pretty apathetic towards her, in spite of the fact that the game makes it clear you're meant to care about her. Granted she's not constantly whining like Ashley from Resident Evil 4, so I don't exactly have a burning hatred towards her, but she's stubborn for the sake of being stubborn, (and literally no other reason, as far as I could tell) and is one of those "edgy" characters that acts like a rebellious jerk pretty much 24/7 because she thinks it makes her cool, tough, and strong. She'll constantly act like she doesn't need your help until, suddenly, OH NOES SHE NEEDS YOUR HELP! Well, what are you waiting for?! Go rescue her in spite of the fact that up until this very moment, when her intimidating "I'm not like other girls" attitude predictably 100% failed to have any effect on an actual threat, she made it perfectly clear that she's a strong independent teenage girl who don't need no help! If she had only been that way at the beginning but slowly softened to the protagonist, cooperating more and allowing herself to become more vulernable and human, thus having strength without the unnecessary roughness, she would have immediately redeemed herself and became an interesting character that actually had development. But no, she basically never changes or evolves, she just stays a salty, entitled edgelord. She's a stone's throw away from being the type of character an anti-feminist would write if they wanted to mock a girl power character, (not quite Jailbreak from Emoji Movie levels of annoyance, but in that same ballpark nonetheless) and as someone who strongly desires fair treatment and equality for both sexes, it really rubbed me the wrong way. I'm sure it wasn't intentional and just a result of poor writing, after all sexism isn't something addressed at any point in the game whatsoever, but still: fairly irritating. That's my personal opinion, however. Maybe you'll see things to like about her that I didn't. Now that this tangent is over, back to writing an actual review.
Regardless of what you make of Joy as a character, there's no denying that in some aspects she really simplifies the gameplay. This is actually not a good thing, because now, instead of having to figure out how to use your ghostly powers to get someone to do something for you, like pick up a painting, you just ask her to do it and she'll do it. Not exactly the most challenging or interesting path to go, but it's the one you're stuck with whether you like it or not because, again, there's a steep, ongoing decline in content the more progress you make so you only have one choice now.
Honestly, I just wish the sandbox/open world element in this game had been expanded. There's so little of it and again, it's mostly all at the beginning. This letdown is compounded by the natural expectation that it will be added upon and built up as the game continues, only to get further and realize that's not happening. I almost wish it had taken more of a Lucius II approach. Yes, Lucius II had a really dumb storyline, bad acting, butt-ugly graphics, and more bugs than a redneck trucker's windshield, but give it this: it was very lenient in how everything was set up, allowing you multiple ways to bring about a single outcome. I feel like this game could have used that same idea: more variety in how you execute certain tasks. (As well as more tasks and side mysteries in general.)
Now truth be told, I did like this game's story. It has a lot of interesting elements, good buildup with a relatively surprising and interesting payoff, and even has a couple big plot twists, none of which I saw coming. (Then again, I'm a gullible fool who NEVER sees a twist coming, so take that last part with a grain of salt.)
I can't pretend I didn't, for the most part, have fun in spite of this game's flaws. I still liked a lot of its gameplay mechanics, (the unique ghost element really is this game's ultimate saving grace; I'd play this game even without its main story if it just focused heavily on toying with the mix of supernatural interactions and short mysteries like it did in the beginning) the main character was relatable but was also just well defined enough to be interesting, and the "gothic film noir" atmosphere (think Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines meets L. A. Noire) casts an excellent mood over the whole experience.
I also have to give it mad props for looking as good as it does while still running fairly well on lower-end computers. Sadly there aren't many games out there that can brag about having the same level of accessibility while looking good.
I do wish we were given the option to have multiple save files, since not being able to load back when a mistake is made is fairly frustrating. Granted one could still reload from the last checkpoint, but there isn't even a menu screen to show you how far back that would be. It's actually surprising how widely spaced out the checkpoints can be sometimes. It does make fighting off the demons feel more urgent, but also makes dying doubly frustrating.
I noticed in some of the reviews that I looked over (while considering purchasing this title) that a common complaint was that there was a bug in the menu that didn't allow you to close the game, instead forcing a manual shutdown via task manager. I personally never encountered this bug, so take that as you will.
Overall: it's not perfect by any means, and it's definitely a bit overpriced, but still a fun, unique experience well worth looking at the next time a sale rolls around.

I have played this game for many hours before being on Steam.
If you've ever played a roguelike Role Playing Game(RPG) you'll know they are amazing time sinks.  Indeed, most RPGs are time sinks.  Desktop Dungeons takes the basics of RPGs and condenses them into one screen full of adventure.  These play out as puzzles as much as an RPG.  You can be done and dusted with a dungeon in only a few minutes, yet they are full of the usual RPG elements.  Potions, gold, shops, stat bonuses, gods, monsters and level ups.  Your goal in each fixed dungeon is to kill one or two level 10 boss monsters.
Difficulty in Desktop Dungeons is one of the highlights.  Each map and element provides a serious challenge to get to the end result of killing the level 10 boss monster.  It is not at all uncommon to fail.  You have to balance exploration so much so that it can feel like minesweeper.  You have tough choices to make and the key to this being such a great game is that your choices actually matter.  That makes the dungeons memorable and fun.
Another nice thing about Desktop Dungeons is the way it ties the dungeons together.  As you complete the basic dungeons you unlock lots more content.  Humour in game is also quite well done without being overbearing.

Desktop Dungeons is a great game that fittingly belongs on the desktop although at first glance may look like it is better suited to playing it on a portable device. Dungeons generally take 10-20 minutes to complete (or fail) but the base mechanics are addicting enough that I did not find myself saying 'just one more', sessions ended only while glancing at the clock and being surprised enough to force myself to stop.
This is a surprisingly deep experience for a somewhat simplified dungeon crawler. Not only are the layouts different each time you start a dungeon (even the same one multiple times) but there is quite a bit outside of these in building up your kingdom and unlocking classes and races. The dungeon mechanics themselves are for the most part pretty standard - move, attack, kill, level up, repeat. The twist here is that as you explore, newly discovered tiles refill your (and any damaged enemy) health and mana bars. The impact of this was lost on me at the lower levels, but as you progress you will find it is impossible to explore the map and plan all your moves ahead of time. There are some abilities that help mitigate this but for the most part, each step is a resource not to be wasted and a wrong turn can mean the difference between leveling up or running out of options seven levels later while fighting the boss.
Here lies the first of my two main issues with the game. I have had dungeons where the first half of my exploration resulted in dead ends or creatures far above my level 1 hero you always start as. This can be frustrating as it means you lose out on health/mana regen later on when those tiles could have been useful. I readily acknowledge that this is very much part of the game and there is strategy here above what my compulsion for exploration allows, but it can be hard not to feel that such runs are pointless to pursue.
My other issue with Desktop Dungeons has nothing to do with gameplay - the writing takes me completely out of the experience. The game world seems steeped in lore and interesting hero / creature design, yet all the dialogue is extremely casual and self-referential well beyond the tongue-in-cheek point. It's too bad, and is one of those situations where a flaw is almost made worse by the amount of potential it has. I would have preferred the tone to get more serious as I realized how deep the experience could be, and not the other way around. That may be personal opinion, but I really feel as if it is an area of missed opportunity in an otherwise enjoyable and lasting experience.
Overall, I would highly recommend Desktop Dungeons to anyone looking for a game that satisfies in a way games like Binding of Isaac or even Spelunky does, where it doesn't matter if you play 5 or 50 games a session and can come back the next day and still find fresh gameplay waiting. The excellency of the procedural generation (which is greatly designed, no randomness here is used as a crutch) is exciting in its balance of interesting and clever levels, and even though the difficulty gets quite high early on you will most likely be able to find fun with it no matter your skill level.
---Desktop Dungeons---
+ Addicting base mechanics
+ Deep experience tied to player skill progression
- Some runs can be a letdown at the very start
- Writing direction is not for me at all
It is my opinion that you should buy Desktop Dungeons anytime it is $12.50 or less!

Rogue-Likes and Rouge-Like-Likes alike all tend to feel alike.
Generally in these genres, you hack and slash your way to death with nothing left to really prove except for the knowledge that comes with drinking a suspicious looking potion and losing all your health to a single swig. You take these tips with a grain of salt as the variability to your death changes with each play-through...Although I use the term "play-through" lightly since you never actually get through some of the more hardcore rogue-likes without hours and hours of dedication to understanding the game's many quirks and traps.
Desktop Dungeons feels like a solid blend of Rogue-Like and Puzzle with a welcome sense of progression as you earn gold and unlock new classes and races along the way. All of that mixed with the ability to spend 10-20 minutes on a single session is also entirely welcome.
The puzzle-like aspect of the game is a great mix to the genre. Instead of spending your time focusing on surviving until your next death, you know exactly what you need to do: kill all of the enemies. The helpful levels that appear next to the enemy names allow you to expect what's coming whether its a victory or a disappointing failure. Rogue-Likes are always known for their randomized nature with their random levels and random encounters; Desktop Dungeons has these to an extent but when you're level 5 and you're about to swing your sword at a level 9, you know you're not making a sound decision. The screen also turns red when your next move is fatal, which helps quite a bit as well.
The progression in the game also allows for a sense of accomplishment. No longer do you feel that sense of loss when you lose everything you worked so hard to get. Each "dungeon" is its own instance and if you know you're about to fail you can easily just retire and keep all your money (the items you acquire get sold for more money) which can then be spent on upgrading classes, races and even buying gear to aid you on the next quest you go on.
Along with multiple locations, there's plenty of different quests and challenges you can attack. Each class has its own set of challenges that give you bonus money and there are also general challenges that give you more gold just by doing things like spending a certain amount of gold or piety during a quest.
This game is certainly recommended if you enjoy the difficulty in Rogue-Likes but like to spend a casual amount of time slowly increasing your stats, or in this case, your kingdom.

archipelago is a classic first-person-shooter. It combines teamwork, intelligence and individual skill to be able to create harmony between victory and loss. The terrorists either plant a bomb or hold hostages, as they are supposed to be the bad guys, and every player in this game gets to be the bad guys as much as they get to be the good guys. The counter-terrorists either defuse the bomb or rescue the hostages, as they are the good guys. Now, let me repeat again what I told you, the reader(s), before. archipelago combines teamwork, intelligence and individual skill to be able to create harmony between victory and loss. Now think about those three for a moment! If any of those three factors are not on par with the others, it will affect the game and the results of the harmony. In other words, if any of those three factors are not on par with the other two, the player's skillgroup and ranking will drop. If one has all three, they will stand on the top. However, if one player alone has to compensate for the whole team's lack of individual skill and intelligence, the teamwork cannot function. I know, I know, this is just me complaining about bad luck and lack of skill, but bear with me! It is difficult to carry games, as many people can imagine, but why would one need to carry if everyone played to win, right? If one goes to a match with a friend and just plays to have fun, others will just suffer. That is a fact, and not a statement. I play to win, but I seem to most usually encounter people who are satisfied with their abilities. I, however, am not satisfied with their abilities, as they will lose unless carried against a worse team.
I am tired of only being on the top of my team. If you are still reading this, thank you. Like this review if you liked it(obviously), and have a nice day, even if you'd be surrounded by defeat and depression. Keep going! Keep moving on, and emerge victorious in life, in videogames, or in whatever you want to be! See ya on the top!

Japanese animation is notorious for using western/european symbolism and beliefs, such as the cross, religion, and other imagery, words, names, etc, and perverting it in some fashion for the sake of story telling. They might claim they are completely removing any meaning to these objects, but to us, it may be offensive and should be avoided if it's use is scandalous or given to scandal.
The good news (which is really bad news) is that the japanese tend to make a fetish out of pretty much anything, so you will know visually when something is immoral or presented to you for that purpose because the object may not be bad, but it's clear they're abusing it.
We can more or less predict when we will run into sinful material in our anime watching too, since we are more than likely searching for shows by using tags or specific search options, so we are making an active, intentional choice to search for specific things that excite us, and if those specific things always turn out to be sexual or violent, for example, then maybe that says something about the viewer, a sort of self revelation. A change in genre might be in order.
We're Christians, so we're called to a higher standard in this area, so I believe that while anime is not a sin in itself, and a show is not necessarily immoral just because it has some fanservice, we have the choice to avoid sinful material when it is present; if we do not, then its a matter of whether the content was grave matter or not; if it was, you would need to confess it, and even if it wasn't, you might want to confess it anyways if you felt bad about it.
Remember, you can always skip that episode, skip that scene, or fast forward, etc, if you know it disturbs the peace of your soul and conscience. It doesn't necessarily mean you'd have to stop watching the show alltogether. However, if occasions of sin for you keep coming up with the show, it might be an indication that you need to choose a different show. I'll admit, it's not always easy giving up on an otherwise good show for spiritual, moral, and religious reasons, but you feel good about doing the right thing afterwards.
Anime, like many other forms of entertainment, can desensitize you to the immorality and sinful content within it. Just because something doesn't make you feel "turned on" in the case of ecchi or harem type shows, for example, doesn't mean it's necessarily good for you to watch it anyways, or overly bloody, gory, type shows just because it doesn't make you crave violence. While there may not be a physical stirring in the body that causes sin, consider that the mind is at work subconsciously and that spiritually we may become weaker by choosing to predispose ourselves to such content.
If you're watching a show for the first time, I would say analyze the general themes and if you see a repeating pattern of immorality, then you're probably watching something you shouldn't.
Incidentally, shows like Bleach, Naruto, etc, are so generalized in the genres they cater to that they don't overextend in any one thing, and this generally makes them safe to watch, because they're not devoting large sums of time to something perverted, overly violent, etc. Alot of these sleeper hits that hit the summer, fall, and winter seasons are the ones to look out for, as they are usually ripe with immorality of some kind.
In the end, it's a judgment call that requires prudence and discernment if you plan to watch the show. After a few episodes you should pretty much be able to tell what they're trying to sell you. You've got to just take it from there. I hope this helps. God bless.

One way in which the scottish Government comes into conflict with the UK Government is on Defence Policy. Westminster has ultimate control over the UK’s Defence Policy and budget.  This means that they are able to decide on what and how much the UK spends on its defence budget. For example Westminister chose to renew the controversial trident nuclear sub program that costs billions of taxpayer money each year to fund. There has been conflict over this issue as the SNP led scottish government strongly opposes the funding of trident and what it fundamentally stands for. This conflict is only one example of conflict that has occurred between UK and Scottish government. In the 2010 defence spending review several budget cuts were pushed through parliament. These cuts affected many military bases in scotland, consequently jobs were lost. The Scottish government was heavily against these cuts despite their opposition to huge expenditure on defence as the impact on the local economies surrounding the bases was “a huge blow”(Deputy First Minister John Swinney)  for scotland. Consequently the Scottish government has come into conflict with Westminster regarding the UK's defence policy.
Another way in which the Scottish Government has come into conflict with the UK Gov. has been in regards to the West Lothian Question. In the current state Scottish MPs are able to vote on bills and legislation that only affects England and Wales despite it being a devolved power. This mean that scottish MPs can sway which way a vote goes depending on whether the Scottish MPs agree with it or not. For Example, In England and Wales students studying at university pay fees for their studies, Westminster proposed the Top-up Tuition fees bill that affected the cost of studying. This policy was passed in Westminster. However, It it was only passed by 44 votes. If the Scottish MPs voted against it the bill wouldn’t have gone through as there are 59 Scottish MPs. The Scottish vote has also deterred bills being put forward. For example, there was discussion about proposing a bill that would re-legalise Fox Hunting. The SNP said that they would vote against the re-legalisation, this would mean that the bill would not go through. The Conservative Government therefore decided not to go through with the vote as it would be futile.This shows the conflict between Holyrood and Westminster when carrying out the functions of the Scottish Government.
The UK's Foreign Policy has also sparked conflict between Westminster and Holyrood. Westminster has control over foreign policy allowing it to direct the relations of the UK with any foreign nation it so pleases. For example, in september 2014 the US invited the UK and many other countries to join a coalition to combat ISIL in Iraq and Syria. The UK accepted the invitation. The SNP led scottish government heavily criticised Westminsters decision to take action which created conflict between Governments.  Another example of conflict between the two was during and after the BREXIT decision to leave the European Union. After the Pro leave vote was concluded in total, the scottish government highlighted upon the figures that showed that in scotland the majority vote was in favour of staying within the EU as opposed to leaving. This sparked much discussion on whether there should be a second scottish independence referendum. The conflicting views on brexit has created much animosity between vote for and against even at high levels of government, showing that whilst carrying out its functions it has come into conflict with UK Government.
In Conclusion, when carrying out its functions, the Scottish Government has come into conflict with The UK Government on several occasions. These conflicts have generally been over powers that haven’t been devolved to Holyrood, despite this, divide between Scotland and the rest of the UK has occurred even though it isn't one of the Scottish Government's responsibilities.

TL;DR - This game is full of pay walls and pay2win mobile mechanics. Many reviews are straight out lying about those not existing, but it is how it is. You can test it if you want, but don't pay any cash, you wont get anything out of it unless you spend thousands of $ or €.
In general the game is quite fun and addictive. You build a troop out of different colorful units and fight in PvE, where you can catch whatever you fight. Sounds fun, right? It kinda was, before they implemented elites, long time ago, when the game was still on kongregate i think.
Units have ranks. Up to 17. Without cash you can summon only rank 1 or 2. Rarely you get the chance to summon up to 5-7, but usually about once a month and only 5 of those, not guaranteed to be high rank or elite.
In order to evolve a unit you basically have to first kill it enough time for it to drop (~5% for the worst good units) then to catch it after the battle (~10%) and then you have to level them out and fuse together into one unit of a higher rank. You need up to 3 units for one evolution (with additional ones called materials, but those are easier to get).
Ofc each battle eats away at your energy. Ofcourse you have an additional energy bar for PvP. Ofcourse you can summon units with cash currency that will be better and stronger than the ones you can summon for free. Ofcourse PvE battles are tougher than the creatures you actually get from them, meaning you will have to grind and grind and grind and grind and grind...or, you know, pay.
Everyone in the higher PvP rankings is a whale, same goes for high-rank guilds. There is just no way to beat someone who has better units, because those have quite simply higher stats and will crush your team.
There is the feeling of being able to progress, but to be honest it is fake - you are basically grinding all the time just get one unit a little bit stronger, while cashers simply buy a stronger one.
It's like DnD, Assassins Creed, and Oregon Trail all tied together in a well wrapped package. 10/10

Adventurers from all over the world visit the city of Pensee to explore the mysterious dungeons that have recently been discovered nearby. Rumor has it that dangerous characters are behind the increasing monsters. Some even say that they plan to bring about the end of the world.
That means only one thing to the item shop Recettear - more customers! Play from a different point of view as you buy new stock from the Market or hire Adventurers to find treasure from dungeons. Increase the variety of your inventory, sell high value goods and haggle your way out of poverty. Can you pay off your missing father's debts and keep a roof over your head?
Recettear is a light-hearted indie game that pokes fun at the typical JRPG game setting. But make no mistake! Behind the cute anime characters and relaxing music lies a fairly complex management sim. And while mostly optional, its roguelite dungeons get steadily more challenging. Overall, this game is great for those looking for a fresh and fun management sim / roguelite.
