Hard Reset is one of those old-fashioned shooter games... first person, no cover, no blind shoot, it's circle strafe and lots and lots of weapons. The plot is simple: You're Fletcher, working for "The Corporation" holding the perimeter of Bezoar city against incursion of killer robots from the outside. When a breach in Sector 6 happened, you're the closest unit to respond, and you must defeat the robot minions, from small swarmers (size of dogs) to gorillas (they charge you, hard), to shooters and more. There are 4-12 secrets per level for you to discover. Some are quite visible, but you have no idea how to get to (some require strategic demolition of certain walls, just like Doom).
The plot has a couple twists and the voice acting... well, falls to the cliche at times. But the cutscnes are rendered in comic book style (albeit with sprite animations) to make for a unique look.
Another uniqueness to the game is plethora of environment kill objects, i.e. the proverbial 'exploding barrel', except in this game, they are all over the place. Explosive gas containers, barrels, high voltage fans, trash collectors, heaters on walls, they all explode or zap everything around them for a few seconds when hit. And you get extra points for using enviro-kills rather than your own ordnances.
Your guy gets three area of upgrades... body, projectile gun, and energy gun. Each area has 5 items that can be purchased / upgraded, and each item can have up to 2 additional upgrades. You come with plasma (for energy) and rifle (for projectile), as well as simple shields (i.e. you have 1 of each). As you advance, and collect N.A.N.O. the currency, whcih are "yellow/gold" in the game, you can eventually spend them at upgrade machines to buy the upgrades.
Certain enemies are more vulnerable to certain types of weapons, so you'll need to switch things up a bit. The enemies are helpfully color coded to help you sort out which is which.
There are PLENTY of boss battles, but basically, defeat all the minions that rushes you, then when the boss starts glowing red on certain sections, shoot those sections. Those areas don't glow red until you defeat the minions, so you can't concentrate on the boss alone. There are probably several groups of these vulnerable points you need to destroy before you can destroy the boss, while its minions hound you.
And there were many many levels. When you die, you are sent back to the nearest autosave / checkpoint, with one death recorded against your accomplishments on this level. There are plenty of achievements, such as time spent, how much of the level's NANO did you gather, how many kills, how many envirokills, damage done, damage received, and so on.
There are some jumping puzzles, but nothing too dramatic. There is no crouch, so it's shoot only.  Some secret areas requires extended attempts at jumping and running.
All in all, Hard Reset is an old fashioned shooter with a better than decent plot and lots of action, but the call for enviro-kills seem to go against the shooter philosophyit adopted. It however, is a lot of fun to play.

The cool thing about Recettear is that it's setting is that of a typical fantasy RPG town, but the gameplay is nothing like that. You're already familiar with the setting and the tropes, but it's a new experience since you come at it from a different angle.
You are a young girl who is severely in debt to a bank run by fairies (millenial problems.) To pay off the debt you convert your family home into an item shop for all those fantasy RPG adventurers that wander through your town. The core of the gameplay is just buying merchandise and then selling it to your customers. There are however some other variations on that, people in the town can help you out, you can market your stuff in various ways, and you can venture out into the wilderness to gather merchandise directly from the source (dungeons and monsters) rather than buying it all wholesale.
So the core gameplay is pretty simple, but unless you're already an economist you'll likely find it pretty intimidating at first. I know I did. I made all the payments for my debt but each time I only just barely was able to meet each installment. Every time it got close to my due date I stressed out and pressed all my customers even harder in order to get by. It was actually fairly stressful.
So if you're interested in becoming an episode of Pawn Stars: JRPG Town this is a great game. But don't say I didn't warn you if you end up blowing a blood vessel.

As someone who has been waiting 6+ years to play Owlboy, it’s a bit unfortunate to say that I have mixed feelings about this game. It deserves a thumbs up simply because the good outweighs the bad, and I'm sure there are people who'll love Owlboy to pieces despite its flaws. It’s great for what it is, but there’s some untapped potential here that I hope will be improved upon if there’s ever a sequel.
Personally, I loved the universe, the amazing soundtrack, the beautiful graphics, and the protagonist (despite the fact that Otus never says anything). Interacting with the NPCs is always interesting and a lot of the time they say or do genuinely funny and adorable stuff.
Otus’ gunners/companions aren't as likable as I feel they should be, considering that they're always around (since you need them for pretty much everything). Well, the exception being the last one you meet - at least he's got a bit of backstory and is somewhat relatable. I wouldn't mind a bit of dialogue/banter from them when you're flying around doing whatever needs to be done, since Otus (being a mute) is obviously silent all the time and the cutscenes are few and far between. Sometimes it feels like you're just doing levels for the sake of it and not to achieve anything, at least until you bother to read the reminded to see what your actual objective is.
My only real problem with this game, though, is the difficulty. It's literally so easy that I don't think I needed more than five tries on the hardest boss - and that wasn't even the final one. There's no learning curve or need for tactical thinking in this game, you just shoot enemies and make the slightest effort to dodge their attacks - and that's the solution to winning every fight. You sometimes have to switch your gunners mid-fight, but you can usually win with whichever one you're currently carrying.
Puzzles aren't challenging either, and I say that as someone with sub-par visual intelligence. Even finding every single coin in the world was fairly easy.
The most difficult part in Owlboy is actually completely optional, and that is the mini-game that you only have to succeed 100% at if you wish to get every achievement (you'll use WASD to move Otus normally, but I couldn't complete the mini-game until I tried the arrow keys instead. Too bad I discovered that after 2 hours of messing up).
I guess I hoped for more challenging gameplay to go with the story, but I enjoyed the game nonetheless. The world is extremely detailed and feels very alive, so getting immersed in it was no problem at all. Level design is clever and there's even a day/night cycle that makes the environment even more beautiful.
Completionists will get more out of the game as the story is only about 7-ish hours long, but I’d say that Owlboy is definitely worth picking up regardless of what type of gamer you are; just don't buy it believing it's anything other than a casual, easy-going experience.

DreadOut is a third person horror game where your only defence is your camera. Sound familiar? You play as the silent protagonist Linda on a school trip, only you've seemingly taken a wrong turn and ended up in an abandoned town. Eventually night falls and things go wrong, and you must search the town, solve puzzles, and fight off ghosts in order to find your classmates.
Combat is similar to Fatal Frame. You use your smartphone's camera to take pictures of ghosts. However, you'll only damage them if you take a picture and the right time indicated by a glitch on the screen. When you die there is no game over screen, instead you go to "limbo" where you must run toward a light in order to continue. Each time you die, the space between you and the light gets bigger which can get quite tedious.
Exploration is very rewarding in this game. You can blast through the story in a few hours if you wish but you'll be missing a lot of content if you do. There are many hidden ghosts to find and taking pictures of them reveals some of the folklore behind them.
If you're a fan of the Fatal Frame series you will almost certainly enjoy this game. However, this game is much more than a Fatal Frame clone. The Indonesian setting and ghosts are very unique and the game has a wonderfully spooky atmosphere. While the graphics are very dated and there are quite a few bugs I'd still highly recommend this game to any horror fan.

Below is a summary from the full review on my personal blog:
I've had the fortune of playing quite a few really good indie games, and indie developers seem to be the only ones who are really developing good, serious horror titles. DreadOut is NOT one of those games. At virtually every step, the game suffers from near-crippling design flaws and glitches. Character movement is slow and clumsy, the camera gets stuck on geometry in the game and gets spun around, dialogue is cringe-worthy. Even the game's core mechanic (taking pictures of ghosts with your smart phone) is prone to malfunction, which renders one of the mid-game boss fights and some of the puzzles almost unplayable.
All the time I spent trying to figure out how to overcome the game's technical and design shortcomings resulted in a complete desensitization to any atmosphere that the game may have been trying to build, and the lazy, predictable jump scares just plain don't work.
Every time you die, you have to walk through Limbo. And each time you walk through Limbo, the distance to the end is longer. During this time, the game likes to display useless and insulting hints and messages to the player. One such message says "Thank you for purchasing a legit copy of DreadOut." Thanks for reminding me that I really wish that I hadn't bought it.

I got Hard Reset on sale. I purchased it because I liked the Blade Runner vibe in the screenshots and trailers. Having just finished it, I can honestly say I would not have been disappointed even if I had purchased it at full price.
Hard Reset is a run and gun that does not reinvent the wheel, but what it does, it does very well. The graphics and level design were great. The difficulty level, while at times frustrating, was neither too easy nor too difficult.  When it seemed like I had died 10 times in the same fight, I would step away from the game, but its fun, and I always came back for more.
The weapons system is very simple - two highly upgradable guns. The upgrades were great - some of them more than others (smart gun and RPG were my favorites.) You can also upgrade the health system in a variety of ways. Its not overly complex, but it mixes things up a bit.
Some people have complained about the repetitive look of things and the recycling of enemies. I actually really loved the art design of the game (the more human than human signs were a nice touch), especially in the Exile portion of the game, which has a completely different color palette than the main section. I didn't think the number of varying enemies was any less interesting than in say, Doom or Half-Life. I learned, as the game went on, how to handle different kinds of enemies with the weapons at my disposal.
Another complaint I have seen is that Hard Reset is "story lite." This is true, but not to the extent I feared. The story/ concept is delivered in a format that mimics a comic book (which I thought was kind of cool), and while it isn't overly deep and doesn't have much in the way of character development, it compliments the game sufficiently to keep my interest. More than anything it serves to break up the "chapters/ levels" of the game and give context to the environment. This is NOT Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but its not just an arcade shoot-em-up either.
I clocked about 29 hours before I was done with the main game and Exile DLC, but I went back a few times to try to find the "secrets" and to raise my level scores. These small elements give the game some limited replayability, and the overall length of the game is fantastic for the price. I have seen some say that it seems to drag on, but honestly, for my money, I would rather have a longer game than a shorter one, especially these days.
Best of all, I had zero issues with this game - no crashes, no freezes, nothing. It just played right away and worked straight through to the end. When I would get swamped with enemies at times, my frame rate would drop, but given the sheer amount of activity on the screen this never suprised me or inhibited my play. Its relatively rare these days to find a game that isn't half broken on release, but Hard Reset is on that short list for me.
So, all in all, kudos to the developers for making a GREAT run and gun game. I was thoroughly entertained and definitely recommend Hard Reset.

TL;DR - It sounds like it'd be cool, but it isn't.
A great concept poorly executed. Essentially a supernatural, watered-down LA Noire with the theme of the Crow, accompanied by a little Max Payne 1/2 narrative style. Unfortunately the whole is certainly not greater than the sum of its parts as this game feels like an indecisive mess. It's not really adventure since the game won't progress until you have found all the clickable items at a "crime scene" to which you must simply pick the correct clue. Don't worry if you get it wrong, main-character-whos-name-I've-already-forgotten will let you know and kindly mark it as wrong until you select the appropriate one via process of elimination, that is, if you actually somehow manage to pick one of the obviously incorrect clues. It's not RPG or action since, well, it lacks elements of both save for the 15 second long final boss "fight" that is about as action packed and tense as running to the kitchen to stop a pot from boiling over. What this game could call itself is a lightly interactive story with player navigation between the chapters and minor stealth gameplay.
The majority of this game is spent navigating from one section of the foggy, New-England themed map to another, wherein the story segments occur. The city of Salem--yes, the game is about witches, sort of-- feels, just void. With the exception of collectables, only cut and paste NPCs with the same handful of voiceover lines populate the city. Even the NPCs point out the monotony of the collectables with a fourth wall joke while being mind-read. The developers
this was boring. There are a few side missions in the city, all of which can be solved in anywhere from 3 to 10 minutes. The story sections such as the graveyard, museum, church, and mental institution, while sometimes atmospheric and pretty to look at, are almost as void as the city map. Cutscenes, some talking from uninteresting/pointless characters, interacting with useless objects/escorting whats-her-face, and the aforementioned "crime scene" mechanic that sometimes involves the use of a cat to linearly platform to inaccessible clues are about all you can expect from a story section. Except for the demons.
Demons. This is about the most coherent and almost enjoyable gameplay mechanic the title has to offer, but like the rest of the game, the developers manage to squander this opportunity as well. With the exception of the final "boss" and a randomly placed ghost train straight out of Ghostbusters 2 that will instakill you if one of your pixels is in its path during the museum section, the Demons are the sole enemies in the game. There is only one kind and it would appear that the art department took some liberties with the design by essentially copying the Fade Demons from Dragon Age. The stealth-based encounters consist of choosing one of the plentiful and conveniently located hiding spots to which you rush them(they are deaf) from behind as they very slowly patrol a 10 foot line and perform a two button QTE. That's it. When you encounter the first one, you feel and hope that the game will begin to get difficult and even creepy. It doesn't. They are nothing but an attempt to pad the length of the game. By the way, the devs kindly let you see them through the walls too. Wouldn't want things to get too difficult.
The story? A dark antihero teams up with an angsty gothic teen to solve his own murder so he can join his murdered wife in heaven. Yeah, the Crow basically. There's an endless supply of great to decent adventure/detective games on Steam. This isn't one of them.

I could just about copy and paste my D:OS review for D:OS 2. The short versions is that if you liked D:OS you'll like 2. If you didn't enjoy the first you won't like the second. So if you have experience with the first title, there's your answer. You can stop reading now. The rest of this review is aimed at those who haven't played the first game.
I thought the first was a GOTY contender in 2014 and I think #2 is a GOTY contender in 2017. But some of the flaws that remain are all the more glaring because this is the 2nd time we've seen them. So let's start with those flaws.
The obscure quests still remain from the original and you often have no idea how to move a quest forward or where to go next. The quest log is still quite useless. Some screens are too much of a pixel hunt and the highlight button doesn't highlight most objects. The difficulty curve is even higher this time and takes the same type of leaps that the first did which leads to frustration. The game is still difficult, doesn't hold your hand and more than occasionally nut-punches you. Be prepared to get frustrated from time to time. Also, I've had an issue with saves that don't seem to actually save. Save now, save often...and make sure it saved.
And like the first, this is overshadowed by the best turn-based combat ever to appear in a RPG. This is the meat of the game and it's sooooo tasty. There are many options on how to approach a battle and you can use environmental barrels (water, oil, poison) to shape the battlefield. Every encounter is a combat puzzle and most of them are fun. Sometimes an encounter seems impossible and then you figure out a strategy to make it relatively easy. For example, there's a battle in this game when you're blindfolded. The first time you approach this you're likely to get spanked. But a quick duck around a corner, a few blind AOE fire arrows to help block an approach and suddenly this becomes easily doable as you've re-formed the battlefield into a flighting in a phone booth.  This series remains the high-water mark of RPG combat. As AOW3 is to 4x games, DOS is to RPG games.
The back stories of the starting characters are great and your party members seem to be far more developed this time. The voice acting has been consistently great and the music and sounds are still top-notch. The environments are quite beautiful and quite detailed though they are sometimes so busy the game delves into a pixel hunt. The races are really quite neat and there's a couple here that are fairly original which isn't easy to do in an RPG. The RPG aspects just feel more fully fleshed out in this version. The synergy between the NPCs doesn't seem to be very good to start but after a few rough bumps the first two levels it's easier to figure out how you want to blend your party.
The AI is quite good to the point of being frustrating. You can - and will - get stun locked in certain battles. The balance between spells and classes seems to be a bit off right now. But we also know Larian will continue to do a great job of supporting their product. They did a great job in the first and they've already released multiple patches in the second. A game this large is going to have bugs and Larian does a great job of squashing them. But know there are some severely unbalanced battles, especially in Act 4, and those need to be re-done to make them even close to fair.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game. If you're new to the genre, beware that you're diving into the deep end of the pool. But it's worth the jump.

+ The atmosphere is truly stunning. You really feel a sense of awe when you stumble upon an ancient tomb, or a sense of dread when you enter the creepy necromancer's creepy basement. The art design and soundtrack nail the atmosphere time and time again.
+ The combat! The combat is my wet dream, I'm a huge fan of Xcom and love turn based combat, but I've seen it done wrong too many times. Divinity absolutely gets it right. The sheer variety of ways to kill your enemies means I'll be playing this game far past the first play through.
+ The difficulty. I wasn't aware beforehand that the Divinity series is known for it's difficulty (much like Xcom and Dark Souls) so I was surprised to find out how damn hard it is. But that's a good thing. It's incredibly satisfying to win a fight that when it starts you're thinking, how the hell am i going to get out of this one.
+ The main story. This fits in with the writing category but I think it should have it's own section. As I said I've not yet finished Act 2 but so far I'm completely hooked.The story does a great job of gradually making you feel more and more badass. It's the familiar trope of starting out as nothing and gradually getting more and more powerful but it does it so well. I don't want to say too much because spoilers. Just trust me, it's friekin' dope.
These are the things that stand out to me personally but there's much more to love. I've never written a review before but felt I needed to express my appreciation of this great game. I could go into more detail but I kinda wanna get back to playing.

Chances are that when asked about games you consider to be classics or personal favourites, you have a handful that you fondly remember and can still pick up and play even today. As such,
is, by no means, a perfect game nor the "greatest" game. It suffers from issues that have polarised many in the community, from the supposedly awkward combat to the infamous elevator rides. Yet even after nearly 5 years and dozens of playthroughs, (across multiple platforms), it still remains a personal favourite.
Though released under the thumb of everyone's favourite publisher, the period around the release of
also saw the equally excellent
appear, marking the triumphant return of BioWare and Western RPGs in a whole new way. You are once again placed in the boots of Commander Shepard and are weeding out the remnants of indoctrinated Geth when a new threat, known as the Collectors, reveal themselves, turning the tables on you and your crew in an incredible opening sequence. Abandoned by The Council and now working under the orders of the pro-human extremist group Cerberus, you must once again build yourself up from nothing, gather your crew, prepare yourself and travel through the Omega-4 relay to end The Collectors once and for all.
A heavily stylised and cinematic experience, BioWare's so-called space opera features some of the best writing around, easily quotable and frequently amusing. Regardless of your opinion of BioWare and the controversies in recent years, it is difficult to deny the depth of characterisation and investment that the studio has brought to the
series. From the opening titles all the way to the end credits,
has a quality that others still aspire to and fail to achieve. You will grow attached to your crew but in different ways compared to other playthroughs, especially with the romance and loyalty mechanics. The game allows for what can only be described as true role-playing, in a more accessible medium than that of pen-and-paper.
From the character customisation to the dialogue wheel to the open-ended Paragon/Renegade morality system, you are free to shape your Shepard however you wish and determine the fates of not only your crew but the galaxy itself. With the addition of the import save file feature, playing through the series carries further weight as for every choice there certainly is a consequence; many of which are severe and often unexpected, especially in the final mission where everything and everyone is on the line. Successfully pulling off the aforementioned Suicide Mission without a single death is truly epic and will stay with you long after the credits roll and Jack Wall's excellent soundtrack finishes.
As it is action-oriented, the squad-based gameplay features an impressive range of enemy types and classes, six of which are available to Shepard and complement specific weapon loadouts and cross-class abilities with your team of four per mission. Although the game goes to great lengths to encourage experimentation with a good range of weapons, you'll most likely have a loadout well and truly established for each character within a few hours, with exception to the researched upgrades later in the game. Finite magazines have replaced the overheating component of previous weapons, which significantly affects the style of combat between the two. You'll be taking cover and pausing more often, relying more on biotics than the first especially to get through the various layers of protection.
The tactical UI has been cleaned up a bit and there are other significant changes from the first game. For one, there isn't an inventory or loot system. At all. The top-of-the-line weapons are simply found, bought or researched. Weapons are assigned prior to missions and medi-gel is frequently littered throughout levels, now used only to revive teammates. Shepard's N7 is the centrepiece in terms of armour, featuring modular customisation, but other parts and sets can be found or bought. Over all, combat is certainly more streamlined then the chaotic firefights of the first game, but feels more realistic and enjoyable. Shepard no longer feels like a demi-god, instead like the lone soldier fighting tooth-and-nail against all odds that they're meant to be.
The galaxy map and vast array of missions will take you from the heights of glorious Illium to unsettling space stations to the seedy underbelly of Afterlife and Omega. In terms of graphics,
isn't the best looking game for its time, choosing more of a gritty, contrasted artstyle that BioWare's heavily modified version of Unreal Engine 3 allows for but still looks great all the same.. even when wandering around the Normandy for the umpteenth time. AI is surprisingly quite good, significantly better than a lot of other games, with only the rare kamikaze or doorway block. There were occasional minor framerate drops and in terms of bugs, I encountered some clipping and camera issues but nothing significant or game-breaking. A quick reload usually fixes most of the few that remain. Having played this for hundreds of hours on the PlayStation 3, the experience has been pretty good on both platforms.
The only major criticism here is due to the Steam version, rather than the game itself, and the lack of DLC. Already having owned all the available DLC on console, the Digital Deluxe edition contains the "Cerberus Network" DRM, (which, at the time of writing, apparently has been shut down), with the only meaningful addition being Zaeed Massani as an additional companion. The best content, like the Lair of the Shadow Broker, Kasumi and The Arrival, costs more than twice the initial price of the Steam edition, let alone when it's on sale. Besides the fact that this is overseen by Electronic Arts, the fact that DLC costs more for a game that is over half a decade old is unacceptable.
Do I recommend
for everyone? No. In fact, I know many people who hate it with a passion, and that's fine. It certainly isn't for everyone. But this is a Steam review, so let's continue in the not-so-objective manner.
It is a captivating ride from start to finish with thousands upon thousands of lines expertly delivered by the cast, bringing Shepard's crew and the complexities of the alien worlds and relations to life. The triumph of
is that it captures not only the sci-fi epic but the humanity that underpins it. The love and effort that BioWare have put into crafting this is second-to-none as the game constantly drives you into exploring and, above all, determining how you play.
For a genre that is so overused, parodied and often mishandled,
is a truly epic example of a game done right and the pinnacle of the BioWare RPG. How much enjoyment and investment you get from this ultimately comes down to personal preference, though coming from someone who knew nothing about the series going into their first playthrough, I'd ask that you give it a chance. Even just on sale, it's worth it.
Though I'd recommend that you experience the trilogy from start to finish, this also stands proudly amongst the best in its own right. This and
may be a far cry from the days of
or KOTOR but still remain a personal favourite.
Just like old times.

Really though,
Do what any poor f***er lost in the desert should do and look for trees! Pick up rocks, plant fiber, and branches along the way. Make a pickaxe asap to bash motherf*****s and collect resources. Wait to make clothes. Crafting takes too long right now. Mr. Johnson likes to breathe anyway.
Water, water, water. Eat the bugs you find; haven't gotten sick from them yet and you will need tons of plant fiber, which is where you find them. Raw turtle meat will get you sick probably. First: Great job, Funcom. This game is already so feature complete. As a veteran of every other game you have launched, this is by far the smoothest yet. RIP AO Launch.. plz remake this game in a few years with an AO-based skin =)
#Jubilation:

(this section is longer than the above, but please do not take that as my dislike for the game, rather my passion for seeing a smooth experience):
- Death should remove portions of corruption or it should slowly go away on it's own (much slower than dancers remove it). I wandered into a cave with corruption without knowing what it was doing and dealt with a day of half hp/stam. - Bark... as stated in numerous threads. We need a bark gathering device. In 1x, the entire game is bottle necked around stuff that grows on every tree in the game but only comes out 1x. As a solo player with iron tools, I am in a circle of "get more bark" to support actually using the tools that I then turn around and use to get more bark. - Teleporting mobs.. I'm fighting one hyena.. then two.. I kill them. Suddenly two more (the same ones?) are attacking me out of nowhere. I kill them. Now another is hitting me from nowhere again. I'm wondering if I'm standing on a quick spawn point or perhaps just blind? Watching replay footage of from my stream, I can see where the area is clear before I start harvesting, so it feels like teleportation to me.
- Mob agro range.. I can't explain what the rules are for hostile mob agro. Combine this with the teleporters and it makes for interesting risk analysis. Fun.. but still interesting.

Desktop Dungeons is an interesting game and worth looking into, but it's not quite the 'roguelike-lite' that it advertises itself to be. Each dungeon is one level (occasionally with a sublevel with more treasure or more enemies) and your adventurer always starts fresh at level 1 at the beginning of the dungeon, so there's no characters that carry over from dungeon to dungeon. The most notable difference between this game and other roguelikes is that monsters in dungeons do not move and do not attack until you attack, which causes the game to become more of a puzzle game than a genuine roguelike- the challenge comes not from the monsters themselves but rather budgeting your resources and defeating the monsters in the correct way to give your hero as much power as they need to defeat the boss monster and defeat the dungeon.
That's not saying Desktop Dungeons isn't entertaining or worth looking into, though. As far as being a sort of time-waster to play inbetween ordering a pizza or during a break at work or something, it fits perfectly since each dungeon could take at most 15 or 20 minutes to complete. The gameplay suits itself well to playing in short bursts rather than sitting down for long sessions and as such is a perfect fit for the busy gamer looking for a more intricate experience over Bejeweled or games on Facebook or something.
That being said, I'm not entirely sure this game is worth the $15 price tag. Maybe wait for it to come on sale for $10 or less, then go ahead and make the dive.
One final note: The soundtrack, made by Grant Kirkhope (Banjo-Kazooie, Goldeneye, Perfect Dark) and Danny Baranowsky (Binding of Isaac, Super Meat Boy) is excellent and fits the game well. Makes the dungeon-crawling a lot more thematic and interesting than it would have been otherwise.

I wonder how much of the 8.9 hours I spent was actually playing the game, and not consulting a youtube playthrough to figure out what the hell to do next. Good effort from a first-time Indie developer, but there's room for improvement.  I don't regret the purchase, but only because I got it on discount.

Metro Last Light Review :
Pros & Cons for the metro series :
1. Great atmosphere
2. Gunplay is awesome
3. Graphic is gorgeous (expecially the redux version)
4. Great story
5.Survival horror
6. Challenging(on ranger hardcore difficulty)
Cons :
1. Minor bugs
About Metro Last Light :
Both Metro are awesome games and one of the best survival horror games available on the market. What i like about Metro Last Light is it improves some of the mechanic that was present in Metro 2033 . I also love how each level is structured and designed to reward exploration . Running out of filters ? u might wanna check around the corner because there might be some laying around . Taking this kind of mechanics and give a Ranger hardcore difficulty and u get one hell of a challenging game . Bullets and resources are hard to come by and even your military grade bullets (currency) can be use for spare ammos. Adding to that challenge , the enemy also hit very hard especially the monster . U will die in 2 / 3 hits if u dont come prepared .Playing the game in the highest difficulty really enhance the survival horror aspect of the game and it will be one hell of a ride .
How does it compare to Metro 2033 ?
I would say that it doesnt change too much from the original but both of them did somethings better than the other .
I would recommend playing metro 2033 first and then play metro last light to get the full metro experience .
This has been an awesome game and I am excited for Metro Exodus to drop next year .

This game has been on my favorite's list practically since I bought it.  Yes, it is alternate WWII setting, but instead of a bloody dance between super-powers, it is a small country, caught between an aggressive and yes, genocidal opponent and large, super-power type allies that don't really seem to think that this one small country is all that worth committing to.  Don't get me wrong - the battles are fantastic, and the tactics of what type of soldier to use where, when, and the micro-tactics of which individual's strengths best fit a role are fascinating, and that's the point - this game is far more about the actual people doing the fighting.
- One of my favorite things about this game is the fact that there are no white or black hats - you have to command soldiers who may be a pain to work with, or are terrified, or are so gung-ho that they are practically nauseating.  There are officers on both sides that I want to strangle, and others that I feel great sympathy and respect for.
I nominated this game for the "Villain Most in Need of a Hug" award because of one of those invading commanders (two actually, but one in particular) because they is used as a tool, and thrown away when that is most convenient...  Yet they are a person, and chooses to make their final sacrifice all the more meaningful.
And if the touchy-feely-emotional-connection aspect that I'm describing doesn't attract you, hey, you get to deal with tanks and fighters, train them, earn money to improve them and their gear, and play through some truly fantastic tactical puzzles.  This is a great game, and may be the finest war-game you ever play - that's for you to decide.
p.s. get the DLC's - they are worth it.

Pretty good FPS! Old-school in the sense of Painkiller and Serious Sam, rather than DOOM and DukeNukem.
The level design isn't as interesting as the latter, but the game still has room for a few secrets for you to uncover. Each weapon is unique, with various uses, although the slow upgrade system doesn't encourage experimentation with the weapons (it's balanced for you to have 80-85% of the upgrades by the end of the game).
Still, even though it may take a while, each weapon is pretty satisfying.
Wave uponh wave of enemies. The big problem is how resilient they are to damage. Even a rocket launcher is rather inneffective... Then again, I played on Hard mode. It's... really hard. Sometimes frustrating, putting high damage enemies with you into very small spaces.
But, despite that big flaw, the game is still a hell of a lot of fun!
Visually, it's nothing short of impressive, with a huge, cyberpunk city. The lighting system is pretty good as well.
Then, there's the physic's system. It's a big part of what makes this game awesome to play! Everything explodes and breaks apart, and you can basically shoot everything long after they're dead. It gets a bit too resource intensive, but it's worth it.
The levels are a bit too long to my taste (usually 40minutes +), seeing how much you die. Checkpoints are really unforgiving as well, with the game lacking a "quicksave" feature.
But hey, if you're looking for a game that is purely about the shooting, with little other distractions, definitely check this out!

I've only recently touched upon FPS games, and Hard Reset is definitely one of the toughest FPS I've ever played so far [Normal Difficulty].
Weaponry:
The game offers a total of 10 different weapons, 5 for the mechanical side and 5 for the plasma side. Its supposed to keep you interested and excited for the next weapon you can unlock the next time you visited a shop, but once I got the homing plasma gun, I found myself not needing the other plasma guns anymore. This gun has homing functions, x-ray vision, infinite wall penetration, multi-missile, and high damage. Why would you even consider the other options?
On the mechanical side though, the guns are a lot more balanced. Eventually towards the end of the game, I rotate around 3 main weapons, shotgun, rpg, and homing.
Gunplay:
This is where the game gets slowly dragged out over time. Enemies are really hard to destroy, and even with maxed out weapons I find myself struggling with the mini-bosses rush attacks. Speaking of rush attacks, it's extremely frustrating to find myself getting ambushed EVERY SINGLE TIME. At no point in the game I'm able to spot an enemy before he spots me, and being the terrible fps player that I am, I had to cheese my way through tons of battles via homing plasma behind/inside some large crate. However, it is fun to shoot and feel more experienced killing them after dying multiple times. The 3 boss fights [including the DLC] are really well thought out battle designs, so kudos for that.
Exploration:
I pretty much blazed through the game, not bothering to attempt getting all those secret nodes, but for gamers who are collectors this game would be amazing. In fact, if you wanted to do a 100% run, it will most likely take twice as long as if you were blazing through it. A few secrets are quite obvious though, probably placed so that you don't feel like such a noob for getting 0/X secrets per stage. Progress itself is fairy linear, as eventually you have to reach point A to unlock point B, but the journey during these two points are pretty action-packed, especially for the DLC, where they really upped the ante.
Story:
Hilariously bad, halfway through the game I didn't bother to keep up with what the conversation was about. Voice acting is horrible especially for the main character, his personality comes across as dull and whiny 99% of the time. Each time he has to argue with the professor in his mind, he speaks like an angry 12 year old who can't understand simple explanations. I see that they went for some sort of comic art style with minimal animations, it kinda works but feels very lazy and budgeted.
Overall:
I would still recommended it to anyone who is interested, but I wouldn't play this all over again, normal is enough of an adrenaline rush for me, collectors and fps veterans would definitely love this game.

A cyberpunk shooter by (some of) the makers of Painkiller, and very much in that style (that is, old-school shoot-em-up).  Looks great, and the levels are well-designed.
The upgrade system is a little wonky: you have two guns, which can each be upgraded into other types of guns within that guns' style.  One is an energy weapon, the other a conventional rifle: the energy weapon is upgraded into a rail gun, &c. while the rifle can be upgraded into an RPG, shotgun &c., with about 10 different weapons in total with most all having an alternate firing mode.  These were relatively easy to switch between, but tedious to scroll through (I would advise using the bound keys for specific guns early, as I used the mouse scroll and ended up blowing myself up with the RPG several times intending to use the shotgun).
The story is mostly non-existent.  One gets the feeling that they ran out of funding, or something, as the cut scenes are all hand drawn (as though they were still storyboards), and the plot seems half-cocked at best (I could not even begin to tell you what the story is about).  But it, appropriately, goes mostly unnoticed, taking a backseat to the gameplay.
tl;dr: Story sucks, but looks good and plays about as well.
I'd give it a B

At first and foremost I have been a Dungeon Keeper 1 & 2 fan since I play computer games! I think that this fact is pretty relevant for this review. It is tha digging and room building that I loved quite muche these days and still do. Besides being the evil guy is always quite tempting, isn't it? Of course it is! Therefore I am really happy that War For The Overworld managed to breathe new life into this uniue genre. What follows is a list about different game mechanics that I like and don't like.
Rooms:
WFTO managed to bring the rooms that the player built in Dungeon Keeper back to life and developes it further. The player needs ingame to dig for new space and build rooms in that space. These rooms vary in size and purpose even more than they did in Dungeon Keeper. The player uses these rooms to attract humanoids and beasts, trains them and makes them happy or uses rooms to increase the own power with spells.
Rooms get 1+ from me!
Spells:
What I like is that WFTO did't just copy rooms and spells from Dungeon Keeper into the game, but created many unique spells that come in form of, well spells but also in potions that can be made in certain rooms. Also rituals let the player feel quite evil and unstoppable while he fullfills the ritual simulatiously with preventing the heroes from docking at the door.
Also Spells get 1+ from me!
Traps, Weapons, Buildables:
The player not only builds rooms, but also traps and other stuff to make the underground its home and its enemies hell. The buildable stuff that the player can choose from varies a lot, but I dont want to tell you about this for spoiler reasons. See youself and have fun!
Buildables get 1+ from me!
Downside!:
WFTO also has its problems, at leat with my computer. At a certain point ingame it starts to lag and can be stopped by turning down the graphics. I believe that this is a problem that will be solved as I write this review, because the game just released to version 1.0 and will be updated further.
Conclusion:
WFTO is the Dungeon Keeper successor that I always wished to get! Well okay I cant get to the overworld which I wished for after Dungeon Keeper 2, but damnit! We have enough games for beating somebody up in the overworld.
In my opinion WFTO is a musthave game for fans and newcomers!

Every day I started this, the controls randomized themselves. One day O was my accept-button, one day it was square and one day it was triangle. (Using standard PS4 controller with DS4Windows which works flawlessly in all other games).
Using the configuration tool that comes with the game does not help at all (it mixes up your controls even more and you end up accepting by pushing left etc).
The max resolution is 1280x960. That may have been good in the year 2000, but it's 2016 now and this game really looks bad at 3440x1440. If you run it windowed you have to use third party software like ShiftWindow to force this thing into borderless mode. It won't take over your window-resolution but stay at 1280x960.
There are many options in the config tool that let you downgrade the graphics to i386-niveau but nothing that actually lets you improve it. I think my graphics cards didn't even wake up from desktop mode while displaying this thing at it's max FPS of 60.
All in all this game, albeit being a PC only release, feels like a super bad console port with Consolitis so strong, I'm surprised it doesn't infect my other games.
Apart from the technical amagheddon that this thing (I'm not calling this game) represents, it can actually be fun. I will not go into those details as it's simply not worth playing for a PC gamer.
I can write mods for Skyrim and fiddle with NWN 2 configs for days but I simply don't see why I should endure the unwillingness of devs to create a remotely playable game on the main game platform: the PC.

Hand of Fate is a Hack & Slash Rogue-Like/Lite Card Game, and a well good one at that.
It's different, new, and a great blend of genres. You sit a table with a mystical dealer. About to play a game with your memories as the cards. You select the cards you want in your deck. Pick your class (DLC), and your boss plus it's effects. (Note: There's also Endless Mode, but that doesn't let you pick cards for your deck. It takes all your cards. It also gives you pain cards, and makes enemies harder with each floor.) You'll get your starting equipment depending of how far you're in the game. When you begin a game you start on an entrance card. With facing down cards around it. You'll have some food which will be used when you move, or lost with food pain cards, or you use it in an encounter. Food will heal you for 5 HP whenever you move. But if you have none you will starve, and lose 10 HP. When you move to a faced down card it will reveal the encounter, and you'll be drawn into a memory. You could be talking to some solders wanting helmets, meet a vampire wanting some of your blood for money, Get a quest from a dying hero to finish his job, see a shop, or just get into a simple fight with some bandits. All this is done in a nice way with the card flying up showing you the card's art. You'll get some text explaining what's going on, and sometimes you'll have options to input. Like a simple "No" or "Yes" to entering a shop. Or it could be to give 5 food or 10 to a priest. Or maybe it could be to ask for some information concerning all these portals to the underworld? But not all things are gotten easy. Sometimes you'll have to pick a success card from a shuffle. Getting a failure card might lose you your chance with the card, make you draw pain cards, or course you. Most cards results in fights. So you enter a 3D to dodge, bash, hack, slash, and slay your foes. All the cards have a story, and some are only the begin to a bigger one. Each cards has a token. Which when you've for filled the cards requirement you'll get, and once the run is over will unlock new cards. New cards can be all from equipment, encounters, food or health cards. Some will be locked to your deck till completed. Once you've explored a floor enough you'll find the "Exit Card" which will bring you to the next "Floor" if you accept. Each floor is relatively the same. But the floor will look different, and the cards will be different. Once you go through enough floors you'll fight the boss. It will be a fight with a boss that has special abilities. 4 minions, and sometimes a tool of some sort. Defeat them, and you'll unlock the next one till you've beat them all. There's a lot to unlock, and a lot to master. Learning the cards, and the enemies is a fun, and engaging. All around a great game, and highly recommended if you like Hack & Slash or Rogue-Like/Lites.

I beat it on my first try without any resets besides the main character. I'm funny. Here are my tips if you want to experience the game blind and figure stuff out yourself don't continue reading.
TIPS: Adventuring doesn't really pay too well in the items you get i would try and stay away from that if your not experienced.It can pay off sometimes usually maybe once in the beginning and occaisionally if you know what your doing. I try to stick mostly to the shop.
Always try to have more items to keep your store fully stocked for when people buy stuff.
Try to go shopping in the morning slot, both the market and the guild are open to buy stuff. Don't go in the middle two slots because that's when the most traffic comes. Also night time the market isn't open.
This is the most important thing!!!!I know it sucks at first to price items cheap at first but you need to start pricing items barely over 100%  The customers don't start with bringing in a ton of money to buy your stuff at high prices also they will only pay a certain amount over 100%. The more times you don't have to haggle with the person the more you can get from them the next time and the next time. It's not an exact science so you gott feel how uch you can get away with raising it. Also haggling is in my opinion bad. If you sell and buy many items in a row without needing to haggle because you know how much they will accept then it raises the consecutive EXP bonus you get which is invaluable  with the perks it gets you. The most valuable is new items in the guild and market. Others are great too.
Don't slack off on a due date. If you have over the amount of money on due date don't skip the day. go invest it in more items  and make enough money back that day to pay off the debt. You need to know how much you can make in a day though pay attention to that and oonly spend what you think you can pay back quickly on due date day.
Try to have some cheeper items  for people who want multiple and don't carry enough money for two big items really helps prevent an impossible sale. This also helps for cheep people like the little girl. Don't worry if you give her good deals she carrys more  money like everyone.
Last but not least I don't have a tip for the girl who tries to sell her crap for absurd prices sorry she's just a combo breaker lol.

Full disclosure: I bought in during Early Release, however I did not play the game extensively until 1.0.
This game is, by and large, a deep spiritual successor to the great Dungeon Keeper of old, complete with the same narrator in the background, along with the witty humour and dungeon base building concept.
It is brought to the modern day with a more modern control scheme, graphical fidelity, and delivery. If you've ever been a fan of base-building games and/or wanted to be the bad guy, this is your game. Fan of the DK of old? Its back, baby!
+ Great successor and spiritual remake of Dungeon Keeper, down to the narrator V/O and core mechanics
+ Expands on the formula by ading new minion types (with different mechanics rules), minion behaviors, and artifacts that add new abilities
+ Looks great, feels just like a Dungeon Keeper game, and even sounds right, complete with the minion V/O you can hear from time to time.
- Release jank, and lots of it. No doubt it'll get fixed, but as I'm playing this right as 1.0 has hit, its evident.
- Performance and stability issues, from crashing on exit, to FPS slowdown when a lot of worker minions are spawned.
- (AT RELEASE, will likely be fixed by the time you read this) No Skirmish or Multiplayer Lobby working yet, as they've had to remove them to fix showstopper bugs.
- Sudden difficulty spikes that can run away from the player, particularly the Dwarven survival campaign mission.
- Options menu feels a bit bare
- "Possession" mechanic, whilst its in the game, feels just as janky as the original Dungeon Keeper one, complete with odd camera POV, lack of feedback on weapon swings, and when being damaged.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a weirdly named game where you get the role of a detective investigating his own death. It happens on Salem, the city that burned witches back in the day.
The main mechanics are:
- Walking around trying to find clues;
- Pressing X to write down those clues;
- Pressing Y after getting enough clues and try piecing it together in order to find out what happened.
You also find collectibles throughout the game. Press RT to reveal and X to collect them. After collecting enough of them, a cutscene appears telling a story. The cutscene comprises of text, images and a voice narrative.
Sometimes there are demons and you have to hide and execute them stealthily. I found this part to be REALLY boring and just a mechanic added in order to increase the game value. It didn't work though.
The game is interesting enough for the 7 hours it takes. Any more of that and I wouldn't make the matter of finishing it. The ending is interesting but far from mind blowing. Get this on a 75% off sale if you can.

Mass Effect 2 took Mass Effect 1 and made it better, what a sequel should do. However, with overall improvements and refinements, other things had to suffer.
The game picks up shortly after mass effect 1, and the normandy is out on a routine trip. However, they are shot down by a large mysterious ship, and Shepard goes down with the normandy. Two years later Shepard is revived by the corporation Cerberus, who played a small role in the previous game. Shepard has no other choice than to join cerberus, since they are the only ones who belive Shepard's reaper claims, and also have the funding to back it up. The focus is not on the reapers however, since several human colonies across the galaxy have been vanishing with no trace of humans. Shepard must build a new crew to take down this unknown threat, save as many as possible, and prepare for the inevitable reaper invasion.
Pros:
+ Graphics have seen a huge upgrade, the textures, antialiasing and screen effects look a lot better
+ Combat feels far superior, and weapons have far more visual impact
+ Customization of weapons and armor has been simplified
+ Voice acting is fenomenal
+ Long campaign with entertaining side missions
+ The new crew is nice, and all their dialog is well written
+ You can tell your squad where to take cover, a mechanic the first game sorely needed
+ Choices have a huge impact on the story, even more so than in the first game, and everything you did in the first game is transferred to Mass Effect 2. No replay of the game is the same
+ Mining for minerals is quite fun and enjoyable
+ Awesome sci-fi soundtrack
Cons:
- The story sadly takes a back seat in Mass Effect 2. It's not nearly as deep as the first game, and feels like it was squeezed in as filler between the stories of ME1 and ME3 in an unnecessary way
- Romance with Liara is locked off to a DLC pack. If you romanced her in the first game, you need to get the DLC in order to get her on the normandy and continue the relationship
- There's yet again a 62 FPS cap, but it's a lot more tricky to get rid of than in the first game. For me it wouldn't even launch with 144hz settings
- People who were fans of the deep RPG elements of the first game will be dissapointed, the upgrading has been radically simplified, however, I did not personally have a problem with this
- SPOILERS B0SS:
My cons are merely nitpicks, and I wholeheartedly reccomend Mass Effect 2. It Absolutely deserves a 9/10
Dont think about it ...Just please ....please ....BUY IT ~!

This game is not for everyone and I'll keep the review spoiler free.
Simply put, the genre's are Horror and Supernatural, if that one even exists.
You go around snapping photos of ghosts while trying to find your classmates and teacher to escape the haunted village.
Now why would I say it's not for everone?
-The story itself wouldn't make sense, especially the ending, if you aren't good with mythology or understanding what's going on.
-Limbo, after death, can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to travel through if you die multiple times. To avoid this, go to the Experience Settings and then press the cute little button that fixes Limbo at a certain distance.
-It is dark and maze-like. The first level, the school, is more of an open area you need to explore and find objects to continue with the story. Sometimes it can be very confusing and getting lost can be easy. Some parts are harder to complete than others but you could always cheat and look up a guide if you need one.
-Some ghosts/monsters are unforgiving and can kill you many times before you figure out a strategy or way to survive.
-Graphics aren't that bad but for people who want beautiful design, yeah probably not the game for you.
Why is it good?
-Various ghosts that have nice design and give a good and scary vibe.
-Music. Music. Music, It fits perfectly, or at least well, in the game. Some of it is in a different language but it really doesn't matter much.
-Each ghost gives you lore, in a journal you have, after beating it.
-The Horror genre is very present and is heavily present throughout the game.
-The scenery isn't bad, even with somewhat old graphics.
-It's well worth your money on sale.
-Of all the Horror indie games I've played throughout the years, this is one of my honorable mentions. It fills out it's role well and doesn't copy paste objects repeatedly or even repeat the same sounds a hundred times over (unless you sit there for an hour listening :P)
-Easter Eggs like UFOs.
-Sorta has Side Quests.
Overall, if I were to rate this I would give it a 7/10.

DreadOut is a survival horror game that combines Indonesian folklore with gameplay mechanics similar to the Fatal Frame series.

The most frustrating aspect of DreadOut is how unclear the objectives are. The objectives are most vague and rarely offer any helpful direction or advice to advance in the game. Most of the game time logged in the game will be trying to figure out the puzzles and how to advance to the next section.
Whilst it is not the most graphically impressive game, DreadOut makes up for that with an interesting story and setting. If DreadOut had a bigger budget, this game could have been even more brilliant.
Regardless of the faults, DreadOut is a game that all fans of horror ought to try.

Just really fun combat and movement (double-jumps, wall-running, sliding, dashing, teleporting, climbing, etc. it's all here - including zero-g combat in space with a jetpack), lots of different styles of weapons and warframes, lots of quests, mission types (from stealth missions and heists avoiding cameras and laser grids, to assassinations, sabotages and defences, to just killing lots of enemies) and lots of objectives, many of which you decide to set for yourself. There is also tons of customisation options both for progression and appearance. There is just so much to do in this game and it's more horizontal progression than vertical progression, so you don't really leave friends behind and can always play together.
Play solo or with friends, pick whatever difficulty of mission you want, pick what objective you want to achieve next - follow the story or just go get a weapon or warframe you want to try, it's up to you. Sure, some stuff needs to be unlocked, or maybe you need to get lucky with a drop, but it's more like running a 10 minute mission 5-6 times to get the drop you want, or looking up on the wiki where you need to go to get it, than the gated linear progression and tiny chance RNG lotteries of other games.
The devs support the game really well - there are fixes and patches almost every day, which don't interrupt you in your mission until you complete it, then you might have to log out and back in again to get a short patch - and the devs seem to add lots of content to the game regularly. Probably my only criticism so far is that it's not a game you can really play or understand everything without using the Warframe wiki occasionally to look stuff up, as some things are not always explained that well in-game.
The bottom line is that Warframe is just a good time, no strings attached - it doesn't pressure you to spend money on it (you mostly pay for either skins/aesthetic options or as a shortcut to something you can earn in-game), it doesn't pressure you to log-in or play every day - it's just there when you want to play it and it's just fun, like video games used to be - it's not a gambling simulator designed to milk money out of your wallet, like so many games these days. This game actually lets you make your own choices about your progression and work towards the items you want, not what RNG decides to give you.
Of course it's free-to-play, so why are you even reading this? Just play it and make up your own mind!

The game is very fun for a while but after a couple hours you start to realize how complicated things really are. It's nice at first and you feel great, but then it gets very grindy and your progress gets stuck until you level up enough. You also need to get Food in order to get to play the stages. So, playing in general.
The game clearly gives you a lot of cool things for a good first impression and then says "Okay, throw money at me now. Please." Lots of microtransactions for literally everything, and the game constantly reminds you of that. They're not straight up required, but the game would be a lot more enjoyable if you did just because of the grinding in general.
There's clearly a bunch of content with evolutions for your characters which is really nice and a thing to look forward to, but the grinding required to get the component characters to that level (Note: You would have to get those component characters first), as well as getting your account to the required level, is a big turn off. Or it was for me, at least.
Art style is that art style you would normally expect from a browser game. It's not horrible, but it's not beautiful nor distinctive.
Gameplay is just click a thing and ocassionally move your characters in an attemp of strategizing since different characters in your formation, as well as enemy units, all have different stats and passive effects. I'm sure that last part gets a lot more complex eventually, but the gameplay is still the game. Click a button to move ahead and kill dudes. I don't have an issue with it, but that's just how it is.
Overall I'd say it's a fun game to play if you're bored and don't feel like doing anything, but have in mind that it requires time and commitment in order to reach most things that you want, which is not the kind of game I'm looking for when I look for a game to play when I'm bored and not feeling like doing anything.
But again, that's just me. If you like playing browser games and spending a lot of time and effort (Or money, even) then you should try this.

A great game truly worthy of the RTS genre. Best on PC for sure, it has a massive unit cap of 1,000 mobile units and several settings to play on with several game modes and a campaign to boot. It also supports offline co-op/versus and you can play Skirmish against one or many AI units on whatever setting you like. It's not to hard to figure out and get the hang of but even on normal (the lowest combat setting) it won't just hand you victory. It will make you work for it and you will enjoy every second of it. That being said I wouldnt recomend this to anyone who is impatient or bad a strategy games because this requires lots of sitting, planing, waiting and running the numbers on what has to be shut down in order to conserve energy untill new generators can be built. It's all about two things, How well you play chess and your understanding of Economics. You have to be able to outwit your enemy while trying not to waste resources. My strategy is to hole up in a well defended location and build strength while I coax the enemy into making the first few moves so that i can see how harsh they want to play. All in all it is an amazing game and if you like to think a lot and plan and strategize then this is the game for you.

I was wary of this.  I played a ton of alpha, even after I had unlocked everything and finished all the levels.  It was a lot of fun, and I appreciated the minimalism of the game.  I paid for the advance copy something like three years ago, played the game, then stopped and sort of put it behind me for a while.
Then, just a couple weeks ago, I saw that it was released on steam.  While I thought about looking up my copy of it, minutes later I received a message saying because I paid in advance I got a steam key!
So, I cracked it open.  And for a brief minute, I was shocked.  This isn't the blocky spreadsheet I remember!  Where did all these graphics come from?  Why are these characters saying things?  A town?  I miss my grid of things!
Of course I got over that quick.  What I wasn't sure about is what changes there would be, and after playing about 10 hours of the game, I am excited to say that I think they've put an amount of polish on top that has made the game even more nuanced, more complex and overall, well, more.
The base aspects of the game are the same.  You are in a dungeon with monsters levels 1-10.  Killing them nets XP, but killing monsters of a higher level than you gets you exceptionally more experience.  And you will need to kill higher level monsters, because otherwise you are unlikely to level high enough to kill the boss.  Lucky for you, the monsters are pretty lacksadaisical and tend to just stand around in the same spot, and won't strike unless you strike first.
It also has a clever mechanic where revealing tiles in the dungeon is the prime method of regaining life and mana (aside from leveling, which refills all your life and mana). The monsters also refill their life, though, so you can't just take anything out by regaining your life over and over.
It sounds simple, but when you count class skills, items, gods and so many other factors, there is just so much to this game.  And the random generation of levels makes every game, even of just random games, a thrill and a different experience.  And I love the way they build level by level as you experience more and more - the learning curve here is a big improvement on the original which pretty much threw you right into the fray and you had to guess what would be hard or easy.  Frankly, that never bothered me because a game like this that lets you take your time, you learn in your own way, but I appreciate what they've done here.  It opens up pretty fast anyway, and I think your particular sense of play can lead you towards certain classes as the most fun or interesting.
So basically.  I'd recommend this.  A lot.

This is one of those greats that unfortunately never got the marketing to get the mainstream appeal it deserved when it was released on PS3. Even then it was a beautiful looking game where the Cel Shaded artstyle often makes it look the scenery look like a painting. The story is very well thought out, and makes use of some interesting parallels to real world events despite the world being a more fantastical one than our own.
Even with its large cast of soldiers to acquire and pick from within your platoon, they still put in the effort to make each of them stand out and have their own quirks and reasons for getting involved, even if a lot of them don't get as much focus as some of the key ones. The included DLC helps bolster this as well, adding in a short campaign revolving around one of the main Antagonists involvement in the war and a few others focusing on a specific subgroup of your Militia and their misadventures.
As for the gameplay itself, its an interesting mix of a classic turnbased tactical rpg and a third person shooter, Its got a bit of a learning curve and ends up being a bit remenicent of the old XCOM games but once you figure out how to properly command and move your troops into position it actually keeps things exciting and feels quite satisfying as you find better and better ways to clear maps with higher score rankings.
Well, and theres not much more thrilling than running a Shocktrooper through enemy lines in order to rescue a fallen comrade before they end up dying. Its a game where your troops live or die due to how good of a commander you are, and while its not really a brutal game difficulty wise, especially if you take advantage of all the different RPG elements for upgrading your troops, the risk of potentially losing characters you've grown fond of adds a lot more impact to the game. Well, if you don't just savescum your way to flawless victories, I mean you still have to make the shots but at least that way you don't have to worry as much about someone actually dying.
Also, as far as tanks go, the Edelweiss is a pretty cute one. Theres also girls with rifles and/or giant lance shaped bazookas, if those are your fetish.
The PS4 Remastered Version that just released has slightly better graphics than the Steam release, but if you don't have access to a PS4, or just like delicious Steam Sale pricing more than slight texture and shading upgraded, its definitely worth getting the HD Steam port instead.
Or well, you could also just be like me and either double or triple dip on buying it over and over again, cause really the game is worth buying twice at least. I would have bought it three times if not for just playing my brothers copy back on PS3. Its definitely a game worth coming back to though, which is why its my nomination for the Time After Time Steam Award.

Hand of Fate is a Hack & Slash Rogue-Like/Lite Card Game, and a well good one at that.
It's different, new, and a great blend of genres. You sit a table with a mystical dealer. About to play a game with your memories as the cards. You select the cards you want in your deck. Pick your class (DLC), and your boss plus it's effects. (Note: There's also Endless Mode, but that doesn't let you pick cards for your deck. It takes all your cards. It also gives you pain cards, and makes enemies harder with each floor.) You'll get your starting equipment depending of how far you're in the game. When you begin a game you start on an entrance card. With facing down cards around it. You'll have some food which will be used when you move, or lost with food pain cards, or you use it in an encounter. Food will heal you for 5 HP whenever you move. But if you have none you will starve, and lose 10 HP. When you move to a faced down card it will reveal the encounter, and you'll be drawn into a memory. You could be talking to some solders wanting helmets, meet a vampire wanting some of your blood for money, Get a quest from a dying hero to finish his job, see a shop, or just get into a simple fight with some bandits. All this is done in a nice way with the card flying up showing you the card's art. You'll get some text explaining what's going on, and sometimes you'll have options to input. Like a simple "No" or "Yes" to entering a shop. Or it could be to give 5 food or 10 to a priest. Or maybe it could be to ask for some information concerning all these portals to the underworld? But not all things are gotten easy. Sometimes you'll have to pick a success card from a shuffle. Getting a failure card might lose you your chance with the card, make you draw pain cards, or course you. Most cards results in fights. So you enter a 3D to dodge, bash, hack, slash, and slay your foes. All the cards have a story, and some are only the begin to a bigger one. Each cards has a token. Which when you've for filled the cards requirement you'll get, and once the run is over will unlock new cards. New cards can be all from equipment, encounters, food or health cards. Some will be locked to your deck till completed. Once you've explored a floor enough you'll find the "Exit Card" which will bring you to the next "Floor" if you accept. Each floor is relatively the same. But the floor will look different, and the cards will be different. Once you go through enough floors you'll fight the boss. It will be a fight with a boss that has special abilities. 4 minions, and sometimes a tool of some sort. Defeat them, and you'll unlock the next one till you've beat them all. There's a lot to unlock, and a lot to master. Learning the cards, and the enemies is a fun, and engaging. All around a great game, and highly recommended if you like Hack & Slash or Rogue-Like/Lites.

War for the Overworld -Pre Release Review
Gameplay & Mechanics-
The game play is pleasant, the developers did a good job on the fluidity and ease of controls.  The camera is locked into a overhead mode, this sometimes is annoying when trying to verify your dungeon layout and design.  I did not notice any skill hotkeys; however, I might have overlooked this feature in a menu/sub-menu. This game offers the player four types of usable skill mastery's. Building magic, Attack magic spells, Minons, and Defensive structures.  Playing through the first three campaigns offers little insight to the end game viability of building magic and/or defensive skills.  defensive skills as you quickly learn in campaign 3 take up a specific amount of MP based on the structure from your mana/energy pool.  This limits the amount of defensive structures that a player is able to build. I did notice however; while tinkering around in skirmish mode, advanced walls do not take up MP/energy. Unfortunately once built, the walls cannot be sold or taken down.
Value--------------------------
Currently keeping in mind that the game is in pre-alpha, I would not purchase this game again if I had the chance.  The negatives outnumber the positives on this one.  My advice save your money until game hits 50/70% off.
Pro's-----------------------------------
Wity humor
Dungeon design tools are solid
Non game destroying bugs "this is a good thing in my book"
Solid minion diversity
Con's-----------------------------------------------
Camera is locked in overhead without a way to rotate
Minion's are capped (in skirmish I was only able to get 9 in each type of minion roughly 40-50 minions)
Defensive structures limit spell usage and have a low cap (about 15 Mix & Match)
Worker minions are limited (if you go over "via build spell" limit they take MP away like defensive structures)
Minions are inefficent, for example they leave tiles unclaimed when making rooms that are not square. (dont forget you cannot rotate the camera to correct this)
Minion AI is inefficent when fighter minnions are rallyed to a specific location (with complex dungeon design)
Review------
My review is based off of 5 hours of campaign and skirmish tests of a alpha/pre-alpha game. As such the released version of the game may differ greatly from its current state.  My review is only meant to offer my opinion of the game as it stands today 04/01/2015.  I believe this game has potential however; several other emerging games might offer more $/hr of enjoyment value.

After the debacle of another game I bought into for Early Access, I had my doubts about this game.  I re-installed today after reading the notes and came upon a pleasent surprise.  Dungeon Keeper 1 is among my top favorite games to play.  This game, while not quite there, does fill the void that game left after DK2 appeared to be it.
After some time to play, I want to give some more information about the game for those out there.
Notable Problems:
1. Sluggish Gameplay: At the moment, they just quashed a major problem by fixing the issue with the memory leak.  This helped deal with some of my slowdown issues, but it hasn't fixed them all.  I'm not on a state-of-the-art model computer.  At the same time, I am running a decent setup that can handle a good chunk of modern games at higher settings.  I haven't tried out my laptop, yet I will get around to that for a final detailed review.
2. Place Holder Text: A majority of this did get fixed.  Some place holder text does remain however.  Also, there are times when text will break and return to a placeholder setup.  This happened to me on the second to last level with some creature texts.
Minor Issues:
1. Saved Game issue - Encountered this one today where my saved game files were out of arrangment.  I had to fish around to find the one that I wanted.
2. Tactics:  At the moment, the computer can be downright stupid at times.  It'll do nothing or do a simple, one direction, brute force attack wave that can be counter with ease.
3. Level Design: Each level feels similar to the next with little change in design.  Only one level really caught my eyes, standing out from the rest.
With all of that said though, this is not a Caveat Emptor/Buyer Beware notion.  Instead, I recommend it as a buyer being aware this game still needs some fine tuning.  I applaud the developers for sticking with the game vs. simply releasing it then splitting with some extra $$$ to line their pockets.  Several updates have been released since launch to fix notorious issues, and, in a week or two imho, the game will start to work even better than expected.
