I bought this game EA and initially refunded it after having a frustraiting time with the game over a year ago. However after playing and sinking 50 hours into this game. I've got to say this was a suprisingly good RPG. Now obviously there is something that has to be said about this game. It does NOT hold your hand. And combat, especially on the higher difficulties can be torture. Yet this oddly adds to the charm of the game once you accept it. Another aspect which is difficulty and potentially frustraiting is the quest system, specifically the quest log. The quest log is sometimes ambiguos and really only records information you find and may ponder. So a secret code or location won't be found unless you search every location, every book and ask every npc. This can be tedious at first but after the first 10 hours it easily becomes routine.
Aside from the above mentioned, the game can be easily broken down into pro's and con's below:
Pro's:
- Good story.
- Interesting quests.
- Enjoyable combat system.
Pro's/Con's (mixed feeligns):
- Some areas are locked off by higher level NPC's, if you go to these areas before you are ready you will get slaughtered.
- Some quests reference area you don't know about, you spend ages looking for them only to give up. And then find out that it was actually another location entirely, this is not conveyed well in dialogue.
Con's:
- Crafting system isn't particularly good, It's great for making potions and stuff with recipies learnt from books. But unfortunatly the rest of the crafting system for combining items is fairly poor, requiring mix and matching of 4-5 different items to make something, and if you have an inventory full of random items, it can get ridiculos how many combinations you might have to try to make something new.
- The difficulty of the game fluctuates as it progresses in an odd manner, normally you expect a game to start off easy and gradually get harder. This game starts off hard, becomes easy in the middle with a few exceptions and hard again at the end. This makes it particularly frustraiting as you slog your way throught he game initially, blitz through the middle only to hit a brick wall at the end.
- The ending. It seems the choices in the game made little to no difference, and the summarisation of your journy at the end (which is basically all that chances) is ambiguos. Now whilst this leaves you to make up your own opinion of what happened, the game might say in one ending that you win, but you also lose. And in another which is fundemantaly similar to the other ending that you win, technically you lost but you still win. Which frankly is confusing, plus the romance option in the game seems to in my case just up and left despite what her character said.
- Picked up useable objects added to the abilities bar. Might not sound annoying, but when you pick up arrows and potions and they fill out your abilities bar, you have to constantly clear them out. Hopefully this is fixed by a patch or mod.
TLDR/Rating;
Ultimatly, whilst this game does have a few annoying flaws such as random items added to your abilities bar, fluctuating difficulty and an ambiguous quest log. It does not detract from the overall expirience from Divinity: Original Sin 2. Make no mistake however this is not a normal RPG. This is an RPG I would class as a mix between Dragon Age: Origins and Baulders Gate. If all of this however is irrelevant to you, and you are just wondering if the game is worth the price in terms of hours/price paid, then be rest assured it most definatly is. After 50 hours I can safely say I didn't complete every quest, and I am looking forward to doing a second run.
Final Rating: 8/10.

Summary: Detective game with great atmosphere and interesting stories
Pros:
- Well written stories, both plot and side stories, which showcase a wide array of deaths which could leave a person feeling "unfinished". The main story itself has quite a few hooks and doesn't reveal too much too fast.
- The collectibles all add to the story of this game, either by letting you get to know the characters more, feeding you more information so you can try to figure things out before the game tells you, or tell you (sometimes gruesome) stories of other people
- The music and visuals combine to give various areas in the game a very creepy feel and it is well done
- The "combat" in the game is a puzzle with multiple choices which work. If you want to execute the demons, you have to figure out a good way to approach them.
- The investigation part is very well done. While getting all the clues helps, you only need the clues which give you the answer to complete the investigation
Cons:
- If you play with a controller, the game can sometimes be picky about whether or not you are over a target. It doesn't happen often, but it is something to be aware of.
- There are potential glitches which can cause you to trigger some cutscenes twice. Again, this does not happen often.
All in all, the game is very enjoyable and I would highly recommend it if you like detectives and interesting stories!

Years ago, I found this gem in the bargain bin in Wal-Mart and instantly fell in love.  For an old game it still runs well and was one of the few games (even today) to be optimized for four cores.  It needs that power to run because you will have awesome battles of an epic proportion. Each player can have up to a thousand units on the field at any one time.  Even for an RTS game with thousands of units being rendered at the same time the units are well detailed and animated.  Sup com is also the only game I have that supports multiple monitors, which is nice.  It is too bad that there is no longer any supported multiplayer, but Sup Com Forged alliance does have multiplayer with Forged Alliance Forever, which is run by fans of the game around the world.  The fans of Sup Com have even added support for mods and up to 12 player games, which is astounding with the fact that each player can have a thousand units.
Great Game, I recommend getting both Sup Com and Sup Com Forged Alliance. For $3.74 it is a steal and even for full price, it is worth it.
I do not suggest getting Sup Com 2, which was developed by a different company and the multiplayer is truely dead.

Hey everyone!
Here is my little list of what I find good and bad about this game. I only played singleplayer so far so can't speak for how it feels and plays online! At the end, I'll put a link to a playlist I made for those who want to see what I saw and did!
Positive:
- The game looks really beautiful, quite some details in it's textures and models and I've had my share of amazing views.
- There is more story than most survival games, it isn't a must for me personally but this one is based on the Conan universe so it should be there.
- The way you build things is really well made, it's easy and it looks good, yet it seems you can still make it how you want.
- The feeling of the game is also something nice, it's dangerous and many things feel new for the first time.
- There seems to be quite a diversity in monsters from what I've experienced so far, didn't get very far yet so I'm sure there will be more surprises!
Neutral:
- This game is quite hard, but that might be because I'm alone, I'm sure in a group it's a lot more doable. As soon as a few enemies are on me, I'm a goner, and some enemies are impossible to defeat BUT that probably because I'm alone and not high level and with bad gear!
- You need to grind quite a bit, both for level and for resources. The leveling part, seems everything you do gives you some experience, which is nice. But you need to be higher level in order to craft more things and get further without dying. As for the resources, this is probably a singleplayer problem again, as with a few people you get those materials very fast most likely.
Still, this could be fixed to make singleplayer/co-op a bit different from multiplayer. Less materials required and some faster leveling would be welcome! But it could be me who is just bad. xD
Negative:
- The game has a bit of bugs, didn't get anything gamebreaking so far as it runs smoothly on my PC, but I had a teleporting crocodile once or twice. The humans don't animate the first seconds they charge on you, etc.
- It isn't very singleplayer-friendly right now, but I guess it might change in the future!
- I wish you would get more of the basic things, like a chest or the basic walls for a home from the beginning. You need to unlock them through leveling up your character as you get points this way. I mean, it was a bit annoying to grind a whole level just so I could make a small wooden chest to store things in and then another level to be able to build a house.
Unlocking armour, weapons, more building stuff like that would probably be fine or just make it a bit faster to unlock it. The list of things you can make is huge and after some hours playing, I didn't get much and I feel a bit stuck, as if I just have to grind levels now to unlock the next armour so I can finally move further in the game. But it could really just be me who's bad.
Now, as last: here is the link to my playlist if you're interested!

Last Light is a great sequel to 2033 that very subtly improves upon aspects of the first game and also treads some new ground. By that, I mean it's not immediately apparent in the beginning, where it feels like "more of the same" but as the game progresses, the improvements and differences slowly surface.
The atmosphere is still great, if ever so slightly more fleshed out and this is aided by a bigger variety of locations in the aptly named Venice, the quirky and colorful Theatre and the eerie Dead City. Ofcourse, this is in addition to the familiar endless tunnels, the cobweb ridden catacombs, the barren surface (which is a lot less whiter this time around) and the usual grim goodness that we love.
The level design (which I found a little weak in the first game) is slightly better with less awkward enemy positions and better, smoother opportunities to stealth your way through. Gunplay is pretty much the same, with only two new snipers bring added. However, I did feel like the combat AI is a little too aggressive even on normal difficulty, but one could see it as an extra challenge.
Coming to the mutants, the Nosalises and Watchmen are still super jumpy, the Demons are unpredictable and the new additions, the swamp inhabitant Shrimp family probably takes the cake for the most annoying. But there is a bigger spread between scripted encounters and the ones resulting from exploration.
The counterpart for the Librarian encounter from the first game isn't quite as epic or heart pounding, but it does serve a different purpose (spoiler).
The horror factor is upped a little bit, but it's still a survival game first.
The story is done well too. Artyom feels more a like a character than just the mute guy you control. His interactions and arcs with the half new, half old cast of characters feel genuine. The story of the dark ones and how it ties in with our Ranger's is handled neatly too. While 2033 showed us the desperation of the world, this game shows us a more hopeful side. There are a few questionable things and some plot device moments, but this is forgivable given that it does service the game well and never compromises the structure.
I did encounter a few technical hitches. The game sometimes goes into a black screen between chapters and there is the rare glitch on the surface sections, which is probably due to the fact that the game wasn't designed for a exploration oriented experience. But none of these things are gamebreaking and it actually runs pretty well for the way it looks.
TLDR:
So to sum it up, it is more of the same from 2033, plus some more. The plot isn't a grand sequel and is pretty much a continuation, but it resolves satisfyingly some of the recurring elements while also introducing its own. You likely bought this as a bundle with the first game, and even if you found yourself unpleasantly dragging through that, I'm willing to bet that you'll be pleasantly surprised by the end of Last Light.
The Metro games, for me don't stand for a central theme or concept. They're not reflections of the human condition or anything like that. What they are, is a great shooting/stealth experience with a decent challenge, believable world and investable characters. But if you want them to be any of the former, they sure are strong enough for that.

Really not my sort of game, despite me trying my darndest to enjoy it, for I have friends who love it. Thirty hours in and it still only makes limited sense to me (and no, I'm not a complete and utter idiot). Far too much seems dependent on luck, for a start. Event pop-ups occur where you can make some rather limited decisions, and there will be cases of 'fourty-percent chance something you don't want happens, sixty-percent something you do want happens'. Quite a lot of cases of that, in fact. If that makes for enjoyable gameplay for some people, then have at it - I'm not stopping you. For me on the other hand, constantly saving so that I can reload if I get buggered over by RNG isn't what I'd consider to be fun (or I guess you could play ironman mode and let fate take its toll, though I rather play the slots at a casino than this all day, for they offer about the same level of entertainment and cost the same, what with this game's ludicrous amounts of DLC).
Most of the game seems to consist of waiting. Wait for your piety and prestige stats, both of which are doing some very subtle things you probably won't realise at first due to the tutorial mode failing to teach you much of anything. You can speed things up, but then I suppose it's just a case of waiting for the things you want to happen but faster. Apparently there's strategy involved, but if you can make sense of it you're doing better than I did. Infantry units get combat bonuses when standing on certain terrain for example, but good luck telling what sort of terrain you're on as it's pretty damned hidden away - I only figured out how to tell about twenty-five hours in. If you do realise what's going on, good luck telling if that bonus is ACTUALLY having an effect and isn't bugged, like a lot of things in Crusader Kings 2 seemingly are.
Then there's the fact you have no actual goal to achieve presented to you. Some people love that, apparently, take Minecraft's success for example (though even Mojang decided to add an 'end boss' to their game). I personally just sit there and wonder "why did I pay for something that's telling me to make my own fun?". If you have any hobbies, I'd go do those instead. You could say that you should aspire to take over the world - well, okay, but is it actually enjoyable? Only if you're a particular sort of person, it seems, as I'd be bored to death by the time I manage it; most of the game involves nothing but waiting. The game just isn't fun - I tried the multiplayer, and when it wasn't "desyncing" (which was a CONSTANT issue, desyncing being tantamount to a crash as you had to exit and restart the game when it happened to someone) for half the game I was tabbed out and talking to people on Skype, as the only convenient way to play multiplayer is on the slowest setting - after all, having people pause when they need to is impractical - and thus the only 'gameplay' I was experiencing was, yet again, waiting for stuff to happen.
I'd like to try and deconstruct the individual mechanics of the game from my limited understanding of them, but really, there's no point. If you're not already playing Paradox's "grand strategy" (a genre I'm pretty certain they alone make games for) games, chances are you won't enjoy this. I'll end this on something objectively bad about the game - its DLCs, or more aptly put its micro-transactions. Multiple, tiny and worthless 'infantry packs' for soldier units you barely pay attention to and multiple 'portrait packs' for the already rather poorly rendered ruler images. Then there's the DLCs that actually add gameplay content - supposedly, they come with free patches that add content even without you purchasing the DLC when they're released. That sounds great and all, but then you hear that those patches have a tendency to come with a host of game breaking bugs and it apparently takes Paradox forever to fix anything. Great. Though I haven't actually purchased any of the DLCs, I have experienced them via my multiplayer escapades, and they seem extremely limited - essentially, think if you modded Super Mario Bros, for example, so that you're running around as Peach instead of Mario. That to me is what the DLCs appear to amount to, what with them consisting of apparently exciting new features like "new start dates" and new rulers to play as, or then you have the Way of Life DLC, where you pay for about five-hundred words or so packaged into event pop-ups that are just more of the same RNG nonsense as before. I suppose that's all great if you already enjoy the concept, but where the game's appeal originates from I cannot even fathom. I never felt like I was applying much strategy (though I suppose you do with extreme patience), I was never having much fun, and I think my friends enjoy the game more than they would otherwise because of their apparent interest in history (which this game pretends to have a lot of, that being historically accurate gameplay, which is also a complete lie as you'll never truly play the lives of infamous rulers, the game simply isn't even nearly sophisticated enough to achieve such an experience). If you want to learn history, great - but read a book, don't play this game.

Digital Happiness return to Steam with their second game in their popular DreadOut series with Keepers of the Dark. This is not a sequel but rather a standalone horror game that takes place in the same universe as the original. Once again a developer has done a very thorough job in explaining their game in the Steam description so without attempting to repeat everything contained within it I’ll explain my own personal thoughts on the game.
I feel it necessary to compliment Digital Happiness on an outstanding ‘how to play’ feature available from the main menu. It’s a great way to handle a tutorial so that players know the ins and outs of gameplay before they begin so that they can best savor the sensory experience that they are about to embark upon. For those who never played the original and are starting here, which it is entirely possible to do, this is a must read section.
I agree with those who have made the claim that providing skills, abilities and experience points would have added much more variety to the game than what is present. It’s probably the biggest downfall of the game. The other, in my opinion, is the non-SLR camera perspective. I’m not a big fan of the behind the shoulder camera as I feel that it eliminates too much of the potential screen and as you can’t run while in camera mode you can’t get away from that perspective. That said the graphics of the game from an overall perspective are as they should be and help immerse the player into the atmospheric horror experience. However, the combat mechanics desperately need working on.
The actual horror featured within the game is top notch. The jumpscares are well designed and the enemies are a refreshing take on the genre. However, I do have a minor bone to pick with the final boss. I felt that the developers didn’t make it as challenging or as ghastly as what the build up – which began in the original game for those that played it – should have been.
The game has been Steamified with trading cards and ten achievements. This gives you something to aim for within the overall context of the game.
It’s not the best horror game that I’ve had the opportunity to play this year but it is far from the worst. In all, DreadOut: Keepers of the Dark is a middle of the road game that will genuinely appeal to lovers of Asian mythology and certainly to those who have played and enjoyed the original. There is much to appreciate here but many important facets of the game will aggravate players as well. It is worth its modest asking price.

It is really hard to review a game so soon after release, however I can not help but notice the game has improved significantly. Some of the earlier reviews are now missing the real state of the game.
What am I ? I am in a clan of 10 people on a x1 unofficial server. No offline raiding, no avatars. This review is about my experience, not the one of a solo player or in a very small clan, keep that in mind.
To sum up the game, it's basically a better ark.
+ The Good
- Engage in savage PVP, build your base and level up in order to dominate others. No dinos, breaking through bases takes a lot of effort unlike RUST (when you get to stone buildings at least), so the the game revolves about brutal melee combat and killing your enemies on the field.
- More balanced and fun than ARK. No dinos to tame, you won't need to stay 4 hours straight to protect your capture. No dinos will crush all your base in one swipe.
- You have to deal with monsters hunting across the lands, dungeons full of vicious creatures and demons, other exiles... it's quite nice to fight different kind of enemies.
- Conan universe. The game is immersive, you feel like living in a barren, barbarian, desertic world. I like the oriental-themed style. And the thrall system is brillant, that I am sure devs are going to expand.
- The game suffers from lag and rollback issues but the devs managed to make one patch everyday since launch and the game is now in a playable state. It is still early access though, bugs still do exist and it's far from perfect. You would have asked me yesterday if the game was playable I'd have said no. Now this is much better.
- Funcom seems a very serious company and did not disappoint seeing how much work they had put at release, even releasing a patch on sunday. This game has great potential and the devs are more professionals than some other compagnies.
- Levelling takes time but it is not too long either. The XP you get is mostly from combat, so be prepared to kill stuff. I think the devs should rise the EXP you get from crafting.
- The Bad
- As an early access game it is still plagued by bugs, lags etc... so either you are patient and you will like the game for what it has to offer, or you want a game free of all these hussles and you won't like CE at all.
- Melee combat is better than most survival but it is still not as good as pure combat titles such as chivalry, war of the roses etc. You hit, you have to manage your stamina, dodge and you can't parry (you can only block with a shield). The one with the best gear and stats will kill any noob easily.
- Unbalanced. Ranged combat is impossible due to lags and the ridiculous range of bows/xbows, some weapons are far stronger than others etc... and avatars seem far too easy to summon. For now.
- Somehow a lack of content especially at end game.
- Offline raiding is still a thing, so pick an unofficial server that has rules against it if you want to. Otherwise, build on a cliff and destroy your stairs everytime you disconnect. Keep in mind this won't prevent avatars from wiping your bases... Again, choose a server with the ruleset you like.
- As in similar survival titles, there are things easily abused (blocking paths with unbreakable walls, farming people over and over etc...). Keep calm and find a good server...
* Should you buy this ... ?
- If you are patient and understanding of what early access means, ie enduring bugs, lags, wipes etc...
- If you like other survivals games, and want a more balanced experience around PVP.
- If you have a lot of time to play
- If you have people to play with.
Grade of the game : GREAT POTENTIAL.

I need to get a couple of cons out of the way very first:
There are a couple of segments that require you to do a couple of ridiculous things to move the plot forward - things very simple, but made no sense in context, that I got stuck on for 15 minutes at a time. And you'll know exactly what i'm talking about when you get there.
The music just loops over and over again with like 3 or 4 different 20-30 second loops. So it's going to get tiring.
Now with that out of the way, what I can tell you is that this was a very fun, neat, little futuristic sci-fi game. There are two episodes with the 3rd one TBA (Although at this point in time I don't know if it'll ever be made) and each episode will take anywhere from 30min to 1hr max. It's a point and click adventure game, and it tells the story through beautifully drawn anime-esk comic strips. There is no voice acting so you'll have to read everything, but that's ok. It works well.
The story has a couple of "choice branching" options but nothing major or game changing. But it will change dialogue paths slightly.
The story itself revovles around the planet, which is in chaos and is uninhabitable because of a past nuclear war - therefore everybody lives inside of a sealed dome to protect themselves from the outside air/radiation. You have the government who runs the "city" known as the LSF and then the resistance known as the Dissonant Octave.
You join up with the resistance to bring freedom to the world, and end up uncovering a whole lot of conspiracies along the way.
And that ending though, WHAT A TWIST.
All in all It might be worth it at full price if you're really into point and click adventures, but i'd probably wait for a sale at which point it's definitely worth it!

Flying Wild Hog are a developer I've learned to love because of their unrelenting old-school design philosophy. They hand you a variety of interesting and unique weapons, add in a no-nonsense upgrade system, then throw you into a well detailed and absolutely gorgeous world and throw large numbers of fairly challenging enemies at you to overcome until they turn you into a badass. Coming out a year before the equally awesome Shadow Warrior, Hard Reset is an arcadey, clunky first-person romp through a near-future, lightly-cyberpunk city that flew almost completely under the radar.
Much like Shadow Warrior, Hard Reset is a game that puts everything together really well, and gives a strong level of immersion that's missing from most games these days. I caught myself feeling like I was a detective inside a Blade Runner movie, trying to figure out what was going on while fighting off hoards of robots and passing through grimy city streets under the classy neon embankments, which, at times, is a real pleasure.
* The Flying Wild Hog Engine was built specifically for this title and is absolutely gorgeous while still performing really well
* The production value is clearly high, and it feels a lot more solid and well designed than just about any other indie title
* Extremely good content updates and freely released DLC which adds to the game deserve special mention
The settings and characters for this game give a ton of possibility and are really a blank canvas. It's a shame then, that what could've been an extra special experience ended up being merely an above average game due to a very forgettable plot and story and Comic-book intro scenes and good voice acting help the world come alive, but don't add much to the story or suspense.
* Feels like a corridor shooter at times and tends to feel very samey towards the end, despite the wide variety of weapons and upgrades
* For an FPS, it has lacklustre boss fights and a forgettable ending purely because of the lack of consequence, again because of the story
Priced at £9.99/13.49€/$14.99 at the time of review and clocking in at 8 hours gameplay, and with all the new content being released for free, Hard Reset is good value. It's also routinely on sale for as little as $4.99 on Steam and $1.49 from various Indie Bundle retailers.
* There's a fantastic Developer Artbook with characters, landscapes and plenty of concept art which is definitely worth a look.
* There's a free demo available on the Steam Store Page below which gives a good feel for the title

Speedrunners is similar to the name of the game. It's a 2D semi-platformer where you race other players (or bots) around a looping map.
But that's where the standard starts to become different. This game can get very competitive very quickly. There are items, some of which are more over-powered than others. You also have a grappling hook which can cling to certain types of ceilings and swing you forward, with reasonable physics.
All of the maps are indefinitely looping. There is no set number of laps or anything of that sort. The way you win, is by making the other players fall behind too far, so that they get pulled off the screen. If you leave the screen, you're out for the round. If there are other players when the first player is out, or after a set time, the screen will progressively get smaller and smaller to the point where it is about the size of a modern smart-phone. When that happens, a different level of competitive atmosphere and individual skill kicks in.
Speedrunners is an amazing experience that I feel is less popular than it should be.
If you like chaotic, platformers that are very competitive, then pick this one up for sure.

Just because your game has familiar and playable parts doesn't mean you can't combine them in unique ways. Hand of Fate shows as the standout example, taking influence from collectable card games, roguelikes, choose-your-own-adventure novels, and modernized brawler combat to portray something more than the some of its parts.
The conceit is that you're in an endless game with the mysterious dealer, progressing through increasingly dangerous paths through the medium of shuffled cards. You can change these cards before a game to try and give yourself an advantage, or futher discovery by putting in a potentially trecherous encounter for yourself. Just as you can stack the deck, though, the Dealer will stack the deck against you more and more to counter that.
Adventuring through the lands, you can buy equipment drawn from the shuffled-in deck to try and improve yourself, or perhaps grab a blessing to get a futher edge onwards. But you have food to worry about as you explore, keep your supplies fresh or pain and death await.
Challenges tend to come in either a choose-your-own-adventure roleplaying format or a combat/dungeon exploration format. The choose-your-own-adventure ones go through a mini story, often with chance elements that are hard to win. But maybe that's not so much a worry when you're encountering them in the future for as long as you have them in the deck. The combat itself is very familiar if you've played any of the Batman Arkham games or even Dark Souls, as it has the mix of different attacks and additional timed counters to spice up the flow - often focusing on mobs of enemies at once.
There's a sense of style that keeps things held together, whether it be the hammy game master you're playing against, or the mini-stories the adventure challenges give whenever you encounter them. Matter of fact, the chained quest lines in this game added in over time have really made a difference.
I really only have minor niggles with the game, if mainly to do with there being too much reliance on chance or the food survival mechanic being overbearing, but that's really it,
If you're looking for something different that's still extremly approachable and will give you hours of fun while you're at it, look no further. Can't wait for the sequel.

This game is one of the best MMO's I have ever played and I have played very VERY many.
Early game is a little grindy with quests and learning game mechanics such as land ownership, farming / animal husbandry etc. Although it goes by pretty quick.
End game is very rich with this game you have loads of PVP/PVM opportunities with serverwide raids, interesting dungeons and intercontinent/faction warfare. Along with the newest additions of player created and run empires. By empires I mean real empires, stand alone continents built by the players and run by the players.
A quick break down of Pros/Cons
Pros:
Massive class selection with ability to switch classes/skill trees at anytime with no real money only in game currency
Rich PVP experience from 1v1 to small groups to massive scaled battle for territory.
Ultimate sandbox MMO experience with land ownership and literally writing the games history with your gameplay
NO SUCH THING AS GEAR/ITEM SATURATION  this is in my opinion one of the worst things that happens to MMO's is saturation of economy. Gear and high level items as well as gold are all sucked out of the game through mass RNG and a constant need to purchase things from NPC's "perfect gear" is not just a matter of grinding a dungeon for months.
Wonderful Guild/Family/Group/Raid mechanics one of the most streamlined interesting structures for grouping I have seen and yes I said Family. You can declare a family with your friends or real family for that matter which is basically just a smaller grouping if you want to multi guild but still pretty cool
Combat is one of the most polished and excellent experiences I have ever had and somehow they manage to actually balance 130+ class combinations. Now yes there are some class combinations that just don't perform to standard with some of the more popular ones but that is mostly classes that don't have much synergy.
Ability to buy in-game subcription using in game gold see cons for details
The ability to do WHATEVER you want you can literally go the entire game without ever interacting with PVP or even heavy PVM for that matter. Yeah a few mobs at the start of the game but you can literally just be a carebear farmer and actaully be really useful.
Vehicular excellence. Sure MMO's have mounts of different types but you will never find yourself walking in this game once you've reached late game. With gliders, mounts, airships, public transit wagons, cars, motorized longboards, tractor like vehicles, boats, galleons etc. etc. the list grows. With each of these their own uses and mechanics. Naval warfare. I wish I could go into more detail but I don't want to write a whole page on nothing but vehicles this is long enough.
Cons
Some pay to win aspects with ability to buy in-game items that allow non-subscribers to buy subscription using the item thus putting "gold buying" into the game double edged sword though as aforementioned in pros I think this is a pretty common thing in most MMO's though
Too many choices. It is hard to stick with a class and although you can be any class at anytime and switch as much as you would like getting optimal gear for each of those classes is difficult and takes a lot of time. Rendering multiclassing in an optimal PVP set up difficult
Lots of chance for griefing. There are many ways to grief but this is a side effect of being so sandboxy. People can and will steal/destroy your things if youre not careful. That being said you can avoid this relatively easily.
TL;DR Whiney kids don't belong here, PVP is not P2W they're mostly just bad. Gorgeous asthetics, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic gameplay substantial world worth a play.

Reccomended to me by so many people, I finally got around to playing Owlboy. And if I had to explain it in one word, it would be: "polished".
This game is not only beautiful to look at with its "hi-bit" graphics, you will definitely notice the orchestral score. The characters are a bunch of loveable outcasts, flying around with Owlboy feels great and the game has a fair share of awesome moments. It rewards people who like to just mess around and discover - not only with collectibles, but also with minigames and even emotional scenes. None of that is compulsory, you can finish the game just rushing through it, yet it is breathtaking how much care and attention to detail went into this game.
If you have 20 bucks to spare, you really can't go wrong with Owlboy. It's a lot of fun and while it felt a bit short - it was more like I didn't want it to end yet. I'll definitely come back to it someday and wholeheartedly reccomend it to anyone.

This review is for the game ''Crysis Warhead'',a first-person shooter video game,developed by the video game company Crytek(Budapest).
The game was published by Electronic Arts and released in Semptember 16 on 2008(in North America) for Microsoft Windows.The game uses the CryEngine 2.The game is only available for Microsoft Windows.
Plot
You are Michael "Psycho" Sykes,a former British SAS Sergeant and member of the Raptor Team,a squad of mostly American soldiers who are invested suits with advanced technology.The story takes place on the other side of the island in which the original game <<Crysis>> is set and after you split up with Nomad(the main protagonist of the first installment) you go hunting the Koreans.Psycho has to engage through numerous of tasks and orders throughout the game in order to discover a container which envelops an alien war machine.You will have to secure that container(in some point you lose it)and kill a big bad alien (a Red Hunter) and you proceed to the exctraction.A last attempt (cinematic) is being made by Colonel Lee to accumulate the container,a fight scene follows but he fails and gets thrown off the ship leaving him to the mercy of a massive alien warship.O'Neill takes off with the container, as Psycho kicks back.
Character:As it has been stated you take control of a former British SAS Sergeant and member of the Raptor Team,Michael "Psycho" Sykes whom only from his code name (Psycho) you can understand that he is not the most conventional obedient military soldier.Even though he acts all tough and macho he does not take the life of a Korean(stating he was unarmed) and that wouldn't be fair.But as the story progress he watches his crew mate die helplessly,he snaps and kills by drowning a defenseless Korean soldier.After that he becoms a killing machine,always sticking to the mission and after he destroys the alien forces he successfully retrieves the container and leaves alongside O'neil having completed his mission.
Gameplay:Updated and refined gameplay of the original game.Newer graphics engine(CryEngine 2).Includes all the standart weapons from the original game with the addition of futuristic weapon builds,the introduction of Mini-SMGs which you can dual wield,EMP grenades and the PAX weapon which will be used on the destruction of the exoskeleton of the Red Hunter(last boss).
Multiplayer:The game comes with <<Crysis Wars>> ,a multiplayer mode.Even if this game is 6 years old you'll be surprise to see how many people still play crysis 1.
Recap:Like it's predecessor this game is a must buy.Breath-taking graphics,simple yet enjoyable story,challenging gameplay and exceptional first person shooter elements weave the greatness of this game.Only thing i dislike is that it's really smal.Took me only 6 hours to finish the whole game.I guess if you go around the map and kill everything it could last about 8-10 hours.Maybe more.
Thank you Crytek Developers for this wonderful game.
P.S If you are into the game's story you will like this game even more(like that's possible).Throughout the game you can listen audio clips from four years ago which explain a lot about the original game <<Crysis>> even about the successor <<Crysis 2>>.I am not going to say anything more.Buy the game,play it thoroughly and find out yourself :D

A shorter, honed in take on Crysis, Warhead delivers a slightly tweaked take on the original game in a more linear, but excitement packed expansion.
There's a distinct change in tone between Crysis and Warhead and whilst the game largely plays the same, having a more vocal and at the very least charismatic main character gives Warhead a more personal touch than Crysis ever had. Coupled with gameplay changes, from minor changes to suit usage for increased usability and general effectiveness as well as overall level and encounter design, there's a different experience available here. It is much more focused on what it wants to deliver and does so at the expense of vast open enviroments, but not so much that there isn't plenty of room for you to breathe and negotiate the areas you're in. There's a perhaps greater emphasis on action as you're carried from encounter to encounter, but this generally feels like an improvement over potentially mundane driving sequences in the original.
The only major criticism I have of the game is its length. Whilst it maintains a brisk pace from start to finish, it does end after not too long a play-time, howerver it doesn't feel like a let down given its approach as a sort of side-quest from the main game. Of questionable worth in of itself, as an addition to Crysis it provides a really fun accompliament such that if the original was of interest, Warhead should certainly not be ignored.

Jack is a member of the local force, in a world where downtown is equal to a prison, at least, for the upper citizens, not aware of the reality. However, one day, his pregnant wife got killed in an explosion and he never recovered from that. Now ousted from the force, he's contacted by the same terrorists that need his help. Is what Jack always believed in really the truth?
Return NULL is an episodic adventure game in a dystopian world, where those living downtown are oppressed by the authorities, without really a perspective to survive and with the truth being hidden to the upper citizens (though they can be thrown down to what is described as a prison/jail). The story is interesting as we meet Jack before the death of his wife and after he's ousted from the forces because of the depression that followed. While Jack wants revenge, he's convinced that maybe the truth isn't the truth and is now ready to take down the society he once swore to protect. Everything is centered around plans of a bomb, even in the second episode.
However, I will only concentrate on the first episode as the second is available as a DLC and I will not spoil it. So, this introduction is interesting as you're leading a depressed yet determined Jack in the streets of this upper part of the city, not realizing of what is really happening down there (Jack himself isn't really sure of what to find, even if he knows the truth about it) or being afraid of the local forces, as people are taken and never seen to return.
The gameplay is a point-&-click game: you speak with people, you interact with them, you find items, you solve puzzles. There is nothing extraordinary added to Return NULL on that point and it's working perfectly. However, as it's a game with choices to make, you can expect some impact on the story (nothing really major, apart on the dialogues). It's just the way you will behave with people and how you will blame yourself on your wife's death. Besides, you can be met with a gameover as you have some action in the game.
What I liked in that game is also the graphics. I loved how the characters are depicted in a comic style. However, there is no real animation in the game. You're just in a static background. Jack isn't moving around, you're just pointing on where to go or where to interact and it's done like that, like in a casual adventure/hidden object games.
I also liked the soundtrack. However, there are no voice acting. You just read the dialogues as in a comic book.
I really liked this first episode though I found it short, even if some parts of it seems long (but it's the time taken to find how to solve some parts). It was a good premise for the story to come and for the price, it's not a waste of money - at least, for the first episode. I'm giving you a warning ahead for episode 2: I don't know what happened but it wasn't as good as this one.
I'm still waiting for episode 3 to make a conclusion for the whole series....

A fantastic but short first person shooter if you wish to kill some time. This game adapts some elements from old school first person shooters such as Quake. There's no reloading, no objective markers telling you where to go, no in game scripted cutscenes, and best of all, no regenerating health. I got in game on sale for $1.49 from bundle stars. It was definitely worth it without a doubt. But if you're expecting an fantastic Oscar award winning story from this game, you're not going to get any. Personally, when it comes to fps games, I for one do not care about storytelling aside from Halo and perhaps Bioshock, because when it comes to fps, I want experience whatever action the games deliver, which this game definitely does. There's action in every step of the way.
But in case, you're curious, the game storyline honestly makes no sense, but like I said, who cares. You play as Major James Fletcher, some kind of cop, soldier, detective guy who has to fight his way through this futuristic looking city of Japan known as Bezoar through hordes of corrupt machines. To be honest, you're going to fighting the same exact machines over and over to the point where you might be bored of them. But don't worry, after the confusing ending from the 2nd boss fight, you will get to play the Exile Dlc, which will the continue the story.
Gameplay wise, like I said, you have to pick up health and ammo, which is what I prefer a lot in first person shooters. There are 2 weapons to carry but you can keep upgrading them to do amazing things such as turning your assault rifle into a shotgun and shoot pellets that stun enemies.
Above all, Hard Reset is a nice looking, fast paced first person shooter which you barely see nowadays. It's very short and you can beat in just a day so get it when it's on sale. If you enjoy classic styles in fps games, then pick up this game.

Hand of Fate is a very unique game that combines a story rich "Choose your own adventure" RPG, with deck building elements, and Batman/Shadow of Mordor encounters and combat.  Also did I mention it’s a roguelike as well?
One would assume this to be a disaster in the making with all these features vying for the players attention, but in reality it is an oddly perfect fit.
While you play the game against your foe, the Dealer who takes delight in commenting on almost every action you do.  Once again another potential recipe for disaster averted due to the crisp excellent voice performance that sets a strange level of immersion where it indeed feels like a game within a game.  The dealer always has something witty, interesting, deep, or teasing to say about every card that is played.  He even catches on to certain situations like where he happens to notice you milking a card for all its worth in multiple plays, or makes note on your lack or abundance of certain resources.  There’s so much dialogue that not only does it remain fresh; it paints a 2nd story reflecting the lore of the main game, not just the one you are playing.
The music is quite good, though the tracks are limited and you will find yourself hearing the same battle song over and over again.  The game is a good deal for what it is and you will find yourself playing game after game as the difficulty starts to ramp up to unfair levels of play.  Since it is in part a game of chance, it is certainly something you will have to accept. Despite being from 2008 - this game still looks beautiful.  It's a real pleasure to hide within the lush jungles of the island.  You really do feel like you are in a real forest.  Turtles included. !!
The gameplay of crysis is pure FPS nirvana.  The weapons are pretty cool but they need a little more reactivity and rebound.  Sometimes it seems like enemies are being tazered rather than blown away by a big gun.  It leaves you in the middle of gameplay wondering if they really have gone down permanently or just received a gentle blast.
But gameplay is enjoyable and the shotgun has the desired effect at close quarters.  Grenades are also effective and realistic.  The very best weapon is the experimental gun you receive at the end of the game.  It totally destroys the large alien floaters and their smaller counter parts.  One shot does the job.
It would have been fantastic to have this beast of destruction earlier on in the game.  But - it isn't.
I love Crysis.  I hate multi player centered games and I only enjoy the single player campaigns and crytek give you a decent chunk of gameplay.  Varied and interesting.
The voice acting is generally very good but the main character's voice does not match his appearance.  It isn't terribly out of place but it didn't match up.  But the main character actor does an excellent job.  There are a couple of shameful acting moments but they are generally few and far between.
Crysis is everything we want in a FPS.  Big guns and aliens and tactical planning in the moments of gameplay - mean you can be creative in silently sneaking up on your opponents or go in with guns blazing.
I really enjoyed blowing up the armoured vehicles but sometimes got confused with their selections in the menu.  It meant that I sometimes blew myself up - mistaking the detonator in my hand for another explosive.
The speed mode of the suit isn't really that fast - I thought it would really make the character zip across airfields or swamps but it is kind of sluggish.
Perhaps a few seconds more in the cloak energy mode would have been nice.  It runs out VERY quickly and left my behind clearly visible to enemies as I tried to reach that last hiding place.  But that in itself is quite thrilling and led to some funny situations.
Crysis warhead is a really cool game and I heartily recommend it.   8/10

ME2 is an excellent sci-fi RPG.  It's not perfect, but the story, the universe and characters are generally well done, and the third-person shooter gameplay is quite satisfactory.  Would strongly recommend playing ME1 first to get the full experience!
+A decent cast of characters.  Some old friends from ME1, and some really cool new guys (MORDIN!)
+Great universe, rich with lore learned from the characters as well as supplementary information from the Codex
+Lets you make important choices through dialogue, and also quick time events (aka "interrupts") during dialogue!
+Nice variety of weapons that are distinct from each other, and no hassle of inventory management
+Combat is fun, with the option of pausing at any time to give orders to teammates and cast abilities
+As before, a nice variety of abilities ranging from tech, mass-manipulating, and pure combat
+Gotta love the humor in this game.  Some of your teammates can get rather snarky.  Even the dialogue between no-name citizens changes whenever you pass by them, and they talk about the darndest things.
+Do your choices matter in the long run?  Are your teammates' opinions of you really that important?  Trust me, they are.  Try not to cry.
-Resource gathering minigame for upgrades, etc. is boring.  Most, if not all of it should have been accomplished in missions
-Level design is linear, and can get somewhat boring.  Some of the major planets were quite disappointing because of how they limited your travelling to only mission-designated areas.
-One of the dumbest plot holes I have ever seen in a game. It deserves its own bullet point.  I'm referring to
Seriously, such lazy writing.  Only for that part, though.
-While some of the new characters were interesting, others felt like re-hashes of characters from the first game, or just plain bland.

At the moment, I'd say it's only decent. But I would highly recommend buying Euro Truck Simulator 2 instead for the moment, as it comes with much more content.
ATS has good feeling to it and driving around is still as enjoyable as it was in ETS2, but it's really limited until more locations come out and it has it's share of flaws too.. Mostly when it comes to traffic jams, since most of the traffic lights are really badly designed and sometimes AI cars get stuck forever, also in city areas you feel like you are being stopped by every single light there is, instead of having well flowing traffic if you drive within the speed limits, like they are in real life in most places.
Another critique I'd give for the lack of speed signs and that they are way too small to even see.. As a person who likes to play these kind of games from simulator perspective, I hate having to watch the GPS all the time. It makes the game feel more like a game where you follow lines and numbers, instead of being truck simulator where you are supposed to a "feeling of driving a truck".
The best addition to the game is ability to customize GPS route for yourself, and even tho it's a minor complain, I'd love if the default way to make route would be from first to last, the game defaults to you choosing the route in backwards order (you can select to flip it in game, so it's not a big deal, you just have to do it every time), so I would like if it would remember your selection, on how you like to plan your route (I personally use it for collecting roads that I haven't been driving yet, and it works decently well..)
Also I would like it if you could see what routes you have been driving and what you haven't from under the suggested GPS route, but at the moment it blocks the road completely until you drive past it. This has been also problem in ETS2, but it's not that big of a deal. Especially since you can customize your routes now from the scratch.
Overall, I would recommend this game for anyone who already has ETS2 and has grown bored of it, but I would also recommend waiting until it gets way more states than it currently has.

If you can find my user review for the original Crysis I noted how the quality of its level design seems to fall off a cliff later in the campaign. A lot of other people will probably tell you this too. Warhead feels as if Crytek made it specifically to address that problem. It’s pretty much a more tightly-designed package of Crysis levels with a couple new weapons and vehicles.
If you were actually interested in what the original Crysis game’s story was about I don’t know what to say, but Warhead’s is slightly better. It’s kind of like the difference between Predator and The Rock respectively, the latter being slightly less cheesy, but still bombastic in its own way. Warhead follows Psycho (the British guy) and features a somewhat decently played-out character arc between him and a new supporting character. That’s all I think I can really say about it.
Aside from the original game’s suit powers, a new grenade launcher, EMP grenades which weaken nanosuit-equipped enemies (who are far more common in this expansion) but you as well, drivable APCs, and a couple new kinds of mounted gun, Warhead’s selling point is its superior level design compared to the original game. Luckily the level designers managed to stay strong throughout.
Crysis is a game that, behind its graphics, is hailed for open-ended mission design reminiscent of GoldenEye or Thief with huge maps. Ironically, almost all Warhead’s missions are pretty linear compared to the first game’s. But it manages to be linear without feeling like a Call of Duty-style corridor. It’s a very “wide” sort of linear.
The first mission ends with an open-ended base infiltration similar to some levels from Crysis, but after that everything is technically a straight line that still manages to give you a lot of options in how you play the game. The vehicle chase sequence immediately following that infiltration somehow doesn’t feel like a scripted event but instead simply has you follow a target within an open area. This is followed by what is, actually, a pretty well-done boss fight to contrast with the first game’s mediocre final boss. Afterwards there’s a section inside a battleship where Crytek actually manages to play some scripting tricks on you without automatically controlling the camera or putting you in a quick time event or anything. It’s almost more Half-Life 2 than Black Ops in this way. Warhead makes even its literal tunnels dynamic enough to let players have a say in how they tackle each combat situation, including a train section.
Visually, Warhead looks slightly better than the original Crysis but hasn’t had nearly as many mods made for it. Fortunately Crytek actually tried to optimize Warhead a bit so for most people the game should run better than Crysis. Warhead’s highest graphical features also aren’t locked behind DirectX 10.
Compared to the first Crysis, Warhead is kind of like the same meal with the same ingredients but prepared more diligently after the chef got some experience.

Crysis Warhead is the official expansion for Crysis, set from the perspective of "Psycho", your Jason Statham look-alike on Team Raptor.
Graphically speaking, the game runs a bit smoother than Crysis, but this is largely because of a lower default LOD scaling distance which results in more pop-in and lower res textures, generally speaking. Not terribly annoying, but graphics nerds will be very upset. What is upsetting is the persistent memory leak problem that I had with the game, which I have confirmed others have as well. Scope in lag, quick turning lag, lag in vehicle segments and cutscenes all result from an overloading of RAM with leaky memory. It needs to be patched.
Gameplay wise, it is largely an improvement, with the introduction of many great new features. New weapons, such as the grenade launcher and sidearm smg, AT mines, claymores, and more. New vehicles, like light apcs/recon vehicles with mini-guns and 20mm cannons, and new em-placed weapons as well. The auto ammo pick up feature is very welcome, especially seeing as it also allows you to pick up scopes and attachments automatically. Level design is good, allowing stealth and assault paths for taking down objectives, except when it isn't. Driving missions feature heavy forced action and no stealth, and are confusingly and sometimes inadequately designed. In addition, the game is generally more linear than it's predecessor.
The story is ok, but it's nothing special, focusing on what Psycho did between Crysis' "Assault" mission and the return to the carrier. His ultimate goal is track down what first appears to be a nuke but later is revealed to be an intact alien marauder corpse. The side story which involves Psycho's relationship to a pilot named O'Niell is a bit iffy, but has a good ending ultimately. I was not a fan of 3rd person cutscenes in Warhead, as the 1st person ones in Crysis were some of my favorites. I understand that Nomad is the main character of the series, not Psycho, and that's why this is done, but considering the majority of the game is played in first person anyway...
Ultimately though, Warhead delivers more incredible Crysis gameplay in an incredible visual package, from a refreshing perspective. There are just a few hitches along the way.

First off let me start by saying that I love the concept and I really liked Euro Trucker 2.. I've been waiting a long time for the American version because.. well I live in America.  The game its self is basically the same thing as Euro Trucker 2 which is perfectly fine (read reviews about the Euro version for in-depth info) but there are 2 things that cause me to down vote the American version of the game:
1.  Why start on the west coast for the first release?  That's about as far as you can get from what real trucking is like in the US.  California is a bunch of tree hugging hippies, massive conjestion, liberal regulations that making trucking there a joke.  You can't even drive classic trucks in that state because of their insane laws so why choose that to start off in?  I would have much rather have seen the midwest, south, even the east coast for the first version.  I've driven all over the US and California is about the last state I would have stated with.
2.  The 1st one was more of me ♥♥♥♥♥ing, this one though is really why I downvote the game.  The developer made the decision to change the scale of the game in the American version which blows my mind.  I can't understand why they would do this as logically it makes no sense.  In the Euro version when you drive from country to country it feels like you are long hauling.. I'm not saying that I spend hours in front of the computer for 1 route but you do get the experience that you really are trucking.  In the American version when you drive from LA to San Deigo you can barley get the truck up to speed before you arrive at your destination.. to be honest it's really bizzare.
It seems to me that the developers think that the 'fun' in this game is backing up the truck to unload and going from stop light to stop light when you arrive at a town.. and that's not the case at all.  The real fun in this game is being on the open road, having your radio tuned to some red neck station and chilling out drinking a beer trucking down the high way... that's what it's all about.  The Euro version had this, the American version doesn't come close.
The scale change for America was a big let down, yes I know that if they kept the same scale that they had in the Euro version that it may have taken a few hours to drive from the west coast to the coast.. but honestly that's not a bad thing.    People who are crazy enough to do that, more power to them... that's long hauling in America and trust me there is plenty to see that would have justified the content being created (DLC, more money for them).  As it stands now I think the developer missed a huge oppurtunity to take advantage of the US market but not understanding it's love for driving and the potential revenue that could have been captialized on.

Do you like Final Fantasy Tactics or the Ogre Battle series? Do you enjoy XCOM? Do you like anime? If you answer "yes" to any of those questions, you owe it to yourself to try this amazing game. Particullarly so if you enjoy turn based tactics game. So, what's so good about this game? Let's dig right into it.
1. STYLE: This is, probably, the most obvious feature of this game. It looks incredible. Cel-shaded graphics tend to age way better than realistic ones, and even though this is a PS3 era game, the graphics are extremely pleasant to look at even today. The game mixes celd-shaded characters with an anime look with a beautiful kind-of-grpahite-looking aesthethic that's just a joy to behold at every time.
2. SETTING AND STORY: Let's state this: the story is good. Let's frame this statemente: the story is good for a JRPG title. It's, of course, plagued with tropes you've seen a million times before, and almost every character has that one defining characteristic that makes his or her entire personality. Unlike other japanese anime-inspired games, however, this is not a major issue since it's not overplayed, and the story presented here keeps a very serious and even mature tone at times. Since this is technichally a "war" game, it's refreshing to play a teen-oriented game that doesn't shy away from complicated subjects such as death and racism. Don't get me wrong: it's still a japanese, anime-stylized and teen oriented game, which means fanservice, stupid over the top♥♥♥♥♥♥like Valkyrias doing flips over tanks and overly-dramatic dialogue, but, for what it is, it could have been so much worse.
3. GAMEPLAY: This, in my opinion, is the defining feature of this game. Gameplay is thight as it can be. Simple in its basis - thus, easier to explain to a newbie - but very deep on the long run. The game is divided in two major parts: your headquarters, where you level up your units and equip them with whatever new stuff you've developed, and the proper action scenarios, which are played out in turns. During your turn you position your units, move them around the map trying to get to vantage points or hiding areas and then attack the enemy, trying, most of the time, to take their camps and win the map, while the enemy tries to do the same to you. Both systems complement each other very well and you get a real sense of becoming more and more like a seasoned millitary man the more you advance in the story. The most important part, though, is  that the game never feels boring or repetitive, even though you're basically doing the same thing over and over. Since it's so well paced, you never feel like being "cheated". I've played in the Hard difficulty and it certainly is hard. I've had to replay many maps multiple times, trying to get the "perfect" combination of units and positioning in order to advance. It's challenging, rewarding and I've never felt like it was cheap.
4. VARIETY: The game never feels stale because it's always throwing new stuff at you withouth being overwhelming. No map is played exaclty like the one before. I remeber one map where I had to stop this massive, gigantic tank, taking out its turrets from a distance and then disabling it's engines, WHILE stalling it with debris on the field, WHILE running away from a psychotic killing machine that was constantly on my heels. Another map tasked me with killing two smaller, yet still gigantic mortar-spewing tanks located at both edges of the map, WHILE avoiding constant mortar fire, WHILE dealing with respawning snipers on the ledges above my camp, WHILE trying to contain their infantry so they didn't occupy my base camp. I had to replay both maps at least 3 times before I realized where to move and how to counter each of the many different threats that kept popping up. This makes each map feel very intense and packed with obstacles, which is why I never play more than one or two at a time. Yet, when you finally manage to overcome adversity and win, it feels incredibly rewarding.
5. EXCELLENT PORT: 1080 HD resolution, has both keyboard and controller support, keeps both the original japanese and english audio files with subtitles, can create different save files. Nothing to say, one of the best PC ports I've seen.
6. LONGEVITY: Each match can last from 10 minutes to 60 minutes, depending on your playstyle and the different objectives. This makes it a game that's better appreciated by playing it in spurs instead of one long sitting.

Owlboy is one of (if not the) pinnacle of pixel art in video games. Playing Owlboy feels like playing a genuine piece of art, in both its painfully detailed visuals, charming designs, and FANTASTIC orchestral soundtrack (played by an actual orchestra!). Owlboy is a joy to look at and listen to, and the story/concepts are fun (although the plot takes a while to pick up), and for that I would definitely recommend it.
However, I won't lie and tell you that its gameplay is anything close to groundbreaking or amazing. The gameplay is not bad so much as it is simple. Since the core mechanic that makes it somewhat different to other 2D sidescrollers is that you can fly, there isn't much platforming. Instead there is more focus on puzzles and spammy shoot-em-up combat, but neither of these are very complex at all. The earlier puzzles are trivially easy, and combat doesn't pose much of a challenge outside of a a couple pretty good boss fights. I say 'earlier' because I feel the gameplay as a whole picks up in the last third of the game or so.
Definitely check out Owlboy if you are looking for an awe-inspiring graphical and musical experience, but don't expect much of a challenge from its gameplay.

August 2015 review of this fine title.
This is a four-player game based around running through a maze-like course faster than your opponents. Obstacles are all over the place, switches change the map layouts, pickups can help change the course of the race. Think Mario Kart, but without laps, where the objective would be to make everybody else crash. Graphics are tight, gameplay is crisp, sound is good. That's the positive.
The negative is that this game works best with an active community. It's really fun if you're playing with friends. But if you're looking for online multiplayer, it might be too late to have a good time. You're reading a review of a game with 8,000+ positive reviews but a daily active playerbase in the range of ~500 players. This may change if/when SpeedRunners exits Early Access, but based on the player count histories of other titles on Steam, I'm not sure I'd count on it.
For: People with friends, fans of Mario Kart.
Not for: People who mostly play single player games.

Let's write a review on this. An ongoing one, editing it as I play it more and more.
The game is an indie attempt to immitate Fatal Frame experience.
It promises a horror experience and I can't describe how strict I am on this genre.
I love horror and I can't find many games that can absorb me into their reality and also make me feel horror.
So is it good? Let's see.
The controls are not so good. The sprites are also not nice, only the main character is really sophisticated.
Voice acting is bad. Seriously. What saves the game from being a disaster, is that most of the horror time, is not in those voice acting scenes.
The sound has also some issues.
It is obvious that the game has many flaws.
Like the flowing water on the graveyard, in the begining of the game.
The riddles are not well set and many players will probably have a hard time to solve the first one.

Nothing was fitting well, not the gameplay, not the music, not the surrounding fx, not the sound fx, not the gameplay, neither the mechanics no nothing. I can't even figure out if there is a scenario. I just woke up somehere and that's how the game begins. Really? Oh well they might unravel some of the scenario later.
And I was right, I reached the abandoned school. And it was there that I pooped bricks.
No I am dead serious. For some reason, the music, the atmosphere, the graphics, the sound fx, the enemies, the gameplay mechanics, all of a sudden all the elements merge together very well, in a way that they make me feel threatened. Yes it isn't perfect, it's far from it, but it delivers when it comes to fear, because I am used to horror. I am not getting scared easily.  They managed to scare me, it is good enough for me.

To be a bit more honest, that game suffers from 4 very bad problems :
- the enemies are all faster than you. You can sprint to bypass that peculiar issue, but given that you can only sprint forward, that the levels are quite small, and that you can't shoot while sprinting, it's basically useless,
- the levels are very beautiful, but sadly, they are filled with invisible walls. Graphically, you're moving in a futuristic town, but in fact, the game could just be a bunch of rooms and corridors,
- I do not know how explosions are programmed, but a wall will never protect you from an explosion. I did the test of hiding myself in a container (three walls and a roofs) and yet I still took damage from explosions,
- and the most annoying problem : that blur each time you get hit. No matter if that missile took 75HP or one, your screen will get blurred, making it impossible to see how your health is. And if you're ganged up on by enemies, you're done for. They'll constantly knockback you and kill you extremely quickly.
Otherwise, enemies are fairly challenging, with a very decent tracking (that's a nice way to say "you'll fail almost every evade and get charged by that giant angry robot"), but your weapons are diverse and powerful enough to not turn the fights into a chore.

This action-packed, challenging FPS is very reminiscent of Croteam's legendary Serious Sam games where you are swarmed by dozens of enemies almost at any given time and you need to shoot through hoards and hoards of robots who are hell-bent over tearing your insides out.
BUT, unlike Serious Sam games, the levels in which you fight these ever increasing number of enemies are MUCH more confined and closed when compared to the former game's large, arena like levels. This will probably lead to a lot of frustration as you barely have any room to maneuver around dozens of enemies running towards you or shooting at you. It doesn't help much that the main character runs so slow and his running dash is so short and pathetic it doesn't help at all. Therefore dodging enemy attacks becomes a game of sheer luck rather than skill.
Another negative thing for me in this game was the weapons system. You have 2 main weapons that can be upgraded to embody more shooting modes for different situations (e.g. your standard assault rifle can be upgraded to also accompany a rocket luncher and a shotgun etc.) The problem arises when you are in the heat of battle and need to switch between different weapons in order to utilize their abilities in combat situations. Since this is a fast and frentic game very similar to older shooters, it becomes really awkward to switch from a weapon to another one and THEN selecting the desired shooting mode with the mouse wheel. Sometimes you barely have time to think because of all the chaos happening on screen and switching guns can lead to untimely deaths.
The graphics look gorgeous albeit repetitive. The DLC included extends the base game by a few levels which look different and are a welcome addition to the abruptly ending vanilla game.
Sound and music are very nicely done and fit the action perfectly.
You should definitely not expect any coherent story in this game. This is a action shooter at heart and doesn't give two pennies about storyline.
Make sure you use environmental explosives and traps as much as you can because they will save your life and help you defeat the baddies with more ease.
All in all, I can describe this game as Serious sam in the future and with much more cramped, tight levels. It'll take around 10 hours to beat counting the Exile DLC. Base game will take around 6 hours to complete. It got a bit repetitive for me halfway through because all you are basically doing is pushing switches to get to the next area to kill more enemies. there are a couple of boss fights that are amusing if nothing else.
If you know what you're going in for, then expect your adrenaline glands to pump non stop. This is a very solid shooter that knows what it wants to be and what it wants to do is take you back to the sweet haydays of golden shooters of past while relentlessly challenging you with every encounter. A casual gamer will find passing some of the levels pretty hard.

At the time of writing this review I have nearly 200 hours invested into this game. Please understand, this does not happen. I'm the kind of guy who MIGHT get a dozen hours out of a single-player game, MAYBE 30 if it's an RPG.  But to think that I can get 200 hours or more out of a single-player game is crazy. So what is it about this game?
1: The history.  If you are even considering this game you must have some interest in history.  Most people, including myself, didn't know much about the middle ages other than castles, knights, and christians killing muslims killing christians.  But Crusader Kings II shows you so much more: There are the Vikings to the north, the Picts in what would become Scotland, there are Leon, Castile, Aragon, and other minor kingdoms that would someday become Spain, the Muslim presence on the Iberian Peninsula, the Orthodox Byzantines facing Catholics on one side and Muslims on the other, even the Indian kingdoms that existed during that period.
2: The alternate history.  This is definitely the biggest selling point.  Sure, you could start as a duke in the British Isles, form the kingdom of England, and then just duke it out with France for the next 400 years. Or, you could go out and conquer the entirety of Catholic Europe, assimilate the Germanic Saxons and Norse, show the Byzantines the error of their ways (with the pointy end of your sword) crusade against the heathen Muslims and even take India for good measure.  So much detail has gone into the potential for kingdoms that were just a mino blip on history's radar.  You can play as the Byzantines and reform the Roman Empire as well are re-unite the two branches of Christianity.  You can have a Jewish ruler who re-conquers Jerusalem, re-forms the Kingdom of Israel, and rebuilds the Temple of Solomon to usher in a golden age of prosperity for the Jewish people. You can even reform a pagan religion such as Germanic to bring it on par with the mainstream monotheistic religions.
3. The variation.  You will never see the AI play two games the same way.  Take France for example.  In the Charlemagne starting point, France starts split into two kingdoms, Western Francia and Middle Francia. In some games, the two empires will merge to form the Empire of Francia.  Other times, They will combine with Italy to form the Holy Roman Empire. And still others, they will be wracked with so many rebellions that they will splinter into a half-dozen smaller kingdoms.  Likewise, the Byzantines or the Abbasids (the major Muslim power) can expand and expand and expand, or fall apart at the seams. The game has endless playability because you CAN NOT play the same game twice.
Now, if you're still considering whether to get this game, understand that you will EASILY invest 50 or more hours before even getting a grip on the basics. As of writing this, I just had to restart a game I played for 20 hours easlily because of a bad choice in when to turn from tribal government to feudalism.  But I'm still learning about the game, even with 200 hours. I've sat in this chair for 12 hours straight at times, that's how good this game is. But understand that it is quite a hefty time investment, it's not something you can play for 15 or 20 minute sittings.
