A slick, gritty, and fast paced shooter. Brilliantly combines simple and manic old school play with an impressive upgrade system. And there is a RIDICULOUS amount of environment destruction that is both useful in combat and pretty to watch explode.

Most negative comments are about the combat. I assure you these people also hate Dark Souls, Ninja Gaiden, and probably Batman games too. They are used to the hand holding in the many modern games and hate a challenge.
Without a doubt it can be very tough, but it is fair. If you are fast and smart you can survive just about any encounter. The fighting gives you very generous slow motion moments to decide whenever you want to counter, dodge or attack in the moment. It becomes difficult when you are facing multiple enemies and a boss, but all of them have tactics. You will encounter these bosses again and again, and you learn them. Eventually you'll know all the tricks and all the moves that AI will have in stock for you and you'll develop your own strategies of dealing with them.
Cons: If you are looking for a game that will let you build a god deck with all the best items and will let you blow through all the encounters, this isn't for you. Your deck building influences the kind of experience you are going to have, but it doesn't make you powerful. There is always a lot of chance involved.
This game is well worth it's full value.

Wow, where do I begin?
First off, Larian Studios is a company who respects the people who play their games.  Did you notice the price of the game?  Did you also notice that shiny Divine Edition with the awesome artwork and music?
I know that one thing I didn't notice was a bunch of content locked behind a paywall (Destiny has me jaded at this point).
DoS2 as a game respects the players more so than any game I've played since the good old Morrowind or Baldur's Gate days.  The way you explore this world they've crafted for you is completely up to you, because Larian Studios are a company who *respects* the way you want to play their game.  Any number of the bizarre scenarios you may find yourself in during the potentially 100+ hours of content can be reacted to with an equally large number of solutions.  You will get as much out of it as you invest into it, creativity will get you a long ways and will feel very rewarding.
The voice acting is wonderful, and every NPC in the game is fully voiced.  Even the narrator is voiced, the only lines that won't be read to you are the things you select to say for yourself (which is standard).  You really get the feeling that the NPCs have a life of their own and that the world is moving on with or without you.  The marks you leave on the world are very real, every monster/creature/villain/person you slay will never be back.  You may walk through the area much later and expect some battle with skeletons that you remembered from before, but this isn't Pokemon.  Once you kill something it never comes back.  Including you.
Perma-death is handled interestingly in DoS2, your character can die like any other, permanently.  It's got something akin to the D&D equivalent of resurrection with scrolls and spell you can buy from some vendors.  They won't be affordable for at least 10-20 hours into the game however, if you find yourself frequently dying in the first 10 hours of the game expect to empty your coffers on resurrection scrolls instead of that shiny sword you've been eying. Combat always feels really good, and there's unlimited creativity you have when you're going about it.  The environment is entirely interactive.  Want to use a barrel as cover?  Sure. Screw the barrel, I'll make it rain and freeze the ground and then combine my boots with nails in the crafting menu, now they're slipping all over the place but I can walk around like a champ.  Or sneak through the fight all together.  Or talk your way out.  There's so many ways to handle it.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game.  I've beaten it with about 65 hours but I was playing with no companions and with a Lone Wolf perk, there were SO many things I didn't see.  I've got 6 campaigns in progress and I'm still finding new stuff every day.  You'll thank yourself for getting this game.

Murdered: Soul Suspect’s first red herring comes five minutes in. As dead detective Ronan O’Connor, you are promised an enormous and exciting ghostly skillset with which to solve complex crimes, right wrongs, and gain unbridled access to the real-world town of Salem, Massachusetts. But by the time the credits roll, that promise has only been partially fulfilled. Being a ghost in Murdered is enjoyable in fits and starts, yet the use of your powers is brutally limited, resulting in an almost entirely scripted and therefore watered-down afterlife experience.
Our hero Ronan is a roughly sketched amalgam of every anti-authority, lone-wolf detective popularised in film during the late ‘60s and early ‘70s; a gravel-voiced cliche under a fedora. Yet the mystery lying at his feet is more unusual than most, as Ronan has a series of bulletholes in his chest and his ‘unfinished business’ is to discover the identity of his own killer.
It’s a powerful whodunnit set-up, which kept me invested - just - for the ten hours it took to reach the reveal, despite narrative shortcomings elsewhere. An insistent yet irrelevant sub-plot involving Ronan’s wife, for example, evokes a particularly clunky romance novella, while the thoughts of possessed citizens that Ronan is able to hear are oddly mundane. The supporting cast fails to make an impression too, save for Joy, a spirited young medium - terrifically voiced by Entourage actress Cassidy Lehrmam - who deserves more screen-time.
Similarly, Salem, with its rich real-life history, feels wasted as a setting. Murdered’s small sandbox, (truly the loosest use of that term), offers little variation in environment and restricts the player's natural instinct to explore it at every turn. One of its more interesting features; a ghostly overlay of parts of the town during its most notorious years in the 1600s, is mostly used as an environmental trick to prevent you from going beyond the game world’s close confines. The explanation for this feels arbitrary: Ronan can’t pass through other ghostly matter because he’s a ghost, and he can’t access three quarters of the town’s buildings as they’ve been ‘consecrated’ by Salem’s citizens. The developer didn’t have time to make a bigger, more interesting world, in other words.
Such limitations extend to your toolbox. While Ronan can, theoretically, do all the cool things you’d want a ghost detective to be able to do: walk through (some) walls, analyse the ghostly residue of a murder scene, interrogate other ghosts, possess humans and animals to influence them and read their thoughts, and move objects about like a poltergeist - you’ll rarely find any use for his abilities outside of the tightly scripted story which you’re funneled through.
This is particularly frustrating considering Ronan’s investigations in Murdered require very little actual brain work. The business of solving puzzles, which boils down to ‘analysis’ of a crime scene by either collecting every clue using your ghost skills and selecting the most relevant one, or linking together a series of clues to form a cohesive timeline of events, equates to meaningless busywork as the solution is more often than not blindingly obvious from the get-go.
The ability to scrutinise the ghostly residue of a dramatic memory captured in a three-dimensional still - the killer searching for a victim, for example, or a cowering victim sobbing in terror - is perhaps the most ridiculously simplistic in Ronan's investigatory repertoire. It’s hard to feel the developer is taking us seriously when our multiple-choice descriptors of someone pleading for their life are words like Scared, In Charge, Calm, Tense or Confident. For a game centered on a murder mystery, it’s baffling that Murdered is devoid of any real, challenging sleuthing.
When the answers aren’t so obvious - and generally this is when the task at hand, not the solution, is obtuse -  there seems to be no consequence for failure. Even when you don’t guess the most relevant clue on your first attempt, there is no option but to get to the answer eventually through process of elimination. While you are rated on your ‘detective work’ on a case by case basis, the judgement seems meaningless; no branching storylines are shut off from you for screwing up, and there is no overall rank offered at the end to make you want to try again and do better.
Enemy encounters, which are few and far between, offer more room for freedom and tactical thinking. The only way to dispose of Murdered’s genuinely frightening soul-sucking demons is to get immediately behind them, and the only way to get immediately behind them is to hide in the residue of individual ghost souls, which are tightly packed together and therefore create a sort of teleportation system for Ronan.  It’s a neat, fun idea, and one that is bizarrely underutilised and unexplored for a game trying to sell an atmosphere of danger.
A multitude of side quests pump a little life into Murdered. Populated throughout Salem are ghosts who, like Ronan, are stuck between this world and the next by virtue of their unfinished business. Ronan can help these people move on by solving their conundrums, and while the process of doing so is no more satisfactory than it is in the central quest, many of these encounters are memorable stories. Helping a guy who can’t remember who was behind the wheel in a drunk-driving accident, for example, or revealing the heroic nature of a death to someone who thought otherwise, are nice little human touches in a larger story that regularly serves to remind you of the futility of death...

It's been out awhile, and yes it has a few minor problems still, but the game is a cinematic masterpiece filled with creepy atmosphere and on-edge moments of spooky little girls and creepy creatures and unsettling moods.
The ending is a bit disjointed, bland, and unfulfilling, but the game makes up for it in the journey to get there. Lots of sleuthing and clue-finding along the way keep you occupied for the 8 to 10 hours it will take you to finish this game.
Ronan has been murdered (gasp! spoiler, but you knew that already) and he has to piece together what has happened and why he has been caught up in this past-meets-present mish-mash of mayhem in creepy ol' Salem, Mass.  The streets are filled with spooky ghostly spectres, and you're constantly tasked with finding the next clue to what happened to you. You also have to solve the case of the Bell Killer, as well, and find some missing persons. As sidequests, you have to help the dearly departed gain some closure and help them move on in the afterlife. You're part medium, part detective, and part ghost... live a little!
It's worth fighting the slightly wonky controls to get clues to appear, and there's very little combat (except for some frequent quick-time-events later in the game; there is also an .ini hack to prevent those from becoming tedious).
Very good game: the story (except for the ending) is interesting, the atmosphere is loads of creepiness, and there is way more sleuthing than slashing. Get it on sale and you won't be disappointed.

Full Disclosure: I main Sebille because she hits all the right buttons for me, so if my review seems gushy about her, you can (and, if it bugs you, should) blame my tastes.
I've been playing since earkly access, back in May, 2017, or so, so I have a lot of experience with it, especially the first act, and have enjoyed it all the way. As I'm writing this review, I have just arrived in the third act of three.
I'll start with talking about the gameplay. It's extremely dynamic, and great fun in battles, encouraging you to (carefully) set up traps for enemies or otherwise catch them in things like suddenly electrified water or the like, though, I admit, I prefer a very straightforward approach (EG, with Sebille, backlash, then whack with other special abilities, using AP gaining abilities as well to keep up the damage), which is perfectly viable as well. Out of combat, it can be mildly annoying, especially in areas where there are walls nearby or lots of items belonging to people. Hello, accidental theft and fines. On the bright side, you can travel to any waypoint you've discovered if you'd rather not walk all the way across the island to get to that one spot you were at, plus the teleporter pyramids return.
On the characters: their characterization is surprisingly deep, and at times deeply interwoven, especially between Sebille and Ifan (no spoilers and romance is optional but they speak to a lot of the same people for similar reasons), and at times a bit silly in a good way (Mostly Lohse's doing), and they play their parts to the hilt. Sebille's attempts to find her former master, and kill him, as well as Ifan's growing internal conflict with his past are especially interesting. The voice-acting is also great, adding a surprising depth to their characters, with only the town crier and the randomly interacting NPCs in the second act being annoying, and you only need to go there for buying and selling, say, every level up.
Difficulty: It can be hard at times, though I find that's almost always because you've picked a fight you're too low-level for (albeit, there are times when finding properly leveled fights, or even those you're overpowered for, can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ or the foe has a VERY annoying aura effect. My advice: quicksave often (default: F5 on the keyboard), because there are also a few badly placed autosaves here and there and you can go a long time between them, causing you to lose a lot of progress just by hitting one (as I had happen to me a number of times). However, the abilities and weapons are well balanced, as long as you keep up with the upgrades, though I can see why some think rogues are overpowered. For example, my rogue Sebille may not be my number one damager, in base damage, (that being the Crossbow wielding Ifan) but she packs a ridiculously big punch when she can get behind an enemy, more often than not taking away at least 3/4 of their psysical armor, due to auto-critting backstabs, and a huge critical multiplier.
Environment: While you do play in a 3/4 view, the environment is still amazing, doing a great job of setting the mood for a given area (dark, dank caves and lush forests both give off the right vibe), though occassionally, they'll cause a bit of camera screw (plus during Early Access, my scroll button broke, making this problem even worse until I got a new mouse).
Sound: Oh, the lovely soundscape. The music, which is done with whatever instrument you chose at the start (I like the tondela, personally), provides the mood in battle and out. It's good enough that sometimes, when I'm asking "where should i go next" or just wanting to chill after a tough battle, I'll just sit there and listen to the music, since I find it so relaxing out of battle (in battle it's much more pumped up and kind of ominous, which works great, especially in an epic battle, like the one at the end of the first act).
Conclusion: The game is great, all around, with great dynamism and fun throughout, even if it's a bit tough in spots (plus the badly placed autosave problem). All in all, I give it a 9/10

It's weird that most reviews focus on free-to-play aspect of the game. As if all ftp games are bad by default. It's not like this. I've played a lot of ftp games without paying anything and enjoyed a lot of them.
This game is one of those that I enjoyed. I played it on Kongregate and got to level 40 before I got bored with it.
About the game: you make a team of different units with a lot of passive skills and clear dungeons in turn-based combat where you press forward button and see your team moving one step forward (unless they are blocked) and turn actions resolve - archers shoot, healers heal, some abilities trigger, some units die, etc. You can change formation of your units in a team, you can use some one-time boosts, you can order everyone to focus on one enemy. When enemy units die they sometimes drop souls that you can capture and have them join your team. Outside the battle you can evolve units by combining several lower tier ones into higher tier ones. Depending on certain circumstances (time, level, elite status) units gain a certain bonus to their stats after evolving. Later in the game you can also upgrade your castle that gives minor boosts to units/skills/evolution and provides some extra daily income.
There are several types of stages that are available in the game: campaign stages (each node has 3 difficulties and has a certain setup of enemies so you can farm them for units that you need), daily challenges (each map requires a certain team composition and provides special rewards), weekly portals (they have certain enemies required for higher tier evolutions and access to them changes depending on the day of the week), pvp (these are just battles against other player's teams).
Special currency: main currency that you buy for real money can be easily acquired while playing the game. You gain small amounts for finishing each campaign mission for the first time, you gain small amount from the mine in your castle, you gain some for daily logins and most important source - you gain some for finishing several daily missions. You will need that currency mostly to unlock extra slots for your army, but even default amount of slots (50) is enough to keep a good amount of captured units if you don't suffer from "I must keep them all!".
Pros:
1. Easy to learn (but rather intricate due to a lot of passive skills) turn-based battle system
2. Interesting evolution system
3. Easy access to special currency
4. Interesting process of farming/grinding for units to evolve if you enjoy such things
5. You can continue to max unit stats after evolving the unit by doing daily challenges for special units that boost them slightly
Cons:
1. Energy (Food) system that I personally hate in such games (though it's is not very restricting in this game)
2. PVP had a lot of enemy teams that were really strong and you could not understand it before choosing to attack them (this may have changed after I stopped playing the game)
3. Farming/grinding for units can become rather boring after a while because chances to get exactly what you want (a certain type of unit with an elite status) and then to be able to capture it were really low (this may have changed too after I stopped playing the game). I remember there was an item that allowed to breeze through the level by auto-advancing and giving a huge boost to attack power. Even with that item, that allowed to clear a map in less than a minute, it took a lot of time to farm for certain types of units.
Anyway the game was really good and enjoyable for a while, so I recommend trying it.
Forgot to mention: on Kongregate this game has 3.8/5 rating with almost 2m players (it's amount of players who tried the game, not the current amount of players I believe).

This game feels more like it belongs to a Mobile App than something that should be on Steam.
I've played and seen similar games within the Mobile App stores; this game in particular seems to have a combination of systems utilized: The fusion/max-level bonus evolution system found in multiple card game RPGs, and the battle system is reminiciant of the "advancing army" style of play. This style of gameplay isn't as common as other types of games within the Mobile market, but it is present.
That's about as much good I can say, however. There's definitely many more bads to goods to this Steam App:
When I played the game, the game felt a bit laggy while controlling my characters or navigating the menu. I don't know if it's my OS that caused this, but it very quickly got irritating.
The UI doesn't feel modified for a PC. Often, I have difficulty selecting the unit that I want to move, which doesn't help considering the already-present lag. When I try to click a unit above another, I'll end up selecting THAT unit instead. There's also grammar and font issues, as well, which is something one SHOULD fix when porting a game from the Mobile market.
Finally, when I tried closing the window with Alt+F4 or the corner button, it instead kept bringing me to the Gem Purchase menu. I get that the game is free-to-play, but this seems like a very underhanded move, especially when all I wanted to do was close the game. This part here was the nail in the coffin towards my feelings about this game; it felt less like a legitimate attempt at a good game and more like an attempt to desperately harvest money from players.

Crusader Kings 2 is a behemoth of a game.  If you've never played a grand strategy game before (like me, before this) you will be intimidated by it's depth.  There are a staggering number of buttons to click, screens to read, information to digest, filters to apply, and characters to interact with.  You will likely grope around in the darkness and barely survive, at first.  Then the magic starts to happen.  You learn how to properly apply your advisors, how to marry for alliance vs. how to marry for stats, how to get those elusive claims on neighboring territory, and so on.  You will pillage the English coast as Viking raiders.  You will make pilgrimages to Jerusalem, hajjs to Mecca, blood sacrifices to Kali.  Feel like taking control of a lowly duke in Sicily and reforming the ancient Roman Empire over hundreds of years?  Go for it.  Unite the three great empires of ancient India and become Samrat Chakravartin?  Do it.  Play as William the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Charlemagne, Alfred the Great, Saladin, Mansa Musa, Genghis Khan - or play, like I first did, as a mere count in Dublin and work your way up to Emperor of Britannia.  Or start out in Rus and form the giant Russian/Slavic blob to collide with the Golden Horde.  My point is, if you're into history like me, you will be able to live out any scenario from the past and form it to your liking.  Assassinate your children, marry your sisters (Zoroastrians I'm looking at you), seduce your Steward's wife, hunt mythical white tigers, launch crusades, throw parties.  Conquer territory and cement your family's reputation in the history books.  BUY THIS GAME.
A few tips - as big of a game as this is vanilla, the major DLCs are must buys.  They are constantly going on sale, so don't buy them at full price - wait for a sale and scoop 'em up then.  I'd recommend Sword of Islam, Legacy of Rome, The Old Gods, Rajas of India, and Way of Life first.  Charlemagne, Sons of Abraham, and The Republic are also awesome, but not as crucial as, say, The Old Gods.  Save Sunset Invasion for last, if at all.
ALSO, bonus points for listening to Dan Carlin's Hardcore History podcasts while playing.

I nearly♥♥♥♥♥♥myself when I heard that someone was making a spiritual successor to the Dungeon Keeper series.  Dungeon Keeper II stands as one of my favorite games of all time, and I still remember my disappointment when I heard Dungeon Keeper III had been cancelled.  After playing several beta builds of War for the Overworld, I think I can comfortably say that this game is the one I've been waiting for.
Stepping into the game, I was amazed with what these guys have accomplished so far.  The creature and level design does sway a bit "grittier" than Dungeon Keeper, but it doesn't detract from the feel of the game.  The rooms are exquisitely detailed, which comes across especially well in the first-person view.  The creatures are also gorgeously and creatively rendered, and each unit is fairly easy to pick out among the throng of minions churning around your dungeon.  The interface is already fairly intuitive, with a few niggles here and there.  It can be difficult to select the right minion out of a crowd, and certain vital functions--the "rally" command, for example--can be a hassle to get to.  The game could also benefit from remappable hotkeys, or any hotkeys whatsoever, for that matter.  The devs have stated that hotkeys and remapping are coming in a later patch, though, so I wouldn't dock any points over it.
The tech tree is extensive and well-done, with some solid improvements over the Warlock research tree from Dungeon Keeper II.  The tree is sorted into three "veins of evil," with your cultist accruing "sins"--research points, basically--which allow you to unlock "aspects," granting access to new rooms, minions, spells, and rituals.  It's all pretty straightforward once you get used to it, but the tutorial doesn't do a great job of explaining how the tech tree works.  You can fumble about with trying to attract a specific minion, only to find out later that the minion's specific room and requirements are tied up somewhere in the Veins.  It's not a huge problem, however, and I'm confident the devs will add a better tutorial in the future.
The campaign's still on the way, which is the part I was especially looking forward to, so it's impossible to give a solid score at the moment.  However, what the devs have accomplished so far is incredible, and very much in the spirit of the original games.  If you're a fan of the Dungeon Keeper series, or a fan of base-management games in general, I would definitely recommend checking out War for the Overworld.
UPDATE 11/26/2017:  having played through the full campaign, I want to emphatically state that Brightrock Games have accomplished something incredible with this game.  If you've been waiting for a follow-up to the fantastic Dungeon Keeper games, you owe it to yourself to play this.

When you buy American Truck Simulator, you are buying two things - an excellent base game, and the promise of significant expansions/DLC/improvements over the next years. The game as it is now is already excellent - the world, although maybe a little small compared to Euro Truck Simulator 2, seems far more detailed and far more alive than some of the parts in the base ETS2 map.
Of course, the game engine is pretty much the same and it will feel very familiar to ETS2 users. There are, however, plenty of things to enjoy in ATS - from challenging deliveries to long open roads, not to mention those great American trucks.
With California and Nevada in the game at the time of writing this review, the world can feel a little small. In my current 33 hours of gameplay I have visited all major towns and have explored over 75% of the map, something which would have taken far, far longer in Euro Truck Simulator 2. On the other hand, with a free Arizona update coming soon and the promise of significant map expansions through DLC, American Truck Simulator is only going to get bigger and better over time.
This is a great single player experience, that can also be enhanced through multiplayer play with the Truckersmp mod which is easy to install and free. If you are tired of driving around California and Nevada on your own, join up with some friends and join a convoy!
A great single player and multiplayer experience that promises to get even better as more content is added to the game by developers. Well worth it for people who enjoyed ETS2 - it is more than re-skin and it is also a great introduction to those who sneer at or have not had the pleasure of enjoying truck simulation.

Warframe has to be one of the best free to play games i've played, it's up there with Path of Exile.

It's free so give it a try, you have nothing to lose other than the disk space it occupies and the time it takes to download/install.

As for how it manages to stay  free to play; Microtransactions.
You can buy Platinum (An in-game currency used to buy items from the market and from other players).
You can also buy various packs such as Prime Access, Prime Vault and the various packs which give you an item mod. (All of these also give you Platinum)

None of the items purchasable with real-world money are obtainable only with said money.
You are also able to earn Platinum without spending any extra money by trading with other players. (This is how most people get Platinum and is honestly the best way to do so.)

There are also a number of skins for various  pieces of gear that are created by the community (TennoGen) these items cost, and are only acquirable with, real-world money. These TennoGen skins do not affect gameplay in Warframe in any way, they only affect your FashionFrame rep.

9/10 would recommend to everyone i know.

Although the game carried some complaints along the way (mainly because of its pricing for being an indie game), Owlboy is a great and truly gorgeous game.
Graphic 12/10
Simply looking at the trailer/picture will be more than enough to show just how gorgeous the game pixel art is. It is extremely well-made and lively. Hitting trees/bushes will cause them to move around. Running around in certain map will have the map cycle between day and night time. There're also Otus, the owlboy, facial expressions throughout the game when he feels sad, happy or just shocked that are just funny to look at all the time.
Story 8/10
In this game, anyone can be a hero, as long as you have the courage to carry on. The game doesn't outright force a "YOU'RE THE CHOSEN ONE! DO SOMETHING" that most game use. There are so many moments in the game that will have you feel really sad or happy in this game. The pacing is also great and prevent the player from feeling like they're trying to drag out the story.
However, it does suffer from some issues that will be noticable near the end of the game where you feel like you had little impact and the whole thing is happening because both side are just acting like idiots when they are spewing the solution to each other before they fight.
Gameplay 7/10
With all the flying and the switching, the game isn't too slow or too fast. You fly around, collect coin, do stuffs and unlock new upgrades or hats. It's basically everything a platforming game should have.
But why only 7/10?
Because it does have its issues. Coins are ridiculously annoying to get 100% with the ridiculous amount of hidden wall in the game. Only a few of them will have the hints attached that there's a hidden wall here. Majority of them have you revisit the place again and hug all of them. Combine with having to take a trip back and forth due to lack of instant-travel option, it's a real pain to backtrcak.
After about 60% into the game, there's almost nothing new to discover in the game and all the exciting moment are pretty much gone. The game enter a period of frustration where enemies try to cheap-kill you instead (you will hate monkeys) until you get new stuffs to just disable them with ease again. The "Exciting chase/rush" moments are pretty much gone and boss fights are no longer as fun as they all become a "Dodge all my random projectile attacks and hit me X times to deal damage. Do this 3 times to win".
Fortunately, because the game length is quite short, you don't get to have to deal with this kind of frustration for far too long to the point the game becomes too stale/frustrating to keep going.
Music 10/10
Grab the OST DLC If you can.
Other factors -15 / 10
Not enough bird puns, owlboy is actually a human boy and that red thing is a nose, not a beak. Such betrayal. UNforgivable.
So while the game does have issues, if you the type of player who want to enjoy playing some relaxing platforming game and story instead of bashing the heck out of your competition face, considering purchasing this game. Even with such a price, you won't regret it because the game quality is that high.

For a free to play game it is one of the best! The grinding may not be for everyone but I still enjoy it. Fun to play with friends. Plenty of action. The community is one of the best I've ever seen. The developers are always listening to their playerbase and seem to care about the game and it's players a lot. The continuous updates add new content to the game which adds even more things to do so veterans and new players alike have something to do/look forward to. For a new player however the game may seem hard to understand or get the hang of at first considering how much it takes to learn the numerous mechanics. This is why I reccommend new players pay close attention to any tips the game gives, but mostly ask the community for help in region chat or if playing on steam asking in the Players Helping Players thread. The game has a deep lore that fans can really get into. The gameplay is actually really solid. There are tons of weapons and Warframes to try. Each one very unique. The combat is fast and action packed most of the time. The guns and melee weapons are great, but the overpowered feeling you get from your Warframe's abilities is what really sets it apart from the rest. With your Warframe and weapons cutting down hordes of enemies feels amazing. Another note is that the "Marketing Model" is pretty solid. You definitley don't need to spend a single cent on this game if you don't want to. Mostly you pay for a premium currency called Platinum. This currency is used to get things faster. Say you're building something, which takes 3 days. If you want, you can rush the process to get it instantly with Platinum. There are also numerous cosmetics you can buy for Platinum as well. There's also things you can buy with Steam Money if you play from steam. Say you want a Warframe and don't want to build it yourself, well you can pay Platinum to just buy it already built. Sound like you need Platinum for a lot of things right? Well you don't need it, you can gain access to almost every item, warframe and weapon as you progress through the game. Mostly by gathering resources, getting the pieces, crafting it and waiting. Again this game has a fair amount of grinding going into it, but if that doesn't turn you off then I'd say it's worth it. But back to the topic of Platinum, you can actually get Platinum without using real money. In the game there is a trading system for players where you can trade items, special weapons, and "prime parts". And through trading these players can trade their Platinum for the piece you have. So when I said you don't need to spend a single cent on the game, I was not lying. But still purchasing Platinum to support the game if you like it I feel isn't so bad. Not to mention there are daily rewards that have a rare chance of giving you 20% 50% or even 75% off your next purchase of Platinum within 2 days. I tend to take advantage of it when I see the 75% off. Anyways I would definitely reccomend people to try the game. If you like it, then welcome to the game! If not it was nice that you gave it a chance. Maybe down the line you'll try it again and you'll have found it better than you remember. Sorry for rambling. Short version is: Give it a try!

Hand of Fate is at it's very essence is a 3D card game with some basic combat elements. You swap cards in and out to build a better deck so you can fight the bosses at the end of each run. What separate it from it's card brethren like Hearthstone is in Hand of Fate everything is a card. From encounters, events, enemies, and the bosses themselves are cards. On top of these cards the dealer himself has a deck which along with your cards are than arrayed on the table in different configurations, and the match up of the two decks serves as the game's board. As you move along the board the dealer also serves as the narrator and draws you into the experience. I only wish the story wasn't paper thin, but it is serviceable. The only major fault I have with this game is it's combat system. How it works is when you land on a card that isn't either gain gold, health, food ect, or lose gold, health, food ect. A 3D world is generated with your generic character and whatever armor and weapons cards you have happened to pick up. There is nothing inherently wrong with this system, but compared to the deck build aspects this part is a let down. All and all I would highly recommend this to people who are fans are cards games, or those looking to try a new and interesting game

+ Excellent sound effects

Final major edit: The game past Act 1 simply isn't finished. It's not polished at all.
Dialogs are wrong/missing, quests won't trigger/are broken, plots can't be progressed. Characters won't recognize you did something downstairs, NPCs spawn as the wrong model, combast are imbalanced as can be, etc. etc.
The first 20 hours of the game is perfect, Fort Joy is divine. The rest needs a lot of work and attention to bring it up to that level of quality. Get this game on sale down the line and it'll blow your mind once it has been tidied up.
Quest updates are out of whack. Interactions with companions are HORRENDOUSLY shallow. It basically is one of two things - take *one* step per act towards their quest. Other than that, you and your companions make a remarka bout things that happen. It's A or B. A is "i agree with the thing" or B is "I disagree with the thing." That's it. Your companions have no dialogs of depth or character development otherwise at all.
You'll get randomly stuck in dialog windows and unable to leave them. You'll be oneshotted before combat even can begin and the only way to win is by cheesing with metagame knowledge.
Don't get me wrong, the first 25 hours of this game was the MOST fun I've had in any game. If DOS:2 finished after Fort Joy I would have been disappointed at the length but happy with the game.
Everything after Fort Joy has been a hot mess that has gotten only messier and hotter. I feel nothing but frustration when NPCs repeatedly fail to recognize things I have done. That guy? I already talked to him, I can't kill him. No, I can't talk to that person for you, they're dead. Yes, I have both halves of this item you want, but you don't recognize it.
It's a lot of sloppy, sloppy stuff that should have been cleaned up before proper release. Larian should apparently have put the whole game out there for EA, because again, Fort Joy is AMAZING. It's perfect in balance and completeness. There were only a few little tiny frustrations or things that were out of whack with dialog or quests.. but that was the exception to the rule. In act 2, it becomes the rule. The game becomes a sloppy, slipshod mishmash of frustration.
Some boss encounters hit less hard, have less health, and less armors than the first mobs you fight off the boat into act 2. They're eyerolling-ly easy. And this wild variation in balance becomes the new norm. It's just.. so frustrating because the game was absolutely, perfectly wonderful for the first 20-some hours, but it tanks so hard. Going from a 10/10 to a 6/7 out of 10 is a big drop, it's disappointing. Until they take time to polish up the majority of the game after Fort Joy, I can't recommend it.

I await the day I get off the island and see the whole game through. I'm starting to think that this ♥♥♥♥ing island is the entire game, but I can tell that the developers put a lot of damn work into a marvelous game that will make you feel like you're sitting at the DnD table experiencing the best storyline of your lifetime.
The game is addicting, and hooks you with different storylines that make you want to come back onto the game everytime you open Steam. The combat is very difficult, yet very fun. The core element that makes the combat so fun is it's difficulty, it makes this ARPG have a sense of a RTS inside of it. You have to be smart about what moves you make, how you make them, and how you can use the enviornment around you to your advantage.
To give you an idea of how much I approve of this game, this is the first review I've ever really written (I've wrote a few half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥derpy ones before). I believe this game, and its hard working developers deserve the Game of the Year award due to the amount of work they put into a game that was funded by a KICKSTARTER!
This game shows you how GAMES are SUPPOSED to be made! This game isn't created by EA, Ubisoft, or some other company that pumps out half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unfinished games to the public yearly just to pump in cash from fans of the older games who want to see if they have FINALLY fixed their beloved franchise. You don't come across a Halo Reach or a childhood memory quality game often nowadays, but this game will make you feel like a child again wanting to come home already so you can hop on your character and continue the storyline that you left off engrossed in.
Please purchase this game if you love DnD, RPGs, RTSs, or anything of the sorts! These developers deserve the money, and YOU deserve a GOOD GAME for once instead of rubbish games like CALL OF DUTY INFINITE WARFARE!

I have tried many MMO in the past few years and one thing I found peculiar about ArcheAge is that, despite its pros and cons, it is by far the most complete MMO I have ever came across. It has such variety and it offers so many features to explore, that I could never find another MMO that was this complete (and it wasn't by lack of searching):
- pve and pvp (both in constant update, with new features being constantly released, to provide for endgame players)
- castle sieges
- intra/intercontinental world events
- naval battles
- land/naval trade system
- underwater exploration and treasure hunting
- pirate faction
- trial system
- pets and mounts
- gliding system through the use of custom gliders
- housing system with multiple house and farm models (including marine houses and aquafarms)
- several land and sea vehicles (skates, cars, farm vehicles for land trade runs, ships, submarines)
- guild system
- nation system
- several events throughout the year (not just during Christmas/Halloween/etc, but during the whole year)
- new content released periodically
And I might still be forgeting something xD
Edit:  Trion Worlds has completely changed the whole game. They changed the housing system, the farmimg system, the crafting system, the combat system, the guild system, the naval system... it is now a completely different game than the one I used to play. I ended up quitting and have no idea what kind of game it is now, so I am changing my review for this game from Positive to Negative, as I can no longer vouch for this game. Maybe it's still a great game for new players, since they never got to know the old system.

I've played Conan Exiles for over 60 hours now and I'm really enjoying the game.  Yes, it's riddled with bugs at the moment, but that's to be expected with an early access title.  There are two major issues that I hope they address soon.  First, I'm constantly losing sync with the server, requiring me to log out and log back in.  Second, when I log in, it takes a long time for all of the player placed building pieces to render in.  In a hevily built area this can take a couple of minutes sometimes.
Aside from that, I'm lovingthe game.  It's a great change of pace from more "gun based" games like Rust or H1Z1.  The scenery is amazing.  My friends and I spent a couple of hours just going around the map just sight seeing.  It's obvious that the map designers and artists took a lot of time creating a beatiful and interesting world.
I love the PvE aspects of the game.  These kind of games are a lot more fun when there is more to do than just fight against other the players.  The AI could probably use some work, but the creatures are already fairly challenging, especially when you get caught in a pack of them.
As I write this, the game has only been in early access for less than a week.  The development team has already released several significant patches to address issues.  I know they have a lot of work ahead of them, but I think this game is just going to get better as time goes on.
Hopefully the BR plague never spreads to a different game.

***Review from a experienced survival game player that has a little over 1200 hours combined in titles like 7 days to die, ARK:Survival Evolved and Rust***
I feel like i need to recommend this game because a lot of people are downvoting it for problems that are currently there but i do not think the game deserves a downvote because of those problems. Actually the only main problem that i currently experienced is the lag on the servers. Because of this me and a friend thought lets just wait for them to fix these problems and we'll try out the game on a private server with just the 2 of us for now.
Since we're playing with the two of us we're having a blast. No lag issues at all, havn't even encountered a lot of gamebreaking bugs except for the crafting que getting messed up a little which i fixed by just relogging into the server. There is plenty of PvE content currently available to have your fun with just a friend.
I also saw some complaints about the graphics of CE? Well i really don't know what that's all about. Yes the graphics of this game are not mind blowing but in my opinion they do look nice and atleast they are properly runnable. Do you get♥♥♥♥♥♥fps? Well i have a I5-5670K (not overclocked) and a gtx-980 and if i'm not also running my server at the same time i can play the game with around 45 fps on ultra. I currently have 8GB of ram and when i'm running the server (for 2 players) i'm using around 90% of that. When i'm running the server i play on medium graphics settings, this way i can run the game smoothly at around 50 fps. And well  it might be just me but i still don't think the game looks like crap in medium settings. The things that i mainly noticed when going from ultra to medium is the rendering distance (objects that are further away arn't displayed in full graphics)
Conclusion:
I'm having a blast with this game already on my private server and i'm looking forward to the day where funcom fixes the lag issues for bigger servers. I do hope this will be soon ofcourse, but even without being on big server i can already see i'm going to enjoy this game for quite some time in it's current state. There is already plenty of stuff to do even when you only go for pve. There are no problems with the graphics at all in my opinion. I'm really excited for the stuff that is currently on the development roadmap and think this can become one of the finest survival games out there.
Oh and for the people that are saying it's just a ARK/Rust ripoff
First of all if you're really going down this road everything is a minecraft ripoff (atleast that was my first survival game with mechanics like hunger, gathering and building)
I played both ARK and rust for a lot of hours
CE is also a survial game and i think it's really weird how mad people are that CE has some aspects implemented into the game that look a lot like the mechanics of Rust/ARK. ARK and Rust are both very succesfull if not the most succesfull games in the survival genre. In my opinion looking at your predecessors is always a smart move. So what if they used stuff from other games? Don't we all just want the perfect game that has done everything just right? Why would you try to invent a whole new system for every detail of your game when a previous game in the genre already had a great system that worked really well? Why would you try to keep reinventing the core of survival games while it already has a solid foundation on which new mechanics could be build. I'd rather have them focus on new refreshing things in the genre like the thrall system (yes this game has npcs which you can enslave) or the religion system (you can get bonusses and really powerfull avatars if you bring offerings to your chosen god).
i really hope this game grows up to be the best survival game in the genre. I really think the potential is there and i'm excited to see where the game will be in a few years. That combined with the fact that i'm already having fun in it now makes me say it's worth the 30 euro it currently costs.
I'm really sick of all the hate every EA title gets. They are games in development if you want a finished product just don't buy it. Meanwhile i have like 1300 hours combined in all my EA titles for maybe a total of 100 euro combined? (some bought in sales some instantly) In my opinion that has already been well worth my money. For games that arn't even finished yet, i think that deserves a little support instead of all the crying about the bugs that they warned you about in advance.

Though there isn't that much variety in turns of battling (bascially move really fast/dodge/attack, repeat), there is enough skill challenge to keep it fairly interesting. Hand of Fate is more than the sum of its parts: everything comes together to give you 12 short and relatively enjoyable rouge-like levels in story mode. Chance has more of an effect in your ability to beat a level than most games, and sometimes luck will go against you. Only had really bad luck in one level out of 6 so far, which perhaps means the odds are stacked in the player's favor. Three consecutive pain cards was indeed painful; lost 60 health right before boss, lost boss battle, needed to repeat entire level.     7/10: Would randomnly lose 60 health again.

I was interested enough to buy it after playing the demo, but don't feel motivated to keep playing after the first few hours. The main character is a grinning idiot doormat in debt slavery to a fairy who won't tell her the actual amount owed on the family shop. The shop-keeping system is kind of interesting (as I would hope) but quickly bogs down in randomness and odd design choices. For instance, for days on end armor was arbitrarily low-valued, making most of my stock basically impossible to sell at a profit even as a massive debt payment came up. About 1/4 of your customers walk in not to buy anything but to sell you random garbage with insane dialog: "Want this [bowl of stew] I found in the forest?" "It's time to sell this family heirloom, [a chocolate bar]!" (I'm disturbed by the little girl who keeps selling broken god statues.) You get berated if you don't buy these things and lose out on experience point combos. Haggling consists entirely of raising or lowering a number; there's no rhetoric, advertising, personal relationships, competition, offers of throwing X in, &c. Character interaction is entirely scripted and consists of your character grinning against insults and attempted murder.
There\'s an XP/level system for the shopkeeper, unlocking features like expanding the store. That's fine, but according to Internet guides, the actual rules defy both common sense and the actual tutorial. You're supposed to sell at a *minimal* profit because this somehow makes you more experienced and causes your endless array of generic customers and named, abrasive jerks to become richer. The two points I like here are that the shop can have a distinct light/dark or plain/gaudy rating (though this affects almost nothing) and that it's in your interest to give a good price to adventurers wanting to upgrade their equipment (though they also buy equipment they can't use).
You get some of your item stock by hiring adventurers to explore the random dungeons next to town, this being a generic RPG world. In this mode you control the hero while your own character and her debt-master follow passively. At first I liked this gameplay because there's a variety of enemy movement patterns to figure out, requiring some thought to avoid damage. But since you're fighting the same few enemies over and over (red slimes! yellow slimes!) and your tactics mostly consist of "hit with sword" anyway, the novelty wears off and you're back in random dungeon land, where everything is a meaningless grid of halls and rooms and you\'re hoping the random number gods will stop granting you bits of wooden armor when there's a 200,000 coin payment due Thursday. Besides "vendor trash" items you also collect random ingredients that fuel nonsense recipes for turning items into more valuable items. Eg. iron+bug traps to make a cute maiden's bracelet; adventurous clothes plus fur and walnuts or something to make chainmail. The rules don't make sense, there's no real plot, I don't like the characters, and there's not much to the gameplay.
So, at this point I think I'll abscond with my stock of used candy apples and discount armor. Hopefully the fairy won't see me sneak out.

Please excuse the lack of 100% achievements. I thought I could handle an FPS, but then I took insane for a spin. Hard Reset is like an unrelenting Olympic gymnastic coach who never gives you a moment's break. Are you sure you are out of the blast radius? Нет . You miscalculated your shield recharge time? Nein. You thought a few heavy headshots would kill a charging monstrosity in time? 不. Did you think you found good cover from? No. In the first level of the game I felt like I deserved a parade at every check point.
But soon enough, I realized I was just being lazy. I loved Doom, Quake, and Unreal Tournament growing up. I had babied my FPS muscles and was suffering from atrophy in the L33t skillz area. With that in mind, I stepped up my game and started being more careful, more precise. I still died a lot, but now I was learning. I still felt supreme satisfaction, but I also gained a newfound respect in the balance. The game was trying to train me, and get me used to playing a shooter where I don't just respawn 2 seconds away, automatically regenarate all my health, or kill enemies in a few hits.
All that being said, Hard Reset is not perfect. The story could not really hold my attention, though the art was kind of nice. The load times can be a longer than comfortable. I despise the autosave system: I could have a perfect run all the way up to one point, only to be killed out of nowhere and have to try to recover my balance in the next load. I also feel like I should point out that it is not the hardest game ever made. I make it sound extremely tough, but I do not consider myself really great at shooters. Challenge is very subjective: I found Hotline MIami to be moderately diffiuclt on my old trackpad, but I cannot play War of the Roses or Megaman to save my life.
Hard Reset feels extremely refreshing and satisfying, while familiar at the same time. It has been bundled and been on sale frequently, so this is a solid, engaging experience worth checking out.

At the start this game got off on the right foot. Corporation run lifestyle with robots sabotaging things? Sweet, right up my alley. After the first few kills I was still having fun. Upgrades for weaponry with a slick UI that was built into the game so it felt extremely fluid. The world felt, albeit deserted, lived in in a way.
Seconds later I started to notice the glaring flaws with the game. While attempting to sprint away from a horde of enemies, I found out that sprint only lasts for maybe a second or two, quickly giving me false hope of getting out of the situation unharmed while I sought better cover. I noticed that the two guns, an EMP rifle and a standard assault rifle, had no real difference other than looks. I upgraded said weapons to allow one to give me an area effect and one with a grenade. The area effect was useful, but still allowed enemies far too close for comfort, and the grenades were just...useless. "Oh well, maybe they need more upgrades." I lied to myself as I pressed on. Soon I found myself becoming irritated by the obvious pickups just out of reach in a crouch-able area. I tried every button then went into my key bindings, low and behold there was no crouch button.
Soon after these flaws arose, thinking I was lucky, I attempted to jump on a few crates to hurdle a barrier to get a secret pickup. Right as I reached the top, I was met with an invisible wall. I groaned and moved on, and within a few short moments I was met with the irritation that caused me to quit the game: "This barrier is self-powered, you've got to find a way around it." I do recommend this game, with some reservations.
The premise was really interesting, and the visuals and voice acting were great. Where it fell flattest for me were the "investigations." I normally hate using quotations for emphasis, but it's really warranted in this case. They were so laughably straight forward and simple that I actually tripped myself up the first two questions, because I thought there was no way it would be so obvious. If you're expecting something more in depth a la LA Noire you'll be disappointed. It quickly became evident that the investigations were there just to push you from plot point to plot point, no critical thinking need apply. I had seen that in other people's reviews and they're spot on.
There aren't that many side quests either- I had thought there would be more investigations into the cases of people in the afterlife. There are four, and again those are really simple. The other side quests are basically collection quests. I don't mind a game that focuses more on character or plot, but it would be nice to have solid investigative gameplay to round it out, particularly for a game that seems to market itself that way.
It just feels really unbalanced - the casual gamer appeal of simple puzzles combined with the dark supernatural detective theme feels like they're playing to two separate audiences at the same time.
That said, I definitely thought it was worth picking up and playing if you enjoy these genres. Just don't expect too much out of the gameplay, and get it on a good sale.

If you're thinking about buying chivalry and you don't know if you'll like it, for example you've never played a melee focuse competitive multiplater game before (I know they're aren't many) these are the things you should know about Chivalry:
~ It's not like Mount and Blade, it's much smaller scale and controls quite differently, if you haven't played M&B the controls should be easier to learn in one way, but conceps such as "dragging" a little difficult to pick up. Chivalry is difficult to learn and difficult to master but they key to success is patience, peristence and not trying to tank 3 dudes by yourself.
~ It's hard for new players to get into without being interested with the medieval setting or you aren't the most paitient person when it comes to online games, and the low level servers only teach you bad habits that work against you in the long run.
~ Community is simultaneously the best and worst, new players will be shown no mercy for team damage and people will criticise how you play mercilessly. But at the same time there are some of the wittiest and hilarious bunch out there. The playerbase is old and low level servers are usually barren outside sales and learning to play against 1000 hour veterans can be a huge test of ones fortitude...
~ The only microtransactions/dlc in the game are purely aesthetic such as weapons skins and character skins, weapons are unlocked purely based on amount of kills done with specific weapons.
~ The weapons that you can unlock aren't inherently better than the starting selection although there are some weapons that are virtually useless for competitive play and others which are abused to the utmost for easy kills.
~ Not in any way representive of actual medieval combat... But still fun as hell...

Artillerists is like a really bad, unbalanced version of the old boardgame Battleship, which has been re-created as a video game quite a few times and much better than this.
This is a complete guessing game, at least to the extent that I have played it. You can earn money to spend in an upgrade shop (the Artillery, where you buy "abilities"), but you have to grind out guessing games to earn the money.
Whereas this is obviously a Battleship style game (obvious even before you purchase the game), what you don't know ahead of time is how unbalanced it is. By the third mission of the main campaign, you have 2 mortars in a 6x6 grid. The mortars take up one block each, so you can only take 2 hits and then you lose. The AI has more than 6 blocks of units in a 6x6 grid, and the game gives you no idea how many the AI has at the beginning of each mission. I haven't made it past the third mission of the main campaign (as of this review) because this is just a pitiful waste of my time when I could be watching paint dry instead.
The AI also has "abilities" to hit multiple blocks, whereas you are stuck with grinding to buy lesser abilities early in the game, and they are really expensive and underpowered, particularly when the AI has some♥♥♥♥♥♥that can hit like 5 blocks at once as well as at least one airstrike (which hits 2 blocks) by this third mission.
You can use radar and airstrike abilities if you have purchased them at this point, but they are very expensive. When I say expensive I mean you will grind out clicking on grids trying to win missions in order to gain money. There are side-missions in which you can gain money, but the clicking and guessing is just horribly boring. In the game Battleship it's essentially the same, except you know what you're up against (the same units as you have, and there is a little more fun to the minimal planning and some strategy involved even though it amounts to guessing).
This is just a poorly thought out game. Nobody likes an unbalanced guessing-game. There are people that pop up with irritating dialog as well, which just makes it even more annoying because that makes more clicks to grind out.

NOTE: Artillerists was originally a free mobile game with in-app purchases. The version on Steam costs money to buy, but is the full product.
PROS:
+ It's basically the classic game, Battleship, but on land using artillery pieces instead of naval warships
+ Easy to pick up and play
+ No time commitment
+ The developer is willing to listen to feedback and adjust the game
+ There's an upgrade system where you can acquire new units, more units, and extra weaponry
+ It's cheap at $3.99 USD
CONS:
- It's basically Battleship... which means there's very little to see here that's even remotely new
- Poor graphics that look slightly better than the original Tropico (which came out in 2001)
- Skirmish Mode is locked by default until the player has completed the entire campaign
- Money is hard to get so you'll always be at a disadvantage (in terms of unit numbers and power) against the AI
- The campaign is full of unnecessarily long still-frame cutscenes that must be watched every time you play
- Dialogue is badly written (likely the result of poor Russian-to-English translation) and the attempts at humor are cringe-inducing, especially the female reporter who appears out of nowhere to make comments about her hair
- Single player only
- No Steam Cloud
RECOMMENDATION: Unless there are some major changes to the game, I can't recommend Artillerists. It's not a terrible game (I've certainly played worse), but that's not exactly a ringing endorsement. I'd suggest skipping Artillerists unless you're so desperate for a Battleship-like game that you're willing to overlook this game's faults.
The only reason I even bought it was because I like Battleship and this game is on sale for 25% off its already very low price tag. Losing $2.99 USD (or in my case, $3.36 CAD) is hardly a major ordeal and not enough for me to request a refund.

The critical foundation of any fantasy card game is the strategic use of cards. It's the development of your own customized deck. Combining cards in your customized deck to provide multipliers in combination with other cards, for use against a specific opponent. Hand of Fate is the most perfect name for this game because literally there is no strategy in developing your own deck, it's all left to Fate.
Issues
-Right off the bat, getting the chance to pull an equipment card is so rare, the whole point of having a customized deck is almost useless.
The default size of your customized deck grows every level, decreasing the chances of you pulling any one card. For instance, I believe the start deck size is near 20 cards and since the chance of getting an equipment card to pull is less than once per level, this means the chance of pulling any one card is less than 5%.
It's almost as if the dev's intentionally made the user deck larger as you advance levels, as a way to nerf the effectiveness of the cards and having a customizable card deck, in an attempt to make the game more difficult and stretch the game out. If this is the case, it's a bloody shame because its sacrificing crutial gameplay in an attempt to balance.
If you guys want to play a really good card game then I suggest going to Pokemon or Hearthstone. There is a reason they are so popular because they are REALLY REALLY well done.

Recettear is an item shop management game that includes dungeon crawling, item fusions, and hero item management.  The ability to haggle with customers and handle their special requests ("I want a weapon!") keeps things interesting but the UI, menus, and controls can be a hassle.  The anime style and irritating sound effects do get on my nerves, but I did have fun playing this game in short bursts.  I wish it was more open-ended, but you have strict repayment deadlines that you must keep or else you fail.  Not perfect, not terrible, fun, but not THAT fun.  Recommended if on sale.
PROS
+ You get to run your own item shop!
+ Gathering items to sell and equip via dungeon crawling is fun
+ Haggling with customers and handling special requests adds flavor
+ Leveling up heroes and upgrading shop keeps things interesting
+ Lots of items to collect, fuse, sell, and equip
+ Storyline might be interesting to some (I thought it was silly)
CONS
- Japanese/Anime style may irritate some (girly giggles and constant whining come to mind)
- Dungeon diving is very basic and combat is relatively shallow
- Permanently equipping your heroes is a chore (they have to randomly buy item in store)
- Lots of pointless dialogue including tons of EH's, UM's, OH's, !!!!'s, etc.
- Relatively linear due to repayment deadlines and ongoing storyline
- Clunky controls and confusing UI make it seem like a simple RPG Maker game

TL;DR:The excellently voiced Card Dealer makes all the difference in this rogue-lightlightlight card game! The combat sucks, the cards are nice, the narration is mind blowingly awesome.
While not exactly perfect mostly due to its highly exploitable counter based combat system (melee combat is easily the worst part of this game) this game has a very unique concept which now that it exists seems to make you think "why the hell did nobody think of this before?"
Each round you move your pawn over a path made of cards, one card at a time.
Each card represents some kind of encounter, which can lead to combat, a game of chance, a randomized effect on your character (aka curses and blessings) or having to navigate a dungeon full of traps. You can either do challenges in the form of a story mode where you defeat different bosses or play in endless mode using all the cards you have unlocked.
Combat is real time and very similar to the system used in batman / asscreed games, symbols show you when you should counter, block or dodge. The problem with this is that it leads to abuse since at some point you find out that spamming the counter button while avoiding unblockable attacks is basically all you have to do to win. Your character automatically targets the foe that you can counter so you become almost invincible this way.
Fortunately different weapons and abilities make the combat at least ignoreable if not enjoyable.
What entirely makes up for the lackluster part though is the voice over. The card dealer will speak to you in a deep, smooth voice that will even make the straightest, most bearded, lumberjackiest man in the world feel a little tingle in his scrotum. Additionally the amount of recorded sentences is quite big, enough to rarely feel like you are hearing the same things over and over again.
As a working man i also enjoy that you can easily jump in, play one round and leave it for the day without having to get used to it every time like most big RPGs.
Its a bad game for people who care about the Action RPG aspect, but its absolutely amazing if you are looking for a nice storytelling card game which you can play by yourself.

Whilst some descriptions of this game claim it to be a metroidvania, it is anything but.  Theres very little backtracking, aside from a large scale game length side quest.
The game can be finished in 5 or so hours.  A little more if you wanted to collect all the trinkets and coins.  However, do not let the length dissaude a purchase.  Owlboy overall is a wonderful package that takes you on an amazing journey, and one that you will remember for sometime.
Very few games come along that you say that you wish you could experience playing a game all over again like it was the very first time you had played it, and Owlboy is one of those games.  If you are one of those gamers who question why games are no longer like they used to be, well, Owlboy proves they still make games like they used to.

My first complaint is the lack of a decent tutorial or even a very visible prompt that pressing s is required to move in stealth. The game gives you an easy to see prompt for movement by popping up the movement keys, and pops A over a door which you see your character swipe at and open, indicating it's probably an attack as well (It is). However the game never tells you that you need to press and hold s in order to move stealthily, otherwise your character can move one step and then be attacked because for a stealth game where you will most of the time be moving at a stealth speed, stealth is NOT the default. This is a bad decision which leads to numerous problems. Further the actual stealth gameplay does not seem deep with some of the areas being too tiny to actually do anything. Throw in an autosave feature vs. a manual save combined with autosave and you will be redoing sections if you mess something up in another section and get to sit through the dialogue...again. The unskippable dialogue of people talking that occurs outside of cutscenes, in which the dialogue is skippable.
On top of this, I had the frustration of wanting to quit the game and hitting escape and realizing this did nothing. It wasn't until a frustrated 30 seconds later that I finally realized to open the menu, you need to hit return. ESC does nothing except skip cutscenes, I believe. This goes against gaming conventions and led to another annoyance added on top of the prior ones. It is within this menu that I finally discovered the section that tells you how to play. Also, I'm not sure if it actually tells you but I don't remember it telling me the difference but it does say you can poison people. What's the difference between poisoning them and a regular attack against them? I have no idea as I don't remember it saying.
As for the stelath mechanics themselves. It's essentially a move silently and don't get in their physical way and you'll be fine. There are no ways to really move guards from their positions other than your ridiculously loud default movement. It doesn't matter what surface you're walking on. If it's carpet or stone, stealth movement is silent, default is loud. There are no pots or other objects that you can hit or use to distract the guards. This game lacks depth, nuance, and good feel for the gameplay.

Supreme Commander isn't your usual cup of strategy game. It is more like the big hairy uncle of yours that think bare knuckle boxing teaches character. Supreme Commander takes everything you'll find it in your standard RTS and supersizes it.
From the very first mission onwards you will be overcome with a strange new feeling as you get thrown into a game with an almost unprecedented scale. The maps are not simply bigger than what you are used to, they blow everything previous to oblivion and the maps are not where this massive scale stops. Not only do you control massive armies and giant bases with humongous defensive networks but the units and buildings themselves are beyond what you usually find in an RTS game. Giant robots, massive spaceships and artillery pieces that can throw shells from Monday to Friday. If this game was a car I'd say the owner was compensating for something.
Various design mechanics are hard at work to keep it all from overwhelming you. The zoom function allows to you go right down to group level and all the way out to where you can see the entire map. Instead of having to build new tech every so often everything has an upgrade function allowing old factories to produce the latest and greatest in units, your defenses to stay effective and your resource gathers to not fall behind. The entire game and the buildup of power and technology that happens throughout a game is a very fluid process and only rarely do you find yourself having nothing to do.
Something that shouldn't be ignored either is that Supreme Commander, despite it's scale and the massive amount of units that can appear in a game manages to not only run really well, it also looks good.
Supreme Commander is an RTS on steroids. It's like nothing we've seen for a very long time and it does everything it tries so very well.

The stealth mechanics are rudimentary and poor. There's a huge lack of options to progress through the environment. Your options for dispatching guards consists of a basic attack and well... That's about it. This means that stealth consists of slowly trailing guards from behind or charging recklessly at them to activate the same insta-kill attack. The environment is completely static despite an incredible amount of pots, pans and all other sorts of valuables being bolted down in the environment. Having at least a few contextual objects here and there that could be interacted with to alter the paths of the guards would at least have added the depth of a puddle to the game play. This inability to meddle with the game's script is particularly problematic. It makes the game move at a snail's pace and feel incredibly repetitive. Instead of stalking and preying, you are most often forced to sit and watch unskippable chat blurbs play themselves out again and again before the guards will disperse and you can start playing the game again. Why can't I break some pots, pans or vases or do something in order to break up these oft-repeated conversations? Being forced to sit through these unskippable scenes again and again is worsened by the large number of deaths you will endure due to cheap, trial and error game design.
The game design is extremely cheap, poorly designed and unfair to the player. The game loads each room to approx 1 second of a black screen (your screen is blank but the guards are still patroling and the game playing itself). This leads to countless cheap deaths where you are rushed and killed before you can even see the room you entered. This results in trial and error game play where you compensate for this by running blind in the direction away from the guards who previously killed you during this 1 second black screen. Furthermore guards are often placed right in front of doorways which is just bad stealth game design. The guard pattern is also static and never-changes which is probably a good thing considering these aforementioned issues. Haven't these guys played the original Metal Gear on the NES? For a 2D, top-down stealth game I would not expect these design issues in 2016.
