This game is basically Counterstrike with medieval weaponry and hilarious voice acting.
Reasons to like this game as a beginner: It’s pure fun. The sound effects of dismembering or bludgeoning foes with an array of weapon types will most likely be the highlight of newcomers, along with the fact that even its bugs, crappy graphics and voice macros are something to laugh WITH and not just at. The community manages to help enhance these features. Then you’ll start getting better and expecting to get better. You’ll feel very rewarded when you manage to kill 3 – 5 enemies all on your own, whilst your team cheers you on in the chat-box. Especially if you duck under a swing from an opponent and they accidentally kill their teammate. Just BE WARY to not let it get to your head, otherwise you’ll end up like most of the idiots giving this game a bad review based on the ‘broken mechanics’ and the 'community.' These aspects I will rebuke in the following paragraphs.
People say it has a ‘toxic’ community, and this is simply untrue. The reality is that get your bad seeds with your good ones. Mostly if you stick to routinely playing on a server type, for example the Last Team Standing East US server, you’d find a jolly and friendly bunch there. Meanwhile, if you want people to be directly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by, then be a fool and start going on Duel servers ‘till you bang your head against the desk. Or if you want to be swamped in a sea of anonymity, go ahead and play Team Objective. Furthermore, Torn Banner’s emphasis on applying player-made maps and mods only increases choice and possibility.
Meanwhile, the people complaining about the exploitation of mechanics have a point, but then again they don’t. For example, I feint. I even throw feints in the middle of combos like a production line at work. And I get people shaming me, but I don’t care. I don’t care because the loading screens used to encourage it, and just like feinting: dragging, reverse-over-heading, Vanguard dancing or taking advantage of the Brandistock’s stab delay/reach have all become integrated and defined as the overall current product of the game. If you want to beat these types of players, then you’ll have to find a way to get better; either by being ‘taboo’ (like myself), getting better than them at their own game or by breaking the mould like many other players have before you.
Because these mechanical exploits weren’t apparent on Day 1 to the Chivalry community; they have been founded, learned and mastered. Thus, the community, skill level averages, and very mechanics of the game are constantly evolving. For example, when I used to play it extensively a long time ago, only a hand-full of players (mostly level 40+, which wasn’t common back then) utilised dragging, ‘rainbows’, or simply dashed the crap out of you with a hatchet wielding MAA or rushed you efficiently with a stiletto wielding Archer, etc. The Level 20s were crap, and in the 30s: Knights loved the Bearded Axe’s speed, Vanguards used to dance around like headless chickens and the MAA class would typically dodge forward, stab, and dodge back or exploit the Dane-axe reach. I personally used to take advantage of the alternate swing with the mace when they updated the Mouse layout by mapping alternate strikes to Thumb Mouse Button 1/2 and introduced the pole-axe.
And now? Even Level 20 players can utilise the very skills it took time to establish years ago, whilst the previous Level 40s are now around Level 60 (or mid 50s), have mastered almost every weapon, are probably in a well-known clan and are practically untouchable. Most good archers don’t need crossbows (which fire straight) anymore for headshot accuracy; even when approached for close combat the skilled ones don’t try and rush-stab you like an epileptic bat anymore, and the implementation of Duel mode has made the Javelin thrower type a force to be reckoned with. Most knights these days use the Messer, which is a weapon I favoured back when it wasn’t very popular due to its lack of speed (which many now realise is useful for feint animation, and best of all: dragging animation). Flails are now apparently universally considered as useless. No one ducks anymore because everyone else has all learned to direct their swings lower, or not swing at all. And I haven’t seen one single MAA using a hatchet these days! They all know the Norse sword or broadsword is the weapon of choice.
And this game will not stop growing, either. Funnily enough a lot of the cultural choice of weaponry has also been affected by the constant patches to nerf them, which derived from whiny idiots complaining about weapon x or mechanic y being overpowered. For example, Vanguards generally don’t use the Claymore anymore, because Torn Banner nerfed the damage output. I remember before this that the Claymore was a weapon of choice due to its speed; and the nerf directly affected the way players utilised the Vanguard, and thus indirectly affecting his opponents (of any class) and how they challenged him. Thus my point is we're still learning, and that this game is not yet a final product. You may call it 'exploited,' but you could also call it 'evolved.'
But enough of my analysis. Here are legitimate reasons why Chivalry sucks:
- I feel there aren’t as many players as there used to be. Perhaps this is because the majority are conglomerating in the Level -20 Servers. So you have to wait for a Free Weekend, and when that happens, every server is almost ♥♥♥♥ing full. Still, Free Weekends are a good thing for the game.
- The new interface is crappy. Of course, this is subjective. But it is.
- Torn Banner keep patching stuff that doesn’t need to be patched, yet can’t for example, fix actually annoying issues such as the chat-box resetting every time a new duel occurs in Duel mode (you can imagine how annoying this is when I’m in the middle of replying to someone).
- The new maps, such as Cove, Castle Assault, and Impasse suck (of course, this applies to LTS). This is again subjective, but it is especially annoying as they are the only 3 maps I ever see in LTS along with that Colosseum based magically environment changing one, whilst they remove my favourites such as Dark Forest XL.
- The customization brings originality, and the purchasing of separate items (some made by the WorkShop community is great, but I sometimes wonder why I’m fighting an Agathian that looks like a Mason Nordic Viking with campish bodypaint. Or a tw*t that think's he's Sauron from Lord of the Rings. This is just me nit-picking now.

I have 1000+ hours in this game. Been playing since closed beta. Overall it's the best mmo I have ever played.
First of all, the worst things about this game are the labor system and the RNG regrading. If you try to stay free to play, just realize that you won't be able to craft much unless you are willing to leave your game on overnight to generate some labor. Even coinpurses dropped off mobs require labor to open. I recommend paying the $15 for your first month of patron. After that, you will have oodles of labor. Labor = crafting = gold = never having to pay for your patron with real money ever again. I played for 8+ months after release without paying any real money. I started paying again to support the game and because I wanted to keep more of my gold for myself. =P
If you are lucky, RNG is your ticket to the big bucks. If you are like me and you absolutely hate RNG with a passion, just don't do it. It's that simple. Pay someone else to do it for you. I never regrade anything. I just save up the gold and buy an item that someone else has already regraded. Unless you are super lucky, the cost is about the same as regrading yourself.
A lot of people say that this game is pay to win. While technically you could shell out money  for credits and sell those credits for gold, it would take a rediculous amount of money to buy any gear of worth. I'm talking $300+ for one piece of armor. You need seven. If you add in weapons and jewelry, you are talking about 3-5k real money to gear out one character. How many people do you think are gonna do that? I haven't personally met any. There are a lot of strong people in the PvP, but most of them got there by putting in a lot of hours and a lot of hard work.
Now I'll talk about what I LOVE about this game. =D
Character customization: It's incredibly in-depth. I can spend hours adjusting sliders and making my character truly unique.
Classes: Classes are all really fun and you can switch between them at any time. I hope they add even more in the future.
Crafting: Tons of different crafting professions. If you want to put the work in, you can master most of them on a single character.
Questing: Quests here are pretty average for an MMO. Kill this, collect that, deliver this letter, etc... What I do love is that you never have to do a single quest if you don't want to. If you've got labor, you can craft and explore your way to max level.
Combat: Mechanics are also pretty basic for an MMO but much more dynamic than say WoW. Different abilities chain together in different ways so you can make your combat style very unique.
Mounts/Pets/Costumes: This game is a collector's DREAM. My gear may not be the best in the game but I have a ton of adorable pets and costumes along with plushies to decorate my house.
Housing: I honestly prefer zoned player housing, but Archeage's system isn't bad. On the more populated servers there isn't enough land to go around so you will have to save up or join a guild if you want to farm. There are a ton of different houses to choose from and you can decorate them however you like!
SHIPS: If you love ships/pirates chances are you will love this game. Choose a base ship and customize it how you want. Want to go deep sea fishing and haul several fish back to the mainland to sell? There's a boat for that! Want to be a solo pirate with the fastest boat on the seas? You can! Want a massive galleon with fold out cannons for you and your buddies to man together? It's in there. We have the kraken. We have the leviathan. We have massive ghost ships. Get a fleet together and go fight them for awesome loot. A fan of underwater adventure? Get yourself a submarine like me and go exploring for sunken treasure chests. If you are a trader at heart, get a merchant vessel to haul large amounts of cargo across the ocean for big rewards. Just keep an eye out for those pirates!
Honestly I could go on and on about what I love about this game. I have been playing for 2+ years now and I still haven't tried everything there is to do here. Yes there are negatives, but every game has them. Trion doesn't have good customer support but they also don't MAKE you pay for anything. There are a few cosmetic items that can only be gotten from their high cost packages, but so what? I encourage you to give this game an honest try if you love MMOs.

War for the Overworld has now been officially released with a story campaign I can play through and the love the devs have put into this project has become apparent.
It's messy around the edges and could be perfect with a bit of tidying up, but here's my re-review for you:
War for the Overworld has successfully put itself on the map as the best dungeon "god" simulator we've had for a long, long time. It is incredibly similar to Dungeon Keeper (so much so that I keep struggling to call it otherwise in my Let's Play for it!).
Now, when I first re-opened the game, I was again annoyed that everything seemed a bit bland and grim around the edges in colour. A strange criticism for a game surrounding evil overlords, but one worth adding. I did however have a personal fix for this. One that I haven't had to utilize in years, outside of a horror game. I adjusted the gamma ... though I did so by a whooping 60% brighter.
I can now see the detail the devs have put into some of the blocks, the rooms, the gold veins, the walls and more. It's a very, very beautiful sight to see and one that brings back many memories to the old DK games that WFTO was inspired by. It just seems such a shame that the darkness level is so off that I needed to adjust it by that amount to see the gorgeous detail (something I haven't had to do on any other game in my library or console, since Resident Evil 5 on the 360!).
Would I recommend WFTO to an RTS friend or a friend new to gaming?
As of this re-review, yes I would.
Summary of Pros and Cons:
Pros:
Art team have worked incredibly hard on their designs, with only a few feeling "rushed" or in need of improvement. To perfect this, I'd recommend a DLC release of additional textured skins for monsters. Allowing players to see their succubi with the more traditional tail, wings and hoofs demon look, or the Cultist with an entirely different robe/without hood (take DK2's hero creatures and do one better, especially if you're charging for it!)
Spells very potent and powerful, though mana caps left me feeling like a kid waiting for their pocket money (even with a limited amount of workers and traps!), as mana slowly trickled up again. It's a tough balancing act I suppose, though I'd rather cast more harmful spells with less damage, than a more potent one, waiting for the resources to do so. Dungeon Keeper 1's charging spells did a very good job of that, giving you additional options to take on your foes.
The sound effect team have done an amazing job, leaving me without anything but praise in that department. Music wise, we could use something a bit more noticeable from time to time, with the most notable bit of ambience that comes to mind, being the beating of your dungeon core. Maybe have a track that brings more epic to large scale combat?
Traps are simple, but effective and the rate at which they're constructed is lovely. Constructs are a beautiful addition that allow for a great deal of variety when planning both your attacks and defences and bring in a truly unique mechanic to the familiar game play style we have come to love.
This now feels like a suitable replacement for the game-play style of the Dungeon Keeper games, though it has also put itself on the map with unique mechanics only found within WFTO.
The animations that are in the game look very nice and flow very well! This is a bitter sweet bit of praise that I'll elaborate on in the cons section...
Cons:
Certain lines of dialogue appear time and time again and just aren't bold enough in their dark humour to be as funny as the standard we've seen before. The Cultist is constantly testing my patience and leaving me to consider home schooling my workers, simply so that I can hurl the cultists into the torture chamber, due to lacking a suitable means of gagging them. The narrator is especially bad for this, with introductions nattering on for far too long, quips being far too frequent and notifications severely needing a "Toggle Vocal Notifications Off" option.
It's not that I don't appreciate him telling me that a Gnarling has entered my dungeon, but at times it almost sounds as if he's telling me "A Gnarling has picked his nose and flicked the snot. Just thought you should know." some things need a verbal notification, whilst others could do nicely with a quick icon to let you know.
Animations! Where art thou? I want to see the creatures roaming idle around my dungeon, DRINKING in the tavern or playing darts! I want to see the creatures walking about exploring the halls, or performing a unique idle animation to give more character! You have amazing animators on your team, so I cannot stress how much this would add to breathe life into your key actors, the monsters themselves! Picking up minions, dropping them and by ALL THAT IS EVIL, give them a unique and satisfying reaction (for us ;) ) to being slapped!
The right click is not being utilized as well as it could, and it would be nice to see a grand overview of the mini map, akin to DK's right click to enlarge and snap to location. Breaking out of possession should be a right click motion. You need to be given the ability to maim your enemy as quickly as possible through the eyes of your beast, so again, "Attack" should be your default ability upon possessing a monster.
Placeholders. Ladies and Gentlemen, you know this is absolutely unacceptable for a fully released game, though I have no doubt at all that this will be updated in time.
I now consider WFTO a fun game to play, that has delivered quality for the money I originally paid way back when. If you are sitting on the fence about buying this, I would say go for it. You will find a fun game full of love, though one that is currently in a late state of Early Access.

This game will attract people in pursuit of a way to sake their Dungeon Keeper cravings, but unfortunately the execution of War for the Overworld just seems very off to me and I'll try to explain why.

The original Bullfrog games carried a lovely sense of character behind their cartoony characters with a mix of gritty in there, though the monsters featured in War for the Overworld (Monsters being the most critical desired feature for this kind of game), all lack a true sense of personality and shine, with none of them really standing out and saying "Hey look at me! A fun, short little old school style FPS with real fast shooting and circle strafing, made by the same guys who made Shadow Warrior 2013. May not be the most polished or fancy game on the market, but still worth your time. The weapons are all varied and fun to use, and come with upgradeable characteristics that you can use to specialize your arsenal.

I've had a keen interest in economics for some time.
On the side of that, we have Recettear; a game that is about managing a store as a means to pay off a debt left by your (possibly deceased) father, which sounds kind of cliche. However, there aren't many games that come to mind which result in handling stock and trying to make a profit off them (or at least try to do better than break even). Your starting week will probably end up being pretty confusing, even with the 'tutorials' and tips given to you by Tear as you go along, but it's generally a game that doesn't really want to hold your hand, which makes the game more enjoyable when you do realize how the market works.
You attain goods through "second party" sources, which you then must sell at your own accord to customers that will buy what they desire. As a footnote, each character has their own threshold of how much of an increase over the base price they will generally be content with. It's mostly about experimentation, and knowing what your customers want to fulfill their window shopping into actual purchases (adventures will rarely buy anything outside of weapons/armor etc. but do sometimes request other goods), so having at least one of each selection will help your store and profits as the weeks pass.
Generally, your success for each week may or may not be enough to pay the debt, but one thing to note is that Recettear has no true end. If you do happen to fall on the payment, you still maintain everything you have, which allows you to keep trying new approaches to making good on each weekly payment the next time around. It's not a particularly challenging game, but it does require you to think about your investments, and what to sell. That said, if you consider Recettear as a stock market... it should give you a push in the right direction if you follow through.
While Reccetear does have an anime theme style, it doesn't really detract from the game itself. You can even turn off the voice acting cuts that crop up every now and then. You'll be reading text boxes throughout anyway.
An enjoyable and interesting experience, for sure. Give the demo a try. Highly recommended purchase if it ever goes on sale and/or if you like the concept of buying/selling. Mmm, meta.

This game is bonkers.
Let's talk about it right away, it has its price, and I believe it is fair for such a masterpiece.
I played this entire game and have earned all the achievements in under 18 hours, so it IS quite short, however, it's an adventure game, which unlike a roguelike or most free to plays is never repetitive. The truth is I plan to play it all over again to have that second playthrough where you know what's going on and notice these details and references you didn't understand before.
The graphics are unbelievably beautiful and smooth, and the soundtrack is as good as Undertale's.
Owlboy is hard, too. As a veteran gamer, I went through it without much problems but clearly the difficulty may increase the game durability quite a lot depending on your skill.
But the thing is, the game throws new stuff at you ALL the time, never letting you get bored and introducing new mechanics and epic battles.
It has fights, it has infiltration, it has exploration, it has challenges, expressive characters, numerous secrets, cutscenes, sidequests, it has a nuance between good and evil, so that you'll ask yourself if you are doing the right thing at several points in the game (can't tell more without spoilers, but get ready for some plot twists), it has a soul of its own.
Really, think about it, this 20 hours game took 9 years to be released, playing it is as powerful as reading a very good book.
Also get ready for the feels.

Very unique game. Though at its core, it's a simple stealth game with occasional puzzles, its unusual setting (I wish there were more games taking inspiration from Islamic myths, it would be a welcome change from common high fantasy tropes), excellent atmosphere, and the way its mechanics reward different ways to play truly make it shine.
+ Great visuals, taking their inspiration from Persian art. The lighting was also very well-done. Play this at night with dim lighting, it's even better.
+ Amazing sound design. From your character's footsteps to the patrolling guards' distinctive skipping, as well as ambiant sounds here and there, or the characters' "voices", everything is near perfect.
+ Simple but effective mechanics. You can go full stealth, massacre everything in your way (making further stealth attempts harder, but exploration easier), and use traps against the enemies (though they usually work better against you).
+ Two endings. You can get the first one in a couple of hours, but you will likely miss half the content of the game by doing so.
- A few repeated puzzles, particularly the "rotating wheels". Some of them are a bit unclear as well.
- Later parts of the game focus less on stealth and more on traps and teleporters, so it's sometimes hard to know what to do next.
8/10 Definitely get this if you're into stealth games, Islamic culture, or both.

I had high hopes for
and right from the opening title screen I found myself enjoying the inspiring music and getting transfixed with the world it was building with just those two elements. I even lost myself to apparent metroidvania style of level design and the little bits of flying I got to do. The dialogue was fairly witty and making Otus mute was an interesting take on the silent protagonist trope that I adored right off the bat.
Then I had to go to the first dungeon and found myself enjoying the game less. The flying had quickly become far too slow and I "fixed" this by air dodging everywhere instead. That was forgivable because, "hey, it's like Ocarina of Time! You just roll everywhere anyway, right?" But man does flying feel like the worst thing after having to traverse open areas with it. I found myself wanting to not explore anything because it meant I have to fly everywhere, and I'm the kind of person who 100% goes left when the game points me toward the right.
The combat in this game, in no respect, ever wowwed me. When I learned that it was a twin-stick shooter, I was on-board but skeptical. I figured there would be some fairly immediate upgrades to make Geddy's blaster feel less slow and crappy, so I was immediately excited when I got Alphonse! Until, that is, it turned out that his blunderbuss took what felt like a year and a half to fill up. The idea, of course, is to blast away with Geddy then switch to Alphonse and do a chunk of damage, so I get it, but it's bad. Nothing you do feels quick and powerful, but boy howdy do the enemies have the reverse issue!
I was having a good time with the game during the second dungeon area, which is a bit of a stealth mission done simply and elegantly, and I was ready to go on to the next big level! And then that level threw you into so much frustration that after I was done SMASHING into it with my beaten and bloody head, I immediately quit the game feeling cheated.
I respect games that take a tough-but-fair approach. Part of that approach is to make sure your players feel like they're getting stronger with the characters. I was ready for a game, priding itself on its SNES/Genesis style, to be difficult-yet-rewarding, but part of that is giving your player ample
in the game to keep them going. I don't need much. A simple blaster upgrade for Geddy, a timer reduction for Alphonse's shotgun; anything that would make you feel just a little more powerful would be great. Instead, you take your thousand coins, go to a shop with a shopkeeper who's punchline is that she beats her employees, and then buy a health upgrade and a freakin' hat or two.
At the very least, this game is pretty. With artwork this fantastic, I can tell Owlboy's look took nine years of tweaking and changing and reworking and deconstructing and rebuilding to get it just right. I can give nothing but a massive kudos to the artists and musicians of this game. The presentation is lively. This game truly gave me that nostalgic feeling of a late SNES title like Super Castlevania or Demon's Crest, or even Chrono Trigger but with a lot more polish and the power of a PC to back it up. Even the story I found myself enjoying despite it being a fairly on par experience.
But beauty is only skin deep. When you get down to the skeleton of a game, the gameplay, it's all rather feeble and dusty.

I have felt no actual reward for taking time in battles as my characters still die, a lot. I take the high ground? Doesn't matter. I start the battle behind my opponent? Doesn't matter. I take cover? Doesn't matter. I use spells in combination to maximize effect? Doesn't matter. I divide and conquer? Doesn't matter. I use strategic matchups? Doesn't matter. I overload with healing? Doesn't matter. I overload for damage? Doesn't matter. I rush in with no plan and just start swinging? By pure chance, that was the only battle where I didn't lose a character.
To make matters worse, every encounter leaves me with significantly less than when I started. No problem, right? It is an open world game, right? Sure, completely open and small, too small. I spend most of my time running around in circles picking up odds and ends (Buckets, baskets, fish bones) to sell to buy more ressurection scrolls. I steal all the food and potions I can possibly find but just can't keep up with what is needed to win fights. Ultimately, I have become a petty theif in the game, wasting hours of time stealing crap to subsidize my inept party of fighters. And that is the game, five minutes of prep, ten seconds of actions, and you fail. F8. Five minutes of prep, ten seconds of action. You barely win. Thirty minutes or recouping losses. Continue with the story line.
The second issue is the math in the game. I'm level 4. My enemy is level 4. I do 20 damage with my most powerful attack, a magic battle ax. He shoots a plain jane, run of the mill, every day bow... 21 damage. That is stupid. On average, it takes my character about eight rounds to kill an equal level enemy. It takes that same enemy about five to six rounds to kill me. I have a ninety five percent chance of hitting? That means I hit about seven of every eight attacks. Perhaps I've missed something, but the statistics always seem to favor the enemy, as they never miss.
The next issue is the world. It is truly open, if you're clever, and has a lot of neat secrets. It is also much more realistic than some games where a shop keeper in a podunk village might sell you a "Greatsword of Fire" or some other marvelous item. However, the open world is also boring. It is a series of shops that don't have crap worth buying and a series of fifteen step quests all based around just happening to bump into the one item you need to get the next dialogue box. There are a handful of skirmishes to help you get close to the level you need to be to not get totally clobbered. But, just like real life, close only counts in horshoes and hand grenades.
Last is the pace. This game is slow. I love slow games. I have dominated every Thief game ever made. I enjoy old school wanderlust RPG's. Pillars of Eternity seemed to go way to fast for me to truly enjoy to maximum extent. Yet this game just seems to grind on and on and on.
Ultimately, description of what is wrong is can be described thus: You don't count the time spent winning. When you play Divinity: Original Sin 2, you count the time spent not losing.

M:SS is a unique sort of adventure game. There's not really any action in the game, no brawling, no shooting, nothing, so if you're looking for that, don't bother. If you want to experience a supernatural detective story, however, you may feel right at home. The game does a lot of things right, but doesn't always hit the mark.
You play as a kid-with-troublesome-past-turned-detective-ghost. The meat of the game is exploration and solving "the Bell killer case". In order to do that you can explore the main hub area of the game, Salem, as well as about 7 or so levels. All of these can be freely explored and revisited once you've unlocked them in the story (I think you can even resume the game after beating it to collect everything). Speaking about collectibles, those are undoubtedly what will - hopefully - capture your attention the most, since the main game itself is abysmally short if you just rush through. It took me about 8 hours to finish it and I've found about 95% of the collectibles. Most notably are the ghost stories, one of which you can find in every level including Salem. For these you just have to reveal and collect specific items, some of which are very well hidden, to unlock a narrated short story. It's actually kinda fun to listen to them. Of course, if you're lazy, you can just look them up on YT...
Apart from that there are scenes from your life, notes from your dead wife, notes about the killer, etc. I'd say the notes about your past with your wife are probably the most interesting, the rest is ok-ish, but it's nothing that would make the story better. The other stuff at least makes you care a bit about Ronan.
The main gameplay mechanic, however, is finding clues and solving cases. I gotta be honest here, there's nothing much to it. You basically just go around the room, look for interactions, listen to the narration and put 2 and 2 together. Most of these cases are very logical, however, finding some clues or interpreting them correctly can just be a case of trial and error in my opinion, which doesn't really make this mechanic all that great. Luckily that doesn't impede your progress (unless you can't find the relevant clues), just your "score"...you can try as often as you want and there are no up- or downsides to it from a gameplay viewpoint.
The most outstanding feature of the game is probably that, since you're a ghost, you can walk through walls and such. The game feels like an old school FPS with no clip mode activated. Lovely, but it can also be disorientating, and your ghost form can't cross all thresholds. Each level is also at some point populated by demons (3 or 4), who patrol an area in a set radius. If they spot you, you better hide. You can either completely ignore them and rush through most areas or take your time to stalk them yourself and dispatch them with an easy button press...it's, frankly, quite boring and clearly a mechanic that was tacked on. At least it feels like it. And that's a general problem with the game: it feels fresh, but also at times unfinished. There "could" have been so much more, but instead it's just a glorified item collector with a pretty decent story (which imho is the main attraction here). For example, you can also help some ghosts find their final rest, but with most you can just "ask them a question" and that's it...or just talk to them, but they don't have anything to say. That just feels weird. I mean, what's with the questioning? It feels as if the devs intended to do more with that but either ran out of time or budget or just scrapped the feature for another reason and left these remainders in the game.
Visually the game is also not a stunner, despite using the Unreal 3 engine. Since the game plays at night anyway, and you're dead...there's very little colour, very little distinction. It just feels a bit "bland", but you could argue that was intended and fits the theme...still, it feels so boring and most locations don't have that "oh, this is cool" feeling to them.
There's also a few bugs and movement issues at times, as well as severe performance issues that shouldn't be there in a game such as this. Luckily they don't impact the gameplay at all, but they're still annoying. Not sure if it's the game's fault or Win 10's.
I'd say wait for a deep sale and give it a whirl.
It's good, real good, maybe even the best!

So what does the title Qasir al-Wasat actually mean? It’s meaning is relatively simple and cleverly ties into the game’s story. Qasir al-Wasat means the palace in the middle and that is precisely the game’s setting.The game’s Steam description, below, does a very good job in explaining the game. So rather than focusing on that I’ll jump immediately into my opinion on the actual game play. I’m not generally a huge fan of games where you’re dead in one hit and have to start over from a checkpoint but I was definitely a fan of this game. The setting is brilliant and the narrative that begins with the introduction really suckered me in. I genuinely felt as though I was experiencing Syrian culture. In a world where many people are far too easy to dismiss the culture because of world events its a real treat to see something that is so easy to immerse yourself in. It’s content is something that even those who hold ill-formed prejudices should be able to gain enjoyment from.
I’m a huge fan of how the stealth mechanic works. It also happens to be the most important mechanic in the game – present in almost everything that you do. If you move into lit areas enemies will see you therefore you need to be careful where you are at all times. But that is only the first layer of the mechanic. Arguably the most important part, certainly the most compelling from my perspective, is if you kill an enemy and get blood splatter on you you’ll become visible to enemies even when you’re out of the light. There are pools of water spread throughout each map that allow you to cleanse yourself of the blood and to return to a fresh status. These are well placed throughout the game with most or at least many serving as a checkpoint (I didn’t die everywhere so I’m not one hundred percent certain).
The puzzles, of which I would consider most games of being, are fantastic and helps make the action-adventure a thoroughly enjoyable experience. There are a number of ways to move throughout the majority of the areas of the game and each will result in making the next part of the game either easier or more difficult. It’s a game where you can choose to attack and kill everything in your path or try to play as sneakily and stealthily as possible. Some rooms will require you to kill your enemies where as others can be conquered without getting blood on your hands, literally.
I really do not have much to criticize. The only thing would be considered trivial. I believe that you’re thrown in at the deep end and not quite in the best way possible. I died a few times in the very first room. It took me a couple of minutes to work out exactly what I had to do and then I was set. The game is difficult, intentionally so, and you will die often. A few of the hits do feel as though you’ve been cheated but they’re easy to overcome and it’s not really a big factor in the game. Otherwise it’s a truly wonderful experience and one of the best that I’ve had this year.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to everyone. I think there’s something here for all gamers and there truly is no content here that anyone could consider insulting. A truly great game.

If you love Arabian Night, you'll love this little piece of masterpiece.
Heavily focusing on stealth and one-punch death, players will control Subtle - a mystical creature summoned by a sorcerer named ah-Saahir with an assassination task: to eliminate 3 different targets and retrieve an extract of poison coming from their special weapons.
Once Subtle has completed the task, the game will be over, but the game's story line and secret is hidden so well that players can actually trick ah-Saahir and take time to explore his dark secret, motivation that makes him summon you from the beginning and what's hidden inside the palace that you take place in. The game focuses quite well on sound and visual as they're essential to the stealthy gameplay. With the ability of staying (Almost) invisible and one-hit kill, Subtle can walk around in the palace without having to kill (Almost, again) everyone on its path. But without its powerful poison, each kill Subtle makes will leave blood on its body, making enemies recognize it quickly, so trial 'n error will happen A Lot during the exploration.
The palace's design is well-done in a way that makes every room seem to be connected along with the characters in-game, making them look more life-like rather than repeated AI doing what they're programmed to. Secrets are also well-hidden and will force players to explore everywhere in order to solve puzzles and dig into the immersive story line. The sound and visual, again, are executed and prepared so pleasing that they represent a miniature version of your favourite Arabian tales when you were young. Puzzles are also designed well, making your grey matter work hard enough to solve them all.
The downside of the game is the clungy control during in-game and even in menu, especially when changing the binded keys. Sometimes you won't be able to use some buttons like the Examine one in a room or the dialog will be frozen, but these glitches don't happen too often, fortunately. Depending on your system's rig, V-sync may not work well and will create screen tearing while Subtle is moving around.
But overall, this game is a gem packed with tons of secrets that beg you to solve them in order to see what's behind the curtain. Totally recommended to try right now or you can wait until Steam sale comes.

At first glance, Qasir al-Wasat might look a little bit simple and rough on the edges but this is misleading. Within a few minutes of gameplay, it's easy to notice the qualities of this game - and there is a lot of them.
The mechanics are spare but very clever, with a surprisingly amount of depth. Aside from the stealth mechanics, there is a plethora of puzzles, branching paths and secrets that rewards patience and observation. The art direction is atmospheric and full of details, showing a deep commitment to craft and research. The plot is very straightforward at the beginning but is much more intriguing and complex than it seems. It is also one of the most unique and creative settings seen in a video game, with small vignettes and lush descriptions that result on a very rich and interesting lore. I would also recommend a good pair of headphones for the eerie sound design and music, which adds a lot of immersion and mood.
Not all of these elements are perfect, but they are very coherent and consistent with the themes of the game, resulting in a sum that is greater than the parts. I would recommend this gem to everyone that is looking for a challenging gameplay that trusts the player intelligence while offering a unique setting and story.

This is not a review that calls the game really bad.
In fact, it has a nice mood, I like the "dialogues" if you could call them something like that, the humour etc.
But, I probably won't play the game anymore. Why?
It takes too much time to let things happen:
Some small spoilers ahead!!!
There you are wandering through nature, screen after screen, nothing happening - no interaction, nothing -, the artwork nice but nothing special. Is the intention to show you, that you have to be patient? Perhaps.
Then you find a fireplace. You now have to search for firewood. But, you gotta be kidding me, there's lots and lots of it and you have to go back many screens. Then gladly something a little bit more fun happens.
After that you are back at the fireplace and have to be patient again, while nothing really is happening.
OK: While I played, I thought about my life and hobbies. I work. In my work, I have lots of situations where I have to be patient. Then I love to paint, there patience is needed, too.
In games, I want things to happen, I don't want to wait through minutes of situations that give me the feeling of waiting screens.
So, I decided to paint. That's more productive and more fun. Because the game now felt for me like a waste of time. Why was I playing? To come to another situation, where I have to patiently wait for some nice jokes? No.
So, if you want to kill some time, have time to kill and don't mind the slowness of the game, just try it! I think it's made with lots of love.
If you want more entertaining games, if you want things to happen a little bit more faster, think about, what I wrote - if you want to!

While I haven't finished the game, I have played for almost 40 minutes, which was more than enough for me to decide that; no, I do not recommend this game.
Edit: I went back to the game and played for another hour. Everything you see until the * is what I wrote for the first 40 minutes, and everything after that is what I wrote for the next hour of gameplay time.
Going into Faria, the first thing that instantly puts me off is the graphics. While the game uses several assets that look good on their own, these do not go together. The characters are generated from MV's character generator, and look REALLY out of place compared to everything else that's pixellated. There are a lot of cut-offs in maps, and the maps are usually not really fun to explore. While the maps start out fine at first, they eventually turn into empty meadows of grass, flowers and trees real quick. The cliff tiles are used really weirdly, and sometimes do not make sense.
The game has some pretty well written and advanced degree dialogue, but it pretty much disappears after the first 15 minutes as the game just turns into a walking simulator. And even as someone who enjoys walking simulatos, the game just felt empty and boring to me. A lot of the walking simulators I have played atleast give you dialogue and beautiful environments to help make themselves fun to play, but FARIA just lacks any kind of unique-ness. One thing you definetly do not want to do in a walking simulator is make the player super duper slow and force them to backtrack. Which the game does. It does have running, but you have a limited amount of stamina, which isn't that bad at first, but quickly gets annoying.
After around 35 minutes into the game, you are supposed to find firewood to start a campfire. While the idea doesn't seem bad, it requires you to walk all the way back and just gather wood lying all over the place, because apparently even after getting like 20 she still wants to ''let's keep going!''. This is about when I dropped the game, because walking all that way was just way too tedious.
The game does have several branching paths in the maps, but they usually lead to nowhere, and if you have a game that's set up like it wants you to explore, you should definetly reward the player in some way.
Other than that, the only issue I have would probably be the resolution. While many may disagree with this, I really hate large resolutions and fullscreen. I would much rather play a 640x480 or smaller/slightly larger than play a game that is 1024x768(which I believe is the resolution size, but am not 99% sure). While I'm not really breaking off any points or downrating the game simply for this issue, I would still like to be able to play the game in smaller resolutions~
It's a shame, because Faria feels like it could be enjoyable if it offered more than it currently has, but is just really boring and bland in it's current state. I'm totally up for giving the game another go if it was actually updated to offer more content, or if it actually gets better and the game doesn't repeat the same mistakes(because ain't wasting my time walking through the same meadows again for 6 hours), but right now, it's just... nah.
*
So, I decided to go back into the game. I must say, it does get better. But sadly, not better enough to change my review to postive. And right afterwards, after around 40 minutes(again) the game goes downhill once more.
So, there is a lot more dialogue for the next 40 minutes of gameplay, and it's actually pretty silly and nice. However, the game is still filled with cut-off tiles, passability issues and semi-poor mapping. The music, which I forgot to talk about when I first wrote the review, is actually pretty good and -mostly- fitting (though the music in the dark cave is just too cheery, imo, hence the reason I said ''mostly''). Since the next hour of gameplay introduces a new character, I'll talk a bit about the characters in the game.
So, Fiona has some pretty silly and nice dialogue in this next 40 minutes, but she still doesn't have a personality that makes me like her. She mostly just feels like she is there to satisfy the ''playable character'' role, and despite her silly dialogue she just feels generic and boring.
We later on get introduced to Skye, who is also the main reason things went downhill for me again. While she is cute and, just like Fiona, has some pretty silly enjoyable dialogue. She is a lot more unique than Fiona as a character, because unlike Fiona, her LACK of personality is what makes her likeable. She mostly doesn't know what's going on, and gets easily distracted, which makes me like her way better than Fiona.... in theory.
You see, another major problem the game has is that it takes way too long to display the next sentence or words of dialogue, and Skye commits this the most. You usually have to wait atleast 10 seconds for her to say a 5-10 word sentence, because there is a second or two of pause between each letter she sprouts out. Even before she is introduced, people tend to wait 3 seconds to display ellipses(oh, and there are also a few ellipses that are incomplete and have only 2 dots instead of 3, but I didn't mind this all that much). This is a fantastic example of the horror genre being done properly in a video game. I didn't know much about it going in, only that you played as a girl with a camera who fought ghosts, so I set the bar low thinking it might just be a bad Fatal Frame knockoff but it's very original despite the parallels. First let's talk about some horror tropes and how the game handles them because a lot of games screw this up...
Jump scares are here but they're not the ONLY thing that's here. There's is a lot of tension, build up, anticipation, not knowing what you're going to find around the next corner, etc. In other words, there is a strong focus on the psychological aspects of horror and the game doesn't just rely on jump scares. There is also plenty of times where the tension builds up to... nothing. Yes, even nothing is important in horror. If the audience learns that tense moments always lead to a horrific payoff then the tension melts away due to familiarity. It just becomes systematic. Here they mix it up often enough that you never know exactly what to expect and that keeps you on edge.
Darkness is another trope often done wrong but this game handles it in a fairly unique manner. You do have a flashlight and it is better to use the flashlight than not use it but the flashlight itself isn't the best way to light your surroundings. When you bring up your smartphone camera, the world gains an even lighting that makes it easier to see things. Being in camera mode is slow, however, so there's a good balance between moving quickly in low light and switching to your camera to see better. The game also avoids two horror game DON'Ts: flashlight cone of light and batteries. The flashlight has a fairly wide arc of light (although the engine sometimes renders things in darkness that should be lit, this is an engine issue and not a design issue) instead of a narrow cone which is great and it doesn't require batteries/fuel which is fantastic. That's just the beginning, though, because later you get an SLR camera which has a completely different lighting mechanic. Instead of a flashlight you have the camera's flash. The flash lights up the world VERY well but only briefly and when you bring up the camera you're left in the dark until you take a picture instead of having the even lighting of the smartphone. This is a whole new dynamic and you have both the camera and the smartphone so you can switch between them as you like which gives the player choices and different ways to explore the world.
Now, onto combat/puzzle mechanics. These almost entirely revolve around the camera. Many ghosts you can just take pictures of when the camera shows static but sometimes you need to work out a pattern or a discover a weak point in order to be able to kill a ghost before it kills you. Puzzles are also mostly about taking pictures of the right things or noticing differences in the world between the world as you see it normally and how you see it behind the camera's viewfinder. While it seems very simplistic, the game keeps everything fresh throughout. Each ghost and puzzle is going to have it's own little twist. There were a few fights and puzzles in the game that I was really impressed with and I don't want to spoil.
As for the story, the game does a great job of giving you the backstory through little newspaper clippings and whatnot while giving you the present day story though cutscenes. There are some aspects that probably could have been fleshed out a little better but overall you'll know what's going on by the end. At first it seems like a normal little haunted town but there is a bigger central plot that comes into play near the end so I can't say any more about it.
As for criticisms, I have plenty. This is an indie game on a budget so it does have some flaws but overall the great experience overshadows all the flaws. The one flaw I have the biggest complaint about is Limbo. When you die you end up in Limbo and you have to run into the light to get back into the game. Normally this running section gets longer and longer the more times you die and it gets REALLY annoying. There are items you can collect to shorten Limbo, however. IMO, the shorter length should be the standard. The first time I played I missed an item so I wasted many, many minutes running in Limbo during boss fights where I died frequently and I feel that was just a big waste of my time. (Edit: Turns out there is an option in the game for "Fixed Limbo Length". Wish I'd known about that earlier. Turn it on to save yourself some grief!)
There are also some little quibbles like the low res textures (some are like N64 quality, I know this is indie but sheesh), some audio levels being unbalanced (sometimes a BGM would kick in quite loudly for what I had my volume set to), a few glitches here and there (nothing game-breaking) and some of the ghosts can have particular quirks that make it hard to fight them (one ghost I needed to aim the camera slightly high or I couldn't get static to take a picture and I was completely frustrated before figuring that out) but none of them are enough to detract from this great gaming experience. I highly recommend it even at the full $15 price tag. Pick it up if you enjoy horror games.

The Mass Effect Trilogy is perhaps the greatest creation in science fiction in over a decade. Its scope and scale dwarf any movie, the characterization and emotion compete with any novel and its graphical flair and design eclipse any comic book or graphic novel.
BioWare has built an entire company around compelling narratives and interesting companions, and this expertise is demonstrated with unparalleled deftness in Mass Effect 2. The fully voiced dialogue is tight and economical, yet shows a range and depth reserved for the best movie scripts.
With its Seven Samurai backbone, Mass Effect 2 packs a great deal of world-building and character development into a tight narrative arc. Introducing totally new worlds and new characters who will immediately become familiar locales and friends thanks to the richness of their presentation. These people and places will be exploited for greater emotional heft in Mass Effect 3.
The actual gameplay is a competently executed cover-based shooter - taking ques from Gears of War especially. While the nuts and bolts of combat are solid and work well, they are decidedly not the centrepiece of the game or development effort. Combat is best seen as a highly enjoyable diversion between the addictively immersive dialogue trees - and that's okay. That being said, firefights are far more fluid and interesting than the original Mass Effect's stilted and often slow-paced battles. Position, mobility and powers matter a great deal more; this is the highly kinetic World War II to the stolid and static attrition of The Great War.
To say much more would be rob the reader of some joy from the game. It is one of exploration, elaboration, discovery and immersion.
If you've ever liked an episode of Star Trek or devoured Battlestar Galactica, you owe it to yourself to jump into the Mass Effect's vision of the Milky Way.

I waited long before buying this. I've watched the development from day 1, tested the "unofficial" version and finally decided it's time.
Considering i spent literally lots of hundreds of hours in the Dungeon Keepers, and adding the confidence, commitment and love the developers show for their project, i can safely predict what this will become: GLORIOUS!
It looks and feels almoust identical, except the modern graphics of course. Well, modern is not quite right. It still looks dated, but not compared to that old original DKs. Well does that matter? HELL NO! It's more than adequate and gameplay > graphics!
Although WFTO tries to clone DK in every aspect legally possible (even the "...has entered your dungeons"-voiceover had exactly the same melody) i've notices some minor additions that won't change gameplay but makes it more fluid. Like different rallies for workers (YAY!) and warrios. Or a flag to forbid workers to dig there (YAY!) or groupings (YAY!).
Why reinvent the wheel? It already was perfect.
Sure, a recommendation based on a tutorial and a sandbox is quite risky (as there is not much of a campaign here yet), the basic gameplay-skeleton looks and feels "right".
THIS IS THE SUCCESSOR WE'VE ALL BEEN WAITING FOR TOO LONG!
Even if it does not add much new things, it revives one of the best game/gamplays of all times. Although i still play DK2, this will end an era and start a new.
What about Dwelvers? They're damn brilliant too, and even a lot cheaper. But they're having a different approach. Taking the master and bringing in their own vision. This is totally fun too, but it's not DK3. Not visually and not gameplay-wise.
Get then both if you can!
If you can't, get this one if you prefer the "darker" original gamplay and get Dwelvers if you want some creative fresh ideas added to an already superb gameplayconcept.
tl;dr:
You're into RTS? You like a game that does not take itself damn serious? You're quite fed being the "good" fighting the oh-so-bad? Give this one a try! But only if you think this will really suit you, otherwise WAIT until it's done! Without the campaign you'll stuck with the sandbox. The campaign will decide it's final faith (and multiplayer of course).
Alternative? Except the masters itself, there is only Dwelvers. Maybe "Dungeons 2" (time will tell). Besides there are no games (to my knowledge) that come even close to this gameplay and fun. Period.

This game is much better than I thought it would be. The Turn-Based strategy mixed with real-time 3rd person combat is pretty well done, much better than I imagined it.
The map is populated with enemy units, with your own placed prior to the mission at specific control points. You have a variety of soldiers to build your own squad with, including Snipers, Heavies, Troopers, Scouts, and Anti-Tank units. Each individual soldier have several individual traits and personalities that make them unique and suited to different environments and situations, making pre-planning worth while. Knowing your soldiers strengths, weaknesses, personality, etc., even down to who they work best with and who they don't. Mix in equipment and upgrades, not to mention a customizable tank, and this game doesn't fall short on the prep. It's simple enough for the less forward thinkers to jump in to battle, but a good strategist makes the difference (and yes, permadeath exists).
Once the battle starts, the fighting takes place in turns. You have a certain amount of command points, which you need to move your units. You spen command points to select units to move from an overhead map, then move them from a third person over-the-shoulder perspective. Each unit has a stamina bar, which determines how much you can move the unit around. When you aim, you're stuck in place Resident Evil style, allowing you to take your shot. Your unit shoots, then your opponent shoots in turns. You have a choice of weapons and tools, which vary based on what unit you've selected. You've got some support squadmates, like an Engineer, who disables mines and repair the tank, and some support tools, which includes a healing item and ammo packs. As stated above, some individuals have unique skills, which can affect the battle in a lot of ways, such as a unit with the Tank Killer trait do more damage to tanks, misandrist characters won't work well with male sqaud mates, and so much more. As the commander, you can issue orders, such as a retreat, heal, damage boost, accuracy boosts, morter support, etc. There's a lot to do and take in, but the game's difficulty curve does a good job of introducing all this stuff to you slowly and thoughoughly.
Once that's done, a story happens, and it's a great story. You can press A or Space to continue the story. There's main missions, side missions, challenges, and so much more.

TLDR: Is good RPG/Tactical game; you should buy.
I don't review often, just not my thing but for Lord Larian I shall. Played the early access 4 times solo, each time having more fun then the last. Decided to play early access a few times with some friends and had a total blast and some serious laughs. Now at release and loving every second.
RPG elements are excellent and have consequences such as being so much of a scumbag we got a villain tag that unlocked some awesome new dialogues. The world shows clear signs of love and depth, have never had a moment that shocked me out of that all important immersion. Dialog, story and lore are compelling and have me hooked. Game is also fully voiced and is incredibly well done with only a lack of varied accents.(In my opinion) If you like RPG or are a D20 player looking for a good game, this is your winner.
Combat mechanics are tight with some few little knit picks such as ocasionally inaccurate AOE/LOS markers for skills that cause some mistakes that are inevitable with such varied terrain and not game ending. Tactician difficulty is tough but fair, requiring you to turn every battle to your advantage, sometimes even striking an enemy first while a party member distracts them with friendly words. Meanwhile lower difficulties allow for bizarre character combos being viable. The evolving battlefield is fun but requires you to think really hard about every spell you fling. The AI is also ridiculously smart, they know everything about your character except the arsenal you wield. Having spells, abilities, bombs, scrolls and arrows means the only time you cannot to anything is a result of your mismanagement of resources. Only real qualm is resistances existing only for magic as a second line of defence while armour only has dodge and hp. Certain enemies being immune/resistant/absorbing to damage types is interesting while physical only has to deal with dodge.
General mechanics are diverse and well developed, theft and murder being my favourites. Item RNG occasionally seems less helpful but guaranteed drops and well stocked shop keeps help alleviate that. If you take a diverse team items are plentiful and rarely useless but if you take a single type team you can tear though enemy defences at a breakneck pace. Only negative is the camera does not ignore the blocking wall closest to your camera resulting in you needing to use the tactical top-down camera that makes the game seem so less pretty.
Balance is fair and even but the elf nerfs before release makes them very unattractive for tactician or permadeath mode compared to all other races. Undead are amazing and used right get the min-maxer blood flowing.
Graphically the game is fantastic and beautiful and runs fine on my 1080, then again what doesn't. Spells and abilities are showy and well made, wish I could point out examples but they are all good.
Overall the game is fantastic and must have for any RPG or Tactical game lover who wants maximum bang for buck and to back a shining diamond in the pus-filled cesspit we call a games industry as well.

Let’s start from the beginning shall we?
Owlboy is a 2D platformer developed over the course of 9 years with little to no funding (with the money coming from the devs pockets) and currently avaliable for PC. The game has been one of the most awaited indie games since its first announcement back on 2008-2009, sporting HD Quality pixel art, a huge world and an emotional story
Although many say its a Metroidvania (and the early shots and demo pointed towards it), the game is actually an action/exploration plataformer with some Metroid elements (namely the sequential progression through adquisition of new abilities) and Zelda-like dungeons.
The game puts us into the cloak of Otus, a mute young owl who lives on a small village named Vellie which is overseen by his mentor Asio, a strict and demanding owl. Alongside his good friend Geddy, they guard Vellie and help its inhabitants. His life changes one day when pirates attack his hometown and steal a treasure from it, thus beginning his journey.
It has 2 main mechanics: Otus’ ability to fly freely anywhere and grab objects and people, thus the game follows an upwards sequence of progression instead of the more traditional right-side. His grab ability allows Otus to carry a variety of objects to help him reach new places or solve the dungeon puzzles, be it by interacting with the object or throwing it against monsters. Grabbing people allows them to tag along and, if they can, assist Otus with offensive options. With that being said, Otus has no offensive means to defeat enemies himself, instead stunning them for a short period of time on which you can run away. Otus moves at a pleasant speed both walking and flying, and his jump trayectory can be controled as well (akin to Megaman), so he makes floaty jumps.
Across the journey, Otus will also meet people that will be always avaliable for him to call and assist him at all times. Without spoiling anything, their abilities provide more efficient ways to deal with most situations and will prove to be valuable as you go along.
The game has the options to control with keyboard/mouse, or a controller if so you wish. I haven’t tested on a controller since I no longer have my X360 controller, but on keyboard and mouse it controls very nice. You use the keyboard to move and change/call partners, and the mouse to aim and interact with your companions and the world.
Owlboy is a more relaxed and chill game compared to other options, which can be appreciated right from the start. Though it does have its energized moments, the game goes at a more pleasant pace, allowing you to take your time and not stress yourself.
The world of Owlboy is colorful, big and filled with small secrets and caves all across, its most shining quality being that its an scenery to look at and delight on the amount of detail on it, from the greens of Vellie to the heights of Strato, inside the caves below or the Owl structures. With its stylized presentation and crisp sprites, Owlboy easily scores being one of the best looking indie games of the decade.
The music adds more flavor to the journey, each piece having a distinct personality for every place in the world. Just listening to the title screen music sets the mood for the game’s story, it knows when to play, where to play and how to make it pack a punch. The choice of instruments is also very fitting too, with energetic compositions of strings and flutes for the overworld, booming and imposing trombones and percussion for the pirates, just to name a few.
Story-wise, Owlboy’s is centered around Otus’ coming of age, which gets to you soon thanks to the lighthearted and more emotional moments, as well as the more intense parts, without being out of place. Its a rollercoaster and a blast, all in the good way. I could go on and on, but then I’d be spoiling.
Gameplay wise, it works really well and the game is also relaxed on this aspect too (which is fitting with the more artistic elements previously mentioned), but is not free of some small flaws and maybe a nitpick of mine.
Soaring through the sky and exploring with Otus is always a delight and the owl and partner abilities are all satisfactory to use. Monsters roam every most places, but they can be either dealt with quickly or just be left alone, so in most cases you can ignore monsters if you want.
The world also has spread across every place series of ring trails from which you’ll be getting the game’s currency, in order to obtain some small trinkets and some upgrades too. Is not mandatory to obtain these but they certainly come in handy for the later parts.
Though the game does not have much flaws really, it does have one glaring issue: the complete absence of an in-game map. Such a tool is practically a must and seeing how the game does not have an option for a map seems rather confusing, especially because (given the topic of the game) owls do map their environment. Though exploration is encouraged and works great, a map would have been a very welcomed addition to avoid some moments where the player may get lost.
Some minor flaws are found only on the beginning of the game but I consider these as nitpicks: at times one can see rocks that look like they are covering some kind of secret passage and are honestly kind of misleading because those stand up from the rest of the scenery. Also would have been nice if Otus could defend all by himself against enemies instead of just stunning them, at least against the small ones after a certain point if you want. It does feel a bit like a chore to be changing partners just to get rid of small pests while exploring the overworld; and the ability to put down things on a more tactful way instead of only throwing them. I get Otus is a bit of a ditzy but even then its weird to just toss things to put them down.
A command to make partners stand aside instead of just respawning them would have also been welcomed, since there were times I did need to get something or enter somewhere but they stood in my way, it takes just a moment but it can get a bit annoying. I also have an issue where there’s a certain ability that makes a prior one completely useless and still occupying space. And also to give the option to resize the window, the game looks really gorgeous, but I’d like to have it not taking quite the share of my screen if I play windowed.
And, maybe its just me, but the game’s writting starts a bit too mean spirited, I’m not saying its bad but it is kind of jarring given the situation when it happens and the rest of the game. I also would have liked if the last upgrade could have been obtained a bit more early to use it more, as well as a certain secret for lore, but I guess it is justified since that upgrade is mighty good and that secret gives a whole new layer of complexity to the ending. It would have also be nice to have other hidden collectibles around, like a medallion of sorts or some artifact to use, the coins only last for so long and in some areas the game almost gives them to you quite generously, it sort of makes it feel a bit short (maybe it is just me since I’m a more explorer type of player). And also the minigame: I am a bit upset that it had to be a mandatory element for the completionist and also a sort of abrupt change of pace, but it fits within the story itself so I guess it was a tough call.
Though with few flaws (well, few and a relatively big one), Owlboy is a charming game that definetively was worth the time spent on it, both by the devs and myself. Despite some of my personal issues, I really did enjoy all the way through and I feel that it does deserve more exposure and acknowledgement. Its a project of love that aims not to be the best game ever made but being a pleasant experience.

PC gamers tend to be open to a much broader range of game genres than console gamers are, so it was no surprise to see this game get a higher score when it hit Steam.
I was first introducted to video games through a computer and though I love all kinds of games, adventure games were my stock and trade. When this game was first announced, I thought it sounded like a solid concept. I was slightly disheartened to see it's low scores...but when most console gamers play mostly FPS and sports titles...it wasn't a shocker.
Now I understand this review is very late, but I have an older PC, so my titles are limited.
The story of this game is the most ingaging I've played in a long time. The gameplay is what you would expect from an adventure/mystery game. I've read reviews complaining about "all you do is walk around and pick things up."(News Flash Hardcore Gamers!: That's what you do in an adventure/mystery game.) I don't remember this game being advertised as anything other than that...

I think that the strength of Metro Last Light is not in its characters or story, but is instead in the environments the game takes place. The Metro is home to extreme ideologies, interesting communities and nightmarish hallucinations. When you travel to the surface of 'Dead Moscow', the sheer amount of enemies, the need for you to use a gas mask everywhere and the equally disturbing nature of it makes these times harrowing.
Coupled with a potentially crushing survival difficulty which emphasises you needing to learn when to fight, how to conserve your resources and balancing exploration with simply staying alive, Metro can be a very challenging game.
I really hope that in the upcoming Metro:Exodus, they improve on fundamental aspects like the combat and stealth systems whilst simultaneously keeping the eeriness that makes the Metro games unique. Personally, I really hope that the new world will sometimes force you to go to the surface, make Dead Moscow even more dangerous and have a large degree of interconnectivity. The bonus level 'Kshatriya' from this game provides the developers with a solid foundation for this.

Overall:
Game that delivers on the horror front, but fails everywhere else.  I can't recommend this to anyone but someone who loves the horror genre that has absolutely played every other horror games.  It's too bad, because it absolutely nails the horror, and I can see it had a lot of potential and good ideas on the horror.
The Good:
- Scare factor.  The atmosphere feels creepy and unsettling at all times, and there are also jump scares on top of this.  Even if you expect a scare, the thing that you see and experience is so unsettling, it will give you the heebe geebees.
- Ambient music fits in nicely with the unsettling atmosphere.
- Sound effects and sound design come from accurate places that aids you in discovering the ghosts and other weird things.
The Bad:
- Gameplay feels clunky.  You basically shoot ghosts to death ala Fatal Frame with your camera.  The game design seems solid, but the terrible animation combined simplistic AI that beelines straight towards you at all times doesn't feel exciting at all.
- Level design is bland.  Lots of empty rooms and empty hallways.  This causes you to run around for a long time with almost no action in between.
- Item discovery is barely passing.  The game draws a blue halo around the item you can interact with.  It's really hard to see which items are interactable.  I randomly clicked around whenever the blue halo came up seeing if I can hit something.
- Animation is barely passing, and characters float around.  I'm talking human characters, not the ghosts.
- Graphical assets.  Textures are worse than games from 1998, and polygon counts are low other than some human characters.  I'm sure they could've purchased better looking stuff from Unity store.
- B-level dialog and story.  I enjoy cheesy stories, but this was too much.

I can't belive i havn't written a recomendation for this game yet. Supreme Commander is one of if not the best RTS of all time. At it's heart it is a reimagining of Total Anihiliation, a very old RTS. The thing that makes SC so special is the scale of combat. Your not using 2 or 3 dozen units, you are using hundreds, the normal unit cap is 250, but can be increased to 1000. The maps range from 2 player close encounter maps, to giant maps that can easily fit 8 players no where near the other. This leads to a type of scale in the game that you just don't get in other RTS. 2 of the interesting things about SC is that resources generated are a steady stream, not "collected" or gven in "chunks" like most games, and your starting unit is a commander, a super powered unit that can easily take on any other unit (or even swarms of them) for quite some time. If you like RTS games buy this.

As we grow and develop, we often see someone in a different light. Whether it is from their looks, how they carry themselves, or that after knowing them for a long time you just cross over to liking them more. Developing a crush on the person. Worrying whether or not they will be accepting and go out with you, or even that they are single. With how much “The worst thing they can say is ‘No’” is said, it is still heartbreaking being turned down.
Confess My Love goes on the premise of, well, confessing your love. You play as Willie, who admired his classmate, Liza, from afar for a while. Planning to tell her that he loved her on this fateful day. With 20 endings to look forward to, you go forward hoping that Willie’s heart is not broken in one of them. Every ending playing off on how you might of felt in your own experience.
I do recommend looking at a guide for this game, as even if you figure out the general way of getting endings, there are some that stray away. Ith that said, most of the endings are timed based. Which in turn makes Willie more prepared in his words as you wait longer and of course Liza’s responses change along with it. Other endings depend on items and interacting with the other character Julie. With only the last few dependant on you doing the other endings, as well as timing and items, to achieve them as items do appear over time.
As the ending is really a twist that you really only think about after a certain amount of endings, I will not spoil it for you. But it is chilling and it is only amplified by the soundtrack switching it’s usual light hearted but fast paced theme when confessing. And at the end very heartbreaking, especially with all that you go through. Though I will say that I love games that play with how it can interact with files or the computer. The game tells you what is going to happen, and it happens on our side.
I really like the pixel art they decided to use, though the indication of an important item was of center to the interaction point other than one of them. With the character portraits, I also wonder why they only have one of them show completely. They do show Willie’s on the title screen, but Liza’s is the only one to completely show. It kinda can be linked to what the ending tells you, but it does seems like they were not finished.
+ Pixel art
+ Music
+ Interesting way to tie in multiple endings to the storyline
+/- Some grammar issues
+/- Most character portraits seemed unfinished or just not included.
Confess My Love brings a simple story line of a boy finally confessing to his crush. Containing multiple endings tied to timing, items, and/or interacting with Julia. If you have a free day and not feeling the games you already have, try this out. It will certainly make your boring day interesting.
