DreadOut is a good horror game with solid action, decent story, and difficult&simple puzzles. Common questions that everyone asks is "Is this game good?" and "Is this game really scary?" Let me answer these questions for you.
Simple answer: Yes. It has everything I expect from a horror title. The atmosphere is dark and gritty, the story has solemn undertones, there is lore that you unlock and can read from your journal, and the music fits this title perfectly. The music really made me feel like I was somewhere terrible and I needed to get out immediately. The controls are also responsive and simple. If you can allow yourself to immerse into the story, it's a very enjoyable experience. There are also three endings and different costumes for Linda. The costumes are unlocked when you complete the game once and are accesible from the rear of the van at the start of Act 1 (Not Act 0). Giving it some decent replayability.
No, the game overall is not that scary. Reason being, your smart phone doesn't run out of batteries. This is a constant sense of security in itself. Secondly, you can take unlimited pictures without worrying of running out of film... Remember dying in Fatal Frame because you ran out of film? Yeah, that will never happen here. HOWEVER, if you want to expand upon this and ask if the ghosts themselves are scary then my answer is yes. The ghosts are very scary, the sounds they make, the movements they make is all very creepy and unsettling. But again, most of the ghosts are easily dispatched save for the bosses and a few tricky ghosts.
All that aside, there's a lot in this game if one takes the time to look for it. I found many hidden things in this game that I really appreciated like UFOs in the sky, hidden ghosts, and other small recognizable details. These things won't break immersion because they're extremely difficult to spot. The puzzles are questionable in places, I found some puzzles clear and easy to solve but some puzzles were unclear. Example: I spent many hours running around a school looking for a solution to one puzzle. The solution was an object I ran past several dozen times.
That is really the only time I can think of where a puzzle was unclear. The rest are simple.
Ghosts have some strategy to them. For example, some ghosts take more damage when aiming for their head. Also, some ghosts are invicible unless you hit a certain part of their body. Bosses are tricky and can kill Linda very quickly if the player is unprepared. Ghosts will disappear into walls... So if you're in a tight hallway and you encounter a ghost, it's best to run up and down the hallway. There is a lot of dodging in this game, it's not always as simple as standing and snapping pictures. And each ghost has their own fighting style. That alone kept me playing.
The only real negative I can give this game is they removed high resolution textures during a 32-bit patch. The developers plan to release a patch to fix this.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. The cons, imo, are minor and are outweighed by the pros. Some aspects reminded me of Fatal Frame, Silent Hill, and even The Grudge (which is a horror movie I quite enjoyed.) I recommend buying it at sale price, it goes on sale often.
P.S. In Act 1, instead of going into the haunted town, you can turn around and run back down the road. Run and be free!

Whether you'll see it as a good game or not depends on what you're looking for.
It's mini golf with crazy, themed type courses. Think of mini Golf courses that sometimes feel like obstacle courses but exaggerated to at times extreme levels.
You have the ability to customize the appearance of your ball (i.e., change the colour of it, give it a hat once you unlock said hat or even use silly things up to and including an acorn in place of a ball). This can work out to some pretty silly looking balls that hopefully will only get sillier once they add more options.
Unlike other Golf games, when you aim and select the power level of your shot, you *won't* get an estimate of where your shot will land. You also cannot see an overview of the hole you're currently on, which can lead to "where the heck am I aiming for?" moments for some holes, especially when you're new to them.
If you're someone that doesn't play a lot of Golf games but has (for example) played Golf in GTA V and enjoyed it, don't expect this game to be a similar experience. This is far more causal and (in my opinion and from my limited experience with it) is not a Golf game one will enjoy if you try it take it seriously and not getting a low score is something that will bother you.
If you're someone that likes trick shots (i.e., bouncing from one thing to another to another etc.) some of the holes seem to beg for them. Doing a perfect trick shot is always awesome. However, since you can't survey the hole beforehand, it can often involve already knowing the hole and a lot of trial and error.
In short, if you want a silly mini Golf game you can play with others (but also alone if you're like me and have no friends) that's easy to jump into, this might be worth your consideration.
However, if you're looking to get low scores and to take it seriously and/or want something more realistic where you (for example) have to take into consideration which club you're using, wind speeds etc. then this may not be for you.

Owlboy was a game I honestly expected to be the big indie darling of the year. It looked fun, simple and beautiful. I was very ready to watch a brand new indie mascot emerge and hang with the likes of Meatboy, but sadly I feel Owlboy will be a soon forgotten character. It's visual art style is one of the few interesting parts of the game. Gameplay and overall game feel are terribly bland by comparison.
Owlboy starts off in a lovely little town full of characters to talk to, houses to enter and small places to explore. This set a great tone for the game almost like that of a Zelda adventure, but it doesn't continue on this path. Although it continues to expand the lore and allow you to talk to a bigger cast of NPC's as you progress through the game, it starts to become a nuisance. I have a huge problem with the amount of exposition presented in the game. Most indie games with interesting lore (or even AAA games for that matter), give you the option to dive into the deep expository elements of the game. The key word is option. Owlboy chooses to make the story of the game unavoidable, with a false sense of importance. Especially for a game so short, I just don't care about the finer details of the 'owl lore'.
The gameplay doesn't make up for this expostion overload. It lacks variety, despite seeming like it will have some with multiple companions. The game suffers mostly from a slow pace. The games flying mechanic is great at giving a sense of freedom, but the pace severly stunts this feeling. You'll be spending most of the game auto-targeting enemies and mashing the shoot button, with the occasional stealth section oddly enough. The game lacks any serious upgrade feature, and the shop acts mostly as a way to track your collectables. The few upgrades you do end up receiving happen later in the game, and judging by the difficulty of enemies and bosses, you wont really feel the difference. Most enemies are quite easy, and there's no real penalty for death.
To end on a high note, I must stress how great the art style of this game is. The environments are always new and interesting, the characters are cool and well designed, and the game mixes a good variety of light and dark tones. I haven't seen an indie game in quite sometime that  has such a solid art design as this. It has no gimmicks and it serves no ultimate purpose to the gameplay. It's just beautiful.
With all of this said, I hope to play future D-pad Studio games and enjoy them, taking the faults of Owlboy into consideration.

It is no secret that I have a huge love for both indie games and emotional games.
Owlboy from the Norwegian developer D-Pad Studio manages to capture everything I love in games. From beautifully crafted pixel-art visuals and wonderful music, through its amazing gameplay that combines elements from Zelda, Metroid and flying games to its humor, emotional moments and great and often relatable characters. The first few minutes themselves managed to make me love the game.
I dare to say that Owlboy is one of the best looking games of 2016. The pixelart is this game is often breathtaking. The attention to detail, beautiful scenery and really nice looking and expressive sprites with a sort of Zelda-esque style make the game really pleasing for the eye.
As for the soundtrack, it's equally beautiful with many wonderful orchestral pieces mixed with some ocasional electronic bits. The music often manages to build up atmosphere and sometimes even play on your emotions.
The best way to describe the gameplay is that it's a mix of Zelda and Super Metroid where you can fly. One of the main features is carrying things while flying which has many uses in solving puzzles etc. You also get to carry your buddies who will, for the most part, be attacking the enemies for you.
On your adventure you'll get to explore the world including several big open areas and a few big dungeons, full of puzzles, challenges and a lot of secrets, some of which are hard to find. It all works nearly perfectly with some very minor issues. The game isn't the longest, but it's an acceptable length for this type of game, especially if you want to enjoy the game to its fullest by 100% completing it.
Not gonna reveal anything about the story as I think it's best to experience it without any spoilers, but all I can say is that in many ways, it is similar to games like Mother 3 or Undertale, with very memorable and often very relatable that you really care about, many humorous moment as well as emotional moments that might drive you to tears. It might not be everybody's cup of tea, but I hold games like this really, really dear.
Overall: 10/10

Hand of Fate is an excellent little game that features several components. The strongest one is the game's setting, the dialogue with the mysterious Dealer character, that represents many archetypes from popular narrations - fortune teller, sorcerer, Goethe-style devil that tempts, tests and confuses the main protagonist. The tarot cards and their mysticism provide an excellent background for the game events, each game being a unique story, of hope, struggle, and of course misfortune. The art is superb, and the pacing is brilliant, the game is both rewarding and attractive when played for the first time.
Combat is somewhat mediocre, with constant bullet-time slowdowns which IMO breaks its rhythm, and the system is not deep enough, the roll move is overpowered solution for most threat, so you end up rolling around constantly with occassional attacks of opportunity. Some combats also feature damage sponges that prolong the fights unnecessarily, with similar patterns repeating overa and over again.
Overall, a fresh idea and setting, highly recommended!

One thumb up, one thumb down (mixed review)
Pros: Really good atmosphere, art, voice acting, writing, music, and charm.
Cons: Terrible design choices in the new armor system (0% crowd control or status affliction chance while armor is up and 100% chance while armor is down) - makes encounter solutions incredibly repetitive and thus fairly boring, as they are too easy to "solve" via chained, 100% success rate crowd control. Also, on tactician there are not more enemies, but instead enemies just get huge boosts to their stats (armor included), making fun, hybrid parties bad, pushing you to use a more-repetitive either all physical or all magical party. The first Divinity Original Sin also had more chance involved (hit/miss chance for both attacks and crowd control), which this sequel pretty much eliminated, which makes fights very snowbally and predictable (and thus somewhat boring) towards the mid to end portions of the fight.
Poor, lazy loot design choice as every level up your lower level equipment becomes extremely outclassed by current level equipment found by tediously going to merchants and buying their newly updated wares. Also, loot attributes are randomized on most equipment so loot while adventuring feels way less special and lovable as you ditch them frequently for current-level loot with higher numbers (feels like Diablo 3 or Borderlands - games with the same lazy, constant slow-drip dopamine design choice).
Only 4 action points without a way to increase them (unless using OP lone wolf), makes fights much less tactical compared to the first Divinity: Original Sin 1 in which you slowly increased your action points as the game progressed, allowing fun combos. In this game you will use your most powerful skills/spells at the start of almost every single fight and then your second most powerful skills in the second round. Also, because action points are more sparse, scrolls and potions are used less frequently as they take precious action points away from using the aforementioned most powerful skills/spells. It makes the combat much more repetitive than the first Divinity: Original Sin.
Initiative system is botched. The turn order is now a round robin system as enemies always get a turn in between your characters, no matter how high your or their initiatives are. This makes fun multiple character combos less possible as enemies will often move or teleport before you have a chance to perform the full combo. Example: one character casts rain on the floor, enemy moves out of the water, and your second character can no longer electrocute the water with a lightning spell.
Stats are dumbed-down. Google Divinity:OS 1's stats and then Divinity:OS 2's stats and see the difference for yourself.
Small selection of damage-dealing magic spells (with many of them locked behind the anti-fun source system which forces you to spend a few and far between source points to use them).
Conclusion: If you liked the first Divinity Original Sin you will probably enjoy this one as well, even though most combat mechanics were changed for the worse. If you are looking for a superb, deep crpg experience similar to the past greats like Baldur's Gate, you may be disappointed.

Mixes cards and dungeon exploring to a result that's both satisfying and interesting. Hand of Fate challenges you to chase down 12 bosses before you can challenge the dealer himself.
Each boss quest is like a dungeon adventure, where you choose from cards on a table. Whatever is picked is what you'll have to face. These range from random events, to equipment pickups, groups of enemies, travelling salesmen and lots more. For each step you take on the map, you consume one food. As the story progresses these settings may increase and various curses will make your adventures more difficult.
The second part of the game is in the combat, where the game switches to a third person action game. Overcome them and you'll move on.
All in all it's an enjoyable mix of two different game genres that I cannot recall to have seen before Hand of Fate did it - and it works surprisingly well.
Rating: 8/10 - Play it!

Murdered: Soul Suspect is third person adventure video game developed by Airtight games and published by Square enix in 2014. The main theme of the game is Salem’s history of witchcraft and ghosts. In the prologue you were killed by mysterious b to ell killer. The whole game is about find out who is he and why he killed you. This hunt for your own killer will take you roughly 8 to 10 hours.
As told before the theme is the Salem’s history of witchcraft and ghost stories. Once you were killed your soul is stuck in this realm. Only way to get out is find out who killed you and why? The story here is interesting. and the main characters here have a proper backstories, their interaction with one another is believable, but most of the back stories are optional collectables, This game is filled with various types of collectables some of them are fun some are not. You are also given a chance to help some other ghosts which is a fun diversion from main story.
The game has its own fair share of flaws. For one It's has many bugs, and the difficulty is also. Since you are already dead almost nothing can kill you. So the designer came up with the idea of daemons that eat souls. But it is so poorly implemented that after some missions they just feel annoying. Whenever you enter an area you are free to find the clues collectables but if you want to leave somehow these daemons show up and you have to use the so called "stealth". which feels like a chore. So after half way of the game i fiddled with config and disabled these monsters from detecting me. Yes i was that frustrated from these daemons.
So is the game worth the asking price. Well kind of, I really recommend all of you to play this. But don't pay full amount. wait for the sales for reduced price. As a whole it is a satisfying experience to play this game if you can look past the minor annoyances

A faithful, intentional sucessor to the Dungeon Keeper franchise. It lacks some of the quirky charm, but is very impressive regardless. There have been very rapid developments in the past month or so which have left it feeling more like a game than a beta, and even if there is still a way to go, things are looking good.
- The design is frankly, beautiful. it captures the feel of the classic dungeon keeper games perfectly.
- The UI is... less impressive. It's functional, but feels somewhat rushed in places.
- The creatures are interesting, but lack some of the character that the Dungeon Keeper creatures had.
- Sound effects are a little repetitive, but tend to be very nice.
Overall, it's a beta and it shows. Some things seem missing - animations occasionally feel like bland placeholders, there aren't a great variety of levels to play and so on and so forth... That said, it's already an impressive game and I can only see it improving as times goes on.

Crysis Wars (The multiplayer addon that comes with the game) has a mod called Mechwarrior : Living Legends. Any old fan of the Mechwarrior franchise losing faith in Mechwarrior Online or anyone with a thing for giant robots should try it out. Well worth the price of this game, at any price level! Despite the mod having ceased development, there are still a few people playing, and they are ususally rather helpful to new players.
As for the base game, well, It's okay, but not fantastic, and definitely not remarkably better than standard single player Crysis. There's a few new toys to play with and looks as good as expected, but it boils down to the same "Kill hundreds of Korean Soldiers for a few levels before wierd space aliens come" formula.
Stock multiplayer is either lacking in players entirely or is riddled with hackers. Avoid it like the plague. Fortunately, there are various multiplayer mods that are quite popular without the unpleasant cheaters, like the aforementioned Mechwarrior: Living legends, and the Crysis Wars EX mod, which provides an improved version of the stock multiplayer (Which is quite fun in the first place), with additional weapons, maps, vehicles, game modes to keep you entertained.
Overall, if you're an avid fan of Crysis or its sequels then you should look into this for a quick and dirty booster for your Crysis addiction. To anyone else, the fantastic mods should keep you hooked for a while, but you're not particularly missing anything special if you've tried any other Crysis title.

TLDR; Excellent run-and-gun game, but I felt let down a bit by the ending, it felt decidedly 'unepic'.
Well, OK it was a "Walk cautiously-and-gun" game. I've played this game twice, now. If you play it on  Easy, you'll see an arena type area, and go "here we go again and run in" If you play it on normal, you will see an arena area and go "oh no I'm going to get smashed again and try and sneak past (not gonna happen)"
Some of the 'unique' things about this game,
You can't crouch (whatdya MEAN I can't get through there)
there is limited ammo (slowly recharges over time, but plenty of pickups from fallen bots)
BUT there is no reload. all your ammo is in one big clip! it's so great!
The Smart Gun on the NRG is OP Forget your rifle, max this as fast as you can, then go for you rifle's rocket launcher
you only get 2 guns, but they get a snotload of alt fire modes
RPG elements through choosing what to upgrade... either gun, and choose from a variety of mods, or buff yourself with extra health / armour/ scanner/radar/medkit etc (I suggest getting the money-raqdar ASAP... before you get any gun upgrades)
Gameplay tends to be tight corridors that lead into arena style rooms.
Annoying things
You can't crouch
invisible walls. If they don't want you to go through there yet, you can't parkour it.
arena battles, doors auto lock until you finish the fight, even though they work perfectly before and after the fight.
the jumping/platforming bits (mostly for secrets) felt wrong. your character's movement through these sections is hard, as you move so fast by default, and
no quicksave (it auto saves before every arena, and right before any parkour-to-your-death bits)
The story was a huge let down thus far, even though it's open for a sequel, it felt like they finished in the middle of the story. Killing the boss didn't feel like taking down the baddies, merely  getting him out of the way so you could get through the next gate. (compounded the storyline)
things i liked
Secrets are REALLY worth taking the time to find. that extra cash allows you to build up your weapons much, much faster.without them, you might only have half the stuff unlocked by the end boss fight.
on Normal, I was panicking about every corner, setting off the next wave of enemies.

you have real speed in this game, making a truely run-gun experience. Similar to Shadow Warrior (If you've played that, It's by the same guys, but you'd know that by all the references to HR in SW)
the -nomagazine mechanic in the guns
graphically beautiful

So, A good looking FPS shooter with no quicksave (not a bad thing), RPG elements,  engaging and tactical combat (different enemy types are wiped out best by different weapon mods), and a few quirks. Hard Reset is definitely an old school style shooter.  The game gets fairly difficult at times so dying repeatedly in certain areas is to be expected.  The story isn't amazing but the cutscenes are done in animated comic book style which is pretty cool.  The original campaign isn't too long, but combined with the Exile DLC, this game becomes a bit lengthier.  Because the DLC adds on more levels without including more weapons/upgrades, the game becomes harder, especially if the upgrades chosen before entering the DLC levels were purely offensive like I did.  The enemies become much tankier so getting upgrades on health, defense, and ammo are definitely needed.  On the other hand, the level design were more varied, which is a plus, and felt better overall.
Technically, there are only two weapons, but each gun has multiple modes.  For example, one gun can transform from an assault rifle to a grenade launcher while the other can morph from traps to a rail gun.  Choosing the proper weapon and mode on the fly takes a while to get used to, but becomes fairly satisfying once you get the hang of it.  If your mouse has extra buttons, it's probably a good idea to hotkey the weapon swap to one of them as pressing the keys for it always felt a bit awkward for me.
It's got a decent length campaign mode as well as other replayable modes, which I haven't tried.  While the story isn't quite there, I would recommend this if you want to play an old school shooter game.

Great little cyberpunk classic FPS with some modern features thown in. And by "modern features" I mean the good ones, like upgrade system and not the bad ones, like regenerating health or QTE.
This game works like this: you got two guns, C.L.N. and N.R.G.. First one shoots bullets, the other one shoots plasma. However, you got upgrade stations scattered everywhere. You buy upgrades from them for nanites, which you either find in secret places (yeah, this game has secrets, another good feature) or get from shooting robot baddies. Those upgrades are mostly different modes for your guns. C.L.N. gets usual stuff like shotgun and rocket launcher, N.R.G. has more exotic things, like close-range lighting gun or sniper gun that shoots through walls. For nanites you can also purchase alternative modes for those gun modes: shotgun can get paralyzing darts, lighting gun can have EMP blast.
Game itself is pretty intense, you have to move a lot to avoid getting shot, blown up, rammed, stabbed etc. Game has  an impressive amount of enemy types and loves to mix them up to keep it fresh. Graphics-wise, game looks gorgerous and system requirements aren't demanding, but I did experienced some slow-downs, especially when lots of things exploded on the screen. Level design is good but some mind find it repetitive because levels take place only in a city, or (after free DLC arrived) in a junkyard. Soundtrack is pretty good, too.
This game does have story... but it's main feature is being skippable and is there only to explain why you are shooting robots. Also this game has an annoying feature of posting huge waypoints with giant text that says "GO THERE". You can turn it of, through. The main problem with the game, in my opinion, is low shot length, you can beat it in 3 hours. 3 enjoyable hours, that is, but still! This problem was somewhat solved by afromentioned free DLC, which adds 3 more hours of gameplay. Interestingly enough, this game came out in 2011, way before Early Access on Steam, when it's became the norm for unfinished games to come out for full price and leave gamers waiting for eventual full release.
Due to all this, I would recommend getting this game on low price (the price without discount is 15 USD, if I am not mistaken) to all classic shooter fans.

This was a fantastic game, and a lot more satisfying to play than I expected.
Owlboy has a beautiful pixelated aesthetic that left me just sitting there staring at the background at times.  The animations are spot on, with expressive characters and enemies.   The music was beautiful and the sound design... well it was okay.
The game plays well and I was expecting to find the "always flying" gameplay to be dry but the enemy designs kept things interesting.  I found that I struggled with the controls at times, but that was my own issues I'm sure.  I had to play with the right stick settings of my steam controller quite a bit to get a setting that felt right to aim with.
The difficulty curve was a bit on the wonky side.  It provided a little challenge for most of the game but then about 2/3 of the way through it goes through the roof for about an hourish and then gets far too easy.  The boss design was nice, and most were fair but challenging.  Once you figured out the patterns it just becomes a problem of execution... which causes some of them to drag on awhile.
Overall I like it and will be rejoining the game to find the rest of the coins and investigate a few things I couldn't figure out on my first playthrough.
Besides all the rubberbanding issues, I can already see this game is going to have alot of potential to a great game once it's finished.

While there are definitely a handful of things that could improve the game, the experience as a whole is a very cool, unique, and fun game play concept that hasn't really been done before, and for that I very much look forward to future installments.
The execution is very clean, from the music, voice acting, card design, environment, etc. Some of the issues are with the mechanics though, like the inability to rotate the camera in battle, how the "counter" system works, and other foundation level things like that.
My one main complaint was the lack of a feeling of progression as you go through the levels. Every single level, you start with basically the same default gear. Sure it upgrades as you progress, but the point being, there isn't any of the enjoyment/excitement/satisfaction of finding new loot, at least in the traditional sense. You may get a card for a new awesome weapon, but there is a good chance you won't get to use it any time soon, or technically speaking, you could make it through the rest of the game without getting a particular equipment card that you've unlocked. Because of that, I don't really view this as much of an RPG, instead it's more of fantasy game wrapped around an action framework.
All and all, I loved the fresh approach, and many aspects of the game, enough that I would in fact recommend it.

Overall, my views of the game are quite mixed.  It is definitely a hit in terms of its high bit art and orchestral score, but isn't the best in terms of raw gameplay value.  The story has its moments and is full of memorable characters, but overall it isn't anything you haven't seen before.  It shines best in little moments rather than in sweeping arcs.  The level design feels fine for the most part, as the environments blend puzzle solving and combat well enough.  It isn't perfect though, as hidden rings in random walls doesn't feel clever in any way, and sometimes enemies are placed poorly (like transition tiles).  The flying controls also don't feel tight enough to justify Stratos's thorn maze.  This shouldn't be suprising though, as the game's mechanics are easily its biggest shortcoming.  Fighting can feel a bit clunky, which probably explains why they never try to do too much with the combat in the first place.  It feels like it only exists to pad out the game.  From what I remember, the game doesn't have a lot of variety in its puzzles, because while each dungeon will have its own gimmicks that are clever, the game has far too many times where all you need to do is get a bomb to chuck at a cracked wall, which prevents me from remembering anything else in detail.  Speaking of which, there are plenty of times where you'll want to pick something up, and end up spawning your partner instead, which just makes the game feel unpolished.  I feel like the price tag is too much for what you get, so try to get it on sale if you can, but I am still very happy I got Owlboy.  Also, ♥♥♥♥ that cannon minigame.

I have never loved and hated a game so much at the same time.
The concept is brilliant - it's a roguelike that uses the randomization of cards to change your game each time. You build a deck of possible items and encounters, and the dealer mixes in additional ones depending on the boss you're challenging. Every game plays out differently, and the encounters can have numerous different resolutions (based on how well you can pick from cards a la 3 card monte). As well, there are tokens to earn, which unlock new items and cards. It's compulsively playable and always different.
And always frustrating - the combat model isn't great, and there's a fair amount of slowdown (especially when going into stores). The variations on combat (trap rooms, for example) are creative but not expansive enough. And the final boss battle is insanely hard - I finished all the other major challenges in less than 20 hours, but I've put in 7-8 hours on the final sequence by itself, and only beat it on easy (and just barely managed that). But even with those frustrations, I consider it one of the best games I've played this year, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the sequel improves on it. Highly recommended as long as you have a high threshhold for frustration.

From the orchestral soundtrack punctuating every environment and story beat to the gorgeous display of 'hi-bit' pixel art craftsmanship Owlboy is a feast for the senses.

Hand of Fate is an action, indie, RPG game developed by the Australian company, Defiant Development. This is one of the best action based tabletop simulators so to speak. The gameplay is very unique with a system which is enjoyable and challenging at the same time.
The story of the game is quite simple, your goal is to defeat the narrator of the game, the fate weaver.  The campaign mode contains 12 bosses that need to be defeated and after each four rounds you gain additional bonuses while the enemies become stronger. The game essentially plays as tabletop adventures with cards shuffled face down and your main hero being a pawn moving. Many times the path has different shapes which can make it tricky when it comes to planning your route.
The three main stats that are used in this game are health, gold and food. Health is usually either lost or gained in combat/traps/boons, gold can be gained in multiple ways while food is the resource that makes everything more challenging and interesting in Hand of Fate. Each movement costs one food and it is also used in many events which adds a whole new depth to the game.
The other important factors in this game are the gear and blessings/curses. The hero can gain during his adventures multiple pieces of equipment as well as blessings from various events. Combos can make a huge difference in this game and some pieces or blessings can save your life. For instance, one blessing found during the game let me re-draw any attempt during chance cards, saving my butt many times when I could have ended up in a sticky situation. The system itself is based on four factors: success, huge success, failure, huge failure which usually will either reward you handsomely or make you cry. Another factor that makes this game insanely addicting is the tokens. Each time you resolve a challenge at the end of the round, you unlock new tokens which adds additional ways to customize your deck.
The game excels in particular in the music and storytelling department. The music is absolutely amazing and combined with the storytelling of the fate weaver, it makes the experience even more refreshing. Each time you activate a card the story teller will make a snarky remark depending on the outcome.
After the player finishes campaign mode, the game can be continued in endless mode which functions similar to the campaign but with points given for successful actions, the floor number reached as well as your other stats. This in turn can provide a very long and amazing experience in which you can either unlock the cards you missed or simply enjoy Hand of Fate. After each floor the game becomes harder due to the extra trap cards added.
Overall, Hand of Fate is one of the best tabletop simulator games I have ever played which makes it a must-buy. I give the game a 9/10, a must have to any tabletop/RPG/card games fan.

This is an interesting one. Not very original, but still interesting. The premise is simple: you're Willie and you're alone in a classroom with Liza. You want to confess your love for her. Then you choose what happens. That's pretty much it. The game itself is very short, one playthrough lasts 5 minutes at max, and getting all the endings takes about... You know what, I don't really know. For me, it took 2 hours, but that's after a lot of trial and error in trying to figure things out and whatnot. Until you realise how the game itself works and which objects and interactions are important, you'll probably be stuck working with nothing but trial and error for most of the time. For a game this short, I don't think it'd be too much of a problem, but you have to read the dialogue over and over and over again for every playthrough. You can make it go faster by holding CTRL, but it doesn't help too much.
With that said, the story (or what little there is of it) is actually pretty good. Like I said, not very original, but it is good for what it is. There are a total of 20 endings that I won't talk much about because they're quick and somewhat easy to get. The translation is a bit off in places with things like typos and some words and phrases that sound a little too weird (For example, instead of what I assume should have been "Must be my imagination", it's "Must be an illusion"), but you shouldn't have a problem with understanding it, so that's a minor problem.
Confess My Love takes a leaf out of Undertale's and OneShot's books by having the game change a little bit for every playthrough. For example, after the first playthrough a new character will show up, or after a few more you'll get new things to interact with and even new dialogue. This combined with the number of endings pretty much just lay it out to you that this game is intended for multiple playthroughs. So don't just get the first ending and be done with it, there's a whole lot more to do and learn.
All in all, the game isn't bad. It's quite good in fact, but it's not a masterpiece, not that it needs to be. It's a humble little game telling it's own little story. It just has that sort of indie charm about it, like the developer(s) just made the the game they wanted to make and put their all into it. If you have an hour or two to spend, check out Confess My Love. It's pretty cool.
EDIT: Oh, and I know my achievements don't show me getting all endings, but for whatever reason I didn't get achievements until after the first hour or so. Not sure if that's a glitch on my end or if that's just a bug that needs fixing.

The Good: More Crysis, better balancing of open environments and closed, more big aliens to kill
The Bad: Nothing really new, still requires a monster to run, story is still lacking
The original Crysis was a technical phenomenon with a lot of great elements that worked, and Warhead is the exact same game with a different setting. This is both good and bad, but more positives than anything. You play Psycho, one of the special forces soldiers who was sent in with the original game’s Nomad. This is his story and what happened to him while separated from Nomad. While the core story of Crysis wasn’t too interesting there is a better mix between the open world and corridors. The game still gives you the option to choose to approach each objective by sneaking, sniping, driving, or guns blazing.
The game has more of a variety of objectives such as a train ride, and killing the larger aliens which can be pretty fun. There aren’t any new weapons, and everything is pretty much the same. If you’re looking for Crysis 2.5 with this you’re going to be disappointed. While the game plays exactly like the first there are more cinematic moments such as running from a giant alien, and towards the end the game gets really epic. There are more aliens involved this time around instead of just mostly KPA soldiers. I still would have liked to see different alien types, and maybe make the game a bit more scripted since the game is so short.
The game still looks the same with no graphical improvements at all. You still need an ultra powerful machine to run this on highest settings with DirectX10. Even my monster computer struggles to keep the FPS at a non-choppy rate during large firefights. The game is also more forgiving this time around as I only died maybe a dozen times during the whole campaign. The mass of enemies are easier to take on since the game seems to feel more balanced and the close quarters environments seem to be designed for this too.
While I wish there would have been new weapons, new enemies, and totally new locales it works with the game’s story. Warhead will really make Crysis fans happy and add an extra 4-5 hours and give you more of a back story to what happened to the strange Psycho.
--Score: 8.5/10

ArcheAge is a great game ruined by misinformation spread by uninformed players.
Let me start off by saying that I agree the game is pay to avoid grind, but I don't think it's pay to win for the sole fact that there is nothing in the cash shop that will give a player a sheer advantage over someone who doesn't spend money. If this game had no cash shop, people could still argue that it is "Pay to Win" since the best gear int he game isn't bound, and is bought with gold. A player could buy gold from an illegal gold selling site, and still get the absolute best gear in the game. I was even someone who would spew that the game was pay to win before even putting any time into it until I started playing. Another issue players will bring up is patron, saying how it puts them on an uneven playing field. ArcheAge is a free to play game, and the company running the game needs to make money somehow. Trion/XL games can't just give a game out for free, because they would end up bankrupt. I personally think patron is fair, as you can obtain it in game, or pay 15 dollars, which isn't really a lot of money.
The combat in ArcheAge is tab targetting, and in my opinion it's done really well. The combat feels really fast paced, and you constanstly get new skills while leveling. This can be overwhelming from someone who hasn't played many MMOs, but it keeps the combat feeling fresh, and not feel worn out as you progress through levels. You can also mix the classes together to build your own class, though some are stronger than others, and some of the classes aren't even worth playing.
ArcheAge also allows you to level every class and profession to max level on a single character. This makes it so you don't need to make a new character everytime you want to try something different, but you still need to level it on your main character. This is something that not many MMOs adopt, but it shys away from the need to have an alt, which for some people can be good or bad.
Leveling is pretty standard to what you'd see in other MMOs. ArcheAge will have you going from quest hub to quest hub while following a main story. I personally haven't bothered to pay attention to the main story, so I can't really say how good it is, but the game does a good job with questing making you kill a variety of different monsters, so it's never the exact same thing over and over again. A player also won't really struggle looking for new places to level or quest, because the game does a good job at pointing you into the right direction. Again, for some players this can be too much hand holding, and make the questing boring. Most people blow through the questing though, and ArcheAge does a good job at letting you mindlessly grind out levels.
ArcheAge starts to show its flaws when it comes to the labor system. The labor system is a way of gating progression, and making it so players can't do everything. If you don't pay 15 dollars a month, or spend 1300 gold in game, you will regenerate 5 labor every 10 minutes while online up to a maximum of 2000. If you pay, you will regenerate 10 labor every 5 minutes whether you're online or offline, up to a maximum of 5000 labor. You can use this labor for different things like gathering, crafting, and unidentyfying items. This is one of my only issues with ArcheAge, as it's a way to artifically stop you from progressing. There are items that you can buy, and unlock in game that will restore labor, but they have a cooldown. This is where the cash shop begins to be an issue, because you can use these potions on different characters on different servers and still regain the labor. This allows players who buy these potions on one server to benefit a character on another server. This is one of the biggest flaws with ArcheAge.
The end game in ArcheAge is what sets this game apart from most MMOs on the current market. You can choose your won adventure, and do whatever you want. If you want to do dungeons or just kill bosses, you can do that. If you want to be a pirate and rob people out at sea, you can do that. If you want to find hidden farms and steal another players crops, you can do that. If you want to fight 1v1 in an arena setting, you can do that too. ArcheAge has some of the best end game in any MMO, because you have a ton of options on what you can do. This is why I reccomend ArcheAge. The game has it's flaws, and it can be incredibly grindy, but no game on the market has the end game that ArcheAge does.
Despite the bad rep this game has, I still think it's worth trying. People will call this game pay to win before even setting foot into it, and I was one of those people. Now that' I've actually started playing the game, I realized that the issue is not as bad as people make it out to be. In it's current state, I would give ArcheAge a 7.5/10, but if they reworked the labor system, and made changes to how gearing works, it would bump my raiting to a 9.5/10.

Probably one of the first actual "sandbox MMOs" to reach western markets, and it did what it said it would
-> large open world to explore
-> Crafting
-> Farming (and trading)
-> huge battles and events
-> other stuff, bla bla bla...
BUT!
This game has had a steadily declining playerbase since the launch.
They created a huge amount of hype surrounding the release and had several server issues, forcing them to open multiple servers to host the amount of interested players. Sadly, because of poor company management and an over-the-top focus on microtransactions, most of the servers became next to empty, other than the couple of extremely dedicated players. So they were forced to merge several servers to keep multiplayer content (raids/dungeons) accessable for new players.
That's all fine and dandy, but seeing that most of the community consists of these "hardcore" players, the dungeons still remained empty, excluding newer players from most of the interesting content. The merge also "cleared" all the land players had bought, forcing them to buy it all again. Sadly, 90% of all buildable land was taken within the first 4 hours after the merge. I guess that's what a higher player-base means.
If you're into MMO's, I recommend this game, but play it with a couple of friends (5 is the max party size).
The community is not incredibly friendly towards newcomers, but maybe you'll find someone who is. It's 50-50.

This game is very cinematic; between its mostly turn-based and dialogue-option-heavy gameplay, the great writing and voice acting for the Dealer, and its excellent atmosphere, this is a great game to play with a friend in a dark room (no, it's not horror or jump scare trash). I picked it up after seeing it on a late-night stream, and I've since had friends watch it via Steam broadcast and heckle me to go disturb that ancient tomb because there might be loot in it. It even draws heavily enough from traditional storytelling and keeps its (most visible) video-gamey mechanics simple enough that I could imagine even someone who doesn't play video games enjoying it as a spectator/backseat player; try it with a family member or loved one and leave a comment here about how it goes! I mean that.
That said, it's also enjoyable alone. I've spent enough nights with the Dealer, on hard mode because I like a good roguelike challenge, dying over and over at the hands of vampires or old gods or that bloody kraken that isn't even the final boss or what have you. His dialogue is intimate, and like I said, he does a great job setting the tone and atmosphere of the piece; like so many adventurers before you who have tried and failed, you have wandered into his parlour, and you now play a magical card game built from memories of your adventuring life that may very well have your immortal soul hanging in the balance.
I admit to having been spoiled by free MMOs, to having sinking thousands of hours and zeroes of dollars into individual games skew my perception of value, but most non-free games feel outrageously expensive to me for what they offer, especially when they're short. Hand of Fate is a glorious exception, one of the very few games that I have not once regretted buying, an honour limited among my Steam library to it, FTL, and possibly Portal 1.
tl;dr 10/10 shining ♥♥♥♥ing diamond of game design buy it now

Great game that relies on the choices you make as well as fighting skill and some luck.
You have a deck of encounter cards, these get arranged into dungeon levels which your hero steps through. The challenge being that you have to balnce your health, gold and food as you go so that you survive in the long term. You start off with a fixed deck of cards, but each encounter is usually part of a chain that you progress through, so the one you just completed is discarded and then in your next game the new card will be added. This is how new loot and gear are also added to the mix.
Not all encounters are combat related, with text describing a situation, then offering some choices to make. There are some that present you with a sort-of luck based success/fail (its one of those follow the card as they are shuffled mini games) which can be frustrating, but its a mechanic that works.
Some may find the combat either too simple, or get annoyed by controls, camera,etc, but I think it works well since its not the sole focus of the game and so doesn't drag on too much.

This game is very enjoyable and scratches numerous genre itches. The game is set up with a character and the character is given a deck that you improve each game. As you unlock new quests, items, and other "tokens" in the game this serves as a permanent change to your deck. This also works with creatures, as you progress the deal will also get a harder and more robust deck. Every time you die in the game, your character and progression through the story has to restart, but any tokens you won are permanent (so it is sometimes worth dying and having to restart the game so long as you have a change at a permanent token). The combat is fun and fast, fairly easily button smashing with some strategy. The game is fast past and designed well enough that you can pop in and out of games. 10-15 minutes can be enough to actually make progress. I normally prefer very long and in-depth games that take 100s of hours, but this is something nice to break it up, or if I want something that is better on controller. Honestly you should pick up this game if you are in the mood for something different.

Metro: Last Light is pretty cool, I guess.
You play as Artyom, a man who lives in the Moscow Metro because some jerks with big red buttons decided to push the big red buttons and kill us all.
During World War 3 in 2013, a war I apparently missed, it all got too hot and everyone decided to nuke everyone. Major cities across the world were burned away in nuclear hellfire and most of the human race was wiped out. Fortunately, 200,000 residents of Moscow managed to avoid being turned into the skeletons form Terminator 2 by hiding underground in the Moscow Metro station.
It is now 2034, and the Metro has taken on a society of it's own. Less than 50,000 people of the original 200,000 are alive in these Metro tunnels, but they have formed their own brand of society and go about their day to day lives working, exploring, farming, and of course, waging war.
Because what screams post-apocalyptic Metro tunnels more than Nazis fighting Communists?
Metro: Last Light is a first person shooter where you, playing as Artyom, must travel through the Moscow Metro in search for the last Dark One, a survivor of a race of strange creatures that were wiped out in the last game. But after being captured, Artyom is cut off from his faction, the Rangers of the Order, and has to travel through a hostile Metro while fighting Nazis, bandits, mutants, your mother, and several other enemies that want you dead.
Metro: Fast Food puts a big emphasis on resource management, ammo and supplies CAN be scarce within the metro tunnels if you're a big stinky man who doesn't know how to manage his things properly. Artyom is a very sneaky fellow, and usually has the advantage of not being seen when he goes into a new area. As long as you stay out of sight and avoid light sources, the enemy shouldn't be able to see you, allowing you to plan out your attacks and pick off stragglers and loners as you see fit. Or you can just avoid them all together and stock everything like the hermit you are.
The game gives you a lot of options for handling enemies and dangerous situations. Not only are all of the weapons weighty and crunchy to fire, but you also have a knife that lets you dispatch enemies quietly as well as throwing knives for when you want to do your best ninja impression. Not only that but you can carry three firearms at any given time and customize them to meet most situations. A silencer for when you want to be sneaky, IR scopes so you can see in the dark better, and even a suppressor for your shotgun because 'No Country For old Men' was a rad movie.
You also have two types of ammunition, or at least two types of ammo for weapons that can fire Soviet 5.45x39mm cartridges. See, I did my research.
These "golden bullets" have become a currency in the Metro tunnel. The way it's explained is that the bullets aren't backed by any kind of currency standard like the NCR money was in Fallout, but instead they're prized for their stopping power and penetration. So you have a choice to make, hold on to these bullets and spend them as currency, or use them in your gun if for any reason you feel as though the shoddy and poorly made dirty rounds that are manufactured in the metro just wont cut it.
The game is linear, but honestly, what do you expect when you're walking through a literal metro tunnel. The game does open up and allow you a bit of freedom when you enter stations with enemy encounters. But for the most part, you're on the rails, no pun intended. It's not a bad way for the game, considering how narrative heavy it actually is, and I never really felt all that oppressed when going through it, there's still enough room to scavenge and hunt for supplies in between sneaking and fire fights, which is more than you can say for most linear games.
But should you play Metro: cockfight?
The game's linearity may ward you off, and the mutant fights feel like nothing more than events that happen only to drain your resources. The boss fights are fairly boring, but they only happen twice or so throughout the entire game.
I would say Metro works as a nice gateway for people into the Eastern European Post Apocalyptic genre. It shares many similarities with another series of the same genre known as STALKER, who both borrow heavily from Arkady and Boris Strugatsky 1971 classic novel: Roadside Picnic. It's a very different take on the genre than you might be use to. There's this overlying feeling of...I don't know, hope I guess. There are crazies and freaks in the Metro, but it's not like raiders and bandits completely outnumber and overwhelm the decent folk like the modern Fallout games, and it's not like Mad Max where everyone is living off borrowed time and outside of things like ghosts and mutants, it feels more grounded in reality.
The people aren't living off borrowed time, they picked up where they left off and struggle to make with what they can. Don't get me wrong, living in the Metro tunnels would still be a terrible and dreadful experience, but if you held on, if you struggled and fought with everyone else, you can make a life for yourself in those dark, old tunnels. And even though you might never see it, maybe, just maybe, your children, or your children's children can stand on the surface world without radiation suits and gas masks, and can build a new world from the ruins of the old one. Maybe there is a light at the end of that tunnel...

TL;DR: It is a simple game with too many translation errors to make the story driven game worthwhile. It's a decent time waster for a free game, but only because it is free.
I didn't want to write a review until after I completed the game and unlocked all the achievments. For a simple story game it is rather flat. For the most part all you do is wait beside a girl's desk while you waste time in order to unlock different dialogue options.
The puzzle portion of it was the most interesting part.
The controls of the game were very annoying to use, but they were manageable. It made getting some of the endings rather bothersome as you were timed.
At first I thought this might have been made by a child, but I then realized that it was made by someone who doesn't speak English as their native language. I let pretty much all of the atrocious translations slide, but there were a couple of things that would have translated no matter what language you spoke. Some of the later endings had squares instead of spaces. They were clearly not meant to be there and just seemed like lazy editing to me. Another thing is they spelled the main girl's name wrong at the ending scene. It was spelt correctly the entire time until the very end. It just seemed like the creator got sloppy nearing the end and just wanted to finish the game.
Overall it was a decent time killer, but that's all it was. The translation errors made the game almost unplayable. As a story based game, I don't think I should have trouble reading the story. Reading some of the other reviews I am not sure what they saw in this game that "made them cry", but there really wasn't much substance to the story.
Personally I would not recommend this game, but seeing as it would probably be fine in its native language AND it's free I will give it a thumbs up. This probably took some time to create. Overall I would probably say 3/10

7/10 - Good
THE GOOD
This game has an excellent premise which opens up a lot of doors for a unique plot. By far, the game's strongest point is the story; not nail-biting-edge-of-your-seat, but well told and keeps you guessing.
Character design and voice acting is very well done.
Investigation sequences make you think and feel like a real detective, searching out clues and narrowing them down to the most important in order to solve the case
THE BAD
This game is rather short (approx 9 hours).
There are very few side objectives other than the "find this many hidden objects to unlock an achievement" sort of thing.
Diversity of gameplay is lacking, featuring only two main mechanics of play: sneak mission, and investigation sequence.
The world is technically "open" but it only serves as a corridor between objectives.
Little to no replay value.
CONCLUSION
I would recommend this game to people who enjoy a story-driven experience that doesn't focus much on complex gameplay. If that's what piques your interest, Murdered: Soul Suspect is well worth your time. (Recommend buying on sale, though.)

I really enjoyed this game, though with a big caveat.
The combat system is terrible. I became so frustrated with it that I looked up how to disable the demons' awareness in the game's files. I recommend this to all players who, like me, are playing this for the characters and story and not for the once-in-a-blue-moon exorcism.
WIth that out of the way...
Character. I thought the two main characers, Ronan and Joy, had a lot of personality. I loved their banter and teamwork. I wasn't really expected Ronan to be as memorable a protagonist as he was. Thanks to the bits of lore you find throughout the game, you learn a lot about Ronan's backstory and his relationship with his dead girlfriend, Julia. Usually, games that pull the dead girlfriend card don't bother to dive into what their relationship was actually like before she was fridged. It made Ronan and his motivations feel more real.
Worldbuilding. There are a lot of collectibles in this game, but they all serve to flesh out the character backstories and Salem's history. I really enjoyed collecting all the tidbits of information so I could context on the town. The ghost stories were all super spooky, and I wish I had the foresight to complete them all. All of the NPCs have unique dialogue you can hear when you read their minds, which i thought was a cool touch.
Also, this game is just overflowing with atmosphere. Definitley one to play with the lights off on a spooky night.
Plot. I love mysteries in every medium. While I picked up on some narrative hints long before the protagonist it, the twist at the end made me gasp. I thought it was really well done. The different portions of the game were also really unique. Even when returning to a place I'd been before, I never felt like I was doing the same thing all over again.
Mechanics: As I mentioned before, the quicktime events the game uses for combat were frustrating, especially since combat isn't even the primary goal of the game. However, the investigative and interactive mechanics were really fun. I thought the ways Ronan could find new information, even as a ghost, were really inspired and unique.
Graphics: The cutscenes were really good. They don't get too gory, but there are some disturbing scenes as you see some really messed up murders take place.
I do recommend this game to players that want to play an atmospheric, creepy, supernatural murder mystery. Just do yourself a favor and tweak the files so the demons don't frustrate you.

Another positive about the game is the variation. You will sail across the sea one moment, and sword fight the next.
You will also fire at ships and attempt to board them, a similar mechanic has you attacking towns and i'm not a fan of this. The idea is using the wind to dodge shots from forts and get to land. But the wind changes at random. The idea is to leave if the wind isn't in your favor, but leaving can be just as hard which has got me killed. The graphics and sound design get the job done for a dosgame, though I found my crew yelling YO-HO-HO when they see a ship to be really annoying. Those are my biggest issues with the game. First, because I need to get it out of the way: This game is AWESOME!! Anyway, on with the review...
MURDERED: SOUL SUSPECT is the story of a criminal turned cop named Ronan solving his own murder. The game takes place in Salem, Massachusetts, USA.
Ronan is killed at the beginning of the game by a serial killer who has been terrorizing the town. The moniker this killer goes by is the "Bell killer". You spend the rest of the game tracking him down. The games is really fun, and makes you think in certain places. The characters will sometimes make you laugh out loud, but they never say anything super unimersive. Story wise, the game is really good and I always found myself wanting to go do that one side-quest or to finish this story mission - and then immediately feeling the same about the next side-quest or story mission... I wanted to experience the story.
Performance wise, the game is also really good, running at 23 FPS on a computer that should NOT be able to handle this game. I have a moldy potato laptop (It doesn't even deserve the moniker microwave) from 2011 with integrated graphics processing (No GPU) and the game is playable (With a few lag spikes every once in awhile).
In the voice acting and general "feel" departments, the game is also really good. There wasn't really had any times were the voices felt out of place or badly recorded. As to the general atmosphere and "feel" of the game, this is another place where the game shines. The town FEELS like a town that has been scared S***less of a serial killer. And aside from having all of the Cops playing Deus Ex while their working (Jeez Square Enix, you just couldn't resist could you), they feel nervous, scared and angry that this is all happening right under their noses - and they are especially scared now that one of their own has been killed (Ronan is a cop, remember).
I REALLY like this game, but I do have a few complaints, the biggest one being the demons. The developers but in an 'enemy' creature called a Demon (And they DO look pretty demonic), and I think these demons ruin the game. I like challenging games - A LOT - but the Demons are ridiculous. The game gives you no weapons and the ONLY way to kill a Demon is to sneak up behind it and press a random combination of buttons to kill it. I wouldn't have a problem with this, except that the Demons can track you down REALLY easily (It's like they have homing beacons) and once they see you, it's basically impossible to get past the area as the demons will swarm you and kill you. The solution is to change a setting in the AI coding so that they ignore you
.
The other complaint is that you can't change the key bindings - at all. The default control scheme isn't BAD per se, but I think it could be done better, and I would have REALLY liked being able to rebind the keys to what I wanted.
+Story
+Gameplay
+Optimization
+Game atmosphere
+Voice acting
+Level design/investigations
+Also, you get to control cats... And it's even better than it sounds
-Demons (There is an easy fix for this tho)
-You can't rebind the keys (And the default controls could be better)

TL;DR - Fun game, but play with friends if you want to make the most of it.
Probably one of the first actual "sandbox MMOs" to reach western markets, and it did what it said it would
-> large open world to explore
-> Crafting
-> Farming (and trading)
-> huge battles and events
-> other stuff, bla bla bla...
BUT!
This game has had a steadily declining playerbase since the launch.
They created a huge amount of hype surrounding the release and had several server issues, forcing them to open multiple servers to host the amount of interested players. Sadly, because of poor company management and an over-the-top focus on microtransactions, most of the servers became next to empty, other than the couple of extremely dedicated players. So they were forced to merge several servers to keep multiplayer content (raids/dungeons) accessable for new players.
That's all fine and dandy, but seeing that most of the community consists of these "hardcore" players, the dungeons still remained empty, excluding newer players from most of the interesting content. The merge also "cleared" all the land players had bought, forcing them to buy it all again. Sadly, 90% of all buildable land was taken within the first 4 hours after the merge. I guess that's what a higher player-base means.
If you're into MMO's, I recommend this game, but play it with a couple of friends (5 is the max party size).
The community is not incredibly friendly towards newcomers, but maybe you'll find someone who is. It's 50-50.

In Hard Reset, you play a man with a metal eyes and no knees, in his quest to shoot every last robot ever.
I would summarise the plot more, but I genuinely can't. I just don't understand it. However, the characters in the game seem to know what's going on, and I'm more than happy to let them handle the major decisions. I'll just shoot the robots, thanks very much.
The plot is revealed to the player via cutscenes which have a pretty great animated comic-book style to them, bringing back fond memories of games like Max Payne.
Gameplay is fun. The environments are impressive and reward player exploration. They have no shortage of things to blow up, and no shortage of things to blow them up with, because instead of picking up guns along the way, you start the game with both of the guns you will ever need, one gun that fires bullets, and one that fires plasma. When you pick up "nano" (the currency), a bar on your HUD will fill. When you reach 100%, it gives you one unlockable slot at an upgrade point, which gives your guns extra functionality. Buy a shotgun slot, and your gun gains the option to fire like a shotgun, etc. Thus you can scroll through each weapon's abilities like you would in any other FPS.
It's a very neat concept, and one that comes in handy during intense firefights - of which there are plenty - switching between the plasma guns and the bullet guns to gain any advantage against the robot swarms.
The music is pretty awesome too, and really sets the tone of this cyberpunk futuristic sprawling mega-tropolis. Not being too familiar with this sort of music, some of the tracks that play during combat remind me a bit of Pendulum, which I like.
Visually, the game is a treat. The city looks grungy and run down, with worn paint and chipped metal contrasting nicely with garish neon and arcing electric bolts here and there. There's no problem at all telling what's environment and what's enemy, like in some games I've played, so you won't get your health chipped away by something you just can't see.
This all sounds pretty great, right? So what's bad about the game?
Well in my first sentence, I said that you play a man with no knees. Well that's pretty accurate, as you CANNOT CROUCH in this game. This is pretty irritating when you feel like taking cover might be helpful, or when there's a chest-high gap in a fence that you can't POSSIBLY get past.
The most glaring example of this is probably in one of the warehouse levels, when a girder has fallen to approximately face height, blocking off a short path to the level exit. You don't even need to crouch to get past that. Just bend over by like five degrees. But no, you're forced down the other route that has explosions, fire, and angry robots just itching to taste your flesh.
Another thing that annoys me is that your guy can - and will - get ganked, usually by enemies called Gorillas, that charge-slam you ever few seconds. It becomes very easy to go from full health to dead, trapped in a corner, being beaten by Gorillas, which is where another one of my niggles joins in:
No quicksave/load. This kind of speaks for itself. Fast, frantic shooters like this NEED quicksave. In games like Alien Isolation, where not being able to save is legitmately part of the game, because the survival thing is supposed to be tense. In games like this, where you play a stompy god of hellfire, slowing down the fast-paced fun is irksome.
Weapons. I really like the weapon system in this game, but it becomes very obvious quite early on that there is a right choice. That choice is the electric mortar. Area of effect attack instantly blows up the generic foot soldier robots, and saps the others. Switch that out with the grenade launcher, and you can very quickly turn the screen into an orgy of exploded robot parts. I've discovered no other combos of guns (as of yet) that can measure up in terms of fast, widespread, heavy damage.
To conclude: Hard Reset is a bloody fun game, that will keep you entertained for as long as you care to play it. It's most assuredly worth the asking price.

Dreadout is a third person horror game developed by Digital Happiness and published by PT Digital Semantika Indonesia, which was released on Steam in mid-2014 after successfully being greenlit.
The game play in Dreadout is almost identical to that of Fatal Frame. You play the role of Linda Meilinda, a young girl who is on a trip with her high school class mates. The game is played in third person. You will be using your characters smart phone and camera to fight the various kinds of ghosts you will encounter – you’ll also use them in a number of puzzles as well.  An interesting element I found in Dreadout is that you don’t actually “die”. When Linda does “die”, you’ll wake up in a dark place surrounded by candles and you run towards the light, typical eh.  When using aiming with your phone, the camera will change to first person and you’ll just be looking through the phone’s screen.
I was really left feeling let down by the graphics in Dreadout. All of the textures are horribly low quality; the polygons can actually be seen visually on most of the models too! Don’t even get me started on the janky animation of some of the characters in the game as well. I was almost on the floor laughing at one of the characters run cycle, it was just horrendous. I was playing the game on 1080p resolution as I was recording, but I tested it out on 4k, it even then still looked poor. Extremely disappointed here as it based on the Unity engine so I would have expected a real high quality looking game.
There isn’t much to sale about the audio on this either; there is some generic “horror” music in the background that conveniently only turns on when something is about to happen. It is certainly not on the level as say Outlast or Amnesia with their top class sound effects. The voice acting is really awkwardly done as well, I can only assume it has been dubbed over in English because some of the lines really don’t feel natural, and the people who are saying the lines, are clearly not being paid enough, or just don’t want to be there.
Dreadout is a fairly difficult game; there is no tutorial level or any sort of in game assistance, you are just left to work it out yourself. Whilst the game play is fairly simple to get to grasps with, the game does not explain how you are supposed to use your in game equipment to aid you; for instance you can use your phone to control candles by holding the viewer over them; something which is used in a puzzle, but there are no clues pointing to that.
All of Dreadout’s levels are fairly sizeable; each of them has a decent number of Easter eggs and collectable items to find. Some of the collectables even unlock in game bosses for you to deal with for extra achievement points if that is your thing! The collectables are all hidden well across the level and will lead you down some interesting paths to find them. The level design is probably Dreadout’s most redeeming factor.
I finished the game in just over two hours. There are three chapters to the game; the first one is really short and has no real story to it, but the last two contain the bulk of the plot and game play. The majority of people that have played the game don’t even normally play the first chapter since it glosses over most things anyway.  Other than achievement hunting, there is absolutely no reason to play this game more than once; the two hour play time is very short as well.
I didn’t run into any bugs or glitches in the game per say, just the really bad graphics and poor sound effects. It can run at 4k resolutions and multiple graphic options aid you to get the settings just right for your rig. It seems the game did have a few annoying bugs when first released, such as option changes not being saved when quitting the game, but these have all been ironed out as of writing this review.
Sadly this isn’t going to come out very favourably from me; yes the game play is OK, but it is fairly slow paced and unoriginal. Graphically this game is appalling and quite frankly, there are so many much better horror games in this genre out there at the moment; I am fully expecting people not to agree with this, given that it already has a “Very Positive” rating on Steam. This is one of the few games to include a demo, so if you are on the fence about picking it up or not, you may as well try the demo first.

A very fun game with many of the FPS tropes like being in an empty room, hit the objective, and suddenly a fight for your life. Environmental kills abound since the level designers use them as props as well.
You have 2 main weapons, a bullet-gun, and an energy-gun. You can upgrade them to have up to 5 "modes" with each mode having an alternate ability. I only used the energy gun twice when the bullet gun ran out of ammo, so I can't say how it works fully.
The bullet gun has a machine gun mode (alternate zoom), shotgun mode (alternate EMG mini-grenades that stun whatever they hit), grenade launcher (alternate gravity well that sucks enemies in and traps them in a small space), RPG (alternate laser guided), and proximity mine (alternate manual detonation).
The ammo system is a shared pool, in that all of the bullet gun modes use bullet ammo, just in varying quantities based on the strength of the mode. RPG using the most and machine gun using the least. So no running around for machine gun ammo when you have 40 grenades lying around.
You start with just the machine gun mode on the bullet gun mode, and the default energy gun mode, and collect orange upgrade packs lying around called 'N.A.N.O.' which come in large or small sizes. Once you have enough of them, you can upgrade your gun for an additional mode, add an alternate fire, or pimp the primary fire out more.
Small N.A.N.O. packs are all over the place and are like a trail of breadcrumbs in some otherwise hard to navigate areas. The larger N.A.N.O. packs are usually hidden behind crates, breakable walls, or areas you have to parkour to.
There are some really OP combinations with the guns, like using the gravity grenade to hold trash mobs together in a bottleneck, then kill all of them with one grenade. Because the explosion from the grenade breaks the gravity well, for a larger charging mob, you hold them with the gravity grenade, then hit them with an RPG for a one-hit-kill.
I would recommend getting the shotgun, grenade launcher, grenade alternate fire, RPG, then the laser guided alternate. Towards the end of the game you will pretty much need the RPG to take out some really annoying flying mobs. Proximity mines are fairly lackluster and use ~40 of your maximum 240 ammo for one proximity mine.
As for the story, it uses a graphic novel format between levels, with basically no story told during gunplay. The ending doesn't really feel like one. Kinda like the ending to Half-Life 2: Episode 2, the devs called it an ending, but they player is left wanting more.
