I love the idea around Dungeons and Dragons, the idea of roleplaying a story with chance and rewards is fun. Hand of Fate is quite similar, except instead of stat cards you build your own adventure by implementing story cards and equipment cards. Story Cards really bring out the DND from this game. After each boss battle depending on the choices you made during your adventure, you will get these tokens. Every time you unlock a different coloured token you get a card which continues the story you started. Each coloured gem represents a different story, for example the blue gems and cards tell the story of a mighty Minatare which you are trying to track down and kill. These cards make up short but interesting stories which are very well written!
Card Overview
You then have your basic cards which tie everything together, these include merchant stops, crucibles and things like that. These fill in the gaps when you’re not continuing a story.  And finally as I mentioned before, you have your equipment cards. The equipment cards that you put into your deck make up the equipment that you will find and unlock during each session of the game.
Combat/Gameplay
I really like the deck building component as it allows you to choose which stories you like and want to continue and what equipment you would like to use during these stories. Eventually you will earthier get ambushed or attacked by something and this is when the game changes from a DND card game to a third person hack and slash. Now I’m going to be honest I felt that this was the one area in the game that needed improving. There were times when the combat felt a bit slowly paced for me. I would have liked to see them try a system similar to Shadow of Mordor where they have finishers that happen but don’t stop the combat from progressing forward. When I hit Q to counter an enemy in Hand of Fate, time instantly slows down which in my opinion puts the combat to a halt instead of letting it progress. I know some people might enjoy these sequences but for me personally, it felt too slowly paced. The easy solution for this problem would be to add a feature in the settings which allows you to turn it off.
Performance
The game is not very graphically demmanding at all, the occasional partical and or spell effects cause my FPS to drop slightly down slightly to the high 80's, but even on ultra with everything cranked up I didn't see any notible game breaking performance bugs. However what I did see were your standard texture pop in and AI glitches. Occasionally you would see an enemy AI get stuck in a wall and some times you would load into a level only to find that the textures were extremely blurry for a few more seconds than they should have, but these are minor annoyances with the PC port itself and didn't have any noticable impact on my play expirience overall.
Music
As for the music, I found it be very good! I loved that when you landed on a merchant card, the music would instantly swap to the merchant sound track. I even found myself humming along to quite a few of the songs, they were catchy and fit very well with the games overall theme. We need more music like this in gaming today, bloody excellent!
Atmosphere
One of my favourite parts about this game, besides the deck building because im a sucker for anything card or DND related, was the atmosphere. The game, over the course of 16-20 hours builds this ever changing atmosphere. The candles around the table, lighting up the dark and gloomy catacombs and the spiders rushing across the table towards the dealer. The developers knew how to transport you into their game’s world through any means necessary, hell even the dealer continues to speak while you’re in combat because if he was talking, then immediately stopped because you got attacked that would instantly break your emersion in the game, Defiant Development has done a stellar job with creating this world of Bandits, Rats and mages and honestly I wouldn’t change anything to do with the games atmosphere as in my opinion it Is right on the money with no compromises in sight!
Boss Battles
Finally, before I conclude this review, I would like to talk about the bosses in the game. Each time you play Hand of Fate, you will eventually encounter a boss. Now the bosses in this game are very well done, before you dive into the boss fight the game provides you with a few details which include: The boss’s weaknesses and the boss’s abilities. I’m also very glad to say that the bosses in the game are very different in character design and in combat. It’s very refreshing to see a game that doesn’t just slap a different coloured model in front of you and call it a boss fight.
Conclusion
In conclusion, Hand of Fate combines Dungeons and dragons Deck Building with third person, hack and slash combat and does it successfully may I add. I really enjoyed this game and I struggled to really find any problems with it and the problems that are there are very minor and aren’t game breaking in the slightest. Also……its 24.99 on the steam store, I mean if you weren’t already convinced to buy the game, I’m sure the price has. The game is dirt cheap and gives you a very memorable and enjoyable experience.

If you don't have a controller don't buy this game. The targeting is finnicky enough with Analog, I can't imagine using WASD.
I'm struggling as to whether or not I should recommend this game, and I don't think I can. The game starts out really fun, and it stays fun for quite a few runs. I've almost beaten it at four hours, and I don't know if I will end up finishing it. The Endless Mode sounds like it could be pretty fun with the right deck, but after starving to death on the last tile of the game thanks to an awful combination of curses and cards, as well as all the other BS this game has thrown at me, I just couldn't play it anymore.
As I said, the game starts out really fun, and it stays fun for quite a few runs. Then you start running into the problems.
The combat is really easy for anyone that's played an Arkham game. That is, when the game actually lets you do well in combat. Combat features a fixed camera, and incredibly small arenas with (as far as I've seen) at most 10 enemies. It also doesn't let you interrupt your attacks, which causes you to not be able to dodge. Combat also has a targeting problem, so occasionally you'll hit the wrong enemy. The power attacks that some enemies do are unblockable, and uninterruptible, which will cause you to get hit when you face one of the bosses for the twentieth time. Unless I missed it, the game also doesn't explain how to do finishers on enemies. As for the difficulty, in the early levels its easy, and in the later levels it just feels unfair. Don't bother trying to increase the difficulty before you get all your food upgrades though, because if you do you'll run out of food and probably end up starving to death.
I will say I really enjoyed the different gear you could get.
The card part about it was really good. I really enjoy that aspect of the game, and how you can choose which cards you'll be finding. Some of the cards however, are incredibly annoying, and basically only worth it to unlock whatever the card unlocks. Also some of the special cards, basically stories told through a couple cards, like The White Minotaur, or the Kraken, they were cool, but you're not gauranteed to find them during a run. That's fine I guess, it was a bit annoying not finding them, because I really liked them, but that's just the type of game it is. My problem with them, is that at a certain point, you have to find them, then roll the dice on whether or not you'll actually get to move on. I was doing one of them, spent 6 turns walking between cards, and then ended up failing because I got unlucky. This was with a blessing that let me reroll my successes and failures as well.
Also the Ratmen. The Ratmen are the worst enemies in this game. They will end your combo because you killed them. Why does this happen? Because they leave a cloud of gas that will damage you over time, and you'll end up running over it at least once thanks to the usually small arenas. They also have a ranged enemy that throws 1-4 knives at you very quickly.
Maybe I'll change this review to be a recommendation later, but as of now it just gets too frustrating for me to recommend.

Owlboy is the very definition of the dedication that can come from the Indie space. The game was in development for about 10 years from D-Pad Studio. While the gameplay doesn't fly as high as I would have liked, the story and animation do help to pick it up to some extent.
Before we can talk about the gameplay, we have to talk about the story and aesthetics. Owlboy may not have the graphical wow-ness of something like Hyper Light Drifter, but the animation quality is one of the best I've seen. Character details and the backgrounds look amazing and right out of a late-gen SNES title.
The story follows Owl in training Otus who has spent his life as a mute. Considered a failure by his mentor, Otus is thrust into action when pirates invade. The story continues to get darker, especially for a 2D game, but I don't want to spoil it.
While this is a 2D platformer, you won't be doing as much jumping compared to other titles. Otus is free to fly around for the most part, and performs a spin attack. Otus has to rely on his friends as his spin attack won't hurt enemies.
Early on, you'll gain the ability to teleport his friends directly to Otus. Carrying them, each person has an attack that you can make use of for combat and puzzle solving. Because you are free to fly, this meant that the developers had to figure out other ways to add progression.
Special coins can be found and cashed in for various items. Coins are usually located in hidden chests or rings that you have to fly through. The dungeons themselves feel right out of home from a Zelda game.
Each one has the standard design of one unique quirk that you have to work around. Due to Otus not having a real attack, you need to rely on your best friend to do the bulk of the damage. While combat is not the focus of the game, there are plenty of arena fights and a few bosses to deal with.
As you play through, you'll unlock a total of three friends that will allow you to find more hidden areas and coins.
All around, Owlboy is a good game, but the gameplay can't match the high flying atmosphere.
Owlboy is unfortunately an example of how a unique mechanic doesn't always lead to amazing gameplay. A lot of your time spent in the game will be air rolling across wide rooms. The different dungeons never try to build on their initial quirk. Once you've solved one puzzle, expect to do it repeatedly throughout the dungeon. Outside of your three companions, no new abilities or systems are introduced.
Due to the flying mechanics, there is very little platforming outside of the final area. The problem is that nothing was really added to replace platforming as a challenge.
The combat system is the weakest part of the game, but is used the most. I would have liked to have seen more bosses that require other tactics than just fighting.
Depending on how you play it, Owlboy can be beaten in a few hours if you skip the cutscenes. Outside of hunting coins and three mysterious items, there's no reason to go back to the game or advanced challenges to find.
From a technical point of view, I had some issues with quickly performing commands using the grab button. There were cases where the camera transition between screens did screw me up in terms of dodging attacks.
Owlboy is an average game with a story and animation style that attempt to elevate it higher. If you're looking for a great platformer, I can't recommend Owlboy. This is one of those games that is greater than the sum of its parts, but how high it flies depends on what you're looking for in a 2D game. I didn't want to give it a thumbs down, but at the same time, there's just not enough in terms of gameplay for me to recommend it.
I understand the community that invested and had to wait so long for the game, but I really enjoyed it, it's a great game with a few layers of fun and chaos. 9.8/10

TL;DR at bottom
I honestly wish I didn't have to say this, but...
The game just isn't that great.
Before you rail into me, I'll at least name off some pros:
-Animations are smooth during cutscenes. The color choices are nice, and overall the game LOOKS good...... in most cases. More on that later.
-The game is at least... trying? It's certainly making some good things here and there.
-It finally came out at least. I'm surprised it even came out this year.
-The soundtrack is actually very well-done. Congrats to whoever did it, you did a superb job. Just wish your music was used more often rather than restricted to cutscenes.
Now for the unfortunate cons.
-The animations can become very cluttered and the whole screen can become messy and disastrous. I know that a riot is MEANT to be chaotic, but it's hard to explain the exact problem. Instead, I'll give an example.
During the Arab Spring riots, at the last mission, the police and rioters duke it out. Rioters are all aggressive, police have lethal weapons, etc. This is meant to be the massive climax.
Instead the end result is a complete and whole inability to even accomplish anything. The only way I managed to beat this stage was by breaking the game itself, even moreso than the game already is. I tried shooting tear gas and smoke and advancing slowly, but all the police retreat (there's no way to set formations for all units except with the radio, which just puts all units on top of each other. Think if in Total War you tried putting all your archers on ONE place rather than spread them out).
I then also tried being lethal to disperse the crowd, but the handguns do jackshit, the tank does one massive lethal shot and then all other shots from the tank do nothing (not even running over protesters does anything, I think it's a glitch), and the shotguns are so ineffective at dispersing the units that it's stupid.
-The rioters are far too easy and the police are far too hard. The rioters can practically just put their hands up and sit down and the cops just simply can't do anything about it when you're playing as the rebels, and during aggressive riots the rioters just simply toss things at the cops and they continously retreat, not employing any tactics that you'd actually expect to keep a formation.
And when playing as the cops, there is no way to improve morale except through the radio (which barely does anything anyway). Your units will often begin retreating at crucial moments, and it's damn near impossible to get much things of substance done during the very hectic parts.
For example:
In one of the Indignagos riots, there's a bunch of miners with fireworks launchers and rocks. You have only 6 officers to disperse a crowd of 40. These 6 all have rubber bullet rifles.
Now, IN REALITY, this would be fine. The units would hang back and shoot and their firing on the crowd would disperse them EVENTUALLY, or totally derail everything and reinforcements would be called in (which you can't do anyway, so what's the point).
INSTEAD, the recharge rate of these rifles is so long that there's really nothing you can do about the rioters tossing rocks at you and shooting rockets at you. Instead your men just stand there and take it until they eventually run away and you lose the mission. I eventually beat it by glitching out the rioters by just sending my men as high as they could go on the map, sending them all the way to the right, and waiting. I ended up doing this very often in a lot of police scenarios.
on another note for the drastic power difference between cops and rioters: cops can't call in reinforcements, rioters can. The men you start the match with as the cops are the only men you got and if just ONE unit runs away, the whole game is pretty much over.
However, as the rioters, you can consistently call in new units.
On top of all this, lethal weapons do almost nothing to disperse a crowd. During the Arab Spring riots where the crowd is immensely violent and hostile, I decided that, realistically, I shouldn't even bother using tear gas and smoke. I already tried doing it before in previous riots and just ended up failing miserably, so I decided to go fully lethal.
The result? We all retreated due to cooldown times and an inability to continue and focus fire. Oh, and friendly fire. I can understand when a unit has a shotgun and hits a friendly unit in front of him, but a sniper rifle hitting a friendly unit? Who's just meters before him? Really? How bad of a shot can you be?
Last gripe is that the game ends up looking like a total mess. I tried watching it in spectator mode so that I could probably just view how the cops would fight against the rioters, and maybe even see if the beatdown and arrest animations held any weight, since I barely saw any cops end up truly hammering down on a rioter, and all I saw were rioters tossing rocks at cops and the cops running away because of it.
Oh, and final gripe: performance and bugs. I have had the game crash about 6 times and had to restart my computer once due to the game locking my screen at one point. There are also numerous instances of the UI disappearing and the graphics completely fizzing out. It's nuts.
Honestly, I'm disappointed, but think that with more work this game could become immensely wonderful. I'm definitely open to speaking to one of the developers about the issues of the game, if they're willing to listen.
TL;DR
An overall pretty and well-sounding and probably well-intentioned game that results in being a mess that isn't really interesting to watch nor to play, with absurd difficulty ranges.

I hardly ever write reviews, but this game is exceptional so I really felt I needed to share some comments of this masterpiece. So I bought this when it was in early access. I did enjoy it back then, stopped playing it for a while because I wanted to have a new experience for the full release and now I've started again and it's alot of fun. The game has so many aspects and I will try to list the ones I like and dislike.
Pros
* Tactical and immersive combat (turn-based). Combat also has good graphics/animations.
* Good character customization
* Fun and well-written dialogues and voice acting (everything is voice acted!!)
* Good roleplaying opportunities because of the amazing quest system, both in single-player mode and multiplayer mode.
* Many items to loot and find throughout the world, and you can craft and combine items yourself!
* Graphics are beautiful - sometimes I just find myself gazing at the water. It's unbelievable good looking environments.
* The game lets you be creative in both character, combat, questing and crafting (let's not forget to mention the Game Master mode!!!)
* You feel like you have a great sense of freedom because the game opens up for new and creative gameplay and roleplaying. I truly felt made choices made an impact in the game and the joy of exploration never ends.
* An incredible good price for the huge amount of content and hours it will give you.
Cons (not many to be honest)
* Can be hard to find decent groups in multiplayer, unless you have friends to play with of course.
* Time consuming, however you can play it in your own pace so it's really not a con for me, but maybe for others.
Last but not least, being a pen and paper roleplayer irl, this game really give me those kind of vibes (especially with Game Master mode). The immersive roleplaying aspects of this game is just amazing! Love it! Thank you Larian studios! Now go buy this game and play it!!
tl;dr: Buy this game, now.

OK. Let's call this an early review, shall we?
I had absolutely no intention of trying this game. Much less liking it.
In all fairness I downloaded it because:
A) it was free
B) I needed a break from Shroud of the Avatar (at 450+hrs) before their final wipe
C) I read some reviews and they were all over the place with their very strong likes and dislikes...which always makes me curious.
D) Did I mention it was free?
Anyway, I had really no idea what the game was all about other than it was yet another fantasy MMO and the graphics looked pretty good.
Then a funny thing happened on the way to the shoe store. I find myself sitting here at almost 1:00am EST after having binge played for something like 7 hours and....I'll be damned. This game has genuinely caught my attention.
The game looks great. The game plays very smoothely. I LOVE the fact that you can choose three different classes and effectively morph into one class. I honestly forget the name of mine,,Helldiver, Hellspawn..something like that. I have tinkered with the last of the three classes a few times, so forgive my lack of attention to detail.
Whatever the name, I am having a ton of FUN. Yep...there's the word.
FUN.
Now there is no doubt a LOT OF♥♥♥♥♥♥going on that I haven't even begun to discover or scratch the surface of. The in game mechanics hint at a deep pool of needed technical know-how I simply wasn't prepared for. Crafting looks wonderfully complex. The 3 class system is very intricate and must be a min-maxers wet dream (or worst nightmare..not sure yet).
I can see where this game will appeal to both the hand holder crowd (yes there are "!" over quest giving NPC's heads) as well as the go anywhere do anything crowd...as there is simply a ton of♥♥♥♥♥♥off the beaten path.
Now...I am fairly certain there is a P2W aspect to this game as there are about 50 different forms of "currency" in the form of merit badges and some weird coin...starts with a "G" and so on.
But this paying actually does not bother me in a "free" game. You SHOULD invest in a game you enjoy playing. In lieu of a standard $15/mo payment structure which, let's face it, is antiquated and will soon be a memory, these games have to make money somehow. It has been proven time and time again that MMO'ers like to play dress up and don't mind paying cash money for stuff to put on their proverbial "Ken Doll".
I'm kewl with that. I am cool with a game like this that really is as of yet undefinable to me charging a few bucks for add ons. Gotta keep the lights on somehow, right?
At the end of the day, after...maybe 10 hours of playing....I like it. I like it a lot.
I would recommend this to anyone who is looking for an outlet for their time while taking breaks from other MMO's they are trying not to burn out on.
I give this one 4 shrooms out of 5.

I read about Darkside Detective about a year ago and was eager to play a new point-and-click adventure full of light-hearted references to the X-Files and Twin Peaks.  Unfortunately, in-jokes and puns are all this game has going for it.  Darkside Detective isn't very good.
I enjoyed the graphics, and some of the jokes made me chuckle (the characters of McQueen and Dooley are goofy, but they make for a decent "buddy-cop" couple), but the core gameplay is too simple, and unsatisfying.  All of the puzzles have obvious solutions, and are of the "add this-to-that" variety - most of the puzzles in any one room can be solved by using a key item from the room just next door.  I suppose the gameplay's shortcomings could be overlooked if the story was compelling, but it's just a formulaic pastiche of tropes from supernatural television shows, horror movies and other, better adveture games.  There's nothing original here.  What's worse is that for a supernatural game involving a detective, the episodic stories in Darkside Detective don't have a mystery that ties them altogether at the end.  Each little story happens - and then there's a final story, and that's the end.  There's nothing nefarious, nor amuzing behind the Spooky Door - just some shlock about a zombie mobster.  It's Scooby-Doo stuff, but without the charm.
I can't recommend anyone download this game; in terms of narrative and in terms of gameplay, this one is a letdown.  It's too bad, I really liked the premise, but the designers don't seem to have grasped that adventure games are more than solving obtuse puzzles and pipe-games.

I highly enjoyed Dreadout.  It's like a mix of Fatal Frame, Silent Hill and Resident Evil, all in one.  It wasn't perfect but was alot of fun to play and I definitely squeezed as many achievements out of it as I could.  Don't know if I'll replay to change the ending yet again by doing the one conversation differently, but I might.
In short summation, you play as Linda, an Indonesian college student whose field trip runs into an abandon town, haunted school and more.  The story (while not insanely complex) keeps you wanting to go through it.  To be honest as far horror games go, this one wasn't terrifying but just ground you down with a constantly foreboding atmosphere which I really liked.    As mentioned, graphics are somewhat in the ps2 area but the enemies look great (I thought), the vision switches are cool and the scenery isn't THAT bad.  Some character models are a bit awkward but it didn't break the game and the sound design more than made up for any graphic glitches.
For some odd reason and you can call me a blasphemer, I actually enjoyed battling through this more than the Fatal Frame games.   Yep, I'm stupid but I loved this game because there were a few key scenery switches that kept the journey intersting and a limited number of choices that differed the outcome.  You won't manage too large of inventory, so it's never too difficult to progress though a couple of the puzzles might stump you for a few seconds.  Combat is a little awkward and I died a bunch in a few fights (damn you scissor ghost) and not at all in others (the big, giant awesome looking beastie that throws Pocongs at you).  Despite the fighting not having a frenetic feel to it, you gotta be quick with your camera and keep mobile for some of the opposition.  The enemies, the lore behind them and the enjoyable battles is what made this game a blast for me.  Quite frankly, I thought the boss fights were excellent.
I didn't have too many problems with the controls, but sometimes in combat they will bring you down.  Linda ain't the fastest draw in the East by any stretch of the imagination and sometimes you might get hung up on some scenery and get your butt kicked.  If there is a sequel (which I hope there is), they do need a bit of tightening but for the most part it was solid and in some strange way that awkwardness of control made the boss fights a real threat.
The story is well-done for the most part although I can't help but feel it could use some sort of fleshing out and deeper explanation.  I guess it makes sense well enough but it can be a bit muddled.  Voice acting ranges from right on the money to Resident Evil 1 cheese, but survival horror nuts are not strangers to this.  Not much else to say here...it's a flawed game but a very fun one!  I'll break this review down before writing you all another essay (oops, too late, already did!).   Oh yeah, okay, one more thing.  The idea of dying, ending up in limbo and running your way out is good on paper but HORRIBLY executed in the game and a major drag especially during the tougher parts.  Make sure you explore and grab a few of the collectibles that shorten this time.  I did and it made things not quite as bad, but it'll still get you yelling at the computer.
Pros:
-Great atmospheric horror (not scary but it wears on ya)
-Combat can be awkward but is alot of fun, kind of like the underrated Cursed Mountain
-Interesting story that makes you want to press onward
-Good mixture of exploration, battles and puzzle solving (feels well-balanced)
-Reminds of old classic survival horror and some parts are really challenging
-Very cool monsters and way entertaining boss battles.
-Excellent sound design (music, atmospheric cues, etc.)
-Some cool unlockables and achievements
Cons:
-Graphics aren't bad.  Beautiful in some places, stale/dingy in others.
-Interesting story but payoff doesn't quite satisfy
-Voice acting is hit or miss
-Sometimes controls will get you in trouble
-Running to the light after death is a pain in the a**...like, to the point of detriment and not really wanting to play the game anymore...but somehow the game is fun enough and you'll be like sh*t I"m comin' back!
Overall rating:  7.8/10

Hard Reset [Extended Edition]
When I first heard about the game in question, I was a bit doubtful. A sci-fi themed game in an action-oriented/arcade style gameplay. It would have seemed to put together all of the stereotypes but, after sometime from its debut, I decided to try and play it; found on some sale for a very few bucks. The graphic and the art style are sleek and polished; the cyber-filled world quite unique and well made; the sound compartment surprisingly well done. So, you're gonna ask "what about the downsides"? 'cause I can say, they're there.
The game's self-professed "old school" (and I shall open a discussion topic about that, perhaps) mechanics are just dull and flat as you basically run through a mega-hallway - that is the world it-self - divided into chunks of areas, that I'm gonna call "arenas", where you are flooded by hordes of enemies and you don't have an "escape route": the door/passage/you-say-it that you've just passed through will suddenly close/crumble/whatever and you'll have to figure out how to kill'em all without dying. That's wouldn't be of any concern if played at low-level but, if like me, you play through a hard difficulty level.. prepare to die and suffer a lot: enemies will just take forever to die, literally; even the smaller-cuty ones, will lasts for too much what you'd expect. Boss fights? Repetitive - as every other fights - and frustrating.
Luckily, here comes the last aspect of the game and a positive one. "Customization". Yes, you can upgrade yourself and your arsenal by using exp points you'll earn killing enemies and picking up special bonuses, let's call'em that way, and spending them at some "upgrade-machine vendor" integrated in the world. You basically starts (and finish) with two weapons, one for each kind like "standard" ammo and power energy; each of them can be upgraded into 4 more weapons for a total of 5 per kind. Every weapon has a primary and secondary mode as well an upgrade. So, you'll have plenty of variety to experiment with though you'll end up using the same two model that best suites you. You can also upgrade your armor/health/utilities, like more health, more resistance to damage, and on..
So, by the end what happens? Well, later on - and not too late - in the game there were times in which I just wanted it to be over; too repetitive in the mechanics and playing it on hard's just too hard: it is not the smart hard, at all, it is the frustrating one that ruin it all. The world itself is well presented; quite varied plus the good points I've already explained.. but the negatives' quite ruined the feast as the game ain't balanced at all. At all. Summing it all up:

Art: 8
Sound: 8
Music: 6**
Gameplay: 6
Uniqueness: 8
Partial: 7.3
F.F.: 75%***
*not latest gen but still very appealing
**bland, uninspired and repetitive music score
***Frustration Factor: game's far too unbalanced on higher difficulty levels but some situations give relief upon completion

I kind of hate this game.  Playing it well requires constantly harnessing the diversity of your arsenal, and I am just not good at fighting with more than one gun at a time.  It is often difficult for me to assess a situation rapidly enough in the middle of battle—while my brain is consumed with the effort of dodging, shooting, and navigating to health and ammo pickups just in the nick of time—to see an opportunity for a better tactic represented by one of my other weapons.
So it has been an extremely frustrating experience, particularly because I stubbornly insist on sticking with Hard difficulty to the end (just regular Hard, mind you; there is worse available, if you wish for it).  I can only play one level per session because it's such an exhausting ordeal, and I've spent the entire latter half of the game wishing it would end already.
Yet, objectively, I recognize that Hard Reset is a very good first-person shooter of the old school style.  There are moments when I actually manage to adapt and perform well, and it is quite gratifying.  I certainly do recommend it.  Just be honest with yourself about who you really are before you make that purchase.

Owlboy is ok. I spent the first ~3 hours playing offline, so my playtime does not reflect the fact that I have completed the game.
The pixel art is obviously incredible, and gives many characters most of their likability. The soundtrack is enjoyable, though not as memorable as some other games.
I have a few larger complaints and a few more nitpicky ones, but let's start with the big things first.
During my playthrough, I felt like I spent about half of my time in dialogue or cutscenes, instead of actually playing the game. While there's an open world, there's only one "main" town, and even then you only visit it intermittently, and it doesn't get that "home base" feeling. There are no shops in town, and the NPCs have relatively little dialogue (~2 dialogue interactions per instance). The NPCs you carry with you have more character, but everyone else just felt flat, with each character having their singular Trait. Additionally, despite having this large open world, there is veeeeery little to do outside of the main storyline, which leads to a lot of useless open space with maybe some enemies thrown in, and almost no reason to return to places with your new partners outside of the lackluster coin collection. Even when you do collect the coins, they are only usable in one "shop" - mostly to achieve health powerups. The cannon minigame was fun, though.
As far as gameplay goes, of the three NPCs you partner with, only two get more than ~2 hours of gameplay, and the last partner only has his gimmick / power used for one level.  Enemies or platforms will occasionally come out of nowhere from across a screen transition, and, while the game is by no means difficult, these sort of "surprise!" deaths sometimes felt cheap and led to me having to repeat sections that were otherwise very easy. Boss fights are very often just groups of normal enemies, and have little character. Levels feel largely the same, and more often felt like they were driven more by gimmicks than tied together by a central mechanic.
These nitpicks don't ruin the game, but still felt like they made the game less enjoyable than it could have been. There are several stealth areas, which honestly do not feel like they fit the game very well. The game does not teach you some of its mechanics, and discovering them on your own without any signaling can be tiresome - the direction you are facing affects whether or not you are able to spin the "screw" platforms, for instance. Not every object that you're able to "screw" with your spin move looks the same, and sometimes are not visually distinct from the rest of the level. The controls are passable, but not great, and cycling through your partners while also trying to dodge around in a fight can be a chore. This is especially when you waste the cooldown on the shotgun thinking you had a different partner out. It's not game-ruining, but it can be bothersome. The same can be said about the lack of a map system.
Overall Owlboy is definitely not *bad*, but it feels like it could have been so much more. If I could give the game an in-between score I would, but really  I didn't feel impressed by any of the game's level design, mechanics, or story. Geddy is great though.

As only a dabbler in Rogue-lite games, I was not expecting to enjoy Hand of Fate nearly as much as I did.  Now I could sit here and attempt to describe all of the gameplay elements that go into Hand of Fate, (Rogue-lite action rpg with CCG-style deck-building and progression) but that doesn't really describe what the game IS or why I enjoy it so much.  This game pulled me in, and really got me into the " just one more run" Rogue-lite mindset in a way most others in the genre have not.
The basic premise of the game is that you construct a deck of equipment and encounter cards and use it to try and defeat each of the dealer's decks of minions.  Each deck progresses over several randomly laid out "dungeon floors" constructed from the encounter cards you chose, plus a few from the dealer.  The goal is to get to the bottom and defeat the deck boss, while unlocking new cards and equipment along the way.
The difficulty curve in this mode is really nice (especially for a Rogue-lite), by which I mean that most action rpg veterans will find that they breeze through the first few deck challenges purely on the strength of their combat.  That, however, does not last.  As the game progresses, unlocking more cards and building your encounter and equipment decks around the specific challenges of an enemy deck becomes more and more important.  This is the part of the game that keeps hooking me back in.  I'd find myself failing a run, but super-excited to start a new one just to see what the new cards I unlocked did.  Also, the artwork for the cards is really really well done and the dealer character has some of the best voice-acting (and one-liner writing) I've heard in a game for quite a while.
A few minor gripes:  The controls for the combat sections aren't quite as tight as I would like (read: as tight as in Arkham City / Asylum), but they are more than adequate by action-rpg standards.  That said, the combat can get a bit repetitive after a while, as the combat system itself doesn't have quite the depth of a full-on action rpg.  Different weapons and abilities help some, but the 15th time you draw a 6 of Scales does start to feel grind-y.
Endless mode is a bit of a mixed bag: it's more of the traditional rogue-lite experience (starts off relatively easy, and just gets continuously harder until you die), but without any of the custom deck-building from Story Mode (it just throws every card you have into the mix).
Final word:  If you like Rogue-lites, I highly reccomend this one, especially if you're also into CCG-driven mechanics.  If you don't like Rogue-lites at all, I'm curious why you're still reading this review, but if you got this far, this one *might* be worth giving a chance, especially since the difficulty curve starts out a bit more forgiving than most of the genre and doesn't really start ramping up until you've cleared 4 or 5 decks.  That said, it is still a Rogue-lite, which means you will occasionally have the runs that end in 4 moves because you drew the hardest 2 monsters in the deck after losing your shield and half your health to bad luck.

Just a thoroughly enjoyable, absorbing, brilliant game that will suck you in and eat up days of your life. I genuinely had to get everything that I wanted to do in a day done before I booted this up, because I knew once I did I wouldn't be moving for 8 hours.  It's very rare that I find a game that I just want to play for hour after hour, day after day, and when I'm not playing it I'm just looking forward to getting back into it. Starcraft, Rome Total war, XCom EU are on that list, and now VC joins them.
VC is 50% Visual Novel and 50% "TBS-with-a-twist" first time through, and you should only consider it if you like BOTH types of game. (After the first run through you'll not bother with the story and jump straight into missions, but doing that first time round totally defeats the object of the game). The game is broken down into chapters, and each chapter tends to have about 5 or 6 story segments and one big fight. If you're just after combat and action, you'll be frustrated. Having said that, I don't usually play VNs, but the story in VC is so engaging and the characters so likeable you'll get totally wrapped up in the epic storyline. Alternate-Europe gets swept up into war, local people become war heroes, concentration camps are liberated, characters you get to care about fall in love or suddenly die. Magic happens. Giant, battleship-sized tanks explode.
I say TBS-with-a-twist because VC uses a mechanic I've not come across before. It IS turn-based, but the defenders can still react. As an example, if your active character runs 50 metres, hunkers down in cover and lobs a grenade at an enemy 20 metres away with his back to you, it's all good. If you start your turn and decide to run face-first into an enemy with a heavy machine gun pointed at you, he'll mow you down. I'm used to TBS games where I can simply saunter up to an enemy and stand one hex in front of him while he's miraculously frozen in time doing nothing, so VC's system is certainly more realistic. It's better than XCom's Overwatch option too, as that's just a one-free-shot deal, whereas one defender could happily mow down your entire squad on your turn if you decide to be an idiot.
You can see the artstyle from the screenshots. Some people may prefer cutting-edge, ultra-realistic 3D graphics and won't like this, but personally I absolutely loved it. If you're a fan of Japanese animation, Studio Ghibli-type artwork it's a real treat.
There are a couple of minor flaws. First up, like many people I messed up with the confusing save system. As others have commented, it's easy to think there's only one save slot because scrolling on the save screen is not at all obvious. Unlike a lot of games that track your campaign progress and keep a record of the fact that, for example, you've completed 12 out of 18 chapters, each save is COMPLETELY independent in VC, so if you mess up and save a new game where you're on the first mission over your save file where you're at the final mission, it's all permanently gone. This wouldn't be an issue if the possibility of multiple saves was more obvious, but if you're pre-warned it's no biggie. I managed this because I'd got to the final mission but was getting pooned because my squad was under-powered, so I  was doing an optional side-mission, which was very long and in multiple parts, to get more xp. I had to call it quits for the night so I saved halfway through. The next day I was horrified to realise that this side-mission was now literally my only save, and when I wanted to switch back to the main campaign I had to start at the very first mission again. I hope that makes sense - in a nutshell, be aware of the possibility of multiple saves and use many of them to be safe!
Here's the interesting point though. With most games, if you play 40 or 50 hours and then by being a total tard you lose ALL your progress, you'd usually (1) scream yourself hoarse (2) put your fist through your monitor (3) put a jihad out on the feckin developers and (4) delete the game in a ragequit and swear never to play it, or anything by the developer, ever again. In my case, after only a minute of kicking myself, I realised that this meant I would have to start the campaign all over again, AND THIS WAS A GOOD THING BECAUSE THIS TIME I COULD DO IT BETTER! Remember I said I was getting pooned in the final fight because my squad was under-powered? The xp you get to upgrade your units is based on how well you complete each mission. Since I was scraping crappy wins with a C or D rating most of the time, and not doing side-missions, my xp had been limited and my squad were all about level 11 or 12. When I re-started, I was getting A or B ratings and playing all side-missions, so when I got to the final fight they were around level 17 or 18 and had a much easier time.
Well, if you're still reading, you must genuinely be thinking about trying VC, in which case the advice is simple: do it, you'll love it!

Valkyria Chronicles is a little gem I never expected would hold my attention so firmly.  The game is effectively a small unit tactical strategy in the same vein as UFO: Enemy Unknown and similar games.  Your units use points to get around and have  one significant action per activation.  People who know this style of game will undestand this mechanic.  However unlike other versions of this mechanic you may activate untils based on Command Points which allows you to activate the same unit several times if needed though each time they have a reduced Action Point pool.
The game was ledgendary on Sega and the port is a little clunky but still quite usable.  The biggest frustration is driving the tanks.
The graphics is intended to look like a comic book.  A series of animated sequences in panels.  The game play has the same look but using 3D models with rag doll physics.  So it keeps the feel of a comic book but has more modern engine.
The real attraction to this game is the story. Once you get to know the characters you will put hours into the game to follow the story to its conclusion.  In addition, every character and soldier in the game has a back story you unlock during game play.  A single run through the game wont unlock them all so finding about about everyone takes some effort.
Overall I think I'll be playing this game through at least two more times.  I will probably come back to it over and over for years to come.  Highly recommended and worth it.

I see a bunch of negative reviews from long-time, hardcore players who have fallen out of love with this game.  But you're not an experienced player if you're reading this trying to decide whether or not to give it a try, are you?
So: as a player new to this game, let me share my experience.
I love it.  There is some learning curve to the combat (the controls could be a bit more intuitive), but once you get the hang of them it's SO rewarding.  It feels visceral and fun.  You feel like a total badass in combat.  Looks and feels fantastic.  Solid.  Definitely the best medieval combat I've ever played.
Yes, there is team damage, it happens.  War is Hell and messy.  If you can deal with that, you'll have fun.
How to maximize your fun:
1) Don't take it too seriously.
2) Do the tutorial.  It's a bit buggy but genuinely useful.
3) Play on the low-ranked player servers to begin with.
4) Start a private server and practice your skills against bots between matches.
5) Learn the different weapons and get a feel for their timing and ranges.
6) Almost-empty servers are a good place to have fun without so many enemies and learn from more experienced players.
7) Learn how to use stab and hack and the alternate attacks.  Bind them to their own keys.
Maybe it won't be a game you play for years or get seriously competitive about.  But so what?  For the money, you absolutely get more than a fair share of entertainment value!  Absolutely recommended!

Chantelise is a very charming game about a goofy girl who exemplifies quite a few silly anime girl traits! Example: She names her item shop Racettear (pronounced: Racketeer, as in someone who engages in dishonest and fraudulent business dealings). She doesn't know any better! She is silly anime girl! YOU GO GIRL!
Anyways, I highly enjoyed this game. I love simulation games but usually run out of patience for the saminess of them. This one kept my attention by having a third of the game be an action RPG! In order to fill your shop with items, you can either buy them low and keep them to sell high later when they are suddenly in demand (in what is apparently the most trendy town EVER), or you can take an adventurer who you have become on good terms with into a dungeon so he/she can risk their lives to get you items! This makes it well worth your while to cut them deals on equipment they will use, even though they try to buy EVERYTHING exploiting your friendship like the little leeches they are! Oh, sorry about that. I love all my adventuring friends! Even the clueless one who doesn't know how she got to said random dungeon map in the first place!
I digress. This game is a LOT of fun if you enjoy simulator games and action RPGs. The Action RPG element is a bit repetitive because it's randomly generated maps with random spawns, but it does mix it up with map rules. When you enter a new map, it will add a rule, like Monsters 2x Damage or Player 2x Speed. Also, your in dungeon bag gets full quick if you go more than 4 levels, so there is some tedium in bag management. But overall, it is the same combat each delve, unless you switch up who your regular dungeon runners are. If you run with person A mainly, then you try to take person B, just remember, the levels are specific to that character.
The other thing to mention is, it's very much a time management game. Each day you have a number of slices of the time pie. If you dungeon delve, you may only get to open the store for one slice of pie (and Recette LOVES her pie). So if you do nothing but dungeon delve, by the time the deadline comes up to pay your father's absurd debt which he dumped on you because he wanted to go adventuring (a lot of jokes at the expense of standard RPGs).
Lastly, this game's final third is Japanese dating sim style, without the dating. You can go to different spots around town, taking up pie peices, to talk to characters, learn more about characters (like Tear, the other half of Recettear) and the adventures you use... I mean borrow? This leads to the recruitment of more than one adventurer if you are in the right place at the right time.
All in all, this game is worth it if you like anime games, simulation games, action RPGs, and quirky anime humor!

They likely wouldn't have had to, if you could reliably control your character in fights.

Hand of Fate follows in the foot steps of great games. There is a single character narrating your adventure. In this case it is your opponent, the dealer. It has roguelike elements. The game actually grows as you play it. It has a story and an endless mode. It is an adventure rpg with randomized dungeon encounters. You attain powerful gear, and your character also gains power as an individual. Your choices matter. While there is a random element, you can overcome it with skill. The combat is simple and fluid. This is a direct game with a lot of charm and some poignant humor.
In spite of all of these features Hand of Fate is simply a good game. It's overpriced at $25, grindy, and easily becomes repetative. The story mode is short, and endless is simply a good way to unlock more cards for your deck. There are three difficulties: apprentice, adventurer, and warlord. The wildcard dlc adds more, but they don't feel very different. Each adds a few cards to the deck if you grind through them long enough, but it doesn't feel worth the tedium to accomplish it. I'd recommend picking up this game at $15 or less on sale.
There are a few other complaints I can see people having. Here they are. Some people might complain that you cannot play as anything other than a male who hardly looks different  than the bandits. There is very little representation of female characters, and it's hardly positive. An elven maiden who grants a boon, a mother who can't provide for her children, a princess in need of rescue. a pair of lovers (the girl is rather flighty), a bandit's nagging wife, an angry spirit, and the queens of each of the suits. Lastly the Descent to the Underworld free dlc adds a new enemy that seems like it is a reskin of the plagues standard melee unit, but that's about it.

Hand of Fate is a nice roguelike-like game where the dungeon is generated based in a deck of cards you unlock as you play.
This means that, like in roguelikes, the whole of your adventure is randomized each time you play, and the more you play the more new toys to play with you unlock. Each time you die you lose everything and start from scratch, but your unlocks remain: If you unlock a weapon, you can find it in all your runs from then on - think Binding of Isaac, but each room in the dungeon is a card with its own event instead, and not all rooms have combat.
Once you're done with the storyline mode, where you can unlock most stuff, you're given the endless mode which is the meat of the game: Just survive until you get bored/killed/starve. You can unlock stuff playing on endless and, if you get the DLC, you're offered a set of "characters" that change how you play the game by setting specific rules to each play session like being unable to carry any extra equipment or making chance events easier... while making your character suck at combat.
It's probably not a game for everyone. There's a lot of text to be read since the game is presented in a mostly text mode (Each event has some narration that's put on the screen), and the combat can get frustrating on harder modes or lower levels of the dungeon. Still, if you're into roguelikes and card games there's little not to like here and you're sure to enjoy it at least one bit.

At this moment, I can't recommend the game.  The pixel art is beautiful and thematic, the sound is great, and watching police and protesters clash in a game is pretty thrilling.  I think the game handles the subject matter it deals with appropriately and in an adult way, and the idea of presenting you with tactical choices that have widespread consequences (even if it's just a newspaper page) is well executed.
Having said all that, the gameplay struggles.  There are big issues with the control, feedback, mechanics and balance.  On the challenging difficulty as police, there seems to be no way to actually achieve the objective most of the time because the protesters are way more under control then they are when you play as the protesters.  When you play as the protesters, they seem to run away at the drop of a hat and don't rejoin the fray.  Am I doing well?  Why are the protesters I'm beating with expandable batons rubberbanding back into the crowd?  Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ time's up and I've only cleared Tahrir square half way, guess I have to try again.
There is also no explanation of the weapons as police.  What's the difference between the different grenade launchers?  Why do I have a budget?  Can I eventually change the number and type of my squads in story mode, or is that just a versus thing?  Can I select my squads with a hotkey instead of clicking them?  I don't know.
Most of my issues with balance are when playing as the police, and I'm confident the developer will fix some of these issues in a few more versions, so I'll come back to the game in a couple of months. Nice presentation but a little basic. I'm a big fan of point-and-click adventures and story/comedy focused games in general so I was really excited to find a new, well-reviewed adventure game to play. Unfortunately Darkside Detective doesn't really have enough depth or cleverness to it to really deliver.
This game has likable characters and a fun setup but the stories and jokes don't really feel like they had much effort put into them. Everything feels like it was written as a first draft and they didn't bother to improve on it. A lot of the comedy just consists of direct references to pop culture (Ghostbusters, Gremlins, Dr Who etc.), which just made me cringe most of the time. On top of that, the gameplay is way too simple to really keep your attention. It's not just that the puzzles aren't difficult or elaborate enough, it's that you only have one task to do at a time and you can pretty much always predict how you're going to have to solve it. There aren't really any moments where you have to think laterally you just encounter a problem, immediately deduce how to solve it and then wonder around looking for whatever object you need.
Creating a silly, breezy game around this dark subject matter is a great idea, it's just a shame they didn't build on that premise with some compelling stories and puzzles. If you're a fan of point-and-click games I'd recommend steering clear as you'll likely just be bored and disappointed.

The title Crusader Kings 2 falls under the so-called grand-strategy games. The term is well-earned in this case and before you start the game be warned that there is a steep learning curve. Do not pick up this game if long-winded games that requires hours of hours to finish is not your thing. Do pick it up if you like games like Civilization, Alpha Centauri, or Europe Universalis. Having said that, and perhaps you do not know these titles, lets get into what Crusader Kings 2 actually is.
Like all grand-strategy games Crusader Kings 2 is (but need not be, I will get back to this) for instance about creating a dukedom, kingdom, or empire, keeping those under you happy less they revolt, and creating a proper army. Unlike many other grand strategy games (outside of other Paradox titles) this game is actually historically correct for medieval europe, the middle east, and India. That is right, did you ever want to play as William the Conquerer? This game gives you that opportunity.
That immediatly leads to 'need not be' clasule I said before. Unlike other grand strategy games you do not play a 'faction' or a 'nation', but you play as an individuel e.g. Ghengis Khan. The game doesn't end when you die, however, no it follows the rise (and fall) of your family as your dominion grows on the map. Depending on your succesion laws you might be playing as your oldest, youngest, or even a random family member. You might even go super modern and have daughters rule on purpose, not 'just because' the male line ended as was more the case in the time period between 769-1452 AD (which how long the games played out assuming you have two DLCs).
The game features cultures (e.g. German, Anglo-Saxon, Berber, Russian, Visigothic, and Tamil) as well as religions (e.g. Hindu, Catholic, Coptic, Karasite, Tengri, Sunni, and Germanic) and this including with recently conquered, traits of a person, your history with them perhaps, can all influence what people think of you. Wil you marry out a daughter for an alliance, or perhaps with that genius of a man so you can get him to court and get a good advisor? This is all dependent upon you.
Thanks to all these features, as well as the fact that once the game starts randomness kicks in and the historical accurate timeline is lost, means that you will never(!) play the same game ever again. Mechanics wise yes, but give it enough time and the map will look quiet different from last time, different kings and emperors, and perhaps e.g. the Byzantine empire might have fallen by 1100. What will you do? How will you influence medieval Europe? I say it is time to find out and play Crusader Kings 2 for yourself.

At the time of writing this review (2/5/2017) I have nearly 60 hours invested in the game since release, so I've played enough to experience the good and bad of Conan Exiles.
First of all, I'd like to adress the negative reviews that are being left for this game because of the server stability issues, bugs, etc.  This is an early access game.  In todays world most people expect things to be perfect when a game releases, early access or not, but they completely have forgotten what exactly early access is.
Early access is a completely unfinished game.  It will have bugs, it will have issues.  This is to be expected!  Early access games have not gone through rigorous testing that say a completely finished AAA game gone though before release.  Early access, for lack of a better way of explaining, is you getting to try out the game while it is still in development, so you need to understand this and be patient that eventually these issues will be fixed as development advances.  Now with that said, I will move on to my review of the game itself...
I absolutely love it!  The world of Conan Exiles is expansive.  The graphics are absolutely breathtaking.  I remember the first time I came across one of the many temples, and looking up at it all I could say was, "wow".  Wandering the desert, looking up to the sky and seeing a massive sandstorm coming straight for you is an amazing sight to behold.  Until you get settled and start to gain XP, life is rough.  It seems around every rock there is some sort of creature waiting to kill you.
So far, I have not felt that this game is too much of a grind to get XP to level up.  There is always something to explore, somewhere new to go, something to kill.  Building is fun, but seem to be a little clunky and not quite where it needs to be yet, but I am overall happy with the building mechanics.  And the fact that the game allows you to build upwards on cliff faces is fantastic.  You're able to build some very unique bases in places you could not do in other games of this genre.
In closing...yes, the game in it's current state needs work, there's no doubt about that; however, the dev's are actively addressing issues and putting out patches regulary.  I believe that this could potentially be one of the best survival games ever made.  Yes, I said it.

Oh Archeage...Where do I begin...
Edit: this review was based off of the Kraken server (Used to be Enla) which was a merge of two different servers, from the start of Kraken everything went wrong and that is where most of my cons come from. If someone comments just be aware that their experience may not be the same due to being on a server with more stability. This was not just my view on the game but an overall assessment made by a guild of over 40 people. and a close estimate of population would be a 1:1:3 Haranyan (us) : Pirate (Purple and same faction reds) : Nuian (Red), so we were completely out numbered when it came to world PvP and trade runs.
Pros -

Cons -
-Literally can not play without dumping about $50 a month into the game.

- RNG with expensive regrading.

-Pirate and Purple faction members recieve hardly a punishment for ruining your trade run that you waited 2 weeks for (roughly..15 mins inside a prison which they can just break right out of and steal someone else's gold.) Edit: it takes 2 weeks if you want good mney. Using larders on your land gives you the most profit out of any trade pack unless you make PvP packs at abyssal and can get them out safely. A larder takes up most of a week to grow and if you had a mercant ship like I did, you can fit 2 weeks of larders on your boat for max profit. Nearly 90% of us relied on this on money whenever the PvP areas were out of peace and making a trade run in or out would be impossible due to Purples and Reds.
-Plots are only available to subcribed people so that free 8x8 you get at the beginning of the game is a joke.
-Labour points make it impossible to find something to do for an extended amount of time. (A trade pack costs Labour to make AND to turn into gold! If you're out of labour by chance don't expect to make any money)
-Only way to get Labour points if you are not a subscriber is to literally AFK while you sleep by hitting on a dummy since there is a 15 min AFK kicker which Trion added after people would AFK...to get the labour they needed...to do anything in their own game...they really just took away the only way you could make a profit in the game. GG 10/10 would play again any day.
-Small amount of content
-Game is 90% PvP based and typically your faction will always lose.
-PvP is only won based off of gear score and not skill.
-In PvP there are counters for every class and more often then not, you're getting countered.
-To switch a class you have to Pay...
-To recover lost experience you must..you guessed it, pay. But wait! you pay with Labour that is based off of your level AND the level of the creature you died to!
-Land hackers and plot spammers make it hard for land trading to happen seeing as how everyone can see when a building is going to be demolished.
-Land hackers own 85% of the land
-Top level guilds have a Monopoly on trading and dungeon running.
-Unless you are in said top guild you will likely have no help with content or protection in PvP zones which you HAVE to travel through to make a good profit.
Example of your in-game, late game Regrading experience: Pay anywhere up to 900 Gold for a Superior Red Charm, 450 for a Lucky Moon/Sunpoint to increase your chances to double proc, and 45 gold for a weapon/Armor scroll. Add on to that a fee for even attempting to regrade. At the medium level of Unique (Level 5/9) this all together gives you a roughly... 30% success rate, a 10% double sucess rate, a 45% fail rate, and a 15% double fail rate. So for a Grand total of 1,400 Gold (roughly 2-3 weeks of grinding) you have a better chance of losing your current grade rather than going up. The system is in no way rewarding and gives absolutely NO COMPENSATION for those (over 95% of players) who get a DEGRADE (that's right, Trion believes in reverse upgrading) to try and work their way back up to that same point. Instead you are forced to keep your subscription rolling so you can farm your plots, store your materials, make trade packs and larders, and transport them across the ocean for the most money with the chance of: your own faction stealing from you, the enemy faction stealing from you, and pirates stealing from you. If you lose all those trade packs guess what, you get a 5% profit off of what they turn in, which usually be Gilda Stars, something that is completely worthless unless you are wanting to upgrade a house to a much larger version (The land around your house must be empty, fair warning: it never is). It is an endless loop of farming, trade running, and regrading for high level subscribers. And it NEVER pays off for the majority of players. Out of my 830 hours I spent at least 800 of them doing trade runs and PvP to try and get my trade packs back from all 3 sides. The highest level I every got to was Unique simply because I never had the money to try regrading higher. I can not tell you how much money I spent on this game trying to get to that level where most of the PvPers were, most of the Guilds who did end content even REQUIRED you to have these ridculously expensive weapons and armor so they could clear them out quickly and easily, basically making those with poor luck lose out on content.
Speaking of Content, you remember those other 30 Hours I missed out of my record? Yea thats your entire leveling experience. 30 Hours. I made it to max level in only 12 hours, the rest of it all was just side quests for money and items I could sell on the Auction. And btw, you can not fully use the auction unless you are a subcriber or use real dollars to by a liscence. You have to pay...to use an MMORPG essential...Let that sink in. I wanted to like this game, I really did but the endless grinding that never paid off simply wasn't worth it. I had friends who lost entire armor sets due to that 5% break chance above unique, it was almost like a 5% pass rate vs a 95% fail/break rate, something that should only exist at the Mythic level. This game is so pay to win that I could have paid for a majority of my college supplies with the amount of money I put into this game, hell probably even part of my tuition. The only reason to play this game is if you want a place to throw unused money at with no profit in return.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale surprises and delights on a level that I didn't expect from such a small game. There are many facets to this game that are on the surface missed, but appreciated after many hours playing the game.
The story is rather simple, you are left with the care of a shop and are required to pay back a debt that your father left you with, so capitalism and careful planning are your only means of digging yourself out of this debt. At first the requirements seem staggering, as each week you progress you're required to pay back more than the last, but the game is forgiving and if you miss a payment you'll restart in a better spot than when you first started your game.
This game truly shines if you enjoy item management (as I do, clearly), as well as RPG elements that aren't extraordinarily deep but yet very enjoyable. The shop management experience found in this game, as well as the bartering that you're required to do to excel, is something that I had never experienced before and found it delightful.
Sound for this game is so-so, and could be better but certainly doesn't detract from the overall appeal of the game. The graphics work well for what the game is looking to accomplish. Unfortunately, the supported resolutions require me to typically run the game in windowed mode (I have multiple monitors that are connected to my desktop, and it's a hassle to go full screen with Recettear). This is a minor annoyance, but certainly something that won't affect all players.
Finally, the controls work well for the game, and I typically play with a connected controller. The support for the peripheral has proven to be one of the largest draws for the game, as I can kick back in my chair and play for a couple of hours with relative ease. I use a wired Xbox 360 controller, but I'm sure that other similar configurations from either the 360 or One will function just as well.
Overall, I recommend Recettear for anyone looking for a new and unique experience. As far as idle games go, Shonen Idle Z is one of the less interesting titles.
You're thrust into a shonen anime world and must battle your way through increasingly difficult enemies. It's a sound premise, but the excecution is lacking. First of all, there are a lot of microtransactions which get in the way. You're forced to progress at a snail's pace if you don't pay up. Second, the visuals aren't all that inspiring, which I suppose makes sense because it's meant to be a shonent anime parody, but that still doesn't save it.
Making your way through the map and killing bosses should probably feel pretty good, but it ends up being quite lackluster because each enemy is only a small, imobile sprite. There's no satisfaction in killing a tiny, immobile sprite boss, especially when you'll need to spam every single one of your skills at once to have any hope of taking less than an hour to win. The party member system is interesting, but you'll find that many of the available members are completely useless, and only a few will actually be worth spending your ascension currency on. By the way, even with party members, your progression will be painfully slow.
The game is also fairly buggy. There was once a bug that kept the game from launching through Steam. Not just for a few players, but for many of us. If I recall correctly, it took a few days to fix what was probably a simple problem.
Overall, I don't really recommend this game. There's too much grind and not enough fun to justify the time spent.

1200 hours into this game, been playing since beta: I can only say it's one of the best Free To Play games I have ever played, period.
The gameplay is boggling, and extremely fun, especially in the early game: It'll provide you with a decent challenge for the 100 hours, assuming you don't purchase a ton of the in-game currency and bypass the grind by buying everything, instead of grinding for it. (Which is half the fun, and the central point of the game)
The biggest 'AW YEAH!' I can give this game, however, is the way it approaches the marketplace: Prime Access is kind of an insult, but the rest of the game's market is extremely healthy and alive. This is because the Developers made the decision to let players trade their 'Real Money Currency', Platinum, with each other freely. Anything that directly affects gameplay, and even MOST of the cosmetics in the game, can be received by simply grinding out items worth something to other players, and then selling them the goods in exchange for Plat. The Devs dont shove it down your throat, instead, they let the market do it's thing, and that gives much more life to the game than most give it credit for.
Thank you, DE, for a healthy economy, and allowing us to trade your premium currency. Warframe overall is a treat, and I always find myself coming back.
But.
There are a few things that could be better: 1200 hours in, I can say that I'm rather officially at the point of having broken the game in a few ways. End-game offers little challenge versus reward, Raiding is kind of a joke due to the Peer To Peer client system DE have based the game around, and the game kinda falls flat. Mind you, I got 1200 hours out of this game, and I'll probably get many more: But DE's boss design and lack of dedicated servers for big-ticket stuff, like raiding, makes the end-game experience disappointing at best, at least for me. Most raids I've ever gone into have been complete and utter messes, better reserved for a much smaller, higher skilled player count. Other players would rubberband around, and anybody you don't personally know can make the entire run fail: Just because they can't follow basic instructions.
It's about as pleasent as herding cats away from the food bowl.
PVP is also a complete and utter joke. So broken it's not even worth laughing about. The network issues glow brighter than a forest fire in the dead of night, and any 'Competitive Edge' this game had was thrown out the window when explosive weapons were allowed into the PVP modes, the Simulor especially. Expect to see people bouncing around in utterly strange, rubberbanding patterns, spamming their Simulor into nearby walls for kills. The PVP takes absolutely zero skill, and the rewards could not be farther from worth such a terrible gameplay experience.
The Early-Mid-Late game progression is great though, and you'll find yourself tinkering with builds, chomping at the bit to try new things and new styles of play, even at the very end of the game. Despite DE's shortcomings in some facets, they are shining beacons in others.
(I sure would like some heavily challenging single-player content for the end game though. Test us by our mechanical skill. Give us a reward worthy of a trial by fire.)
Overall, I can heavily recommend this game to... Everyone, really: Whether you enjoy putting together different builds in RPGs for your characters, you enjoy facing down endless waves of enemies, or if you love hitting sick shots from your rifle into a foes' weak spots. This game has something for everyone, really, and even at 1200 hours, I still have lots of fun with it.
Edit: Some fixes, new ending paragraph.
TLDR: It's basically the Witcher 3 of Free to Play. You'll enjoy it, just avoid raiding and PVP. Download this game and play it already.

Where to begin? I usually start off by comparing to a popular game in the same genre but this one right here... it's quite unique.
So, what is Hand of Fate and why you should try it?
The game itself is played against the Dealer, as you attempt to beat different challenges and combats that he throws at you. They are represented by cards, some designed to help the player, some to hinder and most are a mix of the two, so the difficulty is balanced on the edge. To help you on your quest, you have two decks, Encounter and Equipment, which you set before hand, but each round the Dealer adds his cards into them as well to balance out the 'goodies' you put in.
The cards will vary from straight up story encounters, which usually require the player to make a choice, and may involve combat. Combat is played out top down-ish in a limited area against pre-set enemies God of War style but much more basic. There is nuance to it but not much.
PROS
- Captivating obscure story, challenging you to find out more by unlocking more cards and beating encounters;
- Charming sound design, every clink and slam are in their proper place;
- The Dealer: ahhh, the Dealer... fully voice acted, enigmatic, aloof, sometime even tender towards the player. He will frequently comment on the happenings in game, even remembering the cards you used before. You are never quite sure if he is routing for you or trying to hurdle you and bitter at your progress. Intriguing character and SUPERBLY voice-acted. Probably enough of a selling point on its own.
- Mouse and Keyboard controls are re-bindable and perfectly functional (i.e. doesn't suck without controller). Controller still probably recommended if you got one.
CONS:
- Combat camera cannot be controlled and is sometimes pretty awful;
- Some people will find the totally unfair and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG (tm) to be too hard to handle, such people should STAY AWAY from this game.
- RNG will screw with you. You will die. Repeatedly. Sometimes the Old Gods decide that 90% of your total HP is just about right to take away because you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off......
OVERALL:
HIGHLY recommended to any RPG lovers out there with a bit of collecting cards mixed in. Dripping in polish and a lot of TLC.

Hand of Fate is the perfect card game: everything revolves around doing your best with the cards you have, whenever they're good or bad (mostly bad). It's an interesting mix of deck building, rogue-like elements, dungeon crawling and third person action during battles. You build a deck of events, that will build the path of the dungeons, and of equipments, the rewards you'll get for successful encounters: sometimes you'll have to fight, sometimes you'll have to 'roll a dice', sometimes you'll have to make the right choice. It's a very interesting and well developed concept. Of course the Dealer will do his best to make things worse for you, but as he says "The game is fair and you'll be defeated fairly".
Hand of Fate has a well built learning curve and difficulty curve, knowing when to challenge you and how to do that. Sometimes you'll get frustrated by unfair conditions (like fighting twelve enemies in a small arena), but that's part of the rogue-like nature. I LOVED the atmosphere and the monologues of the Dealer, a very charismatic and interesting character: his presence alone is worth buying the game if you ask me.
There are a couple of downsides, mostly regarding the battle system: a targeting system and a health bar above the enemies would have been useful and made the battle less chaotic; a couple of collisions are off and a very limited number of arenas have some visibility issues in certain points. All around it's a great game, if you like mixing the chance of card games with the risks of rogue-likes. It could use some polishing, but its atmosphere and concept are so fantastic that you can overlook it.

After finishing Mass Effect 1 a couple of days ago, I was eager to start playing Mass Effect 2 as soon as possible. Expecting more of the same, I was in for a few unpleasant surprises. So much has changed that it almost feels like a different game.
CONTROLS:
The controls are so radically different from ME1 that it actually got me killed on several occasions. I felt like my arms had been cut off and then sewn back on backwards! I know that eventually I'll get used to the new controls but they still feel super weird.
WEAPONS:
Reloading? Seriously? Can't buy new weapons, only the blueprints? Really? While I'm happy that I don't have to manually customize every single weapon on every single squad member, this is a bit too simplistic.
MAP:
There was nothing wrong with the maps in ME1. The map in ME2 is hard to read and too colourful. It looks like somebody just resized all the locations to 20x10 pixels and made them into a map. What happened to the ability to add waypoints?
HUD:
Why am I able to "light up" objects through walls? It's distracting. The colour and thickness of the rectangle make things easy to miss. In the first ME game everything stood out great when you placed the crosshairs over an item.
CHARACTER SKILLS:
What happened to all my skills from ME1? Puff! Disappeared into thin air! Now you only get five. Yay! Thank you, Bioware!
PROFANITY:
I don't remember hearing much profanity in ME1. While I'm not against it per se, I didn't expect this from ME2 judging by the tone set by ME1. Completely unnecessary.
