I don't like leaving bad reviews for games unless I really get burned, and I often believe that all games have their good and bad points, but unfortunately there aren't enough redeeming qualities for DreadOut to make me want to keep trying it.
Wonky interface- The controlls for the game use the typical WASD for movement and the mouse for camera control, but the mouse movement is extremely sensitive and dizzying. It almost always gets in the way of taking a good spirit photo or moving in the correct direction. There isn't any way to change the sensitivity.
Little to no storyline imput- Yes, Linda has a journal where she writes updates on plot-related events, but there is no feeling of planned events or order to any of the game's happenings. A little nudge in the right direction would be nice, but this isn't a complete game-ruiner for me.
Tension, scare-tactics and horror- Sometimes you reach cut-scenes, but all the scary stuff happens in the cutscenes and it doesn't really leave you feeling scared because you aren't in control of Linda. You just wait for the cutscene to end and the tension is gone. There are plenty of spooky moments, don't get me wrong, but in order to deliver the right "punch" of panic mixed with confusion, the player needs to control the character during a desperate situation, not just watch events unfold while eating a handful after handful of popcorn until the cutscene is over.
Absolutely no puzzle hints or imput- When the game presents you with a puzzle, you often won't even know its a puzzle at all. There are no hints, there is no moment where you read some cryptic message on a wall that you have to decypher in order to solve a puzzle and continue with the game. The game just drops some weird items or a strange picture or situation in front of you, and after retracing your steps several times because maybe you took a wrong turn somewhere or missed something, and after becoming frustrated and returning to that spot and visiting the DreadOut wiki page, you finally realize that its a puzzle and that NOW you need to start figuring out what to do, but there still isn't any imput on what the puzzle wants from you.
Voice acting and graphics- The characters dont look bad, I'll admit. I'm not a graphics snob, I won't scoff if textures don't exactly line up or if someone's facial features aren't realistic. I have to say though that the voice acting in this game is horrible. Everything sounds cheesy, characters talk over eachother and sometimes audio cuts out. There are plenty of classic old games that have horrid voice acting, but with DreadOut its hard to be scared or on edge when the supporting characters sound so silly.
All in all, I can't do much complaining because I got this game on sale.
I would not reccomend this game to anyone who wants this game because they expect it will be reminiscent of the Fatal Frame/Project Zero series, because you will be very disappointed.

Hard Reset is an FPS in the vein of the genesis of FPS. Combat is quick and based around movement and lots of guns rather than cover and patience.
Unfortunately it feels a bit clunky, you have a jump but it's basically useless and there is no crouch. Sprinting is fairly limited and the screen distorts so much you can't really see anything, leading you to often rush headlong into enemies. As expected you can unlock a plethora of weapons to help you along the way. There are 10 guns in total, each with an alternate fire. The weapons are split into two classes, one firing physical ammo the other firing energy. While I didn't use a number of the weapons or firing modes it was enjoyable to work out the best gun/mode combos for each enemy type. The weapons feel decent and some are pretty fun to use, but the swap time is agonizingly slow.
The level design is that of a corridor shooter but the fact that it is essentially linear is a bit of departure from the days of yore. There are plenty of secrets tucked into corners or behind destructible walls but it's not like you'll be exploring vast open levels to find them. The world is heavily cyberpunk and takes place almost entirely at night in the rain. It looks pretty good for what I suspect is a pretty minimal budget. It's an interesting world that is severely undersold by the story. Mostly told between levels by clunky animated, poorly voice acted "cut scenes" done in a graphic novel style, the story is underdeveloped and poorly explained. I wanted to to care about the story and the world but I just couldn't get drawn in. It just feels like there was supposed to be so much more.
The included DLC, Exile (previously Path to Exile or Extended Edition) is essentially more if the same. There are a couple new enemy types but one of the guns completely removes them as a threat. Partly through Exile I realized I was just grinding and going through the paces.
In the end Hard Reset is just a bit shallow. The potential is there for a much more engaging experience but it just doesn't deliver. If you're a fan of circle strafing this is probably a must have but for generalists or people looking for a deeper cyberpunk world this is a bargain bin/bundle pick up.

Anime-styled story in a "not-WWII" setting. Characters are charming, although they fall into common anime tropes fairly often. The overall story is engaging and has a few strong set-piece moments, while also leaving time for quiet reflective moments.
Combat is very well-designed, and the player units become a force to be reckoned with later into the game, when strong weapons, skills, and equipment have been obtained. The combat system is turn-based, but moving units and attacking occurs in real-time, and the player has full control over which units they will spend their turn controlling. Unit classes are fairly imbalanced, with scouts becoming horrendously overpowered by the end-game. This means that many missions can be cleared while only using a single unit. This diminishes some of the squad tactics and positioning required, which is unfortunate.
Missions do a good job of staying fresh, with different objective types and environmental challenges on a regular basis keeping the player on their toes. The difficulty curve falls off a bit after the mid-game, when the player can obtain some of the late-game weapons and skills for their units. There are a couple difficulty spikes, but nothing too unreasonable.
The art style of the game is gorgeous, and the characters and environments have a gentle color palette and a sketched appearance. It looks good in stills, and even better in motion. The soundtrack fits the game very well, providing both whimsical and serious tracks that fit right in with the alt-history setting.

I tried liking Valkyria Chronicles, I really did. I spent 48 hours playing it and there’s a lot to like here, but the game ultimately proves too frustrating to be worth recommending. This is a game that’s it’s own worst enemy.
First, some of the highlights:
- Unique gameplay that marries RPG elements with turn-based strategy. Think Final Fantasy meets Company of Heroes.
- Interesting setting that can only be described as Dragonball Z meets World War II.
- Good graphics and a varied campaign.
However, there are just too many things that bring the game down:
- Two-dimensional characters that look and sound as if they were created by kids in junior high. Seriously, these people show more emotion when it comes to baking bread than when their entire national army is wiped out.
- The classes are ridiculously unbalanced. Shocktroopers are amazing in 80% of situations whereas Scouts are useless in almost 100% of situations. In addition, 3 out of 5 classes don’t respond when enemies approach. They will quite literally just stand there and get shot in the head.
- There is a ridiculous amount of randomness to when characters hit and when they miss. Leaving you to accept that either you're going to lose some battles out of pure chance or you’re going to have to totally cheese your way through the game, saving after every phase (or even after every turn). Unlike in games like XCOM there is no percentage indicator of a hit or miss.
- The game is long and tedious. Going off of Steam achievements, only 38% of players get the first achievement and a puny 6% actually beat the game. In short, people just give up.
- Tank controls are awful, leaving you to spend half of your movement points just trying to turn the thing in the right direction.

Excellent truck simulator.  I spent some time back in the 70s (before CDL licenses) driving trailer truck, and as long as you are using a steering wheel, shifter and pedals like the G27 from Logitech, the experience is as close as you can get on a PC.
I love backing these long trailers and ATS has more challenging parking spots to plug in and drop your trailer.
I do wish that they had some harley davidson motorcycles mixed into the traffic. I can't imagine driving out west and not seeing a lot of harleys cruising down the highway. That would make it seem more realistic.  You always have to be looking out for motorcycles when driving. It would be even better if they had some motorcycle groups cruising down the roads.
Also, I wish that they would make a feature that would require that you stop and check the load and binders.  Being sure that the load is secure is also the responsibility of the driver, and in reality, the load does come loose as you drive. That would also make the simulator even more realistic. It would be great if someone forgot to check their load when they are supposed to and a big tractor or pipe rolls off of the trailer as you make a corner. That would be a bad situation.
I look forward to seeing Arizona and some other extensions for ATS.  I'll buy them all.
I also really like EuroTruck Simulator 2.  It is a challenge having to drive on the wrong side of the road in certain countries and switching back in others.
I just want to say "Great Job!" to the makers of these simlators.  What a wonderful idea, and you've done so well with both of the simulators, making them very entertaining and enjoyable.

Level 42 Review - Update 6/8/16:
Archeage is not a F2P game. I want to give it a "Yes" recommended, but as F2P I can't. That doesn't mean it's not worth checking out.
I've spent some time with this more and I enjoy what it has to offer. THAT SAID, it really is a P2P game in F2P clothing. It is not worth playing unless you have Patron (subscription). It can be earned in the game through farming things and selling on AH, but really, good luck trying to do that. All the cool stuff does cost Labor Points and YMMV on how you view the Labor system.
Patron lets the Labor Points regenerate while you are offiline, whereas F2P must be logged in to regen and earns 1/2 the Labor Points. Therefore, I would not recommend this game AS F2P. Unless you are planning to have Patron sub, stay away from this.
If you are okay with treating Archeage as a P2P game, there is a lot of fun to be had with building things and its deep crafting system. I built a boat and supposedly I can build a car if I get the plans. Again though, building/crafting costs Labor Points. It's not much of an issue when your points are regenerating while offline or doing other things in the world, but it can be an annoyance when you run out.
I don't know any MMO that has let me build a boat and sail on the ocean with danger around all corners; PvP is everywhere on the open sea.
7/10 would build boats again

A newbie's review (Level 8) -
Review in progress:
I'm just getting started, but I really don't understand the hate for this game. The labor point system is easily overlooked and builds over time.
PROS:
+ Labor points have little to no impact on the battle system (which is somewhere between traditional and action combat).
+ No hard-set classes. You pick skill trees you want to use and can mix/match. Skills rank up the more you use them.
+ Interesting battle system, with combos that can be performed. Skills chain into each other and some can be rapid fired.
+ Game is gorgeous. Sometimes I stop and stare at the scenery,
+ Row, row, row your boat. They give you this as part of the main quest line, you will get a dingy and can explore the sea.
+ Once you have progressed far enough, quests will allow you to "overachieve" and give more items/kills than needed for a quest for bonus EXP. Quests can also be "turned in early," though I don't know who would want less EXP reward from a quest unless they're just totally bored with it and want to end the quest.
+ Walked into what I thought was a town, but it actually was all player-built housing. Interesting to look at.
+ NPCs are interesting, but it's weird/awkward once they're done talking to you... Quest NPCs won't ever speak to you again, unless there's another quest.
+ Story cutscenes paint a nice picture and give an English voiceover telling the story. There's not much action there, but if you like a decent, albeit generic fantasy, story then you will like this.
+ Arguably better progression rate than Black Desert.
CONS:
- (minor) You need labor points for a lot of things; identifying loot, opening "Farmer's Satchels" that drop from mobs (rewards Larceny EXP), crafting, etc.
- Skills rank up the more you use them. Because of this you can't just spend points to level up a skill. Levelling up a skill has to be earned by using. Skill points only unlock new skills.
- Quest treadmill is very strong at the start of this game. (Go here, Kill X mobs, Deliver this, etc.) You will get the impression that "oh just another MMO" until you get futher into it.
- The game mentions housing but doesn't really tell you all that much. Blah blah "Mirage Isle", here's some houses to look at etc.
- Immersion-breaking Korean voiceovers. Sometimes NPCs will spout gibberish when you are near them or finish talking with them. What are you saying to me?! Did that guy just cuss me out?
EARLY REVIEW:
Recommended, but it's not without its flaws.

One thumb up, one thumb down (mixed review)
Pros: Really good atmosphere, art, voice acting, writing, music, and charm.
Cons: Terrible design choices in the new armor system (0% crowd control or status affliction chance while armor is up and 100% chance while armor is down) - makes encounter solutions incredibly repetitive and thus fairly boring, as they are too easy to "solve" via chained, 100% success rate crowd control. Also, on tactician there are not more enemies, but instead enemies just get huge boosts to their stats (armor included), making fun, hybrid parties bad, pushing you to use a more-repetitive either all physical or all magical party. The first Divinity Original Sin also had more chance involved (hit/miss chance for both attacks and crowd control), which this sequel pretty much eliminated, which makes fights very snowbally and predictable (and thus somewhat boring) towards the mid to end portions of the fight.
Poor, lazy loot design choice as every level up your lower level equipment becomes extremely outclassed by current level equipment found by tediously going to merchants and buying their newly updated wares. Also, loot attributes are randomized on most equipment so loot while adventuring feels way less special and lovable as you ditch them frequently for current-level loot with higher numbers (feels like Diablo 3 or Borderlands - games with the same lazy, constant slow-drip dopamine design choice).
Only 4 action points without a way to increase them (unless using OP lone wolf), makes fights much less tactical compared to the first Divinity: Original Sin 1 in which you slowly increased your action points as the game progressed, allowing fun combos. In this game you will use your most powerful skills/spells at the start of almost every single fight and then your second most powerful skills in the second round. Also, because action points are more sparse, scrolls and potions are used less frequently as they take precious action points away from using the aforementioned most powerful skills/spells. It makes the combat much more repetitive than the first Divinity: Original Sin.
Initiative system is botched. The turn order is now a round robin system as enemies always get a turn in between your characters, no matter how high your or their initiatives are. This makes fun multiple character combos less possible as enemies will often move or teleport before you have a chance to perform the full combo. Example: one character casts rain on the floor, enemy moves out of the water, and your second character can no longer electrocute the water with a lightning spell.
Stats are dumbed-down. Google Divinity:OS 1's stats and then Divinity:OS 2's stats and see the difference for yourself.
Small selection of damage-dealing magic spells (with many of them locked behind the anti-fun source system which forces you to spend a few and far between source points to use them).
Conclusion: If you liked the first Divinity Original Sin you will probably enjoy this one as well, even though most combat mechanics were changed for the worse. If you are looking for a superb, deep crpg experience similar to the past greats like Baldur's Gate, you may be disappointed.

At first, I shared in the dissapointment that some have expressed about this game.  And although I feel there is definitely some work to be done to make this game complete, I must say it isn't all bad. Somehow, the game manages to pull me into the story mode after a few plays.
However, some things definitely need fine-tuning. The controls are subpar. It can be difficult to keep control of what is going on at times, as there can be many things happening at once rather fast. To an extent, this is forgiveable playing as the rioters/demonstrators, but not so much when playing as police forces. Police holding the line and other crowd control tactics should be much tighter IMO. Police should be able to at least start out organized and more than capable of synchronous action. Also, live fire should probably be more effective as a means of deterrance.
In general I think the way unit control is handled makes things feel clunky at times. Often when trying to make a move against a certain group of opponents, you end up accidentally selecting another group of your own team. That can cost you dearly when momentum is building against you.
Also, selecting and applying weapons is sometimes a bit too slow in it's response. Again, this can be a problem in certain situations. Perhaps there ought to be a system in place that differntiates between different types of protesters and situations. Like police, protesters can in fact prepare for battle and take it to the police with a relatively small band of close knitted people whereas a bigger protest will always be more volatile, and can in that sense be more difficult to control towards confrontation.
Last, I think this game NEEDS the option to record and replay battles as much of it passes you by in the thick of things. After a good fight, what's better than to check it out from the warm comfort of home?
All in all, it's not a bad game at all. It just needs some more work to really be what it should and can be.
After that, IMHO, time to go deeper with the subject. I for one would support that attempt. There is a great lack of games about euro-style streetfighting, rioting etc. I'm done shooting hookers and ballaz.

Possibly one of the jankiest online multiplayer games I've ever played, including Nidhogg which is notorious for terrible online.
Everything is totally jerky and teleporting everywhere, even with ethernet, a great ping, and good FPS.  That's not to say there isn't skill involved, as many people will say.  There definitely is skill.  But 90% of it is just mastering the jank.  Some people were born into the jank, molded by it.  So they have no idea how bad it really is.  But the game is just chock full of not only immersion breaking bad design and moments, but moments that are awful regardless of immersion.  Hitboxes that are buggy and make no sense, players constantly teleporting around at all times just enough to make things miss, and a lot of problems having to do with tieing movement to camera angle too much.
It is tolerable at best with a bunch of close friends, and that's about it.

This is the most disappointing game I've played in a long time. It promises a pretty fun premise of a character with a lot of agency in a wacky situation (there's also "sexy stuff", but it is skippable).
The game is mechanically sound. The interface works really well, and of all the different things you have to balance in-game, it is explicitly clear on what will do what, which allows you to make informed roleplaying decisions. However, the main character is coerced, belittled, or has her agency taken away in almost every single scene, and none of it is portrayed in a bad way. Almost every character is portrayed as knowing her better than herself, and it leaves me feeling gross. On top of it all, she's helpless in the meta-narrative, especially at the end, where the plot goes off the walls, which I categorically disliked.
On top of it all, all the problems translate into the sex scenes. I went into this being open about the sex stuff, but off the bat, I was grossed out because
And this isn't something that fades into the background, but is consistently reinforced. The second issue, is that although a safe word is established, the player has no opportunity to use it, which seems contrary to the roleplaying style in the other part of the game. When the game is about having a lot of choices to make, the sex scenes happen pretty much without player input. The relationship also seems to develop on its own, too, with nothing in-between all and nothing. The last issue with the "sexy stuff" I'm going to discuss is that while the game touts its skippable sex scenes, it's clear that the sex scenes are longer, more detailed, and basically what people are here for. It is thus incredibly disappointing when one must skip them.
Between needing to skip some sex scenes and wanting to skip all the scenes where the protagonist is put down, belittled, coerced, or otherwise without agency, there are about 3 scenes in the entire game I liked. For a game that I really wanted to like, it just failed spectacularly.

I absolutely love this game. It a mix between a deck builder, tabletop RPG, and a Batman Arkham game. It sounds strange, but it works!
It's part deck builder, so by progressing through the story and completeing challenges, this allows you to gain more cards, which enables you to experience new challenges, face new foes, gain new equipment, etc. The more you play, the more the game expands to help keep things varied.
It's part tabletop RPG, so a lot of the game takes place with you sitting across from the Dealer, moving from card to card, and dealing with the event that occurs as you step on each new card. Gold is used to purchase items and food helps keep you fed, and you'll have to manage both.
It's part Batman Arkham, and this is probably one of the more interesting fusions. As you enter combat, the scenery shifts and suddenly you're in control of your adventurer. You build up combos, dodge roll, and counterattack your way out of trouble using the gear you obtained through your questing.
As mentioned above, I love this game, and it's an absolute steal when it's on sale. I heartily recommend!

NOTE: This review just covers the cons. If you'd like to read about what's good in this game just read one of the positive reviews--I agree with everyone else on the pros of this game, but unfortuantely the cons outweight the pros imo so I focus on them for that reason.
What begins as a wonderful game full of fun and interesting play eventually becomes just another test of player versus sadistic game developers that's so common these days. The more you love this game, the more you'll end up hating it once you near the end.
Unfortunately for players, the way this game ramps up difficulty is to cheat. By the time you reach the last level of the "story" mode (there's no story), the game is so unbelievably cheaty that it robs a very fun game of 100% of the fun it had previously contained. Just so you know what I mean: the last boss battle takes place in a 10 foot square environment so there's virtually no room to avoid the enemies. The problem? Just getting to the battle generally costs you between 30-50% of your health so you always start the battle at 65% or less health (due to curse cards on the last level which hit you every few turns so there's no way to avoid permanent health losses no matter how you play). The enemies surrounding the boss are all invincible until the boss is killed. But you're in a tiny environment so you can't dodge the enemies, and also they all protect the boss so you can't really get to him either. Invincible foes is the game developer equivalent to a slap in the face. It's a big F U to players that makes it very clear the developers enjoy punishing us for playing their game. There is no place in games for invincible enemies--it's a BS way to make a game harder that can only be described as cheating unless the player also has the ability to become invincible.
What is so frustrating about this game is that it has so much potential completely spoiled by anti-player decisions which ruin the fun.
I can't recommend this game because it's the most frustrating kind of game out there: the kind that draws you in, gets better and better, then because of really bad developer decisions becomes just a torture fest of "Can I get that 1 in 100 run where I can pull off a miracle based entirely on luck." I HATE games that force the player to rely entirely upon luck to succeed, and unfortunately by the end of the "story" mode, that's exactly what has happened. The game begins with maybe 25% luck and 75% skill and strategy but by the end it's more like 85% luck, which is FAR too high for any game under any circumstances.
Also worth mentioning (even the most positive reviewers mention this as a negative) is the extremely generic and not-so-great battle system (which is about 40% of what you do in the game). You roll around and endlessly kite groups of enemies until you can catch one of them off on his own and get a few hits in before kiting again. Also, some of the camera angles in this game are so bad they can and will get you killed. I seriously haven't seen this bad of a use of camera angles since the early days of Resident Evil. It's truly shocking how bad the camera angles can be sometimes.
On top of those issues, the narrator drones on and on endlessly and he only has like 8 or 9 things that he says for normal cards you frequently encounter, so you keep hearing him say the same boring thing over and over and over and over. It's maddening. When you first start playing, it's all very charming and wonderful, but by the 400th time of hearing him say the same thing (there's no way to skip or mute his monologues) it's gets really annoying and definitely takes away from the replay value.
I hope the devs make better decisions for Hand of Fate 2, which is currently in development. I feel like this game had great potential and I believe that if they fix these glaring (imo game-breaking) problems they could have one of the best games in a long time. The parts of Hand of Fate that work, WORK. It's an incredibly fantastic game CONCEPT, but unfortuantely miles away from a fantastic game. Fingers crossed, I'd certainly check out Hand of Fate 2 when it comes out. I'd give this one a pass.

I wanted to like this game. I genuinely thought that I would like it. I enjoyed Analogue and Hate Plus and bought this game upon release. What a letdown that was.
Plot - Flimsy. I expected something amusingly outlandish from the premise but somehow got blindsided by the sheer absurdity of it. A cruise for privileged high schoolers becomes the theatre of a game of psychological manipulation and sex. That's about it, a sort of Battle Royale sleazy sitcom.
Writing - Crude. The style is unable to salvage the lack of substance. The story suffers from being delivered in dialogs that feel shallow at best, insipid at worst.
Characters - Mixed. Some characters managed to shine in a few select scenes but otherwise everyone feels terribly underdeveloped. It is fitting that you only know them by a moniker instead of a name as they all can be reduced to mere archetypes.
Art - Mixed. The sprites are fine with a diverse range of expressions and clothing to make up for the lack of facial variety among characters. The backgrounds are pleasantly detailed but sometimes feel overly ornate and jarring compared to the way characters are drawn. The art in the sex scenes is especially pared-down with bodies depicted almost like dolls. Not much disappointment over the absence of the usual Visual Novel gallery feature.
Music - Adequate. Follows the overall atmosphere of the scene, sometimes light-hearted, sometimes tense. Though not memorable, I didn't feel the urge to mute it.
Gameplay - Good. This is a classic Visual Novel with a bit of novelty. An original change is the possibility to keep the conversation going without having to decide what answer to give among a set, answers can then appear and disappear as the situation evolves. Becomes a hassle when replaying in skip mode as you can miss the choices. Interface is well designed and pleasant.
Length - Underwhelming for the price tag. Three playthroughs to unlock everything and finally have an inkling of the plot. There is quite a lot of skipping already read text involved. Not sure of the exact time as I first played the game after buying it on Humble Bundle but about 10 hours in total.
Achievements - Not challenging. It requires playing three times to see everything. Bugs may prevent the timely unlocking of some achievements though.
Sex - Tepid.
Closing thoughts - The game fails to be the 'erotic romantic comedy' it proclaims itself to be and instead dissolves in a needlessly convoluted and messy plot with characters you do not care about having sex that is nothing to write home about.

An interesting title.  It reminds me a bit of Demon's Crest with the wondrous joy of flight being unlocked right from the beginning.  This game screams charm.  Owlboy has amazing 2-d graphics with some of the most expressive sprites I've ever seen in any game, and I've played over 850 in my day.  The music is an interesting mix.  Often uplifting and exciting, it can also be somber, understated, orchestral.  The characters all have their own charm and the game doesn't stray away from unpleasantness in the main story.  That said, it's largely a fun romp through a beautifully realized world.
There are two flaws I've found with Owlboy that I do want people to be aware of.  I feel that at times, it doesn't stay around long enough.  The game is super fun, but feels just a bit short.  I wanted a bit more time to play with Otus and all my friends in the floating world.  We get about 5 serious bosses and a few mini bosses, but I wanted more.  Still, that's not a bad thing.
The other issue is that, no spoilers, the last level is a major pain.  The developers were able to do a great job through most of the game, but the last stage is incredibly frustrating, at least for me.  The devs took something away from you.  And while it only lasts a short time, it's the most frustrating of all the levels.  It's got one of the most striking aesthetics, but the weakest level design.
You should definitely play Owlboy.  Even with its short length and frustrating final level, it's a heck of a ride.  Well worth your time and money for the adventure, the humor, and the charm.

I bought this game in the hopes of further supporting the developers, Flying Wild Hog as I enjoyed their title that they released after this game, Shadow Warrior, however the negative reviews that I kept seeing about this game were and are correct in every regard. This game is sold as Old School but it is not, I grew up playing Wolfenstine, Doom, Doom 2, Quake and so on those were old school, this game is simply a pretender that is unable to put forth even the most BASIC of FPS action and gameplay.  If you hear or read anyone speak of this title and Doom/Wolfenstine in the same breath immediately ignore them as they clearly have never played any of the true older titles as they are nothing alike and that is not a good thing.  Flying Wild Hog used the “old school” phrase as a marketing tool, it is an excuse to use that phrase to get people like me who've grown up playing the real old school shooters into thinking that this game will be ANYWHERE close to the caliber that those titles were and continue to be. Everything in those games was always paced properly, always fair; you never felt like you consistently hit a wall and it didn’t feel like luck to get to the next point. This game, regardless of these “upgrades” feels nothing but a shallow shell of what it tired to do and attempts to hype itself up in order to get unsuspecting buyers. Within 20 minutes, I knew that this game had none of what I found enjoyable in Shadow Warrior, clearly the developers learned many of their lessons from this title, as it is beyond inferior or substandard even for a basic FPS game.
So far I have gotten zero enjoyment out of the experience, the weapons, much like the ballistic weapons in SW, are liken to a toy and do almost nothing to enemies. Enemies that this game's universe has KNOWN about so therefore they should actually do more then just oh annoy them a little which would make you think that humans would have developed weapons to fight beings that are basically computers. With regards to weapon damage and how they work, there appears so far to be no real way to determine if a one weapon is favored for a particular enemy over the other. Part of this is because every single enemy in this title is a damage sponge making combat experience difficult at best let alone figuring out this game’s mechanics, if one can say that it has any. The smallest of enemies do 50 times more damage then they should to the player and take 100 times more damage then they should given how frequently they put the player into the closest of close quarters with these mostly melee driven enemies and their size. I do still see some of this game’s poisonous form spilling out into their work on SW, as the enemies hit you when you clearly put some distance between you and their attack impact point or enemies that have some kind of city sized hitbox for their attack that will hit you not matter where you are in relation to the unit. In this day and age it is absolutely inexcusable that this kind of programming and blatantly unfair gameplay would be tolerated in ANY development studio.
The character you play as seems to be made of paper, thus making enemy attacks even more deadly, dare I say you could right off the bat buy all of starting medical upgrades and STILL not have enough HP to take these unending waves and low amounts of health given. Speaking of your character, he has the lung capacity of a sick new born, he can sprint for exactly 1 meter then becomes haggard, yet we are lead to believe that he is some kind of PMC solder so one would think that he would have some kind of psychical training on top of whatever cybernetics or whatever he may have in him. This lack of stamina will constantly get you killed as enemies will swarm you almost instantly unless you sprint, even though the sprint is rather slow and it barely counts, adding to that the horrible visual effect that portrays the visual of sprinting. Unlike Shadow Warrior, you do not have the ability to dodge, which in this game’s case is a seriously negative omission because it is made by the same people the enemy types or attack types are roughly the same and need to be dodged. Your character however moves as such a slow pace on top of having almost zero stamina makes for even WALKING out of the way or trying to side step an enemy’s attack nearly impossible if not inconsistent.
You my notice that I have yet to talk about the “story line” I have chosen to omit that because as MANY others have talked about that aspect of the game I have really nothing more to add.  The only thing that I will add is that I agree with their sentiment, the story is miniscule it would seem as if someone saw a bunch of science fiction movies and told their 10 year old to write a script while keeping those scenes in mind.  It is confusing only because it does so little to explain anything, this includes the game’s universe, this means the characters and their interactions, this means the locations and their significance, and this means the protagonist and his goals.  All the items that are essential to a proper story and the game provide none of that.  The sad part is that there is a lot of atmosphere within this universe which is obviously taken almost directly from Blade Runner.
The checkpoint system is absolute garbage and the developers felt it necessary to steal away the game’s quick save feature which is in almost Every PC game.  Especially given this game’s insane difficulty this is a crime and there are zero reasons as to why the developers choose to take out the quick save/quick load function or why they made the checkpoints so spread out other then to give the game yet another layer of fake, artificial difficulty. I really do not know how the developers slept at night knowing they made such horrible game design choices and then had the gall to market it as an old school shooter.

The title Crusader Kings 2 falls under the so-called grand-strategy games. The term is well-earned in this case and before you start the game be warned that there is a steep learning curve. Do not pick up this game if long-winded games that requires hours of hours to finish is not your thing. Do pick it up if you like games like Civilization, Alpha Centauri, or Europe Universalis. Having said that, and perhaps you do not know these titles, lets get into what Crusader Kings 2 actually is.
Like all grand-strategy games Crusader Kings 2 is (but need not be, I will get back to this) for instance about creating a dukedom, kingdom, or empire, keeping those under you happy less they revolt, and creating a proper army. Unlike many other grand strategy games (outside of other Paradox titles) this game is actually historically correct for medieval europe, the middle east, and India. That is right, did you ever want to play as William the Conquerer? This game gives you that opportunity.
That immediatly leads to 'need not be' clasule I said before. Unlike other grand strategy games you do not play a 'faction' or a 'nation', but you play as an individuel e.g. Ghengis Khan. The game doesn't end when you die, however, no it follows the rise (and fall) of your family as your dominion grows on the map. Depending on your succesion laws you might be playing as your oldest, youngest, or even a random family member. You might even go super modern and have daughters rule on purpose, not 'just because' the male line ended as was more the case in the time period between 769-1452 AD (which how long the games played out assuming you have two DLCs).
The game features cultures (e.g. German, Anglo-Saxon, Berber, Russian, Visigothic, and Tamil) as well as religions (e.g. Hindu, Catholic, Coptic, Karasite, Tengri, Sunni, and Germanic) and this including with recently conquered, traits of a person, your history with them perhaps, can all influence what people think of you. Wil you marry out a daughter for an alliance, or perhaps with that genius of a man so you can get him to court and get a good advisor? This is all dependent upon you.
Thanks to all these features, as well as the fact that once the game starts randomness kicks in and the historical accurate timeline is lost, means that you will never(!) play the same game ever again. Mechanics wise yes, but give it enough time and the map will look quiet different from last time, different kings and emperors, and perhaps e.g. the Byzantine empire might have fallen by 1100. What will you do? How will you influence medieval Europe? I say it is time to find out and play Crusader Kings 2 for yourself.

First of all, yes, this game has it's bugs and glitches. But the atmosphere is amazing, and that definitely makes up for it.
This game should be played in a dark room, preferably with a set of headphones on.
The atmosphere, the strange creatures and it's creepiness is great all the way through.
The story is kinda like Silent Hill.
You follow a schoolgirl and a few friends and a teacher. On the road they suddenly stomp into a broken bridge. The bridge has never been there before. They start searching around to see if they can get through somehow. They find and search an old school to see if they can find any help with directions, since they seem lost (I guess). Of cause it ends with everyone getting seperated, You are playing the role as Linda in search of her friends.
The voice acting is good, the animation however is kinda clunky and the story is fairly mediocore, though with a great twist at the end. The monsters are creative and scary.
Gameplay was for me a little hard to get used to - I tried starting out with a controller, but after a while, felt mouse and keyboard was the better choice for this game. The game mechanics are quiet simple, you run and walk most of the time looking for clues, and once in a while you have to fight monsters. You fight the monsters by taking pictures of them with a smartphone camera and later on a SLR Camera. Taking their pictures makes the monsters go away.
At times it can be a little hard to know where to go and what to do (mostly in act 1, school area), but it's possible to figure out.
For people who can look past DreadOuts rough edges, bugs and glitches - I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who's a fan of horror games. The sheer horror of facing these weird monsters, trying to find you friends and get out is great. Again, the atmosphere is amazing and is the selling point of this game.

Play as a dynasty leading one of a great host of states from Ireland to India (DLC is needed for several groups, but even the most basic set of characters is a huge amount of replayability), and see your people rise and fall based on an enormous amount of factors - your skill, that dastardly hand of fate, the insignificant details and allies you forgot about, and the Mongols.
The game takes a bit of time to learn, but not as much as many grand strategy games - and as with most Paradox games there are both easy and hard places to start.   Gameplay is exceptionally variable, with events constantly coming up to haunt you (I married my least important son to a countess in Italy for a minor alliance... a decade later and he's my only heir, and she has corrupted him into a monsterous excommunicated idiot), and the future always uncertain*.  The events seem very intuitive and reactive, and every aspect of the game feels like it is impacted by your decisions (from the claims that people look to, to the balance of power of religions, to the genetics of your heirs - the game responds to your actions and gives you feedback: your family might even start naming children after your custom names).
If that doesn't interest you... there's still an extremely robust modding community with tons of alternate scenarios and events.
* If you get enough power, or are very good at playing certain aspects of the game, you can pretty much cruise through poor leaders (or make it very unlikely to get poor leaders).  Unless you're really good or really powerful (in which case, start over and challenge yourself with harder starts or trickier goals), though, your best plans and hard fought gains can evaporate overnight with rebellion, assassination, disease, and Mongols.  The game never gets into a boring plateau, because you are constantly rising and falling (or at least scheming to rise and scrambling to avoid falling).

It's a first-person shooter, set in the future, with secret places, exploding barrels, hordes of enemies increasing in difficulty from start to finish, and a grading system at the end of each level. You also get to upgrade things periodically. If that sounds really generic, and like a bunch of other video games have done it already, then that's because it is generic, and a bunch of other video games really have done it already. Quake 4 comes to mind as the next closest thing, because Doom 3 at least plays with darkness and balancing the flashlight and the other weapons and Red Faction: Armageddon at least has vehicles you can drive. Even Painkiller, which has the same linear gameplay and horde battles as Hard Reset, has you turn into a demon and get instant kills (not to mention it has much more imaginative weapons). In summary, if you've played a sci-fi FPS before, you are prepared enough for the things to which Hard Reset will expose you, and if you liked the other games you played along those lines, you'll probably like Hard Reset, too. Get it while it's on sale.

- Battles lack a "resign" button and for some reason it's impossible to access the system menu during the enemy's turn, which sometimes is infuriating when all you want is to restart the mission instead of waiting the enemy's turn to pass.
- There's no way to delete a save file in game, which is weird.

- Besides the aforementioned lack of incentive to beat the levels properly, even if players decide to do so they need to consciously restrict themselves. The whole point of the inclusion of reaction fire was to avoid players rushing through the level, but including broken orders like Caution and Defense Boost pretty much defeats the purpose. And these orders are there, in front of us, to be used. They are an integral part of the game that players must deliberately neglect so the game doesn't get too easy. In my opinion, this is a serious game mechanics flaw.
- Although I like the story, I get the feeling they interrupt the game too much to talk. I mean, all the time. Sometimes I wished they would just shut up and let me play already, especially when I'm just repeating the mission and have already read the damn dialogue. All it does is having the player mash the A button until it is over.
- I don't like the anime-style highschoolish "I-have-big-boobs-but-I'm-chaste-and-innocent-please-fantasize-with-me" personality of some of the characters. I think it's juvenile.
- Other than that, It's certainly a great game that deserves to be played.

Not really much need to try and express things in spread out detail, because the game is already straightforward with you and puts it in your head of what's going on and what to do, especially when you realize enemies can shoot and kill you during your turn if you don't use strategy. The combat system is very unique and a one of kind, where you can get killed during the turn by realtime attacks, unlike most other turn based games where the enemy doesn't attack until their turn. The story is good and heartfelt, but it's nothing revolutionary.
Everything seemed good when coming from turn based games like Xcom, until you find out something to where alot of people look at and agree as being a major flaw in the ranking/reward system(including me), that eventually might grow on you to the point where you might not want to replay the game. The Ranking/Reward System gives more of a reward to a player, for example, who gets all their troops killed with only 1 soldier left, than someone who actually kills all the enemies and doesn't get any of their soldiers killed or even skilled enough not to take any damage at all, as long as the player with 1 soldier left completed the mission in typically 1-4 turns. I got rewarded more for using "orders" on Alicia to complete "Windmill Plaza" in 1 turn with most enemies alive, than killing all the enemies and keeping all my soldiers alive in a 4-7 turns to complete the missions.
The game gives permadeath with a emotional sad scene of the soldier's farewell speech if a enemy happens to get close and touch the body of a knocked out soldier, BUT yet the game basically encourages people to rush in sloppy and reckless for the most part to complete the mission as fast as possible for the "A rank". The DLC was a disapointment to me, especially the one about the "Valkyrie", because it requires alot of unnecenssary effort to unlock EVERYTHING, but there's a more impactful reward to just do half of the battles for the very powerful gun, instead of the full 3 plus the hidden one just to play as the Valkyrie for ONE battle.
BASICALLY, it's mainly worth playing as a turn based fan for it's unique combat turn based mechanics, but the flawed ranking system just messes up the game for heavy replay value, especially since most of what they promote to justify replaying the game with the "New Game Plus" is it grind through the flawed ranking system to get a "A rank" on everything, rather than actually getting new story possibilites, like I would've liked, especially since the story doesn't give any extra choices to change things in a major way.

Cons:
-Dungeon gameplay, while fun, can easily overshadow the actual game.
-If you read a guide, you pretty much ruin the store section to some degree- half the charm is figuring it out for yourself.
-Numerous "guide dang it" moments.
-Starting hero moves far too slowly for using it to be worthwhile, but you might not figure this out until it's too late.
-Dungeon gameplay, while fun, is kind of both underpolished, and missing the point of the game's marketing.
-Besides survival mode, most postgame content is dungeons.
I give it a hesitant thumbs up, but your opinion might diverge.

You want to pace your way through a good story without much focus on the game itself.
"Oh cool! Solving the mystery of your own murder. So it's a puzzle game... but with ghosts!"
If only.
"Missed opportunity" is perhaps the best way to describe this one. It's not a bad game by any means, but the problem is the lopsided execution of stunning graphics with next-to-no gameplay. The concept is fantastic, but the banality of the actual meat of the game is downright bizarre. You have an adult story sitting on top of a children's educational game that teaches them the importance of nouns.
If you're not too fussed about the gameplay though, this should be a decent bet as the writing and visuals are incredible. It's gorgeously dark and atmospheric, and the characters are engaging enough to have you care about them, despite being a little stereotypical. The twists and turns were very well executed and, if nothing else, was worth a playthrough to enjoy the full story. It's no Ghost Trick (for any DS fans out there), but was clever nonetheless.
The problem is that the actual gameplay felt like an afterthought that was slapped on in order to give you something to actually do. You don't so much "solve puzzles" more "repeat the question" - You're given the scenario of "ah! I can read this person's mind to find out more about my murder. But what can I do to jog their mind about my murder? What can I make them think about... in order to get more details on my murder?"
Answer: "My Murder"
Seriously...? I put this down to being a tutorial, but this actually is how most of the puzzles in the game rolls. Others include a flashback of a terrified person being slaughtered with the caption "This person is _____" and you have to choose between adjectives like "Bloody terrified", "Bored" or "On the brink of sexual ecstasy"... What is this? A mash-up of Reader Rabbit and Hercule Poirot?
I'm not done yet.
The "investigation" scenes involve you finding clues... which consist of walking around a room until you see the 'Interact' prompt appear, at which point you mash the interact button and be told why this clue is important. Collect all 20 and you can proceed by picking the key clues out of the ones you found, forcing you to make the difficult decision of deciding whether to follow possible leads from a murder weapon or a tin of blue paint.
And then we get to the daemons. Bloody terrifying on first appearance and sends a shiver down your spine as you hear their screech, but ultimately become more of a story-blocking hassle than an actual threat. You can hide from them by hopping between conveniently-located hiding places (random husks floating indiscriminately in the middle of nowhere) which basically mean you play whack-a-mole with a daemon until you can sneak up on them and trigger the button combo to exorcise them (I recommend a controller here, as the keys are a bit awkward for exorcising on the WASD setup). If you fail... back to whack-a-mole until they get bored and patrol their little square route again.
The final attempt to flesh out the game are random items dispersed
... with no real incentive to collect the lot other than completionism, ghost stories and reading memoirs from Julia going "Ronan is such a bad boy with his smoking... but he's well fit".
It's such a shame. Unfortunately a good story just isn't enough to hold the game on its own. It screams of potential but feels like a hollowed-out remnant of what could have been an incredible title.

This idling game have "Mixed" reviews, and honestly, it's right where it belongs. I see some good points in it, like feeling of reading some manga. It's definitely not like another "Clicker Heroes" clone. However, I'm not really recommending the game, its pace is somewhat badly calculated, just as the most of clicker games on the market.
Which is worse, the game uses two levels of restarting, to prolong the game process. One is pretty familiar to anyone who have played any clicker or two: you pass some levels, then click "reincarnate" which sends you to the very start, but a little bit stronger this time, with some skill points added. That's fine, but there comes another: once you've seen enough levels, now you can't go to the very start, it's something like "welcome to the brave new world, where all progress goes even sloooower".
And boy, this sucks. I've learned the curve, I've managed to beat through levels much faster than any of my friends, and then what? They might be still in the 1st world, but with almost all achievements completed. And I, who was stronger and faster than them, now stuck in the so called "new game+", which is much slower than its already not so fast world 1 game. And I lost any hope to collect the same amount of achievements as my friends did a long time ago.
And really, what's there left to play for, in that idling simulator, if not for achievements?
There's not so much fun, you know. One last thing that bugs me when I try to restart the game is that the sound settings aren't memorized, as it used to be. And that means, the game will be awfully bleeping every now and then. It's an obvious bug, as I remember that setting used to work just fine, I hoped I muted it forever... But no, one of the last updates made the game worse than it has before.
Oh, anyway, too many words! Don't start Shonen Idle unless you're deep into clicker and idling games, and don't hope to finish it, in any case. In sum, another useless time-swallower, with mark 5/10.

Wonderful concept, shoddy execution.
I've always wanted to see more asymmetric-conflict games on the market: guerilla warfare, public unrest and peacekeeping,  riots and riot control, etc. This game attempts to deliver on that, but it just feels so clunky and underwhelming in play. Some of it can probably be chalked up to early access, mostly the bugs and the lack of explanation for most of the game's content. But it just feels kind of hollow.
First of all, it's very narrow in the options it gives you. Rather than struggling with the decision of containing a riot with nonviolent operations or simply washing it away with a spray of automatic gunfire and then facing the consequences, as I was expecting to see in the Arab Spring scenario, I discovered I was only able to issue a handful of shotguns with atrocious reload times, or a handful of sniper rifles with reload times that implied they were black-powder muzzle loaders. Likewise, when I was hoping to see the police attempt to de-escalate the situation via negotiation, communication, etc., that's simply not an option either.  Almost all of your games on either side will feel incredibly similar, it almost always boils down to "push them that way" or "don't get pushed that way".
Overall it's just bland when it's working right, and frustrating when it isn't. I'll let the glitches slide given early access, but at its core it's just not what I was hoping it would be when I purchased it, and I don't think further development will change that.

I was looking forward to playing this since I first saw it on Steam about a year ago. Have to be honest, I didn't know it was five years in the making. Seems a bit off that the developers took five years to make an Early Access game. Will it take them another five years to finish it?
The game plays like an EA game - and because it was advertised as EA (in spite of taking five years to get to this stage), I expected an unfinished product. All the same, I'm disappointed with it, if I'm being honest. Sometimes I win a level without even knowing why, and sometimes I lose a level without even knowing why. I want to throw a molotov and it ends up somewhere completely different to where I'd intended it to be. I can't always see what's going on - it's just a muddle of pixelated sprites. Things happen too quickly, and it can be hard to do anything in the time given for each level. There is certainly a lot of unplanned chaos, but to be fair, that's what a riot is like.
Am I disappointed? Yes. Is it the end of the world? No. Riot may improve over time, and to be fair it only cost me £8.99, so I won't be starving anytime soon. However, I can't fully recommend this game as it stands, early access or not. Try it for 90 minutes, and if you're unsure and you want a refund, ask for one.

Hand of Fate is a rogue-like-like.  It has randomly generated "dungeons" with random beneficial and detrimental events and effects that either help or hinder your progress.
The story mode:
- gives you a short, multi-level dungeon to defeat
- with the boss of the dungeon being the major goal.
- Can you find and defeat this boss before you die?
- If so, you win and are granted access to the next story mode level/dungeon/boss.
The endless mode:
- is very similar to the story mode, except for three main things:
- First, it never ends... there's no final dungeon floor with a boss on it, and you just keep going until you die.
- Second, you have no control over which cards are included in the deck - they all are, including the ones you hate.
- Third, every floor  grants some sort of curse or other detrimental effect that will usually follow you for the remainder of that run - better hope it's just 5 hp damage or something, which you can generally recover from quickly, and not some intense curse that affects food/gold acquisition.
As you succeed at card events, you will unlock additional cards, including new equipment, new card events, and new bonuses.  In this way, even though your blessings/curses/equipment/etc. don't carry from dungeon run to dungeon run, you do progress.  You are unlocking a deck, much like opening a booster pack in a trading card game.  It's a fun way to progress in a game that otherwise focuses on each single challenging run.
Is it worth buying?  I got it as part of a Humble Bundle, and honestly, I can see myself coming back to play this for years to come.  I don't like buying games at full price, but if I knew there'd never be a deal on this game, I'd probably buy it.  I see it as a must have for any fan of rogue-like-likes.
Oddly enough, it reminds me most of FTL (Faster Than Light), the rogue-like-like where you pilot a spaceship attempting to avoid and eventually defeat the evil fleet that wants you dead.  FTL is another exceptionally good game that deserves your attention if you enjoy rogue-like-likes.

Got this game during the Steam Winter Sale.
Metroidvania is a game genre that there aren't a large number of original, well-made and successful games in, not counting free or fan-made ones. While this game doesn't pull off the metroidvania feel perfectly, it does something else. Something that really speaks to me yet I can't put my finger on it. The pixel-art visuals were top notch with memorable locations and some pretty nice-looking backgrounds and well-animated characters, the soundtrack was beautiful to the point that I am still listening to it while I type this review and while the story wasn't the best around, it was certainly good enough for this kind of game.
The gameplay was interesting, combining the ability to fly around a 2D, open world with the mechanics of a twin-stick shooter. The controls took a little getting used to, but felt nice and smooth to handle afterwards.
Does the game feel like it should've taken 9 years to make? I don't think so. That said, I had only recently become aware of Owlboy's existence and a good game should be good because of its inherent quality, not because of the time it took to make, and I think this game has that inherent quality to it.
In short, I would whole-heartedly recommend this game. A genuine 9/10

I might be a huge fan of rogue-light games, like
, but I'm still surprised to see just how much I got into this one. It's such a weird blending of random generation, board game/card game elements, and brawling that it's hard to believe all that could've worked together in one game, but
surely showed me how it's done.
The theming with all of the narration and storytelling is fanstastic and well appriciated. It's actually surprising to see just how much of that was put into the DLCs too. It invokes that D&D style of love and care in storytelling that makes lonely nights of gaming more warm and inviting. As I said: Very much appriciated.
The fighting begins simple and innocent enough, but, after unlocking loads of card (An event that's quite enjoyable in of itself), you'll begin to realize just how much awareness and management you'll need to worry about as your adventures drag on; especially in Endless Mode. It's still not a hugely complex task in comparison to other brawler games, but it's usually a brief excursion that helps liven up the experiance of play. When you start to form a powerful character, it becomes all the more enjoyable watching 16+ hordes of enemies fall before you as you rake in the spoils of battle.
The free DLCs are a great welcome to the game and I'm still working to try and finish off the last couple of cards involved with them, but the paid DLC that offers a multitude of new characters to play as also adds in some new questlines to experiance. The fact that the character modifiers really do change up the experiance is good enough, but I really do appriciate their lasting contibution to the events deck in the end. Variety of play is something I really appriciate on some nights when I only have a couple of hours to play and, for the price of it all, it's more than fair enough from my standpoint.
The Story Mode really does ease you into the game as it begins to build upon itself, raising the states and difficulty until the final battle. You can fully customize most elements of the game during so too, which really helps when you want to fix things to your favor or work in some new cards to reap their tokens. Endless Mode starts off very simply but rapidly escalates into a really rough experiance and is great for experianced players wanting to test their skills (Works well for unlocking more cards too, in some cases). Story mode is fully replayable, which is great, and Endless Mode is my jam when I just want to dive into play. Everything I need for whatever mood I'm in.
Anything else to gush about? Hmm... I don't think so. This game's an easy recommendation from me, but I will advise against it for a couple of things:
1) There's a lot of RNG in the game that will work hard against you. Not all the time, but at some points. It sucks when you get screwed, but it doesn't wreck you completely; At least, most of the time.
2) This game just isn't for everyone. It's easy to see that from the general game in of itself, but it's just the truth. For anyone that's open to playing a variety of games to play,
is a fairly safe purchase, but not for those types of people that like to stick to their narrow pool of genres. If you're one of those types of people and still want to experiance something weird and new for yourself, I'd probably recommend something else to you.
Want a number rating? I'd say an 8/10; at the very least, a 7/10. It's not your GotY, but there's a lot to enjoy from this game and, if you can get it and the DLC all for under $10.00, then you'll be getting great value from it all.

SHORT REVIEW:
The developers have no idea how to make a videogame.
LONG REVIEW:
I have no idea where to begin on how bad this game is. As a fan of mindless shooter, I can't fathom how flawed the game is in its core.
The character's movement does not feel the player is in control entirely to compensate the chaotic situations that the game constantly puts the player in, as sprinting and jumping are not very fluid. You cannot jump freely while sprinting, you lose a bit of handling while at it, and sprinting lasts for a very short period of time.
All of the enemies (and I mean all of them), have faster movement speed, usually 2 to 3 times faster than the character so the player is forced to be constantly moving with the game's awful controls.
The game seriously lacks variety of enemy types, but it also suffers from their flawed designs. Enemies should be very exciting to fight, but they are incredibly annoying to deal with.
There are self-destructive bots that move in an incredible speed whose explosion radius is massive, shockwave emitting crawlers which lock on you (for the most of the time you cannot avoid them easily) when charging at an accelerated speed, ranged gunners whose projectiles travel as fast as bullets, fast-moving rollers who charge at you to saw your limbs off, and other varieties of the said enemy types.
What's worse is that the game tends to put all of these annoying enemies in a single wave at once in which the player has to rely on variety of lucks or stupid AIs doing funky things to beat.
The game features about 3 different enemy types with different armor levels and different weapons on them. Some of these types have no weaknesses on how to kill them without almost dying. The game still gives you enough regen after a wave to restore back to perfect health, but it is no excuse to design a game where the player is meant to be hurt to almost death situations after every wave. This is the most frustrating part of the game. I died the average of 3 times per chapter, and  after those deaths I didn’t bother changing a strategy and was still able to beat the level I had trouble with, because the enemy AIs were so unpredictable and had no counter-strategy to work with. It was all just luck for the most part. Explosion radius is bigger than the usual player’s predictions in the game’s FOV (and the game basically feeds on explosions), most of projectiles are semi-homing and they also explode dealing damage to the player around even though it misses, small enemies charge at you while you are dealing with bigger enemies and vice versa, and most of them don’t have any counter-strategies to work with. One of my favorite mindless shooter is the Serious Sam series, and the game had enemies that were simply very fun to play against, so I can tell you that mindless shooter does not mean mindless design.
The level design is nothing of stellar, and sometimes makes no sense at all. The game has a hint system telling the player what to do, only when they reach a point. Here's why the hint system is completely useless:
There are points that emit green lights where the player has to go and interact with to advance in the level and it's ALWAYS just as simple as clicking on the button when they reach the point. However, the developers think the players lack brain so it tells them to “click on the button to ... (insert any unnecessary information)”. The problem is that the levels aren’t designed well enough to sometimes let player know where to go in the dark environment, and the game does nothing to assist the player with. It tells the player to click on the button once they reach the only green-lit interactive interfaces which is completely useless. Later in the game, the levels have so many map decorations that are lit green with interfaces that cannot be interacted with. The players are accustomed to click on whatever that has an interface screen and green-lit, and the final levels of the game break this one rule that they’ve been training their players with. Often there will be times where it damages the player for absolutely no reason with some pre-scripted moving objects. There is no way to avoid them, and the game gives you a regen shortly after. The game is the definition of frustration. There were so many flawed designs with no sense of innovation being found from the game, so I had to look up who in the world developed this terrible game. I will make sure to avoid any games from them in the future and so should anyone who wants to have fun with videogames.

DreadOut is a third-person Puzzle/Survival Horror game by Digital Happiness. In it you take on the role of Indonesian teenager Linda, who was on a school trip when not-so-suddenly her group becomes trapped in an old, creepy, abandoned town.
Sounds familiar? Surely it’s the starting point of many a game, but the kind of horror
brings out is one of my favorites. You see, here you’re not hiding from invincible monsters, you’re not running away, and you’re not (really) fighting the ghosts (technically speaking). If you’ve ever played Fatal Frame, you’ll be quite familiar with the play style and ambiance of DreadOut, for Linda is armed only with a camera, and that is all she has to fight off the apparitions and, yes, solve puzzles.
DreadOut is comprised of three different acts (0, 1 and 2), each a bit different than the previous one - act 0 serving as a sort of glimpse as to what to expect, Act 1 setting the pacing, and Act 2 completely changing the pacing you’d gotten used to; all acts follow the same storyline; and while in essence the story might not be out of this world in originality (despite the twists and turns taken and the stories within stories), and while the ghost design might not be anything too different (even if they’re unique to Indonesian lore), the game gets plenty of cookie points for being in a different setting and full of ghost (and thus, cultural) lore.
Controls in the game are fairly simple: You run (stamina dictates you need a break every so often), you walk, you interact with doors and objects, pick items up, and use your phone’s camera to snap photos, solve puzzles, and defeat ghosts. And also to illuminate really dark areas, too. Linda has a ‘sense’ which helps her find all these things, when a blue vignette appears you’re near a puzzle, item or secret, while if it’s red, it means there’s an enemy near.
Although the graphics and textures are a tad dated and will not give an AAA game a run for its money, they’re still fairly decent, and the characters are attractive enough to look at that you won’t be put off by their faces every time they turn around. Despite this, the general ambiance is quite good, and succeeds in making you forget that it’s a game and giving you that creepy feeling every survival-horror abandoned town and building should have. The voice overs are pretty good too, something I was pleasantly surprised with. The music is really good - it’s not always creepy, but it’s still good, and in the parts where it is creepy, it succeeds at it. The game also makes use of silence and sound bites to make you on edge, like playing soft, creepy laughter or crying when you least expect it, managing to create something that truly has you on the edge of your seat.
This is the kind of horror I like, the type that’s more psychological and situational than just jump scares and loud noises, and while DreadOut does have a few jump scares, they’re not quite as obnoxious as the ones utilized in most horror games.
If you’ve never played Fatal frame before, this is how the “fighting” aspect works: All “fighting” is done through the camera. You point it at the evil spirit and snap a few shots, which damages it, and it eventually disappears (unless it’s invincible… then it’ll just leave you alone for a little while). DreadOut has added to this where you don’t just have to snap, but some of the tougher spirits actually have specific weak spots for you to find. I do love this style of gameplay, but I found the ghosts to be a little less scary than the ambiance of the place, and a bit more annoying. It seemed like it took too many shots just to get rid of one simple ghost, so once the initial scare wore off, defeating them was more of a chore. The slightly cramped spaces also made for tricky fights sometimes, becoming particularly annoying during boss fights, making it hard to find their weak spots. At least in Fatal frame when they rushed at you, you had a last-chance shot that made more damage than the others, and a bit more time to run around and find a comfortable spot to snap from. Not so much in DreadOut, where there’s no last-chance shot and less space to run around before the ghost charges at you again. This might work for a more hardcore gamer, for me it didn’t work quite so well.
I feel like the potential in these type of camera-only games isn’t on the fights themselves, and thus they should be easy enough the get past without infuriating you, which doesn’t mean they can’t require some kind of tactics. This, more than anything, is what made it less enjoyable for me than I had anticipated.
I will say, however, that every fight was different from the last, so the originality put on it was really nice to see. When you die in DreadOut you don’t fail. It’s not game over and start over… when you die you enter “limbo”; a dark area with a light ahead of you. You run towards the light, and start back at the spot you were at. Usually with the ghost right besides you, and barely enough time to get your bearings between the animation and lifting the camera before it charges. This is both a cool concept and kind of annoying, as every time you die the length you have to run to reach the light is longer. You can make the length you have to run fixed in settings, though, which I took advantage of.
The puzzles are rather difficult. Sometimes it takes a lot of random snapping of photos and pondering to figure out what to do… which is actually rather good, except when there’s ghosts around making you nervous. Sometimes they were a little too puzzling though, where I would find the blue vignette and walk around and snap shots at everything in the hopes something would yield a result, and couldn’t find what it wanted me to do at all.
If there was one big thing I didn’t like about this game, I would have to say it was the lack of a save-when-you-want feature. The game auto-saves at several parts and does so as well when you exit, which is wonderful and useful for the average gamer, but -and while I appreciate such things- I would also have liked to save at a point I decide without having to leave my game to do so. I also found the save on exit not working all the time, as twice I had to re-do a (short, but still annoying) section when I went back to my game.
There were a few minor bugs through my playthrough; the game would sometimes lag a bit (at random times, not because it was particularly loading anything) and the camera would sometimes “snap” back at a weird angle (I feel it might have been because of the lag, but it seemed like it did it at random times too), but none of them were game-breaking bugs.
And speaking of loading, the loading times could certainly be improved on, as they get a bit too long.
The game has a few items to collect through your play and several documents (besides every ghost encounter filling your ghost lore book with interesting tidbits and stories), as well as some easter eggs; you can also unlock some outfits to wear during replays. There’s also two endings to this hidden gem, which was quite nice.
All things considered, you can tell that despite the dated graphics, the developers have put a lot of thought and care into the game, and you really have to appreciate that. I think this is a solid horror game that does the horror part very good, but falls just a little bit short at the gameplay aspect - at least for my personal taste.
Overall I’d highly recommend it, particularly if you’re a fan of Fatal Frame or similar styled games, or if you like horror games but are tired of jump scares.

This is a thing of underappreciated beauty right here. Thinking of this game harkens back to an era of singleplayer adventures that I greatly miss and wish that there was more of being produced as of late.  I'm glad Metro: Exodus is in the making, but this will always have a place in my heart.
Pros:
-Great, straightforward story.
-The characters are all well built with clear cut motives, depth, and complexity with the exception of the main villain, who is your usual case of villanous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
-I enjoy the combat very much and the stealth even more.  The stealth does significantly ramp up between Spartan and Survivor modes, the latter setting enemies on a hair trigger if you aren't too careful.
-The world the devs crafted here is very believeable, at least in how it's presented in this Disneyland ride sort of orientation.
-Dealing with hostile humans and dealing with mutants are very distinct in their approach.
-Presents a very nice challenge in resource management, but chances are you'll be able to work things out of you scrap all the corners of the level.
-Stealth mechanics work similarly to something like Splinter Cell, though the mechanics can be a bit pressuring given the level linearity.
-The system requirements might seem intimidating, but it's not all that bad, really.
-The DLC on the side is alright, but it's just sorta... meh.
-Great soundtrack.
-You'll finish this game a better person.
-The enemies are generally well coordinated once you tip them off.
Cons:
-The enemies are generally well coordinated once you tip them off.  Setting one off and not taking him down fast enough, they will alert everyone else within a fifty meter radius, and in some cases spawn additional enemies to make matters worse.
-Artyom sure knows when to can it.  Doesn't really speak outside of the loading screens for each level.
-The levels are hella linear, meaning when you're stealthing through an area, there are only a handful of routes you can go without setting off the alarm, and you'll quickly learn where all the secrets are if you aren't too worried about your air supply on the surface.
-More often than not, you'll probably be reloading each scenario with human enemies the moment you are caught, because they'll quickly tear you apart if you're left in the open.
-According to the teachings of Jesus, it is as easy for a rich man to enter heaven as it is for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle.  Not saying I'm religious or anything, but it's to say that getting the good ending is really hard, like follow a Steam guide step-by-step hard.  You'll basically need to go huntng for every last "good" point possible within the game and avoid doing anything that will nullify those good points or earning bad points altogether if you want to get the good ending.  At least the good ending does pay off though.
