I loved this game to death, and I felt like giving it a small review after seeing it in my library again, so this is by no means an instant like or dislike.
Roughly, I'd say if you enjoy turn based tactics game to any extent you're likely to enjoy this given you look a bit at the preview images and video. It's very much an open book from the screen shots alone. Action-points-esque movement will always have a soft spot in my book as well as intercept fire, even if it can be annoying some of the time. Wow, this is an absolutely *epic* masterpiece that is simply one of the best games on Steam. This is honestly not just a must-play for strategy and JRPG fans, but everyone with a Steam account. I'd like to give a few of the reasons why this game is so great, and I'll close with a couple of slight nitpicks that are good to be aware of before you start to play. Overall, just buy this game!
+ The tactical strategy/action battle system is really unique. The game is turn based, but you get to manually control your individual units, so you can place them behind cover, duck down into tall grass, get into position, fire, and then scramble back behind a rock or friendly tank. You’ll be able to command your units’ actions at a very detailed level. It's really satisfying to play a turn-based strategy game where you have so much control over your troops.
+ The level of mission variety is incredibly impressive. It's never just about killing all the enemy troops or seizing the enemy camp. You'll sneak through enemy lines with a wounded comrade, slow the advance of a monstrous tank, storm a castle, fight in the trenches, etc. Every mission is different and you always need to stay on your toes.
+ Beautiful and unique art style. It looks like a storybook in motion, the character designs are instantly iconic, and your entire company of troops has tons of personality.
+ The story is fantastic. It’s quite thoughtful about war, death, camaraderie, and racism. It was really interesting to find that Welkin isn’t the typical anime hero who complains and whines about battle and fighting until he is forced to change his mind. He’s a scientist and a student, but he knows the stakes and he’s committed to the fight from the very start. The art style may seem very “anime”, but the storytelling doesn’t really have any of the “Shinji no baka!” and “Kyaa!” type of stuff that you may be dreading. There are a few brief apperances from a kind of mascot animal and, admittedly, a scene at the beach, but all that is handled with relative taste. Overall, if you like anime/manga war stories like the original Gundam, Gundam 8th MS Team, Macross, or Legend of the Galactic Heroes, this will be right up your alley.
+ So much content. The game is long, challenging, and packed with story and things to do. In addition to the main missions, you get skirmish missions to train your troops, and you can unlock extra story chapters, some of which will give you new missions to play. You also automatically get the two DLC missions, which are great. There's a lot here to keep you busy!
+ You can play the entire game in either the really good English dub or with the original Japanese voices.
= In order to get the best rank in each mission, the game wants you to complete the mission in a certain number of turns, which usually means that you need to play in a very particular way. I didn't really mind...it depends on how much you care about getting S ranks on everything. It's also true that, if you don't care about your rank, you're pretty much open to play each mission however you want, and you can win in all sorts of ways and with many different deployment options. This will mostly come down to how you like to play.
- The RNG can sometimes be a little funky. It’s frustrating to miss a practically point-blank shot with your lance or tank cannon. This gets better as your units level up, but there will be a few annoying "how did I miss that shot?" moments.
- The subtitles for the Japanese language mode are actually "dubtitles"...you're given a transcription of the English dub line, which isn't always exactly what the Japanese-voiced character is saying.

The game, as you've likely already read, is about a young girl having to fight to keep the bank from repossessing her family's shop. In this fantasy land there are three people, adventurers, town folk, and you. You try to manipulate the other two to gain.
Essentially Recettear is two games in one.
The first is entirely about money management, buying and selling, shop upkeep and knowing how to manipulate people best. Think of it as Anime Shop Tycoon the game! Admittedly a lot of frustrating and funny things can happen in this part of the game. At first, with no idea of what people are willing to spend you will mess up.. a lot. I advise keeping a piece of scrap paper close to keep tabs on how much a person is willing to spend total and what percentage of under and over charge you can get away with. You are most rewarded for finding these sweet spots by getting more experience points and thus leveling up and enabling more options for your shop. As previously mentioned some funny things can happen. One time a gentleman walked in trying to sell me a candy under the premise that his great grandmother gave it to him to sell if he should fall on hard times. The candy is worth 300, and so practically worthless. If you haven't caught on the humor comes from the interactions of why people want to buy and sell things. Definitely laughed a few times. Ultimately it can get repetitive and frustrating. You're success or failure largely surrounds an announcement system which tells you updates in trending items, decreased prices and highly demanded items where you can make 300% profits on. The final payment will rely on luck. Another entirely luck based interaction is adventurer items. Adventurers have really bad gear. They ONLY way to permanently give them items is for them to BUY them from you. It doesn't help that EVERY TIME you put out the really expensive armor/weapon/etc for an adventurer to buy some average Joe picks one up for his grandma, wife, or kid to play with. And that item you placed out was also a very hard one to craft, or is on a timer to buy from the store in limited number (once every few days). Yeah.
The second game is a dungeon dive rogue-like hack and slash. Here the adventurer fights, gains levels, and collects treasure. The game developers pulled a Final Fantasy and have a very finite amount of monster models and many, many re-skins. This means that once you have a strategy for a monster you can take on all future monsters of that type. The dungeons also sport a boss after a handful of floors. Boss fights are all variations of the same thing and tend to be very easy and not terribly rewarding. So, speaking of rewards, the monster (and bosses) all have a chance to drop items. These items follow a theme based on monster type and chests can drop anything. This is where the frustrations begin. Toward the beginning you'll dungeon crawl to get items to sell. Later on you'll only do it to find ingredients for crafting recipes.  This is a hit or miss process entirely based on luck. More times than not you'll find yourself grinding the same monsters for a drop and wasting precious time since drops are seemingly rare. There are boss only drops and are even harder to farm because to kill a boss again you need to enter a dungeon again. And did I mention you only get 20 items to carry? Yeah, 20 the WHOLE game. No way to increase. If you bring better weapons or items for the adventurer to use their old crappy items reduce those 20 slots as well. You will constantly find yourself stopping to drop a previously useful item for another, better item. This part is as grindy as a rogue-like can be.
The quick TL:DR-
Recettear is cute, fun, addicting, and very much enjoyable. It is dated, and it's limitations are apparent, but it has a surprising amount of replay value. I find myself loading it up once a year or so just because/10

The first thing you'll notice is that its one of those pay-to-progress sorta games. You can still progress in the game without spending a single dime however Patrons will definitely have the upper hand in earning gold to get high tier gear. To get yourself off the ground you'll need to spend $3 USD for an Auction House permit that works across all characters, but that is the extent of how little you could pay to get an upper hand in the game. Not necessarily a 'pay to win' unless you're interested in PvP. Majority of the pay items are skins, housing (you need to be a patron to own a house/land), and upgrading gear, most of which can be bought from the open market Auction House with a permit and tons of in game gold. As far as storyline goes, each race has a different storyline and perk, with the Harani and Firran allied against the Nuians. The game is fairly open world, with dozens of areas and continents to explore, each quest guiding you along a path through them. However, this game utilizes open world to also support open PvP. Unless you are in Alliance Neutral towns, Mirage Aisle, or Peace time, players of the opposing faction can freely kill you. The upside is that you don't lose any EXP or drop any items like other games featuring open PvP. You still do get rogue players who kill allies to steal their trade packs, but the game offers a justice system that prevents such players from leading faction raids.

If you want a short, comedic take on the occult, with a great number of pop culture references, then this point-and-click is right for you. Though short, full of pixels, and not much else to say without spoiling it, it's a good way to kill an evening. While it reminded me of the Last Door, it certainly has a different mood. There's no creepy atmosphere and ambiance here, only several jokes, and plenty of style.
I hope to see more adventures from The Darkside Detective in the future.

I'm sorry, but, immediately from the getgo I can already see the amount of problems this game has.
I didn't even have to play for all that long to see, and I'm honestly not sure if the developers and whoever else tested this intentionally left things the way they are or if they legitimately thought the game was good to go.
Now hear me out, game rolls a fascinating theme, is unusual and new (in a good way), has charming graphics, neato music and good sound and all that, captures the whole riot atmosphere great, truly. The lil cutscenes are great.
But the controls, UI and well, gameplay of it is seriously questionable at best.
- Selecting units is atrocious and basic, it's as if the game was designed around how RTS's were built prior to the invention of a DRAG AND SELECT box, and since nummerical keys are used to select ITEMS and not UNITS your only way to select and manage units is to either hope that you click the right one ingame, or by selecting their respective unit icon far off to the right.
Oftentimes you can't even tell which unit you have selected either.
Icon tells you have an assault unit selected.
Cool, which one, and where?
- For a riot simulator, it does a pretty poor job at simulating riot police holding a line formation.
Both sides devolve into a brittish pub brawl, or hooligan moshpit, every time.
- Units (or at least riot police) often behave super erratically, and start running or displacing in strange ways, even if everything is fine.
It happens more often with large units, but it's not unusual to see balistic units behave oddly, and even get stuck on lamposts and stuff.
Oftentimes units are also completely unresponsive, completely at random.
Fire smoke launcher? No. Yes. Sometimes. Who even knows?
- Is it INTENTIONAL to have everything unlocked by default?
Is this a BUG or a FEATURE? Because I'm evidently getting unlocks - for things I can already apparently use.
- What exactly DO all of the items even do? The game doesn't tell you anything whatsoever here, aside from the vague tooltip for usable items (ie a radio regroups, stimulants make you angery, stun grenade go boom, super), but what is the difference between all these batons and grenade launchers?
What does "gas mask 0-1-2" mean?
What is the difference between Light, Medium and Heavy defense and why would I pick anything lower than Heavy?
What is the deal with the BUDGET you have, if you can have infinite everything anyway?
What DOES a picture camera do? Why use smoke over stun? Pepperspray vs tear gas? etc
The heck do flags and junk do for rioters?
- Is there no Dicipline/Morale meter or indicator anywhere?
- The loadout for the entire faction you play RESETS every mission, why?
- Difficulty is utterly bizarre too.
Regardless of which difficulty level you play, levels are either absurdly easy, or impossibly hard.
Spikes are caused by extreme wonkiness in controls at critical moments, like the immediate start of a new riot, or unresponsive units with seemingly random behavior.
If the game did a better job at actually telling you what is going on, and let you control things in a more fluid manner, then this wouldn't even be a problem, but christ man, I swear you're fighting the controls more than you're fighting the riots themselves.

TLDR; pretty, frustrating, bland and inoffensive.
This is a game where every platformer trope has been taken wholesale and cobbled together in an inoffensive and cliched manner with the single exception that the main character can fly. There was never a question of "should we put boss fights in the game?", the question for Owlboy was "how many can we cram in there?". A boss fight has never been fun in a video game it wasn't fun doing the same fight 20 times in the 90s it's still not fun now.
Also: collect all the coins to unlock all of the upgrades? Hunting for coins behind secret walls is not a suitable replacement for content. I did not get all of the upgrades because the game was already frustrating, and the game was made all the more frustrating for not having the unlocks they provided.
The controls are frustrating at times, the dodge button cannot be pressed at the same time as aiming, leading to a lot of frustrating clusterf**ks with many trivial (and they are almost always trivial) enemies on screen and you having to devote your thumbs to either killing them, getting hit a lot in the process, or dodging their attacks. The inability to do both left the game feeling clumsy and poorly thought out.
Another bugbear with controls is that there is a dash button that makes travelling through the spacious game MUCH faster. So I played this game constantly mashing B just so I could get through it quicker. There's no excuse for this, it's just dumb game design.
There's also the matter of the few scenes where the game requires a lot of precision for platforming sections where your flying ability has been hampered. These sections would benefit greatly from having fine control and precise input, alas if you have a controller plugged into your computer at all you cannot use the keyboard because for some reason it disables the jump key. Bizarre.
There's also no fine control. So you are better off using the DPad rather than a joystick most of the time. If the joystick is a little left, it's the same as pushing it all the way to the left. Stupid.
The story is middling. Standard "bad guy wants to end the world because reasons" tropes abound. The characters are distinctly individual but I found very little reason to actually care about them.
The protagonist is mute because all protagonists are mute. Nothing new to see here apart from the bullying the main character gets for it.
At many points in the story I got very lost, owing mostly to previously completed level sections being explorable again without any warning that you've been there before. By the time I realised I had already explored that section days before (and forgotten because it all looks the same) it was another 10 minutes of mashing the dash button just to get back to where I started.
The art style is absolutely lovely and it's obvious a lot of man-hours went into it; if the devs had spent as much time on having a vision for their game and sticking to it rather than making concessions for every man and his dog then they might have created something really special.
As it is, I can't recommend Owlboy as anything other than a very pretty, thoroughly samey platformer that will appeal to no-one and offend no-one.

The games broken up by times of day and you're able to visit a choice characters in each time slot.  Helpfully, when you're picking which character to spend the time with, it gives an indication of possible suspicion and votes that can be gained, if any, for the encounter.  The social game is just a matter of gaining votes if you so wish to win The Game, and avoiding suspicion, which can be removed at night if you submit to The Beauty.

What's neat about it is the interaction system, where instead of just always having static text boxes, they sort of flow in and out, not often or jarringly but enough to be interesting and keep you on your toes.  So you can wait to see if choices unlock, or perhaps you already passed up your best option for what you're going for.  Also text boxes are coloured (I believe by 'type' of choice. This might be the most anime game I've ever played.  The Nonary Game is pretty anime...but I don't know this was pretty ridiculous.  I'm pretty sure the plot was supposed to be a commentary on how absurd anime plot lines can be.  At least I'm going to believe that, because if it wasn't meant as a satire...then I'm not to happy with the plot.  The framing device for the plot is just so over the top and absurd.
Your "evil" twin brother makes a deal with you that if you crossdress as him and join his classmates on basically a highschool graduation cruise he will attend your summer school classes after you flunked out of highschool and give you back a motorcycle your father took from you.  That was weird enough.  But, to find out
I also find it hard to believe, and very animey, that this insanely wealthy person hid the fact he has a daughter from the world because he hates her so much.
Despite that very weird and perhaps terrible framing for the story, I did enjoy it quite a bit.  The game really only has two romance options and I felt both were handeled excessively well.  I also just liked talking to people on the ship.  I got the feeling the game felt I was playing wrong though.  As i really just wanted to talk to people and not have sex with everyone.  A lot of the poeple seemed like they were kind of massive jerks or sociopaths...so I didn't really have a desire to attempt to sex them up.  I spent the bulk of the game just hanging out with my cousin.  I liked it quite a bit, I felt they were a fun character.  All the characters were all well developed, it's just I didn't like them so I didn't want to have sex with them.  I also greatly appreciated the soundtrack.  That jazz score was so great.  I'd feel better about paying full price for the game if the soundtrack was included as opposed to it being additional money as dlc.
The one thing I will fault the game for is that basically you are simply choosing who you want to hang out with on the ship.  You don't have enough days/hours to hang out with everyone so you have to pick who you want.  These choices are binary/linear.  Picking some people over others has no impact on the other choices.  It's already scripted out, each character has 5-6 scenes and they play out in order.  Which creates story problems later.  In one example the Beauty showed up in one scene and it was heavily treated like I had sex with her, even though I didn't yet.  In another example even though I was having sex with the nerdy girl the game treated it as if I wasn't.  Also, except for Beauty and the nerdy girl it felt like things I told people in one scene didn't really carry over to other scenes.  If I was super nice to people prior they didn't seem to care in the next scene.  I would have liked my decisions to have more impact on the other people.
I still felt the writing was very well done.  Unlike, most anime the romances here actually felt like real relationships.  I would like to see what this developer could do with a lot more money and a bigger team.  I noticed quite a few inaccuracies with character design from scene to scene (such as a character would say they look one way or be wearing something and the picture would clearly show the exact opposite). I enjoyed the over all interactions with the characters so much though that I would still recommend the game.  But, due to those weird bugs/inconsistances and the choices not having much an affect outside the main relationships I would not suggest paying full price for this game unless you just want to support the dev.  #worth $10

The title Crusader Kings 2 falls under the so-called grand-strategy games. The term is well-earned in this case and before you start the game be warned that there is a steep learning curve. Do not pick up this game if long-winded games that requires hours of hours to finish is not your thing. Do pick it up if you like games like Civilization, Alpha Centauri, or Europe Universalis. Having said that, and perhaps you do not know these titles, lets get into what Crusader Kings 2 actually is.
Like all grand-strategy games Crusader Kings 2 is (but need not be, I will get back to this) for instance about creating a dukedom, kingdom, or empire, keeping those under you happy less they revolt, and creating a proper army. Unlike many other grand strategy games (outside of other Paradox titles) this game is actually historically correct for medieval europe, the middle east, and India. That is right, did you ever want to play as William the Conquerer? This game gives you that opportunity.
That immediatly leads to 'need not be' clasule I said before. Unlike other grand strategy games you do not play a 'faction' or a 'nation', but you play as an individuel e.g. Ghengis Khan. The game doesn't end when you die, however, no it follows the rise (and fall) of your family as your dominion grows on the map. Depending on your succesion laws you might be playing as your oldest, youngest, or even a random family member. You might even go super modern and have daughters rule on purpose, not 'just because' the male line ended as was more the case in the time period between 769-1452 AD (which how long the games played out assuming you have two DLCs).
The game features cultures (e.g. German, Anglo-Saxon, Berber, Russian, Visigothic, and Tamil) as well as religions (e.g. Hindu, Catholic, Coptic, Karasite, Tengri, Sunni, and Germanic) and this including with recently conquered, traits of a person, your history with them perhaps, can all influence what people think of you. Wil you marry out a daughter for an alliance, or perhaps with that genius of a man so you can get him to court and get a good advisor? This is all dependent upon you.
Thanks to all these features, as well as the fact that once the game starts randomness kicks in and the historical accurate timeline is lost, means that you will never(!) play the same game ever again. Mechanics wise yes, but give it enough time and the map will look quiet different from last time, different kings and emperors, and perhaps e.g. the Byzantine empire might have fallen by 1100. What will you do? How will you influence medieval Europe? I say it is time to find out and play Crusader Kings 2 for yourself.

Play as a dynasty leading one of a great host of states from Ireland to India (DLC is needed for several groups, but even the most basic set of characters is a huge amount of replayability), and see your people rise and fall based on an enormous amount of factors - your skill, that dastardly hand of fate, the insignificant details and allies you forgot about, and the Mongols.
The game takes a bit of time to learn, but not as much as many grand strategy games - and as with most Paradox games there are both easy and hard places to start.   Gameplay is exceptionally variable, with events constantly coming up to haunt you (I married my least important son to a countess in Italy for a minor alliance... a decade later and he's my only heir, and she has corrupted him into a monsterous excommunicated idiot), and the future always uncertain*.  The events seem very intuitive and reactive, and every aspect of the game feels like it is impacted by your decisions (from the claims that people look to, to the balance of power of religions, to the genetics of your heirs - the game responds to your actions and gives you feedback: your family might even start naming children after your custom names).
If that doesn't interest you... there's still an extremely robust modding community with tons of alternate scenarios and events.
* If you get enough power, or are very good at playing certain aspects of the game, you can pretty much cruise through poor leaders (or make it very unlikely to get poor leaders).  Unless you're really good or really powerful (in which case, start over and challenge yourself with harder starts or trickier goals), though, your best plans and hard fought gains can evaporate overnight with rebellion, assassination, disease, and Mongols.  The game never gets into a boring plateau, because you are constantly rising and falling (or at least scheming to rise and scrambling to avoid falling).

I wanted to like this game.  I'm not sure exactly WHY I wanted to, but I gave it multiple chances, tried to see some of its flaws as charm and just all around did what I could with it.  Ultimately though, it just couldn't keep my attention.
Its positives are an interesting array of supernatural beasties drawing from Indonesian lore.  The game can be genuinely creepy at time.  It does a good job of capturing the horror feeling.
The flaws all lie in execution.  The graphics are largely a blurry, low resolution mess.  Linda's model is okay although the screen shots on the store page are carefully selected to make the game look its best.  In reality, the game looks like a product for the Playstation 2.  Your fellow classmates look laughable.  The game's pacing feels off and you spend too long just trotting around.  But the worst felt like the controls which often had me over steer or snagged me during fights.  Some battles require you to quickly move around and it just wasn't reacting well.  Compounding this was a death system where each time you die, you have to run back out from limbo, jogging along a blue strip of light.  Unfortunately, each time you die that strip grows longer and it's frustrating to not only feel like you died a cheap death but to now be expected to just jog for 90 seconds before you can play again.
Given better controls and a less punitive system for dying, I might have felt like completing this and been able to enjoy it for what it is.  But after my last jog back from the underworld, the game just felt like a waste of time.

Dreadout is an old school survival horror inspired by Indonesian ghost tales and lore: its roots and the original ghosts they spawned are the game's strong point and provide some interesting encounters that are sadly often blemished by clunky combat and a few annoying bugs.
-great soundtrack and sound design
-original and truly disturbing ghosts
-each ghost needs a different strategy to be beaten thus keeping you on edge
-unsettling, creepy atmosphere mantained through the whole game
-extra collectibles provide background to the story
-below average graphics even on High settings, textures are quite blurry
-wooden animations
-combat feels clunky due to the time it takes to bring the camera up and the slow first-person speed
-boss battles alternate between easy and frustrating
-little character depth
-a few situations can be confusing due to not following the usual rules or not being properly hinted at (e.g. having to use the flash at a certain location, having to actually die at a certain point etc)
-the whole story is never properly explained and, after the end, you're left wondering what exactly happened and why
-despite being a year old and several patches there's still quite a few annoying bugs and while they're not gamebreaking they sure are annoying. I experienced achievements not unlocking properly, camera hits not registering on enemies and a couple scenes not playing properly: all those were solved by a checkpoint reload but the fact they're still in the game shows poor programming
Despite my grievances with it Dreadout is still a pretty decent, if not good, game: the various ghosts are all pretty interesting and, while more unsettling than truly scary, work pretty nicely in keeping you under pressure. The atmosphere is pretty strong and will make you feel uneasy and threatened most of the time.
We never got Fatal Frame on PC so this can work as a poor man's substitute if the Cons list hasn't disheartened you too much: just wait for a 50% or more sale.

On top of that, the English translation is god awful. I've lost count of how many times I went "Wait... that's not what they said!" (I play with Japanese audio)
The combat is what I liked the most about the game.
I particularly like how they managed to make every single mission a unique tactical experience. When I first started the game, I had the fear that the combat may get repetitive soon like it did in Shining Blade, but that wasn't the case at all. Every mission had something different, and each fight felt unique. Each was reasonably challenging, and conquering each with tactics felt satisfying.
Mission design is very well done in this game... except for the repeatable skirmishes. those are like... ehhhhh
One thing don't like is how the mission ratings are based exclusively on the number of turns you take to clear it. If I take a more cautious approach, moving the whole team together and eliminating every threat i see, i'd most likely get a bad rating for taking too long. In most cases, the game encourages rushing tactics. While rushing does make sense in certain scenario, I don't like being forced into this playstyle for every single mission. It would've been better if the game can take other tactical aspect into consideration when giving out mission rating
Overall, I think this game is a flawed gem, but definitely worth a try. The controls on PC take a while to get used to, and the game's mechanisms may be confusing at first, but once you get past that, there's a lot of fun to be had.

The game is a Grand Strategy game which means you do not take control of battles, instead you are in control of the state, deciding its politics and making sure that you become a pre-eminent power in Europe. Now that doesn't sound that as unique as the other games paradox have made, but as well as a grand strategy this is an RPG.
First of all the RPG elements are not like Mass Effect or Skyrim, they are event based which means you decide how certain events go and see where it takes you. You can become a benevolent ruler who is just and kind, or you can become a intricate web weaver, assassinating rivals and killing siblings. You can even become insane or/and possessed!
Now there is A LOT of DLC for this game and that can put you off. But this has not been pulled from the game (well most of it hasn't), instead they have been developed after the main game came out and add a variety of RPG enhancements and events. They also enable you to play different religions and cultures. The DLCs i would recommend are:
Sword of Islam
Legacy of Rome
Old Gods
Sons of Abraham
Way of Life
Charlemagne
They are all the major expansions except for Raja's of India and Republics which i found were a bit lacking and can be left out without any major changes. All the other Dynasty shield packs and song packs are totally optional (although if you are going to buy one song pack buy the Old Gods one).
This game is worth full price and will give you hundreds of hours of game content and will give you an experience you
will never forget. Also if you are unsure then wait for a steam sale and get the game and the major expansions for an incredibly cheap price!

Ok. Well, let's see . . .
This game was okay. It wasn't bad, and it wasn't great. It was barely above mediocre. It had me wanting to know more about what specifically was going on.
The problems begin with the story. It starts off interestingly, but the problem starts with the very cliche writing style. An attempt in a noir-esque world with a protagonist that is your typical noir-esque detective.
The gameplay consists of trying to traverse a world with many areas blocked off because of ghost-like structures that you can't pass through and there are demons. Spoopy. As you progress, the demons get more difficult to get rid of, so it is generally easier to just find a way to avoid them when you get the opportunity.
If you can look past the glaring cliched story and the idiotic detective, you'll begin to have a little bit of fun. There are side stories and quests. The quests are other ghosts that are stuck in this world unable to pass on because of the typical unfinished business. To be honest, they're not worth attempting to explore.
Then there are objects in the side stories that you can find for a typical campfire scary story, and they're okay. I wouldn't really recommend trying to find all of them because it really takes you out of the main storyline and it is a lot of walking around the world aimlessly.
The other issue with the game is that you're not given a save feature. You're stuck with auto-save. And that's balls. Sometimes I just want to stop playing in the middle of an investigation, but then I have to start at the very beginning. Fortunately, the found objects are saved after you get them. You'll still have to start over, but you don't have to go back and find those pesky objects for your journal.
Back to the problem of the story, you will begin to understand halfway through the game what the motive is behind the killings. You aren't really given anything that your protagonist can't see, so it gets a bit frustrating when he still hasn't caught onto the motive. AND HE'S A ♥♥♥♥ING DETECTIVE. IT IS HIS JOB.
Still, I was surprised at who the true bad guy was. And that felt nice. It's hard to explain. I'd just be talking in circles trying to explain, and to be honest, that might just ruin your experience.
I had an idea, but I was only half right. Or maybe like 1/4 right. Things became interesting at the very end.
If you do plan on doing 100% completion, do not enter the final scene area because the only way to go back to the old areas is to make a new game.

The game has a unique weapons system which utilizes two different guns each having 5 weapon modes each, meaning that in escense you have 10 guns, a far cry from the 2 that you are usually permitted to carry.
The style of the game is dark sci-fi and pits you against robotic enemies or varying sizes, shapes and funcations. There's an interesting amount of different levels although visually there is very little to seperate them and this can make them a little difficult to navigate at times. The difficulty with navigation is that you can basically end up getting stuck for where to go and end up scratching your head for a long amount of time.
Other than a slight repetativeness to the level design and gameplay Hard Reset is still a fun game to play through, especially if you're an old school shooter fan with a lot of tolerance for faults.

So this is probably my most played single player game ever, and it's the one that I always go back to when I get really bored. Its main appeal is probably the ability to rewrite or attempt to recreate history. I have all of the big DLC's and some of the rinky dink ones. The only really bad one is Sunset Invasion (it's just dumb). I'm kind of a history buff, so that's probably why I keep going back to it. Obviously I really like the game, but I also see some issues.
Like most Paradox games, it's got a pretty steep learning curve, but this is definitely one of the more approachable Paradox titles. Very rarely do I find myself in a situation where I'm unable to strengthen my country even as a one province realm (okay, if you get invaded day one by your huge♥♥♥♥♥neighbor it's gonna be rough, but by-and-large...) unlike in EU and especially Victoria games.
Sometimes they mess things up on patches; I remember one time they changed some math to do with retinues but forgot to update numbers for Merchant Republics so for a while you could get a ridiculously large retinue army. Merchant Republics are still pretty OP for player characters, but that's another story.
One of my favorite features is that many historical characters have links to their wikipedia articles (e.g. Charlemagne, but also most king level characters and above in starting scenarios, and the more notable dukes and counts).
Obviously the revenue format kinda sucks, but it's just the way of the world now, I guess. Sometimes I feel like Paradox should be a bit more rewarding to folks who buy DLCs piecemeal (there were times during sales where I could have bought the entire game with all DLCs for less than the remaining DLCs would cost during the same sale, but I guess they still got me to buy them, so, whatever).
I have some legitimate gameplay criticisms, but I can't remember any specific ones right now. I will probably update this later when I remember them (if that can be done). Overall Paradox has done a pretty good job improving and balancing the game with updates (for free).

This is a nice game with an interesting plot at its base, your father ran off with a debt and now the debt collectors come to you to collect the debt off. Since you are basically a teen girl and the one visiting is a pretty understanding fairy, they give you the option to work to pay off that debt by opening an item shop.
First let's talk about the gameplay, the controls feel nice, even though they're not the most desirable combination, and interacting with the game elements feels easy and refreshing to do. There are 2 key factors to the game which are: getting items followed of course by selling them to the customers that come into your shop.
Let's focus on the first element: getting the items to sell. Reccetear is pretty inventive here, offering you the possibility to not only buy the items off the market, but also from customers, at a lower price, craft certains items and last but not least, the most intriguing part, sending adventurers off into dungeons to gather said items. The last one is intriguing because you also get to play as that adventurer and decide which items to take or not while fightingthose pesky monster in some nice action combat.
Now as for selling the actual stuff, you get to decide the price for which the item will sell when the customer asks for it in your shop. So, basically, you can oversell most items to customers, mostly depending on who they are and how much they are willing to pay, all within a limit of course (most people won't buy products that are >125% of their price, though the game says 130%, but that's pushing it too far).
*Also, since you got a debt to pay off the game will take more money off you week after week until you pay the debt off, through some necessary plot conviniences.
*The dungeons also are randomly generated everytime you go into one of them which makes it harder to complete them but not that much, and feels like a forced element, since you won't be repeating most of them anyways.
I would try not to talk too much about characters, as they feel very generic and don't seem to have that much thought put into them, basically the foolish main character, which is a girl, the motherly figure and so on. The story on the other hand feels somewhat original (as original as any story can be nowadays) but there's literally no character development, as in everyone ends up remaining exactly the same, whilst also there seem to be lots of plot holes.
The music and atmosphere feel nice, though they tend to get repetitive quite quickly.
Last of all the voice acting is horiffic, there's literally random characters saying a couple of words in japanese every now and again, but I'd rather they either made the whole game voice acted or don't put it at all, seems more annoying then helping when you're reading some text in english and some random character starts saying stuff in japanese (mostly for people who don't understand japanese, I suppose). I didn't find it that annoying initially as I understood what the characters where saying, but it soon become so bad that I wanted to effectively mute the game.
Pluses:
-fluid controls
-great action combat
-well designed item management
Minuses:
-repetitive music
-incomplete/bad voice acting
-poorly designed characters
All in all this is a nice idea done more or less right, and I'd recommend people trying it if you're a fan of rpgs and/or management games in general.
Final rating: 8

This gem by Square Enix combines a captivating story with fine gameplay and immersive graphics and achieves a unique balance between adventure and 3rd person action. The plot revolves around a series of mysterious murders in modern-day Salem, but goes far deeper than that, resulting in a mystery thriller with dominating metaphysical elements and strong psychological tensions.
You play as Ronan O'Connor, an ex-criminal who became a detective and got violently murdered while on duty. As it turns out, he has some unfinished business to resolve so he is trapped between this life and the afterlife until he takes care of those issues. Certain that this has to do with finding his killer, he starts investigating the case as a ghost, aided by a young girl, Joy, who is a medium and thus can see him and communicate with spirits. As he delves deeper into the case though, he discovers that his connection to it is more complicated and darker, and same goes for someone else he is closely related to.
Although the game is basically adventure, the general setup of the gameplay is very similar to the action genre; there are also a few enemies that you can avoid, or be brave and attack them for some spice of action. The characters are well built, with enough background to back them up and make you interested in their personal stories as well as their connections to the main plotline. Ronan is a great character, with impressive and, at times, enjoying ghostly abilities: he can walk through walls, teleport, possess people and hear their inner thoughts and influence them, discuss with other ghosts, possess cats and thus go to places he otherwise wouldn't have been able to, exterminate demons and make certain surfaces appear or disappear.
Aside from the main story, there are a few optional side-quests - simple mystery cases that Ronan is called to solve, being the detective that he is (old habits never die). There are also hidden ghost stories from the past of the town, which reveal once you find certain items related to them. And of course several files spread throughout the town that shed more light to the case and the characters involved.
As the game takes place at night, the atmosphere is dark and compelling, matching perfectly the general ghostly feel that the story creates, aided by several obvious or not so obvious details. There are interior and exterior settings (an apartment building, a cemetery, a church, a museum, an abandoned mansion, a mental institute and of course the haunted streets of the town), all made with great detail and several visual effects that add to it. Interestingly enough, the scenario of the game is referencing historical events and people that existed for real, making the whole story even more interesting, while the ending builds up in an incredible sequence of twists that will surely blow your mind.

So what is ArcheAge? A great idea executed poorly. The amount of hype for this game was immense, and when it finally dropped, well... People were angry. I was one of the people who paid $150 for the Archeum Founder's Pack, and I wish I hadn't. I have never regretted such a large purchase more than this one.
But why? Why is it so disappointing? It's advertised as the sandbox game everyone was waiting for!
Well, I'll tell you. And I'll tell you the few things it did right. Just to be generous.
Pros:
-Looks decent.
-Deep crafting system, but has drawbacks.
-You can level off of your professions. During my few month return, I went from 30-55 entirely by gathering and crafting.
-Large open world map.
-Decent character creation.
-You build your own class, but very few are actually viable.
Cons:
-Toxic community. Very toxic.
-Pay to do anything.
-The economy is messed.
-Crappy endgame. I would have quit again earlier if I didn't roleplay.
-A poorly executed player court system. Your crimes play no part in whether or not you are jailed.
-The ocean is very empty.
-There is a heavy focus on PvP, but only a few builds are viable, and credit card warriors always come out on top. There is no point in trying to enter the PvP scene now.
-Good luck trying to get land. The amount of space is very limited, and the houses are too cramped together. It doesn't look or feel natural. Claiming land is also a Patron account feature.
-Labor points.
Now let's analyze these cons. The community in this game is horrid. Actually, let me tell you a story about this.
I am a very good land grabber in this game. I have never failed to claim a piece of land the second it goes up for demolition, and the crowd that gathers for land is immense. One time, a player was attempting to grab a piece of land as well. And since it is such a desperate struggle for land, it turns every player into a savage. This person told the same lie again and again, saying that it was their family member's piece of land and that I should let them have it instead, and constantly harassed me after the fact. I saw this person saying the same thing multiple times during the same day, and was labeled by them as "a part of the♥♥♥♥♥♥AA community" and told that I was on their guilds "KoS list". Very immature. Land grabs are fair game for anyone. If you can't log in, pre pay your taxes. Log in for your family member. This is the most toxic way to go about such a thing. /rantover
The endgame is just bad. There are only a few dungeons to run, and most players just do PvP. But then, what is the point to that either? Not much. Sure, your guild can own castles and such if you succeed in guild wars, but then you are most likely trashed by the community for winning. People hate people in this game. You will be killed for no reason time and time again. Actually, I have another story about this too.
It was around the time when the game first came out. I was enjoying it, believe it or not, but this may have played a part in my decreasing enjoyment of it. I was just a lowly level 40 or so minding my own business, hauling four trade packs along a route. I was in a PvP zone, and naturally, a player came across my nervous self and attempted to kill me. He was around level 47 or so, and I took him down on my own. I was very happy, but that wasn't the end. I crossed a bridge and started driving along a path, content with my skill and effective use of an uncommon build. But what I wasn't aware of, was an entire guild lying in ambush just behind said hill. When they tried to jump me, I drove back to a nearby spawn statue where I would be safe and meant to wait them out.
I sat there for three hours. Three hours until they decided to "leave". Little did I know, was that they were waiting behind the hill... Again. They killed me this time and stole my trade packs, leaving me with hours of my life I will never get back, and very little sleep that night due to being stalled by that band of barbarians. This is, by far, my worst experience in gaming. Ever.
The last thing I want to talk about is labor points. They are the main reason this game is terrible. At first, it doesn't seem like such a bad system. It keeps the economy in check and prevents players from progressing significantly faster than others, right? Nope. None of that. The economy is already screwed over by APEX, an item that players purchase for real money and sell to players for gold. Labor points are required for almost every task in this game. Even as a patron player, they regenerate too slowly. When you run out, you ask yourself "Why am I playing?" and log off, even as a roleplayer. It wouldn't be so bad if it were just for crafting and gathering, but stuff like;
-Unwrapping items you've crafted.
-Unwrapping coin purses dropped by enemies (the only source of income you would make from killing enemies).
-Planting seeds outside of farm plots.
-Reporting bots. There are a lot of them.
-Paying your taxes.
-Dismantling equipment.
-Receiving mail.
-Harvesting crops on your farm.
-Turning in a trade package that you already spent labor to make.
-Breathing (In a future patch I'm sure).
Yeah, the labor system is messed guys. So is everything else. I've said all I can, really. Just do yourself a favor and don't get yourself wrapped up in this game. You might actually care about it like I did.
GG Trion and XL Games. You ruined a potentially good MMO that many people waited for for years. I hope you're happy.

A pixel art game that has hundreds of characters on screen at a time is just beautiful! The cutscene animations are just awesome. Yeah there's no tutorial, but it's not hard to figure out. The wiki tab in main menu has all the information you need on gameplay mechanics and use of items and all that. They start you off on "too easy" difficulty, which is exaclty that, too easy. Switch it to challenging and you'll be like, "Holy Sheep♥♥♥♥♥♥ These cops don't give an Eff bout Nothin'!" So lawless must be like WTF!
There are nice aesthetic features like the ability to zoom in on the carnage. And when I say carnage I don't mean like riot carnage, i mean like pixel color carnage on your screen. Your epileptic brother should leave the room while playing, may trigger an episode. The water effects from the police wagon fire hose are pretty awesome, reflecting the background and people. Lens flares and film grain add a nice touch. It looks good even though it's a bit minimalistic compared to some pixel arts.
The ability to play as both the rioters and police add a nice replayability to the game, and combined with all the options for equipment and the like there are many variations of each riot to play. You even unlock quite a few extra riot scenarios through playing the main ones. Most of the riot scenarios seem to take place in the 2010's and in Europe, which as an American I appreciate, because I know only about the American riots. So, learning experience as well equals +1 to intelligence.
So if you like pixel art and RTS, you'll enjoy this game.

*very minor spoilers*
A really cute spooky point-and-click adventure game. Very punny if that's your thing (it's mine, and I loved every one of them), if not this game probably isn't for you (or most games of this genre). It was kinda weird to me that it didn't go all out in either serious/dark or silly plot like most point-and-click adventures go (especially a paranormal one) but once I realized that I got into it more for what it was. I really enjoyed the two leads Detective McQueen & Officer Dooley. They have great chemistry and play off each other well enough to keep the cases fun and hold stakes at the end. The subplot about the darkside unit and it's origins and relationship with the city is very interesting and would be great to springboard off of if this game does well enough to do a sequel!
The game itself is kinda short given that each of the 6 cases isn't that long, but given the price and quality I'd say what I got was pretty fair. While short, each case (by my gauge) where mostly just challenging enough. I *tried* not to cheat and most of the logic is pretty sound, but still at least once a case on average I had to look up what to do, but that just might be my shortcoming, it all made sense. The music was pretty nice, as well as the art.
*I DID initially play with my sister, but she quit by the 2nd case because there is a lot of flickering lights used for atmosphere (especially in the 2nd case) and it's migraine inducing if you'r sensitive to it (even with my brightness all the way down, it gave me a headache and I tried to avoid those rooms).
*The only other sensory complaint was fly noises in two screens in the 5th case. They are REALLY irritating (to me personally, most people probably not so much) and I feel like they didn't really add to the camp vibe despite how (disturbingly) real they sounded. Neither of those things took my enjoyment away from playing the game per say (aside from not being able to include my sister), but I feel like they should still be taken note of.
BUT those grievences took up a very small slice of the game, which I could tell was made with a lot of heart, and puns. Lots of puns.
Amazing, that is all.

Had more fun running in circles screaming help as I punched anyone who came near me to death than actually playing the game as it's meant to be.
Team Objective is a pit of despair, as objectives are lost or won solely on which team doesn't have a Vanguards swinging the Zwei back and forth into their teammates. Say hello to the archers!
Free For All is THE place to go if you want to be called an idiot for not 1v1'ing people (Despite there being a duel gamemode)
Team Deathmatch is all Vanguards. If you've ever wanted to hear people screaming at the top of their lungs as they lunge three hundred feet forward, this is the place you want to be.
Duels might be the most amusing gamemode to those that don't take Chivalry seriously, for good reason. Nine times out of Ten, its a Knight using some disgusting cosmetic combination while wielding the Messer or its reskin equivalents. The other tenth chance is to be matched against a Man At Arms, already equipped with the Norse Sword or Holy Water Sprinkler, ready to spam the V button to dodge away from your clumsy attacks or rapidly press x and 2 to have his character burst into laughter at the same time he bursts your head open.
Shoutout to the maybe one or two servers that play Capture the Flag, where the small enclave of players actually play together and use weapons that aren't cheap gimmicks.
If you thought the archers were bad in Team Objective, play Last Team Standing. For extra fun, change to a Knight with a Tower Shield and see how many arrows you can have stuck out of its front. Better yet, don't use shields at all and become the human pincushion as Normal Bows, Crossbows, and Javelins are slung at incredibly high speeds into your poor body. Oh, and if you don't do 1v1s when theres only one guy left on either side, prepare to be kicked.
However, hidden in the mess is Torn Banner's Horde maps. Take NPCs that have no idea what pathing is, put them on a large map that has fire and spikes strewn about, and watch as they mercilessly kick or smack each other out of the way and into dangerous objects. I've never had more fun in this game since I witnessed a King three times the character's normal heights football kick his subjects into a spike after lighting everyone on fire.
In all honesty, the Chivalry is mindless fun. Swatting people with what seriously is just a wooden club, impaling heads against walls with a three foot long javelin, joyfully laughing as you punch an archer to death, or the ever-amusing lines of dialogue just make the game something to come back to. (Though maybe not for 20 dollars. Buy it on sale, trust me.)
The main drawback are the obnoxious level differences. 15 and below servers are seriously fun, but you don't learn anything playing with fellow inexperienced players, which leads to a burning hatred by higher levels when you finally are thrown into 15+ servers. People somehow forget colors (Seriously, what is so hard? It's RED VS BLUE)
The game is plagued by overzealous veterans who will practically burn you at the stake if you mention that the Claymore, Zwei, Messer, and Maul are painfully overused, or that the combat system needs a big redo seeing as by aiming down and crouching will ally a majority of weapons to swing (FOR FULL DAMAGE MIND YOU) in half their normal time. Looking at you, Claymore.
So if you're thinking of buying this, do it when it's on sale, and play with friends. Community's too toxic otherwise.

Disclaimer: my name is in the credits as a playtester, and I received a free copy of the game for that reason, though I have bought multiple copies for friends. I have no connection with Christine Love or the dev team other than my playtesting and a number of mutual friends.
Ladykiller in a Bind is the future of visual novels. Christine pushes the bar in so many ways and refines a huge number of visual and story innovations that appeared, rough-hewn, in other games. In Ladykiller, these innovations are smooth and silky, and as a visual novel developer myself, I'm absolutely gobsmacked at how far she pushed the game engine (Ren'Py) with everything. I keep getting distracted by the subtle animations in the backgrounds.
Anyway. I just need to say that this is one of the best visual novels ever published, and if you're interested in VNs as a medium, or game storytelling in general, you owe it to yourself to play this.
I cannot recommend it enough.

TL:DR This is a beautiful looking game with enjoyable gameplay but I cant recommend it at the full price which is pretty expensive. At about 50% off or more though I would highly recommend it.
Full Version:
Owlboy is a kind of mix of a metroidvania and twin stick shooter. You play as Otus who is an owl (owls in this game are kind of human like owls) and Otus is able to fly. However he isnt able to attack and so relies on his friends who he can carry and who will shoot enemies. This is where the twin stick shooter element comes in as you move Otus around while simultaneously shooting enemies. Each companion has a different weapon which means you'll swap between them for different situations and enemies.
The pixel art in this game is incredible and really is impressive. The areas, characters, pretty much everything is beautifully animated. The games soundtrack is also brilliant and fits really well into the game.
The story is good as well and has some enjoyable characters, particularly your companions. It isnt a very long game but the length feels about right as it doesnt outstay its welcome. There are collectables to search for to pad out the game if you want to do that.
Overall it's a great game but despite that I dont feel it's worth it at its current full price.
Positive points:
- amazing pixel art with the whole game being just beautifully animated. Has a great soundtrack to go with it.
- combining the flying Otus with his shooting companions in a metroidvania style game is an interesting idea and its one that works quite well for the most part. Theres enough variation introduced as the game progresses to keep it from getting too monotonous.
- has a nice story and enjoyable characters. Otus is a mute but stillis a likeable protaganist despite not being able to speak.
Negative points:
-while the bosses were enjoyable enough to fight, I did find that they were a bit too easy. Most of them, including the final boss, I was able to beat on my first try
- Despite it being a good game the full price for this game is quite expensive for what it is

I love the Conan universe, and I can not wait to see the expanded content of this game.
So far, it is just 1 of 5 areas we are given, which in time, we will have access to all 5 areas.
The initial area is huge, a desert/savanna landscape.
The crafting can be in depth, but you must earn your right to craft by leveling up.  And in this game, I feel like crafting equals power.  So essentially you gain more power by getting more crafting recipes.
It still has an old school MMO feel to it, where most mobs argo to you, which can get annoying.  I wish the "mobs" were doing daily tasks, such as eating, chasing prey, sleeping, playing, etc... and only argoed if they were threatened or really hungry.
This game still has some bugs, but that is expected, as this is a beta in which we paid for.  The bugs ranged from floating rocks, to enemies spawning right on top of you.
The game also needs some improvements, like being able to reclaim crafting resources from something you built that needs to be moved because it's in the wrong spot.  Currently, you just destroy the item completely.  And for some crafting items, it takes a while to gather the resources to build it up.
I feel this game should shy away from traditional MMO games, get rid of the enemy health bar, and have more of a dynamic attack feel to it.  So for example if my Strength is high enough, and I have a good enough Tool, if I swing my Axe for the Neck of a Gazelle, I should be able to lop it's head off in one hit.
Avoid the EA mobile travesty like the plague - this is the real deal and deserves every penny put towards it.

Throughout the multiple runs and routes I've played through it has made me laugh, cry, and... well, it made me wish there were more people like the Beauty and the Stalker in the world. It's not a perfect game, of course, there's a few mis-steps here and there as you might expect with the characters and story-- mostly personal preference though: I didn't always agree with the political beliefs and statements of some characters and they ended up feeling a little grating at times, or I agreed with them so much it felt like they were preaching to the choir and stating the obvious multiple times in a row.
When a story is this long (240k words in total, according to the internet) you can't expect it to strike gold with every single scene (and it doesn't), nor are you going to agree with absolutely *everything* an author is trying to say (but does anyone really expect to?) When Ladykiller in a Bind is at it's best though, it is so, so good and I consider it to be one of the best games I own on steam. There's a reason I've bought it for multiple friends (and will continue to whenever a sale comes around) and am working on unlocking all of the achievements.
Ladykiller was my first introduction to Christine Love, and after playing some of her older work I'm pretty sure she has a fan for life.

Overall a satisfying if brief game, set in a slightly bizarre futuristic cyberpunk world, where AI controlled machines have arisen as mankinds primary threat, fighting to gain entrance into the last bastion of human civilization.  The protagonist played is none other than a secret police type, send on missions to halt and uncover infiltrations and deal with them in a violent manner.
Sound great? Sadly, the storyline is a convoluted mess bordering on incomprehensible.  Having finished the game, I'm still not sure what was accomplished and what was going on.  With that major flaw aside, Hard Reset is an absolute blast, and captures the essence of the cyberpunk genre proficiently.
You're given 2 weapons from the word go, and as you progress through the game, granted fairly frequent upgrade to bolster their capabilities and fire modes, rather than replace them with completely new guns. We're not talking minor changes either. but rather unlocking things like charged blast to electro-mortar to smart-gun style upgrades, which you'll find yourself rapidly switching between mid-fight to use deadly combo's to turn otherwise difficult enemies into scrap.
The game starts out relatively difficult, almost to the point of being merciless, so if you're struggling, remember that in the future, lots of the cars, terminals and other machinery are highly volatile and explore with the gentlest of encouragement from your arsenal.
While the graphics are great, and the holographic style waepon upgrade interface is pretty cool,  I find it hard to overwhelmingly recommend this game due to the poor narrative. But, if you're the type to skip cutscenes, you'll probably find this worth your while.  There's potential here in the setting, so lets hope the developers make the most of it in any sequels.

so heres a run down of some Pros and Cons of the game:
Pros:
Epic setting: The setting is fantastic it really does feel like you are living in the world of Conan the Barbarian and it is amazingly crafted the ruins, the rocks, the landscape it all screams feral im going to kill you barbarism.
Beautiful Graphics: The graphics are of the highest quality and it is an absolutely stunning game to look at you can see a lot of time and work was put into these models and textures.
Easy to learn Crafting system with lots of crafting options: alot of people are comparing this game to ark which is understandable as Ark is one of the biggest if not the biggest survival games on Steam at the moment, the crafting system however i feel is more stream lined than ark and feels to me anyways less clunky. Its straightforward you level up you spend points on tech to craft new things (similar to the engram system in ARK) however one thing i have noticed is there is a lot of options for crafting be it weapons, armor or just plain household furniture there are tons of things to make and if you love decorating your home to the extreme conan lets you do this in some fantastic ways.
Religion: Religions in gaming have always been a barely touched upon subject but this game makes it feel like it is not only a key feature but a necessary component to later survival. Think of the religion in Conan Exiles not as a means of worship but as a means to gain access to the games super weapons, Avatars.
Not to mention the Various Buffs you get dependant on your Faction.
Thrall system: so many survival games out there let you use the creatures in the game to better yourselves well conan exiles takes another approach more suited for its setting, throughout the world there are little campsites where NPC's are residing these NPC's will be hostile but if you can subdue them and take them prisoner the game allows you to make them into your slaves via the Wheel of Pain and these "Thralls" then can do an array of things, the cooking, dancing to keep insanity away, blacksmithing (giving you extra crafting options) and they can even defend your base.
right i think thats all of the Pros now onto the Cons:
Cons:
At the moment conan exiles has the exact same problem as what every other early access game has bugs and lag,
The bugs are being fixed as soon as FUNCOM get word of it they seem to be on top of it and because of the fact they are an established Video Game company the chances of them cutting patches and or stopping involvement of this game is going to be next to nothing unless something dire were to happen (please crom dont let it happen, if you do well to HEll WITH YOU)
Now we get to the Lag, as i mentioned earlier FUNCOM is doing their very best to combat the bugs and are cranking out patches left right and center however they have hit a wall when it comes to their servers, basically for those  of you who arent aware FUCOM's server provider over launch week was at critical level and couldnt handle the load of people playing there games so FUCOM are now looking for new server providers for their official servers and for now have taken the Official Servers offline however there are like 9.000 independant servers so you arent going to miss out. So dont let the lack of Official Servers deter you.
Overall im very very impressed so far with Conan: Exiles it is one of the most fun survival games i have ever played and i am really looking forward to seeing the game when it is out of Early Access until then im going to keep surviving in the world of Conan.

So, if you feel like killing some time with some mindless (really mindless) straight-forwarded shooter, get it, it's your money after all, just try to wait for a sale if you're not in a rush.

The game has a lot of entertainment in the main playthrough loop as you struggle to get out of your debt before the deadline either through sheer capitalism or mixing in some dungeon runs to earn extra items to sell in your shop.
The fun in the game for me is getting the story triggers in town (which admittedly might be few and far in between or have very specific conditions that you might be less frustrated if you looked up a guide) and attracting the right NPCs to your shop by remodeling and putting up the right items in thee display windows at the right times.
If you have a favorite dungeon partner then ending a playthrough with getting their true card is a nice goal as well as trying to unlock all the dungeons and NPCs that you can before paying the debt.
While some might not want to read spoilers on how to get the debt cleared on the first run, you might probably be doing yourself a favor reading up a guide on the crafting materials from the dungeons and how to best use them or else they will just be mostly junk that you will sell because it does take some effort to figure out what each one does (and there are a lot of them). Reading a guide on how to trigger the story events might be good for you as well if you don't wish to spend too much time figuring it out.
I like this game a lot and if you just want to experience it, grab it when it's on sale, but I still feel that it is worth the full price unlike some AAA games that have been released for PC lately.
Oh... and don't ever forget the most important thing... Capitalism ho!

I just love this game so much.  The story has that charming "ancient power awakens that will decide the outcome of the war" thing going on, which is an RPG trope that I personally never tire of.  But the thing about JRPGs is that their plots and lore are never the interesting thing about them, it's the characters and their personalities and the way they grow and change together.  And that's simply perfect in this game.  All the characters have real pasts, plans for the future, attitudes, quirks, and feel like real human beings.
Moreover, the character units which in most SRPGs are just clones are instead people with their own biographies, voice actors, lines of dialogue, and even personality traits that actually affect gameplay.  This helps you connect so much more with your squad and helps you really care about them.  My favourite of the optional squad members is Ramsey, the ill-motivated engineer who always acts like she'd rather be doing anything other than her job.
The game is overall so vibrant and animated, the art style is beautiful, the characters live and breathe, and the storyline, even though it's a bit cheesy and contrived, simply serves as a vehicle for getting to know the characters better.  It even brought a tear to my eye on a few occasions, which is what a good JRPG is supposed to do, after all.
The dual audio is a good feature.  I'm playing with Japanese audio to make it feel even more like watching an anime, and I'd recommend that to anyone who thinks they might enjoy that kind of thing.
Pick this up if you like SRPGs or traditional JRPGs, or both.

I really want to leave a positive review for this game and recommend it to others.  I really do.  But after force re-starting my computer for the umpteenth time after trying to launch, I just can't.  This is my biggest gripe about the whole game.
Here are my specs:
Intel i7 - 2600K 3.4 GHz
RAM 16.0 GB
64 bit x64 windows 10 (boy do I miss windows 7 tho)
AMD Radeon HD 6900
All drivers are up do date.
The problem is this - roughly every third or fourth time I try to load a saved game, the game freezes.  I can still hear music, but I can't even ctrl-alt-del out of the game to force close it, it completely freezes my computer and forces me to do a hard reboot, which I hate.  Sometimes when I go back in the game after a re-boot it says there was an error and says reasons have to do with mods.
I have absolutely no mods on this game.  I have only the game I purchased and the updates SCS software did with the new truck.
If they ever fix this I will absolutely change my review to recommend this game, as when it works it is loads of fun.  I had never played ETS2 so I couldn't compare this to that, my gripes about in-game playing would be fines way too high and double if a cop sees you run a red light or hit someone (like it's more illegal if a cop sees you do it) but enforcement can now be turned off.
I do hate the stop lights in the middle of the interstate...and why they put spawn points for AI vehicles at a T junction to an interstate I'll never know.  The only way to actually get on the interstate from here is to pull out, slowly, in front of traffic and force them to stop.
Also the wheels of the truck while turning only turn the full degrees while stopped, not sure what that's about.
When you hire drivers and they 'couldn't find a job, $950 in fuel costs', seems odd that they don't know how to use a phone or the internet.  If SCS wants to limit funds I think it would be more realistic to have a message say, 'XXX called in sick today and could not work'.

For the pros:
Graphics are amazing.
I like the progression to higher levels, more money per level, unlocks to truck upgrades and paint jobs.
Having driven thru CA and NV, the realism for the terrain and landmarks are great, I can't wait for other states to be added.
TLDR:  I would recommend if I didn't have to force re-boot my computer every day.

Owlboy review:
Owlboy is an action/adventure gsme where you play as a little owl called otus. Otus is seen as a good for nothing by his fellow owl students and his teacher asio since he makes many mistakes while learning to become a proper owl. Though otus does have one friend geddy. Geddy is a human unlike otus but they get along very well. our story begins whit asio waking up otus. He informs otus that they have overwatch duty and have to watch for pirates. Suddenly a random trouble maker shows up and otus and geddy start to chase said trouble maker. They run into a cave where they find a weird looking relic. Geddy decides to chip a piece of the relic and to there suprise geddy starts to teleport. this is a big mechanic in the game but more on that later. when Geddy and otus find there way out of the cave there are pirates every where. This leads into a stealth section where you cannot get spotted. Otus and Geddy manage to flee there town safely and our adventure begins. Alot more happens in the story over all and i found the story to be compelling.
Story:7.5/10 charming characters and good lore.
Gameplay wise Owlboy is a blast to sit down and play. Otus cant really do anything to protect himself but that is were geddy comes in. Geddy has a blaster that he can use against enimies that is why the teleporting mechanic is so important. being able to teleport Geddy and eventualy other partymembers by your side by pressing the E button is seemless and works really well. other than that there are many different puzzles to solve through out the story. The puzzles were never chalenging but fun non the less. There are also a few memerable boss fights. They are both challenging and uniqe.
Gameplay 8/10 challenging fun
The best part about owlboy by far is the presentation. The sprites are fantastic and the music is amazing in every way.
It took the develepors 10 years to make this game and the sprites are probaly a big reason for that.
Presiontation 10/10 Fantastic
Verdict: Owlboy is a game whit a breif but compelling story with charming characters and fun dialouge. The gameplay is different, Challenging and Fun. The presiontation is amazing with beatiful sprites and music that made me stop
playing and just listen. And with all that in mind i give owlboy an overall score of:
9/10 PLAY IT NOW

Okay, so... I pretty much knew very little about this game when I picked it up. I was aware that the plot was a big deal and that it was considered to be a good game. I wasn't disappointed.
Let me get something out of the way: the story was, indeed, quite amazing. The narrative goes from the main character being a screw up to showing everyone that he was much more than just a kid by the end, and it has an overall feel-good tone all along. The musical score is also brilliant and uplifting (no pun intended, since you fly around as the titular owl boy Otus). The store page didn't lie about the boss fights: each and every one, considering how simple the game mechanics are, feel well balanced and engaging from the very first one.
That said, Owlboy feels a bit short for an averagely skilled gamer used to exploration games with puzzles. The main source of longevity for the title is just in going through the story again because otherwise it's all about the collectathon for the 100%. Picture this: every area has some coins, which basically once you reach certain amounts you get health upgrades and QoL upgrades for the guys you use as gunners. The final upgrade in this chain grants you invulnerability (no joke!), which by the time you do get it you'll use it for the otherwise considerably-hard final encounter. If you ignore looking for every collectable and just do the actual game you might clock in at around 5 or so hours; that's not bad, but you can understand where I'm coming from, likely.
It should be noted that dying in this game is litterally a minor setback with practically no consequences, given how you are restored to full health and the game likes to auto-save a lot on area transitions and clearing things (such as unlocking a door or collecting some thingamajig).
Should you buy it? I guess. It is a good game, after all. The music really is great and the story is memorable. There's a funny moment here and there so it's not too bad. The post-ending extra area that clues you in on some very important key points of the plot also feels well done.

I just love this game so much.  The story has that charming "ancient power awakens that will decide the outcome of the war" thing going on, which is an RPG trope that I personally never tire of.  But the thing about JRPGs is that their plots and lore are never the interesting thing about them, it's the characters and their personalities and the way they grow and change together.  And that's simply perfect in this game.  All the characters have real pasts, plans for the future, attitudes, quirks, and feel like real human beings.
Moreover, the character units which in most SRPGs are just clones are instead people with their own biographies, voice actors, lines of dialogue, and even personality traits that actually affect gameplay.  This helps you connect so much more with your squad and helps you really care about them.  My favourite of the optional squad members is Ramsey, the ill-motivated engineer who always acts like she'd rather be doing anything other than her job.
The game is overall so vibrant and animated, the art style is beautiful, the characters live and breathe, and the storyline, even though it's a bit cheesy and contrived, simply serves as a vehicle for getting to know the characters better.  It even brought a tear to my eye on a few occasions, which is what a good JRPG is supposed to do, after all.
The dual audio is a good feature.  I'm playing with Japanese audio to make it feel even more like watching an anime, and I'd recommend that to anyone who thinks they might enjoy that kind of thing.
Pick this up if you like SRPGs or traditional JRPGs, or both.
