Hard Reset is a fast paced revivalistic shooter, a tribute to a kind of game that has nearly vanished from the gaming world and has been replaced with the "wanna be realsitic" shooters.
Let me start off by saying the game looks amazing. Graphically impressive with an art style that matches the tone of the game perfectly. Weapon effects, explosions, rain... Everything looks top notch, especially this being the first game of a small company.
Gameplay is fast and brutal. You only have acess to 2 weapons, one that uses bullets and the other electricity. "Just 2 weapons?" you might think. No, not REALLY 2 weapons, as each weapon can be upgraded and transformed into various other weapons at the same time, so the machine gun you start off with will be able to transform into a shotgun, a rocket luncher or a grenade luncher for example. Oh, and every "weapon" has secondary fire, and none of that "aiming down the sights" BS here either. Just run fast and hold down either fire button and have fun.
There's also secret areas to be found, wich hide ammo, health or the currency you need to upgrade your weapons or health/armour and all that.

tl;dr: Good movie, horrible game. Buy under 10$ and use cheats to skip the "enemies".
This product has a good story (also the side-stories you discover), good atmosphere, characters and voice acting.
If it was a movie, it would be pretty good. This is why ratings here are relatively high - people are pretty bad at applying standards to reviews.
However, as this claims to be a games, it has to be judged as such. And it fails in almost every aspect:
- First of all, there is little to no gameplay to begin with. What you actually do as a player is about as much as you do in the Telltale interactive movies (no, they are NOT games).
Just much, much worse.
- There is one type of "enemy" in this game. Not even reskins. Really just one. From beginning to end. To "defeat" it, you have to do a quicktime event (a random combo of 2 buttons, wow). That's it. Utterly horrible.

- The "puzzles" in this game cannot be called such, a 5 year old could figure everything out. Yet this is clearly a game meant for an adult audience.
- The controls work... barely. And sometimes they bug out. Especially the teleporting is unreliable and completely inconsistent.
- Only one other "challenge" is finding items in each level. Really. Finding items in a level in... when did this game come out? 2014? Oh, my. So creative. And finding the last few items is a horrible nightmare as some of them are simply hidden pretty well. So - if you'd actually want to catch them all - you'd be running back and forth in the same level, checking each corner 3 times. This is game design from hell.
- Replayability does not exist. There are no choices here, not even fake ones as in the Telltale products.
I could go on, but you probably get the picture.
Every single attempt at gameplay this game makes just falls flat or is downright offensively obnoxious.
If they had stripped all the horrible "gameplay" elements and just made it the interactive movie they were clearly going for, the ratings for this game would have been higher.
It is no wonder the devs got axed only few months after the game's release. I hope that the artists, sound people and writers got good new jobs - and that whoever was responsible for that "gameplay" did not get a job in the same position again. Some people are not cut to make game design.

Almost instantly Hard Reset brought to mind all those great late-90's FPS games. With a modern touch and great attention to detail, especially with the level design and enemy types, this game is truly both a blast from the past and a blast of fresh air. It is a shame that an amazing game like this has gone so unnoticed. I certainly am very glad that I decided to give it a go. Cool noir-ish style in its story, some very intriguing sci-fi concepts, fantastic gunplay and a gun-focused progression system, this game doesn't really lack anything. The gun system is interesting, you have two guns which have multiple modes of firing and you upgrade them as you go, also unlocking more fire modes, I think this system works very well combined with all the different enemies you'll face. I especially liked shooting the bigger enemies with a shotgun or a railgun, and seeing all the armor plating fly away, yet the buggers kept coming - so many thrilling fights! The boss fights are very enjoyable, the levels have lots of destructible environment and last but not least; this game has a lot of secret places - just like good old FPS games used to have. If you are a FPS fan, you should definitely play this one through.

This is a fun tun-based combat game set in an alternate universe WW2. Rather than using a grid for the turn-based action, you switch to a first/third person mode on the battlefield for each characters movemet/action phase, choosing who to move and how often to move them with your limited action points.
The game doesn't always do a great job of explaining its mechanics, so a lot of it you won't get until you've played 5 or 6 missions and gotten a chance to mess around. There are also a few missions that, unless you look up strategies online first, you won't be able to do well on the first time through. Also, the overall length of the story mode is a bit short, and you don't unlock a lot of the free play options and side missions from the DLC until you've finished it.
All that said, it's a fun game if you like fire-emblem style combat and don't mind a new and interesting take on how to implement that on a full 3d battlefield while staying turn-based. The upgrade system gets to be really fun around the midpoint of the game, especially if you pick a favorite unit or two and rank them way up early by re-playing the missions for extra xp. And once you have unlocked everything, replaying old missions or the side missions with all your units fully upgraded feels amazing, and gives you a real sense of how far you've come.

TLDR version: Doesn't exactly reinvent the wheel and can get repetitive but for any fans of JRPGs or dungeon crawlers, this little gem does more than enough to justify the modest asking price (Pssst this game goes on sale often)
Story and Characters: You play as Recette, a cheerful naive and only somewhat annoying little girl whos carefree life gets shattered when her father disappears and she's left to pay his debts to a fairy named Tear. Your goal is to open the store her father left in order to pay off weekly payments to Tear or lose your home. It's not exactly on the level of the Count of Monte Cristo but for a cutesy game like this it's all the motivation you'll need.
The characters are pretty simple anime cliche, but most are charming in their own right. Tear makes a great straight man to Recette's bubble-headed obliviousness. Charme the thief is a likeable rogue and kind of like a big sister to our lead. That being said a number of characters are very one note and that note is typically "rude and nasty for no particular reason". Still, you have the option to skip any dialog and if your anything like me your finger will fly to that escape key any time you see that irritating rich girl.
Graphics: The visuals are decent, they do their job expressing the world but they aren't very inspired. Customizing your store is the most visually impressive part of the game. Expect to see a lot of brown and gray dungeons copy pasted almost to the point of frustration. Closeups during dialog convey a great sense of personality but the actual models only look OK. Animation is nice and smooth and the frame rate is pleasingly consistent throughout which is all that really matters in a budget title like this.
Audio: Voice acting is all in Japanese and it's cute, if a bit unnecessary with dialog being mostly text. The music isn't really worth noting. It's mostly cute and bouncy MIDI tunes that loop over and over. By far the most awful thing about the game is the ear-bleeding harmonica track that plays when walking around your store. It didn't take long for me to mute the music, and you likely will too.
Gameplay: This dungeon crawling ARPG has just enough twists to the classic formula to really make it addictive. Your time will be split between selling items in your store and running down to the dungeon hoping to find loot to sell at said store. It's easy to assume the selling part would be the weakest but it's amazing how nail-biting selling stuff can be when your next payment is due tomorrow and your still 5000 short. Do you jack up your prices and risk a customer walking out on you? Will anybody buy that really expensive item you absolutely need to sell to make your payment? How much is too much for a chocolate bar? This game manages to make such a mundane idea quite exciting.
The dungeon crawling is also quite fun if a little basic. You start with just one swordsman to dungeon dive with but you later unlock a quick thief, a glass cannon mage, etc. They all have different items to equip, different abilites, and different special attacks so there's enough variety to keep it fresh.  Enemies are generic looking but each one has different attacks and movement patterns, such as knights being able to protect themselves with shields or the winged eyeballs shooting lasers at you. The only real issue I have with the controls is the momentum characters gain while moving seems a bit too much. I found myself walking straight into enemies I meant to avoid or having a hard time wheeling myself around to hit their weak spots before they moved.
What really stands out is the way RPG conventions are subverted. This might be the only RPG I've ever played where my characters level didn't matter to me. After all, the game measures your progression almost completely with money, so while filling your merchant EXP bar grants new perks to make the money pile up, the combat EXP isn't nearly as important. Sure tougher dungeons usually have better loot but the only reason I was happy I leveled was for the HP refill so I didn't have to use any of the healing items I found. I didn't really know or care what level my hero was as long as I could carry out a huge bag of loot.
All in all, Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a fun, cute and simple ARPG well worth your time and money. It's not for everyone and it's not exactly the kind of game that will leave you glued to the edge of your seat but it has novel gameplay and lots of charm sure to appeal to the RPG crowd looking for something different. And hey, if you enjoy story mode and you can play challenge mode and fulfill your fantasy of fighting your ever-growing debt until the massive payments force you into bankruptcy! Sorry, too real?

Spent about 300 hours in game in total I believe, I've been having days where all I did was sleep for 10 minutes, then back to gaming until I was too tired, sleep 10 minutes, back to gaming. It's insane, the amount of things you can do in this game.
If you're not willing to pay, you receive a pretty nice linear game with a solid story and great mechanics, you have your quests, your dungeons, you can even join a guild and go hunt for secrets or big mobs around the world. It's possible to enjoy the things you spend labor points on, though I have to admit it's going to be a rough grind for you. You will have to make money for labor pots to actually achieve anything, or make money to buy things off of other people. But I guess that's what you're paying for, to not waste your life on it.
If you pay though, prepare yourself for the most amazing experience in your life, literally the only reason I had to stop playing was because of the effect it had on my private life, I didn't talk to offline people anymore, I spent less time sleeping, I neglected my studies, it's been a wreck, but I can't allow people to badmouth this game.
If all you want to do is one specific thing like arena or dungeons, don't buy this game, buy this game if you want to immerse yourself in a new world, join a guild, get to know your server, play together or against other guilds, try out different playstyles, go crafting, do traderuns, get to know your neighbours, have practice fights, go fishing, dive from the highest towers in the cities, go farm, do it all, explore ArcheAge.
It has so much to offer if you've never played it, it's an experience way more satisfying than any other game can bring, but you have to allow yourself to like it, don't listen to the naysayers that went into the game with the wrong idea, don't listen to the people complaining about p2w, ArcheAge is a world on it's own, go find your place in it.

Initially I was apprehensive about buying the game due to the small size of it compared to ETS and ETS2, and over scaling making the roads far too short. However, I bought it after playing around with the demo and realising that it is all relative. Don't get me wrong, the map is small, and the longest drive I've done so far lasted no more than 40 minutes (I've spent a couple hours on a single job in ETS2). I have no doubt this will change over time, but I feel SCS has cheated the game by only releasing two initial states.
Pros:
- Challenging driving with longer trailers
- Selectable trailer drop off locations
- Detailed scenery and roads
Cons:
- The map is far too small in its current
- Lack of trucks
- Idiotic AI and overly harsh traffic penalty enforcement
This game is good for people who want a step up from the driving in ETS and ETS2, but I wouldn't strongly suggest people who own those games to get this as it feels more like a DLC or gimick having played the previous two games.

If combining a card game with a combo brawler sounds like the sort of thing you'd be interested in, buy this when it's on sale. At full price, know what you're getting yourself into -- the game is a little too shallow and a little too grindy to be truly great.
Hand of Fate serves up the combo brawling that was made famous by the Arkham games as encounters that are triggered by cards you collect in a game. Is this fun? Yes it is. Is it the greatest combo brawler slash card game crossover out there? It may well be, since I'm not aware of another game that tries exactly the same thing. Is it a good game? Yes. Is it a
game? No, it's got too many flaws for that.
The brawler aspect is a serviceable copy of the Arkham system -- you can move, dodge roll, attack and counter, with a weapon or artifact ability thrown in occasionally. But while it works, it feels a lot more clunky and lacks the grace and move sets of its inspiration. Difficulty is cranked up by having the fights take place in what are often claustrophobically small areas littered with traps. Getting up your combo count, while presented as something desirable, appears to do almost nothing beyond adding motion blur -- you certainly don't appear to become faster or stronger, though frankly it's hard to tell. Even with all that, though, fighting is entertaining enough, if at times a bit frustrating. It's the card game aspect where Hand of Fate really doesn't live up to its potential.
Deck building in Hand of Fate basically boils down to putting in the cards that will advance some encounter questline and throwing out the cards with completed questlines (since, save for a few exceptions, there's no reason to replay them). There's very little opportunity for strategy, save for, say, replacing your big hammer with the sword against undead when you know the next level is about skeletons, which isn't even rock-paper-scissors. Hand of Fate has the superficial trappings of a card game, but it's no more than a paper-thin disguise (literally) for what is at the core a dungeon crawler (certainly not a roguelike) with more randomization in the encounters than usual. And the randomization can be terrifyingly annoying at times, requiring you to replay cards over and over again just because you failed the random checks. Although you can do a little better than raw chance when you learn to track the fail/succeed cards as they shuffle around in a four card Monte, that still doesn't excuse this crime against gameplay.
Even when the randomization isn't annoying, it's all a bit pointless. It doesn't really matter if you, say, draw a sword or a hammer, as long as you set up a draw of
that isn't the starter weapon so you can make combat a bit easier. The way a round of play works out basically varies between "the player got lucky and is now breezing through the combat encounters" and "the player got unlucky and is now having a really hard time getting through the combat encounters". You're almost never really in control during the card section, save for the few times where you've activated effects that let you make meaningful choices (like revealing part of the playing field). It is to the game's credit that it manages to dress up this illusion of control so well before presenting it to the player, but it's still no more than an illusion.
Hand of Fate is a good game, in that it keeps you entertained. It comes tantalizingly close to being a great game, without ever actually achieving greatness. Combat just isn't smooth and varied enough, card progression is too linear and lacking in strategy, the story too shallow and mired in fantasy cliches as it goes on, and the ending (if it qualifies as that) is just downright disappointing, lacking any kind of payoff. While the whole does manage to be more than the sum of its parts, it still left me with the impression that it could have been so much more. Sadly, with the first videos of Hand of Fate 2 up, it seems "more of the same" is what we're going to get.

Been playing games on Steam for nearly a decade now. It is June 25th, 2016, and this is the very first game I have ever requested a refund for.
The game is trash, disguised as a treasure. It seems like a lot of fun on the surface, but once you get about 3 to 4 hours in, you realize that none of the decisions you make matter at all. You follow the same tired formula of "choose to do nothing, and nothing happens, move on to the next card" or " choose to do something and unlock a token, which unlocks a new card". Return to beginning of the loop. There is not a modicum of skill or involved, and very little decision making. Every "success" or "failure" is literally you drawing randomly from cards that say "success" or "failure". You can try to follow them being shuffled, and sometimes that results in success if the same card stays on top twice in a row... but really, it's just pure luck of the draw. Once you realize you're playing an RPG on rails, and your choices don't matter... it gets bad. When you then realize that it's just pure luck to hope you randomly pull the one "success" card out of four cards, so that you can advance the storyline for that one series of cards... it becomes absolutely, insanely frustrating. And that's an awful thing to feel, playing a low-key, deck-building RPG.
The only good things I can say about it is that the production value is quite high. The writing is very good. The art is good. The voice acting for the dealer is excellent. The core idea of trying to merge these RPG, deck-building, action and rogue-like elements is really quite innovative and is what lured me in.
Unfortunately, the gameplay just wasn't thought out in the long run. It is not fun to fail over, and over, and over again when there is absolutely no mechanism in your grasp to try to prevent it. It never goes well in a video game when you remove every semblance of control or input from the player's hands. At the end of the day, you'd be better off just clicking "roll" over and over on a random number generator. That's pretty much what's happening here.

I absolutely can't recommend this game enough.  Beautiful pixel art, gorgeous soundtrack, platformer-style collectables and secrets, loveable characters, and some heartwarming moments for those willing to learn about the inhabitants of the world.
The gameplay is its weakest point by far, but by no means is it bad.  Part DKC2, part Zelda, part Metroidvania.  The difficulty is never very taxing, which may be a negative for some, but I felt like it was appropriately done for maintaining a relaxed atmosphere while still pushing against you enough so that you can feel accomplishment with your character.  Some of the dungeon design was a bit annoying.  I frequently would try to go the "wrong" way to grab secrets before progressing only to take the correct route and be locked out of part of the dungeon for an extended period, making it difficult to remember what routes I had and hadn't looted.  Ultimately, getting 100% of the collectibles was pretty painless, though.  The cannon minigame and the (spoiler) snake riding felt pretty awkward, but I guess it might just be another trait (accidentally) adopted from DKC since they feel similarly out-of-place like DKC3's rocket levels.
Ultimately, it was an excellent game, and I'd say it's worth anyone's time that likes any of the above-mentioned games or just wants a "pretty" experience.  My playtime logged is a bit over what it actually was.  I idled for a handful of hours while taking breaks and also extended the time a bit while revisiting a bunch of areas to get 100% completion.  Most of my Steam friends logged about 8-9 hours to complete the game.
It was worth the 9-year wait.

I have a general aversion to sidescrollers made after the SNES era because they usually end up being♥♥♥♥♥♥poor gameplay wise, and try to sell you with pixel graphics (8 bit! wow!). Sometimes the gameplay works but the graphics are ugly. Sometimes the gameplay works but is so insanely broken or difficult you just want to give up within five minutes because it's garbage.
Welcome to the game that changed my mind, lads and ladies.
Owlboy is, by far, the best game I've played in 2016, and is one of the best games I've ever played. This game is, at heart, a love letter - no, a love novel - written to the Golden Age of sidecrollers. The controls are precise and well thought-out. The art is utterly GORGEOUS, and is likely what pixel-graphics would have become if they had not been succeeded by 3d models. The music and sound design are PHENOMENAL. And that's just from the title screen alone.
As I said, I tend to disdain retro-style sidescrollers for various reasons. They usually try too hard to capture the magic of the glory days, and too often fall short. Owlboy does not. This game was in development for a long, long time, and unlike other games I could mention (cough cough No Man's Sky cough cough), this game has turned out beautifully.
Since people like pros and cons lists, I'll whip one up here. Cons first.
Cons:
- The game has a difficulty spike about halfway through. It's sudden, but not totally unexpected as the game practically warns you that it's about to get toooough. I think it could have been balanced out a little better in difficulty, but it's not impossible, and you definitely improve as you go. All enemies can be defeated by playing the game - and by that, you shouldn't have to look up a walkthrough to figure out how to beat an enemy, even after the difficulty spike.
- There are a few small gameplay segments that seem poorly timed at first, but this could be largely attributed to my using a controller instead of keyboard/mouse. I found myself trying to press the A button, right trigger, and move both sticks at the same time frequently in the last half of the game.
- Rolling to sprint does get annoying after a while, and it does slow down the game unnecessarily.
- The story lacks flesh in a few minor places. Some characters inexplicably disappear.
- While I'm certain it's a design choice, there are some instances where the framerate on animation seems a bit slowed down. It looks more SNES-y, but it is a bit out of place with the rest of the game. If you know the terms, it's like these portions were animated on 2s instead of 1s. They don't look bad, just noticeably different from the rest of the game.
- Possibly low replay value, depending on what one values in a game
-F**K THAT MINIGAME. YOU'LL FIND OUT.
Pros:
- Secrets everywhere. No, like, you're going to have to explore every nook and cranny or look up a guide if you want to 100% Owlboy. The game gives hints but does not point them out blatantly.
- Fluid, responsive controls
- Interesting puzzles that aren't so dense you can't figure them out
- Fairly forgiving respawn system
- Gorgeous graphics
- Superb Sound Design
- Magnificent music
- AMAZING ending (no spoilers)
- Interesting, sympathetic characters. You'll love them, you'll hate them, you'll remember them. Well, except for the handful that just disappear, apparently.
- I mean, this is my GOTY. Seriously. This is the best retro sidescroller, and one of the best games overall, I have ever played - and I've played quite a few. This game did what very few games do - it gave me a story I wanted to see to the end, and the gameplay was fun enough that I didn't want to just go on Youtube and watch a playthrough - I wanted to EXPERIENCE it for myself. It's sorta like Undertale in that it's a story that is definitely best experienced by playing, but instead of just being music and story, it also has amazing art and gameplay.
And yet they sell it for so little. This game is worth more than they're asking for, in my opinion. I hope, if a sequel is planned, it can live up to this "mastapeece."

An erotic visual novel about social manipulation, Ladykiller in a Bind is a game about being stuck in a place filled with terrible people while pretending to be someone you’re not. It’s…very relatable.
(There are sex scenes, but the game is very upfront and clear about letting you skip them at any time if they’re not your thing. There’s also an option to cover up any nakedness with large colorful Christmas sweaters if you want to play on a train!)
As the full title suggests, the game puts you in the uncomfortable shoes of the Beast, who must pretend to be the Prince, her rich and powerful brother, on a week-long graduation cruise. He’s a horrible manipulator, his classmates are just as devious, and the Beast has to play the part without being found out--with the added stress of being caught up in a high-stakes popularity contest called the Game.
The concept of the game uses the classic amnesia trope in a refreshing way; the Beast is going in blind, just like you, and some social situations become minefields when everyone’s referring to something the Prince would obviously know about. Juggling the twin goals of not arousing suspicion and getting enough votes to win the Game is made easier by just how brilliantly the game handles dialogue. Instead of being a classic tree, multiple options will present themselves, and sometimes disappear as the conversation continues. Having been multiple times in the situation of helplessly watching the subject change away from something I wanted to comment on, it was novel to see it used so well as a game mechanic. Some options will make people suspicious; some will get you votes; some will do both, or neither. Sometimes you’ll be pressured into saying something, anything, to avoid tipping people off.
But the game can take a lot of that pressure off you if you need it. You always can scroll back a little bit; take back what you just said, and go down a different path if you’re having second thoughts. As someone with social anxiety, this made me feel so much better. This feature, like many others found in Ladykiller in a Bind, are now things I wish every game with conversation mechanics would use.
What made this game stand out to me so much were the nights, where after a day of saying and doing horrible things to keep up appearances, you finally get to let your defenses down and be genuine with someone you care about; either the Beauty or the Stalker. Both have their own mechanical raisons d’être, but both also give a glimpse into vastly different dynamics. With the Stalker, you take the lead. With the Beauty, you willingly put yourself into the hands of someone else with the promise that she’ll make everything better. Both relationships – all social interactions in the game, in fact--make it clear that there's consent from all parties.
My life is filled with things to be anxious about: I constantly feel that I’m running out of time, that I’m missing important things, that I should be doing so much better than I am at so many things. It’s so easy to beat myself up. But it’s not healthy, is it? Anxiety and depression make it simple to discredit ourselves and be rougher than we need to be when it comes to self-criticism. But there are people in our lives who care about us, who are in a better position to help us get better. We can trust them. It’s okay to put ourselves in their hands, to relinquish that control – to stop hurting ourselves because of all the flaws we see in the mirror.
Video games can teach us important things if we’ll lower our guard and let them in; I learned a very important lesson from an erotic game about frustrated young adults on a cruise ship.

I'm not normally the biggest fan of visual novels, but Christine Love's work has always managed to capture what's best about the genre while minimizing the tropes and stupidity that are unfortunately common to this type of game. Ladykiller in a Bind is no exception.
A fairly simple premise (in which an androgynous woman must disguise herself as her brother in order to win a school-wide contest) gives way to some of the most well-written, evocative and just straight-up compelling explorations of topics such as gender, sexuality, kink, and romance that I've had the pleasure to experience. The characters are all compelling in their own unique way, and the scenes in the story's multple paths run the gamut from hilarious, to sensual, to tender, to gut-wrenching, and just about everything in-between.
This game won't be for everybody, but if you're a fan of visual novels, compelling characters and/or mature explorations of inter-personal relationships, you owe it to yourself to play this.

Crusader Kings 2 is what one would consider a deep end grand strategy, where to suceed one will need to learn the game system thoroughly, and the execution of advance plays will only really occur once the player has emersed themselve in countless hours of gameplay. Although it has a military style, most of the gameplay is centred around intrigue, and the tactical aspects of warfare is not explored. It focus highly personal interaction between a liege lord and its vassals, and stability and advancement depends highly on one's ability manipulate, assasinate, and plot, with the end result being reinforced through open warfare. It is a very deep game worth exploring for those who fancy themselves as strategist.
A draw back to the game is the extensive amount of DLC valuing up to $160, the concept of game content has been vastly commercialised, and many producers tend to sell great games in parts. In my mind the concept of DLC should just be as the term says, downloadable content, content made by producers to improve the dynamics of the gameplay should the player choose to download it. However it should not be charged. Or content that could be unlocked via gameplay, however payable to be unlocked if the player does not have the time to pursue such a path. Considering how most of the DLC does not add significant content to the game, and it could really only be considered extra spice, it should really come as a patch. What should be charged and payable by the players are expansion packs, by definition a package which changes the gameplay signinificantly, to the point where the game does not play the same. Such a significant incremental build up can reasonably be valued to atleast half the game's retail value, a good example for this is the Sims 3 series.
To conclude, Crusader King 2 is a deep strategy game for fevent strategist. However, its dynamics has been mared with improvements to game via producers coming in as payable DLC as oppose to traditional DLC which is free of charge; and is the producers way of saying thank you for joining us. Still a great game, have sunk 450 hrs, would recommend.

Personally, I like this approach. You ignore it until you want to check it, then you get stuff and get better.
The main sell of the game is the art style. It's great to have your character be a late 80s early 90s pulp manga hero type. It's great that the moves are all so memorable from shows and comics and that the reset mode is literal death and reincarnation. Dragon balls are the premium currency for crying out loud.
The gameplay itself is very slow paced. If you don't put cash into the game (I haven't) your progress will be slow. If you see the amount of time I have left this game open while at work or otherwise not around, I will tell you I do not have nearly as many cool things unlocked as the screenshots above. But I am slowly building up my super manga dragon ball collector, and that's fine, for me.

I had a lot of fun with this FPS. Set in a cyber punk styled world, the action is very fast paced with slick and polished visuals to really flesh out the environments. The combat mechanics really shine in this game with a good variety of weapons and enhancements that are upgraded throughout the game. The ability to dual wield weapons, each with a primary and secondary firing option means that there is a large enough variety of weapons that can used in combination to appeal to a wide range of play styles. My personal favourites are the crowd control options combined with a hard hitting attack.
The game story isn't much to write home about, but it provides enough of a  story inbetween frantic bouts of gun play. The long load times between deaths are overly long and probably my main criticism. Level design is well done with some interesting bosses and mechanics. I would say that the difficulty level on normal won't be too challenging for hardcore types, but is well balanced for regular players. The action is straight-up frantic without too much subtlty, so if you're looking for a more tactical or varied game style, you might want to look elsewhere. However, if games like Serious Sam or Pain Killer are more your style, you should definitely consider Hard Reset.

Before we kick off: I'm an idiot. If you were a murderer, you would move to the town I'd worked in to just do what you wanted with a terrified populace as I walked constantly into doors and fell down stairs. However I managed to feel 'smarter' than Soul Suspect. Gameplay is mostly walking around a room finding clues and pressing 'X', before summing up the five last minutes by selecting the three or so clues that answer the question asked at the start. You can't move out of the investigation area so I found myself wandering around waiting for the big X symbol to leap onto my screen. You found a diary page! Let's delve into the tortured life of- oh wait. It's one saying "Diary page of your wife". No story, not even an abridged paragraph. Maybe 10 seconds of spoken dialogue and that's your lot.
Without doubt, Soul Suspect is a lovely looking thing. The buildings and weather are all beautifully rendered, but the people walking around look like mannequins. You can read their minds as well, hopefully offering an insight into- oh no, it's just two or three pre-set phrases.
The concept is great. Solve your own murder? Find peace for restless spirits? Wicked. Spooky! Intriguing! But... not quite. Know what I mean? I found an old timey ghost crying on the beach who remembered nothing of how she died save a boat and a name. All the clues needed to complete this were within five feet of her. Just open your damn eyes! It's like it's
to be clever but just can't quite get there. The relevant clues are all painfully obvious so it becomes a slightly flat point'n'click without the charm of a point'n'click.
As for the combat, let me help you out: use the ability to see through walls, wait for three seconds, sneak up behind the (admittedly quite cool looking 'demons') and kill them off. There is nothing else to it.
I could go on but I'm sure you haven't got this far. If you have, you solved a mystery which is as hard as any puzzle in this game. If you want (like I did) an interesting mystery to solve, try the remastered Full Throttle. Want more humour? Monkey Island. Want a spooky puzzle? The Room and its sequel. They'll do a much better job than this.

In most RPG settings you clear out dungeons, then go and sell the unwanted items to shopkeepers.
In Recettear, however, you are the shopkeeper. Forced into opening a shop by a loan shark fairy to pay off your father's huge adventuring debts, you need to pay off increasingly huge installments each week or lose your home as collateral.
The game starts of simple enough, but as you progress the game will introduce new features, such as customers placing orders for you to fulfil later, and market fluctuations that will allow you to both buy low and sell high, increasing your profits significantly given the right situation. You can even sponsor adventurers to explore dungeons for you, and during these sessions you'll control them as they fight monsters and explore ruins. The main reasons for doing this is to give you ingredients to combine to make better equipment for the shop, and to unlock more adventurers to play as. Some of them will even come to your store and buy better equipment and weapons for themselves, increasing their effectiveness in the optional combat sections of the game. You'll probably even end up giving huge discounts to the adventurers you hire the most just so they'll be powerful and keep coming back for more deals. It's this kind of thing that really adds to the game's charm and helps you care about the side characters as you learn more about them.
The game is actually very forgiving and failure to meet a payment will send you back to the second day with your inventory, adventurer levels and store reputation intact. This makes something that could have been a very frustrating experience stay fun and oddly relaxing, although it is possible to beat the game in a single run if you feel up for the challenge. Completing the game unlocks the ability to start a new game +, survival mode where you need to pay off increasing amounts of debt each week until it becomes impossible to pay back, or simply carry on where you left off without needing to worry about a deadline each week. Combined with the large amount of items you can discover and create this results in a good replay value, especially for completionists.
As for downsides, the game is bad at explaining itself from the first tutorial. Tear will start the game off by telling you to set the prices for around 130%, but this will actually anger most of the customers and will cause less people to come to your store from the very beginning. You're actually better off selling for 106% - 112% until the public start liking you more, causing the shoppers to eventually warm up to buying the later and more expensive objects you can unlock, and raising your combo to speed up leveling. Neither the level combo nor town reputation are mentioned in the tutorials, which is strange considering they're actually very important to succeeding at the game and it can be frustrating until you realize they are both major factors in your progress.
The dungeon exploration is also very repetitive after a while, but is necessary in order to unlock more of the side stories and characters to come to your store. Since merchant levels are more important to success than your adventurers' combat levels you'll probably ignore the dungeons after a certain amount of time to play the markets, especially after you unlock items in the market that make the payouts from these sessions seem small in comparison.
If you're looking for an original take on the traditional JRPG setting and like the idea of running a store in a fantasy realm then I'd strongly recommend picking Recettear up.

It pains me to write this review, but after 1,000+ hours and two toons leveled to max I think I'm in a safe place to critique ArcheAge. Simply put, this is simultaneously one of the most enjoyable and detestable games I've played. It has a huge open world, without loading screens (aside from the dungeons),  complete with soaring, climbable mountains and vast, mysterious oceans. It has a deep and rewarding farming/crafting system, with optional trade-runs to distant regions and continents. When you build your first boat, you feel like you have built a boat with your sweat and tears. When you complete that long trade-run to Freedich Island unmolested, its amazing. When you find someone fun and civil to run around with hunting for sunken treasure, its a great laugh. There are periodically re-spawning world bosses for all the fight against and fun little seasonal events (which usually give out rubbish freebies, but that’s neither here nor there. Its the thought that counts). Somewhere, deep inside ArcheAge there is a really, really good MMORPG.
But then, there is a dark side to ArcheAge.
- It is a Korean Free-to-Play title hobbled by unreasonably grindy, gambling-centric, cash-grab nonsense. The RNG element of this game is simply breath-takingly awful. Success rates for upgrading equipment are so low that you won't even bother grinding for the huge amount of in-game gold required. Purchasable items offered to supposedly increase your chances seem to be utterly worthless and suspect. So, in response to the horrible mess which is regrading, some players prefer to take out their credit cards, purchase a load of labor point restoration potions from AA's cash shop and then sell them in the Auction House for in-game currency. They can then purchase whatever super-weapon they desire from auction. Amazing, right?
- Everything, everything, requires painfully-slowly regenerating labor points (LP) - from opening coin purses, crafting, foraging, farming, mining, logging trees, identifying gear, doing trade-runs, and even ransoming lost XP when killed in PVE (!). The amount of LP used is proportional to the level of enemy you kill and regenerates painfully slowly. To rub salt in the wound, unless you have a subscription, its going to only regenerate when you're logged in. Subs also receive twice as much LP than free players. But either way, you'll find yourself routinely hobbled and prevented from making full use of the game’s economy, accumulating or throwing away loads of gold pouches and unidentified equipment. Because…
- Inventory/warehouse space is extremely limited and there is no way to purchase additional space outside the Auction House or the cash shop (!!). Needless to say, this feeds once again into the ‘Pay to Win’ problem, because inventory expansion scrolls are bought from the cash shop using real money and sold in-game for virtual currency. At 129-200 in-game gold per upgrade scroll, you can make a tidy profit and gain a solid advantage over the poor souls grinding away for pennies.
- The community. Man, what can I say about the selfish, sub-human specimens which dwell in ArcheAge's 'Faction' chat? Lots of unpleasant, trolling, often genital-related, angry, racist garbage in there. Don't bother asking for help, you'll get promptly ridiculed by barely literate pond-life. Alternatively, you'll just get ignored, which seems to be pretty common too (and preferable). Sadly, most guilds aren't much better. Do not trust anybody. Period. For example, if you're doing trade-pack runs, watch everyone regardless of faction. Your own guys will, without hesitation, turn on you, kill you, and steal your trade-packs. Said individuals will then be rewarded by joining the game's 'pirate faction' where they can troll and gank with absolute freedom. Don't expect the game's 'justice' system to help either. Violators are rewarded and punished by the whims of the randomly selected jurors, who are often amusingly related to the offender by guild affiliation. Trading via chat is also strongly discouraged, as glorified phishing is rampant.
- The PVP. Want to have a one-sided battle against people who have been accumulating powerful equipment for several years? Want to be one-shotted by an immortal übermensch who mightily wields the power of his magical, enchanted credit card? Sure you do! Everyone loves unbalanced, frustrating PVP. This might have been fun when the game was in beta, long ago. It isn't anymore. Whether it be the 1v1 arena or large-scale battles, you don't stand a chance against people who have either been extremely lucky with the insane RNG system or have paid for equipment.
This is by no means an exhaustive list of the crap ArcheAge’s developers have tainted their product with, but it gives you a very brief summary of the highlights (or should that be the lowlights?). I cannot in good conscience recommend this game in its current state – there are just too many serious problems baked into the game to say that it is worth investing a lot of time, energy and cash into (and boy, do its developers want you to invest that). If you just want to fire it up, create a ninja mage with jiggling boobs, and briefly explore the world of ArcheAge, sure knock yourself out. But if you want to take it seriously and invest in it, please don’t bother– it will leave your bank account and your soul very empty in the long-run.

American Truck Simulator - The gateway drug to Euro Truck Simulator 2.
As you have likely already seen from others, this is a reskin of ETS2. There is little doubt that ETS2 is a much more complete and superior game experience in "almost" every way. To be fair, ETS2 has been out for a while (2012 I think?)
I have played roughly 40 hours in ETS2 and 9 hours in ATS. (and will probably play 500 more hours in ETS2, and 40 in ATS)
I recommend ATS as its a fun game very much like ETS2 but set in America for those who are not interested in traveling Europe. I actually love traveling Europe and have been over there quite a few times, so its fun to visit places I have been IRL.
There are many more truck models, varied and interesting locations, roads, scenery, and significantly larger area to explore in ETS2. Also once you install something like Promods in ETS2, holy cow...something like 50 more cities and 8 or 9 more countries on top...
So go ahead and drink the light beer that is ATS, and then when you grow bored of that, go grab a pint of stout Euro Truck Simulator 2 and explore strange and new places. (oh and enjoy figuring out how to make that damn round-a-bout in England when driving on the opposite side of the street :))
I will say that I enjoy the loving details that has been put into ATS in creating better city areas, models, and other small unique things. The truck models are great, cities are cool, and once ATS gets more real estate, licensed truck models, etc. It will be a more engrossing experience.
Oh..and the modding community is crazy and already working like mad on ATS in addition to the ocean of mods that exist for ETS2.
Go buy it...I have probably 50 titles that I paid more for, and gave me far less enjoyment.

Quality over quantity.
The main complaints about ATS seem to revolve around "the map is too small", but I much prefer to have a small high quality map than a massive low quality one.
Everything about the map feels like it has been placed by hand - standards are on par with the "go east" dlc for ETS2 (not quite up to the awesome Scandinavian DLC). It is worth remembing the current map in ETS2 took a long time to build, dating back to 2008 with some of the older parts (Germany) starting to feel their age.
It will clearly take a long time to build up the American map, though modders will undoubtedly start providing additions, albiet unlikely to match the quality what is provided by SCS themselves.
Aside from the map, ATS is clearly a re-skin of ETS2, and you know, I am fine with that. Why fix what ain't broken? The interface is familiar and there are a couple of new features here and there.
Given this is priced more like a DLC than a new game, I think it is a very fair deal. While SCS could have gone down the route of churning out a huge map very quickly by having a load of replicated scenery, I am glad they didn't and have focussed on quality, as what we have is a really nice polished product. I am left eagerly waiting for more!

Edit: It has been over a year since I first bought the Sim and started playing it and I am still in as much love with the Sim as I was a year ago. At the moment of this edit, I have logged 843 hours of time in the game. And I don't plan to stop trucking. The Sim has only just started it's life and there is so much more content to come for the Sim. I'm looking forward to the future State Expansions and seeing more Trucks come to the game. You will see people complain that there isn't enough content or that they want new trucks or maps now. But they fail to realize the amount of time it takes to make QUALITY content. Look at all these AAA games coming out with so many bugs and game breaking glitches and issues. That's because those games are rushed to meet a deadline and the company doesn't want to upset their fanbase by pushing the release of the game back and back and back further. SCS does not give us set dates for this reason. And SCS actually put time and care into their content. And with the Public Betas they do for each and every single update, there is hardly any game breaking bugs when the update officially releases. This is due in part because they patch the bugs DURING the Patch Betas, instead of compiling a list and doing it after the patch is released. You don't see many other companies do this. Maybe a few AAA games like Elder Scrolls Online and Battlefield have a CTE (Community Test Environment) to help test patches. But even those don't compare to the level of success SCS' Public Betas have in finding and fixing bugs.
If you've been holding off on getting ATS because you're not sure if it's a broken indie Sim, rest assured. It has next to ZERO bugs when each update goes live. And if there is a left over bug, it is usually found and squashed within hours or a day or two, but so far, no game breaking bugs have ever made it out of the Public Beta alive.
If you're holding back because of the lack of content, the Sim is extremely mod friendly. It has it's own Steam Workshop, a built-in Mod Manager for both Workshop mods and mods from external sites, so there's basically no end to the potential of this game with moddability so easily accessible.
If you're completely new to the Truck Sim community, having never played one before and want to get into it but don't like just plain ol' Singleplayer games, no worries. TruckersMP has you covered. TruckersMP is a mod developed by a team of people that allows online play in both American Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2. A simple google search for 'TruckersMP' will find you the site for the mod.
I hope you found this review helpful. I absolutely love the Sim. It has captured my attention for the last nearly 2 years now and will continue to do so for many years to come. :)

-gameplay is solid (comes across as a sci-fi version of Killing Floor).
-refreshingly friendly and helpful community especially for a free to play game.
-variety of well designed warframes and a vast array of equipment mods/customizations.
-mission finder functionality allows you to co-op seamlessly with others no matter where you are at progression wise in the game.
-huge active player base.
-Warframe at its core is nothing more than a grindfest to deck out your warframes.
-
You spend hours upon hours decking out your warframe for no reason other than to show it off.  Then you start developing another warframe.  Rinse and repeat.  The end-game is known as "Fashionframe."
-Nothing is explained in this game and little is intuitive.  You have to look on the internet to understand how a lot of things work and even then certain aspects of the game are still convoluted.
-A corollary note to my previous point: the story makes no sense and you have no real sense what you are trying to accomplish because nothing is explained.
-You play the same missions and different types of missions over and over.  Even with solid gameplay it can get boring and redundant quickly.
-PvP is obsolete.
Despite all the negatives it is one of the better free to play games out there and is worth giving a shot if you have a lot of time on your hands, have friends that play it and/or can find a good clan, and you don't mind endlessly grinding simply to build cool warframes.  You can always purchase any warframes/equipment with real money but that would ruin the whole point of the game.  I would most likely continue playing this game if there was worthwhile end game dungeons/bosses progression content.

Owlboy is fantastic.  If you really need more than that, read on.
Are you a real gamer?  Are you someone who is serious about the art and love of videogames.  Do you identify as a gamer?  Maybe you've developed a game or game assets, produced fan art, competed at some level, or you have a serious hobby in video games.
If you are, the you will understand what I mean when I say that sometimes a game comes around that you need to play.  A game that you will compare other games to.  A game that will fill a spot in your list of accomplishments or meet a need that's been building inside of you.  A game that is nostalgic, fresh and fun.
You need to play owlboy.  It's not because it's a perfect game.  It isn't.  Owlboy is special.  It's a rare, well done, beautiful game and you will be lesser of your craft if you miss out on playing it.
Controls are very good, tight, responsive, and easy to master.  I played using a controller and I recommend it.
Graphics are absolutely gorgeous 2-d sprites.
Sounds and music are pleasant and mood setting, they are done very well.
Story is gripping.  I will admit, it's not for everyone and the ending may be a tough pill for some - but overall I was entertained and glad to have seen it through (ensure you finish the sidequests to get all the details).
I rate Owlboy a 10/10.  A perfect score doesn't mean a perfect game, it means that to me Owlboy represents the best of what is available right now in video games.

My scores:
world: 9/10
main story arc: 8/10
characters: 7/10
role-playing elements: 5/10
side missions: 2/10 (don't even bother)
loyalty missions: 6/10
presentation: 8/10
combat: 6/10
Detailed opinion:
I've heard a lot about that game, but I'm kinda disappointed. I'm fan of sci-fi genre, and was expecting a lot (Mass Effect 2 is the first game I played). At the end, the feelings are mixed. The story is very good, and the world is detailed and interesting. Characters are a mixed bag, some of the characters are very well written (Mordin, Grunt, Tali, Morinth), some are just dull (Miranda and Jacob). The protagonist itself is also somewhat one-dimensional and doesn't make a lot of sense. For example if you play paragon, you are good all-loving paladin, but has no problem whatsoever killing hundreds of minions during the mission.
The main issue I had with the game, is it's mechanics. It is simply not good enough. You would expect some choices to make from an acclaimed RPG title, but all you can do - is plow though hundreds of dull enemies in a linear corridor-like missions. Many missions start with a good premises (i.e. politics, character development, etc) but no, every goddamn single time it ends up with the same boring killing of hordes of enemies. And the combat isn't even that fun. I never had console and admittedly not very familiar with thirds-person shooter genre, but I do enjoy good fighting. Here the fighting in the game felt really boring and dull. Every time I had a fighting part, I was just thinking to myself "not again" and wanted to get over with it as quickly as possible. Also I didn't see any real difference with taking different companions - they all performed more or less the same, with no synergy or strategy whatsoever involved in choosing them (even if it made difference you don't even know what the mission will be, so you can't make an informed choice).
Another complain I had - is that loyalty missions were very much similar, almost all of them involved some kind disappointment with close relative and again tons of goddamn fighting which often didn't fit thematically. Few were nice exceptions (notably Legion and Jack) but the majority were quite boring. Side missions on other side were complete and utter waste of time. I usually do like to go through all side missions in RPG games I play, but here I stopped doing any side quests completely after a while as they were lacking and real substance or fun.
Anyway, I finished the game and somewhat enjoyed it, but I'm not sure I would recommend the game of play it ever again myself.

Simply Put Valkyria Chronicles is a classic tactical role playing game with turn base point assigned action set to a straight forward book story telling format. I would say probably top 10 all time in strategy turn baeds games. Though very simple for adults, I enjoyed the tactical puzzle solving fun aspects of VC. It remined me a lot of some of the earlier PSP games like Ring of Red and others.
Pros:
A: Beautiful simplistic story telling with a sort of hand drawn simple colored pencil quality.
B: Very easy to learn tactical warfare
C: Neat cut scenes and book storytelling with multiple sections to each chapter. Like watching a book anime movie.
D: LIke other classic turn based games-You have Lancers, Snipers, Machine Gunners, Engineers to use which get stronger as the game progresses. They also have pretty animation abilities they get added. Watch out for Pollen.
E: Some challenging battles that you can either overwhelm or out manuever the enemy.
F: Teaches the children the costs of war. I would caution supervision with younger age groups. Follow the rating.
Cons
1. AI is too crude and not too bright here which can take away from the over all theme.
2. Shooting affectivly can be a challenge do to the camera movement. Caution
3. Though beutifully done. The animation may not be what your used to and may seem crude to today's animated polished cut scenes and games. That is however my subjective take.
4. Full rosters not necessary to mission completions which is a turn off
OVERALL
First remember this game is 7 years old. I would advice three things
A: Go to the workshop and watch others or see videos and see if this is for you. You don't like tactical games or turn based, pass. B: Wait till on sale to buy, Know that a new Valkyria Azure Revolution is coming in 2017 to PC, and rumors of VC 2 and 3 coming out in a condensed format for PC after, so sooner of later you will probably add this if you like the new game. Not a bad addition if 50-75% off.
C: Avoid cheats of this game since there are plenty of how to videos to get past battles. A mistake. It will take away alot of the fun of figuring it out yourself.
I recommend Valkyria Chronicles and a great addition to Strategy lovers. I rate it 3.5 out of 5 stars

I have mixed feelings about this game.
Pros:
- This is, first and foremost, a 3D point-and-click game, and as an avid fan of the genre I found it most enjoyable.
-Great atmosphere, with various extensive areas that have plenty of explore-value. You can breeze through this game if you prefer, or take your time and explore everything (I chose the latter and was not disappointed).
-On numerous occasions you get to possess and play as a cat.
-Loads of easter eggs and collectables if you're into that stuff (I am)
-A lot of narrative was written into this game that is only accessible through the aforementioned collectables. If you get bored by excess backstory then you don't have to engage with it, but if you are into it there's a lot there to enjoy.
-Great game for achievement hunters, though many achievements involve the collectables.

Cons:
-The protagonist is- you guessed it- a jaded, white, flowy brown haired, fedora wearing, tattoo bearing, cigarette smoking dude with a 2edgy4you past and a serious chip on his shoulder. Tbh I'm pretty over this character as it's been done time and time again, and no amount of swaggering, sauntering, or side-smirking is going to make me feel like this character is in any way original or interesting.
- Some awkwardly timed voice-acting means characters cut each other off on occasion, which I found very distracting in an otherwise immersive game.
- Although the story was decent, it definitely got a bit cliche at times (
). There are plot twists meant to keep you interested but that didn't stop me from figuring out what was going on long before the protagonist did.
- Not enough ghosts for you to talk to, and far too many living people who have nothing interesting to say.
I do recommend this game if you're a fan of point-and-clicks and ghost stories, though I don't think I could recommend getting it at full price. On the surface you are a sweet little girl caught in the throws of flash poverty after your deadbeat dad runs off with everything that will put food on the table, may or may not get eaten by a dragon, proceeding to leave you to pay off his enormous debts via an item shop.  In reality, this game is a corruption simulator in which you experience first hand how a little girl can become drunk with capitalism, exploit other small children for their goods then turn around to sell those same goods to the elderly at obsurd prices.  It COULD stop there but it doesnt.  Why be "we can retire early" rich when you can be "I own a back yard pool full of slaves that don't like me." rich, stop by the local adventurers guild to risk other peoples lives for your gain by sending them into a 1000 floor living dungeon that rearranges as they manage to survive. Awsome fun f2p shooter game.  Tip for anybody starting, once you are done with the tutorial quest just try and progress through the star chart.  Focus on unlocking new planets and trying out new frames and weapons.  Keep the ones you like and sell the weapons you don't like, frames you can keep.  Reason I'm saying this is because newcomers often get confused about what they are supposed to be doing.
As far as the f2p aspect goes, it goes like this.  The premium currency is platinum and is used for a variety of things, most importantly slots and reactors/catalysts (AKA potatos).  Potatos you can occassionaly get from events, especially from alerts every other Friday so they aren't a big issue.  Slots  you have to spend plat on, but I would say you get about 100 hours or so of gameplay before you HAVE to get more slots, which is a DARN good amount of quality free gameplay.  Just make sure you spend your first 50 starting plat on a frame slot and two sets of two weapon slots.
As far as getting plat goes, you don't even necessarily even have to buy it.  You can trade for it too if you wish.  Rare mods, prime parts, and syndicate items are the usual things that sell for plat.  If you do want to buy plat, you don't need too much either.  Wait for a 50% off or 75% off log in bonus coupon and put about 5-10$ in and you are set.

The main complaints about ATS seem to revolve around "the map is too small", but I much prefer to have a small high quality map than a massive low quality one.
Everything about the map feels like it has been placed by hand - standards are on par with the "go east" dlc for ETS2 (not quite up to the awesome Scandinavian DLC). It is worth remembing the current map in ETS2 took a long time to build, dating back to 2008 with some of the older parts (Germany) starting to feel their age.
It will clearly take a long time to build up the American map, though modders will undoubtedly start providing additions, albiet unlikely to match the quality what is provided by SCS themselves.
Aside from the map, ATS is clearly a re-skin of ETS2, and you know, I am fine with that. Why fix what ain't broken? The interface is familiar and there are a couple of new features here and there.

At the end of each week the feds come round and charge you a huge amount of cash up front, and if you can't pay they shut your shop down and game over. Overall, buy this game if you are a fan of JRPGs and want some interesting parodical gameplay, but don't buy it if singleplayer RPGs aren't for you as sometimes gameplay is repetative with the whole buy cheap/sell expensive thing wearing off after a bit.

I've played this game on both the Switch and on PC.  This review represents both versions.
First, the good:
+Music.  The music is incredible, and is by far the highest point in the game.  Supremely good soundtrack.
+Visuals.  Great, crunchy graphics and excellent representation in how the game conveys information on the playfield.
The not-so-good:
-Collision.  It feels like everything is an obstacle in the game, and you can see your character getting hung up on areas that you're clearly not even touching.  When you have to deal with this, on top of a ton of enemies all aiming railguns at you, it makes the situation feel needlessly frustrating.
-Menus.  The menus feel clunky and minimalistic, involving a lot of scrolling though inventory, and new items feeling like they're sometimes placed at random.  It's just unintuitive.  There's a lot of space available on the screen, and menu occupies so little of it, and cramps everything into a tiny, inconvenient area.
-BIOS/Mutation/Skill/Whatever you want to call it when you start the game.  There's no reason to take anything other than self-healing.  Health packs are few and far between, you wind up taking excessive damage faster than you can realize in the later levels, and other, cool starting perks, like Blademaster, winds up being usless due to poor developer foresight.  To elaborate on that, that perk makes all weapon drops melee weapons.  There are explosive canisters on the floor in each level, and when they explode, they deal heavy damage to all things nearby, and with a melee only build, you can't safely destroy those.  So, if you're in a cramped corridor with a canister, and tons of enemies, you're likely dead, nothing else to it.  General shortsightedness in game balance makes the perk system almost inconsequential.
I could go on, but you get the idea.  A difficulty curve that ramps up too high, too quick, questionable collision on every wall and prop in the game, tedious, unintuitive menuing, and poor weapon and ability balance make Neurovoider an awkward red-headed step-child in the already over-saturated rougelite genre.  Great presentation can't save this game from its own mechanical issues.

Absolutely love it! 10/10
Edit: It has been over a year since I first bought the Sim and started playing it and I am still in as much love with the Sim as I was a year ago. At the moment of this edit, I have logged 843 hours of time in the game. And I don't plan to stop trucking. The Sim has only just started it's life and there is so much more content to come for the Sim. I'm looking forward to the future State Expansions and seeing more Trucks come to the game. You will see people complain that there isn't enough content or that they want new trucks or maps now. But they fail to realize the amount of time it takes to make QUALITY content. Look at all these AAA games coming out with so many bugs and game breaking glitches and issues. That's because those games are rushed to meet a deadline and the company doesn't want to upset their fanbase by pushing the release of the game back and back and back further. SCS does not give us set dates for this reason. And SCS actually put time and care into their content. And with the Public Betas they do for each and every single update, there is hardly any game breaking bugs when the update officially releases. This is due in part because they patch the bugs DURING the Patch Betas, instead of compiling a list and doing it after the patch is released. You don't see many other companies do this. Maybe a few AAA games like Elder Scrolls Online and Battlefield have a CTE (Community Test Environment) to help test patches. But even those don't compare to the level of success SCS' Public Betas have in finding and fixing bugs.
If you've been holding off on getting ATS because you're not sure if it's a broken indie Sim, rest assured. It has next to ZERO bugs when each update goes live. And if there is a left over bug, it is usually found and squashed within hours or a day or two, but so far, no game breaking bugs have ever made it out of the Public Beta alive.
If you're holding back because of the lack of content, the Sim is extremely mod friendly. It has it's own Steam Workshop, a built-in Mod Manager for both Workshop mods and mods from external sites, so there's basically no end to the potential of this game with moddability so easily accessible.
If you're completely new to the Truck Sim community, having never played one before and want to get into it but don't like just plain ol' Singleplayer games, no worries. TruckersMP has you covered. TruckersMP is a mod developed by a team of people that allows online play in both American Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2. A simple google search for 'TruckersMP' will find you the site for the mod.
I hope you found this review helpful. I absolutely love the Sim. It has captured my attention for the last nearly 2 years now and will continue to do so for many years to come. :)

I have mixed feelings about Valkyria Chronicles. By one side, I really loved this game, I obviously would not spend 36 hours of my free time to play a game I do not like. By other side... there are too many aspects I could not accept, in general I was disappointed and not impressed. Well, I will try to explain.
Best parts of the game are setting and lore. It developed brilliantly, Valkyria Chronicles is not just another fairy-tale about "good and bad guys". It is a tour through a fictional but very realistic world that has its own history and its own problems, like economical and political issues or cultural acceptance of national minorities. There is a lot of attention to small details, well, just look at this glossary, where you can find a lot of various information, from historical facts to weight of anti-tank gun. Look at these maps, where each street has its own name. For example, did you noticed that one of the streets of Bruhl is named in honor of general Gunther, father of our protagonist? Look at biographies of characters, not only major characters but every insignificant infantryman in our squad has its own small story. All this, taken together, creates a magical atmosphere and immersion. I believed in Valkyria Chronicles, I delved in this game and I loved it, but...
...but then, I was faced with characters that inhabit this world, and I felt myself, well... cheated. Problem is, I just can not believe in storyline of Valkyria Chronicles. It filled with obvious cliche, like "war is bad, friendship is good and, despite everything, life is going on". Most situations looks frankly false for me. I guess, story was designed by people, who know nothing about army, relationships and discipline. Watching countless cutscenes, too often I was not sure, should I laugh or cry. My point is... I do not demand realism in game about magical girls called "Valkyrias", but if game pretends to talk about serious issues - such as patriotism, xenophobia, humane attitude to enemies and eternal question "do end justifies the means?" et cetera - I expect that these issues will be highlighted properly. I could not understand, what this storyline actually is... is it a bad comedy or slobbery drama or something else, I do not know. Lack of a good story was especially disappointing for me if compared with brilliantly developed setting, so huge is this contrast.
I do not believe in protagonists. A funny thing is that it was easier for me to believe in personalities of antagonists - commanders of imperial army - who are not stereotypical villains "lets destroy the world because we can", but people with their understanding of situation and their reasons to fight. I even feel slight sympathy for antagonists like Jaeger and Selvaria. And for ending... I am trying to not use memes, but in this particular situation, I simply can not find another word but "facepalm". Just facepalm. This ending is terrible, a classic "deus ex machina" in its worst shape. *sigh*
Well, this was my opinion about storyline. As for gameplay, I have very mixed feelings too. Combat system is quite interesting and promising, but also it has a lot of flaws. It is absolutely imbalanced, to be short: in most missions you will need only one scout to win the battle, and all other units are useless. To be fair, there is a couple of situations where you will need to use tank or shocktrooper, but in most cases all you need is a scout (obviously, this will be Alicia) and several useful spells (they called "orders"). Lancers? What lancers? Engineers? Never seen a single one on the field. Tank? Clumsy piece of ma... well, metal.
AI is terrible. It tends to run in circles like headless chicken and often skips turns without any reason. Of course, flaws of AI are compensated with large numbers of enemies but, surely, quantity will not help the imperial army to stand against unbeatable Alicia.
Surprisingly, despite everything, battles was interesting and enjoyable for me. Well, this is my opinion: Valkyria Chronicles is not a strategic or tactical game. It is a puzzle game. The goal is to end missions in less possible count of turns, and suddenly I found that it is quite challenging. I replayed battles again and again, trying to solve this puzzles, and I enjoyed this, even despite all this annoying "evades and misses". Even bosses can be defeated in one or two turns, and doing so gave me a nice feeling of completion.
Last but not least. Game looks gorgeous, I absolutely loved this art-style. Characters looks attractive, landscapes are beautiful, Alicia is cute and Selvaria has huge ch... well, charisma. Eye candy.
So. I can cautiously recommend this game. If you can push yourself through countless silly cutscenes and accept weird combat system, then you probably will love Valkyria Chronicles. Actually, there is some good fun, buried under a thick layer of husk. In fact, there is only one thing that makes me sad... I am absolutely sure that setting of Valkyria Chronicles deserves much better story.
And, well... if it is one of the best japanese games then I hope that I will never see their worst. Valkyria Chronicles might be decent, but consider it as masterpiece? No, not even close.

Ищем причину потратить 104  рублей по скидке и 419 рублей без скидки, на немного улучшенную дилогию Metro. Частично удается: Metro 2033 Redux стала намного лучше, а вот смысл в покупке Last Light Redux найдут лишь самые заядлые фанаты.
Дмитрий Глуховский написал не шибко интересный роман «Метро 2033» и однажды проснулся знаменитым. Выкладывая в интернет главы и попутно обивая пороги издательств, в один день начинающему писателю и опытному журналисту улыбнулась удача: книгу взялись выпустить на бумаге. С тех пор (2005 год) вышло продолжение «Метро 2034» и скоро ожидается релиз «Метро 2035». Сеттинг франшизы отлично подходит под игровую адаптацию, поэтому появление шутера не заставило себя долго ждать. Обе части, Metro 2033 и Metro: Last Light, хорошо встречены общественностью.
2 игры получили улучшения и доработки, однако реально заметно это лишь в первой — Metro 2033. Потому как в Last Light Redux изменений кот наплакал: «по просьбам фанатов», как говорят сами разработчики, в игру добавили невероятно важную опцию — посмотреть на часы и заглянуть в инвентарь. Чувствуете глубину изменений, за которые просят $15 (или 7$, если уже куплена Last Light)? Ах да, еще тут есть улучшенная анимация ближнего боя и тихих убийств. Этого все равно преступно мало для того, чтобы вновь просить деньги за игру. Такие изменения можно и в патче сделать, на худой конец — в DLC за 1-2 доллара.
Зато с Metro 2033 Redux ситуация совсем другая. Игра вышла в 2010 году и на тот момент выглядела очень недурно: передовые технологии, четкие текстуры, хорошая работа с освещением и при этом относительно неплохая оптимизация. Но время идет, и сейчас шутер четырехлетней давности выглядит не столь впечатляюще. Поэтому 4AGames перенесла Metro 2033 на последнюю версию движка 4AEngine. Результат заметен невооруженным взглядом. Совершенно иного уровня освещение, эффекты в разы красивее, объемный туман и дым, которые хочется развеять рукой. При этом игра избавилась от большинства болячек, вроде беспричинных просадок кадров в секунду, графических багов и других огорчающих моментов из оригинальной версии. Только вот трупы по-прежнему могут проваливаться сквозь объекты: то нога монстра будет торчать из бетонной плиты, то полтуловища уйдет в стену. Также никуда не делись бесконечные орды противников — будут переть, пока не выполните задание. К счастью, таких эпизодов мало на протяжении шести-семичасовой кампании.
Которая все так же интересна, и парочку изменений в Last Light сугубо для фанатов. Приобретать обе части есть смысл, только если до этого не играли в Last Light. Но игры вышли топово!!!!

CONS:

If you're a collectionist buff, you will be annoyed because if you accidentally go into another chapter, you are forever prohibited from going back and collecting things you may not have known you missed. There will be like, 5/10 things to find, and you won't know that you didn't find all the things in the previous section of the level.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a painfully adorable resource management game that manages to make the seemingly dull task of sitting behind a store counter fun and engaging by virtue of its barter system, the ups and downs of the item market, and the almost fiendish  joy you experience when you sell an expensive item for 300% of its base price after you just bought it for 45% of said base price a few days ago.
Add to this a basic dungeon crawler (that however can get rather tedious in the later and larger dungeons), about eight companions to unlock and equip for aforementioned dungeoncrawling, a New Game+ Mode, the Endless (Sandbox) Mode, Survival/Survival Hell mode, and finally the sheer number of items you can buy, find, or craft, and Recettear offers an impressive amount of gameplay for what may initially appear ot be just another random japanese moe blob title.
The only real downside is that you will inevitably develop the urge to feverishly rub your hands together after every good sale you negotiated.

I could spend ages in the customisation menu between stages - just as long as I wasn't holding back impatient fellow players.
The yet-to-be-implemented game saving feature will hopefully spare players the current need to set aside over an hour for a satisfying session.
Bosses feel a little repetitive and would benefit from unique features that set them apart from each other - currently, they all feature weak points, minions, and a lot of bullets - nothing more.
Great for a longer session with like-minded friends on the couch.
