Story mode "complete" as of 10.7 hours, mainly on easy/normal difficulty. I have not completed finding all the various card storylines (example is how you go and give a vampire your blood one card, then you get to go to a vampire auction as you get a token and unlock more story card options).
25 dollars? Kind of expensive, but unique and fun enough game. It's fine enough. I got this game in a humble bundle for 7 dollars. Worth the price I spent.
Gameplay works by getting a deck of cards, which has various events inside it. You have a token on a tabletop, which can move to adjacent cards. Upon moving onto a card, you reveal the event hidden inside, and will have to fight/go for a RNG card choice to complete the event. Pretty fun, the randomness is kind of offputting and I am not sure if its randomness can be "read" or not.
During the story mode version (story mode + endless mode), you choose to fight various bosses from the dealers "court". These bosses are taken from a standard suit of cards, jack to king, with 4 types of enemies - dust (human bandits), scales (lizardmen), bones? (undead), and plague (ratmen/skaven if you're a 40k fan). These bosses have various abilities to make things challenging, and it's ok enough.
Enemies consist of the 4 suits as well as other non-suits enemies like goblins. Entering a battle scene means you go into a top-downish arena to mash wasd and space (to roll/dodge) while left clicking to attack. Standard fare, it's not that difficult and gets kind of tedious in the long run. Until you get damage-locked by a boss, in which case it becomes irritating. Otherwise dodging a lot is required at normal and hard difficulties, getting hit makes you lose health, get to 0 and you die, no stamina bar.
While carrying on the tabletop (i.e. not fighting monsters), you can also get blessings and curses which affect the difficulty level by making it easier or harder, or making things riskier. You need food every time you move to a different card, 1 food per card, run out of food and start losing health every time you move to a new card.
Gameplay (battling monsters) - easy enough
Gameplay (tabletop) - tedious+fun+irritating at times, very RNG based depending on cards/encounters.
Graphics - Not too shabby, better than I expected.
Sound effects - Nice music, nothing I care too much about but I don't dislike it either. Was just... good background soundtrack.
Price - Full? Maybe not. Anything less than full price? Sure. Half price? Might as well.
DLCs - No idea

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Rogue, Card builder with Real-time combat
The Good:
+ When different genres are mixed together the results can be very unpredictable, yet when they work you get a pleasant surprise. Hands of fate thankfully does a successful job of mixing rogue with building a card deck with real-time combat. The game is pretty simple in its execution, you build a deck with equipment and 'encounter' cards, the dealer then mixes in his own cards (usually bad ones). The deck is then shuffled and the cards are placed faced down on the table. Most cards have a game of chance involved, the higher the reward the higher the risk. By completing cards, you then unlock new cards that can be used in subsequent play-through’s, usually resulting in greater rewards.
+ Unlocking new cards and equipment is very satisfying
+ You also have to manage 3 types of resources, health, food and gold. Every time you select a card you lose one food. Run out of food and you begin to lose health after every selection. Certain cards reward gold/food/health. Acquired gold can then be used to purchase food, equipment etc at a shop.
+ To make things interesting the dealer mixes in 'curse' cards in the deck. These cards are numerous and can drastically change the way the game is played. I.e. enemies do double damage, lose gold after every turn etc.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
Combat is a big part of the game and it just isn’t as good as other games. Combat is identical to Rocksteady's Batman games, you have a strike, counter and dodge button. The animations feel stiff, hitting enemies doesn't feel satisfying and the mechanics never change. The combat starts to feel rather repetitive after awhile. I found it strange the developers decided to use real time combat instead of a combat system that used cards which is the games entire premise.
Glitchy achievements.
Conclusion:
This is a great unique game on Steam that is a bit rough around the edges but ultimately provides a very enjoyable and satisfying experience. I understand they are making a sequel which aims to improve many of the weaknesses from this game. If you like rogue-lite type of games and are looking for something a bit different, hands of fate will certainly deliver hours of fun.

Four long years I waited for this game and what I got was a mixed bag. The developers remained silent for a long portion of the games development, pushing the game back every year for
years. All while feeding us information on the game with crumbs of short bursts of PR on their
and the steam store. The community was having its own riot on the forums, begging for even the smallest amount of information in a sea of conspiracies that they took the money and ran from their
campaign (which has yet to be updated. 12/6/2017)
But what about the game?
When I started up the game I was initially surprised. Both factions played differently, however the road to victory is always won the same way. The AI is easily exploitable as you can simply push the other faction off the point so long as you don't do anything violent. My favorite map involved a bridge; I had my shields enter a defensive stance and simply
to the other side of the bridge. I did this for every mission, but only finding the resolution to finish the "No Tav" campaign. However, even this tactic wasn't easy as the cops have the tendency to run away from the battle and ignore orders, forcing you to restart the mission.
Rioters were by far the most fun while still being on the same road of victory as the police. The easiest way to win is to send a group right up to the cops, plop their butts on the ground and tell them reach for the sky as if God himself came down from the Heaven's. Cops will tremble in fear at the sight of Samantha's badly done nail polish on full display. All other items and abilities are useless when compared to the sky-hug tactic.
Speaking of items and abilities-
Police have the ability to choose between
different batons and a wide array of useless items that are the same for every officer class. Armor and weapons increase the cost of officers and their deployment, however there is no clear reason as to why you would pay attention to your cash reserves since you are given a seemingly endless budget. The large selection of grenade launchers, weapons, flags and armor have no visible stats and don't seem to actually matter. I was able to cut my gameplay time in half when I figured this out.
Is it good?
What you get is a mobile game with some pretty pixel art and some tear jerking cutscenes. Even after four years this holiday ham is still undercooked and kicking. The word for this game is "Potential," as it still has the potential to become the perfectly seasoned, oak  roasted ham it set out to be. So long as the dev's are willing to throw it back into the oven.

Went in with no expectations and left 8 hours later think... that was a bloody fun game!
So, imagine a movie from the 1980s, it's about Humans fighting machines, only the movie isn't Terminator, it's some B-Movie Polish Sci-Fi movie starring a guy that vaguly looks like Michael Biehn. They wanted to hire Michael Biehn to be the actor, but sadly the producer had spent the entire budget on the SFX - that's basically Hard Reset.
Forget about trying to make sense of the story, which is pretty off the wall and has liberal use of swear words (like a teenager out of earshot of their parents). For this game isn't about an deep storyline where the plot is a social commentary - no; this game is about one thing... shooting robots. Lots of robots, and causing some really impressive explosions.
That's where Hard Reset excels - making things explode.
It has some of the best lighting effects I've seen in a computer game, which it uses it effectively throughout the game. I'm not one to really care or comment on lighting in computer games, but for once I'm willing to give it a go.
The neon world (insert Blade Runner comparison here) contrasts well with the dark gritty under-streets you start in. Yet that isn't the most impressive part of the lighting, it's the lightning that comes from your gun, or sub-stations that spew out lightning shocks that attack the robots and cause environmental damage. Wonderful stuff. Or the huge fireball explosions that emit from Gas Mains and Pipes. It's all nice stuff.
Also, like all good 80's Movies this game plays host to one amazing soundtrack that underscores the entire gameplay experience. Like classic shooters before it the music kicks in when the action ramps out and dies out as the last robot's motorservers slowly whine down as it dies in front of you. It's hard to describe the soundtrack, but it fits like a glove.
Basically this is a First Person Shooter. It's not ashamed of being a FPS; it grabs the genre and runs with it, only it doesn't stop after the first down... no it continues. It doesn't attempt to re-invent the wheel at any point in the game, so it might get a little stale towards the end, but for me the fun lasted a good 7 hours. It was just refreshing to play a game that knew what it was and tried to be the best it could be at it's genre.
I'm not going to claim it's an 'old school' FPS, as it isn't, but there are some nice nods to previous FPS throughout the game that fans of the genre will pick up on.
The biggest compliment I can really give this game is that I expected nothing, and came away wanting to raise awareness of the game and get more people playing it.

Story:
In an alternate universe Europe is undergoing WWII due to a lack of a multipurpose energy resource called ragnite. The neutral country Gallia is invaded by the Empire for its rich ragnite resources
. The main characters, Welkin and Alicia, end up leading Squad 7 and take part in various military campaigns. As the war goes on the true motives for the Empire's invasion are revealed.
The story is told through episodes. Some of them you play and some you just watch. It is kind of like an anime and there are even filler episodes you can buy responsibly with your military funds, one of which is the anime required beach episode. You can rewatch episodes but you cannot replay campaigns. The only campaigns you can replay are the bonus skirmishes, most of which resemble the actual campaign you played.
Gameplay:
This is a turn based RPG, however you have full control of your character (a unit of your squad) and can aim with them too. There are 6 classes: Scout, Shocktrooper, Lancer, Engineer, Sniper, and Tank Commander. Scouts can move the farthest in one turn and spot enemies more easily than other classes, they have a weak but accurate gun and their defense is low. Shocktroopers can move a low to medium amount in one turn, their defense is good and they can carry a powerful machine gun and flamethrower. Lancers cannot move very far but they are effective against tanks. I believe they can also get a variant of their weapon that makes their lances (rocket launchers) have a wider spread for groups of enemies. Engineers can refill ammo and repair guard towers, sandbags, and tanks. They can heal more effectively too. Snipers cannot move very far and have low defense. In the first half of the game they are pretty much useless because they will ALWAYS miss. Later on you can upgrade your sniper rifle with Aim stat A and they will be pretty useful then. Tank Commanders will always be in their tanks. You will get 2 tanks in the game but in the first half you can only control 1. Tanks can kill other tanks and groups of soldiers and they can break down barricades. You can also use it as a shield for your troops in the back and you get smoke rounds later on.
Although you can aim in this game it does have random elements (RNG). Most enemies will die when you shoot them in the head with a shocktrooper or scout but some will dodge randomly. Lancers and Snipers will frequently miss even on later stages when you have your weapons upgraded. It is not too big of a downer but on the last stage you might have to shoot an armored enemy and they only shot the target 1 out of 4 times. That is 3 turns wasted. Tanks can also shoot armored enemies but they take 2 CP (turns) rather than 1 CP. I said "might" because there is a chance that the boss won't activate those armored enemies (another random element). On a reload he did not and I was able to finish the boss on that turn.
You level up and purchase upgrades for the entire class rather than individual characters. In my opinion I love that feature because you can play the game without too much fuss. YYour squad members can die but you can save them if you get to them in less than 3 turns, complete the mission or reload a save from before. But you get an achievement the first time one of them dies so I was OK after one of mine died. The princess even gives you an award. Joking aside it was kind of sad when my squad member Coby died because they each have their own story and personality shown by their dialogue and unique abilities. Some characters unique abilities and they like certain people. When they are by a person they like (as a friend or love) they get status up. I believe status up makes them less likely to miss or raises their defense. I am not too sure. The character like system doesn't really get in the way of the game but it would help those that wish to use it. Each class also has certain abilities that are unlocked as you level up in addition to the unique ones. While some unique abilities simply give them a status up others change the gameplay. One unique ability, "Hard Worker", allows the character to shoot again. Another one allows you to instantly heal. Certain class abilities can increase damage, or allow better tank repairs. There are some bad abilities too. One called "Moody" prevents you from doing anything on your turn. Some characters are also racist or sexist and will get a status down by the type of person they hate, including Darcsens, women or men.
This is a fun great game and it really is fun planning your moves. The ability to move your character and aim with them is a plus. I only like RPGs if they allow you to control your character in some way, like Mario & Luigi. There is even a New Game Plus. This is definitely a buy.

Valkyria Chronicles' gameplay is comprised of the "BLiTZ" system, a blend of turn-based and real-time combat. You probably know the basics of both, turn-based systems involving planning and strategy, a general map of the area involving what you can or can't see, several different units whom you usually control and real-time systems involving fast gameplay akin to action games, micromanagement, also a general map of the area, etc.
Before the general gameplay starts, you choose your units. After you've placed your units, you're taken into the "Command Mode", the turn-based part. In Command Mode, you get a map of the area, your units and enemy units, and how much "Command Points" you have. Command Points are used to execute orders (specific actions you can use to up a unit's stats or perform other things) and to control Units. When you control a unit, you're taken into "Action Mode", the real-time part. In action mode, you have a bar at the lower part of your screen showing how much "Action Points" you have, essentially how far you can move, which is pretty much everywhere as long as you have enough AP. You can only perform one action (shooting, healing) each time you control a unit. You can move a unit more than once, however they will have less AP until the next player turn. Once a battle is complete, you gain EXP and "DCT"(money) based on the rank you received, which you can spend on leveling up units, and weapon and tank upgrades, respectively. One annoying thing is that while the rank given is primarily based on the amount of turns it took, it feels as if the game wants you to do things a specific way, and if you don't then it will give you a low rank with low EXP and DCT, made even more frustrating when it wants you to do things you wouldn't on a blind playthrough.
Going more in-depth about gameplay, you have to be careful while advancing because all units have a passive attack. If a unit is close enough to an enemy unit, the enemy will begin to attack. All units also have return fire, where if an enemy attacks then the attacked unit will attack back, if they are in range. If you have bases, you can call in for some of your reserved units to join the battle, however if the unit has not arrived yet and the enemy takes the base, they don't arrive. This works both ways however, you can take their base and their reinforcements won't come. Remember that the enemy team is pretty much equal in terms of gameplay mechanics, meaning that they can do all the things listed above.
The A.I. can also be quite stupid. Sometimes you can accidentally lead it into a situation where it will end up using all of it's CP in an attempt to move a couple of meters, completely expose their tank weak spot to me, or one where it would rather take out 1/2 of each tank's health rather than just straight up killing one. You're never going to be playing against revolutionary A.I. that's going to use actual WWII tactics to flank you and destroy your entire team.
Level design is varied, from a small town that's great for shocktroopers to a massive desert which you might want scouts and snipers for. The levels allow use for teaching certain mechanics to prevent the player from being overwhelmed, and as you begin learning how to use the mechanics, the level design will scale with that. There are 2 small difficulty spikes, however that's merely because you're going into the levels blind without knowing what's coming ahead.
This system allows for more strategy, as you will have to think more about your actions because it will mean the difference between a wasted CP and a well used CP. It also allows you to merely go in guns blazing Rambo style if you want, at a high risk however.
The unit classes are Scouts, high-mobility but low health and aren't particularly good at combat. Shocktroopers are opposite to the Scouts, low-mobility but high health and are very good at combat. Lancers shoot anti-tank rocket launchers which will take out a big chunk of tank health, that is if they can even hit the tank at all, as the rocket launchers are so inaccurate they're practically a melee class. Engineers are able to repair sandbags and tanks, restore Lancer, Sniper and Tank ammo, however in other ways are pretty much downgraded scouts. Snipers are Snipers, put them somewhere they can see the battlefield and they can take out most specific units for strategic purposes, however they are vulnerable to enemies in CQC. The Tank is, a tank. They can easily breach through enemy lines and are practically invincible in the front and sides to ordinary gunfire, however they use more CP than other units and are vulnerable in the back, and aren't the most mobile.
Talking class balance, the only 2 that I have a particular problem with are Scouts and Engineers. Engineers are downgraded scouts, and they serve no real purpose aside from just sitting beside the tank and using their attack to repair the tank. Scouts, being highly mobile are able to move across the battlefield and stealthily take out enemies. Despite the game telling you they are not the best at combat, that's not true at all. Using orders given near the start of the game, they're practically shocktroopers with less bullets in the magazine. In later stages where the main objective is to get to the base camp, they're the best bet. Aside from those 2 classes, the others are generally fine.
Valkyria Chronicles is set in Not-Europe, in Not-WWII, a war caused by the demand for Not-Petroleum, by the Not-Nazis, against the Not-Allies, in a story which happens to involve the Not-Jews, hated by both sides and the magical girls who wield powers unknown to mankind, just like in WWII.
The story is certainly cliche, has some strange pacing issues, has the corny Japanese-English translations one comes to expect, and has it's fair share of moments where you're thinking something else could have easily happened and they're just being stupid, however it still has a pretty engaging story with plenty of entries on characters for some great character development, even on seemingly minor characters. Except for the guy at the base who always says "bro". I want to kick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of that guy.
WWII is commonly associated with worn-out colours, usually greens. Not-WWII however, has a vibrant colour palette consisting of bright reds, yellows, blues, blacks, etc. It's much more visually interesting than the theme of WWII would have you think, and combined with the "CANVAS" graphics which makes the game look like watercolour pictures, it's bloody beautiful.
The soundtrack is great. It sets the tone for the story and theme of Not-WWII, swaps to match gameplay and story accordingly and the orchestral style doesn't feel out of place.
The tank controls with KB+M are♥♥♥♥♥♥ the mouse doesn't work on the menus, the FPS is tied to the game speed/physics which is a shame because it's an incredibly well optimized game, running on my piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥with no GPU.
Valkyria Chronicles certainly has some flaws, however it damn well makes up for that in it's gameplay that leads to some intense situations that strategy and thought will solve, visually stunning graphics, great soundtrack and a charming story with memorable characters which makes this game an anime series that you play through.

The investigation mechanic should be great, but its implementation is usually just okay. Other times, the game is weirdly picky about which facts contribute toward a conclusion, and on more than one occasion the expected answer to "what do I know about [thing]?" is just "[thing]." In grainy, prerendered cutscenes, the main character will react with astonishment at details he's already stared at and committed to memory. The investigation into his murderer starts at square one, despite the opening scene showing he knew enough to track down and confront the killer. At no point does this police detective seem to understand how, why, or even
he did.
Since the game has only about eight level maps, the transition between well-developed, fully funded zones and "we're out of money, just make a maze with some combat arenas" is stark. One level (toward the middle, surprisingly enough) is unique in having items that can be examined and generate a little popup description like clues do, but aren't clues and contribute toward nothing. The stealth combat is slow and frustrating; the only way to win is to walk up behind enemies one by one, hiding as necessary if spotted. And you will get spotted, because your movement speed is low, the enemies can turn around instantly at the end of their patrols, and the kill move requires you to hold a button and complete a simple QTE, leading to a surprising number of failures (though maybe that has something to do with using mouse & keyboard to play what is a painfully obvious console port). If you're killed, you get to attempt to sneak-walk behind the whole group again, one at a time. Fortunately, the enemies come in small groups, but even a small group is too large when each kill is so laborious, and the stealth options so minimal.

With a pulse-pounding soundtrack and an amazing visual style, Neurovoider has incredible presentation that sucked me in immediately. Unfortunately, all that audio/visual polish is makeup for a rather plain game with some pretty glaring issues. While it wants to be a frenetic experience of shooting and slashing similar to Nuclear Throne, the design decision to make projectiles vanish after a distance means that the best way of engaging any enemy is to move forward to lure them in, and then backtrack so their shots disappear before they can hit you. Weapons like sniper rifles and the mini-nuke can kill enemies from off-screen, and since your ammo resource is recharging energy, you can just slowly advance while shooting mini-nukes and killing enemies before they even notice you.
Nuclear Throne managed to blend melee and shooting action together by making it so melee attacks deflect bullets. This game features melee weapons, but again, since the best way to beat enemies is to outrange them and there's no way to deflect attacks, they end up being purely suicidal. There are a number of powers that try to address this but it's not enough to make them ever feel viable.
The game's difficulty is also extremely uneven: While most enemies are complete weaklings who are no threat at all, "super-elite" enemies, depending on their equipped weapon, can just ping you with a sniper rifle or fire a massive barrage of rockets for an instakill. This ends up making the game feel like a chore, as you chew through 2000 more meaningless enemies on the next run before being wiped out in an instant.
The game advertises "8736 unique enemies to blow up", but what they really mean is that enemies fall into category of "Sword guy, flamethrower guy, gunner guy", with negligible variations. It comes off as blowing smoke.
I really want to like this game, but ultimately gorgeous visuals and a rocking soundtrack can only drag a boring game along so far.

So, by this time I'm done with the game. Having done most but not all side missions. Worth mentioning that I got it via the Square Enix's mystery box for March which was 10$. For those looking for the punch-line of the review on if it's worth your money or not (29,99$), here it is guys and gals: If you like point and click adventure games, sure, go ahead, it's one of the better of it's kind, you don't see tripple A point and clicks that often. If not, I'd wait for a really good sale. Also keep in mind that the replayability value is low, if any.
Now, into the depths:
*The Plot* : You're a badass detective under the department of the Salem area, an active serial killer is around and you just happen to pick to have your badass moment going-in without back up moment in the wrong place and in the wrong time, getting killed. Surprise, you're now Casper and you get to be a detective in the afterlife trying to solve your own murder while trying not to get killed (again) by demons in the ghost town. The concept in itself is marvelous- who wouldn't want to be a ghost detective? But the execution.. Don't get me wrong, it had it's moments and a few great twists, but for the most time the story felt predictable, the characters felt very shallow and generic and they certainly  did not make me to want to know more about them. I really wanted to buy into the world, but I just could not feel it. Overall, the world building felt weak, if not rushed. It's like reading one of those books that you thought they were okay, but you just wished there was more to them because their description made you expect more. In short : -Average
*The Gameplay*: As I mentioned earlier, the gameplay is point and click for 90% of the time. Those interested in L.A Noire/Sherlock games are out of luck, no observation needed what so ever, your only penalties are that you lose 'ranks' each time you make a mistake, that's pretty much it. Outside that, you go from area to area, you point and click at clues, you get clues, you point and click clues into a sequence and tadam, you're the Sherlock Holmes of the Underworld. Is it repetetive? Very. Is it a criticism? Not in this genre. Outside the point and clicking, you'll get to jog around the world for quite a bit from place to place with occasional simplistic puzzles that for the most part -you guessed it, require you to click on something and see magic happen. I gotta point out that the navigation after some point gets tiring and as a result of the world not feeling very lively, the game would have benefitted greatly from a fast travel option at some point. The devs put some interesting 'invisible' walls around the game so that as a ghost, you cant go through everything, you gotta go through the simplistic puzzles, of course and on top of that, those invisible walls and obstacles which make the world look 'cooler', also make it harder and pointlessly longer to traverse. The side missions around the world although they sometimes have an interesting backstory, are not very engaging for the most part. At some point, the invisible walls get very frustrating, especially once you get your teleport power as they get nonsensical. The weakest part of the gameplay is the combat. It's tedious and clunky. I wish I could demonstrate. There are demons, chasing you around, you have no weapons to fight so you have to hide and execute them from the back. The number of times I was spamming the execution button till it responded  but I left it (you gotta hold it) and failed the quick time event (YES, QTES BOIZ) which most likely resulted to my death or running around for 2 minutes as a result is immense. Not only that but the execution animations remain the same every time and its the same, over, and over, and over.. If you're adding combat, even stealthy combat into your game, you gotta be more creative. A huge spike of irritation comes in the last sequence of the game which becomes unforgivingly hard and 'timed'. I got so frustrated at that point that I finished it on another day. But that's literally the last 5 minutes. Overall, the gameplay, aside from the point and clicking is very average, with the combat being a gigantic unpleasant pain for the player.
*Graphics* : Unimpressive. Although the main character model looks good, the world itself looks mostly uninspired and bland. The textures are pretty outdated and the effects were generic mostly. The character models outside the main character are mediocore. Your enemies are always the same kind, looking exactly the same like someone performed a kage bushin no jutsu (Yep, a Naruto reference). This unfortunately is the same also for the peope around you such as cops and even some ghosts are just so, so uninspired. Overall: Average (probably) for it's time, below average for what it is now.
*Sound, Music, Voice Acting* : The sound of the game is actually good, I found myself enjoying each cutscene after an investigation was over as a result of the robust sound they provided. Its not ground breaking, but it felt more effortful. The music is very repetetive, its definitely not getting any 'extended' remixe's anytime soon, if ever. The voice was okay, the lip syncing was fine but if you were expecting L.A Noire, well, that's not the one.
Is it worth your buy? For 29.99 I'd probably only recommend it to die hard point and click fans that wished for big publishrs to release point and click titles. For the rest, just wait for a good sale. The only thing the game has going for it is it's story which is not as interesting as the cover makes it to be. It's a missed opportunity for a game that would have great potential if you added better combat, a more fleshed out world and made people care for the characters.

- The game is essentially an ETS2 total conversion.  Is that bad? No. Why fix what isn't broken?
- Traffic appears to have some improvement. It still has the blind driver that stupidly runs into you once in a while.
The game has a western US feel to it, driving through California or Nevada. It feels more immersive than ETS2, I find. I'm not far into it, but I enjoy a relaxing drive while listening to the radio.
Suggestions?
My brother was suggesting tandem trucks, box trucks, maybe even expand into tow trucks and big rig tow trucks. I won't mention map expansion as I understand that is the long term plan.
Though I feel like I'm asking way too much for this next idea, but I would love to be able to get out of my truck, walk around, inspect & secure the load, Bring the feet down to disconnect the trailer, hook up any applicable cables/hoses... etc.
I remember the game, Rig'n Roll. It was more story oriented, but I enjoyed it. I liked the story feel to that game. It added a little personality.
A suggestion for SCS, which could generate some extra income:
Implement real advertisements on billboards around town and highways. Lots of potential for some passive income. It could help keep DLC costs down. Or free.

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Rogue, Card builder with Real-time combat
The Good:
+ When different genres are mixed together the results can be very unpredictable, yet when they work you get a pleasant surprise. Hands of fate thankfully does a successful job of mixing rogue with building a card deck with real-time combat. The game is pretty simple in its execution, you build a deck with equipment and 'encounter' cards, the dealer then mixes in his own cards (usually bad ones). The deck is then shuffled and the cards are placed faced down on the table. Most cards have a game of chance involved, the higher the reward the higher the risk. By completing cards, you then unlock new cards that can be used in subsequent play-through’s, usually resulting in greater rewards.
+ Unlocking new cards and equipment is very satisfying
+ You also have to manage 3 types of resources, health, food and gold. Every time you select a card you lose one food. Run out of food and you begin to lose health after every selection. Certain cards reward gold/food/health. Acquired gold can then be used to purchase food, equipment etc at a shop.
+ To make things interesting the dealer mixes in 'curse' cards in the deck. These cards are numerous and can drastically change the way the game is played. I.e. enemies do double damage, lose gold after every turn etc.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
Combat is a big part of the game and it just isn’t as good as other games. Combat is identical to Rocksteady's Batman games, you have a strike, counter and dodge button. The animations feel stiff, hitting enemies doesn't feel satisfying and the mechanics never change. The combat starts to feel rather repetitive after awhile. I found it strange the developers decided to use real time combat instead of a combat system that used cards which is the games entire premise.
Glitchy achievements.
Conclusion:
This is a great unique game on Steam that is a bit rough around the edges but ultimately provides a very enjoyable and satisfying experience. I understand they are making a sequel which aims to improve many of the weaknesses from this game. If you like rogue-lite type of games and are looking for something a bit different, hands of fate will certainly deliver hours of fun.

The game is basically a diablo/old school Link to the Past type game, but running the item shop instead of adventuring. It's surpisingly complex for the chibi anime theme, very analitical, lots of math and statistics, strategically deep with underlying economic mechanics that I'm still trying to puzzle out.  You also hire adventurers to go into dungeons and get items for you, and you control them during their raids, you make decisions about what to stock, what price you offer to each customer, and each costumer has different item preferences and price ranges, and there's a balance between going for maximum profit or increasing your reputation with that costumer. The game has a lot of layers of metagame to think about as well, as new modes become available after the first time you beat it, and much of how you played the game will effect what you can do in those new modes.  You can continue to a sandbox mode, start the game over with new stuff unlocked or go into survival mode where the difficulty exponentially cranks up and you see how long you can last before you go bankrupt.
Each character has a maximum amount of money they can spend, so for some items even if you give them a really good deal, they literally just don't have enough money on hand. As your reputation with that character increases, so does the amount of money they are willing to spend, and you also have to consider how you're going to balance against the mechanics for how you gain experience and level up, which unlocks new abilities, game play features, and items.
There is also some dungeon crawling, which I like, the game has a bit of a harvest moon feel to it, but the dungeon crawling breaks up the monotony, and the characters you send on adventures visit your store, and items you sell them they have available to use in combat, so that's an extra metagame, some times you have a tough choice of selling an item at a significant loss, just because you want your favorite character to get an item they really need.
You only have so much time in each day, so you also have to plan carefully when you open your store, when you go to town, and when you hire an adventurer, and plot elements will open up in town that will advance the story, add new characters, and open up new dungeons.
Many people said they loved the humor.  I'm not seeing it.  A few jokes were pretty good but mostly I found they fell flat, but I know there are definitely some people who love that kind of humor, and besides, you can skip all the cutscenes easily.
You also manage your storefront, the wallpaper, carpets, flooring, and tables you have in your store, that and the inventory on display effects who you attract.  There's obviously an economic element to the game, with fluctating prices opening up opporunities to make lots of money, or to get stuck spinning your wheels with difficult choices to make.
I'm picky about my games, and I haven't dumped this much time into a game in a long long time.  If you like crunching numbers and statistics, deep strategy, games like the original XCOM where you have to manage inventory, manufacturing, and calculate average profit margins, this may be the game for you,  I like games with unique mechanics, a lot of indie games, and if that's the sort of thing you are into you will probably like this game.  And the demo is free and carries over when you purchase the full game, so give it a try.

I've sunk entire afternoons into this game. The characters are adorable and Recette is instantly likable. The story is simple: Recette opens a shop to clear her father's debt with the help of a fairy accountant. Along the way, she meets adventurers to help her gain more items. The gameplay, which can feel frustrating and unforgiving until you make all of the payments, offers a good balance between running the shop and adventuring. The game leaves it up to the player to manage time and money in order to meet each weekly goal.  After this is accomplished, the player can choose to continue in their current save without weekly goals or to play in Survival mode, in which the goals increase exponentially each week.
The gameplay is where this game really shines. The shop sections are engaging as players strive to meet each customer's needs at an acceptable price. There's plenty of ability to customize the shop as well, including expanding, moving tables, and changing the overall atmosphere. I'm a die-hard RPG nut, but these sections were some of the most enjoyable parts of the game for me.
The adventuring sections are really fun too, with the player able to choose from a variety of playstyles in 3rd-person combat. The enemies are challenging but not infuriating and the item drops help the player make more items for the shop.
If anything, the fact that I've already played 45 hours and that I plan to spend many more should tell you something about its quality.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a wonderful game that combines the gameplay of shop managment along with top down hack and slash RPG dungeon crawling. The premise of the game is that the main character, Recet, must pay back a loan in a month with weekly deadlines, where the payment gets larger and larger each week. You encounter heroes in the story and hire them to take you into dungeons to get supplies for your shop. In the dungeon you take control of the hero(adventurer) that is escorting you, to kill the enemies in the dungeon to gain experience and collect dropped items from them. Items can also be found in chests in the dungeons.
The game's art is done in an anime style that I thought was quite nice. When going in the dungeons you have a limited number of items you can collect before you have to start deciding what you want to keep or drop. At first it aggivated me, but I came to understand it made me learn what items were more important making actually think about what I was collecting, so I could properly guide myself into making money easier by collecting the right items and ingredients to create other items that sell for more.
I liked how during the store mode when opening and selling to customers that you had to learn what each type of custmor wanted and their personal views on what is a deal and what is too expensive, making it similar to a real store, because not every customer is going to look at an item the same way. Along with that I liked that it wasn't just selling items that you put on the shelf, but some customers come in to make orders for items some that you might or might not have, which adds extra tasks to complete during each day till the come back for an order, because if you don't have the items on hand, you'll have to try and get said items by dungeoning or making purchases through the market or crafting them.
I liked that the game has a story that evolves over the game. You end up learning about the different adventurers that you employ and run into other characters that effect your shop by either coming into sell you items or buy specific items.
It is quite challenging, most players will end up not making the payment deadline on the loan. I do like that you can continue playing if you don't make the deadline, that it resets you back at the beginning of that week, but it doesn't take items away that you bought or collected that week.
I found the game to be quite enjoyable, watching the shop grow and seeing the quirky silly story of Recet, her shop, and new found friends unfold.
The RPG elements are rather simple, so I would recommend that part to more easy going RPG players, but the store management can get a bit difficult at times, on that I'd recommend it to people that want to play different kind of management game with a funny story.

Ladykiller in a Bind is a smart, funny and well-written erotic visual novel with strategic elements, and is an absolute treat to play, (probably) no matter your sexual identity. The sex scenes are tastefully done and not very explicit, the sub/dom and bondage play is handled with a lot of care and respect, and the characters are all fleshed out and written in such a way that you end up caring a lot about them. (Well, most of them. The President can **** right off)
Different from a lot of other visual novels, the game includes several strategic dialogue and character choices, where you at specific points in the dialogue will have different, time-limited (limited by progressing the text, not a clock) dialogue choices that impact the story and your relationship with the current characters. You also have a limited amount of "suspicious actions" (think Phoenix Wright's penalty system), leading you to balance how you behave and talk based on how much suspicion you've gathered at the time.
At the time of writing I've finished one playthrough (getting ending A, and sleeping around) clocking in at around 6 hours, which is a very respectable time for a game with so many choices and side-character routes to explore, and most importantly - side-character routes I -want- to explore. I'm already itching to go back in and finish the Swimmer's route, figure out the Photographer, being friends with the Athlete, and hopefully get the Boy to some sort of happy ending.

Dag, ya'll.  If there ever was a game I'm mad *I* didn't make, it's 'Hand of Fate'.  A sweet-spot mashup of roguelike, deck builder, narrative choose-your-own-adventure and ARPG, this game swooped in and became my favorite new game in my Steam library(which is pretty substantial at 520+, because I'm a Humble Bundle Hoarder).
The game is really pretty, first of all - very well polished.  The art on the cards is funky, medieval-illustration inspired, and the renderings on the 3D characters are really well done - ragdoll physics as enemies croak are super fun to watch, having them careen all floppy into the edges of the arena.  The random element to the game in terms of the choice cards is shell game style - you see which cards are which, and then you can watch them shuffle before your eyes - you can actually FOLLOW them.  The difficulty arises with multiple shuffles, but it's still great that it doesn't fall to RNG; there is some skill there.
The game is laid out like a tarot spread, and your pawn moves from card to card - you can hop to any adjacent one - and that flips them over, wherein you encounter what's beneath.  Could be a shop, could be an encounter, could be a token encounter - the tokens are a really interesting way to progress the game, and add replay value: each card with icons on the bottom have a chance to give generic tokens, unlocking random cards from the 'common' deck - when you finish a run, the tokens break like seals to reveal new cards.  But there are also storyline encounters - tokens with colored and unique icons - that when broken, give new cards that often progress the storyline for THAT specific card.  You may not reach the objective on the card - in fact, often you're not told what the objective is - depending on how you play you may or may not achieve the card's purpose... but the fun part is putting that card back in your deck to figure out how to defeat it.
Combat is Arkham-styled(when you have a shield), wherein you hit a button to counter when you get the green icons above your head(slap back ranged weapons, slide over and face-smash melee attackers), and red icons are unblockable so you can smoothly dodge-roll out of the way.  Weapons all feel different, they all LOOK cool, and all have different abilities, and not just simple "double damage to undead" type of stuff.  There's that too... but the additions are super sweet, like gaining cash from smacking bandits.
Arguably my favorite portion of the game is the Narrator himself - a mystic with a face veil and a hood who tells the stories of the cards as you progress through the game, and his voice acting is top notch.  He actually comes through with some creepy and cryptic nuggets of wisdom - his narration never seems overdone or trite, there's just enough to keep you entertained, and well crafted.  Listen to him; he reveals secrets, if you pay attention.
This game is a work of art, seriously.  One of the most unique and well crafted experiences on Steam and absolutely highly recommended.

I'll open by admitting the visual novel isn't one of my preferred game formats. I've tried quite a few over the years, but for the most part I lose interest within the first twenty minutes or so. This isn't because of the lack of interactivity or action; it's because, just in general, for games theoretically focused on their textual content, the writing is abysmal.
Ladykiller in a Bind had me hooked before the introductory segment had even ended.
Now I'm not going to tell you the game is entirely lacking in cheesiness - that is, in fact, part of the appeal! What I will say is that its writing is clever, humorous, and, perhaps most importantly, sincere. Scenes that would make me cringe to read in other contexts WORK in this game: they're set up properly, they feel like they're given appropriate weight and respect, and those "uncensored" moments aren't just played for titillation. The plot is, on its face, ridiculous, basically playing a social media popularity contest in an unrealistic setting, and yet through that vehicle it manages to create a variety of interesting, believable, and widely varied characters.
As for the structure and mechanics of the game, the way it approaches your standard conversation branching activity is a bit different from the usual formats of either quicktime style "pick your response before the conversation moves on without you" or "everything hinges on this one choice" that seems most prevalent in these kinds of games. Instead, you get a sort of gradient of choice over the course of a conversation, with options popping up and gradually fading away as they're relevant to the conversation at hand. It lends a sense of realism to the flow of conversation: do you butt in right away as soon as you think of something to say? Do you decide to wait until you can come up with something a little more witty or biting? Are you going to miss your moment entirely trying to think of that perfect response that never comes?
This is a big part of what kept me engaged with the game as I went through it when I might have otherwise lost interest in a core plot that isn't my usual fare, that sense of needing to really be in the conversation and gauge my role in it to decide how and when I need to make a move, if I want to speak up at all, to achieve my goals. It's more complicated than simply "who do I want to make happy?" and then picking whatever seems like it will go that direction as soon as I can. Well, at least it was for me, as I got to know the characters. If you really just want to make your goal "impress X," you can do that, too; it doesn't try to trick you with secretly sabotaging conversation choices. However, as in a real conversation, timing and context is important: what you think might be the best way to get what you want could bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥if you misjudge your audience.
Highly recommended for anyone with even a passing interest in VNs, and even for people who, like me, usually don't find the genre interesting at all. You might be pleasantly surprised.

Valkyria Chronicles is a damn good game. The art is great, the story is good, the VA's are way better than I've come to expect from a localized Japanese games, and the gameplay is a blast.
It does get hard, though. I mean, really hard. Part of it is a normal difficulty curve -- enemies are more numerous and powerful, you have to complete more difficult objectives, that sort of thing. But about halfway through the game, it starts getting cheap. For example, in one later mission, once you capture the enemy camp, two squads of powerful enemies as well as two very scary tanks appear out of nowhere. As soon as you finish that turn, they go and tear apart all your units. It's practically impossible to deal with this your first time in the mission. You will die, and you will start over. Your strategy will totally change because you have this new information, and it feels like you were cheated by the game.
But you can also cheese this mission instead, as you can many of the other difficult missions. For example, the solution to that mission is just to place a unit behind each of the enemy spawns before you trigger them to appear, then destroy both tanks with a single rocket each and finish the mission in three turns. You also get "orders", which let you buff one or more of your soldiers. These are hideously broken. Defense Boost, for example, costs a single CP (unit movement), is obtained early in the game, and lets even your squishiest scouts run straight through a hail of bullets with nary a scratch. It's easy to see how this could be abused in a game where your win condition for each mission is simply to capture the enemy base camp, not to kill all the enemies. Snipers, once you put a few levels into them, can one-shot any visible enemy from across the map. Two of the DLC missions can be completed very early on in the game, rewarding you with game-breaking superweapons and heaps of money and XP.
And the difficulty of the game almost requires it. By the end you're so hopelessly outnumbered and outgunned that completing a single mission without a Wisconsin's worth of cheese takes many hours, assuming you don't just turn it off out of frustration.
But saying it's "cheesing" makes it sound like it's boring, like running through the game with god mode enabled. And it's not! It just becomes its own sort of minigame: I have these very powerful tools at my disposal, but so do the enemies; how do I use them to complete the objective? It's not the game the developers intended, to be sure, but that doesn't mean it's not fun!
And fun it is, this game is excellent. I've had way more than $10 worth out of this game (got it on sale!), and I'd happily have paid $40-50 for it. The tough missions you can't cheese are very satisfying to pull off without any casualties, and the ones where you do shamelessly cheat are fun in their own way. If you're looking for a challenging strategy game, this is the one to get, period.
Has a bit of a learning curve, but if there's a game to get you hooked on grand strategy, this is it.

2)Digging a little deeper into the game - the game's story takes a backseat to it's gameplay. You are equipped with two guns which transform into several types and they can be upgraded throughout the game. This is the only modern mechanic implamented into the game. The game is powered by RoadHog Engine - there are impressive lighting effects, physics and decent textures, but the areas that you will visit are not verried. Almost 15 years ago, I discovered a wonderful game called Progress Quest.
At the time, Diablo 2 and Baldur's Gate and Fallout were trying to seduce players with more quests, more items, more character classes and subclasses, and subitems and subquests.
Progress Quest had the perfect answer to this problem: no graphics, no interaction, no gameplay. Just your stats going up. And a text ticker telling a tale of epic proportions: destroying monsters, getting loot, selling loot, turning in quests. This was the first idle game ever.
I turned into a hardcore Progress Quest player and sought ways to run the game permanently on my school's computer. Then I started multiboxing. I called all my friends and we played online mode while idling on IRC at the same time.
Shonen Idle Z is Progress Quest for the new generation. Sure you have to click sometimes, and this can feel awkward to a seasoned Progress Quest player. But trust me, sometimes you have to add more casual features like sound, graphics or clicking to appeal to a broader audience.
So please enjoy Shonen Idle Z, the spiritual successor to one of the best games ever made.

This game is a masterpiece. Now, that out of the way, lets begin the review! This is a turn-based strategy game with a unique combat system. Unlike games like Fire Emblem where you only position and select units to attack - the Valkyria Chronicles allows you to enter a third-person movement mode called "action mode". In "action mode" you take control of the selected unit and traverse the battle field, while in "action mode" you can have your unit take cover, mantle, hide, and aim for attacks. While moving or preforming certain actions you will loose "energy". "Energy" is what powers your unit, be it tank or infantry. Once you run out of energy you are unable to move but are able to preform actions like aiming, firing, and using items.
Attacking in this game consists of selecting a unit, moving them to a desired location, aiming, and firing, The damage you deal is based on enemy stance, headshot multipliers, and if the have any damage reduction buffs. If you manage to kill an enemy they will fall to the ground in a what I call "Bleedout" mode. While in "Bleedout" the unit is rendered completely immobile and cannot perform actions. If an enemy is touched in "bleedout" they will die and be erased from the enemy roster. This will happen to your units too but death can be prevented by reaching a downed squad member and touching them. This will summon a medic to extract them. Alternatively you can wait 3 turns and not have anyone touch them for them to retreat on their own. When an ally is extracted they can be redeployed after a set amount of turns.
The game has 5 classes of infantry, Scouts, Shocktroopers, Lancers, Engineers, and Snipers. Scouts are one of the backbone memebers of your squad. They have a rifle, hand grenade, and later on a grenade launcher as well as a healing item called "Ragnaid". Scouts are best used for flanking enemies and acting as spotters. As far as combat goes they are nothing extraordinary. Grenades can be used to deal heavy damage to other infantry and light damage to tank treads as well as blow up sandbags. The rifles they carry do considerable damage but are best used to get headshots. Scouts also have low heath but are also the fastest unit and have the most energy. Shocktroopers fill the role as frontline assault units. Their armaments include a machinegun, hand grenade, Ragnaid, and later on a flamethrower. Best used for close and mid-range combat, Shocktroopers are one of the most basic but most useful units in the game. Dealing heavy bodyshot and headshot damage as well as being able to easily destroy tanks, they are one of the most well-rounded unit in the game. They have decent energy and fast speed. Lancers act as anti-armor units with high explosive damage and high health, they fill the need of demolitions. Their arms include an anti-tank lance with 3 shots, Ragnaid, or an optional anti-infantry lance. They are one of the only units that are able to penetrate tank armor. Engineers act as your support units. They are used to disarm mines, heal teammates, repair sandbags and tanks, and deliver ammo to units that use it ( Note; the only times a unit uses ammo is when they use a weapon that has limited ammo, rifles and machineguns do not use ammo but sniper rifles, grenades/launchers, lances do). Engineers are best kept behind the tanks or behind cover. They have a rifle that is the same as the scout's but unlike the scouts they move slower and have less energy. Their arms include a rifle, one large Ragnaid, the engineer's tool, and grenades. Finally we have Snipers, snipers do what else than shoot heads from a distance. They have high-powered bolt-action rifles that have a scope that typically one hits an enemy unless they are behind sandbags. Sniper are the slowest and have the least amount of energy of them all. Their arms include a sniper rifle and a Ragnaid. These units are best kept behind lines and cover for they have very little health.
In the game there is a leveling mechanic. Units don't level individually, instead you gain experience points from completing missions and skirmishes. Using the experience you can access the training field and level up the unit's class altogether. Doing so will raise the unit's health and grant them new abilities and even commands. Commands are used in the battlefield as actions you can ask a "third party" or your squad to carry out. These commands include but are not limited to: sniper support, mortar support, healing requests, retreat requests, and stat bonuses that last for a turn. all of these require "command points" which is our next subject.
Command points are required to move units and carry out commands. Some commands take more "CP" than others and certain units require more CP to use than others, and that unit is...
Tanks!
The tank is where you (the commander) resides during battle. Your tank can be upgraded as well as weapons to enhance their effects like extra damage or extra health. The tank costs two CP to use and has slow speed and decent energy. The tank is armed with one anti-tank cannon, one mortar, and a machinegun. The tank can also only be damaged by other tanks or lancers, bullets deal no damage unless the back of the tank known as the "radiator" is hit. The radiator is the weakest point of the tank. One lance or one tank shell to the radiator and its all over, mission failed. It is advised that you never turn your back to an enemy of any kind. Along the way you will receive a new tank, it moves faster and has less total health but can be outfitted with a flamethower or gattlinggun to replace the cannon.
The enemy also has access to tanks and has 4 different types. The light tank: easiest to destroy, only a real threat to infantry. The medium tank: Has good anti-armor ability and is good at eliminating infantry, has a rear-mounted machinegun to protect the radiator. The heavy tank: extreme anti-armor ability and can destroy infantry with ease. has an extra turret mounted on it that acts as a heavy machinegun that can be destroyed. The tank destoyer: effectively a moving artillery piece, has a very high damaging cannon that cannot rotate, a machinegun, and weak armor comparable to a medium tank.
Each battle has its own twist to it. Some battles you are on an offensive and the enemy will have bunkers and artillery shot down on you. Other times you are trying to hold a position or destroy a key enemy while waves of troops attack. There are also skirmish battles that have no twist and are normally balanced.
In the later half of the game you can upgrade your weapons to deal more damage, have better accuracy, have an added effect like poison, or have more range. All possible with the money you receive from completing missions. You can also buy enhanced uniforms that provide better damage resistance or buy special enhancements for your tank that takes up space on it. There can only be a set ammount of these upgrades but they are worth the times and resources.
That effectively concludes gameplay and the story is wonderful but I will not spoil it in the slightest. The story is up to you to learn and the backstories on the characters are so as well. I wish you a successful war effort Lieutenant!

I can't really add anything to the reviews good or bad that hasn't already been stated better by other people. Right now the servers are a mess, so I've been mostly playing solo or coop. I'll try to hit some things other people don't seem to hit as much about the game.
It's rough, but not on the level of playing an alpha like some have stated. It's more like playing an early beta, but that's what you sign up for with early access. The devs are responsive to issues and even in the few days since it's been released there's been marked improvement. Leveling is easy early on, but becomes harder at a reasonable pace. The word is brutal, and you die alot, but I would expect that from something called a survival game.
Many of the reviews are from people who bought the game for the sole purpose of carping about early access games. It's a game design philosopy that one might not agree with, but spending $30 to air this disagreement shows poor judgment, and anyone who does so is not person who really thinks things through. Disregard the opinions of people who have done this.
One area that Funcom made a mistake on however is adding full male anatomy and a junk slider this early in the process. Nudity is nothing new to Conan art or games (AoC gave us topless females to play with a sweater-kitten slider), and yes, it attracted people to buy the game who might not have already. However, those same people didn't bother to read the early access disclaimer, or they wanted to spend $30 for the sole purpose of giving voice to the sense of humor of their inner fifth grader. As a result the reviews are more difficult to navigate than normal. Time will tell if the early negative reviews will outweigh the added funds to development. However, the fact that the review average rose from 58% to 66% in the course of a week is a good sign.
I like the game, and I think it's worth while even at this stage of early access. If my opinion changes, then I'll update this review. If you're on the fence after watching a few "Let's Play" videos, and reading the reviews, I think it's worth the dive ~IF~ you are willing to endure the trials of early access, and be a part of the game as it grows.
On a closing note, for the fan of Robert E Howard who wants a Conan experience, this does a good job of invoking the ambience of a REH story. It has the same pantheon, and races in the stories and comics, but you don't yet interact with the world in a the same way you might in Age of Conan. There are NPCs, but they are few and far between. This might change, but not likely by a lot. Pulling some freinds and fellow REH fans onto an rp server might quench your thirst, but ultimately the Conan experience is going to be what you put into it.
I give it a thumbs up over all, but I also give the caveat that early access is not for everyone.

There's a lot of good to be found in this game, but it is ultimately let down by its length, scope, and incredibly frustrating 'combat' mechanics.
You play as Ronan, a newly-deceased detective on the trail of the same serial killer that had just taken his life. In his new ghostly form, he possesses powers of teleportation, x-ray vision, and some other supernatural capabilities in addition to his police skills.
The game is fully linear in nature with some detours (small side stories), but ultimately railroads players down a single, short path. Taking my time to look around, I ended up clocking just under 10 hours on my playthrough, but your mileage may vary here. In addition to basically being a one-track experience, the game heavily relies on collectibles to flesh out its characters, setting, and lore; a bad design decision as not everyone may be inclined to seek out every little hidden detail. All Steam Achievements are tied into this as well; if you collect all 242 collectibles, you have 100% completion outside of surviving the final 'boss battle'.
Nonetheless, if you are a fan of murder mysteries, point 'n click games, and supernatural stuff in general, Murdered might be worth a look during a sale (you want to go for 90% off, like I did). That being said, don't expect a groundbreaking ride; interest in the aforementioned things will justify a cheap price tag on this game, but little more than that.
If you have no strong interest in the above genres, steer clear of this game; short on content, zero replayability, horribly implemented and hamfisted combat, some bewildering design decisions, and suffocating linearity (with plenty of walls to stifle your progress) will kill most enjoyment you can get out of this game. Additionally, the developers closed down less than a month after release, which is pretty ironic considering the sense of wanting to get things over with the ending has about it. A shame considering the likable protagonist, but the closest the game comes to outright telling you you shouldn't have bothered.

I'd dearly wish I could give this game a thumbs up and a good review, but I just can't. There's so much here that I'd love to like, but it's all spoilt by bad mechanics and the odd glitch here and there.
First off, I'd like to say that I really like the atmosphere here. It's really quite spooky and well done. I like how there's ghosts that are secondary in that they are just there and will do you no harm etc. I also liked the characters in this game as well. I thought they were acted very well and all gell well together I thought.
Looks are hit and miss, with some stuff looking pretty good, but others looking like sub PS2 quality with very low texture detail, so it's all a bit patchy looking. But there's nthing game breaking here and you'll quickly get used to it all.
But it's the gameplay mechanics that really let this game down. I found it really hard to work out what I needed to do. I'm fine with games that don't hold your hand, but this game has some very obscure mechaincs in place, like finding a photo, then matching that photos position to find a key that opens a hidden area etc. Sounds simple enough, but I had to look a guide up a couple of times, just to see what I actually should be doing, otherwise, I'd just have been walking around in a big loop.
There's also an issue with the actual photo fighting thing. There's a ghost where you need to "shoot" it's red patch on it's back. Despite haveing a camera FULL of shots of the ghosts weak spot, it took me ages to finally get one to "take" and kill the ghost.
Another thing is the Limbo bit when you die. It can take ages to get back into the game from here (and I know you can fix this in the menu), but often, the game will respawn you directly into the ghost that killed you in the first place! A good example of this is the scissor ghost. I've lost count of the number of times I died almost instantly because I got respawned directly onto his attack. This is where I stopped playing.
Such a shame as I dearly want to love this game, but I just can't. My advise? Pick it up in a flash sale (like I did) or download the demo first.

Speaking of the story, however, this main character is easily the dumbest person I have ever encountered in my life, let alone the fact that he's a detective. Ronan didn't die because he was hunting down a murderer, he died because the writers couldn't come up with a good enough excuse for supposedly-respectable police officers to allow this kind of stupidity to act freely in their police department. So they killed him off so that no cops would have to actually deal with how utterly moronic he is. I figured out the story about two and a half hours into the game, and i played a good 5 or 6 hours total to beat it. All along the way, Ronan kept going "Huh, I wonder what this means" when the meaning is so blatantly obvious that a 7-year-old could figure it out, given that this 7-year-old had the utmost basic knowledge on the historical significance of Salem. There was genuinely only one part of this story that surprised me, and even then, it wasn't that impactful because of how upset I was at Ronan for his 6  straight hours of nonstop idiocracy. What really emphasized his stupidity, and I personally find this thoroughly ironic, was when he finally ended up talking with Baxter. Ronan spent the entirety of the game talking about how stupid Baxter is, and when it came down to them actually working together, Ronan had gotten to literally the EXACT same place as Baxter in their search for the killer. Also, overall, Ronan's facial expressions were a huge disconnect. You could tell it was supposed to be a dramatic moment, and Ronan still looked like the infant that I think he really is. Except if that infant were 5'10", had a stubble, and wore a goddamn fedora. Mechanics-wise, it was lacking, but not in such a way that made it hard. Just somewhat tedious. At one point where Ronan should be hauling♥♥♥♥♥across all of Salem, he's instead jogging briskly, taking detours because of how confusing the map is. The teleport mechanic comes in handy, I guess, but honestly it would be so much better if it were just a set distance that you could sorta spam to move faster, instead of having to hold left click, wait for it to charge, and let go, only to travel a repeatedly disappointing distance. Trying to get from the musem to the church was honestly one of the worst sequences for this. I wanted to care about trying to get to the church as fast as I possibly could, but all Ronan could care about was the brunch he was gonna go have with his dead wife after this was all over, resulting in me wanting to start running down my street so that one of us could feel like they were attempting to go quickly towards anything.
tl;dr
story was predictable, Ronan is a moron, and the controls are meh. 14/10 would Julia again.

A well done murder / detective game, Murdered: Soul Suspect was an enjoyable game overall and is worth getting (on a sale) if you’re into this genre.
The plot is straightforward. You play as Ronan, a criminal turned detective who is shot and killed by a mysterious man. Your quest is to figure out the truth behind your murder and why it happened.
Gameplay is mostly good. First off, you play as the ghost of yourself. Therefore, you can walk through most walls and objects which is fun to do. This is carried through the story where characters that are alive cannot see or hear you. You won’t be shooting anyone or have any big action moments. This is story driven first with some puzzles, clue finding scenes and a few small “stealth” parts thrown in.
The puzzles incorporate clues you just found or found in the past. You use them to answer questions the game asks you. “What would help Mary remember?” or “What is Joy doing?” for example. The answers are sometimes illogical but you can just guess again.
Clue finding scenes are exactly what it sounds like. Find all the clues in a particular area in order to figure out what went on.
Stealth sections are the weak point of the game. Luckily, there’s not many of them and it’s not too hard. There are demons that can float around certain areas or inside buildings. To kill them, you need to go up behind them and execute them with a quick time event. However, the controls for this were not predictable and I died several times because the controls wouldn’t respond how I anticipated.
The environment, graphics and sound are all very good. There’s definitely a creepy atmosphere that surrounds the entire city. Although, I found that a lot of the characters looked the same and would mistake certain characters for others.
I thought the voice acting was fantastic. A definite strong point here.
+Turn off VSYNC in the game options
+Enable/force VSYNC in the Nvidia Control Panel
Cinematics will still be 30FPS as they are pre-rendered
One of the biggest complaints I have with the game is the lack of a map. It became frustrating to try and navigate around Salem and forget how to get to certain areas you want to re-visit. The game gives you a navigation marker for your current objective, but that’s it. Throughout my playthrough I was never really familiar with the city. For a game with lots of collectibles, it would have been a great addition.
I initially tried playing with a keyboard and mouse. It seemed to work fine but when entering the in-game diary, it wouldn’t register me trying to move around. I eventually just used an Xbox 360 controller and everything worked perfect.
+60FPS (see note above)
+Good story
+Great voice acting
+Well done animations
+Creepy environment
+No map
+Stealth combat sections
+No save feature, only checkpoints
+Puzzles are too easy
+Steam overlay doesn’t work
+Keyboard/mouse controls broken
Even with a few faults, I thought Soul Suspect was a good game and enjoyed playing it. It’s a little short, with maybe 8-10 hours to complete. Even less if you don’t collect the various collectibles. So at the current price of $30, it’s a little steep. Grab this on sale.

- The game seems lacking, in tucks and map, however they're working on it. The licenses are all that is left for the trucks and the maps are part of the ongoing evolution of the game, ETS2 style.

Do you like driving in real life? Do you enjoy sightseeing and traveling? Good.
American Truck Simulator is a game made in the same engine as Euro Truck Sim 2, and it surely shows especially if you know ETS2 very well like I do, but this is not a bad thing. American Truck Simulator takes advantage of the ETS2 engine and adds quite a bit more to make the experience as authentic as possible.
As it stands now, this game is still being developed, and as such all further remarks should be treated as an early-access review.
Pros:
-GRAPHICS: Absolutely stunning scenery for such a small download, in my opinion this game blows ETS2's scenery out of the water, and if they continue to do this great of a job I really don't think I'll be able to stop exploring the country.
-SOUND: Nothing special, a few background tracks and that's about it, if you've played ETS2 you pretty much know what to expect. The cool thing is you can link song files from your harddrive to play in the game much like the GTA series, and trust me this makes a huge difference to your gameplay experience, crusing the US to your favorite jams is pretty damn awesome. My only gripe with this custom radio system is that the songs are played in exact order as opposed to random, and if you're like me and put hundreds of songs in there, you don't really want to randomize them yourself.
-GAMEPLAY: It's a truck simulator, I mean what do you expect, you drive a truck and deliver cargo. However, ontop of the aforementioned truck driving, you can also; Own a delivery company, hire drivers, buy and modify trucks, free roam to find further career opportunities, and just plain sight-see.
That's all I got for right now, but I've only put 8 hours into the game and I definitely look forward to putting more into it, if you're at all into simulators or driving I can assure you will have fun with this game.

This game does nothing better than completely make you one with the world. At times you'll feel filthy rich, and other times, completely helpless. As you run the shop every day, the game teaches you very early on that you must be as efficient as possible to maximize profit and not lose the game (and your home). Even though collection day seems like a far-off hurdle, you must not remain complacent with your business. All it takes is a haggle taken too far, or purchases made too carelessly to ruin you. As Tear counts your 80,000pix fee only to count 79,860pix....
Well, game over. Your payment is void.
Much like running a business, this game is difficult. You have get it right once. When you lose you have to start over from day one. Fortunately,
, except starting with 1000pix again. Unfortunately, you have to run through all the dungeons from the beginning.
There's a lot to stomach when you first run through the game. Eventually you have to keep track of orders and making sure you have a wide variety of stock. I have notes scribbled on my desk about how one customer never purchases anything at 115%, and how this customer buys at around 125~130% of cost. It can also feel grindy at times when you're in the dungeons fighting enemies.
But what makes Recettear so warm and inviting is the fact that you are so much a part of this world as much as the next NPC. No matter how hard it is to make ends meet in your store, you are still a participant in the town around you. Your business, customers, and explorations are as real and as stressful as you want them to be. To paraphrase Tear, "It's more of an art than a science. There's no map to follow."
There are so many variables to take into account. Recettear is not so much a simulation, than it is an experience.

Visual novels have always had a strange relationship with sex. It’s been an ever present part of them, but the inclusion often being so clunky you’d swear the writer was forced at gunpoint to put it in. Ladykiller in a Bind isn’t like that, as this is a story where sexual relations are front and center. Lots of thought and nuance was put into its portrayal. This isn’t just a breath of fresh air for the genre, but something that felt missing from media in general. It’s unapologetic and honest, and I’m pleasantly surprised to see it on Steam.
Beyond the sex, the level of ambition here is higher than in Christine Love’s previous titles. Branching dialog choices fade in and out depending on context. This means it’s good to have patience and not click the first thing that shows up on screen, as it represents the least thoughtful response by the protagonist. The music is effective at making the game a nice place to spend your time. You get positive vibes simply from having it running in the background.
