I originally bought this game on Humble, my play time with that version is at about 8 hours as of this review.
Ladykiller in a Bind is one of the most competent visual novels I've played to combine comedy and (primarily) lesbian erotica without relying on goofy slapstick or worn out anime character tropes. Attention has most notably been paid to making the characters all feel like interesting people who have their flaws and hang-ups but are fun to be around - even if that fun comes from you pushing their buttons until they snap.
On the side of raw game mechanics, Ladykiller builds on the typical VN style by allowing you to ignore the dialogue prompts that appear on-screen and instead let the conversation continue naturally, new options appearing as new details come up in the conversation, and old prompts disappearing as things move on from where they would be relevent. One small but very useful addition is the inclusion of a tone indicator, letting you know whether the option you are picking will be spoken sarcastically, reasonably, etc. The game also goes out of its way to make clear which options will unlock new paths, give you rewards or penalties, so you won't end up uncertain of why something just happened.
Depending on your reading speed, a playthrough will take 2-6 hours. Exploring all of the main paths will probably take around 6-10. All the paths are dense with dialogue and humor, but this game is priced higher than some people are willing to pay for a VN. I found the price to be acceptable, but not everyone is in the same financial situation and the cost-to-time ratio isn't the best for someone primarily looking for the most playtime for their dollar.
Oh, also the sex scenes are all very good, using the same dialogue system as the rest of the game throughout, and make up about 1/3rd of the game's full word count. Which is a lot.

Take note indie-devs: THIS is how you make a proper twin-stick shooter. Simple, easy to learn, addictive gameplay. Since it contains "rogue-like" elements it is also eminently replayable.
You play a human brain (the last human brain) inserted into a combat chassis to retake a world overrun with partying robots-- like literally partying, speaker systems act as explosive barrels. Obviously the robots don't take too kindly to this.
There are about 20 maps each playthrough with a boss every five or so. Enemy loadouts, like the maps themselves, are randomly generated and the bigger the baddie the better look it drops. Loot takes the form of coins (which recharge your special skill), weapons and modifications for your chassis, which you can swap out and upgrade between levels. This is a very fun process and can take several minutes as you compare stats and spend scrap, which can also be used to re-roll level stats. Combat (depending on your selected difficulty) is fast and hectic, and you will learn to identify who is coming at you from off-screen based on their "alert" noise. This can be very anxiety inducing, especially the gutteral groan of an Elite.
Things I don't like, so you don't think I work for the devs or something: There are three types of chassis to choose from at the beginning of the game, but the Tank class is the only useful one. Each class has a unique secondary attack; all of these are also useless. There are 20 or so "specials" to choose from when you start your playthrough, basically special "powers" you can activate that give you some sort of advantage for a brief period of time before they have to recharge. Sadly, the Healing Skill is, you guessed it, pretty much the only useful one. Not being able to repair on the fly while being swarmed from all sides = game over. I wish there were more than four types of "metaverse" levels, because those are a welcome switch from the regular ones.
Lastly, as others have mentioned, the game lacks a certain sense of depth or longevity, but, as you can tell from my cummulative play-time, this is a matter of personal taste.

Ladykiller in a Bind is my GOTY for 2016.
I've written a lot about My Twin Brother Made Me Crossdress As Him And Now I Have To Deal With A Geeky Stalker And A Domme Beauty Who Want Me In A Bind!! in my continuing efforts to convince people to buy it, but here's a bit of a short form review for you if you just want a simple opinion to determine whether or not to buy it:
Ladykiller in a bind continues Christine Love's excellent and deeply thoughtful approach to games, and is both incredibly funny and very interesting. If you're balking at the price for a visual novel, absolutely don't, it's worth every penny. It has a cast of memorable characters who are in some ways very much fufilling and archetype, but are not two dimension enough to be summed up by that archetype. The dynamics between characters are good, the dialogue is top notch, and the use of choices and branching paths is stellar. If you at all are into the idea of visual novels, or even just reading a comedy with pictures, seriously just buy this game.
If you want to hear a longer form review, here's a longer bit of writing about it:
Ladykiller in a Bind, or Incredibly Long Title No One But Me Actually Uses, is a game about... well, I mean, the title explains a lot of it. The main character is forced to act as her twin brother for a week on a graduation cruise, and encounters a not really a stalker geek and an absolutely a domme beauty, and sometimes gets tied up. In impersonating her brother, the main character can get "suspicion" and if you rack up five suspicion, it's game over. Meanwhile, you also collect votes to win a mysterious game with five million dollars on the line. Also, you have sex with your brother's friends and enemies, probably. There's a lot of sex in Ladykiller, I'm just putting that out there right now. You can have sex with the majority of the cast, and every one of the seven nights ends with the main character in either The Beauty or The Hacker's bed. Speaking of The Beauty and The Hacker, character names in Ladykiller are set by the player. Whenever you met a new character for the first time or another character mentions them before you meet them, a quick info screen shows up and prompts you to pick a name from either one of two suggested choices or a custom name.
Christine Love is one of the very few developers of visual novels interested in poking at what the medium can do. Hate Plus was particularly interesting in a lot of ways regarding the fourth wall, and Ladykiller is a game that subverts a lot of how visual novels work normally in a thoughtful way. I've heard it described as "a power fantasy for socially awkward people" and in a way that's right. In most visual novel type games, you have to pick the right option to get what you want, and then if you pick wrong something bad happens. Mostly you just sit there advancing text until a choice happens. In Ladykiller, there's two main differences. First, options pop up during dialogue without interrupting it, and you choose when to speak up. Sometimes you'll reach a point where you have to say something if you've been quiet for too long, but you can cut off characters all the time or jump in eagerly to agree. Secondly, you generally know the outcome of what you're going to say- if it's going to generate suspicion, or get you votes you'll know. If you're about to lose the chance to say an option, it indicates it, and if something opens up more choices, ends a scene or closes off a character, it'll tell you.
What this means is the game becomes less about figuring out the "right" thing to say, and more about figuring out what you want to result from it. On Twitter in the runup to the release, Christine mentioned that she wanted to make "good easy choices" - "that is to say I’m interested in making it easy for the player to do things they wouldn’t normally do, to do the interesting-but-wrong thing". You can generally be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and absolutely know you can get away with it. The game even gives you an excuse- you're trying to act like your brother, and he's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, go for it! On the other hand, suspicion is pretty easy to reset, so if you don't want to be bound to acting like your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brother, you can be more noble than he would be without necessarily getting game over. It makes for a more interesting dynamic than "which is the right answer" or "which of these answers is the one to get the route you want". The design of the game in general is really nice as well; there's stylish cards for picking where to go during the day, the menus and options are all nice, and there's well done dynamic music. Characters change outfit every day, and will sometimes be wearing something different if you run into them in the bar compared to the library, so it's significantly more dynamic than the standard "ten sprites for the entire game and maybe two outfits" deal.
So, let's talk about humour: Ladykiller in a Bind is ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious. I don't think there's a single other game where I've laughed out loud as often as in Ladykiller. If I posted every screenshot I've taken of lines that made me laugh it'd be a wall. The game is just really funny. That said, Ladykiller is also an incredibly honest game in a lot of ways, and part of that is that it's honest to Christine Love's sense of humour, so if tumblr jokes or general memes♥♥♥♥♥♥you off probably you'll get annoyed sometimes. That's not all of the humour, by any means, but there's plenty of it, with The Hacker especially. I think the humour as a whole easily stands up even if you don't know any of the memes or tumblrisms referenced, however.
Now would be a good time to mention there's a joke SFW option that puts christmas sweaters on everyone in sex scenes! And that brings us to the sex scenes. I mentioned before that Ladykiller is honest, and while sometimes obviously things are character opinions, sometimes things are said that I'm fairly confident are things that Christine Love thinks. And a lot of these are about relationships. The sex scenes are full of explicit consent, jokes, honest conversation, and exploring relationships. Almost all of the characterisation of The Hacker and The Beauty is done in the sex scenes, inverting the normal "get to know this character and then bang them" paradigm. The game doesn't shy away from sex, but it also doesn't treat sex as some kind of ultimate achievement. It's a part of a relationship.
Anyway, I could basically talk about this game forever, but there's a limit to how much anyone wants to read. It's seriously well worth your time and money.

Ladykiller in a Bind is a game about control.  It is also a visual novel with interesting choice systems.  You play as "the Beast" (every character can be renamed), twin sister of scheming weirdo "the Prince".  Your brother has kidnapped you and made you take his place on a cruise ship full of his classmates, who are mostly also scheming weirdoes.  Also, he has arranged a Game to take place on this ship, where everyone is given a vote and the ability to trade it, and whoever has the most votes at the end of the cruise supposedly wins a bunch of money.
Ladykiller revolves around two systems: votes and suspicion.  If you're concerned with The Game, you can work to earn votes from people by (for example) doing what they want or tricking them.  However, many actions also arouse suspicion.  You're pretending to be your brother and do not understand any of his relationships with the other people on the ship, so there is a bit of danger in almost any conversation.  Suspicion is always bad, and if you get five points of it, the game ends.  However, it might be worth taking the suspicion hit in order to change someone's opinion of you from whatever impression your brother had left.
The game is abundantly clear about exactly what effect any option will have.  You never have to guess at the overall outcome of a choice.  When you pick where to go at various times of day, you can see the potential range for vote and suspicion gain for that scene, and when picking options within conversations, you can also see how many votes/suspicion you would gain as well as whether the option might open up more options down the line or just end the scene outright.
The conversation options themselves are mostly interjections.  They appear in the middle of a conversation and allow you to interrupt with something.  If you continue the conversation, they fade and eventually disappear as the moment passes.  However, occasionally there is a consequence for not interjecting, and in those cases the options will not fade until you have made a choice.
To further complicate the votes/suspicion system, at the end of each day you choose to spend time with either the Beauty or the Stalker.  The Beauty will erase all of your suspicion, allowing you to act like a complete fool during the day, and the Stalker will give you votes, making it easier to win The Game, but requiring that you take more care with the rest of your actions.
I primarily wanted to talk about the mechanics of the game in this review, but of course I should also mention that the game has numerous sex scenes, mostly at night.  A lot of the most interesting conversation choices are in those scenes, and you can really alter the tone of your relationship with the Beauty or the Stalker depending on what kind of options you pick.  Like the rest of the game, these scenes are about control, and either the giving or taking of it.
The story is rather silly and I suggest that you not spend too much time thinking about things like how anyone could actually mistake the Beast for the Prince, even if they do have roughly the same face and hair, or how a single school could end up with so many horny Machiavellian backstabbers.  Just take it for what it is and accept that this insanity is happening and that you need to find a way out of it with some shred of dignity hopefully intact (or not!).
Also, the game has a fantastic dynamic soundtrack whose songs change along with what is happening in the conversation.

Pros:
-Clever plotlines and witty jokes. Good use of refrences that are accessable to most players but don't feel pandering
-Fun, casual point and click gameplay. You rarely have more than 3 or 4 objects at any given point and most rooms serve a only one or two purposes.
-Uses an X-Files/Twin Peaks type setting which is rarely seen in video games.
-Both main characters are really likable. Your partner (Officer Dooley) rarely actually helps you, but always has a joke or non sequitur to say
-Looks and sounds really good, regardless of if you're into pixel art or not.
-Most objects are easily defined, and the game rewards you for clicking everything in the room with a joke anway. I only ran into one object that I really coulden't find during my playthrough
Cons:
-Short. Without guides I beat the game in a bit under three hours, clicking and reading just about everything I could find. I hope the creator releases some DLC or similar in the future, I would really like to see some other paranormal tropes explored. This is the main flaw in the game imo.
- 3/6 of the cases are about ghosts or spirits, and one has no supernatrual 'entity' at all. This isn't a universal problem, but personally I wish more supernatrual mumbo jumbo was used
- You never really 'investigate' a scene. There's often a mystery, but you never piece together clues or figure it out as a player. This makes the game a little more casual which is fine, but it's someting to keep in mind if you're looking for a game that requires more deductive thinking.
- There are some cutscenes in one of the trailer that aren't actually in the game. Again, this isn't an awful betrayal or anything, but it's something to keep in mind.
Overall this is a really well made game in my opinion, I just wish there was more of it. It's listed at $13 at the moment, and I can see wanting to wait until a sale drops it to 50% off or so. If you're like me and happen to really like this setting or you really love point and click games, then feel free to pick it up. If you've only got $10 and want to make it last the rest of the month then this might not be the best pick.

It's easy to start up CK II and not get what the fuss is about. Another Euro-centric medieval simulator, like we haven't seen that before. With a snail pace and no sprawling, Total War like combat, it seems more like a "watch time pass" simulator than a game.
But you start a game nonetheless. You chose to start as a small, independent region - maybe the one where you or your ancestors hail from - glory to the motherland and all that. And you just want to learn the ropes, no need to get into anything large. The game starts; you press play and fiddle with the speed. Nothing happens. You leave it on high. Minutes pass; nothing happens. 'OK', let's see what this button at the top left does. You spend the next half hour fiddling with all the info there, trying to make sense of it. From time to time, pop-ups show up, detailing little events that seem to have no impact on the game. 'Oh, cool. This random courtesan fancies me. Who friggin' cares?'.
But one message catches your eye - the neighboring♥♥♥♥♥hat has decided he likes your lands and he'd like to make them his lands. You quickly raise your impressive army only to watch in horror as ten times as many butcher them with ease. Your dynasty ends with its founders head on a pile. Game over.
OK, that went as well as can be expected - can't be be blamed for not winning with the small guy on the first time. You start up another game, this time as the biggest, baddest nation that you see - what greater joy could there be than to steamroll all your punier neighbors into fine grains of dust? As the game starts, you watch with greedy eyes as the gold rolls into your treasury. 'Yeah, time to build some♥♥♥♥♥♥. 'What? It takes one year, costs that much and increases my army by ♥♥♥♥-all percent in this region only?? Screw that, time to slaughter some franks'. 'OK, diplomacy, declare war... Why is it greyed out? Casus Beli??? WTF is that?'.
But no matter, while you were scouring your memory of high-school Latin, the guys to the south have graciously decided to bring the fight to you. 'Pathetic basters, they're like half my size. This is going to be fun'. You raise your levies and merge them into one big glob. 'That skull must mean I'm one deadly S.O.B' you think to yourself. And you march to meet them head on, only to see your guys start to die off before you even get there. 'Doesn't matter' you think to yourself, 'I still outnumber them 2:1'. By the time your armies meet, it's more like 1.5 to 1, and you still barely beat them. But you do. Time to reap the rewards...
Your peasants have taken up arms against you.
Your vassals have risen up to lower crown authority.
Your king has died, only to be inherited by a possessed dimwit.
You have been excommunicated.
The franks have decided that that small little province on the border is theirs and they are willing to drown you in blood for it.
Game over.
At this moment you are fuming. You steel yourself - this stupid game isn't going to get the better of you. You start thinking, 'what's the best starting point?'. You start again, this time as a count in province deep in the heart of a stable empire. You start slow, making friends with everyone. Then your lord and brother dies, making you the new Duke. 'Oh, so I don't have to attack everyone to take their land'. You make a mental note. The years pass; through claim fabrication, key marriages and poisoned wines you grab a few more adjacent duchies. A few gold coins later and you are the King of Bavaria.
This makes the emperor uneasy. He demands that you release a duchy that he claims is rightfully his. You're too weakened from your last conquest to fight him - and it's just a small province anyway. You grin your teeth and accept his demands. And the years pass again; your line is well loved and respected by your emperor and fellow vassals. You are seen as a keen supporter of his Imperial Majesty. But the strangest thing keeps happening. All the bright, attractive or strong princes, they never seem to make it pass infancy. As generations pass, the crippled, the dim and the feeble seem to favored by some unseen force and raise to the crown. Unsurprisingly, your fellow lords are not happy with this rule.
The time has come. You start a movement, to replace the inheritance law with an elective one. A bloody civil war erupts and, after many years, you emerge the victor. You are now next in line to become the most powerful man in Europe. Just. one. more. assassination.
And... the Huns happen. Your empire is too weak and you fail to protect your lands against the scourge.
GAME OVER.
It's morning. You have to go to work in about an hour. You call in sick.
You probably are...

Duration: 40 hours (main game without extras)
Playing Valkyria Chronicles is like watching a Studio Ghibli TV series where in each episode there is a tactical battle that is played in FPS turn-based mode.  Without doing a full review the story was top notch and one of the best I've ever experienced in a video game.  The art style and animations were top quality and the voice acting was also pretty good.  Much of the game will be spent watching these cut scenes which explains the massive 26GB harddrive space needed.
The tactical combat was fun and a wide variety of missions is thrown at the player.  The game starts off easy showing you the ropes before you put your team together Jagged Alliance style.  The characters have a wide variety of personalities and the game is not without humour.
For the actual combat you have a number of command points to move your characters and issue orders.  Once selected it turns into a First Person Perspective for movement.  Characters have a finite number of action points to spend moving and get one attack per activation anytime during their move.  The blend of FPS and turn-based tactical is unique and flows very well.  Defensive fire keeps the tension up.
In between battles there is the headquarters where you can assign experience to your classes, buy R&D, equip found weapons, and a number of other strategic tasks. There are also skirmish battles you can reply if you find your experience of money lacking.
A few negatives keep this from becoming a 10.  First are the tank controls.  Moving the tank in FPS mode almost works but takes a while to get used to.  I spent a couple activations early on spastic-ing in place while trying to inch forward.  Sometimes the controls are hard to move forward just a little to repair sandbags or disarm mines.
Another negative is the mid-game battle versus the giant tank which was almost depressing.  Aside from that though, the battles were great. It was almost information overload once the headquarters is introduced, although it doesn't take long to understand and get into it.
All in all, the graphics, art style, story, squad-building tactical fun is like nothing I've ever played before.  After 40 hours I was sad to see the story end although it did so with Ghibli delight. Overall I have no difficulty recommending this game. 9/10.

Pre-review Note: Mass Effect 3 completes the Mass Effect trilogy but isn't available on Steam. I highly recommend purchasing this for Origin - it's an excellent game and an epic conclusion to the series.
Mass Effect 2:
+ Another amazing, story-driven game by Bioware, where your decisions impact the way in which others view you and how the plotline develops. Become a paragon or renegade through your choices in quests.
+ New locations to explore, each filled with numerous side missions and content relevant to the main narrative.
+ Interesting characters (won't add any spoilers), each with their own personal quest lines.
+ New range of weapons and upgrades, you can even reinforce the Normandy with state of the art equipment.
+ Great graphics, a massive step up from the original title.
+ The game has been streamlined, making it more sleak and professional in appearance compared to the first entry in the trilogy.
- Although Mass Effect 2 looks a lot more refined and stylish than its predecessor, it comes at the expensive of its RPG characteristics. Leveling has been dumbed down a bit, but still plays a role in the game (thankfully).
Overall Score: 9/10

This is a fun pseudo-turn based strategy game that is very heavy on story. Selecting a unit, lining up a shot, using different weapons, and using skills are all turn based with a set number of action points. In an odd twist moment happens in real time; so as you're moving your unit into position you're being shot at continuously and you have to very quickly decide where to go and then mash that action button to freeze time before you die. Beyond that this game ticks all the turn-based tactics boxes. There's unit classes, expierence, and skills. New weapons to capture and research. New global commander abilities to learn (like in Advance Wars). Then finally there's the story. There's a movie's worth of pre-rendered cut scenes in this game and enough text backstory to fill a novel. The more you use a unit the more you learn about them and it fills out this encyclopedia in between battles. If you're looking for a Final Fantasy Tactics level of story, this is the game for you. Graphics, art-style, and music are all top-notch.

Saw this game last year, probably when it came out. Thought it was amazing for numerous reasons. The game itself looked good and promising. I'm a huge fan of spooky games, and I love the lore and mythology behind spirits and cameras.
Honestly, I'm not the best at writing reviews, but I really enjoyed this game I feel it deserves every word I can muster.
I'll start with an analysis and breakdown, then finish with a pros/cons list.
ACT 0 Starts off you off in a bamboo hut  with your trusty Android Cellphone. Pretty sure it's a Razr Maxx, but I could be wrong. Upon picking up the phone you receive a call from your Friend Ira. She sounds distressed and the call starts to glitch out when you suddenly see your first ghost! Upon leaving the hut you walk around and come across a house with your friend Ira Inside and insanity starts to ensue. She eventually tells you that she is unable to leave and only you can get out. She gives you a key to leave the house and  you end up in a tombestone slewn marsh with what appears to be a giant body in rages hanging in a cave. After solving the puzzle nearby, you are thrown into the Intro screen and into Act I as well
ACT I starts off in a car with your friends Doni, Shelly, YanYan, Ira and the teacher Ms Siska. You end up at a broken bridge and walk your way to the other side only to find the entire town deserted. As you continue walking, leaving your friends behind you come across a school and the rest of your friends magically catch up. Linda (the Protaganist) and Ira sit on a bench as Ira begins to talk about their friendship and reveal the story a bit. Doni, Shelly, YanYan,  and Ms Siska roam the school As you guys talk, and a great deal of time passes until it's night time. Everybody comes out but YanYan and if you haven't guessed already Linda goes to try and find him and more insanity ensues in the school. I don't want to spoil the chapter too much, but lets just say you come across a Giant Pig who's Really friendly, Some hookers, and a very interesting Hallway guard.
ACT II After leaving the school you wind up in the village and come across some little gremlins who steal your phone and bag. You start to chase after them until you run into Doni, who is really surprised to see you. He was so scared and lonely he really needed a hug, so he chased you for a little bit until giving up. After losing him you find a DSR camera that enables you to use it's Flash to stun certain enemies and illuminate the area much better then before with your phone. You quickly kill the gremlin and retreive your belongings only to find a lovely cult who gets very upset if you extinguish their candles. In fact, the Giant lady in the sky will have a very stern talk with you afterwards, but you simply cannot continue the game unless you put out their candles. After dealing with PMSing God Lady, you run into your friend Shelly and Siska, who is badly wounded. After getting Siska some rest, she tells you about Ira who is acting strange. You go to find her and Ira asks you to follow her and this is when the game really pops off, as there are two seperate endings depending how you handle the dialogue portion that follows. After talking to Ira, she gives you a key to go see her "sisters" in the mansion and escape, after finding out that you have to first regret ever coming to that place before escaping. More insanity ensues, you see a lady in red with pretty teeth, The Poltergeist doesn't like the dinner party they threw, and an eyeball with teeth talks in tongues.
Whew, still with me after all that? Didn't care and wanted the TL;DR version? Great! Here's the Pros/Cons list.
PROS:
+Horror game. If you liked outlast or amnesia, check this out as it wont disappoint
+You get to play with an Android phone, sweet.
+Graphics are pretty good for a game in 2014 AND Indie
+Only place you'll see a smart phone last over 24 hours while taking thousands of pictures and illuminating everything for you.
+Wonderful Ambiance that really sets the mood for the game. Helps make up for the few lame jumpscares
+Indie game. I have yet to come across one that didn't meet my standards and this certainly delivers.
+Controller Capable
+Runs in 64 Bit
+Good story*
CONS:
-Runs in 64 bit, though recently introduced 32bit. I did not try it so I cannot weigh on it.
-Pre-rendered graphics like hair and paintings look pixelated and stretched. Minor annoyance
-Short game. Bought it and beat it in about 8 hours. Both endings.
-*Not the best at explaining the story and ending. You kind of have to piece it together yourself or search google. Really good ending though once you understand.
-Some parts can be hard and/or frustrating.
-Game is a bit buggy. Had to restart the game client a few times to get past certain events as the scripts didn't execute properly. NOT GAMEBREAKING. Just annoying.
Overall, if you see this review while the game is on sale, DEFINITELY GET IT.  You literally will not be disappointed if You liked games such as Amnesia or Outlast. If you are reading this after the sale... I still recommend getting this game. It is truly amazing for the Horror Genre and I cannot wait for DreadOut 2. I cannot explain how ecstatic I am to see this game go on sale and finally try it. Please give this title a chance.

The game starts with your character being killed by a serial killer and you become a ghost needing to resolve your murder before he can 'move on'.  As you investigate the killer, you'll also help a girl that the killer is looking for (a medium who can see and hear ghosts).
As a ghost, you get to do some neat tricks: pass through some walls, teleport short distances, possess people to read their minds, poltergeist objects. My favorite was possessing cats. It's too bad some of these weren't fleshed out a bit more, as they sound more interesting than they actually are in the game.
The main danger to your character are demons that can kill you. You can kill the demons by sneaking up behind them and killing them with a keyboard and button click combo. You don't have much time to do it so the potential to screw it up is not high but still there. Mess it up and you're probably reloading. The threat is mostly when there are two demons in close proximity to each other. One will see you trying to sneak up on the other.
When you investigate a scene, you get enough information that will lead you somewhere else. You go there, investigate, and that leads to your next destination again. Rinse and repeat. You can't get the investigations wrong and you'll keep looking for clues until the game says you've found enough. Even the dialogs with characters, you don't choose what to say, you only choose the order in which you'll say it. You can wander around the town and do a few side quests (helping other ghosts) but the town is not very big and there is not a whole lot to do other than travel to your next main objective. The progression is very linear. It would have made a good movie.
Despite the shortcomings, I enjoyed the atmosphere and story. The mystery around the killer and the murders were great and had me hooked to the end.

I bought this game when it was on sale for only $3.00, so the price was not an issue for me - but now having played it all the way through I can genuinely say I would not have regretted paying $30.00 for such an enjoyable, atmospheric experience.
Storybuilding was phenomenal - from beginning to middle to end, there was never a dull moment as I was deeply engaged the entire time. I grew attached to the protagonist Ronan O'Connor fairly quickly, especially as you begin to uncover clues about his past. I bought everything the developers sold me about the "ghost realm" and how it functions (such as there being consecrated "obstructions" that ghosts can't pass through - perhaps not the most realistic idea to some, but considering we're dealing with a video game, I found it to be a very reasonable and clever excuse to keep the player's area of exploration streamlined but not restricted). The way that one investigation would lead to the next felt natural and smooth. Towards the end of the game I started to grow fearful that I would be disappointed by the conclusion, but I absolutely was not. From start to finish the plot was well-thought out and brilliantly executed.
The worst part of this game to me are the demon-hunting sequences. In all fairness I've never been much for destroying enemies, but even moreso than usual I found them to be an annoyance. Luckily individual demons follow their own path on a loop, but when there's more than one to an area it can become much trickier to get the timing right. Really, though, it just takes a lot of careful planning and mapping out your steps in advance.
Otherwise, for negatives, the autosave feature is a bit of a pain because I had to leave the game up & running at all times until I finished. That is, you cannot save your game on your own time, the game chooses when to save FOR you. So then if you exit & reopen the game, you'll be started back at the beginning of the last area you entered instead of specifically where you left off. Also, there are some parts of the game where you have to select the "most useful" clue(s) and while I got most of them easily, there were a few where the logic was simply lost on me.

I'll preface this by saying that I have nothing but respect for the developers who worked on the many iterations of this game for approximately nine years. Their dedication is certainly admirable, and their vision, while not fully brought to its potential, is readily apparent when you play the game. Truthfully, the game feels like it was developed by a team solely compromised of artists, not game designers. As players, we need to try to not hype this game up based on its development time or appearance. Look at how long Duke Nukem Forever took.
With that out of the way, however, I couldn't find a way to connect myself to the story, the characters or the world itself. The art, while beautiful, doesn't make up for what, outside of the soundtrack, is a package that feels like it hasn't been properly fleshed out. Both the level and monster designs don't lend themselves well at all to the fundamental mechanics of the game, a conflict that ends up being one of the larger factors that pushes this game into overwhelmingly mediocre territory.
The world is mostly empty and, despite its beauty, I hestitate to even call what you can do in this game world "exploration", with the exception of finding the golden discs, as there's a ridiculous amount of empty space and an almost upsetting lack of things to do, see and uncover.
The story is about as mediocre as they come, despite its fairly strong start given Otus' state in the first five minutes of the game. The characters fall flat, the tale that the developers spun is nothing short of cliché and all in all, it just isn't anything special.
Mechanically, the game is fairly standard twin-stick shooter affair with a few tweaks to the formula. While necessary in the open world, I had a few gripes with the Geddy teleporting system as it lessens the impact of being hit while within a dungeon. It just felt like more could have been done there.
Ultimately, for a game so heavily toting its exploration, being able to 100% the experience in approximately 7-9 hours is laughable, and most definitely does not justify the price point that the game is currently sold at at the time of writing. There's very little worthwhile to find, too, which only cheapens the experience.
Unfortunately, as previously stated, the breathtaking art and suitable soundtrack aren't enough to salvage a game otherwise wrought with mediocrity. If you're looking for a game that offers the exploration you might be looking at this game for, I implore you to check out Rabi-Ribi. They're very similar games, but Rabi-Ribi is infinitely better in execution as a Metroidvania style game. At a similar price point, you will get so, so much more out of it than you will with Owlboy.

Owlboy's not a bad game and honestly it's difficult to give it a thumbs down, but I just found myself really underwhelmed by the game, especially after reading so many great reviews from both critics and players. It's not that I'm saying you shouldn't try it, but I feel like expectations should be tapered a bit.
To start with the good, there's a lot of heart in Owlboy. The art direction is great, some of the best pixel art I've ever seen in a game, and the soundtrack really gives the feeling of a grand adventure. The characters have a lot of charm and the game balances humorous moments and emotional moments really well.
The gameplay is a pretty standard twin-stick shooter, albeit framed in a fun way where Owlboy carries his friends who are in charge of the gunning. The controls are pretty simple and tight as well, so any failures felt like they were my fault. The gameplay is fun at first, but gets old as the game doesn't really have any "upgrades" to add another element of gameplay past what's initially there. After a while, I just couldn't get myself to keep playing.
Unfortunately, I just feel like Owlboy doesn't do anything that some of the top indie games in the past couple of years haven't done better. It sucks, and I'm sure the 8-year journey to develop the game was definitely not due to choice, but I can't help but feel like Owlboy would've seemed so much better were it released years ago like it was planned. It just seems like it was a bit late to the party and the trophies it was going for have already been snatched up by bigger and better games.
Again, not a bad game but just not what I was looking for.

Small, silly, fun.  It can be an action game or purely economic.  I dig it.
As Recette, you take over your deadbeat dad's bills and need to make weekly payments.  To do this, you'll wheel and deal and make the money.
You can choose to stay in town and purchase wholesale and then sell the items retail or you can hire adventurers to go into the dungeon and get items for free (which you control for some action RPG action).  Adventuring is the only way to get some items as well as a way to score items you can buy for free.
Doing stuff takes time.  There are 4 time slots per day that you can operate in.  Going around town takes 1 slot, running the shop takes one slot, and adventuring takes 2 slots.  So you could go into town in the morning (all stops in town count as the same time slot), then go to the dungeon, then sell your loot at night.  Or you could sell, sell, sell, sell!  You get the idea.
I enjoy this game as it is simple, easy with some depth, has RPG elements, and has some grinding involved.  Also, there's a new game+ feature and an endless mode if you manage to pay off deadbeat dad's bills and a variety of characters to unlock for dungeon exploration.  Tired of sword and board?  Take the rogue or the wizard.  Everyone I've played with plays differently which keeps the fun alive.

This game might be fine for you if you're a hardcore fan of twin-stick shooters and are a sucker for the rouge-like formula; however, in my opinion this game is simply a frustrating mess.  A large portion of enemies' projectiles can travel much much further than your own and that combined with enemies constantly shooting at you from off screen even in the earliest levels creates a very frustrating experience.  The game tries to show you enemies that are off screen with (!) symbols but to me this is merely a pathetic band-aid for a much larger problem.  Here's a few ideas on how to fix this, game devs:
- The HUD (especially the top middle piece) often covers a lot of what you want to be able to see.  Make these items much smaller or at least transparent or SOMETHING like that.  It's critical to not be getting hit in these difficult rouge-like games and getting hit because enemies were hidden behind the HUD is extremely frustrating.
- Zoom the view out a lot so that enemies don't have to be constantly firing from off screen.  It's understandable for enemies to fire from off-screen occasionally but I swear 75% of damage on me and the other two friends playing couch-co-op with me came from off screen crap.  Between that and the HUD getting in the way, I returned this game in frustration.
The upgrade system / weapons seemed fine and at its core the game looks like it could be fun.  The music is EXCELLENT!  Fix the above issues and I will gladly buy it again and give it another spin.

Mass Effect 2:
+ Another amazing, story-driven game by Bioware, where your decisions impact the way in which others view you and how the plotline develops. Become a paragon or renegade through your choices in quests.
+ New locations to explore, each filled with numerous side missions and content relevant to the main narrative.
+ Interesting characters (won't add any spoilers), each with their own personal quest lines.
+ New range of weapons and upgrades, you can even reinforce the Normandy with state of the art equipment.
+ Great graphics, a massive step up from the original title.
+ The game has been streamlined, making it more sleak and professional in appearance compared to the first entry in the trilogy.
- Although Mass Effect 2 looks a lot more refined and stylish than its predecessor, it comes at the expensive of its RPG characteristics. Leveling has been dumbed down a bit, but still plays a role in the game (thankfully).
Overall Score: 9/10

I really wish I could avoid the typical "community is toxic" comment, but unfortunately it sums up the Chivalry experience pretty well.
Your first few hours in the level 0-15 servers will be the best. Everyone is learning the ropes (except for smurfs, of course, but I personally didn't meet many) and the battles are therefore a fun and often amusing experience. Apologies for teamkills were often accepted as pretty much everyone was committing them, and there was a mostly friendly atmosphere.
However, once you are kicked out of the "noob servers", the fun ends there.
As this is a rather niche game, servers seem mostly populated by veteran players who have no patience for still unskilled and relatively new players, and have no problem in using their high-tier and sometimes unfair tactics against them.
FFA is a joke. Since the game is called Chivalry, I thought I would honour other people's duels and wait for fights to end before attacking myself, hoping others would do the same. Instead, high-level players will ignore eachother in order to constantly chase down the new players to earn free kills and top the scoreboard.
In the end, unless you don't mind fighting bots who are often more fun than the majority of players, don't bother with this initially promising game.

If you remember the golden age of RPGs with titles like Baldur's Gate I&II, Jagged Alliance, Icewind Dale, or Planescape Torment then this is the game for you. It's a masterpiece at every level, and even had a surprise at release with over 80,000 lines fully voice acted. That's insane, and really makes Larian one of most realiable and trusted names in video gaming. I can't heap enough praise on them, and this time multiplayer is simply astonishing.
+ Darker than DOSI, with a much more compelling storyline and script
+ Unique take on character races. Elves eat flesh to reveal their secrets. Undead heal only with poison, and are engrossing to play.
+ Combat system is one of the best, and the Ai is challenging, especially on tactician mode.
+ Loot is balanced, and rewards the player depending on your choices.
+ Beautiful game, and downright stunning at times. I find myself sitting idle just marveling at some of the game's foilage, and enviroments.
+ It's optimized for lower end systems, and they are saying Mac support is likely as well.
+ RNG elements have been minimized with a tremendous loot system that makes each playthrough unique, but dependable.
+ Highly custimizable skills and talents that truly allow you to make whatever you deem worthy of your time, and party composition.
+ Multiplayer/Co-op are amazing, and even more enjoyable than the solo matches
+ All Origin characters have depth, personalities, and stories that are woven into the fabric of the game. Events will trigger only for certain combinations, or interactions. It constantly surprises you.
+ Fully voice acted (80,000+ lines), and damn good too.
+ The game is gigantic, and the tutorial island takes nearly 30+ hours to get through.
- Addictive, and you will want to stockpile food, and other goodies for your travels.
- The occasional glitch, but they are far and few, and easily overlooked by everything else

another downside is, that in my opinion the grinding system for equipment is really confusing. this could have been done way better and easier.

To say that this is a great game, actually does it a disservice, it is a phenomenally made game with amazing RPG elements and spot on tactical gameplay.   At first I thought the game was a bit overbalanced on the NPC's side,  but ended up finding out that it was just me.  A few key gear purchases and suddenly I was taking out fights that I had an incredibly difficult time before.  The combat does a great job of making you feel powerful while never making it feel easy.  Your tactics matter.  From your choices of companions (and what specializations they have) to the positioning on the battlefield, to trying to create your own ambush instead of getting ambushed is just amazingly done.
The game does not hand hold you along, but at the same time it does not feel hard to keep up with all the different quests and side missions that you have on your plate.  Not every fight is meant to be tackled the first time you see it and the game rewards you for taking out something in an ingenious way with an every increasing power level on your gear.  You are always advancing in one way or another.
I never write reviews, this is probably my first so hopefully that says something.  Such an amazing game, do yourself a favor and buy this!

Being an old-time fan of the venerable Scapeghost by Level Nine, I grabbed this one with high expectations. And it's all there: You get to walk through walls, read people's minds, interfere with TV Sets and solve your own murder case. All that with Unreal-Engine powered graphics, a teenage punk medium and evil demons chasing you - what could possibly go wrong? The intro sequence showing the protagonist's past being inscribed as tattoos on his body was nice storytelling as well, so I was really, really ready to like and recommend this after like ten minutes.
The setting is also fitting, with run-down buildings, a creepy cemetary and, of course, an asylum, all set within Salem which drips with atmosphere all by itself.
And then it feels like the guys or girls with the nice ideas went to do something else, or got fired, or had no more time left.
First, after being introduced with a rich background and ambiguous personality, the characters put all their dimesions aside and do exactly what you'd expect them to, in a mildly stereotypic way that makes them feel like copies from a couple of similar movies you just can't remember right now. This is especially true for side characters. No one expects brilliant writing for every single one-line (to be exact, two-line) character, but whatever chance for creepy, humorous or kinky or otherwise interesting background was given by the setting, nearly none of that was taken. And apart from five relevant persons and a couple of side-quest givers, everyone is a two-line character.
Second, the game mostly progresses through you doing "police work". In itself, that wouldn't be much of a problem, as ghost stories and crime stories usually go quite well together. But this game relies more on your stuff collecting skills than on any form of crime puzzle solving. Any hint you may find has a generic one-line description but you won't ever read one, as you get an informative clip once you found 9/9, 15/15 or 20/20 hints, I think you can guess the mechanics. Any combination or deduction is done by the game itself by letting you choose from some heavily hinted options.
Apart from the main story, there are bonus tidbits scattered everywhere. Once you found x/x of these, you get told a ghost story and go on. Some of the tidbits require jump-and run episodes, some the use of ghost abilities, but there is no other interconnection between them and the rest of the game. Same goes for side quests.
The plot actually does not feel that bad, but the shallow, "consoley" approach to it, repetitive gameplay and thin dialogue, the tedious fights, the linear progression and the lots of walking didn't do it for me. It is an action game without action trying to be an adventure without puzzles. Which is a real pity because it does have production value.

If you had some way of reprimanding these NPCs, that would be fine, but they are characters that you're fighting to protect, and you have no way of interacting with them other than to talk to them to receive their scathing disapproval.
All in all, it's a really demoralising experience, and I have no motivation to pick up the game and continue, knowing there's just going to be another tirade of nasty remarks coming my way despite completing objectives and defeating boss monsters successfully. Consequently, I've sought a refund for this nasty waste of time.

+ Highly polished graphics
+ Fun and engaging gameplay
+ Immersive world; lots of tiny details (e.g. birds, rustling grass, etc.)
+ Excellent and memorable cast of characters
+ Good puzzles
+ Good soundtrack
+ Great story
+/- Difficulty varies from area to area
+/- Gameplay feels both smooth and clunky (in some areas)
- Lackluster ending
- Some bugs here and there
- Feels incomplete on the whole; lots of loose ends
- A bit short; the game can be completed 100% in less than 15 hours
Additional notes:
On the whole, I think the game was worth it and I would recommend grabbing this game. Gameplay progression is excellent - new mechanics are continually introduced as you progress so it doesn't feel tedious at all. The story hearkens back to the good old days where the story revolves around saving the world from an impending threat. The world building is complex and deep enough to leave you interested. I personally love the protagonists in this game, each has a fleshed out backstory so that you can relate to them to some extent. Most of the villains are terrible, only one of them was well written, the rest feels rushed and uninteresting.
Game has a lot of puzzles in it which are not so easy that you would breeze through it and not so difficult that would leave you stuck in the same puzzle for hours. It's got the right amount of difficulty, enough to get your brain to function and think. The gameplay was innovative, I guess, but the gimmick is really nothing special. It plays well, however, and the gimmick is implemented well enough such that it feels natural after the first hour of gameplay.
The biggest letdown to me was the ending. It felt rushed, incomplete, and unsatisfying. I wore a blank face throughout the ending sequence - the development was too sudden and random that I was suddenly felt detached from the story. The world building also feels incomplete; too many questions are left open and never explained throughout the game. There are some areas in the game where you would think may hide some secret lore, but instead what you get is a blank map with nothing in it.
That's all there is to it - the (very memorable) story on the whole is excellent (I absolutely loved everything from the start of the journey until just before the final stage) which more than makes up for the terrible ending. The graphics as well! It's practically pixelated wallpaper: the game as the graphics are consistently top-notch all throughout. Despite some setbacks I think the good points outweigh the bad so I will recommend buying this game.

A great little sci fi point and click adventure game. The puzzles are very logical compared to classic adventure games, and the individual cases means there's no wandering around a massive map with 50 inventory items. Some people might find it a bit simple but I definitely consider that a plus, I'm too old and have more respect for my free time for a proper Sierra/LucasArts grind these days, but I enjoyed this little reminder of it.
The best part though is definitely the writing. I loved the dialogue, all the cases were interesting, and it was very funny (as long as you don't mind a lot of geek culture/90s nostalgia references).
Some people have said it's a bit short for the price, for me it was definitely worth it, 6hrs of entertainment for the price of a cinema ticket. Replayability is fairly limited although I am tempted to go back and look for the last few hidden achievements.
I also really appreciated the free curse removal, finally I can go out at night again!

Not the longest game, nor the most complicated, nor the hardest, but Owlboy was visually and aurally one of the best games I've ever played.
The gameplay is relatively simple, but satisfying, and some parts required multiple redos - as a person who generally enjoys coasting through games and experiencing them, this is preferable to a particularly difficult retro game ala Mega Man.
The story started off slow but a twist in the first half really caught my attention and I played through to the end, really enjoying the interactions between characters in this little world that had been created.
Despite the relatively low playtime/dollar ratio (the time I have now, 9 hours, is having completed the game with some side content, though not close to all of it) I could not recommend this game more highly to anyone who sees it and at the first glance is interested.

Neurovoider is a great couch co-op game for 4 people.  In the beginning of each game "session" you're given the choice  of 3 robot classes: Dash(fastest and squishy), Rampage( balanced medium robot) and Fortress(the name says it all).You also get to choose perk, passive or active, after which you are thrown into the first level. The level objectives are pretty self-explanatory: kill everything that moves, destroy reactors, kill bosses, survive.
The major advantage of the game is the randomness of it. Sometimes you get all elite enemies spawned, sometimes you get lucky and get super crazy gun that nukes half of the screen.  All enemies drop health kits and loot. Loot is separated in 4 different categories: vison, core, transport and weapons. Each class has their own loot, you can't use other class loot, but you can sell it for credits or you can change your class mid-game( which is a big +, in my opinion). After finishing the stage, the intermission comes, where you can upgrade your robot, repair it, sell loot or gamble for the better loot.  randomization system makes game feel like it has limitless amount of guns and upgrades. To sum it up, the gameplay is really fast-paced and can be really challenging( some enemies may oneshot you), but otherwise it wouldn't be fun.
The graphics are nice, but it's the soundtrack that needs to be mentioned. The OST is basically an album "The Wrath Of The Code" by Dan Terminus. The tracks are what gets you into the "crush/destroy" mood, though not all of them are aggressive . If you're fan of Perturbator( Hotline Miami, Furi) you definitely need to check out Dan Terminus.
Controls are slick on both  gamepad and keyboard/mouse. However, the game wasn't optimised for Dualshock 4, which will be recognized as Xbox One controller by the game.
There aren't that many things to complain about. I would suggest devs to add more boss and location variety.
Overall it's really nice game. If you're searching for top-down twin-stick to play with friends, it's a must-have.

What a strange and ridiculous game Crusader Kings 2 is. A fair warning right now, to anyone thinking about buying this game, just be aware this is NOT a casual game. This game requires a lot of time put in to learn the mechanics and systems. You can and probably will make terrible mistakes, even after you've gotten comfortable with the game. RNG will sometimes grant you great boons, and then later take everything from you, and there's nothing you can do to prevent it. You will probably get frustrated at times, and may even rage quit.
It's all worth it though. The depth of your campaigns will draw you in and never let go. I will freely admit I once spent 8 hours doing nothing but play this game, and it didn't feel like a waste. I barely even noticed the time had gone by, as I was too busy forming Ireland. It was worth it, after days of struggling against the neighboring Irish tribes, to finally watch the grandson of the character I started as become king of all of Ireland. My struggle wasn't, and still isn't over. I still have several hundred years left, and I'm just getting started.
10/10
If you have the time, get it. You won't regret it.

We play Detective Francis McQueen, a police detective who is into “spooky crap” (as Officer Patrick Dooley puts it), aka investigating crimes where there is an element of the supernatural – the Darkside – with his fairly useless and slightly corrupt sidekick. The dialogue is sharp, to the point and extremely witty throughout. Almost the entire game is written with humour. Sometimes silly, sometimes downright farcical and often clever. Peppered with smart linguistics and pop culture references, it was a real delight to read. It had me smirking in the very first interaction and that keeps up throughout and it reminded me in many ways of the Discworld game, which is a real treat since I’ve been a hardcore Terry Pratchett fan for two decades.
This is a point and click adventure game, so we must work our way through a series of interactions and logical puzzles to figure out how to progress and solve all six of the Detective’s outstanding cases. There were some moments of guesswork for me – but ultimately everything was entirely logical and made perfect sense, even if I didn’t always quite get it until I’d tried quite a lot of things. Through talking to folks, investigating items, combining things and a couple of simple puzzles, we progress through each spooky story. The gameplay is very minimalist and relatively fast; you don’t control or move your character, only scene changes and there is very little animation. This does mean you move through it at a pace and the bite-size episodic cases make it easy to play in short bursts but still feel very satisfied with what you’ve achieved.
The graphics are very much stylized block pixel 2D graphics, which won’t be for everyone. My husband, for example, hates this graphical style and would never consider playing it – aesthetics is definitely a strong personal preference. I like the graphics and felt they fit well with the overall atmosphere of the game, which is also heavily reinforced by the appropriately spooky soundtrack. The music is serious and really creates the setting for the scene changes – this works incredibly well with the humorous dialogue and gives the game a more cohesive feeling. You are at the end of the day, solving crime here!
The game is short; taking me just 4 hours to complete all six cases (and if you’ve played the demo, that will be five). I didn’t find all the hidden achievements there so there is perhaps an extra challenge for hardcore completionists, but on the whole there is very little replay value so some may question the value. On the settings side this game is bare bones; there no resolution options, no window size options and the game is played in full screen mode which might frustrate those who are used to running multiple monitors and alt-tabbing. The only settings are for sound.
I enjoyed every minute of this game though and would highly recommend it to fans of the genre, or newcomers who like amusing dialogue. A thoroughly engaging and entertaining game from start to finish. Need more!
